docs.title: About
docs.text:
Research edition: The intended scope of this website is to record the history of Barney from its formation through 1950, the latest federal census year for which individual household records are publicly available. As a work in progress, current research extends through 1910. Original records are used whenever available, but some identities, dates, relationships, and locations remain uncertain. Citations are reviewed continuously, and corrections will be made as stronger evidence is found.

Historical language notice: Some quoted newspapers, records, and other original sources contain outdated or offensive language and stereotypes. They are preserved as evidence of their time, not endorsed by this project. Read the full historical language and cultural sensitivity notice.

I grew up hearing stories from the second- and third-generation residents of Barney. It was a town full of character and characters. Sadly, nearly all of those voices are now gone.

My hope is that this website can help recover and preserve some of those stories before they are lost. If you have anything related to the history of Barney and are willing to share it, such as photographs, documents, records, memories, or family stories, please contact me at the email address below.

James E. Jones

docs.title: Barney & Smith Car Company
docs.text:
Barney & Smith was a railroad-car builder in Dayton, Ohio. Its connection to Barney, Georgia, is often told as a naming story, but the surviving evidence supports a more careful account. Later Georgia histories say the Oglesbys named their new station for a principal of the Ohio company because they bought cars from it. No contemporary railroad minute, equipment ledger, postal form, or 1897 newspaper article located in this research confirms that explanation. What the records do prove is that the company had business ties to the Oglesbys by October 1897, sold cars to several railroads serving Georgia, and later controlled a large lumber and short-line railroad operation at Milltown, about thirty miles east of Barney.[1][2]

A period advertisement for the Dayton Car Works, operated by the Barney & Smith Manufacturing Company.

docs.title: From a canal-side shop to Barney & Smith
docs.text:
The business began in 1849, two years before a railroad reached Dayton. Eliam E. Barney and Ebenezer Thresher supplied the capital, while Elijah Packard brought car-building experience. Barney remained a silent partner until 1850 because he still had a year to serve as principal of Cooper Seminary. The first firm was Thresher, Packard & Company. It became E. Thresher & Company after Packard left, Barney, Parker & Company when Caleb Parker bought Thresher's interest in 1854, and Barney, Smith & Company when Preserved Smith replaced Parker in 1864.[3]

The early location was awkward but not irrational. Dayton had water power, canal transportation, and a central position in a region where railroads were spreading quickly. Before tracks entered the city, finished cars traveled by canal boat toward the Ohio River and then by steamboat or barge to a rail connection. The firm also made agricultural implements during its early years, but railroad equipment became its defining business.[3]

The partners incorporated the operation as the Barney & Smith Manufacturing Company on May 16, 1867, with authorized capital of $500,000. Capital rose to $750,000 in 1872 and $1 million in 1882. Eliam Barney remained the active head until his death in 1880. His son Eugene J. Barney then led the company until the end of 1899. On May 27, 1892, the concern reorganized as the Barney & Smith Car Company with $3.5 million in authorized stock. A 1906 increase brought authorized capital to $4.5 million.[3]

docs.title: What the Dayton works made
docs.text:
Barney & Smith built wooden freight and passenger equipment, sleeping and dining cars, baggage and mail cars, narrow-gauge cars, streetcars, and interurban equipment. Passenger-car work involved much more than framing a box on wheels. The plant maintained drawing, pattern, upholstery, cabinet, paint, blacksmith, foundry, machine, estimating, and finishing departments. The company separated its drawing room from the pattern shop in 1883 and hired professional interior designers during the 1880s.[4]

William Voss, author of the 1892 book Railway Car Construction, became assistant superintendent that same year. The company's own history says systematic cost estimating began in 1885 and became a separate department in 1886. Those details place the firm inside the changing engineering and production practices of late nineteenth-century car building.[4]

The Dayton Car Works in 1875. The image appeared in Ohio, the Future Great State and is preserved by Internet Archive Book Images.

The plant expanded repeatedly. It added a separate annex in 1886 and began planning a steel freight-car plant in December 1904. Ground was broken in March 1905, and the first steel cars left the new plant that December. Barney & Smith started taking orders for steel passenger cars late in 1909. After the steel plant finished its freight-car orders in the fall of 1910, it shifted to steel passenger-car work. By 1911 the Dayton property covered about 57 3/4 acres, contained about 85 buildings, and had roughly eight miles of standard-gauge track.[5]

The shift came late. Competitors had already moved aggressively into steel construction, and the company's 1911 history admits that the transition required a much larger drafting force, new sheet-metal machinery, and gas-welding equipment. Later railroad histories identify this delayed conversion as one reason the firm lost market share.[5][6]

docs.title: Depression, adaptation, and labor
docs.text:
Railroad equipment was a cyclical business. Barney & Smith's internal history describes closed or nearly idle shops during the panics of 1857, 1873, and 1893. After 1893, when ordinary railroad-car demand remained weak, the company built electric street and traction cars to keep work moving. The Panic of 1907 brought another downturn that lasted into 1910.[5]

Expansion also changed the workforce. The steel plant needed large numbers of immigrant workers. In 1906 the Dayton Realty Company developed Kossuth Colony in North Dayton, with 80 dwellings, a clubhouse, and a store. A later Dayton account says about 200 Hungarian welders and steelworkers lived there and describes restrictive company-town conditions, including a surrounding fence and payment through company credit. That social history comes from a modern local account, not from the company's celebratory 1911 book, and should be read with that difference in mind.[5][7]

Georgia newspapers show that the works were still seeking skilled labor during World War I. Advertisements in 1916 requested wood boxcar repairmen, car builders, riveters, fitters, reamers, blacksmiths, and tinners. Similar ads appeared in 1917. They establish active hiring, though they do not by themselves identify the contracts that produced the demand.[8]

docs.title: Cars used in Georgia
docs.text:
The newspaper trail reaches well beyond one South Georgia railroad family. Barney & Smith equipment worked on several railroads serving Georgia.

In March 1900, the Central of Georgia placed three new Barney & Smith sleeping cars in service. Numbered 19, 20, and 21, each had twelve sections, a drawing room, smoking room, and lavatories. They ran between Savannah and Macon and between Savannah and Atlanta. Three more twelve-section drawing-room buffet sleepers, numbered 25, 26, and 27, arrived in 1903 for Savannah, Macon, and Birmingham service.[9][10]

The Georgia Southern & Florida ordered a baggage car, a mail car, and four express cars in 1907. In January 1909 the Seaboard Air Line awarded Barney & Smith contracts for 200 fifty-ton steel phosphate cars and fifteen passenger cars. Later that year the Southern Railway ordered twenty-five electric-lighted coaches from the company.[11][12][13]

These orders document a broader Georgia market. They do not prove that the South Georgia Railroad bought the specific boxcars remembered in the Barney naming story. No builder's list or South Georgia Railroad equipment roster establishing that purchase was located.

docs.title: The Oglesby order and the Barney name
docs.text:
The earliest direct connection found between Barney & Smith and the Oglesby businesses is an October 26, 1897, item in The Valdosta Times. It reported that the Oglesby mills at Heartpine and Barney were running full time on an order for one and a half million feet of passenger-car sills for the Ohio Falls Company, Pullman, and Barney & Smith. The sills ranged from 35 to 72 feet long.[2]

That is important evidence, but the timing sets a limit. Barney station was already appearing in the newspaper by June 1897. The October sill order therefore proves a business relationship, not why the station received its name. It also describes lumber sold to car builders, not railroad cars bought by the South Georgia Railroad.[14]

Huxford's Brooks County history, the Brooks County Museum binder, Georgia Place-Names, and Edmondson's later local account all preserve versions of the car-company naming tradition. Huxford says the Oglesbys named the station for one owner of the company from which their railroad bought equipment. The museum material tells a boxcar version. Edmondson adds an unverified visit by Mr. Barney to the Oglesbys in Quitman. These sources show that the tradition is old and repeated, but repetition among later accounts is not contemporary proof.[1]

The most defensible conclusion is simple: the town-name story is plausible, and an Oglesby relationship with Barney & Smith is documented in 1897, but the exact naming act and the claimed car purchase remain unverified.

docs.title: Yellow pine and the Milltown purchase
docs.text:
Wooden cars consumed large quantities of seasoned lumber. Mid-Continent Railway Museum's restoration research on Milwaukee Lake Shore & Western coach No. 63, built by Barney & Smith in 1888, found yellow pine in parts of the surviving car. The museum also identified an earlier lumber relationship with Atlanta businessman George V. Gress. The evidence does not trace that coach's individual boards to South Georgia, but it confirms that southern yellow pine and Georgia suppliers belonged to the company's material network.[15]

Barney & Smith moved from buying lumber to controlling its own supply. On December 22, 1904, its executive committee discussed the need for secure yellow-pine timber and sent Arthur J. Stevens south to investigate. Stevens reported on February 28, 1905. The company then authorized purchase of the Gress Lumber Company operation at Milltown, Georgia.[5]

Contemporary Georgia newspapers reported the sale in mid-March. The package included the sawmill and planing mill, about 50,000 acres of timberland, the Milltown Air Line Railroad from Milltown to Naylor, four locomotives, and fifteen miles of tram road. Barney & Smith organized the Milltown Lumber Company to hold the operation. It bought another 36,000 acres in August 1907, bringing the reported total to about 86,000 acres.[5][16]

A 1906 promotional description of Milltown said the plant employed "an army of men" and shipped millions of feet of car material to Dayton each year. The wording is boosterish, but the basic flow of lumber from Milltown to the Ohio works agrees with the company's own history and other newspaper coverage.[17]

docs.title: The railroad extension that did not reach Valdosta
docs.text:
Barney & Smith's Georgia railroad was the Milltown Air Line between Milltown and Naylor. It was not the South Georgia Railroad through Barney.

In late 1905 and 1906, Valdosta newspapers repeatedly discussed extending the Milltown line west to Valdosta, or toward Nashville and the Georgia Southern & Florida. Reports also floated a freight and flatcar shop in Valdosta. Citizens held a mass meeting, company representatives examined maps and routes, and officers came south to consider the plan. The stories document a serious proposal, not a completed extension or factory. The Milltown Air Line never became a Barney & Smith route through Barney.[18]

docs.title: Sale, receivership, and the end of the Georgia operation
docs.text:
Barney & Smith sold the Milltown mills, timber, tram roads, and related holdings to Henderson Lumber Company in March 1917. Contemporary reports give the consideration as either $180,000 or $186,000. Because the two newspapers disagree, the exact figure should remain qualified. Henderson took over the mills, while the Barney & Smith interest in the Milltown Air Line later returned to the foreground.[19]

When the company tried to stop service and dismantle the short line in 1919, Milltown businesses and residents went to court. They argued that earlier promises of permanent rail service had induced large investments. Judge W. E. Thomas ordered continued operation while a jury resolved the dispute and provided for a receiver if the owners did not comply. The Georgia Supreme Court later allowed the order to stand. In November 1919, a Macon newspaper reported that Barney & Smith itself had entered receivership in Ohio, raising questions about the Georgia court's control of the railroad.[20]

The short line continued under court pressure until Barney & Smith sold it to W. L. Miller and R. E. Carter in August 1921. The buyers announced two daily round trips between Milltown and Naylor beginning September 1.[21]

docs.title: Flood, receivership, and closure
docs.text:
The Great Dayton Flood inundated the works in March 1913. Contemporary Georgia coverage called the plant one of the city's heaviest industrial losers. A Dayton account says workers from Kossuth Colony tore down the colony fence and used the lumber for rescue rafts.[7][22]

The flood did not end the business on the spot. Hiring advertisements and equipment work continued later in the decade. The company nevertheless entered receivership by November 1919. Modern railroad histories disagree on the final marker. One gives 1921 as the end of active business and 1924 as the auction of remaining assets; another uses 1923 as the closing year. These dates probably describe different stages of failure, production, and liquidation. Without the corporate receivership and auction files, a single exact "closed" date would pretend to more precision than the evidence allows.[6][23]

docs.title: What survives
docs.text:
Barney & Smith cars survive in museums and heritage collections, though some have been altered heavily during long service. Mid-Continent Railway Museum is restoring Milwaukee Lake Shore & Western coach No. 63. Northwest Railway Museum identifies its chapel car Messenger of Peace and several passenger cars as Barney & Smith products. Passenger Car No. 563, built in 1883, is interpreted at the Utah State Railroad Museum.[15][23][24]

The company's records appear to be scattered. The 1911 history preserves detailed internal chronology, but Mid-Continent's restorers report that original construction records for coach No. 63 have not survived. That gap helps explain why builder dates, materials, and individual railroad orders often have to be reconstructed from surviving cars, trade journals, railroad records, and newspapers.[15]

docs.title: Findings for Barney history
docs.text:
The research supports five conclusions.

  1. Barney & Smith was a substantial Dayton builder with a documented corporate history from 1849 into the early 1920s.
  2. The company had a real Oglesby business connection by October 1897, but that evidence comes after Barney station was already in use and cannot prove the town's naming.
  3. Later histories consistently connect the town name to the company, so the tradition belongs in Barney's history with a clear label, not as a settled fact.
  4. Barney & Smith equipment served the Central of Georgia, Georgia Southern & Florida, Seaboard Air Line, and Southern Railway. No reviewed source proves a South Georgia Railroad car purchase.
  5. The company's direct Georgia ownership centered on Milltown beginning in 1905. It controlled a lumber company and the Milltown Air Line, not the South Georgia Railroad through Barney.

docs.title: Early Settlers
docs.text:
Early Settlers

Barney’s earliest history began more than eighty years before the town's founding. The Treaty of Fort Jackson, signed August 9, 1814, ended the Creek War and forced the Muscogee (Creek) Nation to cede about 23 million acres to the United States. Georgia organized part of the ceded territory into Early, Irwin, and Appling counties on December 15, 1818. Original Irwin County, covering approximately 5,000 square miles, was then surveyed into sixteen districts containing 6,582 lots—6,421 full lots of 490 acres each and 161 fractional lots—for the 1820 land lottery, which distributed the lots among eligible Georgians.

Source note: James Bagley Clements's History of Irwin County (1932), chapter 2, gives the sixteen-district survey total as 6,421 full 490-acre lots plus 161 fractional lots. The full lots alone equal 3,146,290 acres, or about 4,916 square miles; adding the fractional boundary lots supports the rounded estimate of approximately 5,000 square miles. The Georgia Archives overview of the 1820 Land Lottery independently confirms Irwin County's sixteen districts and 490-acre lot size. Library of Congress catalog record and digital copy.

The first settlement traditions

A familiar Lowndes County tradition says that four settlers—James Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, Drewry “Drew” Vickers, and Alfred Belote—moved with their families into the area in 1821. The surviving published trail begins with William Harden's 1913 history, the earliest account located and fully inspected that assembles this exact group. An unsigned article in the 1922 South Georgia Historical and Genealogical Quarterly repeated the four names and supplied the 1821 date. The article credited its data chiefly to recent Valdosta Times sketches by Hortense W. Baker, and the quartet passage appeared immediately afterward. Because that paragraph had no separate attribution, Baker is a plausible source but cannot be identified as the source of the exact list or wording. Her sketches have not been located. Harden's book and the 1922 article are therefore the earliest located links in the published chain through which the four-family tradition was preserved and repeated.

The earliest published accounts located do not agree on who should be called the area's first settlers. Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollections focused on the Hall settlement and Mount Zion and named a different circle of pioneers. Montgomery M. Folsom's inspected 1885–1886 writings described the Coffee Road, the Hall and Morven neighborhood, and several early residents, but did not assemble the familiar four-man group.

In December 1888, the Valdosta Times reprinted a Quitman Herald story naming “Mr. Frank Rountree and Lawrence Folsom” among the first settlers of “this portion of Georgia.” The story said their descendants remembered that coffee was unknown when the families first settled and was initially cooked like beans when someone later brought it for sale. It also recalled Native Americans visiting Mrs. Folsom “in droves.” Although she feared the visits, she treated her guests kindly and observed their custom of shaking hands on arrival and departure. The account goes on to describe barter for milk and a shared meal. The printed “Frank Rountree” was probably Francis Rountree, but the article does not establish his identity, and he should not be confused with James Rountree. The piece preserves a late family tradition rather than contemporary evidence of the settlement.

The January 1889 article “Correcting a Munchausen Story,” signed “Savage,” linked several settlement traditions in one account. It called James Rountree the first settler of Lowndes County and placed Joe and John Bryant at the old Indigenous town where Okapilco and Mule creeks meet. It also said that Lawrence Folsom married Rachel Vickers in Burke County about 1790, moved to the Ocmulgee River in 1808, lived there until 1823, and later traveled south and west after General Jackson's purchase opened Irwin County. The writer added that “the Folsoms and Rountrees had been used to Indian company many years before Brooks and Lowndes were settled.” The article does not date Folsom's arrival in Lowndes County, identify Rachel Vickers's relationship to Drew Vickers, mention Alfred Belote, or assemble the familiar four-man group.

An article signed “Civilized,” published on October 5, 1895, gave a more definite version. It said that settlement began in 1824 with Benjamin Daniels on the Withlacoochee River and Washington Joyce, Drew Vickers, Lawrence Folsom, and James Rountree on Little River. The writer called these “the first settlements made by white men in the present territory of Lowndes county.” The article also said Folsom's place occupied the site of an Indigenous town, where pottery, knives, arrowheads, tomahawks, and gun barrels had been found. This is the earliest located and inspected account that names Joyce, Vickers, Folsom, and Rountree together as the county's first white settlements. It does not mention Alfred Belote, and its 1824 date conflicts with the later four-family tradition's 1821 date.

J. R. Folsom added another version elsewhere in the same issue. Writing about Cecil and the Coffee Road, he said that the first lands settled were near the watercourses, dated settlement of “the Bryant place” on the Okapilco to 1829, and grouped James Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, and Drew Vickers as settlers east of Little River whose descendants still lived on those places. He did not call the three men the area's first settlers, give a date for their arrival, or include Alfred Belote.

R. E. L. Folsom offered another version in 1899. He called Washington Joyce's 1824 home and ferry the first white settlement in present Lowndes County, then said Vickers, Lawrence Folsom, and a man named Baker came next. He mentioned Rountree elsewhere in the article but did not include him in that sequence, and he did not name Belote. Differences in county boundaries explain part of the conflict, but the accounts also preserve genuinely different local traditions.

An unsigned 1900 article, “A Historical Sketch of Old Lowndes County,” expanded that sequence. It said Thomas Baker established a ferry on the Withlacoochee River where Coffee Road crossed it late in 1823, and that Thomas Futch bought the ferry in 1824. The article then placed James Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, and Drew Vickers on or near Coffee Road east of Little River in 1824. Thomas Baker is therefore a strong probable identification of the “man named Baker” in the 1899 account: the name, river, ferry, and road crossing agree. Because the two articles may preserve versions of the same tradition, the 1900 wording is not independent proof of Baker's identity or the dates.

Neither Harden nor the unsigned 1922 article cited a contemporary deed, diary, tax return, or court record for the four families' move. The account is a durable local tradition, not a proved passenger list with a certain date.

Original records do establish the men in the early county. On November 27, 1823, Newman Pounds conveyed Lawrence Folsom all 490 acres of District 12, Land Lot 187. The deed identifies Lawrence as "of the County of Irwin," proving that he was an Irwin County resident and landowner by that date. It does not establish when his family moved there. Rountree can be followed from Pulaski County into the Lowndes settlement and died after an 1834 attack on the Tallahassee road. Folsom later became a Lowndes county-site commissioner and a Mount Zion trustee. Vickers appears in the 1820 Montgomery County lottery and later Lowndes census, land, court, and tax records. Belote held Land Lot 55 in District 12 and was dead by 1844. Their dossiers also show how much remains unknown, including exact arrival dates, complete families, and the location of every first home.

The old claim that one man was the area's first settler is even less certain. A January 1889 newspaper item said that “Joe and John Bryant” settled at the old Indigenous town where Okapilco and Mule creeks meet. It separately called James Rountree Lowndes County's first settler. R. E. L. Folsom wrote in 1899 that Jose Bryant settled at the old town in 1828. An unsigned 1900 article changed the year to 1823 and added claims about Jose's household, enslaved labor, and first crop. Huxford later substituted John Bryan and Abraham Hunter. John Bryan is documented in Lowndes County, and his daughter Jane Hunter's 1912 obituary associated him with Okapilco. No record yet proves that Jose, Joe, and John were one person. The identity remains unresolved.

The county-organization story now appears on From Irwin to Lowndes and Brooks Counties. The church, campground, trustees, and militia connections are covered on Mount Zion.

What the independent record check established

An October 2026 review tested eighty additional names from the wider early-settler roster against census images, official registers, local records, church evidence, and known identity conflicts. It did not turn the roster into a list of eighty proved settlers. Instead, it separated a small number of direct record findings from the much larger body of retrospective or unresolved claims.

The clearest shared record is a digitized 1836 Lowndes County general-militia return. It names Pennywell Folsom, Thomas Folsom, Ashley Lawson, James J. Joyce, John Hall, John Dampier, David Edmondson, Zachariah Fletcher, Henry Rowell, Samuel T. Henderson, and Cornelius English as privates. It names Abraham Byrd in the same return, William G. Hall as captain of the 660th District, and Joel Gornto as second lieutenant of the 659th District. The return supports each man's district association and eligibility for the general militia in 1836. It is not an active-service muster and does not prove Creek War service.[25]

Federal official registers also name Hamilton W. Sharp or Sharpe as postmaster at Sharpe's Store in 1829 and 1833. Those entries establish the office and locality by 1829, but they do not prove the exact April 2, 1828 opening date reported in later postal histories.[26]

At that stage, the review left most claims unchanged. No named household from the wider roster had been independently verified from a newly inspected 1830, 1840, or 1850 schedule image. Reel and index references were treated as finding aids, not household evidence. The records still require several people to remain separate: the older and younger Ezekiel Selphs; the two Archibald Stricklands in the indexed 1850 household; the 1850 Asahel Renfroe, who was too young to be an adult migrant in 1826; an unrelated William Newton passenger; and younger Simpson Stricklands who cannot be the man already holding office in 1829. Other same-name questions remain unresolved.

The result is a research control, not a new claim that every traditional arrival date is proved. Dates taken from Huxford or another retrospective compilation remain attributed traditions unless a contemporary record independently supports them.

Farms, property, and enslaved labor

Farming, livestock, mills, stores, ferries, and trade supported the neighborhood, as did enslaved labor. Census and estate records count enslaved people in households associated with Alfred Belote, Drew Vickers, Sion and Enoch Hall, Francis Rountree, Hamilton Sharpe, William and Henry Blair, John Pike, James J. Joyce, William Smith, Rev. Joshua Platt, and others. Most federal schedules omit their names. Changing counts cannot be treated as a continuous list of the same people, and matching ages alone do not establish identities across emancipation.

William Folsom, a son of Lawrence Folsom, remained in the area as county lines changed; later accounts connect him with courthouse commissions and Mount Zion. His obituary says he died at his Brooks County home on November 16, 1872, in his seventy-eighth year. Four original administrator's deeds prove that his estate included at least 2,080 acres: all of District 9 Land Lots 492, 519, and 521; 120 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 491; and all of District 12 Lot 323. The estate sold those tracts to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree. The $30,000 administration bond was security for the administrators, not an estate valuation.

Elizabeth Folsom's executor separately conveyed her District 9 Land Lots 493 and 520 to her daughter Edith Rountree for $1,200. Elizabeth's will identifies Edith as her daughter and Charles W. Ryall as her grandson. Together, the will and deeds document a Folsom-Ryall-Rountree-Perry land and family network north of Barney. They do not reveal how William and Elizabeth acquired every tract or establish William's complete acreage.

A surviving photograph shows William and Elizabeth Folsom's broken marble grave marker, with both names and the years 1872 and 1877 visible. Field documentation places the marked graves on their homeplace in District 9, Land Lot 520, contrary to the online description of unmarked graves in the family cemetery. In 1870, Dicy Roberts and her sons Louis and John, all Black, lived in William Folsom's household; they remained in Brooks County in 1880. No record found shows whether any member of the Roberts family had been enslaved by Folsom.

Acts of incendiarism, 1885–1887

A series of suspected incendiary fires struck the Morven district during the two years before Barney was founded. Gum Pond School House burned around November 1885. When another schoolhouse on the same ground burned on November 21, 1886, the newspaper called it suspected incendiarism and noted the earlier fire.

The best-documented cluster began in January 1886. During the same night that Folsom Bridge burned, fire destroyed William Ryals's gin house, a country schoolhouse, and the miller's dwelling at Dr. Bourquin's mill. Kerosene had reportedly been poured on Bourquin's mill, but the doctor discovered the attempt and drove the suspected incendiaries away. The account places Ryals and a Dr. Bourquin in the broader Little River neighborhood, but gives no initials or land descriptions that would fix either residence or the mill site.

A February reprint said that, while residents were preparing to repair the bridge, someone burned its remaining portion and “another country school-house.” The report said there was no clue to the perpetrators. Its description of the crossing as being at “the Rocks” on the Withlacoochee conflicts with the more specific contemporary report identifying the January crossing as Folsom Bridge on Little River, so that geographic wording must be treated cautiously.

The burning continued into 1887. After Stonewall Academy burned in June, a newspaper summary said that four schoolhouses, “white and black,” had burned in the Morven district during the preceding two years. It also reported that three churches, a mill, and other property had been destroyed by incendiaries. The summary did not identify every building or name a suspect.

docs.title: The first settlement traditions
docs.text:
A familiar Lowndes County tradition says that four settlers—James Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, Drewry “Drew” Vickers, and Alfred Belote—moved with their families into the area in 1821. The surviving published trail begins with William Harden's 1913 history, the earliest account located and fully inspected that assembles this exact group. An unsigned article in the 1922 South Georgia Historical and Genealogical Quarterly repeated the four names and supplied the 1821 date. The article credited its data chiefly to recent Valdosta Times sketches by Hortense W. Baker, and the quartet passage appeared immediately afterward. Because that paragraph had no separate attribution, Baker is a plausible source but cannot be identified as the source of the exact list or wording. Her sketches have not been located. Harden's book and the 1922 article are therefore the earliest located links in the published chain through which the four-family tradition was preserved and repeated.

The earliest published accounts located do not agree on who should be called the area's first settlers. Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollections focused on the Hall settlement and Mount Zion and named a different circle of pioneers. Montgomery M. Folsom's inspected 1885–1886 writings described the Coffee Road, the Hall and Morven neighborhood, and several early residents, but did not assemble the familiar four-man group.

In December 1888, the Valdosta Times reprinted a Quitman Herald story naming “Mr. Frank Rountree and Lawrence Folsom” among the first settlers of “this portion of Georgia.” The story said their descendants remembered that coffee was unknown when the families first settled and was initially cooked like beans when someone later brought it for sale. It also recalled Native Americans visiting Mrs. Folsom “in droves.” Although she feared the visits, she treated her guests kindly and observed their custom of shaking hands on arrival and departure. The account goes on to describe barter for milk and a shared meal. The printed “Frank Rountree” was probably Francis Rountree, but the article does not establish his identity, and he should not be confused with James Rountree. The piece preserves a late family tradition rather than contemporary evidence of the settlement.

The January 1889 article “Correcting a Munchausen Story,” signed “Savage,” linked several settlement traditions in one account. It called James Rountree the first settler of Lowndes County and placed Joe and John Bryant at the old Indigenous town where Okapilco and Mule creeks meet. It also said that Lawrence Folsom married Rachel Vickers in Burke County about 1790, moved to the Ocmulgee River in 1808, lived there until 1823, and later traveled south and west after General Jackson's purchase opened Irwin County. The writer added that “the Folsoms and Rountrees had been used to Indian company many years before Brooks and Lowndes were settled.” The article does not date Folsom's arrival in Lowndes County, identify Rachel Vickers's relationship to Drew Vickers, mention Alfred Belote, or assemble the familiar four-man group.

An article signed “Civilized,” published on October 5, 1895, gave a more definite version. It said that settlement began in 1824 with Benjamin Daniels on the Withlacoochee River and Washington Joyce, Drew Vickers, Lawrence Folsom, and James Rountree on Little River. The writer called these “the first settlements made by white men in the present territory of Lowndes county.” The article also said Folsom's place occupied the site of an Indigenous town, where pottery, knives, arrowheads, tomahawks, and gun barrels had been found. This is the earliest located and inspected account that names Joyce, Vickers, Folsom, and Rountree together as the county's first white settlements. It does not mention Alfred Belote, and its 1824 date conflicts with the later four-family tradition's 1821 date.

J. R. Folsom added another version elsewhere in the same issue. Writing about Cecil and the Coffee Road, he said that the first lands settled were near the watercourses, dated settlement of “the Bryant place” on the Okapilco to 1829, and grouped James Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, and Drew Vickers as settlers east of Little River whose descendants still lived on those places. He did not call the three men the area's first settlers, give a date for their arrival, or include Alfred Belote.

R. E. L. Folsom offered another version in 1899. He called Washington Joyce's 1824 home and ferry the first white settlement in present Lowndes County, then said Vickers, Lawrence Folsom, and a man named Baker came next. He mentioned Rountree elsewhere in the article but did not include him in that sequence, and he did not name Belote. Differences in county boundaries explain part of the conflict, but the accounts also preserve genuinely different local traditions.

An unsigned 1900 article, “A Historical Sketch of Old Lowndes County,” expanded that sequence. It said Thomas Baker established a ferry on the Withlacoochee River where Coffee Road crossed it late in 1823, and that Thomas Futch bought the ferry in 1824. The article then placed James Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, and Drew Vickers on or near Coffee Road east of Little River in 1824. Thomas Baker is therefore a strong probable identification of the “man named Baker” in the 1899 account: the name, river, ferry, and road crossing agree. Because the two articles may preserve versions of the same tradition, the 1900 wording is not independent proof of Baker's identity or the dates.

Neither Harden nor the unsigned 1922 article cited a contemporary deed, diary, tax return, or court record for the four families' move. The account is a durable local tradition, not a proved passenger list with a certain date.

Original records do establish the men in the early county. On November 27, 1823, Newman Pounds conveyed Lawrence Folsom all 490 acres of District 12, Land Lot 187. The deed identifies Lawrence as "of the County of Irwin," proving that he was an Irwin County resident and landowner by that date. It does not establish when his family moved there. Rountree can be followed from Pulaski County into the Lowndes settlement and died after an 1834 attack on the Tallahassee road. Folsom later became a Lowndes county-site commissioner and a Mount Zion trustee. Vickers appears in the 1820 Montgomery County lottery and later Lowndes census, land, court, and tax records. Belote held Land Lot 55 in District 12 and was dead by 1844. Their dossiers also show how much remains unknown, including exact arrival dates, complete families, and the location of every first home.

The old claim that one man was the area's first settler is even less certain. A January 1889 newspaper item said that “Joe and John Bryant” settled at the old Indigenous town where Okapilco and Mule creeks meet. It separately called James Rountree Lowndes County's first settler. R. E. L. Folsom wrote in 1899 that Jose Bryant settled at the old town in 1828. An unsigned 1900 article changed the year to 1823 and added claims about Jose's household, enslaved labor, and first crop. Huxford later substituted John Bryan and Abraham Hunter. John Bryan is documented in Lowndes County, and his daughter Jane Hunter's 1912 obituary associated him with Okapilco. No record yet proves that Jose, Joe, and John were one person. The identity remains unresolved.

The county-organization story now appears on From Irwin to Lowndes and Brooks Counties. The church, campground, trustees, and militia connections are covered on Mount Zion.

docs.title: Farms, property, and enslaved labor
docs.text:
Farming, livestock, mills, stores, ferries, and trade supported the neighborhood, as did enslaved labor. Census and estate records count enslaved people in households associated with Alfred Belote, Drew Vickers, Sion and Enoch Hall, Francis Rountree, Hamilton Sharpe, William and Henry Blair, John Pike, James J. Joyce, William Smith, Rev. Joshua Platt, and others. Most federal schedules omit their names. Changing counts cannot be treated as a continuous list of the same people, and matching ages alone do not establish identities across emancipation.

William Folsom, a son of Lawrence Folsom, remained in the area as county lines changed; later accounts connect him with courthouse commissions and Mount Zion. His obituary says he died at his Brooks County home on November 16, 1872, in his seventy-eighth year. Four original administrator's deeds prove that his estate included at least 2,080 acres: all of District 9 Land Lots 492, 519, and 521; 120 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 491; and all of District 12 Lot 323. The estate sold those tracts to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree. The $30,000 administration bond was security for the administrators, not an estate valuation.

Elizabeth Folsom's executor separately conveyed her District 9 Land Lots 493 and 520 to her daughter Edith Rountree for $1,200. Elizabeth's will identifies Edith as her daughter and Charles W. Ryall as her grandson. Together, the will and deeds document a Folsom-Ryall-Rountree-Perry land and family network north of Barney. They do not reveal how William and Elizabeth acquired every tract or establish William's complete acreage.

A surviving photograph shows William and Elizabeth Folsom's broken marble grave marker, with both names and the years 1872 and 1877 visible. Field documentation places the marked graves on their homeplace in District 9, Land Lot 520, contrary to the online description of unmarked graves in the family cemetery. In 1870, Dicy Roberts and her sons Louis and John, all Black, lived in William Folsom's household; they remained in Brooks County in 1880. No record found shows whether any member of the Roberts family had been enslaved by Folsom.

docs.title: Burney Bridge on Little River
docs.text:
Research dossier

Prepared August 26, 2026

docs.title: Scope and conclusion
docs.text:
Burney Bridge was a separate Little River crossing on the old road system between Tallokas and the Nashville, Sparks, and Berlin side of the river. It was northwest of Rock Bridge and Folsom Bridge. It was not an alternate name for either one.

The road story begins in 1869, when Brooks County advertised a new route from Tallokas northeast across Okapilco Creek and through the Colter, Alderman, and Norman neighborhoods to the Nashville Road at Little River. That notice does not name Burney Bridge or prove that a bridge stood at its endpoint. The later road geography makes Burney Bridge the strong probable endpoint, but the connection is not explicit.[1-4]

The bridge itself is directly named by 1887. Later reports show that it was an established regional landmark, a proposed gathering place, and the starting point of a Berrien County road toward the Sparks road. Brooks and Berrien counties agreed to rebuild it in 1903. By May 1904, high water had delayed the work for more than a year even though the crossing carried "a great deal of travel". The original newspaper page confirms that rains swept the bridge away in April 1908.[5-11]

The record then goes quiet until 1941, when a child drowned near Burney Bridge. Federal bridge data now close part of the later gap. The National Bridge Inventory identifies a county bridge built in 1966 on Hempstead Church Road over Little River, approximately six miles northwest of Barney. Its coordinates are within about 15 meters, or 50 feet, of the locally identified Burney Bridge point. The 1966 structure was a seven-span concrete T-beam bridge about 253 feet long.[14-16]

No located record identifies the Burney namesake, dates the first bridge, describes the nineteenth-century structure, proves completion of the 1903-1904 rebuilding, or explains the full replacement sequence between 1908 and 1966.

docs.title: Evidence grades
docs.text:
This dossier uses four grades:

  • Verified: stated in a direct original, contemporary, or official record, or fixed by several independent records without a material conflict.
  • Strong probable: several specific facts agree, but no source states the entire conclusion.
  • Possible: plausible, but the evidence is incomplete or does not distinguish alternatives.
  • Unresolved: the evidence does not support a choice.

docs.title: Location and bridge identity
docs.text:
James identifies Burney Bridge at 31.067920872044272, -83.56471852760521. That point began as a local geographic control, not an official survey coordinate. The federal inventory now supplies an independent check. It places the Hempstead Church Road bridge over Little River at 31.0680389, -83.5646697, about 15 meters away.[15]

The federal location description reads "APP 6 MI NW OF BARNEY". The 1974 USGS Berlin East quadrangle, photorevised in 1988, independently plots the local road crossing Little River at the same place.[16]

This fixes the modern crossing. It does not prove that every older deck occupied precisely the same line. Nineteenth-century timber bridges were often repaired, shifted, or replaced without a surviving plan. The historical evidence converges on the same road and river reach, making the 1966 bridge the strong probable modern successor at Burney Bridge.

The surrounding county geography changed. Before Cook County was created in 1918, contemporary reports placed the bridge where the Brooks, Berrien, and Colquitt area met. The 1908 washout dispatch described Little River there as dividing those counties. The modern crossing remains close to the Brooks, Cook, and Colquitt corner.[11,16]

docs.title: Separation from Rock Bridge and Folsom Bridge
docs.text:
The three bridges belonged to different roads:

Crossing Historical road system Geographic control Burney Bridge Tallokas-side road to Little River, Berrien-side road to the Sparks road, and later Hempstead Church Road 31.0680389, -83.5646697 in the federal inventory Rock Bridge Adel-Quitman Road, later old GA 76, directly north of Barney 31.050137, -83.499369 local control, supported by the 1908 map and nearby USGS station Folsom Bridge Foster and the Hahira-facing road, later SR 122 30.999009, -83.456601 local control

Burney Bridge lies roughly four straight-line miles northwest of Rock Bridge and about eight straight-line miles northwest of Folsom Bridge. The May 1904 newspaper item clearly concerns "Burney bridge over Little river". It should not be corrected to Barney or used in Rock Bridge history.[10]

docs.title: The 1869 opening notice
docs.text:
On July 5, 1869, Brooks County ordered notice of a proposed road "commencing at Tallokas, running Northeast". It would cross Okapilco Creek at or near John Colter's, pass the residences of John Alderman and John Norman, and intersect the Nashville Road at Little River. The notice appeared in the Quitman Banner on July 9 and July 30.[1]

The sequence is unusually useful because it names a start, a creek crossing, three residents, a direction, and an established road at the river. It proves that county officials were trying to create a Tallokas-to-Little River connector. It does not name a bridge at the endpoint.

The route can be tested against later land and map evidence. An original Tallokas tax image from the 1872-1877 volume group records John A. Colter with 735 acres in Land Lots 459 and 468. Lot 459 lies on the locally reconstructed approach from Tallokas toward Burney Bridge. The 1908 Brooks County map shows a developed public-road network through the same broad neighborhood.[3,12]

The local reconstruction follows Lots 458, 459, 460, and 415, crosses Okapilco Creek in Lot 415, briefly enters Colquitt County, returns to Brooks near Lots 490 and 477, and reaches Little River at Burney Bridge. That reconstruction fits the period evidence, but no surviving road survey has yet proved every segment or centerline.

docs.title: The 1870 discontinuance proceeding
docs.text:
The route's early legal history is not continuous on the present record. In July 1870, an application sought to discontinue the road from Tallokas by Colter, Alderman, and Norman to Little River. Work was suspended while the court invited objections through August. No final decision has been found.[2]

The 1908 Brooks County map supplies later evidence that a Tallokas-to-Nashville road existed and appears to follow the 1869 directions through the same broad corridor.[12] This shows that a road connecting those places existed in 1908 despite the unresolved 1870 proceeding. What remains unproved is whether the 1908 road followed the exact 1869 path. The earlier route may have been retained, altered, discontinued and later reopened, or replaced by a road on a similar line. The 1869 notice therefore remains the strong probable beginning of the documented Burney corridor, but it does not prove one unchanged legal road or centerline.

docs.title: County maps and later highways
docs.text:
B. W. Frobel's 1869 Brooks County map contains a faint, unlabeled route in the northern road network that broadly matches the Tallokas-to-Little River corridor. It supplies supporting geography but no bridge name or decisive legal status.[4]

The 1908 Flippen and Hudgins map shows the mature road network around Tallokas, Colter, Alderman, Norman, Okapilco Creek, and Little River. The inspected image does not provide a legible Burney Bridge label at the crossing, so the map should be used to establish the network, not to date the bridge.[12]

The rural delivery map from about 1930-1938 preserves the later northern Brooks road pattern but does not clearly label Burney Bridge or prove which postal route crossed it.[17]

The 1939 state highway map places SR 33 on the old Moultrie-Quitman Road through Tallokas and Berlin and SR 122 through Rock Hill and Barney. The Tallokas-Nashville Road was a separate road that intersected SR 33; the two roads did not follow the same path. The map therefore documents the later numbered-road setting but does not identify the Tallokas-Nashville Road or Burney Bridge as part of SR 33.[13]

The 1966 official highway map retains that broad state-route framework. The federal inventory is more specific about Burney Bridge itself: the crossing remained a county-owned and county-maintained bridge on Hempstead Church Road.[15,18]

docs.title: Earliest located name, 1887
docs.text:
The earliest direct use found is a Valdosta Times article published September 24, 1887. In a discussion of a proposed railroad and possible depot sites, a writer called Sineath Crossroads or Boyd's "the only convenient point from W. R. Ryals to Burney's bridge". The same discussion referred to the Brooks-Colquitt corner and the Berlin post office.[5]

The article does not say when the bridge was built. It does show that Burney's Bridge was established regional geography by 1887, familiar enough to serve as an endpoint in a public argument about roads, depots, and community access.

docs.title: Gathering place, 1892
docs.text: In September 1892, the Hempstead Democratic Club proposed a mass meeting at "Burney's bridge, or some other accessible point" and invited residents of Berrien and Brooks counties. The wording again treats the bridge as a known place and says something about its accessibility. It does not describe its structure or condition.[6]

docs.title: The Berrien-side road, 1894
docs.text:
In May 1894, Berrien County ordered a new public road beginning at Burney Bridge on Little River and running northeast to the Sparks road at Paul Crosby's. The order named Caroline Flowers, B. George, G. W. Ingram, W. B. Crosby, Marcus Wright, S. J. Wright, W. W. Hancock, William Castleberry, James Castleberry, W. W. Giddens, and Paul Crosby along the proposed line.[7]

This is the strongest early bridge-and-road evidence. The order begins at an existing named bridge, so Burney Bridge predates the new road. On the Berrien side, the crossing connected directly to the Sparks road, showing that it served more than a local Tallokas route. The wider road geography suggests a connection with the Nashville road system, but this order does not state it.

The 1869 and 1894 records therefore describe complementary sides of a likely through route. One reached Little River from Tallokas. The other began at Burney Bridge and ran northeast toward the Sparks road. The geographic connection is strong probable. No single record joins the two as one continuously named road.

docs.title: Deep water and the Rowland near-drowning, 1898
docs.text:
On September 3, 1898, B. A. Rowland and his wife nearly drowned while crossing Little River at Burney Bridge. They entered water deeper than expected but escaped. The report appeared six days later in the Tifton Gazette.[8]

The article proves a water-related travel hazard. It does not say whether the danger was on the bridge deck, a flooded approach, or another part of the crossing. It also does not identify the storm or rainfall that caused the deeper water. The safest conclusion is that high or unexpectedly deep water made the crossing dangerous, not that the bridge itself failed.

docs.title: The 1903-1904 rebuilding
docs.text:
In June 1903, the Tifton Gazette reported that Berrien County commissioners had agreed with Brooks County to rebuild Burney Bridge across Little River. The need for joint action fits a county-line bridge. The short item gives no reason for rebuilding and no cost, contractor, material, dimensions, or design.[9]

The work did not move quickly. A May 1904 Adel News report said Burney Bridge was in very bad condition. Rebuilding material had been on the ground for more than a year, but water had stayed too high for the work until shortly before the article. The bridge carried "a great deal of travel", and the newspaper urged the commissioners to take advantage of low water and complete the job.[10]

The chronology suggests that planning or material delivery began before the June 1903 public report. It does not prove when construction started or whether the counties completed that particular rebuilding. No completion notice has been found.

The 1904 report also shows that Burney Bridge was part of an active travel corridor, not an obscure farm crossing. The long delay illustrates the practical problem of bridge work in the Little River floodplain. Water levels could prevent construction even when officials, materials, and public pressure were already in place.

docs.title: The 1908 washout
docs.text:
A Macon newspaper dispatch dated April 5 and published April 6, 1908 says: "The recent rains in this section caused nearly all the streams to rise. The Burney bridge over Little River, which divides the counties of Berrien, Brooks and Colquitt, was swept away."[11]

The original Newspapers.com page was visually read on August 27, 2026, confirming the saved OCR. The washout is verified from the contemporary page.

The 1908 washout supplies an end point for the bridge then standing, but it does not settle the delayed 1903-1904 rebuilding cycle. The article does not tell us whether the lost bridge was the completed replacement, an older span still awaiting work, or an intermediate repair. It also does not say when another bridge opened.

docs.title: The 1941 drowning
docs.text:
On May 29, 1941, twelve-year-old George Berry Croft of the Berlin community drowned while swimming with other children in Little River near Burney Bridge. Reports said he stepped into a deep hole and that his body was recovered about thirty minutes after he was missed.[14]

This was a river drowning near the bridge, not a traffic accident, washout, or structural failure. It proves that Burney Bridge remained a recognized place-name in 1941. The article does not describe the bridge or expressly state that a bridge still stood there.

A separate 1945 accident occurred at an unnamed bridge on Tallokas Road. The available report does not call it Burney Bridge. It cannot be assigned to this crossing.

docs.title: The 1966 county bridge
docs.text:
The strongest later evidence comes from the Federal Highway Administration's National Bridge Inventory. Structure 000000002700470 carried Hempstead Church Road over Little River at the Burney Bridge location. The 2022, 2023, and 2024 Georgia inventory files all retain the record.[15]

The coded record describes:

Field Official value Facility carried Hempstead Church Road Feature crossed Little River Location Approximately six miles northwest of Barney Year built 1966 Owner and maintenance responsibility County highway agency Main structure Concrete T-beam Main spans Seven Maximum span 14.3 meters, about 47 feet Total length 77.1 meters, about 253 feet Roadway width 7.3 meters, about 24 feet Deck width 9.2 meters, about 30 feet

The 1974/1988 USGS Berlin East map confirms the road crossing at the same location. The NBI record grades the inventoried bridge as not eligible for the National Register under its historic-significance code. That classification applies to the 1966 structure, not to the historical importance of the older crossing.[15-16]

The federal record verifies a 1966 successor. It does not reveal what stood there between 1908 and 1966, whether the 1966 bridge reused older abutments, or whether its centerline shifted slightly. Bridge files, county minutes, and aerial photographs are still needed to answer those questions.

docs.title: Name and namesake
docs.text:
Both "Burney's Bridge" and "Burney Bridge" appear in contemporary records. The possessive form in 1887 and 1892 suggests a personal or family namesake, but no inspected source identifies that person. The surname alone is not enough to choose among Burney families or landholders elsewhere in south Georgia.

The name should not be modernized to Barney. The independent 1887, 1892, 1894, 1898, 1903, and 1904 references form a consistent record for one separate crossing. Searches for "Burny Bridge" and "Birney Bridge" found no additional relevant event.

docs.title: What is proved
docs.text: Question Conclusion Grade Was Burney Bridge the same as Rock Bridge or Folsom Bridge? No. The roads, coordinates, and source sequences identify three separate crossings. Verified Did the 1869 Tallokas road end at Burney Bridge? It reached the Nashville Road at Little River in the correct corridor. Later geography points strongly to Burney Bridge, but the notice does not name it. Strong probable Did Burney Bridge exist by 1887? Yes. A contemporary article used "Burney's bridge" as established regional geography. Verified Was a road opened northeast from the bridge in 1894? Yes. The Berrien order began at Burney Bridge and met the Sparks road. Verified Did deep water endanger travel in 1898? Yes. B. A. Rowland and his wife nearly drowned while crossing there. Verified Did Brooks and Berrien agree to rebuild the bridge? Yes, by June 1903. Verified Did high water delay rebuilding through May 1904? Yes. Material had been present for more than a year, but water prevented work. Verified Was the bridge swept away in April 1908? Yes. The original newspaper page says recent rains raised the streams and swept away Burney Bridge. Verified Was a bridge at the crossing built in 1966? Yes. Federal inventory structure 000000002700470 fixes its location and construction details. Verified

docs.title: What remains unresolved
docs.text:
• The Burney namesake.
  • The first bridge's construction date, builder, material, dimensions, and precise deck line.
  • Whether the 1870 discontinuance application succeeded.
  • The exact legal and physical continuity between the 1869 road, the later Burney road, and Hempstead Church Road.
  • Completion and details of the 1903-1904 rebuilding.
  • The replacement sequence between 1908 and 1966.
  • Whether the 1966 bridge reused an older approach, abutment, or deck line.

docs.title: Best next records
docs.text:
1. Brooks County Ordinary and County Purposes Books A and B for the 1869 petition, reviewers' return, opening order, and final 1870 discontinuance decision.
  2. Brooks and Berrien commissioner minutes, bridge books, warrants, contractor accounts, and road-superintendent reports for 1903-1908.
  3. Brooks, Berrien, Colquitt, and later Cook county bridge records covering replacement after 1908.
  4. Georgia Highway Department inventory cards, plans, inspection files, and correspondence for NBI structure 000000002700470.
  5. A georeferenced comparison of the 1869 and 1908 county maps, the 1930s rural-delivery and highway maps, USGS sheets, and USDA aerials from the 1940s through 1966.
  6. Deeds, tax digests, and probate files for Burney landholders near the crossing to identify the namesake.

docs.title: Search coverage and limits
docs.text:
Stored memory, bridge dossiers, road reports, map analyses, coordinate ledgers, saved newspaper OCR, and related genealogy files were searched before online sources. Georgia Historic Newspapers was searched from 1763 through 1960 using exact and proximity variants for Burney Bridge, Little River, Tallokas, Nashville, Sparks, Berlin, road, repair, rebuilding, flood, high water, washout, accident, and drowning. The focused exact-phrase search returned fifteen pages. Relevant original pages from 1869, 1870, 1892, 1894, 1898, 1903, and 1904 were checked.

Preserved Newspapers.com results covering 1850 through 1960 supplied the 1887 article, the 1908 washout report, and the 1941 drowning reports. Fresh access initially failed after two browser timeouts, and public requests returned 403. The original 1908 page was subsequently opened and read on August 27, confirming the washout report. The Newspapers.com and Ancestry links in the source list require the appropriate subscription or account.

Official records checked included Georgia Archives county maps, Digital Library of Georgia rural-delivery and highway maps, the USGS Historical Topographic Map collection, and FHWA National Bridge Inventory files through 2024. Complete county commissioner minutes, bridge books, contractor files, and Georgia Highway Department project files were not online and were not inspected.

This search is broad and reproducible, but it is not exhaustive. The missing county records are likely to contain the first construction, rebuilding, and replacement details.

docs.title: Research record
docs.text: The detailed evidence and reproducible search notes are preserved in:

docs.title: From Irwin to Lowndes and Brooks Counties
Lowndes County organized
docs.text:
Lowndes County was created from Irwin County on December 23, 1825. It initially included the 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th, 15th, and 16th land districts of original Irwin County. The organizing act approved the next day designated Sion Hall's home for the first courts and elections and named Lawrence Folsom, Hall, William Blair, John J. Underwood, and Daniel McCranie Sr. to select a permanent county site. His name appears as “Daniel McCraney” in the legislative volume and “McCranly” in a 1920 reprint.

Hall lived in the Coffee Road neighborhood north of present Morven. An 1846 sheriff's notice placed working saw and grist mills on Hall family property in Land Lot 271; a 1902 correction placed the residence in adjoining Lot 270. In 1826, the statutory court and election place moved to Francis Rountree's home. Later witnesses disagreed about which early Superior Court terms met at each house.

County commissioners selected Franklinville, on Land Lot 50 near the Withlacoochee River, as Lowndes County's first permanent county seat. The small settlement had the county's first courthouse, and Hamilton W. Sharpe later dated its first Superior Court term to the fall of 1829. Franklinville remained the seat of county government until Troupville replaced it in the 1830s.

Several commissioners later held county and state offices. Blair served as an Inferior Court justice and state senator. Henry Blair was the first court clerk and later served as sheriff, legislator, and militia colonel. Underwood owned books and surveying equipment, held Franklinville town lots, and practiced law at Troupville before moving to Florida. McCranie lived along Coffee Road in the area that became Cook County, but federal registers reviewed so far do not confirm the traditional claim that he was Lowndes County's first postmaster.

William Smith was Superior Court clerk by an 1828-era record and Franklinville postmaster by September 1829. He later kept Tranquil Hall at Troupville and Valdosta; his 1880 recollection preserves part of the early court story but does not settle its dates. Hamilton W. Sharpe opened a nearby store in the late 1820s. Huxford dates the Sharpe's Store post office to 1828; a federal register directly proves Sharpe's reappointment when the office resumed that name in 1837. Sharpe also served as a justice, legislator, Methodist lay preacher, planter, and militia correspondent.

docs.title: Thomas County created
docs.text:
The same act that created Lowndes County on December 23, 1825, also created Thomas County. It initially included the 13th and 14th land districts of original Irwin County, along with the 17th and 18th districts and the parts of the 19th and 23rd districts east of the Ochlocknee River in original Early County. An amendment approved December 27, 1826, transferred the 8th District of original Irwin from Lowndes to Thomas.

Part of the land later included in Brooks County therefore belonged to Thomas County from 1825 until Brooks was created in 1858. This is why the Brooks County act drew territory from both Thomas and Lowndes counties.

This 1830 state map shows Lowndes and Thomas counties before Brooks County was created. The land later used to form Brooks County was then divided between those two counties. The map also shows land districts and numbered lots. Carlton Wellborn and Orange Green, Map of the State of Georgia, Drawn from Actual Surveys and the Most Authentic Information (1830), Library of Congress Geography and Map Division. Select the map to open the Library of Congress record.

docs.title: Brooks County created
docs.text:
Brooks County was created from Lowndes and Thomas counties by an act approved December 11, 1858. Senator James West introduced and handled the bill. Shadrack Griffin attended the local convention and later became Brooks County's first state senator, but he did not carry the creation measure. The published act placed part of the county's western boundary along the "Ocilla River," now called the Aucilla River. From the line between Thomas County Land Lots 392 and 437, the boundary ran south to the river and followed it to Florida. The act also directed that public business be conducted at Thomas Folsom's home until the county seat at Quitman was selected.

Folks Huxford wrote that the Grooverville and Okapilco districts of Thomas County wanted to join the new county and petitioned the legislature. According to Huxford, no objection was made and the districts were included. The original petition has not been located. The published act and contemporary coverage in Thomasville’s Wire-Grass Reporter confirm that part of Thomas County was included, but neither gives a reason.

Colquitt County had been created in 1856 from Thomas and Lowndes counties. It received all of the 8th District of original Irwin, then in Thomas County, and only part of the 9th District, then in Lowndes. In the 9th District, the new county included the land west of Little River as far as the river's crossing of the line between Lots 443 and 444; from there, the boundary ran south to the line between the 9th and 12th districts. The 9th District was therefore divided rather than transferred as a whole.

Brooks County's 1858-1859 formation-era boundaries. Source: 1867 Brooks County map, County Maps, Surveyor General, RG 3-9-66, Georgia Archives.

When Brooks County was created two years later, its northern boundary followed the existing Lowndes-Berrien, Lowndes-Colquitt, and Thomas-Colquitt county lines. Brooks received only the adjoining territory still belonging to Lowndes and Thomas. The part of the 9th District already in Colquitt remained there; neither the legislation nor the Newberry Library's county-boundary chronology records a transfer from Colquitt to Brooks.

The original Brooks boundary placed the future Hahira area in the new county. On November 21, 1859, the legislature changed the Brooks-Lowndes line to the east bank of Little River, returning that land to Lowndes after less than a year. The same act ordered Lowndes County to establish a new county seat along the Atlantic and Gulf Railroad, as near the county's center as possible. That seat became Valdosta. The act does not state why that particular land was transferred, but the change was part of the reorganization of Lowndes County and replaced the earlier lot-line boundary with Little River.

RandyMajors historical county lines map

This interactive map shows how county boundaries changed around the creation of Brooks County.
