docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Head: Mitchell James Hiers (age 50, Georgia, farmer)
  • Spouse (not listed in the 1900 household): Josephine Iona Wade Hiers

  • Children in household: Enoch (age 20), Osca (age 18), Nannie (age 16), Ludie (age 14), Maggie (age 13), Ola E. (age 11)

  • The census trail now runs from 1850 through 1910 for Mitchell Hiers/Hires.

  • In 1850 Mitchell appears as an infant in Division 53, Lowndes County, Georgia, in the household of Philip Hiers and Mary Hiers.
  • In 1860 Mitchell Hires, age 10, appears in Brooks County in the household of Philip Hires and Mary Hires.
  • In 1870 Mitchell Hiers, age 21, appears in Brooks County in the household of Philip Hiers and Sarah Hiers, showing continuity but also a name discrepancy for the older woman in the household between 1860 and 1870.
  • Josephine Wade also appears before marriage in Brooks County census households: in 1860 as a child in the household of Thomas Wade and Mary A. Wade, and in 1870 as Josephine Wade, age 12, in the Wade household at Quitman.
  • The Brooks County marriage license was issued 31 Mar 1874 for Mitchell J. Hires and Josephine Wade, and the return states they were married on 4 Apr 1874.
  • In 1880 Mitchell J. Hiers and Josephine Hiers appear in Morven, Brooks County, Georgia, with sons John B. G., George W., John Morgan, and one younger son whose given name is not clear in the summary now in hand.
  • In the 1900 census the household appears under the spelling "Hires" in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. Mitchell is listed with sons Enoch and Osca and daughters Nannie, Ludie, Maggie, and Ola. Josephine and Morgan Hiers are not listed in this household.
  • In the 1910 census Mitch Hires is still in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, with adult sons Enoch and Oscar in the household.
  • A 1933 Brooks County death certificate for Morgan Hiers, born ~1875, identifies his father as Mitchell Hiers and his mother as Josephine Wade; the surname spelling on the death certificate favors "Hiers." Morgan Hiers bears the suffix "Sr." in the death record. This later-life evidence supports him as the household head's son.
  • Taken together, the supplied census summaries support James's point that Hires and Hiers were used interchangeably across this family line over multiple decades.
  • The supplied FindAGrave memorials place both Mitchell James Hiers and Josephine Wade Hiers at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery in Pavo, Brooks County, Georgia. Mitchell's memorial includes a grave marker photo consistent with an 1849 birth year and death on 27 Oct 1911, while Josephine's memorial gives a death date of 4 Feb 1924.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• The census chain strongly supports Mitchell's continuity from childhood through old age, but the exact identification of Philip/Phillip Hiers-Hires and the older woman listed as Mary in 1850-1860, Sarah in 1870, and Mary again as Phillip's wife in 1880 still needs tighter record work before the parentage claim is stated as fully settled.
  • An enumerator or transcription error is one possible explanation for the Mary/Sarah/Mary pattern, but that explanation remains unverified and should not be presented as fact.
  • A supplied family-record compilation identifies Phillip Hiers's wife as Mary Catherine "Polly" Alderman, which would create an Alderman-family connection for this household, but that point should remain secondary until matched to direct records.
  • Josephine's pre-marriage census trail now strongly supports her continuity in the Wade household from 1860 to 1870, but the exact interpretation of the 1870 Wade household structure still needs caution because the summary view shows multiple adults with the same surname and does not by itself resolve every relationship.
  • The exact child list should be limited to the six children named in the 1900 census household; other candidates identified in derivative family trees should remain unlinked until matched to direct records. Morgan Hiers, son of Mitchell and Josephine, is supported by the 1933 death certificate.
  • The 1880 youngest son should not be named more specifically until the underlying image or a clearer extract is pulled.
  • Mitchell's and Josephine's burial placement at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery is now supported by the supplied memorial pages, but the parent, sibling, and full child links shown on those memorials should still be treated as derivative unless matched to direct records.
  • Josephine's exact birth date still should not be stated strongly from the memorial alone, and Mitchell's full life dates are better treated as supported by memorial-level evidence unless a death certificate or other direct record is pulled.
  • Claims about Confederate military networks, broader Alderman prominence, and Hall-lineage context go beyond the currently preserved direct source base for this household and should remain out of the main writeup unless re-documented.
  • Any future connections section for HH#36 should treat the Alderman link as a likely but still secondary-source connection unless a stronger direct-record chain is assembled.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Head: Thomas Nichols (age 51, Florida, farmer) — born Jan 1849 per 1900 census
  • Spouse: Mary A. Nichols (age 48, Georgia) — born December 1851 per the 1900 census

  • Other household members: Fronis Nichols, Villian V. Nichols, Charles Nichols, Thomas Nichols Jr., Leonard Nichols, and boarder Sam Johnson

  • In the 1900 census Thomas Nichols appears in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, as a white farmer born in Florida in Jan 1849. That record says he had been married 34 years, could read and write, owned his farm free of mortgage, and was the father of a household including Mary A. Nichols, Lingenia, Fronis, Villian, Charley, Thomas, Linnie, and boarder Sam Johnson.

  • In the 1910 census Thomas Nichols appears again as the head of household 119 in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, age 61, born in Florida, a farmer owning a free farm, with wife Mary A. Nichols and children Vivian V., Charlie, Tomie, and Lennie.
  • The 1900 and 1910 household records strongly support HH#37 as a Brooks County family centered on Thomas Nichols and Mary Ann Nichols from at least 1900 through 1910.
  • No marriage record has yet been located in the current online search trail. The 1900 census reports 34 years of marriage, which implies about 1866 but is not a recorded marriage date. The 1910 census reports 46 years of marriage, implying about 1864. The marriage is therefore supported by census evidence before 1870, but the exact year remains unresolved.
  • The supplied 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1920 census screenshots describe a different Thomas Nichols/Nickols line: those records place him in Union County and Henry County, then in Huerfano and Pueblo, Colorado, and show Georgia birth rather than the Florida birth reported in the Brooks County household. The 1880 and 1920 Colorado records also place that Thomas with wife Maggie or Margaret J., not Mary Ann.
  • The preserved trail also cites a 20 Nov 1897 Valdosta Times item about a cotton house fire affecting "Mr. Tom Nichols" near Hahira.
  • Positive FindAGrave memorials are cited in the preserved trail for Thomas Nichols and Mary Ann Nichols.
  • Much of the broader material in the old writeup — especially the orphan narrative, self-education story, founding-family language, and large social-history conclusions — depends on interpretation beyond the direct record trail currently preserved in this entry.

docs.text:
• The supplied 1850-1920 Georgia/Colorado chain should not currently be treated as HH#37's pre-1900 life course. It appears to belong to another Thomas Nichols/Nickols and is better treated as an excluded or false lead unless a stronger identity bridge is found.
  • The statement that Thomas was orphaned or separated from his parents between 1850 and 1860 should be removed from this household's claim set unless new direct evidence ties those early records to the Barney farmer.
  • The claim that Thomas became literate between 1870 and 1900 is not supportable from the currently matched HH#37 record trail because the supplied 1870 record appears to be for the Colorado Thomas, not the Barney Thomas.
  • The 1900 and 1910 household details still contain smaller internal issues that should be treated cautiously, including changing parental birthplaces for Thomas, inconsistent marriage timing between the two censuses, and sex labeling inconsistencies for Villian/Vivian and Linnie/Lennie across census years.
  • Mary Ann's placement in the Vickers line, the Bradford connection, and any HH#37 ↔ HH#18 relationship should remain outside the main claim set unless direct records supporting those family links are restored to the entry.
  • The full child list beyond the 1900 and 1910 households needs child-by-child direct support if later names, married names, or exact life dates are to remain in the encyclopedia.
  • FindAGrave is useful for burial placement and any marker-backed facts, but linked relatives and memorial narratives should remain secondary.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Head: Prince Herring, age 30 in 1900, born Apr 1870 in Georgia, farmer
  • Wife: Laura Herring, age 25 in 1900, born 1875 in Georgia

  • Children in the 1900 household: Simon Herring, Minnie Herring, Plinie Herring, and Lizzie Herring

  • The 1900 census places Prince Herring in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, as a Black farmer renting his farm.

  • The same 1900 household includes wife Laura Herring and children Simon, Minnie, Plinie, and Lizzie.
  • The 1900 census reports that Prince and Laura had been married about eleven years, which supports a marriage about 1889.
  • The 1900 census also reports that Prince and Laura could not read or write.
  • The user-supplied 1910 census screenshot places Prince Herring in Morven, Brooks County, Georgia, still farming, with wife Laura and daughters Minnie, Cazzy, Alice, and Fannie in the household. That record supports continuity of the family in Brooks County after 1900.
  • The user-supplied 1920 census screenshot places Prince and Laura Herring in Morven, Brooks County, Georgia, with daughters Sudie, Alice, and Fannie still at home. That record extends the household trail to 1920.
  • The user-supplied 1870 census screenshot shows an eleven-year-old Prince Herring in Militia District 1157, Berrien County, Georgia, in a household headed by Willian Herring and Pheraby Herring. That is a strong candidate earlier household for HH#38.
  • The user-supplied 1880 census screenshot places Prince Herring, age 21, in District 1146, Berrien County, Georgia, single and working in turpentine. That record is consistent with a pre-marriage Prince Herring in the same general county area.
  • The user-supplied 1880 census screenshot for Laura Sharpe places a fifteen-year-old Laura Sharpe in Quitman, Brooks County, Georgia, as daughter in the household of Margarette Sharpe. That is a strong candidate pre-marriage household for Prince Herring's wife.
  • The user-supplied Georgia death certificate for Prince Herring records that he died on 1 May 1924 in Morven District, Brooks County, Georgia, aged 60, married, a farmer, with father listed as Will Herring and mother as Feraby Herring. Taken cautiously, that death record materially strengthens the identification of the 1870 Willian and Pheraby Herring household as Prince's earlier family.
  • Taken together, the supplied census sequence supports a probable life-course trail from Berrien County in 1870 and 1880 to Brooks County in 1900, 1910, and 1920, while the death certificate adds later support for the Will/Feraby parent identification.
  • Positive FindAGrave memorials are cited for both Prince Herring and Laura Sharp Herring at Salem Missionary Baptist Church Cemetery in Pavo, Brooks County, Georgia. Those memorials are useful for burial placement and for pointing to underlying death-certificate references, but the linked relatives and memorial narrative text should remain secondary.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• The 1870 household strongly suggests that Prince was part of the Willian and Pheraby Herring household, and the 1924 death certificate supports that reading, but the parent identification still rests partly on informant-supplied death-record data and should be stated with ordinary caution.
  • The age pattern across the supplied censuses is not fully consistent. The 1870 and 1880 screenshots imply birth about 1859, the 1910 and 1920 screenshots imply birth about 1862 or 1863, while the 1900 screenshot reports Apr 1870 and the 1924 death certificate implies about 1864.
  • Laura's 1880 Sharpe household is a strong lead, but her maiden-name-to-married-name bridge would be stronger with a marriage record or death certificate.
  • The later child list is much stronger than before, but child-by-child direct support is still needed if the entry is expanded into a fuller family reconstruction.
  • Laura Herring's later life still lacks a directly supplied death certificate in this file, even though the memorial provides a strong burial lead.

docs.text:
• Status: Strongly documented household; not yet fully source-exhausted.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Head: George R. Duggan, age 48 in 1900, born Nov 1856 in Georgia, sawyer in a saw mill
  • Wife: Mary "Mollie" Duggan, age 19 in 1900, born Apr 1881 in Georgia

  • Child in the 1900 household: William Duggan, age 1

  • The user-supplied 1900 census image places George R. Duggan in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, as a white sawyer in a saw mill.

  • That 1900 household includes wife Mollie Duggan and son William Duggan, age 1.
  • The same 1900 record reports that George was born in Nov 1856 in Georgia, had been married four years, and was living in a rented house rather than on a farm.
  • The 1900 record also reports that George's father and mother were both born in Georgia and that George could read, write, and speak English.
  • The user-supplied 1870 census screenshot places George Duggan, age 13, in Valdosta, Lowndes County, Georgia, in the household of Archelaes Duggan and Cardelia Duggan, with younger brother William Duggan; it also reports that George attended school.
  • The user-supplied 1880 census screenshot places George Duggan, age 23, in Valdosta, Lowndes County, Georgia, in the household of Arch Duggan and Delia Duggan, and reports George's occupation as carpenter.
  • The user-supplied 1860 census screenshot appears to place George Duggin, age 4, in Lowndes County, Georgia, in the household of Archibald Duggin and Cordelia Duggin, with younger brother William Duggin.
  • Taken together, the 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 census screenshots support a strong Duggan family chain for George across Lowndes County and later Brooks County, though the father's given name appears in variant forms.
  • User-supplied marriage-record images show a Colquitt County, Georgia, license for George Duggan and Mollie Duggan issued 8 Feb 1896, with the certificate stating that they were joined in matrimony on 9 Feb 1896.
  • A user-supplied Valdosta Times page dated 31 May 1890 appears to report that George Duggan had gotten into a difficulty with Wade Moore and suffered a severe hand cut and a stab near the collar bone that was said not to be serious.
  • User-supplied FindAGrave memorial screenshots support burial for George Duggan at Pleasant Grove Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery, Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia, with the memorial giving birth as 1 Nov 1856 and death as 4 Oct 1902.
  • User-supplied FindAGrave memorial screenshots also support burial for Mollie Duggan Windom in the same cemetery, with the memorial giving birth as 3 Apr 1881 and death as 3 Jun 1971.
  • A user-supplied Georgia death index screenshot for Mollie D. Windom reports death on 3 Jun 1971 in Colquitt County, Georgia, at age 90, with certificate number 014896.
  • User-supplied census screenshots trace Mollie after her second marriage to John A. Windom or Windham in Moultrie, Colquitt County, through 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950.
  • The 1910 census screenshot shows John A. Windham, wife Mollie Windham, son Aubry Windham, stepson Willie Duggan, and stepdaughter Carrie Duggan, which supports Carrie as a child of Mollie's first Duggan marriage even though she was not present in the 1900 household screenshot.
  • The 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 census screenshots continue Mollie under the Windom or Windham surname in Moultrie and are broadly consistent with the memorial's later death record.
  • A user-supplied 1880 census index screenshot appears to place Martha Duggin, age 2, in Lower Fork, Lowndes County, Georgia, in the household of John Duggin and Nancy J. Duggin. That record is consistent with the FindAGrave memorial's later identification of Mollie Duggan Windom as a daughter of John Duggan and Nancy Jane Weldon Turner.
  • A user-supplied 1922 Colquitt County death certificate for John Duggan places him in Moultrie, identifies him as a married white male age 70, names his wife as Nancy Duggan, and records burial at Pleasant Grove. That certificate strengthens the case that the John Duggan and Nancy Duggan couple remained in the same Colquitt County setting later associated with Mollie.
  • The preserved Brooks County FindAGrave search was negative, which is consistent with the burial evidence pointing instead to Colquitt County.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• The current file now preserves user-supplied images for the 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900 census entries. The newly supplied 1880 page image strengthens the preserved record trail, though the entry still needs full source citations for each census record.
  • The current file also now preserves user-supplied images for the Colquitt County marriage license and certificate, but a full source citation should still be added.
  • The burial documentation in Colquitt County is still not preserved here by direct image.
  • The 31 May 1890 newspaper item should be re-read directly from the page image or clipping before relying on every word of the OCR extraction.
  • George's month and year of birth are supported by the 1900 census screenshot, and the FindAGrave memorial provides a specific birth and death date plus cemetery location, but those memorial details remain secondary unless backed by a stone reading, death record, or cemetery register.
  • Mollie's later death is now supported by both the FindAGrave memorial screenshot and a Georgia death index entry, and the later Windom or Windham census chain is consistent with them, though the full death certificate would still be the stronger record.
  • The Martha Duggin index entry remains a useful lead for Mollie's pre-marriage household, but the underlying 1880 census image is still preferable for fully settled proof.
  • John Duggan's 1922 death certificate supports the existence of the John and Nancy Duggan couple in Colquitt County, but it does not by itself prove that Martha Duggin of the 1880 household and Mollie Duggan Windom were the same person.
  • The linked relatives and child listings on FindAGrave are derivative and should be treated as clues unless confirmed by direct records.
  • William Duggan is supported in 1900 and as Willie Duggan in the 1910 Windham household.
  • Carrie Duggan is not present in the 1900 household screenshot, but the 1910 Windham household does support her as Mollie's stepdaughter from the earlier Duggan marriage.
  • The current file does not preserve George's 1910 absence by reason of death through a direct death certificate, obituary, probate record, or cemetery record.
  • The old draft's broader socioeconomic and community-role framing went beyond the present source set and should stay out unless stronger direct records are added.

  • Child census audit: confirm every child named in the 1900 household against later census, marriage, death, obituary, cemetery, probate, or draft records; separate proven child links from same-name candidates.

docs.text:
• Status: Strongly documented and close to complete, but not fully source-exhausted.
  • Strengths: George is now supported by a four-census chain, a direct marriage record, a likely 1890 newspaper item, and burial-level evidence in Colquitt County. Mollie is supported by a long later-life census chain, memorial evidence, and a Georgia death-index entry. Willie and Carrie are both supported through the later Windham household.
  • Remaining cautions: The main missing item is a direct death-side record for George. Mollie's pre-marriage identification as Martha Duggin remains a strong but not fully closed identification until the full 1880 household image is tied down more precisely. Cemetery-register or stone-level confirmation would also strengthen the burial side.

  • User-supplied census detail screenshots now trace Walton or Walter Edenfield across 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930, with expected spelling variation between Edenfield and Edinfield.
  • The 1860 screenshot places Walton Edenfield, age 1, in Berrien County, Georgia, post office Nashville, in the household of Oscar Edenfield and Mary Edenfield.
  • The 1870 screenshot places Walton Edinfield, age 12, in Militia District 518, Berrien County, Georgia, in the household of Oscar and Mary Edinfield, with occupation listed as farm laborer.
  • The 1880 screenshot places Walton Edinfield, age 21, in District 518, Berrien County, Georgia, in the household of Mary Edinfield, working on a farm.
  • The user-supplied 1900 census detail screenshot places Walton C. Edenfield as a 42-year-old single boarder, born January 1858, in James McMillen's Barney household.
  • The 1910 screenshot places Walter C. Edenfield, age 50, in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, on Main Street as a married merchant in general merchandise, living with wife Susie Edenfield and daughter Susie B. Edenfield in an owned free home.
  • The 1920 screenshot places W. C. Edenfield, age 61, in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, as a married farmer on his own farm, living with wife Susie and children Susie B., Annie Laura, Willie Ray, and Eddie Hazel Edenfield.
  • The 1930 screenshot places Water C. Edinfield, age 70, in Militia District 1571, Brooks County, Georgia, on South Rail Road Avenue, living on a farm with wife Susie and children Annie L., Willie R., and Hazel Edinfield.
  • A user-supplied 1930 Georgia death-certificate screenshot for Walter C. Edenfield reports that he died on 27 Apr 1930 in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, at age 70 years 11 months 10 days; identifies him as a married white male farmer; names his wife as Susie Edenfield; names his father as Oscar Edenfield and his mother as Mary Henderson; and records burial at Mount Zion Cemetery on 27 Apr 1930.
  • A user-supplied FindAGrave memorial screenshot for Walter C. Edenfield shows a gravestone shared with Susie A. Edenfield, gives birth as 7 May 1859 and death as 27 Apr 1930, and identifies the burial place as Camp Ground Cemetery Mount Zion Church, Morven, Brooks County, Georgia. The memorial image usefully preserves stone text and burial-place wording, though linked relatives remain derivative.
  • A user-supplied family-record page identifies Walter C. Edinfield as the son of Mary Henderson Edinfield and Oscar Edinfield, gives his birth date as 7 May 1859, states that he married Susie Berryhill on 12 Oct 1904, and names four children: Susie B. Edinfield, born 12 Feb 1910; Annie Laura Edinfield, born 11 Aug 1914; Willie Ray Edinfield, born 8 Oct 1918; and Hazel Edinfield, born 11 Nov 1920.
  • A user-supplied 1987 obituary for W. Ray Edenfield states that he was born 8 Oct 1917 in Barney, Georgia, to the late Walter and Susie B. (Berryhill) Edenfield; died in Licking Memorial Hospital; was a retired insurance agent and World War II veteran; was living at 206 Granville Street; and was survived by wife Ida Ruth McDonald Edenfield, daughter Ruth Sharpe, sister Hazel Victor of Tampa, and two grandchildren. The obituary also reports burial in Maple Grove Cemetery, Granville, Ohio.
  • A user-supplied 1 May 1930 Valdosta Daily Times death notice reports that W. C. Edenfield of Barney died Saturday morning at an early hour after several months of ill health and only one day confined to bed; had made his home in Barney for the past 36 years; was described as a faithful church worker and a member of the Church of Christ for the past 22 years; and had funeral services at the Camp Ground on Sunday afternoon at 4:30 o'clock with Rev. Mr. Chapman officiating. The notice names his survivors as his widow and four children: Miss Sue Edenfield of Jacksonville, Miss Annie Laurie Edenfield, Miss Hazel Edenfield, and son Ray Edenfield of Barney. It also names two sisters, Mrs. J. J. Goodman of Brookfield and Mrs. R. C. Roberts of Ocilla.
  • Taken together, those user-supplied census screenshots support a strong multi-decade identity chain for the boarder later seen as Walter C. Edenfield in Brooks County.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Head: Emery Manns, age 21 in 1900, born Jul 1878 in Georgia
  • Wife: Dallis Manns, age 18 in 1900, born in Georgia

  • Other household member: George Manns, father, age 55 in 1900

  • The 1900 census places Emery Manns in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, on sheet 3, dwelling 45, family 45, as a sawmill laborer in a rented household with wife Dallis Manns and widowed father George Manns. The same record gives Emery's birth month as Jul 1878 and reports that he could read, write, and speak English.

  • The present file now preserves a strong continuity chain showing that the 1900 Emery Manns household is the same family later recorded under the surname Manus.
  • In Jackson County, Georgia, Emry Manus and Dallis Tolbert were licensed to marry on 26 Oct 1897 and were married on 27 Oct 1897; the marriage was recorded on 20 Dec 1897. That record directly anchors the couple before the 1900 Barney household.
  • A 1910 census record in Jackson County, Georgia, shows Emory Manus, age 31, with wife Dallis and children including Maud, Grover, John, Adelle, and Willie. The age, wife, and child pattern fit the 1900 Barney household.
  • A 1920 census record in Barrow County, Georgia, shows H. E. Manus, age 41, farming with wife Dallis and children including Grover, John, Adell, Willie, Mildred, Walter, and Marielle. A 1930 Barrow County census continues the same family under the name Emory Manus.
  • Hugh Emory Manus's World War I draft registration card gives his full name as Hugh Emory Manus, birth date 6 Jul 1878, residence Winder, Georgia, occupation farmer, and nearest relative Dalloe Manus. That card ties the later Manus records to the same birth date and spouse line seen in the Barney household.
  • Hugh Emory Manus's Georgia death certificate shows that he died 18 Mar 1939 in Athens, Clarke County, Georgia, while residing in Winder, Barrow County, Georgia. The certificate names his parents as George Manus and Mary Timbs Manus and his burial place as Chapel Cemetery in Winder.
  • The 19 Mar 1939 Atlanta Constitution obituary for Mr. H. E. Manus names his widow, children, siblings, funeral at Chapel church, and burial in Chapel cemetery. Dallas Manus's 11 Jul 1966 Atlanta Constitution obituary continues the same Winder-centered family and names the adult children.
  • Taken together, the marriage record, 1900 census, later censuses, draft card, death certificate, and obituaries support the conclusion that Emery Manns, Emry Manus, Emory Manus, H. E. Manus, and Hugh Emory Manus were the same person.
  • FindAGrave memorials for Hugh Emory Manus and Dallas Manus agree with the death and burial evidence, but they remain derivative support rather than primary proof.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• Full citation details should still be preserved for the 1910, 1920, and 1930 census entries if not already extracted elsewhere.
  • The Manns-to-Manus shift is now well supported by cumulative evidence, but the change should still be described from the records themselves rather than treated as a simple spelling preference.
  • The death certificate names George Manus and Mary Timbs Manus as parents, but the certificate does not give their birthplaces.
  • FindAGrave family links are useful as clues and burial support, not as stand-alone proof of each child relationship.
  • Additional land, probate, church, or cemetery records could strengthen the Winder and Chapel church context, but the present file already preserves the core identity chain.

docs.title: Household #46: Hall, John Byron
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

Under review: One or more details on this page conflict with an inspected source record. Corrections are being prepared.

In the 1900 Barney census, J B Hall headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
J B Hall headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

J B Hall's listed occupation was Saw Milliner.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text:
This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

  • 1904 social notice: A 14 Feb 1904 Savannah Morning News Quitman column reported that Mrs. J. B. Hall and her little daughter, of Barney, were visiting relatives in Eatonton. That fits Lula S. Collingsworth Hall's Eatonton/Putnam County family background and confirms the John B. Hall household's Barney residence after the 1900 census.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation J B Hall Head 36 Georgia Saw Milliner Lula S Hall Wife 36 Georgia — Sarah C Hall Daughter 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: Later records support the daughter’s identity beyond the 1900 census. Sarah C. Hall appears as Sarah Hall in 1910 and Caroline Hall in 1920, 1930, and 1940. A preserved Brooks County marriage record identifies her as Sarah Caroline Hall when she married Zack Taylor Williams in 1945.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Head: John B. Hall, recorded in 1900 as J. B. Hall, age 36, born Oct 1863 in Georgia, working in a saw mill
  • Wife: Lula S. Hall, age 36 in 1900, born in Georgia

  • Child: Sarah C. Hall, age 1 in 1900, born about 1899 in Georgia

  • The 1900 census places J. B. Hall in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, on sheet 3, dwelling 46, family 46, with wife Lula S. Hall and daughter Sarah C. Hall. That record states that John and Lula had been married about three years, that John was born in Oct 1863 in Georgia, and that he worked in a saw mill.

  • The Hall household remains in Barney through the next four federal censuses. In 1910, John B. Hall and Lula S. Hall appear in Barney with daughter Sarah Hall. In 1920, J. B. Hall and Lula Hall appear there with daughter Caroline Hall. In 1930, John B. Hall and Lula C. Hall remain in Brooks County with daughter Caroline Hall. In 1940, J. B. Hall, then widowed, was still living in Barney with daughter Caroline Hall, and the census reports that he had also lived in Barney in 1935.
  • The daughter line is consistent across these records. The child recorded as Sarah C. Hall in 1900 is recorded as Sarah Hall in 1910 and as Caroline Hall in 1920, 1930, and 1940. The preserved Brooks County marriage record for Sarah Caroline Hall and Zack Taylor Williams on 22 Nov 1945 provides the direct bridge to the 1946 obituary survivor Mrs. Z. T. Williams of Barney.
  • The earlier Hall identification is also well anchored. In 1880, J. Bryon Hall, age 17, appears in Township 6, Fairfield County, South Carolina, explicitly identified as the son of John F. Hall and Sarah P. Hall. A likely earlier 1870 Fairfield County census entry for Byron Hall, age 8, fits the same household line. This creates a possible bridge to HH#1, but it should remain unresolved unless the John F. Hall of the 1880 South Carolina household can be proved to be the same man as the John P. Hall recorded in the 1900 Barney census, or unless the 1900 middle initial is shown to be an enumerator error.
  • John B. Hall and Lula S. Collingsworth were licensed to marry in Bibb County, Georgia, on 13 Jun 1896, were married on 18 Jun 1896 by J. W. Roberts, M.G., and the marriage was recorded on 23 Jun 1896. A notice in the Macon Telegraph dated 21 Jun 1896 reported that the wedding took place in Atlanta at the residence or parsonage of Dr. J. W. Roberts of Trinity Church and described Lula as a popular school teacher from Eatonton.
  • A 1904 Savannah Morning News Quitman social column gives a useful small bridge between the Barney household and Lula's Eatonton background: it says Mrs. J. B. Hall and her little daughter, of Barney, were in Eatonton visiting relatives. The item does not name Lula or Sarah Caroline directly, but it fits the 1900 household and the known Eatonton Collingsworth line.
  • Lula's earlier family placement is supported by both the 1870 and 1880 censuses in Eatonton, Putnam County, Georgia. In 1870, Loula S. Colinsworth, age 5, appears in the household of Thos. Colinsworth and Sarah C. Colinsworth. In 1880, L. S. Collinsworth, age 16, is explicitly identified as their daughter in the household of T. M. Collinsworth and S. C. Collinsworth. A Georgia marriage index entry showing Thomas M. Collingsworth and Sarah Mattox married in Morgan County in 1855 fits that parental line.
  • Lula Hall's 1930 Georgia death certificate shows that Mrs. J. B. Hall died 11 May 1930 in Valdosta, Lowndes County, Georgia, at age 66 years, 2 months, and 26 days. The certificate identifies her as a married white female, born in Georgia, wife of J. B. Hall, daughter of Thomas M. Collingsworth and Sarah C. Maddox, resident of Barney, Georgia, and buried at Camp Ground, Brooks County, Georgia. The informant appears to be J. B. Hall of Barney.
  • John B. Hall's 1946 obituary in the Valdosta Daily Times identifies him as an 82-year-old well-known Barney resident whose funeral was held at Camp Ground Methodist Church. The obituary describes him as a farmer, longtime rural letter carrier, and former South Georgia Railroad conductor. It names as survivors daughter Mrs. Z. T. Williams of Barney, brother W. N. Hall of Boston, Georgia, and sisters Mrs. R. L. Lacy and Mrs. W. W. Avera of St. Petersburg, Florida.
  • That railroad-conductor obituary makes John B. Hall a strong candidate for the 14 Oct 1899 Valdosta Times reference to conductor "J. F. Hall" on the South Georgia Railroad. The match is not confirmed because the 1899 initials differ, but the age, railroad, and Barney/Adel setting fit John B. Hall better than the older John P./John F. Hall lead in HH#1.
  • A Georgia Death Index entry for John B. Hall records his death on 17 Apr 1946 in Brooks County, Georgia, at age 82 and gives certificate number 6941. That index entry matches the obituary date and age.
  • FindAGrave memorials for John Byron Hall and Lula S. Collingsworth Hall agree with the reported death dates, spouse pairing, and Camp Ground burial tradition. Those memorials are useful supporting evidence, but they remain derivative.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • HH#1 John P./John F. Hall lead: Possible connection only. The 1880 census explicitly identifies J. Bryon Hall as the son of John F. Hall and Sarah P. Hall, but the 1900 Barney census currently reads HH#1 as John P. Hall with wife Martha. That could still be reconciled through an initial error and a later spouse, but the present evidence does not prove the bridge.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• No death certificate for John B. Hall has been found. The current death evidence therefore rests on the Georgia Death Index entry and the 1946 obituary, which align on date, age, and place.
  • The preserved daughter bridge is now supported by an image-level Brooks County marriage record for Sarah Caroline Hall and Zack Taylor Williams, but the entry would still benefit from a fuller citation or cleaner archival copy if one is later available.
  • The 1920 census reports John B. Hall's birthplace as South Carolina, while other later records in this chain generally point to Georgia. Given the stable household, spouse, daughter, age range, and location, this reads as a single-record inconsistency rather than a break in identity.
  • Collinsworth appears in preserved records with several spellings, including Colinsworth, Collinsworth, and Collingsworth. The variation should be treated as normal record-level surname drift, not as evidence of separate families.
  • A prior reading in this project treated Lula's burial as Sunset Hill in Valdosta, but the death certificate image itself reads Camp Ground, Brooks County. The Camp Ground reading should control unless a stronger contrary record appears.
  • An Ancestry military entry for Thomas Collingsworth currently carries conflicting Union-coded indexing fields and should remain only a misindex lead until the original card and unit context are verified.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: confirm both parents of the household head for HH#46 through direct or near-direct records where possible; mark derivative-only parent links as unresolved until supported.
  • Child census audit: confirm every child named in the 1900 household against later census, marriage, death, obituary, cemetery, probate, or draft records; separate proven child links from same-name candidates.
  • Other household member audit: verify boarders, servants, in-laws, stepchildren, grandchildren, and unrelated residents in HH#46; document the exact relationship instead of assuming kinship.
  • Spouse and marriage audit: locate marriage records, death records, divorce records, or later census records for spouses or absent spouses tied to this household.
  • Direct image review: re-check the 1900 census image and any cited index-only sources before treating ages, relationships, birthplaces, or name spellings as final.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Well-supported household with a strong multi-record identity chain. The possible Hall-family connection to HH#1 remains unresolved.
  • Strengths: The entry now preserves a six-decade census chain for John Byron Hall, direct parent-child anchoring in the 1880 Hall household, direct marriage evidence for John B. Hall and Lula S. Collingsworth, solid parental placement for Lula through 1870 and 1880 censuses plus her death certificate, and a clear survivor bridge from daughter Sarah Caroline Hall to Mrs. Z. T. Williams.
  • Remaining cautions: No death certificate for John B. Hall has been found, so the death case currently rests on the aligned death-index and obituary evidence. The connection to HH#1 is not proven, and fuller archival citation detail for the Sarah Caroline Hall–Zack Taylor Williams marriage record would also be useful if later available.

docs.text:

In the 1900 Barney census, Thomas H Hawkins headed a 6-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Thomas H Hawkins headed a 6-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner, 3 children, and 1 extended-family member.

Thomas H Hawkins's listed occupation was Carpenter.

Reported birthplaces span Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Thomas H Hawkins Head 55 Georgia Carpenter Julia Hawkins Wife 42 North Carolina — James Hawkins Son 18 South Carolina Carpenter Benjiman Hawkins Son 14 South Carolina — Lillie Hawkins Daughter 5 Florida — Clara Ragan Mother-in-law 62 North Carolina —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• 1900 Barney household: Thomas H. Hawkins, age 55, born Aug 1844 in Georgia, was the head of household in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, working as a carpenter. His wife Julia, age 42, was born in North Carolina. Their household included sons James, 18, and Benjiman, 14, daughter Lillie, 5, and Julia's mother Clara Ragan, 62. The census shows that Thomas and Julia had been married about nine years, pointing to an 1891 marriage year, and that Thomas's parents were both reported as born in North Carolina.
  • Likely continuation after 1900: The strongest post-1900 chain now runs through a Duval County, Florida marriage record and two later census households. A user-supplied Duval County marriage record shows Henry Hawkins and Julia Leslie licensed on 17 Oct 1891 and married on 18 Oct 1891. The date matches the 1900 Barney census marriage fields almost exactly. In 1910, a Turner County, Georgia household shows Henry T. Hawkins, 64, with wife Julia and daughter Lillian; the age progression, wife's name, daughter's name, and parental-birth pattern fit the 1900 Barney family well. In 1920, Thomas Hawkins, 76, appears in Jacksonville, Duval County, Florida, with wife Julia. Taken together, these records make it likely that the 1900 Barney household, the 1910 Turner household, and the 1920 Jacksonville household represent the same family, even though the husband's name shifts between Thomas and Henry in the record trail.
  • Julia's likely natal family: Julia appears tied to the Ragan or Regan family. In 1900 her mother Clara Ragan was in the Hawkins household. An 1860 Wilcox County, Georgia census shows Julia E. Ragans, age 4, in the household of Timothy S. Ragans and Clara J. Ragans. An 1870 Columbus County, North Carolina census shows Julia Regan, 13, with Clancy J. Regan and siblings Robert A., James R., Sarah E., and Wesley J. The name forms vary, but the age pattern, North Carolina birthplace, and the reappearance of Clara Ragan in 1900 make this a strong working reconstruction.
  • Ragan sibling cluster: The same reconstruction likely extends to Robert A. Ragan or Regan, James R. Ragan, Wesley J. Ragan, and Sarah E. Ragan, later Sarah E. Green. The Florida and Georgia follow-forward records for those siblings fit the 1870 household reasonably well, but this part of the family remains less secure than the core 1900-1920 Hawkins chain.
  • Same-name deconfliction, Henry Hawkins with Lydia Story: The 1870 Worth County Henry Hawkins household with wife Lidda and child William, and the 1880 Worth County Henry T. Hawkins household with wife Lydia A. and children William A. and Susan A., should not be merged into HH#47 on current evidence. That line is supported by an 1867 Dooly County marriage index for H. T. Hawkins and L. A. Story, by Lydia's Find a Grave memorial naming her first husband as Henry T. "Jack" Hawkins, and by Lydia's death certificate, which names her as Susan A. Hawkins Leonard and identifies her as a Story by birth. The child set, spouse identity, occupation pattern, and the 1880 report that Henry's mother was born in South Carolina all point away from the Barney household.
  • Same-name deconfliction, Wellborn or Suwannee Thomas Henry Hawkins: The Wellborn, Florida burial trail also appears to belong to a different man. The headstone application for Thomas Henry Hawkins, born 3 Feb 1845 and died 29 Nov 1919, places him at Little River near Wellborn, Florida, and ties him to a Florida Confederate unit. That record fits the separate Suwannee County line with wife Sarah J., not the Barney household with wife Julia.
  • 1909 Florida newspaper lead: A user-supplied page from The Florida Star dated 2 Jul 1909 appears to correspond to the previously indexed Julia Hawkins or Ragan thank-you-card notice. Because the page has not yet been fully transcribed, it is best treated as a lead that supports the family's Florida orbit rather than as a fully extracted proof item.
  • Early Thomas Hawkins lead: A user-supplied 1850 Dooly County census image shows a Thomas Hawkins, age 5, in the household of Benjamin and Malissa Hawkins. The age is compatible with the HH#47 Thomas H. Hawkins, but no direct bridge has yet been found, so this remains a lead rather than a settled identification.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • No direct connection to another numbered Barney household is proved in the present evidence.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• The 1900, 1910, and 1920 records together make a persuasive continuation chain, but the identity is not yet closed by a death certificate, obituary, probate file, or another explicit bridge that names the same man across the Thomas and Henry forms.
  • Julia's maiden-name bridge is strong at the marriage record level, but her later-life death record has not yet been added. A death certificate, obituary, or probate item naming her as Julia Leslie or Julia Ragan would tighten the case further.
  • The Ragan or Regan sibling reconstruction is useful and probably right, but it still rests on a mix of census continuity and later index-level follow-forward work. It should remain provisional until more image-level or vital-record support is added.
  • The 1909 Florida Star thank-you-card item still needs a full transcription.
  • The 1850 Thomas Hawkins in the Benjamin and Malissa Hawkins household remains only a possible early-life lead.
  • Negative search result worth preserving: no Brooks County Find a Grave memorial has yet been found for the HH#47 Hawkins household.

  • Other household member audit: verify boarders, servants, in-laws, stepchildren, grandchildren, and unrelated residents in HH#47; document the exact relationship instead of assuming kinship.
  • Spouse and marriage audit: locate marriage records, death records, divorce records, or later census records for spouses or absent spouses tied to this household.

docs.text:
• Status: Substantially upgraded, but not source-exhausted.
  • Strengths: The 1900 Barney household is well anchored, the 1891 Duval marriage record matches the census marriage signal closely, the 1910 Turner and 1920 Jacksonville households fit the same family well, and the major same-name collisions have been sorted more carefully than before.
  • Remaining cautions: The husband's Thomas/Henry name variation still needs a terminal proof item, Julia's later-life record set remains thin, and the wider Ragan kin reconstruction should stay marked as provisional.

docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Edward Bridges headed a 5-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Edward Bridges headed a 5-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner, 1 child, and 2 boarders, employees, servants, or other non-kin residents.

Edward Bridges's listed occupation was Manager At Saw Mill.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Edward Bridges Head 28 Georgia Manager At Saw Mill Eva Bridges Wife 28 Georgia — Nina Bridges Daughter 1 Georgia — John Sharp Boarder 26 Georgia Laborer At Saw Mill James Sharp Boarder 16 Georgia Going to School

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney census shows the HH#48 head as Edward Bridges, age 28, born in Georgia in March 1872, working as a manager at saw mill. His household included wife Eva Bridges, daughter Nina Bridges, and boarders John Sharp and James Sharp.
  • A brief Valdosta Times item from August 1899 refers to "Mr. E. C. Bridges, of Barney," which helps place the same man in Barney just before the 1900 census.
  • The 1880 census in Dooly County places Edwin Bridges, age 11, in the household of J. W. Bridges and Lidia Bridges, with brother Benjamine Bridges also present. That record strongly supports treating HH#48 Edwin/Edward Bridges as part of the same sibling group as HH#19 Benjamin F. Bridges.
  • The 1910 census in Quitman shows Eva Bridger, widow, age 42, as head of household with children Nina Bridger (11), Bessie Bridger (8), E. C. Bridger (6), and Eddie R. Bridger (infant). The same household also includes Rachel Sharpe, identified as Eva's mother, and Jim Sharpe, identified as her brother. That record strongly supports the Sharp family connection and helps bridge the 1900 Barney household to the post-1909 widow household.
  • FindAGrave memorials identify the couple as Edward Caleb Bridges and Susan Evaline Sharp Bridges, buried at Oak Hill Cemetery, Quitman, Brooks County, Georgia, with death dates of 24 Nov 1909 and 24 Jan 1913. Those memorials also identify children including Nina Lee Bridges Wingate and Edward Caleb Bridges Jr. These details are useful derivative support, but they are not the same as direct vital-record proof.
  • A preserved portrait attributed to E. C. Bridges appears to carry the inscription "Yours truly, E C Bridges." This supports the use of the initials E. C. for the HH#48 head, but it remains derivative identification evidence.
  • Newspaper coverage from 1901, 1906, and 1909 ties E. C. Bridges directly to the Oglesby lumber and timber ventures around Quitman. A 1901 Savannah Morning News item reports a large land purchase by Messrs. Oglesby & Bro. and E. C. Bridges involving the Hunter tract northwest of Quitman, with plans for a large mill in North Quitman. A 1906 Valdosta Daily Times article reports construction of the Oglesby & Bridges tram road to the Hunter timber. A 1909 Valdosta Daily Times item reports that the Hunter tract cutting was nearing completion and that the Oglesby mill would begin cutting timber in Taylor County, Florida, adding that the Messrs. Oglesby and Bridges were large holders in the Interstate Lumber Company.
  • The 29 Nov 1909 Valdosta Daily Times obituary for E. C. Bridges states that he died at his home in Quitman on Wednesday afternoon after several weeks of illness with typhoid fever and other complications. It describes him as born in Dooly County, coming to Brooks County about fifteen years earlier, first settling at Barney, later moving to Quitman, becoming associated with the Oglesby sawmill business, serving as manager of the Oglesby Lumber Co., holding interests in other enterprises in Quitman and Florida, and serving on Quitman's board of aldermen.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • HH#19 Benjamin F. Bridges: The 1880 Dooly County household of J. W. Bridges and Lidia Bridges includes both Benjamine Bridges and Edwin Bridges, strongly supporting the conclusion that HH#19 Benjamin F. Bridges and HH#48 Edwin/Edward/E. C. Bridges were brothers.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• The record set supports the identity chain Edwin Bridges (1880) → E. C. Bridges (1899 newspapers) → Edward Bridges (1900 census) → E. C. Bridges (1901-1909 newspapers and obituary), but the exact full-name expansion to Edward Caleb Bridges still rests primarily on derivative memorial material rather than a newly checked marriage or death certificate.
  • The 1900 census screenshot reads the wife as Eva Bridges, while the memorial material gives her fuller name as Susan Evaline Sharp Bridges. The 1910 widow household with Rachel Sharpe as mother and Jim Sharpe as brother makes that identification plausible, but a direct marriage record has not been recovered in this pass.
  • No online marriage record, death certificate, or cemetery register has yet been located for Edwin/Edward Caleb Bridges or Susan Evaline Sharp Bridges. Those items remain desirable, but they now look more like courthouse, archive, or cemetery-office targets than realistic online-only gaps.
  • The 1910 widow household reports five children born, four living, while only four surviving children appear in the home. Additional follow-forward work on Bessie, E. C., and Eddie R. Bridges would strengthen the later family reconstruction.
  • The business narrative is now supported by newspapers and the obituary, but it should still be framed narrowly: Bridges was clearly involved in the Oglesby lumber and timber ventures, yet broader claims about a coordinated multi-household lumber "dynasty" go beyond the present evidence.

Reported birthplaces span Georgia and North Carolina, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William Eatman Head 41 North Carolina Laborer Saw Mill Laura Eatman Wife 18 North Carolina — Ida Eatman Daughter 11 Georgia — Walter A Eatman Son 9 Georgia — Cora Lee Eatman Daughter 6 Georgia — Isa Eatman Son 2 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney census shows William Eatman, age 41, born in North Carolina, as head of HH#49 and working as a laborer at a saw mill. James's review of the original image confirms that Eatman is the surname for the whole household despite muddy index/transcription readings. The household included wife Laura Eatman and children Ida, Walter, Cora Lee, and Isa/Asa Eatman.
  • The 1910 census in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, shows William M. Eatman, age 51, as a farmer, with wife Laura and children Walter G., Cora L., and Ethel G. in the home. That record provides strong continuity from the 1900 Barney household and shows that Laura was still living in 1910.
  • The 1920 census in Barney shows W. M. Eatman with wife Mary Eatman and mother-in-law J. W. Rouse in the household. That record strongly supports the identification of William's second wife as Mary Rouse and shows that he remained in Barney as a farmer after Laura's death.
  • A Lowndes County marriage record shows William M. Eatman and Mary Rouse receiving a marriage license on 31 Aug 1915 and marrying on 5 Sept 1915. This directly anchors the second marriage.
  • William's Georgia death certificate identifies him as William Mann Eatman, white, married, age 63, born in North Carolina, and employed as a farmer. He died at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, on 5 Jan 1922 of Bright's disease. The certificate names wife Mary Eatman, gives Walter Eatman of Pavo as informant, and states burial at Camp Ground on 6 Jan 1922. It was filed 14 Jan 1922 and handled by J. H. Culpepper & Son.
  • FindAGrave memorials for William Eatman and Laura Eatman place both at Camp Ground Cemetery, Mount Zion Church, Morven, Brooks County, Georgia. Those memorials are useful derivative support for burial location and for Laura's reported death date of 10 Aug 1912, but they are not the same as direct vital-record proof.
  • The earlier census chain is now reasonably strong. In 1860, William Eatmon, age 2, appears in Nahunta District, Wayne County, North Carolina, in the household of Burtis Eatmon and Polly Eatmon. In 1870, a likely match appears as William Eatmond, age 12, still in Wayne County. In 1880, William Eatman, age 22, appears in Great Swamp Township, Wayne County, North Carolina, single and working as a laborer on a farm. Taken together, these records strongly support treating HH#49 William Eatman as a Wayne County, North Carolina native.
  • Laura's pre-marriage chain is also workable. A likely 1870 census entry appears in Columbus County, North Carolina, as Lanna Phillips, age 8, in the household of Asa Phillips and Jennett Phillips. By 1880, Laura Phillips, age 17, appears clearly in Appling County, Georgia, as daughter of Asa Phillips and Jeanette Phillips. A Georgia marriage index then supports a marriage between William Mann Eatman and Laura R. Phillips in 1883, consistent with the later household timeline.
  • Mary Eatman's later-life trail is visible after William's death. The 1940 and 1950 censuses place widowed Mary Eatman in Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, in the household of Hattie Fields, where Mary is identified as sister. Those records strengthen the case that Mary Rouse Eatman survived William by decades and remained connected to her own family network.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • No proven cross-household tie established: Earlier suggestions about a possible lateral connection from this household into the Knight family remain outside the proved claim set until direct marriage or death records support them.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• The evidence now supports the core identity chain William Eatmon/Eatmond/Eatman (1860-1880 North Carolina) → William Eatman (1900 Barney) → William M. Eatman (1910-1922 Brooks County). Even so, the exact parent identification should still be stated from the census chain, not as something proven by the death certificate, because the death certificate leaves both parents unknown.
  • The 1920 census gives William an age that points to a birth around 1851-1852, while the 1910 census and 1922 death certificate point more closely to 1858-1859. The 1920 age is best treated as a one-record error rather than a broken identity chain.
  • The exact marriage record image for William Eatman and Laura R. Phillips has not been recovered in this pass. The 1883 marriage is supported by an index entry and by the later census sequence, but it is not yet anchored by a checked county-level license or return.
  • Laura's FindAGrave memorial supports a death date of 10 Aug 1912 and burial at Camp Ground Cemetery, but a direct death record or cemetery register has not yet been added here. The earlier claim that she died in Miami, Florida should not be treated as established on the present evidence.
  • The entry now supports the census-proven children Ida, Walter G., Cora L., Isa/Asa, and Ethel G., but a complete child reconstruction beyond those directly observed household members remains unfinished. Earlier claims about additional children, exact birth dates, and later marriages or deaths should be treated as provisional unless separately documented.
  • The older version's claim that William spent time in Yarmouth, Hampshire, England is not supported by the records reviewed in this pass and should be omitted unless direct evidence turns up.
  • The prior lateral claim connecting daughter Ida Eatman to the Knight family may yet prove true, but it is not needed to establish HH#49 and should stay out of the main entry unless supported by direct marriage or death records.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: confirm both parents of the household head for HH#49 through direct or near-direct records where possible; mark derivative-only parent links as unresolved until supported.
  • Child census audit: confirm every child named in the 1900 household against later census, marriage, death, obituary, cemetery, probate, or draft records; separate proven child links from same-name candidates.
  • Other household member audit: verify boarders, servants, in-laws, stepchildren, grandchildren, and unrelated residents in HH#49; document the exact relationship instead of assuming kinship.
  • Spouse and marriage audit: locate marriage records, death records, divorce records, or later census records for spouses or absent spouses tied to this household.
  • Direct image review: re-check the 1900 census image and any cited index-only sources before treating ages, relationships, birthplaces, or name spellings as final.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Well-researched core household with several direct anchors.
  • What is solid: 1900, 1910, and 1920 census continuity; William's 1915 marriage to Mary Rouse; William's 1922 death certificate; derivative burial support for William and Laura; workable early census chains for both William and Laura.
  • Remaining cautions: The first marriage to Laura still needs a stronger county-level marriage record if one survives; Laura's death still lacks direct vital-record proof in this file; the full child list and later child follow-forward work remain incomplete.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
James Bailey headed a 6-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner, 3 children, and 1 extended-family member.

James Bailey's listed occupation was Farmer.

Reported birthplaces span Georgia, North Carolina, and Virginia, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation James Bailey Head 30 North Carolina Farmer Elsie Bailey Wife 26 Georgia — Festus Bailey Son 7 Georgia — Rosa Bailey Daughter 1 Georgia — Owen Bailey Son 3/12 Georgia — Hannah Flow Mother-in-law 68 Virginia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
James Bailey and Elsie Bailey were married in Brooks County on 1 Aug 1895. The marriage record gives her name as Elsie Flawnoy, while the 1900 census records her mother in the household as Hannah Flow. Taken together, those records support treating Flawnoy, Flow, and Flournoy as surname variants within the same family.

The 1900 census securely places this family in Barney. James was a North Carolina-born farmer who could read and write. Elsie was born in Georgia. Their household included three young children—Festus, Rosa, and infant Owen—and Hannah Flow, who is explicitly identified as James Bailey's mother-in-law. That relationship provides direct evidence that Elsie was Hannah's daughter.

By 1910, the family appears in Hamburg, Madison County, Florida. James Bailey, 39, and wife Elcy Bailey, 36, were still together, and the household included Festus, Rosa J., Owens W., and Carrie. James was working as a laborer in turpentine, showing a shift from the 1900 Barney farm household into Florida wage labor.

The Flournoy family network around HH#51 is supported by several records. In 1870, Polly Flournoy appears in the Brooks County household of John and Hannah Flournoy. In 1880, the same household includes Mary Flournoy, who may be the same person under a different everyday name. In 1900, Pollie Flournoy heads HH#185 in Barney. Her 1923 Brooks County death certificate names her mother as Hannah Flournoy. Those records support a documented Flournoy kin network in Brooks County and Barney, and they strengthen the connection between HH#51 and HH#185.

A 1920 Quitman household headed by Fess I. Bailey with wife Elcie and daughter Carrie likely represents the next generation rather than James Bailey's own household. Because the record was not tied to James directly, it is better treated as probable continuation of the family line rather than as firm evidence for James's later residence.

docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • The exact relationship between Pollie/Polly Flournoy of HH#185 and Elsie Bailey is strongly suggestive but not stated directly in the surviving records reviewed here.
  • The 1880 Mary Flournoy entry is likely the same person as the 1870 Polly Flournoy and the 1900 Pollie Flournoy, but that identification still rests on cumulative evidence rather than an explicit statement.
  • A 1930 James Bailey entry in Trenton, Mercer County, New Jersey, with daughter Rosa Williams may fit this household, but it should remain provisional unless bridged by stronger evidence.
  • No securely verified death record, burial record, or later-life record for James Bailey or Elsie Bailey has been preserved in this entry.

docs.text: Well-researched through the 1895 marriage record, the 1900 Barney household, the 1910 Madison County household, and the reconstructed Flournoy family network. Later Bailey-family continuity remains partial.

docs.title: Household #52: Shuman, Simon
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Simon Shewman headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Simon Shewman headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

Simon Shewman's listed occupation was Laborer Carpenter.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Simon Shewman Head 23 Georgia Laborer Carpenter Mary Shewman Wife 15 Georgia — Cilla Shewman Daughter 0 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Simon Shewman in Barney as a young carpenter with wife Mary and infant daughter Cilla. The surname appears in several forms across the surviving records, including Shewman, Shurman, Shuman, and Schooman, but the age pattern, household members, and locations support treating those entries as one family line.

In 1910, the family remained in Brooks County under the spelling Shurman. Simon, then 32, was still working as a carpenter. The household included wife Mollie and children whose names align closely with the 1900 family and its expected expansion, including Cilla, Will, Felia, Mary, Aron, and Simon. By 1920, the family appears in Albany, Dougherty County, where Simon Shuman, 47, worked as a driver in a wood yard and the household included Mary, sons Will, Aaron, Simon, and John M., daughter Ruth, and grandson Willie Jno. In 1930, Simon Schooman, 55, appears in Precinct 6, St. Johns County, Florida, with wife Mary and children John, Ruth, and Tinie. In 1940, Simon Shuman, 60, appears in Brunswick, Glynn County, with wife Carry and sons John, Henry, and Charles.

The 1880 census in Ways Station, Bryan County, includes a four-year-old Simon Shuman in the household of Simon and Cylar Shuman. That earlier household is a plausible and likely fit for HH#52, but the parentage link still rests on cumulative evidence rather than a direct later record naming those parents.

Contemporary newspaper coverage ties Simon Shuman to the Hampton Smith case in June 1918. The Tampa Tribune of 22 Jun 1918 reported that Simon Shuman, described as being from near Morven, had been arrested and lodged in the Brooks County jail at Quitman. The Macon News of 25 Jun 1918 and the Atlanta Constitution of 26 Jun 1918 then reported that he had been removed from the Quitman jail to an undisclosed jail for safe keeping so that he could face trial rather than mob violence. Those reports support the conclusion that Simon was arrested during the crisis and moved out of Quitman for his protection. They do not by themselves establish the final disposition of the case.

The 1900-1940 census chain makes a strong case for long-term continuity of this family through Brooks County, Albany, St. Johns County, and Brunswick. The later shift from wife Mary or Mollie to wife Carry in 1940 also suggests that Simon may have remarried, but that transition should not be treated as proved until supported by direct marriage or death records.

docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • A marriage record is still needed to document Simon's union with Mary or Mollie and to identify her maiden name securely.
  • The transition from Mary or Mollie in 1930 to Carry in 1940 likely reflects a later marriage, but the supporting marriage or death record has not yet been added here.
  • The 1880 Bryan County household of Simon and Cylar Shuman is a strong candidate for Simon's family of origin, but the parentage link remains inferential until a direct linking record is found.
  • The June 1918 newspaper reports document arrest and removal for safe keeping, but they do not show the final court disposition.
  • A 1950 Simon Shiman entry was reviewed but is not used here because the reported age does not fit the 1880-1940 chain.
  • A direct death certificate or similarly strong later-life record for Simon has not yet been integrated into this entry.

docs.text: Well-researched for the 1880-1940 census chain and the June 1918 newspaper coverage. Important gaps remain in Simon's marriage record, the transition from Mary or Mollie to Carry, and the final records for his later life.

docs.text:

docs.text:

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Eli Dukes Head 75 Georgia Farmer Hulda Dukes Wife 60 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
In the 1900 census, Eli Dukes appears in Barney, Brooks County, as a seventy-five-year-old Black farmer living with his wife Hulda. The census states that he owned his farm free of mortgage. That is the strongest household-level evidence now in hand and establishes both the residence and his status as a landholding farmer at the time of the census.

The 1890 Brooks County property tax digest also places Eli Dukes in Morven District and shows him taxed on 30 acres in Land Lot 278 of the 12th Land District, along with taxable personal property. Taken together with the 1900 census, that digest supports a cautious conclusion that Eli Dukes was a Black landholder in Brooks County before the 1900 enumeration. At present, however, the available evidence does not support broader claims about a long multi-decade employment network, unusual economic strategy, or a fuller reconstructed life history.

The tax and census entries are a probable continuity lead, not a completed identity or deed chain. The original tax row assesses the 30 acres at $150. That is a tax assessment, not a purchase price.

docs.title: Original-record checks: tax year and separate probate families
docs.text:
The tax-volume opening leaf is printed “1890”. In the same Brooks > 1890 viewer sequence, printed page 36, image 209 of 225, places Eli Dukes between John W. Sharp and Hattie Roberts in Morven militia district 660. His row reads 30 acres, lot 278, land district 12. The opening leaf supplies the year; the viewer sequence supplies the Brooks County context. These two images do not establish when he acquired the land, a conveyance to Hulda, or the relation of other same-name tax entries to this household.

A surname match in probate is not enough. A September 4, 1865 guardianship bond, page 53, appoints John W. Dukes guardian of Taylor, Henry C., Millard T., Florence C. and William Dukes, explicitly called the orphan children of E. C. Dukes, deceased. John W. is the guardian, not their stated father. Separate letters on page 30 appoint John W. administrator de bonis non of E. C.’s estate. No relationship to Eli or Hulda is established by either instrument.

Earlier minor-heirs accounts beginning on page 57 identify Nancy Dukes as guardian. A tuition voucher on page 67 uses “Est. Edmund Dukes” and names Taylor, Henry and Millard as tuition recipients. The closing oath and filing are dated May 30, 1861; recording occurred February 19, 1863. These records help distinguish the E. C./Edmund estate group. They do not link that group to this household or to lot 278, and Nancy’s guardian role alone does not establish maternity.

docs.title: An 1880 candidate household and farm: age conflict remains
docs.text:
An 1880 population schedule, Brooks enumeration district 4, printed page 84, dwelling 762/family 778, lists Eli Dukes, 35, a Black farmer, and Mahulda Dukes, 39, his wife. The index reads her name “Mahalda.” Both are recorded as born in Georgia, with Georgia-born parents. The original page heading says Morven; the index labels the place Quitman. There are no children in that numbered household, but that does not establish that the couple never had children.

The July 8, 1880 agricultural schedule, page 36, row 5, records Eli Dukes as an owner, with 5 tilled acres and 25 acres of woodland or forest. It values the farm, including land, fences and buildings, at $100; implements at $10; livestock at $60; and estimated 1879 farm production at $100. These are schedule categories, not a land purchase price. Several neighboring names occur in the same order in the population schedule, supporting a link between the two 1880 records.

The name pair, Brooks location, farming occupation and 30-acre total make this a useful candidate for the later tax and census household. The age discrepancy remains substantial: the 1900 original clearly gives Eli January 1825 and age 75, not the birth year about 1845 implied by the 1880 age. It gives Hulda April 1840 and age 60, with 35 years married. Neither original reading is silently changed to make the records agree. The 1880 farm has no lot number, so its 30 acres alone do not identify it as lot 278.

Two automated suggestions were screened out of this identity chain: an 1867 voter return is from Pike County, and an 1865 Brooks marriage joins Elijah Dukes and Mary E. Glenn, not Hulda. No migration, alias or earlier marriage is inferred from those suggestions.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Obtain the deed or other conveyance behind the verified 1890 tax entry. Keep lot 278 distinct from later or disputed lot readings until the instruments connect them.
  • The relationship between the Morven District land entry and the 1900 Barney household should be treated as probable continuity within Brooks County, not as proved identity across every possible Eli Dukes reference, until additional records are found.
  • Resolve the 1880 Eli/Mahulda candidate against the 1900 household, especially Eli’s twenty-year birth-year discrepancy. The inspected 1870 name-search result pages did not establish a matching pair; they were not an exhaustive county image search.
  • No death, burial, deed or probate instrument has yet been securely attributed to this Eli and Hulda household. The separate E. C./Edmund Dukes probate records above do not fill that gap.
  • The current evidence does not support the earlier inflated claims about a nine-employer labor network or other broad economic interpretation.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Evidence-supported, but narrow. The household is anchored by the 1900 census and a probable 1890 tax continuity lead. An 1880 population/agricultural pair is now documented as a candidate, with Eli’s age conflict unresolved. Land acquisition, death, burial and estate identity remain open.
