docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Charley Causey appears in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, as a Black farmer living with his wife Hattie and their children Mary, Joe, Pollie, and James. The census states that he owned his farm, but that the farm was mortgaged. That record anchors the household clearly and shows that the family had reached farm ownership by 1900, though not free of debt.

A Brooks County marriage record shows that Charles Causie and Hattie Roberts were licensed in September 1890 and were married on 18 September 1890. That record fits the 1900 census report that the couple had been married about nine years. The surname spelling in the marriage record differs from the later census spelling, but the timing, county, and spouse identification support the conclusion that this is the same couple.

The family can be followed forward in later censuses. In 1910, Charlie Causey remained in Barney, Brooks County, with Hattie and a larger group of children, and the household was renting rather than owning. In 1920, the family again appears in Barney, with the surname rendered as Cansey, and the household was still renting. By 1930, Charley Causey was widowed and living in Bibb County, Georgia, with younger family members in the household. In 1940, Charles Causey appears in Macon as a widowed roomer and laborer. Taken together, those records support a long continuity from the Barney household into Charley's later life, while also showing shifts in residence and economic position over time.

Two later death certificates strengthen the family identification. Joseph Jackson Causey's 1932 death certificate names Charlie Causey as his father and gives Joseph's birthplace as Barney, Georgia. Lessie Lee Webster's 1938 death certificate names her parents as Charlie Causey and Hattie Roberts. That certificate also states that Charlie was born in Crawford County, Georgia, and Hattie in Wilcox County, Georgia. Those later records help confirm that the Barney household, the 1890 marriage, and the later Causey family records belong to the same family.

An 1880 Crawford County household headed by John and Adaline Causey includes a sixteen-year-old Charles Causey of the right age to fit the later Barney man. That identification is plausible and is strengthened by the later death certificate evidence placing Charlie's birthplace in Crawford County, but the connection still rests on cumulative rather than single-record proof.

  • Hattie's exact birth year varies slightly across records and should be stated cautiously.
  • No land deed, tax digest, foreclosure, or probate record is yet in hand to explain the shift from ownership in 1900 to renting in 1910 and 1920.
  • Charley's death record and Hattie's death record have not yet been added.

docs.text:
James Harrell appears in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, as a White sawmill laborer living with his wife Lucy and their four children, Charley, Clyda, Mamie, and Ralph. The census gives his birth as August 1862, reports that both of his parents were born in Georgia, and shows that he could read and write. The family was renting rather than owning its home.

Beyond the 1900 census, the family's earlier and later movements remain uncertain. No confirmed 1880 census placement, 1910 census continuation, marriage record, death record, or burial record has yet been added for James, Lucy, or their children. For that reason, the household is better treated as clearly anchored in 1900 than as fully exhausted.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
William Jones appears in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, with his wife Georgie and infant daughter Annie. The census gives William's birth as June 1873 in Georgia, describes him as a sawmill laborer, and shows that he and his family were renting their home. The household was newly formed, and the timing fits the Brooks County marriage record for Mr. William F. Jones and Miss Georgia Berryhill, licensed 16 Dec 1898 and married 22 Dec 1898.

Georgia's identity is well supported by the combined record trail. Her 1935 Florida death certificate identifies her as Georgia Emaline Jones, born 3 Oct 1880 at Quitman, Georgia, wife of Wm. F. Jones, with parents J. W. Berryhill and Wealthia A. Patrick. That parentage fits the Berryhill family already present elsewhere in the Barney community, and the 1910 household adds a strong internal link because Robert L. Berryhill was living with William and Georgia as a brother-in-law.

William can be followed beyond Barney through a steady Florida census trail. In 1910, William F. Jones, Georgia E. Jones, Annie J. Jones, and Robert L. Berryhill were in Lakeland, Polk County, Florida, where William was working as an auto mechanic in a railroad shop. In 1920 the family remained in Lakeland, and Annie appeared there as Annie Rogers with her husband Norman Rogers. William was still in Polk County in 1930, 1940, and 1950. Across those records he was described in work connected with auto repair, a delicatessen, and farming.

The family identification also reaches backward with useful support. In 1880, seven-year-old William Jones was enumerated in District 394, Montgomery County, Georgia, as a son in the household of Russell Jones and Jane Jones. Memorial evidence identifies those parents more fully as Corp Russell Blackshear Jones and Jane Nicholson Clark Jones. Annie's later identity is also well anchored: her 1964 Tampa Tribune obituary for Mrs. Annie J. Rodgers of Lakeland named her father as W. F. Jones of Lakeland, linking the Barney child in 1900 to the later Rodgers family in Florida.

docs.text:

  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • The 1880 census directly supports William as the son of Russell Jones and Jane Jones, but the fuller names Corp Russell Blackshear Jones and Jane Nicholson Clark Jones come from derivative memorial evidence rather than from that census itself.
  • A direct death certificate for William F. Jones has not yet been added. His later life is well traced by census and memorial material, but the death record would strengthen the final link.
  • The 1930 census appears to conflict with other records on William's birthplace and his parents' birthplaces. That inconsistency should be preserved as a record conflict rather than harmonized away without further evidence.
  • Georgia's death certificate gives her parents as J. W. Berryhill and Wealthia A. Patrick. An 1880 Berryhill household image would still be useful if a childhood census placement for Georgia is wanted alongside the later death-record evidence.
  • Annie's identity as the daughter from the 1900 household is now strongly supported by the 1920 Lakeland household and her 1964 obituary, but her marriage record to Norman Rogers or Rodgers would still be useful as an additional bridge.
  • The exact form Rogers versus Rodgers should be preserved as the records give it until all later records are compared together.

The 1900 Barney household, the 1898 marriage record, Georgia's 1935 death certificate, the 1880 William Jones childhood census placement, the later Polk County census chain, and Annie's 1964 obituary now support the household well. The main remaining gap is William's direct death record.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation James Norman Head 42 Georgia Farmer Louise Norman Wife 42 Georgia — Ella Norman Daughter 19 Georgia — Nancy Norman Daughter 17 Georgia — Malissa Norman Daughter 15 Georgia — Madie Norman Daughter 14 Georgia — Perish Norman Son 12 Georgia — John Norman Son 10 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows James Norman and wife Louise Norman with six children in the household: Ella, Nancy, Malissa, Madie, Perish, and John. That record is the Barney anchor for this family, but the later evidence makes clear that the same man appears in other records as William J. Norman and William James Norman.

The identity chain is now fairly strong. In 1860, James W. Norman, age 1, appears in Colquitt County. In 1870, William Norman, age 12, appears in the John Norman and Nancy Norman household in Colquitt County. In 1880, William Norman, age 22, was head of a Colquitt County household with wife Louisa Norman and Margaret Register in the home as a sister-in-law. In 1910, William J. Norman, wife Louisa, and children from the earlier Barney household were still in Barney, Brooks County. In 1920, W. J. Norman and Louisa were still in Barney with daughter Meadie in the home and a younger daughter Nancy, age 13. In 1930, the indexed household appears as William J. Normens and Luizer Normens, but the ages, place, and household pattern fit the same couple.

Louisa's maiden name is now supported by more than one record trail. The 1860 Colquitt County census shows Louisa Register, age 5, in the household of Joel P. Register and Elva Register. In 1870, Louisa Register, age 15, was still in Colquitt County with Elvy Register and Margaret Register. The 1880 Norman household then includes Margaret Register as a sister-in-law, which fits the same Register family. Louiza Norman's 1933 death record also supports the Register connection, though the parental fields on that record should still be handled with care.

The later-life records support the same broad identification. Louiza Norman died at Barney on 4 Jul 1933, with burial listed at Sardis Cemetery. A Brooks County death index entry for W. J. Norman gives a death date of 21 Jul 1934. Memorial material for William James Norman and Louisa Register Norman is consistent with those records and places both burials at Sardis Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery in Colquitt County.

The parentage case for William James Norman is stronger than it was, but it is still a mixed-source conclusion. The 1870 census directly places William in the household of John Norman and Nancy Norman. A compiled Alderman family source identifies Nancy Alderman as the woman who married John Tillman Norman, and memorial material identifies the father more fully as John Tillman Norman. Taken together, those sources make John Tillman Norman and Nancy Alderman a well-supported working parentage conclusion, though the claim would still be stronger with a direct marriage or probate record.

Several child identifications also need to be handled carefully. Memorial material supports later identities for Ella Norman Alvis, Mary Melissa Norman Castleberry, and John Thomas Norman, but those links should remain derivative support until each child is bridged with direct marriage, death, or later census records. The Nancy problem is clearer now than it first appeared. A Brooks County marriage record shows Nancy Norman marrying Charley Morell on 28 Jul 1901, which fits the older Nancy who was age 17 in 1900. Memorial material for Nancy M. Morell gives a birth date of 4 Aug 1882 and a death date of 13 Jul 1907, consistent with that same older daughter. That makes the Nancy in the 1920 household, age 13, much more likely to be a younger daughter of the same name. Even so, the younger Nancy has not yet been traced forward with direct evidence.

docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The full marriage record for William or James Norman and Louisa Register has not yet been added.
  • A full death certificate for W. J. Norman has not yet been added; the present death evidence is a Brooks County death index entry.
  • The parental fields on Louiza Norman's death record should be used cautiously until matched against other direct family records.
  • The link from the 1870 John and Nancy Norman household to the fuller names John Tillman Norman and Nancy Alderman is well supported by compiled and memorial sources, but still needs a direct record if the entry is to present the parentage as settled fact.
  • The later identities of Ella, Malissa or Melissa, and John are supported by memorial material, but direct bridge records are still wanted.
  • The older Nancy is now substantially clarified through her 1901 Brooks County marriage to Charley Morell and memorial support as Nancy M. Morell, but the younger Nancy from the 1920 household has not yet been traced forward with direct records.
  • The exact readings Perish and Meadie should be checked against the original census images if this household receives a final source-exhaustion pass.

The core Barney family is now well anchored in 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930, with earlier Colquitt County census support and later death-record support for both spouses. The largest remaining gaps are the marriage record, W. J. Norman's full death certificate, and direct bridge records for several children.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows Thomas Rozier and wife Sallie Rozier in a stable in-town household with two young children and Sallie's sister Mattie Hitch in the home. Later records make clear that this household is the same family later recorded under the fuller name Thomas Alligood Rozier.

The identity chain is strong. In 1860, T. A. Rozier, age 5, appears in Robeson County, North Carolina, in the household of Simpson Rozier and Manerva Rozier. In 1870, Thomas Rozier, age 14, appears in Robeson County in the household of Simpson Rozier and Maria Rozier. The 1938 Georgia death certificate for Thomas Alligood Rozier gives his birth date as 3 Nov 1855, birthplace as Lumberton, North Carolina, father as Simpson Rozier, and mother as Maria Carlyle. The mother's name varies across the records, but the early North Carolina census trail and the death certificate align closely enough to support the identification.

Thomas's marriage is now directly documented. Brooks County marriage records show Mr. Thos A. Rozier receiving a license on 9 Jun 1892 and marrying Miss Sallie A. Hitch on 19 Jun 1892. A Foster newspaper item from 2 Jul 1892 independently reports that Thomas A. Rozier of the firm of Rozier, Conoly & Co. had married Miss Sallie Hitch, daughter of the late Dr. R. M. Hitch of Morven. Additional Foster items from 1892 and 1893 place Thomas in the naval-stores business during the family's early South Georgia years.

The later Barney records show long continuity. In 1910, Thomas A. Rozier and Sallie A. Rozier were still in Barney on Main Street, with children Hazel H., Robert C., and Katharine in the household, along with Mattie Hitch and nephew Martin Rozier. A corrected U.S. postmaster appointment ledger places Thomas A. Rozier first in the Barney sequence on 26 Jul 1897 and then reappoints him on 20 Feb 1906 after intervening appointments for Tobe G. Robinson, Blackmon H. Culbreth, Andrew W. Voight, and Moses W. Wesberry. A 24 Oct 1903 Atlanta Journal notice independently supports the Tobe G. Robinson appointment, reporting that Robinson had been appointed postmaster at Barney, "vice Thomas A. Roseir, resigned." The notice should be cited with the printed spelling, but it likely refers to Thomas A. Rozier. A 1911 Valdosta Times article on a Barney lots sale later refers to T. A. Rozier as the Barney postmaster and mentions his commodious residence. A 1912 Macon Telegraph article names him as a director of the Georgia, Alabama and Western Railway Company. A 1909 ad for Poland China pigs, several 1913-1915 Barney social columns, and a 1935 Macon Telegraph birthday profile all support his continuing public presence in Barney without requiring the stronger civic claims used in the older write-up.

The 1930 census continues the same family in Barney. Thomas A. Rozier, age 74, and Sallie A. Rozier were enumerated on Main Street with Mattie M. Hitch, daughter Hazel K. Stanhope, and grandsons Thomas A. and Fred H. Stanhope in the home. The home value reads as 1000, not 2500. Thomas's 1938 death certificate states that he died at Barney on 27 Oct 1938, gives his occupation as farming, and names Morven as the burial place. Memorial material is consistent on the fuller name Thomas Alligood Rozier and the basic family links, but it should remain derivative support, especially where cemetery naming details differ from the death certificate.

The child identifications are also much firmer than the old entry suggested. The 1924 Atlanta Journal marriage announcement for Hazel Hitch Rozier states that Mr. and Mrs. T. A. Rozier of Barney announced her marriage to Harry Hurst Stanhope in Washington, D.C., on 17 Dec 1923. Sallie Rozier's 1958 obituary names her survivors as Mrs. T. F. Lanneau of Barney, Mrs. H. H. Stanhope of Sarasota, Florida, and R. C. Rozier of Quitman, which supports the later identities of Catherine, Hazel, and Robert. Those later-life links are well supported, though any detailed biographical claims beyond what these records actually say should still be kept modest.

Local oral history holds that Thomas A. Rozier built the first house in Barney. That tradition fits his early prominence in the community and the documentary record showing him as postmaster, property owner, and a visible civic participant, but the specific first-house claim should still be labeled as tradition unless supported by a direct contemporary deed, newspaper, or other documentary source.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The precise relationship of Martin Rozier in the 1910 household should be documented more fully if that person becomes important to a later family-network argument.
  • The mother's name in Thomas's early-life records varies between Manerva and Maria; the death certificate favors Maria Carlyle, but the difference should be noted rather than flattened.
  • Thomas's burial location should be handled carefully because the death certificate and memorial material do not use identical cemetery wording.
  • The oral-history claim that Thomas built the first house in Barney is worth preserving, but it should remain explicitly labeled as tradition unless a direct contemporary source is found.
  • Detailed claims about Hazel's education and federal employment were part of the earlier entry, but they should not be restored without direct supporting records in hand.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Strong household reconstruction with a solid North Carolina-to-Barney identity chain, direct marriage and death records, postmaster documentation, and good newspaper support for Thomas's community presence and the children's later identities. The remaining work is mostly cautionary cleanup: tighten a few derivative claims, resolve cemetery wording if desired, and add direct support before restoring any expanded biography for Hazel or stronger town-founding claims.

docs.text:

In the 1900 Barney census, Lyman Avera headed a 4-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Lyman Avera headed a 4-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 2 children.

Lyman Avera's listed occupation was Laborer Saw Mill.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Lyman Avera Head 29 Georgia Laborer Saw Mill Bessie Avera Wife 29 Georgia — Arnold Avera Son 4 Georgia — Arley Avera Daughter 2 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census captures a young family at an early stage. Lyman Avera was a saw-mill laborer, he and Bessie had been married five years, and they were renting their home while raising Arnold and Arley. That household can now be followed with much more confidence than the earlier stripped-down entry allowed.

The marriage record provides the cleanest starting point for the couple. Brooks County issued a marriage license for L. H. Avera and Bessie E. Tillman on 30 Aug 1895, and the return states that they were married on 1 Sept 1895. That record firmly identifies Bessie's maiden name and anchors the family in Brooks County just before the 1900 census.

The earlier identity evidence is now stronger on both sides of the couple, though not every point is equally secure. In 1880, Lyman Avera, age 11, appears in Berrien County in the household of Willis and Elizabeth Avera, and that record fits the later Barney and Colquitt County man well enough to serve as the likely earlier placement. For Bessie, the 1880 household of Harrison and Sarah A. Tillman includes a child entered as Berry Tillman, male, age 8. Based on the image itself, that appears to be an error made by the enumerator in the original census entry rather than a later transcription problem, and the child is very likely the later Bessie E. Tillman. Even so, that point is best stated cautiously.

By 1910 the family had moved into Colquitt County, where Lyman appears on the Moultrie and Adel Road with Bessie and children Arnold, Arlie, Alma, Amos, Henry, and Nellie. The 1920 and 1930 transcriptions continue the same family line through Colquitt County and then Lakeland in Polk County, Florida. The 1940 transcription and image review bring the family back to Colquitt County and also clear up an important relationship point in the household: Alma Sharpe should be read as daughter, not granddaughter, with Jeff J. Sharpe as son-in-law and Thelma P. Sharpe as granddaughter. The family surname in that cluster should be normalized as Sharpe; an earlier Shorpe reading was a transcription error.

Later records tie the household together across Georgia and Florida. William Franklin Avera's World War II draft card gives his birth as 21 Oct 1911 at Moultrie, Georgia, places him in West Palm Beach, Florida, and names his father as Lyman Henry Avera, then living at 315 S.E. 3rd St., Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia. A Tampa Bay Times death notice and obituary published on 15 Dec 1958 identify Lyman Henry Avera as age 87, state that he died the previous day at a Largo rest home, give his residence as 1256 Bermuda St., Clearwater, and say that he had moved there about four years earlier from his native Moultrie, Georgia. The obituary also links him back to Pleasant Grove and names children including William F. Avera of West Palm Beach and Mrs. Alma Sharp of Savannah.

The result is a solid household reconstruction from the 1895 marriage through the 1958 obituary, with the main caution now shifted away from the core family chain and toward the wider Tillman network. Compiled family-history material and memorials do suggest links among the Tillman, Avera, Killebrew, and Norman families, but those broader network claims should stay in the category of supporting context until they are built from direct records.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • The 1880 Berrien County Lyman Avera is a strong earlier-life candidate, but the identification still rests on continuity rather than an explicit bridging record.
  • The 1880 Berry Tillman entry appears to represent Bessie, but because the census records the child as male and under the name Berry, that identification should remain carefully phrased.
  • Bessie's parentage as Harrison Tillman and Sarah Ann Duckworth Tillman is supported by compiled family material, but still needs direct-record support before being stated as settled fact.
  • Find A Grave remains derivative support for Bessie's later-life dates and burial unless matched to direct cemetery or death-record evidence.
  • The wider Tillman-Killebrew-Norman connection is plausible and worth preserving in research notes, but it should not be overstated in the household narrative without direct documentation.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched household with a direct marriage record, a coherent 1900-1940 census chain, supporting military and obituary evidence for later family continuity, and a substantially clearer reading of the Avera-Sharpe branch than before. Remaining work is focused on tightening the earliest identifications and the Tillman parentage question, not on rebuilding the core household from scratch.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows Jefferson Withers and his wife Amie as a newly married couple with no children in the household. Jefferson was working as a farm laborer, and the census reports that he had been unemployed for four months during the year.

This record also gives a compact but useful profile of the household. Jefferson reported that he was born in April 1859 in Georgia, and that both of his parents were born in Georgia. Amie, age 22, was also born in Georgia. Both were marked as able to read, write, and speak English.

At present, this census entry is the only documented record in hand for the household. It supports a careful description of the couple's status in Barney in 1900, but it does not yet support a broader identification, a later life narrative, or conclusions about parentage, migration, or death.

The bracketed database alias sometimes shown for Jefferson should not be treated as proven from this record alone. Likewise, the present evidence does not justify distinguishing him from similarly named men elsewhere without direct supporting records.

docs.title: Household #61: Roberts, Isaac "Ike"
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Ike Roberts headed a 2-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Ike Roberts headed a 2-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner.

Ike Roberts's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Ike Roberts Head 24 Georgia Farmer Ardonia Roberts Wife 22 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows Ike Roberts and his wife Ardonia as a newly married couple farming in Brooks County. The census places Ike's birth in March 1876 and Ardonia's in July 1877. It also reports that both were Georgia-born and that neither could read or write at the time of the census.

The strongest earlier record in hand for Ike is the 1880 census entry for Isaac Roberts, age 4, in the Quitman district household of Prince and Lucy Roberts. That household provides a plausible parent set for HH#61 and is the only Roberts family connection presently supported by direct evidence. Isaac appears there with older siblings Harriet, Louisa, Zillianna, Thomas, Harrietta, and Prince, plus younger brother Mitchell.

The later census chain in hand supports continuity for the same household after 1900. In 1920, Ike Roberts appears in Barney as a 50-year-old rented-farm operator. In 1930, Isaac Roberts appears in Brooks County militia district 1571, age 55, still renting. In 1940, Ike Roberts appears again in Barney, age 66, this time on an owned farm valued at $150. Taken together, those records support a long residence in the Barney area and a modest shift from tenancy to ownership by the end of the documented timeline.

The 1910 census entry previously attached to this household should be removed from the proved chain. That record is for Isaac C. Roberts, age 23, with a wife named Dura. Its age, household structure, and spouse do not fit the 1900, 1920, 1930, and 1940 records for Ike Roberts and Ardonia. At present, no correct 1910 census match is in hand for HH#61.

Ardonia's identity is strengthened by a consistent set of name variants across the later records. She appears as Ardonia in 1900, as Idonia in 1930, as Ardonis in 1940, and as Ardona in the Brooks County death index. A likely earlier match is the 1880 Jefferson County, Florida, household of Lindsay and Nancy Drew, which includes a two-year-old daughter named Ordonia Drew. That evidence fits the later age pattern and the uncommon name, but it remains a probable identification rather than a proved one.

The Thomas County marriage record for J.C. Roberts and Ardonia Drew on 25 December 1899 is promising and should remain with the file, because the bride's name matches well and the date fits the 1900 census report of a new marriage. Even so, the present evidence does not prove that J.C. Roberts and Ike Roberts were the same man. Until a direct linking record is found, that marriage should be treated as candidate evidence rather than settled identity proof.

The Roberts cluster analysis for HH#61 should stay narrow. John Roberts of HH#29 and Octavia Roberts of HH#129 are white households and should not be used in the Black Roberts family network for Ike Roberts. The only documented anchor is the Prince Roberts household in 1880. Robert Roberts of HH#184 and Frank Roberts of HH#189 may belong to the same broader Black Roberts network, but no direct relationship to Ike has been proved from the records now in hand.

The death indexes extend the household beyond the census record. Ike Roberts appears in the Brooks County death index with certificate 18945 and a death date of 10 Aug 1942. Ardona Roberts appears in the same index with certificate 9262 and a death date of 1 Apr 1943. Those index entries support the end dates for the couple's documented timeline, but the full death certificates are still needed for stronger family detail.

docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • A correct 1910 census match for Ike and Ardonia Roberts has not yet been located.
  • The Thomas County marriage record should not be treated as proved for HH#61 until a record directly links J.C. Roberts to Ike Roberts.
  • The 1880 Ordonia Drew identification in Jefferson County, Florida, is plausible but not yet proved.
  • Full death certificates for Ike Roberts and Ardona Roberts are still needed.
  • No burial record or cemetery identification has been confirmed from direct evidence in hand.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Substantial evidence in hand. The 1880 Prince Roberts household, the 1900 household entry, the 1920, 1930, and 1940 census records, and the two Brooks County death-index entries support a solid working reconstruction for Ike Roberts and Ardonia Roberts. The main unresolved points are the missing 1910 household, proof that the 1899 J.C. Roberts marriage belongs to Ike, and fuller documentation for Ardonia's earlier Drew family identification.

docs.title: Household #62: Stuart, James
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

Source review, September 20, 2026: The 1900 and 1920 originals, Turner’s draft card and marriage entry, and Malory’s death certificate were inspected. Corrections below retain conflicting ages; the 1930–1950 narrative was not revalidated in this review.

In the 1900 Barney census, James Stuart headed a 5-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
James Stuart headed a 5-person household in the 1900 Barney census with his wife, Lucy, and three children.

James Stuart's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation James Stuart Head 27 Georgia Farmer Lucy Stuart Wife 24 Georgia — Korey Stuart Daughter 3 Georgia — Laura Stuart Daughter 3 Georgia — Turner Stuart Son 5/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: Turner’s original draft registration and marriage entry are linked below. Korey, Laura and the later children remain separate research lines; no descendant identities are inferred from surname alone.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The new census sequence makes HH#62 much stronger than it first appeared. James Stuart can now be followed in Barney across five federal censuses: 1900, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950. The surname appears as Stuart in some records and Stewart in others, and the given name also shifts in later enumerations to Jim and Jines, but the location, age pattern, household members, and occupation line up well enough to support a continuous identification.

In 1900, James Stuart appears in Barney as a 27-year-old farmer with wife Lucy and three children: Korey, Laura, and infant Turner. The record reports a September 1872 birth, a marriage year of 1894, and six years of marriage. It also shows that the household was renting and that James could not read or write. Korey and Laura are both reported as 3, but their birth entries differ: December 1896 and February 1897. These inconsistent dates do not establish twins.

By 1920, James Stuart was still in Barney, now age 50, with Lucy, son Turner, sons Joe and Frank, and daughter Rosa Mae. Also in the household was his father, Malory Stuart, age 97—not 87 as previously stated here. That detail is especially important because it gives the first direct generational link in the line now in hand. The 1920 record also shows James as literate and farming a rented home farm.

A World War I draft card adds direct evidence for Turner. The card is for Turner Boy Stewart of Brooks County, Black, born 19 Dec 1899. That birth date fits the infant Turner in the 1900 household and the 20-year-old Turner in 1920. The card also shows that Turner was still tied to Brooks County as a young adult. The original nearest-relative entry reads Jim Stewart, rather than the index’s John. The card does not label his relationship; its name and Barney address are consistent with James, but the card alone does not prove fatherhood. Registration is not evidence of military service.

Turner can then be carried forward into his own marriage record. Brooks County issued a license dated 31 July 1920 for Turner Stewart and Penny McCall, and the certificate shows they were married on 1 Aug 1920. The entry was recorded August 12, 1920. It is a strong name/place/time fit for Turner in James’s household, but names no parents.

The 1930 census continues the same household in Brooks County militia district 1564 on Barney and Berlin Public Road. James Stewart, age 57, appears with wife Lucy, age 56, and son Frank, age 15. He was reported as a farmer working on his own account, and the household was still renting. The age at first marriage was recorded as 23, which fits reasonably well with the 1894 marriage year reported in 1900.

In 1940, Jim Stewart, age 68, and Lucy, age 69, remained in Barney on a farm they now owned, valued at $250. The record still identifies Jim as a farmer working on his own account. By 1950, the same couple appears again in Barney as Jines Stewart, age 79, and Lucy Stewart, age 78. That 1950 entry extends the household's documented residence in the Barney community across half a century.

This sequence changes the research status of HH#62 from a thin single-record household to a well-anchored long-term Brooks County family. Even so, several important gaps remain. No direct marriage record is yet in hand for James and Lucy, no death certificates or burial records have yet been tied to them, and Malory Stuart's earlier placement and relationship network still need direct work.

docs.title: Original father–son evidence and age conflicts
docs.text:
The 1920 original, ED 46, sheet 8B, lines 81–87 lists James, 50, Lucy, 50, Turner, 20, Joe, 18, Frank, 8, Rosa Mae, 6, and Malory, 97, father, widowed. The record explicitly identifies Malory as James's father.

The death certificate for Malory Steward, file 30062, records his death in Barney, Brooks County, on December 18, 1921, and explicitly identifies informant James Steward (Son). It reports age 100, Georgia birth, and unknown parents. It also says “Single” and “Not married,” conflicting with the 1920 widowed entry. Neither age is accepted as an established birth date. The burial field has not been securely read; no cemetery or grave is assigned.

These records strongly support connecting James’s father with the uncommon-named older man in household 66, but his 1900 birth entry, May 1830, conflicts with the later ages. They do not name James’s mother. Lucy in household 66 is not automatically his biological mother, and the 1880 child “Stewart A.” is not automatically James.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• James’s father is explicitly named Malory in the 1920 household and corroborated by the 1921 death informant’s relationship. James’s mother and Lucy’s parents remain unresolved.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • A marriage record for James Stuart and Lucy, likely around 1894, is still needed.
  • Resolve Malory’s conflicting ages and trace his earlier household without assuming that every child-name variant identifies the same person.
  • The children Joe Stuart, Frank Stewart, and Rosa Mae Stuart should be followed forward in later records.
  • Turner’s draft card names Jim Stewart without a relationship label; use the census chain, not this label alone, to support identification.
  • Turner Stewart's marriage to Penny McCall should be followed into later census, death, and cemetery records.
  • Resolve Korey and Laura’s conflicting reported ages and birth dates; twins are not established.
  • Death and burial records remain needed for James and Lucy; Malory’s 1921 death certificate is now inspected, but his burial, probate, land and church trail remain open.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Substantial census chain in hand. James Stuart or Stewart can now be traced in Barney from 1900 through 1950, with a strong likelihood that all five records belong to the same household. Turner's World War I draft card and 1920 marriage record add useful bridges from the childhood household into the next generation. The next priority is to add vital, cemetery, land, and earlier-generation records so the family can be placed more securely before and after the census trail.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Isaac L Hues Head 33 Georgia Farm Laborer Sallie Hues Wife 28 Georgia — Asa Hues Son 7 Georgia — George Hues Son 6 Georgia — Rachel Hues Daughter 3 Georgia — Chester Hues Son 7/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The household is no longer limited to a single 1900 census entry. New records strongly suggest that Isaac L. Hues of Barney is the same man later recorded in Colquitt County under heavier surname distortion as Isaac L. Huker or Hues in 1910 and as I. Leonard Hughes in 1930, with a 1937 Colquitt County death certificate for Leonard Hughes completing the line.

In 1900, Isaac L. Hues appears in Barney with wife Sallie and four children: Asa, George, Rachel, and infant Chester. The census gives his birth as October 1866, reports that the couple married in 1892, and shows Isaac as a farm laborer in a rented household. One useful detail in this record is the parental birthplace pattern: father born in North Carolina and mother born in Georgia.

That same parental pattern appears again in the 1910 census of Warrior District, Colquitt County, where Isaac L. Huker, age 42, is living with wife Sallie E. and children James A., George M., Chester, and Sallie M. The age, wife's name, Georgia birthplace, and father-from-North Carolina and mother-from-Georgia pattern all fit the 1900 household well. The record also suggests that the family had shifted from Brooks County into neighboring Colquitt County by 1910. One unresolved point is the oldest son: James A., age 17, may be the same child listed as Asa in 1900, but that identification should remain provisional until another record ties the names together directly.

By 1930, the likely same couple appears in Robinson District, Colquitt County, as I. Leonard Hughes, age 63, and wife Sallie Hughes, age 59, with daughter Dollie May Hughes, age 23. The household detail again reports a Georgia-born man with a father born in North Carolina and a mother born in Georgia. He was farming on rented land and was still unable to read and write. Dollie May may be the younger daughter recorded as Sallie M. in 1910, but the name difference means that point should also remain cautious.

The death certificate for Leonard Hughes, who died in Moultrie on 14 Feb 1937, makes this identification still stronger. It gives a birth date of 20 Nov 1867, occupation farmer, burial in Sardis Cemetery, and parents Asa Hughes and Millie Wilkes. The informant was D. H. Hughes of Hahira. The age, location, and household pattern make this a strong fit for HH#63, though one detail does not line up cleanly: the death certificate places Leonard's father in South Carolina, while the census records consistently report North Carolina. That conflict is not unusual in late records, but it should be noted rather than smoothed away.

A newly found marriage record for Asa Hughs and Emily Wilks, dated 4 Feb 1867 in Tattnall County, gives direct support to the parent names reported on Leonard's death certificate. The spelling differs slightly from the death record's Asa Hughes and Millie Wilkes, but the names are close enough to treat the marriage as strong corroborative evidence rather than a coincidence. It does not by itself prove that Leonard was their son, but it materially strengthens the case that the death certificate points to a real Hughes-Wilks couple in Georgia.

A Florida death index entry for Sallie E. Hughes, a white woman who died in Dade County in March 1962, may be relevant to the same family. The name fits well, and the timing would be plausible for the widow of Leonard Hughes, but the index entry alone is too thin to prove the identification. Until a full death certificate or another linking record is found, this should remain a lead rather than a settled conclusion.

Taken together, these records support a solid working identification for the household and show that the surname moved through several forms in records: Hues, Huker, and Hughes. The family appears to have moved from Barney in Brooks County into Colquitt County by 1910 and remained there through Leonard's death in 1937, with a possible later Florida death record for Sallie still needing confirmation.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • A marriage record for Isaac or Leonard Hues-Hughes and Sallie, likely about 1892, is still needed.
  • Leonard Hughes's death certificate should be weighed against earlier census evidence because it gives the father's birthplace as South Carolina rather than North Carolina.
  • The Asa Hughs-Emily Wilks marriage record supports the parent names on Leonard's death certificate, but Leonard still needs a direct record tying him to that couple.
  • James A. Hughes in 1910 may be the same person as Asa Hues in 1900, but that needs direct confirmation.
  • Dollie May Hughes in 1930 may be the same child as Sallie M. in 1910, but the name difference needs explanation.
  • Rachel Hues from 1900 has not been securely located in later records.
  • A 1920 census placement for the household is still needed.
  • The Florida death index entry for Sallie E. Hughes, died March 1962 in Dade County, should be tested with a full death certificate or other Florida records before being accepted.
  • Burial, cemetery, probate, land, and church records should still be gathered for Leonard, Sallie, and the children.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Substantial census and death-record chain in hand. HH#63 can now be followed with good confidence from Brooks County in 1900 into Colquitt County in 1910 and 1930, with a strong likely death record in 1937. A possible Florida death index entry may point to Sallie's later life, but that still needs confirmation. The main remaining work is to tighten child identifications, find the missing 1920 household, document Sallie's later life and death, and push the family back into earlier records.

docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, James Kelly headed a 2-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.text:

James Kelly's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation James Kelly Head 24 Georgia Farmer Elizabeth Curls Mother 56 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The household can now be followed much farther than it first appeared, but the first step is correcting the 1900 entry itself. In the census detail provided here, James Kelly is not living with a wife named Jennie. He appears in Barney as a 24-year-old farmer in a rented household with Elizabeth Curtis, age 56, who is listed as his mother. That detail matters because it changes the household structure and suggests either that James's mother had remarried or that Curtis was her later surname.

A strong later census chain likely follows the same man into Lowndes County. In 1910, J. M. Kelly, age 34, born in Georgia, appears in Cat Creek District, Lowndes County, on Valdosta and Milltown Public Road. He is married to L. H. Kelly, age 39, and the household includes daughter Lois Kelly, age 7, along with three Simpson stepchildren: Willie, Marion, and Iveree. The age, birthplace, and initials fit the 1900 James Kelly well, though the jump from a Barney household with mother Elizabeth Curtis to a Cat Creek household with wife L. H. Kelly still rests on census alignment rather than a direct bridging record.

A World War I draft registration card helps firm up that identification. The card is for James Madison Kelley of Barney, Lowndes County, born 4 Feb 1876, working as a farmer. It names his nearest relative as wife Larruh Kelley. That record is valuable for two reasons. First, it gives the likely full name behind the census initials J. M. and Jim M. Second, it ties the Lowndes County farmer directly to a wife whose name fits the later Laura, Laurah, and L. H. Kelly pattern.

A Lowndes County marriage record tightens the case further. On 11 Jan 1904, J. M. Kelly married Laura Simpson in Lowndes County. This fits the 1910 household especially well, because Laura Kelly appears there with three Simpson children in the home, making it very likely that Laura was formerly Laura Simpson and that the stepchildren were from her earlier family. The marriage record also helps explain why the wife's name appears later as Laura, Laurah, Larruh, and L. H. Kelly in different records.

The same line continues well in later censuses. In 1920, Jim M. Kelly, age 44, born in Georgia, appears in Cat Creek with wife Laurah Kelly, age 50, and grandson Aubry V. Kelly, age 9. By 1930, James M. Kelly, age 54, and Laura H. Kelly, age 59, remain in Cat Creek, and the household includes son Aubrey H. Kelly, age 19. In 1940, James Kelley, age 65, and Laura Kelley, age 69, are still in Cat Creek. The sequence is unusually steady in age, place, spouse name, and initials, and the draft card and marriage record strengthen the case that these records belong to one long-running household.

The 1950 census then appears to place the same couple in Ray City, Berrien County, in the household of Lois Carter. That record lists James M. Kelly, age 74, as father, and Laura Kelly, age 79, as mother, alongside head Lois Carter, age 47, and her son James Carter, age 29. If that identification is correct, Lois Carter is very likely the same daughter Lois Kelly seen in 1910, and the record carries the family one step farther into the next generation.

A Georgia death index entry provides a plausible endpoint for James. It lists James M. Kelley, white, age 75, born about 1876, resident and deceased in Berrien County, with certificate number 2338. Those details fit the man in the 1950 Lois Carter household unusually well and are consistent with the broader census and draft-card sequence.

A February 1951 Valdosta Daily Times obituary strengthens that reading. The notice is headed "J. M. Kelley Is Laid To Rest" and identifies him as James Madison Kelley of Ray City. It reports that final rites were held Wednesday at 11 a.m. at Ray City Baptist Church and states that he died Tuesday evening at his home. The obituary also names the officiating ministers as the Rev. John W. Harrell of Lakeland and the Rev. E. L. Todd of Valdosta. Even from the imperfect OCR, those details fit closely with the James M. Kelley already traced into Berrien County.

A Find a Grave memorial supplies a likely burial place and family grouping, though it remains derivative evidence rather than proof. The memorial for James Madison Kelley gives the same 4 Feb 1876 birth date already seen on the draft card and reports death on 12 Feb 1951 in Berrien County. It places his burial in Beaver Dam Cemetery at Ray City and links him to spouse Laura Brickle Kelley and child Lois Gertrude Kelley Carter. Those details fit the census, marriage, draft, obituary, and death-index pattern well, but the memorial should be treated as a secondary summary unless backed by cemetery, death-certificate, or obituary-level confirmation.

Taken together, these census records move HH#64 from a thin one-record household to a plausible fifty-year chain from Brooks County to Lowndes County and then into Berrien County. The 1904 marriage record materially strengthens the middle of that chain by connecting James M. Kelly to Laura Simpson before the 1910 household appears, and the 1951 death index, obituary, and memorial all fit the probable final stage of his life. Even so, important gaps remain. The main unresolved issue is the relationship between the 1900 James Kelly living with Elizabeth Curtis and the later James M. Kelly married to Laura Simpson. The evidence points that way, but the case still needs direct records outside the census trail.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • The 1900 entry should be checked again against the original image to confirm every household member and to make sure no wife was omitted in the current extraction.
  • Elizabeth Curtis, listed as James Kelly's mother in 1900, needs follow-up records to explain the Curtis surname.
  • The 1904 marriage record identifies Laura Simpson as James M. Kelly's wife, but more records are still needed to document her earlier Simpson marriage and children.
  • The connection between the 1900 James Kelly of Barney and the 1910-1950 James Madison or James M. Kelley of Lowndes and Berrien Counties is strong but still needs a direct linking record.
  • Lois Kelly in 1910 and Lois Carter in 1950 appear likely to be the same person, but that should be confirmed with marriage or other family records.
  • Aubry V. Kelly in 1920 and Aubrey H. Kelly in 1930 are likely the same child, but the middle initial variation should be noted.
  • The Berrien County death index entry for James M. Kelley should be followed with the full death certificate.
  • The 1951 obituary should be checked against a clearer image or clipping for any survivor, burial, or cemetery details not captured cleanly in OCR.
  • The Find a Grave memorial points to Beaver Dam Cemetery and gives Laura Brickle Kelley and Lois Gertrude Kelley Carter as close family, but those details should be confirmed with direct records.
  • Death, burial, probate, land, tax, and church records are still needed for James, Laura, Elizabeth Curtis, Lois, and Aubrey.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Substantial census chain in hand. James Kelly can likely be traced from Barney in 1900 to Cat Creek in Lowndes County in 1910, 1920, 1930, and 1940, with a World War I draft card and a 1904 marriage record filling the middle of that sequence and a probable final placement in Berrien County in 1950. A Berrien County death index entry, a February 1951 obituary, and a matching Find a Grave memorial likely point to his death and burial, though the full death certificate is still needed. The household is much better documented now, but the next step is to add death and other non-census records that can prove the family links suggested by the census sequence.

docs.title: Household #65: Ryall, Charles Wesley
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Charles Ryall headed an 11-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Charles Ryall headed an 11-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 9 children.

Charles Ryall's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Charles Ryall Head 50 Georgia Farmer Mary W Ryall Wife 40 Georgia — James Ryall Son 17 Georgia — Mary Ryall Daughter 20 Georgia — Jessie Ryall Son 18 Georgia — Bruce Ryall Son 13 Georgia — Ruth Ryall Daughter 11 Georgia — Bascum Ryall Son 9 Georgia — Kittie Ryall Daughter 7 Georgia — William Ryall Son 4 Georgia — Nesbitt Ryall Son 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The census record set now gives a much clearer frame for Charles Wesley Ryall than this entry had before. In 1850, Charles W. Ryall appears in Lowndes County as a one-year-old in the household of Isaiah B. Ryall and Rachel Ann Ryall. In 1860, a Charles W. Ryals, age 11, appears in Brooks County in the household indexed under J. B. Ryals and Rachel Ryals. Those two census placements fit the same child well, though the father's given-name form should be checked against the original image because the indexes suggest either Isaiah B. Ryall or J. B. Ryals.

By 1880, Charles had established his own household in Morven, Brooks County. That census shows C. W. Ryall, age 31, farmer, with wife Ruth G. Ryall, age 24, and three small children: Lula Ryall, age 3; James W. Ryall, age 2; and Marietta Ryall, age three months. This record gives direct support for the first marriage household and confirms James W. and Marietta as children in the home.

The first marriage is now directly documented as well as inferred from the census chain. A Brooks County marriage license authorized the marriage of Charles W. Ryall and Miss Ruth G. Alderman on 13 Jan 1876, and the return states that they were joined in matrimony on 25 Jan 1876 by J. C. Johnson, M.G. That image-based record is stronger than the index entry alone and corrects earlier uncertainty about the exact marriage date.

Ruth G. Alderman can also be placed in her parental household before the marriage. In 1860, Ruthie Alderman, age 6, appears in Brooks County in the household of William Alderman and Catharine Alderman, with siblings James and Mary. In 1870, a Rutha Alderman, age 13, appears in Brooks County with Catharine Alderman, James Alderman, and Mary Alderman. Taken together, those two census entries fit Ruth G. Alderman well and provide direct context for her Alderman family placement before her 1876 marriage to Charles.

The later records for Mary point to the same sibling network. In 1880, Mary W. Alderman, age 18, appears in Morven as the sister of James C. Alderman in a household that also included Catharine Alderman as mother. Read together with Ruth's 1860 and 1870 placements, that evidence shows that Ruth G. Alderman and Mary W. Alderman were sisters of James Alderman, the man treated elsewhere in this project as Household #180. Charles Ryall therefore married two Alderman sisters, first Ruth and then Mary.

Within the broader Ryall network, Charles should also be read as the brother of William Raiford Ryall of Household #70. That makes him the uncle of Annie Elizabeth "Lizzie" Ryall Jones of Household #71.

The 1900 Barney census shows a later household headed by Charles Wesley Ryall with wife Mary W. Ryall and nine children at home. The census states that Charles and Mary had been married fourteen years, placing the marriage about 1886. That timing is now supported more directly by a Brooks County marriage record for C. W. Ryal and Mary W. Alderman. The license was issued on 15 Jan 1886, and the return states that they were married on 25 Feb 1886. Mary can also be placed just before that marriage in the 1880 census at Morven, Brooks County, where Mary W. Alderman, age 18, appears as the sister of James C. Alderman in a household that also included Martha J. Alderman and Catharine Alderman. Together, the certificate and the census trail explain why the household includes older children who appear to belong to the earlier Ruth G. Ryall household and younger children born after Charles's marriage to Mary.

The family can also be followed into Florida. In 1910, Charles W. Ryall, age 61, appears in Precinct 1, Santa Rosa County, Florida, with wife Mary W. Ryall, age 50. The household includes Robert B. Ryall, Bruce C. Ryall, Katie Ryall, Willie T. Ryall, Nesbitt Ryall, Terence Ryall, and Gussie Ryall. That record is important because it carries the family beyond Brooks County and gives direct support for Robert B. Ryall as part of Charles's household, even though Robert was not present in the 1900 Barney enumeration.

Mary can then be followed through the next three censuses after Charles's likely death. In 1920, Mary W. Ryalls, age 59, appears in Sebastian, then in St. Lucie County, Florida, as a widowed head of household. Living with her are sons Bascum C. Ryalls, William R. Ryalls, and Nesbit B. Ryalls, along with daughter Gussie M. Ryalls. In 1930, Mary W. Ryall, age 68, appears in Sebastian, then in Indian River County, as mother in the household of Bascum L. Ryall. In 1940, Mary Ryall, age 80, appears in Sebastian as a widowed head on West Side Dixie, with son-in-law Roy Clark, daughter Augusta Clark, and housekeeper Irene Brannon in the household. Taken together, these three records extend Mary's Florida residence across three decades and fit well with the 1949 obituary's statement that she had been in Sebastian since 1907.

A World War I draft card gives direct detail for another of Mary's sons. Nesbit Bernard Ryall registered on 7 Sept 1918 while living in Sebastian, then in St. Lucie County, Florida. He reported a birth date of 22 Dec 1898, worked as a bookkeeper for the Hendry Mercantile Company at or near Eau Gallie in Duval Precinct, and named his mother, Mary W. Ryall of Sebastian, as nearest relative. The card gives strong support for the identity of the Nesbit or Nesbitt Ryall found in the 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1949 family records.

Find a Grave memorials now provide a likely later burial location for both Charles and Mary. The memorial for Charles W. Ryall gives a birth date of 10 Jun 1849, a death date of 18 Jan 1913, and burial at Sebastian Cemetery in Sebastian, Indian River County, Florida. The memorial for Mary Wright Alderman Ryall gives a birth date of 21 Nov 1860, a death date of 28 May 1949, and the same burial place. Mary's memorial also reports a 25 Feb 1886 marriage in Brooks County to C. W. Ryal and identifies her parents as William Alderman and Catharine Wells Alderman. Those details fit the household reconstruction well, but they remain derivative until supported by direct records.

A May 1913 Fort Pierce Tribune legal notice gives stronger contemporary evidence for Charles's death and estate. The notice, published in the County Judge's Court for St. Lucie County, is headed "In re Estate of Charles W. Ryall" and calls on creditors, legatees, distributees, and others with claims against the estate of Charles W. Ryall, deceased, late of St. Lucie County, Florida, to present them within two years. It is dated 38 March 1913 in the OCR, almost certainly 28 March 1913 or a similar late-March date, and is signed by Mary W. Ryall of Sebastian, Florida, as administratrix. Even with the OCR defects, the probate notice firmly places Charles's death before late March 1913 and shows Mary handling his estate in Sebastian.

Mary's Miami Herald obituary gives stronger late-life detail. It identifies her as Mary Wright Alderman Ryall, a pioneer resident of Sebastian, and says she died at her home early Saturday. The notice says she came to Sebastian from Brooks County, Georgia, in 1907 and was a member of the Sebastian Methodist Church. It names surviving daughters Mrs. Kitty Booth of Jacksonville and Mrs. Gussie Clark of Sebastian, along with sons Bruce C. Ryall and William R. Ryall of Sebastian and Nesbit B. Ryall of Wabasso. It also reports funeral services at Sebastian Methodist Church with burial in Sebastian Cemetery. The OCR is imperfect in places, but the core facts fit the family found in the earlier censuses and memorials very well.

Robert can now be followed farther than that. A California death index entry for Robert Bouquinne Ryall reports that he was born 18 May 1883 in Georgia, died 13 Mar 1949 in Los Angeles, and had a mother whose maiden name was Alderman. That combination fits the Brooks County Ryall family unusually well. It supports the identification of Robert B. Ryall as a son from Charles's first marriage to Ruth G. Alderman and helps explain the middle initial B. seen in earlier records.

These records do not prove every element of the older compiled Ryall lineage, but they do support a solid core reconstruction. Charles was born in Georgia about 1849, was the brother of William Raiford Ryall of Household #70, and stood one generation above Annie Elizabeth "Lizzie" Ryall Jones of Household #71 as her uncle. He was married first to Ruth G. Alderman by 1880, then to Mary W. Alderman by 1900, and had moved to Florida by 1910. Ruth and Mary can both be placed in the William and Catharine Alderman family, and the evidence shows that they were sisters. A printed Ryall family history matches several of these broad outlines, including the Charles-Ruth marriage and some of the child identifications, but it should be treated as derivative support rather than controlling evidence where it conflicts with direct records such as the 1876 marriage return. A 14 Oct 1899 Valdosta Times item naming Charles Ryall among Barney-area farmers adds a small contemporary local reference.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#65 to HH#69 Hardy Ryall: Hardy Vickers Ryall of HH#69 was Charles Wesley Ryall's nephew, the son of Charles's brother William Raiford Ryall.
  • HH#65 to HH#70 William R. Ryall: Charles and William Raiford Ryall fit the same Isaiah B. Ryall and Rachel Ann Ryall sibling group, and the evidence in both entries supports reading them as brothers.
  • HH#65 to HH#71 Edgar Jones: Annie Elizabeth "Lizzie" Ryall Jones of HH#71 was Charles's niece through Charles's brother William Raiford Ryall.
  • HH#65 to HH#180 James Alderman: Charles's wives Ruth G. Alderman and Mary W. Alderman were sisters of James C. Alderman, making HH#180 the clearest documented Alderman connection for this household.
  • HH#65 to HH#191 John H. Ryall: John H. Ryall of HH#191 belonged to the same William R. Ryall branch, making him another nephew of Charles and adding a second Ryall-Alderman tie through his marriage to Libbie Alderman.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The 1850 and 1860 census entries strongly suggest that Charles was the son of Isaiah B. Ryall and Rachel Ann Ryall, but the father's name form should be checked on the original 1860 image because the index gives J. B. Ryals.
  • The 1886 marriage to Mary W. Alderman is now supported by the certificate image, but the officiant's name should be checked again against the original image if we want a fully confident reading.
  • Ruth's middle initial as G. is established in the marriage record and later household context, but the 1860 and 1870 census entries should still be checked against original images if we want to tighten every element of her identification.
  • Mary W. Alderman's 1880 placement with James C. Alderman and Catharine Alderman fits the broader family reconstruction well, but the original image should still be checked if we want to confirm every indexed household relationship.
  • Lula Ryall in 1880 should be compared with the later child list to determine whether she died young or married before the later censuses.
  • Jessie Ryall in 1900 is a strong candidate for Jesse G. Ryall from compiled family material, but the identification should be tied to direct records.
  • Robert B. Ryall appears in the 1910 Santa Rosa County household and is likely the same man as Robert Bouquinne Ryall in the California death index, but the identification should still be strengthened with additional records such as later censuses, marriage, or obituary material.
  • The 1910 children Bruce C., Katie, Willie T., Nesbitt, Terence, and Gussie Ryall should be tied carefully to the 1900 Barney children, especially where name forms differ.
  • Bascum in 1900 appears as Bascum Ryall and in later Florida records as Bascum C. or Bascum L. Ryall; the continuity looks strong but should still be checked across original images and any other records.
  • Nesbit Bernard Ryall is now supported by a 1918 draft card, but he should still be followed into later census, marriage, or death records.
  • Mary's obituary now gives direct newspaper support for her residence in Sebastian, her church, named children, funeral, and burial at Sebastian Cemetery, while the 1913 probate notice gives contemporary estate evidence for Charles; direct death records and cemetery records are still needed, especially for Charles.
  • The earlier multi-generation Ryall lineage beyond Charles's apparent parents should remain cautious unless supported with direct records.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: This household is well documented. Direct census support is in hand for Charles in 1850, 1860, 1880, 1900, and 1910, and both marriages are represented by Brooks County marriage records. The Alderman side is much clearer than it was at the start of this pass: Ruth G. Alderman and Mary W. Alderman both place into the same sibling group with James Alderman of Household #180. The Ryall side is also clearer in the project-wide family structure, with Charles placed as the brother of William Raiford Ryall of Household #70 and the uncle of Annie Elizabeth "Lizzie" Ryall Jones of Household #71. For Charles, the 1913 Fort Pierce Tribune probate notice shows that he had died by late March 1913 and that Mary W. Ryall was acting as administratrix in Sebastian. For Mary, the 1920, 1930, and 1940 censuses add a long widowhood trail in Sebastian, while the Miami Herald obituary gives direct newspaper evidence for her 1949 death, Sebastian residence, church membership, burial place, and surviving children. The remaining gaps are narrower: a direct death record for Charles and fuller child-by-child follow-forward work.

docs.title: Household #66: Stuart, Malery
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Malery Stuart headed a 2-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Malery Stuart headed a 2-person household in the 1900 Barney census with his wife, Lucy.

Malery Stuart's listed occupation was no occupation listed.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text:
Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Malery Stuart Head 70 Georgia no occupation listed Lucy Stuart Wife 65 Georgia —

Original household boundary check (September 20, 2026). The 1900 original, ED 9, sheet 3B, lines 99–100 contains only Malery, 70, and Lucy, 65, in dwelling/family 66. Lucy, age 24, belongs to James Stuart’s separate household 62 at lines 75–79. Her duplicate placement here has been removed; this is not evidence of two wives or three residents in Malery’s household. Lucy in household 66 is recorded as born March 1835, married forty years, with ten children born and two living. That count is not a named list or proof of which children survived.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No children reside in the two-row 1900 household, but the 1880 children named below remain open research lines. A child’s absence from this household is not proof of death.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Malery Stuart, also recorded as Malrey Stewart and Malery Stuart, can be placed in Brooks County from at least 1880 through 1900, though the surviving record base remains thin. In 1900, he and Lucy Stuart appeared in Barney as an older Black couple living alone in a rented household. The census gave Malery's birth as May 1830, Lucy's age as 65, and the length of the marriage as about forty years, pointing to a marriage around 1860 if that report was roughly accurate.

The earlier census places the family in Morven. In 1880, Malrey Stewart, age 49, appeared with wife Lucy, age 50, and five children in the household: Laura, 15; George, 12; Mary A., 11; Stewart A., 8; and Joseph, 3. The original, ED 4, page 93/330A, dwelling 827/family 844, lines 7–13, explicitly records those relationships and Malrey working on a farm. Lucy is reported born in North Carolina, unlike Georgia in 1900; her age 50 in 1880 also differs from the later age progression. These conflicts remain unresolved.

A George Stewart entry in the 1890 Brooks tax list remains a possible follow-forward lead for the son, not a proved identification. The earlier narrative’s name/place/age comparison does not supply a parent bridge; that original George entry was not re-inspected in this review.

A Morven tax page in the Brooks 1878–1882 volume explicitly aligns C. W. Ryall, under “Name of Employer,” with Malory Stewart. The uncommon given-name variant, locality and nearby Ryall households in both censuses support a likely connection to this man, but the tax row names no wife or children. The individual tax year has not been established from that leaf; the collection’s generic “1890” citation is not its date.

A second original tax page has Malory Stuart’s employer column blank. Colen E. McRae appears beside Miller entries farther up that page, not on Malory’s row. This does not disprove employment at another time; the earlier reported McRae connection remains unverified. Neither entry establishes kinship, a pre-emancipation relationship, land ownership or a purchase.

docs.title: Later father–son evidence and death
docs.text:
The 1920 original, ED 46, sheet 8B, lines 81–87 places Malory, 97, widowed, father, in James Stuart’s Barney household with James, Lucy and their children. The 1921 original death certificate for Malory Steward, file 30062 records December 18, 1921, Barney, Brooks County, and names James Steward (Son) as informant. These are direct father–son statements and strongly support linking the older man here with James of household 62.

The death certificate reports age 100, Georgia birth, and unknown parents; it says “Single” and “Not married,” unlike the 1920 widowed entry. The later ages conflict with the 1900 May 1830 birth entry. The records are not harmonized into a single birth year or marital history. The burial field has not been securely read, so no cemetery or grave is assigned.

Neither source identifies James’s mother. Lucy here is not automatically his biological mother, and the 1880 child Stewart A. is not automatically James. Searches of first-page 1870 and 1910 census results did not identify a secure earlier or intervening entry; those searches were bounded, not exhaustive.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • The reported marriage about 1860 should be tested against Brooks County or nearby marriage records if any survive for Malery Stuart and Lucy Stuart.
  • The 1880 children Laura, George, Mary A., Stewart A., and Joseph should be followed forward through later census, marriage, death, and cemetery records.
  • The 1890 George Stewart tax candidate needs original-image review and a parent bridge before assignment to the 1880 son.
  • Find the specific source for the reported Colen McRae association. The inspected pages support a C. W. Ryall employer entry and a separate blank-employer entry, not that claim.
  • Malery's name may appear in variant forms such as Malrey, Malary, Mallary, or Mallory; those variants should be checked in census and county records.
  • The 1920 father relationship and 1921 son-informant statement support the James link; resolve the older man’s age conflicts and seek James’s mother without assuming she was Lucy.
  • Malory’s 1921 death certificate is inspected; his burial remains unread and unassigned. Lucy’s death and burial, and both spouses’ probate, land and church trails, remain open.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: This household is better anchored than it was at the start, but it is still thin. The 1880 and 1900 censuses establish Malery and Lucy in Brooks County across two decades, and the inspected tax page adds a qualified C. W. Ryall employer association. The 1920 and 1921 originals supply a direct James–Malory father–son bridge and a qualified December 18, 1921 death identification. The George tax candidate remains unassigned. Conflicting ages, Lucy’s later life, burial, probate, land, church and other child trails remain unresolved.

docs.text:
