docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Dave Trison Head 33 Georgia Laborer at turpentine still Lula Trison Wife 29 Georgia — James Trison Son 8 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
This household is documented securely in the 1900 census, but almost nothing beyond that single record has been tied to the family with confidence. Dave Trison appeared in Barney as a Black laborer in the turpentine industry, with wife Lula and son James. The census states that Dave was born in North Carolina, that both of his parents were also born in North Carolina, and that Lula was born in Alabama. Those details suggest migration into south Georgia, but the family's path has not yet been reconstructed from earlier or later records.

Dave's occupation places the household within the naval-stores economy rather than the more common farming pattern seen in many nearby households. The census reports steady work, with no months unemployed during the year, and indicates that Dave could read and write. Those details may help distinguish him from other men of similar name if additional records surface.

The main problem is identification. The 1900 household is indexed as Trison, and the available screenshot supports that reading at the index level. Even so, the original handwriting appears faded enough that the surname should not be treated as fully settled without another record. For now, the safest course is to treat Trison as the documented census reading while leaving open the possibility that the original name was read incorrectly.

No firm connection has been established between this household and any other Barney family. The record remains useful because it captures one Black family tied to the Brooks County turpentine workforce in 1900, but the household is still thin and should be handled cautiously until the name can be verified and the family tracked beyond this single census entry.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • The original census image should be reviewed again at the highest available resolution to test whether the surname truly reads Trison.
  • The surname should be retested under close variants, including Trison, Tison, Tyson, Tryson, and other plausible readings from the faded handwriting.
  • Dave should be searched in 1910 and 1920 under both turpentine and farm-labor patterns in Brooks County and nearby counties.
  • Lula and James may be easier to trace than Dave if the surname shifted in later records.
  • The reported marriage about 1891 should be tested against Brooks County and nearby county marriage records.
  • North Carolina origin for Dave and his parents should be treated as a clue, not a proved migration chain.
  • No cemetery, death, probate, land, church, or labor-camp records have yet been tied to this household.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: This household is still lightly documented. The 1900 census gives a solid snapshot of Dave, Lula, and James in Barney, but no supporting record has yet been linked with confidence. The next gains are most likely to come from surname-variant work, marriage records, later censuses, and labor records connected to the turpentine industry.

docs.title: Household #68: Hayes, Burton
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Burton Hayes headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Burton Hayes headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

Burton Hayes's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Burton Hayes Head 39 Georgia Farmer Etta Hayes Wife 26 Georgia — Maude Hayes Daughter 7 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Burton Hayes appears in the 1900 Barney census as a farmer with wife Etta and daughter Maude. He can be traced across a long record trail that begins with an 1880 Brooks County census entry, continues through tax digest records in the 1880s, and then follows the family through four federal censuses, a Brooks County marriage record, Florida death records, newspaper notices, and cemetery memorials. The earlier version of this entry overstated his parentage and birthplace. The newer evidence gives a firmer picture of the household, but some points still need to stay open.

The 1880 census places Burton Hays, age eighteen, in the household of Sarah E. Hays in Quitman, Brooks County. That record is a solid early anchor for Burton himself, but it does not support the previous claim that he was living with James H. Hayes and Candis Hayes. Until another direct record ties him to specific parents, the Sarah E. Hays household should be treated as the proven 1880 placement and the parentage question should remain unresolved.

Burton appears again in Brooks County tax digest material for 1883 through 1887 in the Morven district. The available digest image does not show taxable land ownership for him. That fits the later census pattern. In 1900, 1910, and 1920 he was consistently working as a farmer, and the later censuses indicate that he was renting rather than owning his place. Taken together, the tax and census records support a life of steady farm work without clear evidence that he ever held land in his own name.

The marriage record adds a useful layer of precision. On 30 June 1892, B. Y. Hayse married Miss Etta Maulden in Brooks County. That record confirms both Burton's middle initial and Etta's maiden name. The name forms vary across the file set, with Burton appearing as Burton Hayes, Burton Hays, Berton Y. Hayes, and B. Y. Hayse, while Etta's family appears as both Maulden and Mauldin. The records fit well enough in date, place, and family structure to treat those spellings as normal variants rather than separate people.

The census chain from 1900 through 1920 is strong. In 1900 Burton and Etta were in Barney with daughter Maude. In 1910 the household remained in Barney under the form Berton Y. Hayes. In 1920 the family was in the Williams district of Brooks County, where Maud Bonnard was back in her parents' household with children of her own. That 1920 entry gives the clearest bridge between the Barney household and the later Florida records because it shows the daughter as a married woman while keeping the older household intact.

Burton's birthplace is less settled than it first appeared. The 1880, 1910, and 1920 census material points toward Florida, while the 1900 census gives Georgia. His Find a Grave memorial gives a specific birth date of 3 June 1862 and places his birth in Brooks County, Georgia. That is specific enough to note, but Find a Grave is still derivative evidence. For now the safest reading is that Burton's birthplace remains unresolved pending a death certificate or another direct record.

The later Florida material is much stronger. Burton's Florida death index entry records B. Y. Hayes, white male, dying in Hillsborough County in 1925. His Tampa Times death notice says he died at his residence in Oak Park, that funeral services were held on 17 June 1925 from the F. T. Blount funeral home, that burial was in Riverview Cemetery, and that he was survived by his wife and one daughter, Maud. By 1940 Mary E. Hayes was a widowed grandmother in Hillsborough County in the household of Esther Lassiter. In 1950 she appeared again in Hillsborough County as Marietta Hayes, a widowed head of household who was unable to work. Those records fit the widow of Burton closely in age, place, and family position.

Mary Etta's own late-life records sharpen the Maulden line. Her Find a Grave memorial identifies her as Mary Etta Maulden Hayes, born 22 August 1871 in Georgia and buried at Bethlehem Cemetery in Plant City. Her Tampa Tribune obituary, published 23 September 1953, states that Mrs. Mary Etta Hayes of Dover died in a Tampa hospital, that services were held at the Dover Church of Christ, that burial was in Bethlehem Cemetery, and that she was survived by sisters Lizzie Abbott and Maggie McMillian, brothers Lawrence, Joe, and Willie Mauldin, and four grandchildren. A Florida death index entry for Mary Etta Hayes in Hillsborough County in 1953 supports the obituary and cemetery record.

This household now reads as a well-documented Brooks County family that later shifted into Hillsborough County, Florida. Burton's land status looks modest throughout the record. The main unresolved issues are his exact birthplace and parentage, not the identity of the household itself.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Burton's parentage remains open. The 1880 Sarah E. Hays household anchors him in Brooks County, but no direct record yet ties him to named parents with confidence.
  • Burton's birthplace remains unresolved. Census records lean toward Florida in several years, while the 1900 census and his Find a Grave memorial point toward Georgia.
  • Maude's married surname appears as Bonnard in 1920, but Burton's obituary OCR is too rough to treat the daughter's married surname there as settled without a cleaner image or another record.
  • Burton's death certificate would likely settle his exact death date, birthplace, and perhaps parentage.
  • Mary Etta's death certificate would help confirm her parents beyond the derivative memorial and obituary evidence.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented household. The identity of Burton, Etta, and Maude across the core census and Florida records is strong. The remaining work is mostly cleanup around Burton's origins and direct-record confirmation of late-life details.

Hardy Ryall's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Hardy Ryall Head 22 Georgia Farmer

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Hardy Vickers Ryall was the son of William Raiford Ryall and Edna Vickers Ryall and belonged to the large Ryall family network clustered around Barney and Morven. The 1880 census places three-year-old Hardy V. Ryall in his parents' Brooks County household, providing the childhood anchor for the man who appears as an independent young farmer in Barney in 1900. A later compiled family-history source, Georgia Salzburger and Allied Families by Pearl Rahn Gnann, gives the same parentage and the full form of his name, but the family book is best used as supporting evidence rather than as stand-alone proof.

The 1900 census shows Hardy renting a farm in Barney and living on his own at age twenty-two. He could read but not write. By 1910 he was still in Barney, single, boarding on First Avenue, and working as a salesman in general merchandise. The shift in occupation is real, but it was not permanent. His World War I draft registration card, completed at Barney on 12 September 1918, gives his full name as Hardy Vickers Ryalls, states that he was born on 8 May 1878, identifies him as a farmer, and names Mary Ada Ryalls as his nearest relative. That record ties the 1900 farmer, the 1910 boarder, and the married man of the late 1910s into one continuous identity.

His wife can now be identified with much more confidence. The 1900 census places Mary A. Folsom, born in May 1891 in Georgia, in the Berrien County household of John M. Folsom and Mattie Folsom. A Lowndes County marriage record shows H. V. Ryall and Mary Ada Foleson marrying on 16 August 1911. The surname appears there as Foleson, which should be treated as a record variant rather than forced into a single spelling. Later records, including her 1950 death notice and cemetery memorial, show her as Mary Ada Folsom Ryall.

The later census chain is steady and persuasive. In 1920 Hardy appears in Hahira, Lowndes County, with wife Mary A. and son Keith, although the surname is indexed there as Ryles. In 1930 he was in Sebring, Highlands County, Florida, working as a carpenter in the building trade, with wife Ada F. and sons Keith M. and Myrl Neil. In 1940 the same family remained in Sebring, where Hardy was working as a night watchman. In 1950 he was still in Sebring, now widowed, living in the household of his son Keith M. Ryall and daughter-in-law Madelene G. Ryall. Taken together, those records show movement from Brooks County to Lowndes County and then to long-term residence in Sebring.

Mary Ada's death is supported by a contemporary newspaper notice. The Tampa Tribune of 18 January 1950 identified Mrs. Mary Ada Folsom Ryall of Sebring as the wife of H. V. Ryall and reported that she died at her South Lakeview Drive home after a long illness. Her Pinecrest Cemetery memorial gives 29 May 1891 as her birth date and 7 January 1950 as her death date. Because the newspaper notice and memorial do not fully agree on the exact day, the safest present statement is that she died in Sebring in January 1950 and was buried at Pinecrest Cemetery.

Hardy's later life is also well documented. A 7 May 1972 Orlando Sentinel profile, published around his ninety-fourth birthday, describes him as Georgia-born, recalls his first trip to Florida in 1906, notes that he married a woman from neighboring Lowndes County, and names two of his children, Myrl Nell Simpson and Keith Morgan Ryall. The article is a late-life feature rather than a primary vital record, but it fits the broader documentary pattern. His Social Security Death Index entry gives a birth date of 8 May 1878 and a death date of April 1975, with his number issued in Florida. His Pinecrest Cemetery memorial gives the more exact death date of 23 April 1975.

The older version of this entry overstated the broader Folsom significance. The present evidence supports Hardy's place within the Ryall family and supports his marriage to Mary Ada Folsom, daughter of John M. and Mattie Folsom. It also makes a Pounds connection plausible through Mary Ada's mother. What it does not yet prove on direct records alone is the longer founding-family descent chain previously asserted for this household. That larger lineage may be right, but it should remain secondary until documented generation by generation.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#69 to HH#70 William R. Ryall: Hardy Vickers Ryall is securely identified as a son of William R. Ryall and Edna Vickers Ryall through the 1880 census, later life records, and the consistent Brooks County family cluster.
  • HH#69 to HH#71 Edgar Jones: HH#71 represents Hardy's sister Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones, whose records reinforce the same William and Edna Ryall parental household.
  • HH#69 to HH#65 Charles Wesley Ryall: Charles Wesley Ryall of HH#65 was Hardy's paternal uncle, the brother of William Raiford Ryall, linking Hardy's household back to the older Ryall-Alderman branch.
  • Possible Folsom-Pounds connection: Mary Ada Folsom appears to be the daughter of John M. Folsom and Mattie Folsom, and the line may connect into the Pounds family through her mother, but that relationship still needs direct-record confirmation before it is treated as settled.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Mary Ada's exact date of death should be checked against a death certificate or cemetery record because the newspaper notice and Find a Grave memorial do not fully agree.
  • The immediate link from Mattie Folsom to the Pounds family appears likely but should be supported with direct records before being stated as settled fact in this entry.
  • The longer Folsom founding-family descent used in the previous draft should not be restored without a record-by-record proof chain.
  • Additional Florida records may refine Hardy's exact burial details and late-life residence timeline, although the present identification is already strong.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented. The census chain from 1880 through 1950, the 1911 marriage record, the 1918 World War I draft card, the 1950 death notice for Mary Ada, the 1972 Orlando Sentinel profile, the Social Security Death Index, and the Pinecrest Cemetery memorials provide a coherent record of Hardy Ryall's life from childhood in Brooks County to old age in Florida.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Mary Ryall Daughter 40 Georgia — Mary Ryall Daughter 20 Georgia — William H Ryall Head 55 Georgia Farmer Edna Ryall Wife 48 Georgia — Mary Ryall Daughter 18 Georgia — Charles A Ryall Son 16 Georgia — Nina Ryall Daughter 13 Georgia — Sarah Ryall Daughter 11 Georgia — Edith Ryall Daughter 8 Georgia — Drewry Ryall Son 6 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
William R. Ryall of the 1900 Barney census is the same man who appears across an extended census chain in Lowndes and Brooks counties from 1850 through 1930. The records support identifying him as William Raiford, or Raford, Ryall, though the exact middle-name spelling varies in later derivative material. In 1850 he appears as a four-year-old in Lowndes County in the household of Isaiah B. Ryall and Rachel Ann Ryall. In 1860 he was fourteen and still in that parental household, now in Brooks County. Those two censuses give the clearest documentary base for placing him in the Isaiah and Rachel family.

By 1870 William had formed his own household in Brooks County. He was a farmer, age twenty-three, living with wife Edna and infant son Isaiah. The 1880 census shows the family at Morven with a larger group of children, including John H., Annie E., Hardy V., and Minnie Lee. By 1900 William and Edna were still in Brooks County, heading one of the larger Ryall households in the Barney area. The household links directly to several later encyclopedia entries, especially Hardy Ryall in HH#69 and Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones in HH#71.

The later census trail is steady. In 1910 William was still farming in the Barney district with Edna and younger children at home. In 1920 he appears again in Barney as W. R. Ryall, with wife Edna indexed as Eva and son D. W. Ryall in the household. In 1930 William and Edna were elderly parents in the household of son Drew W. Ryall on the Adel Road. Taken together, those records show long residence in the same local part of Brooks County and a family network that remained closely settled.

A Brooks County property tax digest for Morven District 660 associates William R. Ryall with 1,080 acres between 1883 and 1887. He therefore held substantial land in the Morven area during his middle years, a fact that helps explain the size and continuity of the family household in later censuses.

Edna's identity is now on firmer ground than it was in the earlier draft. A likely pre-marriage appearance is the 1860 Lowndes County census entry for eight-year-old Edney Vicker in the household of Malinda Vicker. More important, Edna Ryall's 1938 death certificate states that she was born in Lowndes County, Georgia, identifies her parents as Henry Vickers and Linnie Bradford, and records burial at Camp Ground Cemetery. That death certificate strongly supports the conclusion that William's wife was Edna Vickers Ryall and that the 1860 Edney Vicker entry belongs in her background.

William's own 1933 death certificate is equally important. It states that W. R. Ryall died at Barney on 11 April 1933, identifies him as a farmer born in Georgia, names his parents as Isaiah Ryall and Rachel Anne Folsom, and records burial at Camp Ground Cemetery. That record does not stand alone, but read together with the 1850 and 1860 censuses it strongly supports the identification of his parents and ties the older Barney farmer back to the earlier Lowndes and Brooks County Ryall households.

The Confederate service claim appears plausible but should stay tied to the records that support it. William's Find a Grave memorial says he had a Confederate pension application in the Georgia Archives virtual vault, states that he enlisted in 1864 at Madison, Florida, with the 1st Florida Battalion Cavalry, and notes that within the pension paperwork Edna said they married on 1 January 1881. That marriage date conflicts with the census evidence, since William and Edna were already together with a child in 1870. The safest reading for now is that either the pension statement referred to a later formalization, or one of the records contains an error. Until the original pension file is checked closely, the conflict should remain visible rather than smoothed away.

The present evidence supports several things with confidence: William was the Brooks County farmer seen in the long census chain from 1850 to 1930; he was husband of Edna Vickers Ryall; he was father of Hardy Ryall and Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones; he held substantial land in Morven District during the 1880s; and he was buried at Camp Ground Cemetery after his death in 1933. The broader Folsom and Vickers lineage significance may prove correct, but the older version of this entry leaned too hard on status language and on conclusions better handled as documented family connections rather than as claims of special rank.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#70 to HH#69 Hardy Ryall: Hardy Vickers Ryall in HH#69 is directly tied to this household as the son of William R. Ryall and Edna Ryall.
  • HH#70 to HH#71 Edgar Jones: Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones in HH#71 is directly tied to this household as daughter Annie E. Ryall in 1880 and later as Edgar Jones's wife.
  • HH#70 to HH#65 Charles Wesley Ryall: Charles Wesley Ryall of HH#65 fits the same Isaiah B. Ryall and Rachel Ann Ryall sibling group and is best read as William's brother, making HH#65 the uncle-generation Ryall branch for this household's children.
  • Broader Ryall-Vickers-Folsom context: William's death certificate names his parents as Isaiah Ryall and Rachel Anne Folsom, and Edna's death certificate names her parents as Henry Vickers and Linnie Bradford. Those records place this household at an important junction of several Barney-area family lines, though each generational step should still be stated only as far as the direct evidence allows.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The Confederate-service claim for William H. Ryall is plausible but not yet source-exhausted. His Find a Grave memorial reports a Georgia Archives Confederate pension application and says he enlisted in 1864 at Madison, Florida, with the 1st Florida Battalion Cavalry. Because the same summary creates a marriage-date conflict with census evidence, the page should keep the service claim tied to the memorial/pension-summary evidence until the original pension file is reviewed.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The exact middle-name spelling, Raiford versus Raford, should be treated cautiously until a direct-life record settles it.
  • The full Confederate service and pension file should be reviewed directly rather than relying on memorial summary text.
  • The marriage-date conflict between the census record and the pension-related statement still needs resolution.
  • Edna's mother appears on her death certificate as Linnie Bradford, while the 1860 household is headed by Malinda Vicker; that relationship likely fits but should be mapped carefully.
  • The broader Folsom and Vickers lineage claims should be stated generation by generation only where the supporting records are in hand.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented. The household rests on a strong census chain from 1850 through 1930, reinforced by William's 1933 death certificate, Edna's 1938 death certificate, Brooks County property tax evidence, and cemetery memorials. A few lineage details and the marriage-date conflict still need direct-record cleanup.

docs.text:

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Edgar Jones Head 30 Georgia Farmer Lizzie Jones Wife 25 Georgia — William Jones Son 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows Edgar Jones and wife Lizzie Jones as a young Brooks County farm household with one infant son, William. Later records make clear that this was Edgar Jelks Jones and Annie Elizabeth "Lizzie" Ryall Jones, a couple whose documented life stayed centered in Brooks County while some of their children later spread into Florida and beyond.

Edgar can be followed across a solid census chain. In 1870 he appears as an infant in Brooks County in the household of Malachi Jones and Cornelia Jones. In 1880 he appears as eleven-year-old Edgar Jones in the household of Frank Jones and Cornelia Jones in the Nankin district. His 1928 death certificate gives his parents as M. F. Jones and Cornelia Powell, which fits the census evidence well and helps tie the childhood and adult records together.

Annie Elizabeth Ryall can also be placed securely before her marriage. In 1880 she appears as Annie E. Ryall, age six, in the Morven household of William and Edna Ryall. That record links HH#71 directly back to HH#70, where her parents are documented as William Raiford or Raford Ryall and Edna Vickers Ryall. It also links HH#71 sideways to HH#69, since Hardy Vickers Ryall was Annie's brother.

Their marriage is no longer inferential. A Brooks County marriage record shows Edgar J. Jones and Lizzie Ryalls licensed on 31 December 1897 and married on 2 January 1898. That record explains the later sequence of names used for Annie across the records: Annie E. Ryall in 1880, Lizzie Ryalls on the marriage record, Lizzie Jones in the 1900 and 1910 censuses, Elizabeth Jones in 1920, Annie R. Jones in the 1955 death index, and Annie Elizabeth Jones on her son James Edgar Jones's World War II draft registration.

The later censuses show a growing family that remained in the Barney area. In 1910 Edgar J. Jones and Lizzie Jones had children Frank, Sarah E., Leon, and Hermine in the household. In 1920 E. J. Jones and Elizabeth Jones were still in Brooks County with children Frank, Sarah Edna, W. Leon, Harry P., Mildred Mae, James E., and Willie, along with Edgar's father M. Frank Jones in the home. Taken together, those records show a stable, multi-generational farm family rooted in the same local community for decades.

The direct William Leon Jones line can now be carried further, but with a FamilySearch profile-cleanup caution. The clean FamilySearch profile for William Leon Jones, MX6P-75T, is attached to Edgar and Annie and has seven sources, including the 1910 and 1920 census records, his Georgia World War II draft registration, Social Security Death Index entry, Georgia death-index entry, and Find a Grave entry. That profile still shows no spouse or children and is flagged by FamilySearch as a person who may have children. Separate thin FamilySearch profiles for William L. Jones and Mauree P. Folsom expose the William/Mauree couple and a son, William Eugene Jones, while a stronger Maurie Folsom profile ties Mauree to Perry Lee Folsom and Ida Harris. FamilySearch record search also exposes a GenealogyBank obituary-index result naming spouse Mauree Folsom Jones and children Barbara Moody Jones Brown, Bernice Jones, Billy Jones, and Edgar Lee Jones. On that basis, William Leon Jones's branch is now extended to Mauree Folsom and their children as a record-supported working continuation, while the profile split and missing attached sources remain explicit cleanup targets.

The 1900 census presents one unresolved but understandable family question. The household includes a one-year-old son William Jones, while later records show a son William Leon Jones born in 1906. The most likely explanation is that the first William died young and the name was later reused for another son, a common pattern in the period. That reading fits the evidence presently in hand, but it should still be treated as probable rather than final until a direct death or burial record for the first child is found.

Edgar's death certificate adds several useful details. It states that Edgar J. Jones died in Brooks County on 10 July 1928, was a married white farmer born in Georgia, named his parents as M. F. Jones and Cornelia Powell, and was buried at Mt. Zion on 11 July 1928. His Find a Grave memorial gives 11 July 1928 as the death date, but that appears to be a confusion with the burial date, so the death certificate should control.

Annie's later records are also strong. Her obituary in The Valdosta Daily Times reports that Mrs. Annie Ryall "Lizzie" Jones died on 21 February 1955 at the home of her daughter Mrs. Mae Becton near Barney, was a member of Mt. Zion Methodist Church at Morven, and was to be buried in Camp Ground Cemetery. The obituary also names her surviving children and siblings, including Hardy Ryall and the other Ryall brothers and sisters that connect her firmly back to HH#69 and HH#70. A Georgia death index entry for Annie R. Jones matches the obituary date, county, and age.

The memorial evidence is helpful here, though still secondary to the direct records. Find a Grave memorial no. 83938146 for Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones and memorial no. 83938009 for Edgar Jelks Jones confirm burial at Camp Ground Cemetery Mount Zion Church in Morven and reflect the same family links shown by the census, obituary, and death records. Used carefully, they reinforce rather than replace the primary documentation.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#71 to HH#70 William R. Ryall: Annie Elizabeth "Lizzie" Ryall Jones is directly tied to HH#70 as daughter Annie E. Ryall in the household of William and Edna Ryall.
  • HH#71 to HH#69 Hardy Ryall: Hardy Vickers Ryall of HH#69 was Annie's brother, and Annie's obituary names him among her surviving siblings.
  • HH#71 to HH#65 Charles Wesley Ryall: Charles Wesley Ryall of HH#65 was Annie's paternal uncle, the brother of William Raiford Ryall, linking this household to the older Ryall branch that also married into the Alderman family.
  • Jones parental household connection: Edgar J. Jones is tied back to the earlier Jones household of M. F. or Frank Jones and Cornelia Powell through the 1870 and 1880 censuses and his 1928 death certificate, though the exact relationship wording between Malachi Jones and M. Frank Jones should still be tightened with additional records.
  • Direct descendant continuation: William Leon Jones, son of Edgar and Annie, married Mauree/Maurie Pansy Folsom. Their child group is now supported by FamilySearch record-search results and obituary-index evidence, including William Eugene "Billy" Jones, Barbara Moody Jones Brown, Edgar Lee Jones, and Emery Bernice/Bernice Jones, but the FamilySearch profiles are split and need source attachment or merge review before being treated as a clean tree structure.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Annie's full death certificate would be useful for confirming all late-life details and parental information in one direct record.
  • The first William Jones in the 1900 household is still not traced by a direct death or burial record.
  • The memorial death date for Edgar conflicts with his death certificate by one day; the certificate is the stronger source and should be followed unless another direct record appears.
  • The exact relationship between Malachi Jones and M. Frank Jones should be spelled out more fully if additional records are gathered for Edgar's parental household.
  • William Leon Jones's FamilySearch profile is under-attached: the profile tied to Edgar and Annie has no spouse/children, while separate thin William L. Jones and Mauree P. Folsom profiles expose the spouse/child bridge. This needs merge/source review before the tree itself is clean.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented, with the direct William Leon descendant line newly extended but not profile-cleaned. The household now rests on a strong run of census records, a direct marriage record, Edgar's death certificate, Annie's obituary and death-index entry, cemetery memorials, and later family corroboration through James Edgar Jones's draft registration. The main remaining loose ends are the fate of the first William Jones from the 1900 household and the split FamilySearch profile structure around William Leon Jones, Mauree Folsom, and their children.

docs.text:

Sebran Kelly's listed occupation was Day Laborer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Sebran Kelly Head 36 Georgia Day Laborer Ella Kelly Wife 32 Georgia — Cleveland Kelly Son 12 Georgia — Charley Kelly Son 9 Georgia — Olin Kelly Son 5 Georgia — Earnest Kelly Son 3 Georgia — Early Kelly Son 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows Sebran Kelly and Ella Kelly as a Brooks County family with five young sons and a reported marriage of about fourteen years. Sebran was a Georgia-born day laborer, and both husband and wife were reported as Georgia natives. The household no longer looks like a one-record family. Later Florida censuses track a closely matching family under the surnames Kelly and Kelley and under given-name forms that include Sebran, Sebron, Seabram, and the initials S. C.

The clearest early anchor outside Brooks County is the Sumter County marriage record for S. C. Kelley and Ella Wingate, dated 30 August 1885. That record fits the 1900 household well and provides a documented Sumter County origin for Ella before the family's appearance in Barney. Additional Sumter County Wingate records now place Ella in a broader local family cluster, but they do not yet settle her exact parentage. In 1870 an Ella Wingate, age four, appears in the household of Franklin Wingate and Sarah J. Wingate in Sumter County. In 1880 an Ellen Wingate, age eighteen, appears in the household of F. C. Wingate and Sarah Wingate in the same county. Those records show that Ella belonged to the Sumter County Wingate cluster. The exact relationship among the Franklin, F. C., and later Lawrence Wingate lines remains unproved through primary sources, and the 1870 and 1880 Ella or Ellen entries should be treated as strong contextual evidence rather than a completed proof chain.

The later census sequence is strong. In 1910 the family appears in Branford, Suwannee County, Florida, under S. C. Kelley. The children in the household closely match the 1900 Brooks County family, including Cleveland, Charley, Olin or Orin, and Earnest, along with younger children born after the Barney census. In 1920 Sebron C. Kelly appears in Branford with wife Mary and children including Irvin, Minnie, Nettie, and Winnie. In 1930 S. C. Kelley appears in Alachua County, Florida, still with wife Mary and several younger children. In 1940 Seabram C. Kelly appears in Lafayette County, Florida, again with wife Mary. Taken together, those records point to a single family line that moved from Georgia into north Florida over several decades.

The main unresolved issue is the name of Sebran's wife after 1900. The Brooks County census and the 1885 marriage record point to Ella Wingate Kelly, but the later Florida censuses identify the wife as Mary. Several explanations remain possible. Ella may have used Mary as a first or middle name in later life. Sebran may have remarried between 1900 and 1910. One or more records may also have been read or indexed imperfectly. For now, the safest wording is that Ella Wingate is securely tied to the 1885 marriage and to the 1900 Brooks County household, while the exact relationship between 1900 Ella and later Mary still needs direct confirmation.

The children's sequence also helps tie the records together. Cleveland, Charley, Olin, and Earnest continue in ways that are broadly consistent across 1900 and 1910, while younger Florida-born children appear in the later censuses. Early Kelly, the youngest child in 1900, has not yet been followed securely into later records under that exact name, and may have been recorded later under a nickname, middle name, or variant reading.

No reliable cemetery memorials have yet been identified for this household. The Find a Grave memorials reviewed for Thomas Christian Kelley and Ellen Wood Kelley from Jones County, Georgia, belong to a different family and should not be used for HH#72.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#72 to Sumter County Wingate cluster: Ella Kelly is strongly associated with the Sumter County Wingate cluster through the 30 August 1885 Sumter County marriage of S. C. Kelley to Ella Wingate and through the 1870 and 1880 Sumter County census placements of Ella or Ellen Wingate in households headed by Franklin Wingate and F. C. Wingate.
  • Possible connection to HH#102 Ben Wingate: The HH#102 line also traces to Sumter County through Benjamin Wingate's death certificate, which names his father as Lawrence Wingate and gives Sumter County as the birthplace for both father and son. The HH#72 and HH#102 households appear to belong to the same broader Wingate family cluster in Sumter County, Georgia, but the exact relationship between those lines has not yet been established through primary-source evidence.
  • No proven Kelly-to-Kelly link: No evidence currently proves any relationship between HH#72 and HH#64 James Kelly beyond the shared surname.

  • Ella Wingate's exact parentage within the Sumter County Wingate cluster remains unsettled. The households of Franklin Wingate, F. C. Wingate, and the later Lawrence Wingate line appear to belong to the same broader family cluster in Sumter County, Georgia, but the precise relationships have not yet been established through primary-source evidence.

docs.text: Partially reconstructed and materially improved. The household is now supported by the 1885 Sumter County marriage record, the 1900 Brooks County census, a strong later census trail through Suwannee, Alachua, and Lafayette counties in Florida, and contextual Sumter County Wingate records that place Ella within a broader local family cluster. The major remaining questions are Ella's exact parentage and whether the later wife Mary is the same person as Ella Wingate Kelly or a second wife.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Mary Clark can be followed across a useful four-census chain in Brooks County from 1870 through 1910. In 1870 she appears as the wife of Fortune Clark in Brooks County, with children Henrietta, Malinda, Margaret, and Edward in the household. That early census gives her birthplace as Georgia and places the family near Quitman. In 1880 she appears as Mary J. Clark in Morven with husband Fortum Clark and children Henrietta, Margaritte, and Edward. Those two censuses anchor the family before Fortune's disappearance from the record.

By 1900 Mary was a widow heading her own household in Barney. The census describes her as a farmer who owned a mortgaged farm. Living with her were son Ed Clark, daughter Ida Clark, and Henry Hunter, listed as an adopted son, along with three boarders. The same entry states that Mary had borne five children and that three were then living. That count fits the broader household pattern reasonably well, though it still leaves open the identity of the missing child or children between the 1870 and 1900 records.

The 1910 census places Mary J. Clark in the household of Coleman Rountree and Maggie Rountree, where Mary is recorded as mother-in-law to Coleman and mother to Maggie. That entry gives direct support for treating Maggie Rountree as Mary Clark's daughter and links this household to the Coleman Rountree household treated elsewhere in the encyclopedia. The 1910 census also reports that Mary had borne five children, with two then living, showing that one more child had died between 1900 and 1910.

Two later records help extend the lives of younger household members. A Brooks County marriage record dated 5 Jan 1924 shows Ed Clarke marrying Mary Larkins. The surname appears there as Clarke, which should be treated as a spelling variant rather than as a separate man. A likely later record for Henry Hunter appears in his World War I draft registration in Brooks County, dated 12 Sept 1918. That card gives his birth date as 23 Apr 1884, residence on Quitman Route 1, occupation as a laborer, and nearest relative as Addie Hunter. The draft card strongly suggests that the Henry Hunter in Mary's 1900 household remained in Brooks County into adulthood, though the age on the card does not align perfectly with the 1900 census age and the identification should remain slightly cautious.

Several points remain unsettled. Mary's birthplace is Georgia in 1870 but Virginia in 1880, 1900, and 1910. Fortune or Fortum Clark is present in 1880 but gone by 1900, yet no death, probate, or burial record has been located. Ida Clark is present in 1900 but has not yet been traced forward in a secure later record. No cemetery memorial has yet been found for Mary Clark or Fortune Clark in the Brooks County searches used for this revision.

docs.text: • HH#73 to HH#122 Coleman Rountree: The 1910 census places Mary Clark in the household of daughter Maggie Rountree and son-in-law Coleman Rountree, giving direct evidence for the Clark-Rountree connection.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented for the core household structure from 1870 through 1910. The census chain establishes Mary with Fortune or Fortum Clark, then as a widowed head of household, and finally in the Rountree household of her daughter Maggie. Ed Clark is carried forward by his 1924 marriage record, and Henry Hunter likely appears in a 1918 Brooks County draft registration. The main remaining gaps are Mary and Fortune's end-of-life records, Ida Clark's later life, and supporting property records.

docs.text:
This household is documented securely in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. The entry shows Allen as a married Black man born in North Carolina in April 1870, working as a turpentine laborer and renting a house. Julia is listed as his wife, born in Georgia in May 1881, and Irene appears as their one-year-old daughter. The census also reports that Allen's parents were born in North Carolina.

The main interpretive problem in this entry is the surname. The indexed transcript reads Dena, while the original census image may read Devane. The handwriting is faded enough that the surname should remain uncertain for now. For that reason, follow-up research should consider both Dena and Devane, along with nearby variants such as Devan and Devaney where appropriate.

At present, no additional record has been found that securely follows Allen, Julia, or Irene beyond the 1900 census. That means the household should be treated as a thin but valid census-based entry rather than as a fully developed family reconstruction. The 1900 census does show the family as part of the Barney turpentine labor population, but there is not enough evidence yet to make stronger claims about migration history, kin ties to nearby households, or later life events.

docs.text:
Albert Love is securely documented in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. That entry shows a Black man born in North Carolina in May 1865, single, renting a house, and working as a turpentine laborer. He was living alone, and the census states that both of his parents were born in North Carolina. At present, this 1900 household is the only firm record anchor for the Albert Love of HH#75.

Earlier and later census candidates have been reviewed, but none can be accepted as the same man on the present evidence. An 1880 census record for Albert S. Love in Ball Ground, Murray County, Georgia, should be rejected because that individual was white, born in Georgia, and living in a household that does not match the 1900 Barney profile. A 1910 census record for Albert Love in Attapulgus, Decatur County, Georgia, should also be rejected because that man was reported as born in Florida, with a Florida-born mother, and was already married to Sarah A. Love. Those facts conflict materially with the 1900 Brooks County entry.

Because no other primary record has been found that fits the 1900 Albert Love securely, the household should remain a narrow census-based entry. The 1900 census does place him within the turpentine labor population in Barney, but there is not enough evidence to reconstruct his earlier family, trace him forward with confidence, or connect him to any other Love household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Adam Allen is securely documented in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. That entry shows a Black man born in North Carolina in May 1870, married, literate, working as a turpentine laborer, and living in a household with his wife Patsy and daughter Leana. The census also states that both of Adam's parents were born in North Carolina. As a household record, the 1900 entry is clear and stable.

The complication comes from a Brooks County marriage license and return for Adam Allen and Henrietta McLeod. The license was issued on 7 September 1897, and the return states that Adam Allen and Henrietta McLeod were joined in matrimony on 13 October 1897. That marriage record is also a solid primary source. It does not fit neatly with the 1900 census, which names Adam's wife as Patsy and reports that the couple had been married for two years.

Several explanations remain possible. Patsy and Henrietta may have been the same woman under different names, Henrietta may have died and Adam may have remarried before the 1900 census, or the marriage record and census may belong to different men of the same name. Leana's age adds another layer of uncertainty, because she was about eight years old in 1900 and therefore predates the reported two-year marriage of Adam and Patsy. At present, no additional primary record has been found to resolve the family structure of this household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Frank Golding is securely documented in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. That record shows a Black man born in Georgia in April 1859, widowed, literate, renting a house, and working as a cashier. He was living alone, and the census states that his mother was born in Georgia. Within the Barney enumeration, his occupation stands out because most nearby households were tied to manual labor, especially turpentine work.

The earlier census material supports a probable multi-census identification. In 1870, a Frank Golding age eleven appears in District 7, Chatham County, Georgia, in a household with Mary Golding and other Golding family members. In 1880, a Frank Golding age twenty-three appears in District 16, Liberty County, Georgia, listed as a Black single day laborer born in Georgia, with his mother also reported as born in Georgia. Those details fit the later Barney household reasonably well. The age progression is workable, the surname remains consistent, and the Georgia birth pattern aligns across the records.

The earlier draft also cited a possible 1896 Atlanta city census entry for Frank Golden. That reference may be useful, but it should be treated cautiously unless the underlying record is rechecked directly. Even without that 1896 item, the 1870, 1880, and 1900 census records provide a plausible working reconstruction for Frank Golding's adult path from a Chatham County household to an 1880 Liberty County labor record and then to the 1900 Barney household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Walter and Alice Wooten are securely documented in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. That record shows Walter as a Black farmer born in North Carolina in April 1869, with both parents also reported as born in North Carolina. Alice, his wife, was likewise born in North Carolina. The census states that the couple had been married sixteen years and were renting their farm. No children were present in the household.

Alice is documented again through her 4 January 1926 death certificate from Nashville, Berrien County, Georgia. That record identifies her as Alice Wooten, a Black married woman age fifty-seven, born in Sampson County, North Carolina, with parents named as Toney McDuffie and Claresy McDuffie. The certificate also gives her spouse as W. H. Wooten. Taken together, the 1900 census and the 1926 death record provide a reliable core profile for the household and establish Alice's maiden family as McDuffie.

The surviving evidence is useful but still limited. The present record set supports the Brooks County household in 1900 and Alice's later identification in Berrien County in 1926. It does not yet establish when Walter died, whether the couple remained together continuously after 1900, or whether any children were born to them and lived elsewhere.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
William Williams is documented securely in the 1900 census at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. That record shows a Black household headed by a North Carolina-born turpentine laborer, with wife Sarah and two young sons, French and John. It is the anchor record for the family and the clearest direct statement of the household in 1900.

The later census material supplied by the user suggests that this family can probably be followed beyond Brooks County and beyond 1900. In 1910 and 1920, a man recorded as Henry Williams appears in a household that matches the expected family pattern closely. In 1930, the head appears as William H. Williams, which narrows the gap between William and Henry but does not resolve it. By 1940, Sarah Williams appears as a widow, and by 1950 a Sarah Williams of the right age appears in the household of Willie Tolbert at Lenox, Cook County, Georgia. Taken together, those records support a likely continuing census chain for the same family across six enumerations.

The main caution is the head's name. The 1900 record calls him William Williams. The later records reviewed here use Henry Williams and then William H. Williams. That pattern may reflect ordinary name variation, a middle name, or reporting differences between enumerators, but no direct record yet explains it. The structure of the household is close enough to keep the later trail in the reconstruction, but the identification should remain probable rather than final until a marriage, death, or other direct record ties the names together.

A 14 October 1899 item in the Valdosta Times naming "B. Williams" among Barney-area farmers should stay outside the core proof. The initial does not match the known 1900 head securely, and the notice may refer to another Williams family in the area. The FamilySearch profile is also best used as clue-level support rather than as independent evidence.

  • A death record and burial record for Sarah Williams have not yet been found.
  • The 1950 Lenox household should be tied more directly to this family before Willie Tolbert is treated as a proved child or close relative.

The present evidence supports the 1900 Barney household securely and gives a likely census trail forward through 1950, but the unresolved shift between William, Henry, and William H. still needs direct-record follow-up before the identification can be treated as final.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Amos Radford in Barney, Brooks County, as a married Black household head born in North Carolina in June 1866. His wife Missouria was also born in North Carolina, and the household included three children born in Georgia: James, Thomas, and Lillie. The schedule states that Amos worked as a woodsman, that the couple had been married three years, and that they lived in a house recorded as owned.

A Brooks County marriage record dated 17 June 1897 shows Amos "Rodford" marrying Missouri Wootin. The date fits the 1900 census report that the couple had been married three years. The handwritten license and return are especially useful here because they preserve the surname forms close to the event itself: Amos appears as Radford/Rodford in the record set, and Missouri appears as Missouri Wootin/Wooten.

By 1910 the family had moved to Precinct 17, Volusia County, Florida. Amos, then age 43, was enumerated as a Black or mulatto farmer on his own farm, owned free of mortgage. Missouri was still in the household, and daughter Lily B., age 12, remained with them. James and Thomas were no longer present. That absence is not enough to place them elsewhere, but it does show that the household had narrowed by the time the family reached Florida.

The 1920 census appears to preserve Missouri after Amos's disappearance from the record, though under a distorted given name. In Osteen, Volusia County, a widowed Black woman enumerated as "Missine Radford," age 36 and born in North Carolina, headed a household with daughter Litter/Little/Littie Bell Lonn and son-in-law Willie Lonn. The combination of surname, birthplace, widowhood, Florida location, and the daughter whose name fits Lily/Lillie makes this a strong probable continuation of the same family, but the entry is not explicit enough to treat the identification as proved beyond doubt.

The earlier 1880 census also offers a plausible but still unproved lead on Amos's parentage. In Tatoms Township, Columbus County, North Carolina, an Amos Radford, age 15, appears in the household of John and Charity Radford. That entry aligns well with the later Amos on name, approximate age, and the later reports that both of Amos's parents were born in North Carolina. Still, without a direct parent-linked record, the 1880 household should be treated as a probable identification rather than a settled one.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • Missouri Wootin's maiden surname invites comparison with HH#80 Walter Wooten, but the present evidence does not prove any relationship between the two households.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:

  • No direct record has yet been found naming Amos's parents.
  • The 1880 Columbus County, North Carolina Amos Radford in the John and Charity Radford household is a good match, but still inferential.
  • No direct death or burial record for Amos has been verified in the present evidence set.
  • Missouri appears likely to be the widowed "Missine Radford" in Volusia County in 1920, but that identification remains probable rather than certain.
  • The later lives of sons James and Thomas Radford have not yet been traced.
  • The possible Wootin/Wooten connection to HH#80 remains unproved.

docs.text: Well-supported core household. The 1897 marriage record and the 1900 and 1910 census entries establish the family securely, and the 1920 Volusia County widow appears to be the same Missouri with their daughter. Parentage for Amos and any wider Wootin/Wooten kinship remain open questions.

docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places John T. Morrow in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, as a white farmer with wife Minerva "Minnie" and nine children still at home. By that date, the family was plainly well established in the Barney community.

The census chain is now fairly solid. In 1880, John T. Morrow, age 31, was enumerated at Morven, Brooks County, with wife L. J. V. Morrow, age 29, and children John W., Eliza A., and Sallie. In 1900, the same couple appears at Barney with the household expanded to include William, Lillian, Eliza, Sallie, James, Thomas, Caddie, Charley, and Nancy. In 1910, John F. Morrow, age 60, and wife Laura J. Morrow, age 57, were still in Barney with James and Nancy in the home. Together, those three censuses show the same household across thirty years in the same part of Brooks County.

The later widow entries also help identify Minerva "Minnie" Morrow as Laura J. V. Delk Morrow. A Brooks County marriage index entry shows "Liv Delk" marrying J. T. Morrow on 22 December 1871. In 1920, Mrs. L. J. V. Marrow, age 68, appears in Barney as mother-in-law in the W. E. Phillips household. In 1930, Laura J. Morrow, age 78, appears in the same family cluster in Brooks County as mother-in-law in the William E. Phillips household. Laura Jane Virginia Morrow's 29 June 1930 Brooks County death certificate ties the chain together directly. It names her as Laura Jane Virginia Morrow, widow of John Morrow, daughter of John Delks and Jane Hodges, with W. E. Phillips of Barney as informant. Read together with the 1880 wife recorded as L. J. V. Morrow and the 1900 wife recorded as Minnie, those records support the conclusion that the 1900 Minnie was Laura Jane Virginia Delk Morrow.

Earlier material is less secure. A Laura J. V. Delk, age 8, appears in Brooks County in 1860 in the household of John W. Delk, which fits the later wife and supports the Delk maiden-family identification. A 1860 Heard County census entry places John T. Morrow, age 9, in the household of Joseph E. Morrow, age 46, and Eliza G. Morrow, age 45. That record fits HH#84 John T. Morrow reasonably well on name, age, place, and family structure, and it gives the Heard County origin theory more weight than it had before. Even so, it is still one step short of proof, because a direct bridge from that child in 1860 to the adult John T. Morrow in Brooks County has not yet been found. A possible 1870 John Marrow in Brooks County may point to the same line, but that identification remains uncertain. Find a Grave memorials for Joseph Ewing Morrow and Eliza Jane Walker Morrow are consistent with the 1860 Heard County household and with the broader family hypothesis, but they remain derivative support rather than proof of John T. Morrow's parentage. A memorial for Sarah Winfrey Walker McCoy, identified there as Eliza Jane Walker Morrow's mother, also fits the broader Walker and McCoy network, but it too remains a clue rather than direct evidence for HH#84.

The daughter lines are clearer than they were at the start of this review. Laura's death certificate first pointed toward the Phillips household because W. E. Phillips served as informant. That link is reinforced by additional records: a Brooks County marriage record shows Ruth Morrow marrying Wm. Earnest Phillips on 19 April 1913; the 1920 Barney census shows Ruth Phillips, identified as Ruth Morrow, in the W. E. Phillips household with her mother listed as L. J. V. Morrow; and the 1930 Brooks County census again places Ruth Phillips with Laura J. Morrow in the same household cluster. Those records support the conclusion that Ruth, or Nancy Ruth Morrow, was the daughter who married William Earnest Phillips and remained in Barney.

The Sallie line is also much better defined. A Brooks County marriage record shows Sallie Morrow marrying Jno. Delk on 7 December 1905. The 1910, 1920, 1930, and 1940 censuses track Sallie Delk in Barney and Militia District 1571 with husband John F. Delk and sons Carl and Hoke, then as a widow with son Hoke still at home in 1940. A World War II draft registration card for Joseph Hoke Delk of Barney names his mother as Mrs. Sallie Delk of Barney, which fits that census trail. Camp Ground Cemetery memorials for Sally E. Morrow Delk and John Flemming Delk match the same household and children shown in the census material, and a Florida death notice and SSDI entry point to Sallie's later death in Orange County, Florida, in April 1966. The cemetery and index material remains derivative, but the full set of records makes it likely that the Sallie Morrow in the 1900 household was the daughter who married John Flemming Delk and stayed rooted in the Barney community for decades.

Camp Ground Cemetery memorials for Nancy Ruth Morrow Phillips and William Ernest Phillips fit the same family and burial cluster, but they should still be treated as derivative support unless backed by direct records. Camp Ground Cemetery memorials for J. W. Morrow and James E. Morrow remain plausible matches to sons from this household, but those identifications still need parent-linked support.

docs.text:

  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • A death record, probate record, burial record, or obituary for John T. Morrow is still needed.
  • The identifications of J. W. Morrow and James E. Morrow as sons from this household still need direct supporting records that name parents.
  • The Phillips daughter question is now largely resolved in favor of Ruth Morrow, but a death certificate, obituary, or other direct record naming both parents would still strengthen the case further.
  • Sallie Morrow's Delk line is now strongly supported across marriage and four censuses, but a direct death certificate or obituary naming her parents would still tighten the proof.
  • Laura's 1930 death certificate should be paired with a clearly readable burial record or grave evidence if the burial place on the certificate cannot be read confidently from the available image.
  • The 1860 Heard County John T. Morrow entry is now a strong lead, but it still needs a direct bridge to the adult John T. Morrow in Brooks County.
  • The possible 1870 Brooks County John Marrow entry needs more corroboration before it can be treated as this same John.
  • The Joseph Ewing Morrow and Eliza Jane Walker Morrow memorials support the Heard County hypothesis, but they do not by themselves establish that HH#84 John T. Morrow was their son.
  • The Sarah Winfrey Walker McCoy memorial may help connect the line to the Walker and McCoy families, but it remains derivative support and does not close the case.
  • The wider Delk, Hodges, and Lashley connections should remain outside the core proof until they are tied in through marriage, death, probate, land, or church records.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-supported census reconstruction, but not fully closed. The 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930 censuses now give a strong multi-decade chain for John T. Morrow and Laura Jane Virginia Delk Morrow, and the Ruth Phillips and Sallie Delk evidence materially improves the child identifications. John's death and burial and several son identifications still need direct-record support.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Georgian Lashley in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, as a widowed farmer with three children still at home: John, William, and Annie. The same entry reports that she was born in November 1856 and was the mother of five children, four then living. That count helps frame the household and suggests that one child had died before 1900 or was counted differently in later material.

The broader census chain is now reasonably coherent. In 1860, G. A. Jones appears in Milford, Baker County, Georgia, in the household of L. Jones and M. Jones. In 1870, Georgia Anna Jones appears in Mitchell County in the household of Levi J. Jones and Mary Jones. Taken together, those entries support the identification of Georgian Lashley as a Jones daughter from that family, though the 1860 initials-only entry still calls for caution. A Mitchell County marriage record dated 30 May 1876 then records the marriage of a bride indexed as Georgin James, with alternate readings including Georgianna Jones, to George W. Dashley. The handwriting and index do not line up perfectly, but the record matches the place, date, and couple well enough to use it as the working marriage record for this household, with the name-reading problem left open. By 1880, Georgia Lashley appears in Baker County with husband George Lashley and children Tommie and Ida; Ida was eight months old at enumeration, which fits a birth in late 1879 or early 1880. In 1900, Georgian is a widow in Barney. In 1910, a female entry recorded as "George H. Lashley" appears to be the same woman, still widowed, renting a farm and living with son William H. Lashley; that entry again reports five children born and four living. In 1920, she appears as "George Ann Lashley," mother in the Willie Lashley household. In 1930, she appears as "Georgian S. Lashley," again as mother in the William H. Lashley household. In 1940, she appears in Briggs, Brooks County, as "Mrs W. G. Lashley," age eighty-two, widowed, and identified as mother in the W. H. Lashley household. The 1940 census and the Brooks County death certificate place her at the end of her life in the same community.

Taken as a whole, the record points to a long residence in Brooks County after the move from Mitchell County. The repeated child counts and household ties make the 1910, 1920, and 1930 entries more convincing than they first appeared. The death certificate strengthens several points that had been less secure: it gives her as Georgianna Savannah Jones Lashley, born 7 November 1856 in Mitchell County, names her parents as Levy Jones and Mary Cawley, identifies her as widow of G. W. Lashley, and places her burial at Mt. Zion Camp Ground. It is still a late, informant-based record, so it adds weight rather than closing every question by itself. Some child identifications still need fuller direct-record support.

The evidence is enough to describe Georgian as a widowed Brooks County farm woman whose household can be followed from childhood in the Jones family through old age with son Willie. It is also clear that daughter Annie married into the Morrow household already documented at HH#84. What the record does not justify is treating every later online detail as settled fact.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Daughter Annie Lashley married J. W. Morrow on 4 February 1910 in Brooks County.
  • J. W. Morrow's 1939 death certificate names his parents as John Morrow and Laura Delk, tying Annie's line directly to HH#84 John T. Morrow and Laura Jane Virginia Delk Morrow.
  • Find a Grave memorials for both J. W. Morrow and Annie L. Lashley Morrow align with the death and burial data already in hand, and they reinforce Camp Ground Cemetery as the family burial place, but they remain derivative support.

docs.text:

  • George Lashley's full identity, death date, burial place, and parentage still need direct-record support, though the marriage record and death certificate both strengthen the reading of his name as G. W. Lashley.
  • The full name "Georgianna Savannah Jones Lashley," birth date 7 November 1856, and parent names Levy Jones and Mary Cawley are now supported by the death certificate, but as late informant-supplied details they should still be weighed alongside earlier records.
  • Ida Lashley Baker, Tommie Lashley, John Lashley, and Willie Lashley still need cleaner parent-linked tracking across marriage, death, census, or burial records.
  • Annie Lashley is now directly tied to J. W. Morrow by the 4 February 1910 Brooks County marriage record and can be followed in Brooks County through the 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses. J. W. Morrow died in Barney on 15 February 1939, and his death certificate names parents John Morrow and Laura Delk. By 1940 Annie appears as widowed head of household in Barney, and by 1950 Annie L. Morrow appears in Barney with brother John W. Lashley in her household. A Georgia death index entry for Annie E. Morrow, who died 26 December 1959 at age 71, is consistent with this line, but the full death certificate is still needed before that final step is treated as settled.
  • The 1910 "George H. Lashley" entry now looks very likely to be the same widow from the 1900 household, but the original image should still be checked carefully for every field and adjoining context.
  • Any claimed Jones-family links to other Barney Jones households should remain outside the core proof until supported by direct records.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented household, though not fully closed. The census chain from childhood through death is strong enough to support Georgian's identification as a Jones woman who became a widowed Lashley in Brooks County, and that reading is reinforced by both the 30 May 1876 Mitchell County marriage record and the 1940 death certificate. Annie's line is also well anchored through her marriage record, five census decades, and her husband's 1939 death certificate. The marriage record still needs careful name-reading, and George Lashley's later identity and death, along with some of the other child identifications, still need firmer direct proof.
