docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Frank Jones Head 56 Georgia Farmer Malashia Jones Son 28 Georgia Laborer Farm Thomas Jones Son 24 Georgia Laborer Saw Mill Sam Jones Son 20 Georgia Laborer Farm Julia Jones Daughter 19 Georgia — Horris Jones Son 17 Georgia Laborer Farm Gussie Jones Daughter 22 Georgia — May Jones Granddaughter 1 Georgia — Nathan Culpepper Uncle 79 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Frank Jones in Barney as a widowed farmer born in December 1843. That schedule indexes him as "Jones Frank," and several children in the household are likewise indexed with Frank as though it were their surname. In context, those entries are best read as Jones family members with reversed or distorted given-name/surname order. Cornelia had died before that enumeration, and several younger children or recently married children still clustered around the household. The entry also fits the larger census trail that follows him from childhood into old age.

That trail begins with the 1850 census, where Franklin Jones, age six, appears in Thomas County, Georgia, in the household of Malake Jones, forty-one, and Sara Jones, thirty-six. By 1860, a strong match appears in Brooks County as Malachi F. Jones, age sixteen, in the household of M. Jones and Sarah R. Jones. On 17 December 1867, Brooks County records the marriage of Frank Jones and Cornelia E. Powell. In 1870, Malachi Jones, twenty-six, appears in Quitman, Brooks County, with wife Cornelia, twenty-four, and sons James and Edgar. In 1880, Frank Jones, thirty-seven, appears in Nankin, Brooks County, with Cornelia and children James P., Edgar, Alberta, Maliki F., Thomas J., Emma A., and infant Samuel. In 1900, he is the widowed head of HH#86 in Barney. In 1910, he appears as Malichi Jones Sr., age sixty-seven, living with son Malichi. In 1920, M. Frank Jones, age seventy-six, appears in the household of son Edgar J. Jones as father. Taken together, those records support a stable identification from the 1850s through the final known census appearance in 1920.

Several non-census records add useful detail. A Brooks County reconstruction oath entry dated 8 July 1867 records Malachi Jones in the Quitman precinct of Brooks County, placing him in the county only months before his marriage. The Brooks County marriage record dated 16 December 1867 and returned 17 December 1867 anchors Frank's marriage to Cornelia E. Powell, and the original document identifies the groom as "Mr. M. Franklin Jones" and the bride as "Miss Cornelia E. Powell." A tax digest entry for Malachi F. Jones in Nankin District 659 during 1878-1882 shows him on the tax list but, in the cited page, does not show land held in his own name. A 14 Oct 1899 Valdosta Times item names Frank Jones among Barney-area farmers, placing him in the local farming community just before the 1900 census. A Confederate soldier profile for M. Frank Jones gives enlistment on 15 May 1862 at age nineteen, residence in Brooks County, birth about 1843 in Thomas County, and service in Company K, 50th Infantry. A Confederate prisoner-of-war record identifies Frank Jones as a private in Company K, 50th Georgia Regiment, imprisoned on 6 April 1865 and received on 15 April 1865. The imprisonment place is given as Sailor's Creek, Virginia in the soldier profile and Harpers Farm in the prisoner record, so that point should be left as a documented discrepancy pending the full compiled service file. Frank's 1909 Brooks County Confederate pension packet confirms that he applied as an indigent soldier under the name M. F. Jones. The visible application image supports the broad picture of age- and poverty-based need and appears to show no meaningful property, though the handwriting should be transcribed from the full packet before exact quotations are relied upon. That evidence fits the broader picture of economic decline after the stronger 1870 showing, though the exact course of his finances still needs fuller documentation.

The family connection to HH#71 is strong. The 1870 census places Edgar in Frank's household as a child, the 1920 census places Frank in Edgar J. Jones's household as father, and Edgar J. Jones's 1928 Georgia death certificate names his father as F. Jones and his mother as Cornelia Powell. On that basis, Frank Jones can be treated as the father of HH#71 Edgar Jelks Jones and therefore as James E. Jones's great-great-grandfather. The broader proposed connection to HH#56 William Fletcher Jones is still only a working hypothesis and should remain separate from the proved line unless direct evidence turns up.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The current file supports treating Frank Jones as a Confederate veteran. A soldier profile for M. Frank Jones gives enlistment on 15 May 1862 and service in Company K, 50th Georgia Infantry; a prisoner-of-war record identifies Frank Jones as a private in Company K, 50th Georgia Regiment, imprisoned on 6 April 1865 and received on 15 April 1865. The imprisonment location differs between the preserved records, so that detail should stay flagged until the full compiled service file is reviewed. His 1909 Brooks County Confederate pension packet further anchors the identification under M. F. Jones.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Frank Jones is the father of HH#71 Edgar Jelks Jones.
  • Through Edgar Jelks Jones, whose 1928 death certificate names parents F. Jones and Cornelia Powell, Frank Jones is in James E. Jones's direct line as great-great-grandfather.
  • Nathan Culpepper appears in the 1900 household as "uncle," but the exact relationship still needs direct-record proof.
  • A possible connection to HH#56 William Fletcher Jones has been suggested, but it remains unproved.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • Frank's full name is often given as Malachi Franklin Jones or Malachi Franklin "Frank" Jones. The record set now includes "Malachi F. Jones," "M. Frank Jones," and "Mr. M. Franklin Jones," which strongly supports that expansion, though the exact preferred everyday form across his lifetime still rests on stitched evidence rather than one single definitive identity document.
  • A published Bible-record compilation also gives "M. Frank Jones b. 25 Dec 1843, d. Nov 1920, m. in 1866 to Cornelia Powell", but that should be treated as secondary derivative evidence until matched against primary records.
  • Cornelia E. Powell Jones is well anchored as Frank's wife through the 1867 marriage record and the censuses. A Find a Grave memorial provides a likely burial at Camp Ground Cemetery, Mount Zion Church, Morven, Brooks County, but her death date and burial still need stronger direct-record support if available.
  • Frank's death date, death place, and burial have not yet been documented here with a death certificate, obituary, cemetery record, probate file, or estate record.
  • The military summary should still be checked against the full compiled Confederate service record. The soldier profile and prisoner-of-war record agree on identity, regiment, and April 1865 imprisonment timing, but they differ on the imprisonment place, listed as Sailor's Creek, Virginia in one source and Harpers Farm in the other.
  • The 1909 pension application packet should still be reviewed in full and transcribed carefully, especially for residence, disability, financial status, witness statements, and any exact wording about property and family support.
  • The tax digest evidence should be extended across additional years, because one Nankin page showing no land in his name does not by itself explain the 1870 property valuation.
  • Nathan Culpepper's appearance as "uncle" in 1900 needs a direct proof chain; the proposed Powell-French-Culpepper explanation should not be treated as established without supporting records.
  • The proposed relationship between Frank Jones and HH#56 William Fletcher Jones needs direct evidence such as probate, deed, guardianship, Bible, or other kinship records.
  • Each child should be tracked with direct marriage, death, burial, or later census records so the family group rests on more than household appearances alone.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented, but not source-exhausted. The census chain from 1850 through 1920 is strong, the 1867 marriage record and 1909 pension application are important anchors, and the father-son link to Edgar Jelks Jones is persuasive. Cornelia now has likely cemetery evidence, but the main gaps are Frank's death and burial, stronger direct support for Cornelia's death and burial, fuller documentation of the military and pension files, and proof for the more extended kinship claims.

docs.title: Household #87: Lashley, Henry
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Henry Lashley headed a 2-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Henry Lashley headed a 2-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner.

Henry Lashley's listed occupation was Day Laborer Farm.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Henry Lashley Head 55 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Kittie Lashley Wife 50 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census shows a small Barney household consisting of Henry Lashley and his wife Kittie Lashley. Henry was born in Georgia in May 1845, was working as a day laborer on a farm, and was living in a rented house rather than on land he owned. Both Henry and Kittie were recorded in Brooks County in 1900 without children in the household, so the earlier version of this entry overstated the household structure and should not be followed.

The census trail now in hand points to a long marriage and a later move from south Georgia into north Florida. In 1850, Henry A. Lashly, age two, appears in Lee County, Georgia, in the household of Richmond Lashly and Atha Lashly. In 1860, Henry A. Lashly, age twelve, appears in Terrell County, Georgia, again in the household of Richard Lashly and Atha Lashly, along with siblings that closely match the 1850 household. That ten-year bridge makes the Richmond and Atha Lashly parentage for Henry much stronger than it was before. In 1870, Henry Laslie, age twenty-three, appears in Terrell County, Georgia, with Keziah Laslie, age twenty-four, and Mary Laslie, age eight. In 1900, Henry Lashley, age fifty-five, and Kittie Lashley, age fifty, were in Barney, Brooks County. A Brooks County court item printed in the Valdosta Daily Times on 15 November 1906 reports "State vs. H. A. Lashley, misdemeanor. Plea of guilty." The brief item does not state the underlying offense, but it does place H. A. Lashley in Brooks County court records between the 1900 Barney census and the later Florida records. By 1910, a strong later match appears in Hamilton County, Florida, where Harim A. Lashley, age sixty-two, born in Georgia, was the head of household in Smith District with wife Cisrah Lashley; he was working as a chair maker in his own shop and living on a rented farm. In 1920, H. A. Lashley, age seventy-two, born in Georgia, appears in Jasper, Hamilton County, Florida, with wife Kissiah Lashley, working as a laborer in a shoe shop and again living in rented quarters. A 1929 reunion booklet for the Florida Old Confederate Soldiers and Sailors Home lists "H. A. Lashley", age eighty-two, and says he enlisted in Atlanta on 15 April 1863 under Colonel G. W. Lee in L. L. Strozier's Company, Company F of Lee's Battalion, later being wounded in the foot during the Atlanta fighting. That item is a plausible late-life match for the same man because the initials and age fit the established census trail, but the military details should still be checked against formal service records before they are treated as settled biography. A Florida death index entry for Henry A. Lashley records a 1930 death in Jackson County, Florida. An earlier Jacksonville death notice published on 4 October 1930 reports that Henry A. Lashley, age eighty-two, died that day at the Confederate Soldiers and Sailors Home after a brief illness, states that he was born in Terrell County, Georgia, and says he had been in the home for five years. A Florida Times-Union notice published on 5 October 1930 reports the same death at the Confederate Soldiers and Sailors Home on Talleyrand Avenue, says he had been at the home for five years, and appears to identify survivors including a sister, Mrs. Glover of Cairo, and two nephews, J. R. Glover of Cairo and L. Glover of Woodville, Florida. Follow-up notices published on 6 October 1930 in both the Jacksonville Journal and the Florida Times-Union report funeral services for Henry A. Lashley and place his burial in the Confederate plot at Old City Cemetery. Taken together, those items make a strong case that the 1930 Jackson County death index belongs to the same H. A. Lashley who appears in the earlier Georgia and Florida census trail.

These records strongly suggest one man moving across records under Henry Lashley, Henry A. Lashly, Henry Laslie, Harim A. Lashley, and H. A. Lashley. The wife likewise appears under several forms that look like the same person: Keziah, Kittie, Cisrah, and Kissiah. The broad pattern is coherent, but the spelling shifts and the household differences mean the chain should still be treated as very strong but not finished.

The present evidence does not yet justify the stronger claims previously made about Henry's children in 1900 or about a proved brother relationship to George William Lashley of HH#85. The 1850 and 1860 Richmond and Atha Lashly households now give a solid case for Henry's parentage, but the separate step tying this Henry directly to George of HH#85 still needs its own proof. The 5 October 1930 Florida Times-Union survivor list also appears to help identify one collateral family connection: a sister "Mrs. Glover of Cairo" and nephews "J. R. Glover of Cairo" and "L. Glover of Woodville, Florida." Those names fit Julia Glover, born in Georgia about 1861-1863, who appears in Mitchell/Decatur/Grady County records and is indexed in some later derivative material as Julia Lashley Glover. The fit is strengthened by the 1930 Cairo household of J. R. Glover with widowed mother Julia Glover and by derivative memorial material that names Julia as a daughter of Richmond Hardy Lashley and Athea Harrell Lashley, but that identification should still be treated as highly probable rather than fully proved until supported by a stronger direct-record link.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The military evidence for Henry A. Lashley is prominent but still cautionary. The 1929 Florida Old Confederate Soldiers and Sailors Home booklet lists H. A. Lashley, age eighty-two, and reports enlistment at Atlanta on 15 April 1863 under Colonel G. W. Lee in L. L. Strozier's Company, Company F of Lee's Battalion, with a wound during the Atlanta fighting. Later Jacksonville notices report his 1930 death at the Confederate Soldiers and Sailors Home and burial in the Confederate plot at Old City Cemetery. Because the entry has not yet tied those details to a compiled service file or pension record, the page should present this as a strong late-life service trail rather than fully source-exhausted military biography.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#87 may connect to HH#85 through the Richmond Lashley family, but that relationship has not yet been proved to the standard needed for a firm encyclopedia claim.
  • The 5 October 1930 Florida Times-Union survivor list makes Julia Glover of Cairo a highly probable sister or near collateral relative of Henry, with J. R. Glover of Cairo and L. Glover of Woodville, Florida as likely nephews.
  • The 1910 and 1920 Hamilton County, Florida records strongly suggest that Henry and his wife later left Brooks County for Florida.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • The 1850 Lee County and 1860 Terrell County households of Richmond and Atha Lashly now provide a strong parentage case for Henry, but a marriage record, death record, or other direct-record link would make that identification firmer still.
  • The 1870 Terrell County household appears to show Henry with wife Keziah and a child Mary, but that child and the exact family structure need confirmation from the original image and later records.
  • The 1900 census records Henry and Kittie as married for twenty-five years, but the apparent 1870 household suggests an earlier union or a more complicated family structure. That discrepancy needs direct review rather than harmonizing by guesswork.
  • The wife's name varies widely across the record set: Keziah, Kittie, Cisrah, and Kissiah. Those forms likely refer to the same woman, but a marriage or death record is needed to settle her name more securely.
  • The 15 November 1906 Valdosta Daily Times court item for "State vs. H. A. Lashley, misdemeanor. Plea of guilty." is useful as a locality anchor, but the clipping alone does not identify the offense or prove by itself that the defendant is the same Henry Lashley of HH#87.
  • Henry's move from Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, to Hamilton County, Florida, is strongly suggested by the census chain but still needs corroboration from land, tax, vital, or cemetery records.
  • The 1929 Florida Old Confederate Soldiers and Sailors Home reunion booklet entry for "H. A. Lashley", age 82, is a strong possible match, but the Confederate service statement should be verified against compiled service or pension records before being absorbed without caution.
  • The Florida death index entry for Henry A. Lashley gives a 1930 death in Jackson County, Florida, and the Jacksonville and Times-Union death notices add age, apparent death date, birthplace, place-of-death, survivor clues, and burial context, but the underlying death certificate is still needed for the informant and strongest identity proof.
  • Julia Glover of Mitchell/Decatur/Grady County, Georgia is now a strong candidate for the "Mrs. Glover of Cairo" named in Henry's 1930 death notice, but the exact direct-record proof tying Julia to Henry as sister rather than another collateral Lashley relative is still missing.
  • The prior claim that HH#87 included adult and teenage children in 1900 should be treated as unverified unless a separate full household image or another census page supports it.
  • The proposed brother relationship between Henry Lashley and George William Lashley of HH#85 remains unproved, even though the Richmond and Atha Lashly family framework now looks stronger for Henry himself.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Partly documented, but materially stronger than before. The 1850 and 1860 Richmond/Atha Lashly households now give Henry a credible childhood-to-adolescence placement, the later census trail from 1870 through 1920 is strong, the 1930 Florida death notices now provide a probable end-of-life placement with death on 4 October 1930 at the Confederate Home and burial in Jacksonville's Old City Cemetery, and the Glover survivor notices now open a plausible sister link through Julia Glover of Cairo. What is still missing is the direct proof needed to settle his marriage, child list, full death-certificate details, and any firm connection to HH#85.

docs.title: Household #88: Wilks, George
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, George Wilks headed an 8-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
George Wilks headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 6 children.

George Wilks's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation George Wilks Head 59 Georgia Farmer Margarett Wilks Wife 44 Georgia — Mary Wilks Daughter 13 Georgia — Florence Wilks Daughter 12 Georgia — James Wilks Son 11 Georgia — Nellie Wilks Daughter 9 Georgia — Maggie Wilks Daughter 7 Georgia — Charley Wilks Son 5 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census shows George Wilks in Barney as a farmer who owned his home free of mortgage. The household consisted of George, his wife Margarett, and six children born in Georgia between about 1887 and 1895. On the face of the 1900 census, this is a second-family household rather than George's first known family.

The broader record trail is substantial, though not complete in every respect. In 1850, George W. Wilkes, age three, appears in Columbia County, Florida, in the household of Jeston Wilkes. In 1860, George W. Wilkes, age eleven, appears in Colquitt County in the household of James R. Douglas rather than with the earlier Wilkes household. In 1867, George W. Wilkes appears in the Georgia Reconstruction voter registry in Dooly County, which helps bridge the gap between the Colquitt County placement and his later settled life in south Georgia. By 1870, George Wilkes was in Brooks County with wife Nancy and children Noah, Judy, and Daniel. In 1880, G. W. Wilks appears in Lowndes County with wife Nancy and children Benjamin N. and Jordy, a pattern that strongly suggests Noah and Benjamin N. were the same child and that Judy and Jordy were the same child under different recorded forms. By 1900, George had returned to Brooks County and was living with Margarett and their younger children. In 1910 and 1920, George and Margaret M. Wilks still appear in Brooks County, with the household reduced to the youngest remaining children and, in 1910, a grandson named Pierce Wilkes. A newly supplied Georgia death index record gives George W. Wilks a death date of 21 February 1925 in Brooks County, certificate number 6388-G. The supplied Find a Grave memorial screenshots match that index by placing George W. Wilkes in Corinth Cemetery near Morven and linking him to wife Margaret Malissa Dugger Wilkes and children including Benjamin Noah Wilkes, Bettie Church Wilkes Hewett, and Nellie Rachel Wilkes Elliott. A newly supplied Find a Grave memorial for Benjamin Noah Wilkes also strengthens, though still does not fully prove, the Noah-to-Benjamin bridge by presenting "Benjamin Noah Wilkes" as son of George W. Wilkes, giving a birth of September 1865 in Georgia and death in 1921, and identifying "Pierce F. Wilkes" among his children. If that memorial reflects real family knowledge, the 1910 grandson Pierce Wilkes in George's household was most likely Benjamin Noah Wilkes's son. A newly supplied 5 July 1927 Valdosta Daily Times death notice for another George Wilkes appears to fit that same descendant line rather than HH#88 himself: it describes a George Wilkes of near Palmetto, Florida, who died of typhoid fever while visiting relatives near Hahira, was buried at Fellowship Cemetery, was survived by a wife and four children, and was identified as a son of the late Noah Wilkes. Read together with the Benjamin Noah Wilkes memorial, that obituary makes it probable that the 1927 decedent was a grandson of HH#88, likely the George Washington Wilkes shown as Benjamin Noah's son. Because the memorial material is derivative and user-edited, and because the obituary has not yet been tied to a direct death record, this descendant-line identification should still be treated as probable rather than final.

Taken together, these records support a two-marriage life pattern. The first marriage was to Nancy, already present by 1870 and still present in 1880. The second marriage was to Margarett, whose reported 1900 and 1910 marriage durations point back to the mid-1880s. The Brooks County Dugger records show a strong pre-marriage candidate in Margaret or Margaretta Dugger, who appears in Brooks County in 1860, 1870, and 1880: age ten in the household of Harvey Dugger in 1860, age twenty-two in the Harvey and Mary Dugger household in 1870, and age thirty-one in the same extended Dugger household in Quitman in 1880. That identification is no longer just a census-based lead. A Brooks County marriage record now shows "Mr Geo W Wilks" and "Margaret Malissa Dugger" licensed on 18 July 1884 and certified as married on 20 July 1884. A newly supplied 1928 Georgia death certificate for daughter Bettie Church Hewitt adds direct family-level support by naming her parents as "G. W. Wilks" and "Margretten Dugg.", giving Bettie a birth date of 6 September 1886 in Brooks County, and placing her burial at Corinth Church. The linked Find a Grave memorials fit those records by naming George's spouse as Margaret Malissa Dugger Wilkes and giving an "m. 1884" notation that matches the marriage record and census-based timing. The census trail also supports a long economic rise from farm laborer in 1870 to landholding farmer by 1880, with continued farm ownership in 1900, 1910, and 1920. What the records do not yet show is the direct marriage proof for the earlier Nancy union, the full death record for George, or a firm explanation for why the 1860 George Wilkes was living in the Douglas household.

The newly supplied Civil War index entries add a possible military lead for George. They identify a "George W. Wilkes" who served as a private in Wheaton's Company, Georgia Artillery, also styled Chatham Artillery, with references to compiled Confederate service records. The name and state fit, but the unit's Chatham/Savannah association sits uneasily against George's known south-Georgia and Florida record trail, and the current evidence does not yet provide an age, residence, spouse, pension file, or other bridge proving that the soldier and the Brooks County farmer were the same man. For now, the military item is best treated as a plausible but unproved identification.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• No documented connection has yet been proved between HH#88 and the other Barney kin networks already established in this volume.
  • The Wilks family appears to reflect a Georgia-origin settlement line rather than the South Carolina migration pattern seen in several other Barney households.
  • The 1910 grandson Pierce Wilkes now most likely points to Benjamin Noah Wilkes as the parent line, because the supplied Benjamin Noah Wilkes memorial identifies a child "Pierce F. Wilkes"; this remains derivative until confirmed with direct records.
  • The 1927 Valdosta Daily Times death notice for a younger George Wilkes likely belongs to Benjamin Noah Wilkes's son rather than to HH#88 himself, but that reading should be confirmed with a death record or other direct documentation.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The military item for George W. Wilks remains a plausible but unproved Confederate-service lead. The current entries identify a George W. Wilkes as a private in Wheaton's Company, Georgia Artillery, also styled Chatham Artillery. Because the unit's Savannah/Chatham setting does not yet connect cleanly to the Brooks County and Florida trail, the page should keep this as a lead until a pension file, compiled service card, age/residence match, or other bridge proves the identification.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The 1850 Columbia County, Florida, Jeston Wilkes household is the earliest strong candidate for George's birth family, but the exact relationship should be confirmed through probate, guardianship, land, or other direct records.
  • The 1860 placement of George W. Wilkes in the James R. Douglas household suggests a disrupted family situation, but the surviving record set does not yet show whether that came from orphaning, remarriage, labor placement, or some other arrangement.
  • The first marriage to Nancy is well supported by the 1870 and 1880 censuses, but a marriage record is still needed.
  • The second marriage to Margarett is now directly supported by the Brooks County marriage license and return for George W. Wilks and Margaret Malissa Dugger, dated 18 and 20 July 1884.
  • The apparent child-name shifts from Noah to Benjamin N. and from Judy to Jordy are plausible census continuity readings. The newly supplied Benjamin Noah Wilkes memorial strengthens the Noah-to-Benjamin reading, but the identification should still be treated as probable rather than final until supported by direct records.
  • Bettie Church Wilkes Hewitt is now directly supported as a daughter of George W. Wilks and Margaret Dugger through her 1928 Georgia death certificate.
  • The 1910 grandson Pierce Wilkes is now more likely identifiable as Benjamin Noah Wilkes's son, but birth, death, marriage, or later census records are still needed to confirm that bridge directly.
  • The Georgia death index now supports George W. Wilks's death date as 21 February 1925 in Brooks County, and the Find a Grave memorials point to Corinth Cemetery near Morven, but the underlying death certificate, obituary, cemetery register, or family documentation would provide stronger direct proof of the full end-of-life profile.
  • The Confederate-service entries for "George W. Wilkes" in Wheaton's Company / Chatham Artillery are a plausible lead, but they should remain unproved until a pension file, compiled service card, age/residence match, or other bridge ties that soldier directly to the Brooks County George W. Wilks.
  • George's literacy reports vary across census years and should not be overinterpreted.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well documented, but not fully closed. The census trail from 1850 through 1920 is strong, the 1867 voter registry helps bridge a key gap, the Brooks County marriage record directly identifies George's second wife as Margaret Malissa Dugger, and the Georgia death index now supports a 21 February 1925 death in Brooks County, with Find a Grave pointing to burial at Corinth Cemetery near Morven. What remains missing is direct proof for George's parentage, the earlier Nancy marriage, the identity bridge for some children across census name shifts, and stronger end-of-life documentation.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Stephen Bourguine Head 72 Georgia Physician Fannie Bourguine Wife 54 Georgia — Stephen Bourguine Son 24 Georgia Farmer Fannie Bourguine Daughter 22 Georgia — Julia Bourguine Daughter 20 Georgia — Thomas Bourguine Son 18 Georgia Laborer Farm

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census shows Stephen William Bourquin in Barney as a physician with wife Fannie L. and five adult children still in the household. On the face of that record, he was born in Georgia in February 1828, had been married about thirty years, and his wife was the mother of five children, all then living.

James later supplied additional census extracts that materially strengthen this household. In 1880, the same family appears in Morven, Brooks County, under the spelling "S. W. Bourginn", with wife Fannie L. J. and children Edward T., Mary L., Stephen W., Fannie F., and Julia A. That census closely matches the 1900 household and confirms the children's names and birth order. A 1920 Barney census record also places widowed or elderly mother Fannie L. Bourquin, age 76, in the household of S. W. Bourquin, age 43, giving a later-life anchor for Stephen's widow and a direct bridge to the next generation. James also supplied the 1930 Georgia death certificate for daughter Fannie Bourquin Eason, who died in Brooks County on 22 February 1930 at about age fifty-two. That record names her parents as Dr. S. W. Bourquine and Fannie Pace, confirms her married surname Eason, gives birthplace Barney, Georgia, and shows that one daughter remained tied to the same local community. The child line for son Edward F. Bourquin is now much firmer as well. A Berrien County marriage record shows "E F Bourgine" and "Sallie N. Parrish" licensed on 15 October 1895 and married on 11 December 1895. A Valdosta Times item of 12 January 1901 adds another useful anchor by placing Dr. E. F. Bourquin in Adel as the lead actor in a local performance of "Uncle Rube," where he played "Reuben Rodney." That article is not a vital record, but it helps bridge the gap between the 1898 Valdosta fire report and the 1907 death material while reinforcing his physician identity and South Georgia residence. Two other newspaper items add more support. The Valdosta Times of 13 August 1898 reported that "the residence of Dr. E. F. Bourquin was destroyed by fire" on a Wednesday morning, with only part of the furniture saved and insurance of $500 not covering even half the loss. A Valdosta Daily Times article of 3 May 1907, titled "Death of Dr. Bourquin," reports that Dr. E. F. Bourquin died at his home in Valdosta on Thursday morning after about three weeks of fever. James also supplied a Directory of Deceased American Physicians entry for Edward F. Bourquin showing death on 2 May 1907 at Adel, Georgia, identifying him as an allopathic physician, and linking him to Emory University School of Medicine in Atlanta. That directory entry lines up well with the 3 May 1907 death notice, though the place detail should still be handled cautiously until checked against the underlying compiled source. Taken together, the marriage record, directory entry, and newspaper items materially strengthen Edward F. Bourquin's identification as a physician, husband of Sallie N. Parrish, resident of South Georgia by 1898, active in Adel by early 1901, decedent on 2 May 1907, and probable Emory-trained doctor. The Mary Louisa Bourquin line is also much better supported now. James supplied a run of later census records showing "Mollie L. Joyce" with husband John W. Joyce in Barney in 1910, "Mary L. Joyce" as widowed head in Quitman in 1920, "Woollie L. Joyce" in Brooks County in 1930, "Mary Jayce" as widowed head in Quitman in 1940, and "Mollie L. Joyce" as widowed mother-in-law in Quitman in 1950. He also supplied a Georgia death index entry for "Mollie B Joyce", certificate no. 5078, age 85, in Brooks County, and a Find a Grave memorial for Mary Louisa "Mollie" Bourquin Joyce giving birth 3 February 1871 and death 7 March 1956. Those records are derivative in part and do not replace a direct marriage record, but taken together with the 1909 church item they materially strengthen the conclusion that the daughter Mary L. Bourquin in HH#89 is the same woman later enumerated as Mollie or Mary Joyce. James also supplied a 1961 obituary for daughter Julia B. Rountree. That item reports that Mrs. Julia B. Rountree, age 81, died in Hahira, names children in the Stalvey, Hall, and Rountree lines, identifies one brother as T. C. Bourquine of Quitman, and describes her as a native of Brooks County and the daughter of the late Dr. and Mrs. Bourquine. The OCR of the parental initials is imperfect, but the obituary strongly supports the conclusion that the Julia A. Bourquin in the 1880 household is the later Julia B. Rountree. A Macon Telegraph item of 14 August 1899 adds useful contemporary context: it reported that "the local physician, Dr. Bourquin" of Barney identified a smallpox case, and doctors from Quitman then confirmed his diagnosis. That article does not prove a new family relationship, but it does directly place Dr. Bourquin in active medical practice in Barney the year before the 1900 census. A Valdosta Daily Times item of 28 July 1909 adds two more useful details. In reporting litigation over a Primitive Baptist church, it said the land on which the church stood had been deeded to the church by "the late Dr. Bourquine, of near Barney", and that "Mrs. Joyce was a daughter of Dr. Bourquine". That article is not a full deed abstract, but it materially strengthens the Mary Louisa Bourquin to Joyce connection and shows that Stephen was already dead by late July 1909.

The new image set also supports Fannie's identification as a Pace by census trail. In 1850, "Frances Pace", age 4, appears in the household of Thomas B. Pace in Twiggs County, Georgia. In 1860, "Francis J. Pace", age 13, appears in the same father's household in Twiggs County. Those two records fit the later Fannie L. Bourquin by age and birthplace, though the marriage record is still needed before treating the Pace identification as fully proved.

One 1870 Brooks County census record appears to capture this same couple under a problematic index entry: "William Bourquin", age 35, physician, with wife Fannie and infant Edward. Because the household includes the right wife name, the expected first child Edward, and the same uncommon surname in the right county, it is a strong candidate for Stephen's 1870 household despite the first-name and age discrepancy. I would keep that record as probable rather than settled until the original image or another corroborating source resolves the conflict. By contrast, the 1850 Chatham County record indexed as "Stephen W Boar" is only a possible early-life lead and should not yet be treated as established identity evidence.

The surviving evidence is stronger than earlier summaries suggested. James also supplied Fannie L. Bourquin's Georgia death certificate, filed as certificate 11539, which identifies the decedent as "Mrs. S. W. Bourguin", widow of "S. W. Bourguin", age 87, born in Georgia, daughter of "T. B. Pace" and "Louise Thorpe", and dead in Brooks County on 26 February 1930. The certificate was informant-based and some fields are faint, but it materially strengthens both Fannie's Pace identity and the reported 1930 death date. He also supplied a Confederate officers card for Stephen William Bourquin from the Military Order of the Stars and Bars card index and a second Civil War soldier profile entry that sharpens the details. Together they identify Stephen William Bourquin as a first lieutenant in Company H, 25th Georgia Infantry, commissioned and mustered on 2 August 1861 in Georgia, with residence in Chatham County, and resigned for disability. That pair of records gives the military claim real direct support and resolves the company letter more cleanly than the officer card alone, though compiled service records would still be useful if we want a fuller service history. Some biographical claims still lack direct citations, including the statement that Stephen was born in Savannah, that he graduated from Savannah Medical College in 1859, and that he married Fannie Louisa Pace on 31 May 1869. Until those records are pulled directly, the safer reading is that HH#89 is substantially improved but not yet fully source-exhausted.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The household likely connects to the Pace family through Stephen's wife Fannie, and the 1850 and 1860 Twiggs County census records now give that connection a stronger footing.
  • Daughter Mary Louisa Bourquin now has much stronger support for connection to the later Joyce household in this volume, because the 28 July 1909 Valdosta Daily Times item states that "Mrs. Joyce was a daughter of Dr. Bourquine", and a later census-and-death-index chain carries her forward as Mollie or Mary Joyce in Brooks County through 1950, though direct marriage evidence is still preferred.
  • Daughter Julia A. Bourquin is now strongly connectable to the later Julia B. Rountree of Brooks and Lowndes County through a 1961 obituary that identifies Mrs. Julia B. Rountree as daughter of the late Dr. and Mrs. Bourquine and names brother T. C. Bourquine of Quitman.
  • The 1920 census places Fannie L. Bourquin in the household of S. W. Bourquin, giving a direct intergenerational link inside the Bourquin family in Barney.
  • Daughter Fannie F. Bourquin can now be carried forward as Fannie Bourquin Eason through her 1930 Brooks County death certificate, which gives death on 22 February 1930 in Brooks County, names Dr. S. W. Bourquine and Fannie Pace as her parents, and states that she was born in Barney, Georgia.
  • Son Edward F. Bourquin is now more clearly identifiable as Dr. E. F. Bourquin through his 1895 Berrien County marriage to Sallie N. Parrish, an 1898 Valdosta house-fire notice, a 1901 Adel theatrical notice, a physician directory death entry, and a 1907 death notice, which together support his physician identification and adult life track.
  • The 14 August 1899 Macon Telegraph smallpox item places Dr. Bourquin in Barney as the local physician and supports the occupational claim with a contemporary newspaper reference.
  • The 28 July 1909 Valdosta Daily Times church dispute item links a Mrs. Joyce directly to Dr. Bourquine as his daughter and shows that land near Barney had been deeded by the late Dr. Bourquine to a Primitive Baptist church.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: Stephen William Bourquin's Confederate service is supported by the Confederate Officers Card Index and a Civil War soldier profile. Together they identify him as a first lieutenant in Company H, 25th Georgia Infantry, with enlistment, commission, and muster on 2 August 1861 in Georgia, Chatham County residence, and resignation for disability. The current record pair supports the core service claim, while a full compiled-service-file review would still be useful for the complete timeline.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Stephen's exact birthplace is still supported only generally as Georgia in the census material now in hand; the specific claim that he was born in Savannah still needs direct proof.
  • The reported marriage date of 31 May 1869 for Stephen Bourquin and Fannie Louisa Pace needs the actual marriage record.
  • The 1870 "William Bourquin" census entry should be checked against the original image and any parallel source because the family structure fits but the first name and age do not.
  • The claim that Stephen graduated from Savannah Medical College in 1859 needs the catalog, alumni list, commencement notice, or another direct school record.
  • The Confederate officer card and Civil War soldier profile now strongly support Stephen William Bourquin's service as first lieutenant of Company H, 25th Georgia Infantry, with commission and muster on 2 August 1861 and resignation for disability; compiled service records or related military files would still help confirm the full service timeline.
  • The 28 July 1909 Valdosta Daily Times item shows that Stephen was already deceased by that date, but his exact death date and burial are still supported in the documented source set mainly by Find a Grave and should be backed by a death notice, death certificate substitute, cemetery register, or probate material.
  • Fannie Bourquin's later-life path is now supported through 1920 and by her 1930 Brooks County death certificate, but burial and any obituary still need direct follow-up.
  • The identities and later lives of the five children listed in 1880 and 1900 still need follow-up through marriage, death, cemetery, and later census records, though daughter Fannie F. is now directly identified in 1930 as Fannie Bourquin Eason, son Edward F. now has a direct marriage record plus directory- and newspaper-based residence, occupation, training, and death anchors, daughter Mary L. now has a strong later-life Joyce chain through 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, 1950, the Georgia death index, and Find a Grave, son Stephen W. Jr. now has a 1948 obituary naming wife Minnie Williams and three children plus a strengthening Hazel lead from a 1915 Adel college notice and the later Hazel B. Briggs death-index entry, and daughter Julia now has a 1961 obituary linking her to the Rountree line. The age given in the 1948 obituary for Stephen W. Jr. appears to conflict with the earlier census trail and should be checked against the original image and death certificate rather than harmonized away.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Source-Exhausted in practical terms. The entry is now grounded by the 1880 and 1900 household anchors, the 1920 widow record, Fannie Bourquin's 1930 death certificate, daughter Fannie Eason's 1930 death certificate, multiple later-life records for Mary Louisa Joyce and Julia Rountree, several newspaper anchors for Edward F. Bourquin and Stephen W. Bourquin Jr., and two military records for Stephen William Bourquin. What remains open is limited to narrower follow-up opportunities rather than major evidentiary gaps: Stephen and Fannie's direct marriage record, stronger direct proof for Stephen's own death endpoint, fuller confirmation of Stephen's medical-school claim, and a cleaner bridge for the Hazel lead in the Stephen W. Bourquin Jr. branch.

docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William Drew Head 39 Georgia Lats Man Saw Mill Emer Drew Wife 33 Florida — Claudie Drew Daughter 4 Florida — Rogers Drew Son 2 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
William Milton Drew can be placed securely in the 1900 Barney household and then followed through the 1910, 1920, and 1930 censuses in Hillsborough County, Florida. Those later records, together with the 1927 death notice for Emma Drew and the 1931 obituary for William Drew, establish a solid later-life profile for the family. The earlier record trail is also strong, though not every point is equally direct. The 1880 Brooks County census firmly places William in the household of William and Missouri Drew, and the 1880 Orange County, Florida, census firmly places Emma in the household of C. H. J. Rogers. A probable 1870 Madison County, Florida, Drew household provides an earlier bridge for William's family, but the state-of-birth details across the census trail are not consistent enough to treat every early detail as settled.

The 1880 Brooks County census is the clearest early anchor for William. There he appears as "William M. Drew," age 19, in the household of William Drew and Missouri Drew, with siblings M. L., Media, Jeremiah, Malachai, Rebecca, and Joseph. That record supports the parentage claim used here, though the family's exact interstate movements between Brooks County and north Florida still need cautious handling. A William M. Drew also appears in Lowndes County property-tax digests in the Hahira-area Folsom district during the 1880s. That tax material is a plausible regional bridge between the 1880 Brooks County household and the later Barney household, but the digest entry alone does not absolutely prove identity.

Emma's side is better anchored in Florida than in Brooks County. In 1880, fourteen-year-old Emma Rogers appears in Orange County, Florida, in the household of C. H. J. Rogers with siblings including William, Wilson, Susan, and M. D. Rogers. A likely 1870 census placement for the same family adds earlier support for the line, but the exact expansion of the father's initials and the full parental reconstruction still benefit from caution. The later newspaper evidence is especially useful here. A 7 June 1908 Tampa Tribune item reports that "Mrs. Emma Drew, of Pavo, Ga.," had come to visit her brother "M. D. Rogers" in the Gary/Tampa area. That brief notice strongly supports Emma's continuing tie to the Orange County and Tampa-area Rogers family.

The marriage of William and Emma was probably about 1894 or 1895, based on the 1900 census and the age of their oldest known child, but the direct marriage record has not yet been located. By 1900 they were in Barney, where William worked as a lath man at a saw mill and the household contained Claudie Emma Drew, age five, born in Florida, and Rogers Drew, age two, born in Georgia. That combination suggests a family transition from Florida into south Georgia during the later 1890s. The 1910 census in Hillsborough County, Florida, shows the family after their return to Florida. William was then working in lumber-mill employment, Emma reported that she had borne five children with four still living, and the household included Claudie, Rogers, Mamie, Leroy, and Emma's widowed mother Clarice J. Rogers. The 1920 census in Hillsborough County continues the same family with William, Emma, Mamie, and Leroy still together.

The child lines are not equally complete, but several are now directly supported beyond the census trail. Mamie L. Drew is firmly tied to William and Emma by a Tampa Tribune wedding announcement of 22 February 1921, which states that she was the daughter of "Mr. and Mrs. William Drew" and reports her marriage to Ward H. Wadsworth. That notice also places William and Emma on Crawford Street near Sulphur Springs and states that the reception was held at the home of "Mr. and Mrs. Roger Drew," giving useful evidence that Rogers Drew had reached adulthood and remained in the same local family network. Claudie Emma Drew's later life is less fully documented in the present record set, but the memorial and survivor material strongly suggest that she was the daughter later represented in derivative records as Mrs. A. B. Paul. Leroy Drew is securely part of the later household through the 1910 and 1920 censuses and through survivor lists in later derivative material, though a fuller direct endpoint chain for him would still be useful.

Emma's death endpoint is now well supported by direct newspaper evidence. The Tampa Tribune of 6 March 1927 reports funeral services for "Mrs. Emma Drew," gives her residence at Pamie and Waters avenues in Tampa, identifies Dr. W. P. Head as the officiant, and states that she was buried in Myrtle Hill Cemetery. The printed age in the notice is not fully reliable in the OCR copy, and derivative memorial material introduces additional age variation, so her exact birth year should still be treated cautiously. Even so, the notice gives a solid death-and-burial anchor. William's death endpoint is similarly well supported. The Tampa Tribune of 6 January 1931 reports funeral services for "William M. Drew, 69, of 3101 Cord avenue," states that he died Sunday at a hospital, identifies Dr. W. P. Head as the officiant, and reports burial in Myrtle Hill Cemetery. A Hillsborough County death-index entry for William M. Drew in 1931 supports the same endpoint profile, and the 1930 census places him in Hillsborough County as a widower shortly before his death.

The Rogers or Rodgers surname appears elsewhere in the Barney census, including Households #99 and #100, but no direct documented kinship has yet been established between Emma E. Rogers Drew and those households. The shared surname and proximity suggest only a possible broader community or family connection. That possibility should remain outside any proved "Connections" claim unless probate, land, marriage, or other direct records establish a specific bridge.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • William and Emma's direct marriage record has not yet been located.
  • William's birthplace is not fully settled. The census trail points both to Georgia and to Florida, though Georgia is somewhat better supported overall.
  • The 1870 Madison County, Florida, Drew household is a strong probable bridge for William's family, but it should still be treated as probable rather than final.
  • The exact expansion of Emma's father's initials in the 1880 Orange County household still needs careful confirmation from additional direct records.
  • Claudie's later identity and the fuller endpoint chains for Rogers and Leroy would benefit from additional direct records.
  • No direct documented kinship has yet been established between Emma's branch and the other Rogers or Rodgers households in the Barney census.

docs.text: Source-Exhausted in practical terms. The household is now grounded by a strong census chain, a solid Florida return trail, direct newspaper support for Emma's sibling tie to M. D. Rogers, direct newspaper support for Mamie Drew's marriage, and direct newspaper death-endpoint evidence for both Emma and William. Remaining gaps are narrower follow-up items rather than major evidentiary problems: the marriage record, the death certificates, fuller control of William's birthplace, and fuller endpoint records for some of the children.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney household is securely the Joyce family even though one index renders the surname as "Joyer." The household number, place, spouse, and children align with the Joyce family, and the census image supports reading the surname as Joyce rather than Joyer. John can also be followed backward through earlier Brooks County census records and forward into the 1910 census, giving the household a solid documentary frame even if some older narrative details need to be pared back.

John's early trail is now stronger than the previous entry suggested. In 1860, "Jno W. P. Joyce," age six, appears in Brooks County in the household of Elizabeth Joyce. In 1870, "John Joyce," age fifteen, again appears in Brooks County with Elizabeth Joyce. Those two records show a consistent early placement, but by themselves they do not prove every parentage claim previously attached to him. The safest conclusion is that John belonged to the Joyce family cluster represented by Elizabeth Joyce and was still in Brooks County across both enumerations.

By 1880, John appears as "J. W. Joyce" in Brooks County with wife "C. V. Joyce." That census provides firm evidence of an earlier marriage before his 1900 household with Mollie Bourquin. The older writeup overstated the identities and later lives of the children in that earlier household. The 1880 image should control any future restatement of those children rather than recycled notes. What can be said confidently now is that John had an earlier family unit in place by 1880 and that the Brooks County marriage license and return identify that marriage as John W. Joyce to Catharine V. Harrington, license issued 2 January 1877 and marriage performed 4 January 1877. A Southern Christian Advocate marriage notice adds corroborating detail, stating that Rev. J. H. D. McRae married "Mr. J. W. Joyce" to "Miss Caddie Harrington" at Rev. John Delk's on 2 January 1877, all of Brooks County.

John's second marriage is much better integrated into the larger Barney network because of the Bourquin evidence already assembled for Household #89. Brooks County marriage records place John Joyce's marriage to Mary Louisa Bourquin in 1892. Mollie was a daughter of Dr. Stephen William Bourquin and Fannie Louisa Pace Bourquin, which links Household #91 directly to the Bourquin family already documented elsewhere in this encyclopedia. By 1900, John and Mollie were farming in the Barney community with four young children: Susie, Ben, Clancie, and Walter.

The 1910 census gives the next secure household anchor. John W. Joyce, age fifty-five, and Mollie L. Joyce, age thirty-nine, were still in Brooks County. The user-supplied image confirms that this later household should be read carefully from the record itself rather than from older derivative summaries. At minimum, it shows John and Mollie still together in 1910 and confirms continuity of the family in the Barney area. It also makes clear that parts of the former entry, especially the treatment of the children across the two marriages, need a more restrained reading than before.

Mollie's later endpoint is supported by the Georgia death index. That index lists "Mollie B. Joyce," age eighty-five, born about 1871, with residence and death place in Brooks County and certificate number 5078. This is good support for identifying the widowed later-life Mary or Mollie Joyce as the same Bourquin daughter seen in the 1900 and 1910 households, although the death certificate itself would still be preferable for full detail. Earlier work also placed John's death in 1911 and his burial at Camp Ground Cemetery, but that endpoint should be treated as strong prior research rather than freshly reverified in the present pass unless the direct death or burial record is pulled again.

docs.text:

In the 1900 Barney census, Allen Carnegie headed a 5-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:

Allen Carnegie's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Allen Carnegie Head 30 Georgia Farmer Ida Carnegie Wife 21 Georgia — Clem Carnegie Stepson (Step Son) 4 Georgia — Einsy Carnegie Daughter 2 Georgia — William Carnegie Son 0 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney household shows Allen Carnegie as a Black farmer in Brooks County with wife Ida and three children or stepchildren. The household is useful and coherent, but the former writeup pushed far beyond what the present record set can prove. At this stage, the entry is best treated as a good early-family reconstruction anchored by census and marriage evidence, not as a fully documented multi-decade case.

The strongest early record currently attached to Allen is the 1880 census, where "Allen Kornegy," age twelve, appears in Quitman, Brooks County, in the household of Henry and Priscilla Kornegy. That is a plausible earlier placement for the 1900 Allen Carnegie because the age, county, and surname pattern fit well, and later records show the surname drifting across several spellings. Even so, the identification should remain probable rather than final until strengthened by additional records linking the 1880 boy to the adult Allen more directly.

Brooks County marriage records now support the Carnegie-Rountree union directly. The marriage license, issued 15 December 1897, authorized the marriage of "Allen Cornegy" and "Ida Rountree," and the return states that they were joined in matrimony on 16 December 1897 by D. W. Hunter, M.G. That record firmly establishes Ida's maiden name and securely anchors the 1900 household to the Rountree family. In 1900, Allen and Ida were living in Barney with Clem, Einsy, and William. The census identifies Allen as a farmer, shows that the farm was rented, and places the young household in its early formation years.

The 1910 census carries the family forward under the spelling "Carergy." Allen, Ida, Clinton, Willie U., and Fannie E. fit the expected development of the 1900 household, with "Clinton" likely matching the earlier "Clem" and "Willie U." likely matching the infant William from 1900. The image also confirms that Allen was farming, was listed as an employer, and was living on a rented farm. That strengthens the continuity of the household, but the children's identifications should still be read as likely rather than absolutely proved until later records are gathered for them.

A later derivative clue points in the same direction for the oldest child. A Social Security Applications and Claims Index entry for "Ida Pinkney" names her spouse as "Allen Carnegie" and her child as "Clent Carnegie." That does not by itself prove the chain, but it makes the progression from 1900 "Clem" to 1910 "Clinton" to later "Clent" more plausible. By contrast, a separate Social Security Applications and Claims Index entry for "William Carnegie" gives a birth date of 12 December 1897 and names parents "Allen Carnegie" and "Ida Paintner." That record does not fit the 1900 household cleanly and should not be merged into HH#92 without stronger corroboration.

What does hold up well already is the broader pattern. The surname moves through "Kornegy," "Cornegy," "Carnegie," "Carergy," and even "Cornego," which is exactly the kind of variation common in Brooks County records. The family also remains in the same county across the presently assembled record trail, and Allen's occupation stays within the agricultural world seen throughout the Barney census. That consistency gives the household a credible core, but it does not justify the previous language about "exceptional" documentation, landownership success, or a complete thirty-year chronology.

  • The 1910 household likely matches the 1900 family, but the children's identities still need later-life records for firmer proof.
  • The Social Security derivative trail supports a possible "Clem" → "Clinton" → "Clent" identification, but that chain still needs an original record behind it.
  • The 1910 image supports Allen's status as an employer on a rented farm, but it does not by itself prove landownership.
  • A 1934 Brooks County death certificate for "Ida May Carnegie," age 26, names her father as "Allan Carnegie" and shows burial in Dixie Colored Cemetery. This is a promising later-family clue, but her exact place in the HH#92 child sequence remains unresolved.

It is not yet source-exhausted, and the former "EXCEPTIONAL RESEARCH" label overstated the present proof. The next pass should focus on later censuses, death and burial evidence, and land or tax material before stronger claims are made.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation John Shaw Head 35 North Carolina Laborer Turpentine Street Hannah Shaw Wife 26 North Carolina — Ann Shaw Daughter 12 Georgia — Albertie Shaw Daughter 7 Georgia — Joseph Shaw Son 6 Georgia — Mary Shaw Daughter 3 Georgia — Mamie Shaw Daughter 2 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows a Black Shaw household headed by John Shaw, a North Carolina-born laborer in the turpentine trade. He reported birth in November 1864, stated that he and Hannah had been married about twelve years, and was living with Hannah and children Ann, Albertie, Joseph, Mary, and Mamie. Both John and Hannah were reported as North Carolina-born, which raises the possibility that the family migrated into Brooks County before the births of the younger children.

The new census chain materially strengthens the household. In 1910, John and Hannah Shaw were still in Barney, Brooks County, with daughter Liza A., son Joseph M., daughters Mamie L. and Inez E., and sons Fred D. and Daniel J. By that point John was listed as a farmer on a rented farm rather than a turpentine laborer, showing a clear occupational shift over the decade. In 1920, the same couple remained in Barney, with sons Fred, Dan, and John L. still at home. That 1900-1910-1920 progression is strong evidence for a continuous family unit in Brooks County.

James then located the key marriage record in Guilford County, North Carolina. The certificate shows that on 9 January 1892, John Shaw, age 22, Black, of Guilford County, applied for and received a license to marry Hannah Donnell, age 18, Black, also of Guilford County. The return shows the couple were married the same day by W. H. Rankin, justice of the peace. The record also names Hannah's parents as Arch Donnell and Susan Donnell. John's parental line is harder to read, but the certificate appears to identify him as the son of John Shaw and a mother whose given name looks like Ada Shaw. That maternal reading should be treated as tentative until checked against a cleaner image or index, but the marriage record is direct evidence that Hannah's surname was Donnell and that the couple married in Guilford County before appearing in Brooks County.

This direct record changes the status of the earlier Ancestry-profile lead. The profile's Guilford County connection and Hannah Donnell identification are no longer just derivative suggestions; they are now substantially confirmed by the marriage certificate itself. By contrast, the separate FamilySearch tree claim that Hannah's maiden name was George should now be treated as inconsistent with the direct record unless another primary source explains the discrepancy.

What can now be said with confidence is stronger than before. John and Hannah Shaw formed a durable Barney household that can be followed from 1900 through 1920, and their marriage is now directly documented in Guilford County, North Carolina, on 9 January 1892. The family appears to have begun in the local wage-labor side of the turpentine economy and then moved into rented farming by 1910 and 1920. The major remaining gaps are the earlier North Carolina placements for John and Hannah, firmer reading of John's mother on the marriage certificate, and the later lives and death records of the couple and their children.

docs.text:

  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • The family's reported North Carolina birthplaces should still be tested against earlier censuses to determine when the move to Georgia occurred.
  • John's mother on the Guilford County marriage record appears to be "Ada Shaw", but that reading should be checked against a cleaner copy or index before being treated as settled.
  • The earlier FamilySearch claim that Hannah's maiden name was "George" conflicts with the direct marriage record and should not be used unless supported by another primary source.
  • The possible connection to later records for John M. Shaw, Hannah, and Inez Shaw Woods remains worth testing, especially because the certificate now supports the Guilford County origin.
  • No death record, burial record, or 1930 census citation is yet attached here.

docs.text: Well-researched. HH#93 now rests on a solid 1900-1910-1920 census chain in Barney, Brooks County, plus a direct Guilford County, North Carolina marriage certificate for John Shaw and Hannah Donnell dated 9 January 1892. That is a materially stronger foundation than the earlier single-census version. The next pass should focus on earlier censuses in North Carolina, a 1930 census check, firmer control of John's parents from the marriage record, and death or burial records that could document the later lives of the couple and their children.

docs.title: Household #95: Dean, Robert - Early Families of Barney, Georgia
docs.text: Household #95: Dean, Robert ¶ In the 1900 Barney census, this household was headed by Robert Dean and included 6 people. The census summary records the head's listed occupation was Day Laborer Still, 1 spouse or marital partner, 4 child or stepchild. Household Snapshot ¶ A good way to read this page is to start with Robert Dean (age 49, born in Georgia, listed as Day Laborer Still). The occupation gives one grounded way to read the household: not just as a census entry, but as people tied to the work, travel, land, stores, churches, schools, and court business of the Barney area. The household was not just the head's name. In 1900 it included spouse or marital partner Martha Dean; children Anna Dean, Katie Dean, Ida Dean, and William Dean. Those names are the starting point for the later family, labor, marriage, migration, and neighborhood trails below. Every listed person in this household was reported as born in Georgia, which makes the page a local-family snapshot unless later records show movement into or out of Barney. 1900 Census Household ¶ Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Robert Dean Head 49 Georgia Day Laborer Still Martha Dean Wife 48 Georgia — Anna Dean Daughter 19 Georgia — Katie Dean Daughter 13 Georgia — Ida Dean Daughter 11 Georgia — William Dean Son 7 Georgia — Children and Later Trails ¶ The household table above already lists the children present in 1900: Anna Dean, Katie Dean, Ida Dean, William Dean. Where a child's adult trail is not identified here, the gap is intentional. The page should wait for a marriage, death, cemetery, obituary, probate, later census, or other direct record before naming a later spouse or descendant line. Family Narrative ¶ The 1900 census places Robert Dean in Barney with wife Martha and four children in the home: Anna, Katie, Ida, and William. That household is the firm anchor for HH#95 . A Brooks County marriage record then ties the couple together directly: R. D. Dean and M. J. Gornto were licensed on 13 December 1880 and married on 16 December 1880. On Martha's side, the evidence is steady. She appears as Martha Gornto, age 19, in 1870 Brooks County in the household of Mary Gornto, and again as Martha J. Gornto, age 29, in the same family cluster in Quitman in 1880 just before the marriage. Robert's earlier identity is supported, though not proved in every detail. The 1860 Brooks County census places Robert Dean, age 10, in William E. Dean's household. A later Dry Lake tax record lists Robert D. Deen directly below William E. Dean, and R. D. Dean married Martha J. Gornto in Brooks County in 1880. Together, those records make William E. Dean Robert's strong-probable father. The 1860 schedule does not state relationships, however, and no probate, death certificate, Bible, deed, or guardianship record names William as Robert's father. The 1870 schedule introduces an important conflict. The young man in the William and Dillilah Dean cluster is written Daniel Dean , age 19, not Robert. Daniel may have been Robert under another given name, a brother, or another relative, but the record does not settle the question. The name Robert Daniel Dean should therefore not be treated as proved. The Florida records belong to a separate, unresolved branch unless new direct evidence connects them. In 1910, Robert D. Deen of Calhoun County, Florida, was about eleven years younger than the 1900 Barney Robert. He and wife Eliza each reported a first marriage of thirteen years. Those details conflict with Robert's 1900 marriage to Martha and with Martha's continuing household at Barney in 1910. The former claim that the Barney Robert began a second family in Florida is not supported by the combined census evidence. Martha's later life is much better documented than Robert's. Her Georgia death certificate identifies Mrs. Martha Dean as a widowed woman who died at Moultrie, Colquitt County, on 10 November 1934; it gives her birth date as 29 October 1851, birthplace as Brooks County, and father only as Mr. Gornto. The informant was W. A. Pippin, a detail that fits well with the later identification of daughter Katherine Kate Dean Pippin. A Find a Grave memorial provides secondary burial support for Martha at Westview Cemetery in Moultrie. The Robert D. Dean memorial at Mashburn Cemetery in Bay County, Florida, cannot safely be assigned to the Barney household head because it is entangled with the rejected Florida identity merge. Connections to Other Barney Families ¶ Martha's documented Gornto background connects HH#95 to the Gornto family network treated elsewhere in the encyclopedia, including the Gornto households in HH#14 and HH#15 . The Pippin informant on Martha's death certificate also supports the later Kate Dean Pippin line. Open Research Questions ¶ Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification. Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure. Robert's full middle name and exact birthplace remain unproven from the present direct-record set. William E. Dean remains Robert's strong-probable father, but a parent-naming record has not been found. Daniel Dean's identity in the 1870 household remains unresolved. The adult trails of Anna, Ida, and William remain incomplete; Katie's later Pippin identity is strong probable. Research Status ¶ The Barney household is well documented. The two-direction surname audit supports the William E. Dean-to-Robert bridge as strong probable, keeps Daniel Dean unplaced, and rejects the former Florida second-family narrative as unproved. docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Robert Dean in Barney with wife Martha and four children in the home: Anna, Katie, Ida, and William. That household is the firm anchor for HH#95. A Brooks County marriage record then ties the couple together directly: "R. D. Dean" and "M. J. Gornto" were licensed on 13 December 1880 and married on 16 December 1880. On Martha's side, the evidence is steady. She appears as Martha Gornto, age 19, in 1870 Brooks County in the household of Mary Gornto, and again as Martha J. Gornto, age 29, in the same family cluster in Quitman in 1880 just before the marriage.

Robert's earlier identity is supported, though not in every detail. A likely 1860 Brooks County match shows Robert Dean, age 10, in the household of William E. Dean. A 1870 Brooks County Dean household with William and Dillilah Dean strengthens the case that Robert belonged to that family. Brooks County tax digest records then place "Robert D. Deen" in the Dry Lake district during the 1870s, which helps bridge the gap between the early Brooks County Dean household evidence and the 1880 Brooks marriage. Even so, the present extracts do not yet prove every step cleanly enough to treat "Robert Daniel" or a Lowndes County birth as settled fact. By contrast, the Franklin County Robert A./Robert P. Dean material does not fit this household and should stay out of the HH#95 reconstruction.

The later record chain shows a second family phase in Florida. In 1910, "Robert D. Deen" appears in Calhoun County, Florida, with wife Eliza H. Dean, children Eliza Louisa and Robert M., and mother-in-law Gerona Cook. The census states that Robert and Eliza had been married thirteen years, pointing to a second marriage about 1897. That later household supports a two-marriage framework, but it does not yet settle whether Ida and William from the 1900 Barney household were Martha's children, Eliza's earlier children, or part of a more complicated transition between the two marriages. The 1920 Bay County census places Robert in Florida again, though the wife's given name needs another close check against the original image before being treated as final.

Martha's later life is much better documented than Robert's. Her Georgia death certificate identifies "Mrs. Martha Dean" as a widowed woman who died at Moultrie, Colquitt County, on 10 November 1934; it gives her birth date as 29 October 1851, birthplace as Brooks County, and father only as "Mr. Gornto." The informant was W. A. Pippin, a detail that fits well with the later identification of daughter Katherine "Kate" Dean Pippin. Find a Grave memorials add useful burial support by placing Martha at Westview Cemetery in Moultrie and Robert at Mashburn Cemetery in Bay County, Florida, but those memorials should be treated as secondary confirmation rather than the main proof for Robert's expanded middle name or birthplace.
