docs.text: Martha's documented Gornto background connects HH#95 to the Gornto family network treated elsewhere in the encyclopedia, including the Gornto households in HH#14 and HH#15. The Pippin informant on Martha's death certificate also supports the later Kate Dean Pippin line.

  • The parentage link to William E. Dean and Dillilah Dean is plausible and partially supported, but still needs a cleaner documented chain.

docs.text: Well-researched and substantially improved, but not yet source-exhausted. The 1900 Barney household, the 1880 Dean-Gornto marriage, Martha's 1870 and 1880 Gornto household placements, Martha's 1934 death certificate, and the 1910 Florida household provide a solid base. The second marriage record and Robert's direct Florida death documentation remain the main missing pieces.

docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Charles Hancock in Barney with wife Nancy and son Emit. That household is the firm anchor for HH#96. The census shows Charles as a farmer renting his place, born in May 1862, unable to read or write, and married for what the enumerator recorded as nineteen years. That marriage length does not fit the direct marriage record, which is more reliable.

The marriage evidence is now clear. A Harris County, Georgia, marriage license was issued on 14 May 1883 for Charles Hancock and "Nannie Grissome", and the return shows the marriage was performed on 15 May 1883. The record appears to use both "Charles Hancock" and "Charlie Hancock", which should be treated as normal name variation rather than a separate identity. This record gives the strongest present basis for identifying Nancy Hancock of the 1900 Barney household with Nannie Grissome of the 1883 marriage.

Later evidence does not yet firmly relocate Charles and Nancy themselves, but it does materially strengthen the track of their son. The 1900 "Emit Hancock", age eighteen, is very likely the same man later recorded as Emmett or Emett Hancock in west-central Georgia. In 1920, Emmett Hancock appears in Big Sandy District, Chattahoochee County, Georgia, age thirty-eight, born in Georgia, with a daughter Mary C. Hancock. In 1930, "Emett Hancock" appears in Tazewell, Marion County, Georgia, age fifty, with wife Etta H. Hancock. In 1940, Emmett Hancock, age fifty-nine and widowed, appears in the Pine Knot district of Chattahoochee County in the household of George Wright, where he is identified as father-in-law. In 1950, Emmett Hancock, age sixty-eight and widowed, appears again in Brantley, Marion County, Georgia. Taken together, these records make it difficult to sustain the older claim that the Hancock household vanished after 1900.

Even so, some points remain unsettled. The present record set does not yet show where Charles and Nancy were in 1910 or 1920, does not yet document their deaths, and does not yet fully prove the link between Emmett Hancock and daughter Mary C. Hancock in 1920 and the later George Wright household beyond the strong circumstantial pattern. A 1910 record for William H. Hancock should not be folded into this household without a direct connection.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: The strongest present family continuation for HH#96 runs through son Emit Hancock, who was likely the later Emmett Hancock found in Chattahoochee and Marion counties. The 1940 father-in-law relationship in the George Wright household suggests that Mary C. Hancock of the 1920 household was likely the later Mary Clyde Wright, but that identification still needs direct-record confirmation.

docs.text:

  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Charles Hancock and Nancy Hancock have not yet been located with confidence in 1910 or 1920.
  • Charles Hancock's death record and burial place have not yet been documented.
  • Nancy/Nannie Hancock's death record and burial place have not yet been documented.
  • The likely identification of 1900 "Emit" Hancock with later Emmett/Emett Hancock is strong, but a direct bridging record would still be valuable.
  • The likely Mary C. Hancock to Mary Clyde Wright connection still needs direct proof.
  • William H. Hancock in a 1910 record remains unproven for this household.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched in its core 1900 household and 1883 marriage framework, with meaningful improvement from later records for the son. The entry is no longer limited to a single census snapshot, but Charles and Nancy themselves still need a clearer later-life record trail before the household can be treated as closed.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation James Nichols Head 21 Georgia Farmer Emma Nichols Wife 21 Georgia — Earl Nichols Son 9/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney household of James Nichols, wife "Emma," and infant son Earl is the starting point for this family in the Barney census sequence. James remained in Brooks County across the next three censuses, appearing in 1910, 1920, and 1930 as a farmer. His 1918 World War I draft card places him at Barney, gives his birth date as 8 March 1879, identifies him as self-employed, and names "Aurelia J. Nichols" as his nearest relative. His death certificate shows that James O. Nichols died at Barney on 22 February 1939, age sixty, and was buried at Mt. Zion near Morven.

The marriage evidence now provides the direct bridge that earlier versions of the entry lacked. A Brooks County marriage license dated 30 November 1898 authorized the marriage of "Mr. James O. Nickols" and "Miss Amelia Lowdy," and the return shows they were married on 4 December 1898. In light of the later record set, those spellings fit the same couple later found as James Oren Nichols and Aurelia Lundy Nichols. The surname variation is routine, and the bride's recorded forms "Amelia Lowdy," "Emma," "Iona," and "Aurelia" are best treated as record variants within the same marriage rather than as separate women.

Aurelia's Lundy identity is now well supported from her own family records. In 1880 she appears as a small child in Jones County, Georgia, in the household of Robert Lundy and Esther Lundy. Her brother A. S. Lundy's 1928 death certificate names their parents as R. L. Lundy and Esther Henderson, and the Jones County marriage record for Robert Lundy and Earther Henderson, dated 9 and 11 October 1875, fits that parental household. The Nichols household records later reinforce the same identification. Delma Humphrey Nichols's 1937 death certificate names his parents as "Jim O. Nichols" and "Aurelia Dona Lundy," providing a strong direct link between the Barney Nichols family and the Lundy maiden name.

The family structure is also better documented than the earlier entry showed. James appears in 1880 as a one-year-old in the household of Thomas Nichols and Mary A. Nichols in Lowndes County, a placement consistent with the parental birth-state pattern carried forward in his later records. The 1910, 1920, and 1930 censuses track the growing family through Earl, Conrad, Delma, Vesta Mae, Lois, and Gladys. Across those censuses James is consistently a farmer, and the ownership columns indicate that he owned his farm free of mortgage. In 1930 the farm was valued at $300.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: The strongest documented connection for HH#97 is internal to the Nichols-Lundy family itself: James O. Nichols and Aurelia Lundy Nichols can now be followed through marriage, multiple censuses, the 1918 draft registration, Delma Humphrey Nichols's death certificate, and James's own 1939 death certificate. The Lundy side is anchored in Jones County through Robert Lundy and Esther Henderson.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • Aurelia's actual death certificate has not yet been added, although the Georgia death index entry for Aurelia L. Nichols in Brooks County aligns well with the cemetery record.
  • The earlier distinction between this James Nichols and another James Nichols said to have died young should not be stated more strongly than the direct evidence allows until the competing child's death or burial record is added to the entry.
  • The census given-name variants for Aurelia are now substantially bridged by the marriage and child-death records, but the literal spellings should still be preserved as found in each source.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household is now supported by a direct marriage record, a five-point census chain for James, a World War I draft card, James's death certificate, Delma Humphrey Nichols's death certificate, Aurelia's Lundy-family records, and cemetery evidence. The remaining gaps are limited and do not prevent a stable identification of the household.

docs.text:

docs.title: Children and Later Trails

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census places John Wesley Nichols and Rebecca Nichols in household #98, where John is recorded as a farmer born in April 1875. The entry is clearer now than it was in the earlier draft. John does not vanish after 1900, and the family did not move to Birmingham as early as that earlier version claimed. In 1910 he was still in Barney, again listed as a farmer, with the census indicating that he owned his farm free of mortgage. By the time of his World War I draft registration on 12 September 1918, however, he was living in Birmingham, Jefferson County, Alabama, at 2510-29th Avenue, working as a grocery merchant, and naming Mrs. Rebecca W. Nichols as his nearest relative. The 1920 census then places John and Rebecca together in Birmingham, where they owned their home free of mortgage.

The marriage and sibling evidence are also stronger than the previous entry suggested. A Lowndes County marriage license issued 31 January 1898 and returned 2 February 1898 records the marriage of John W. Nichols and Rebecca Lundy. In 1880 John appears in Lowndes County in the household of Thomas Nichols and Mary A. Nichols, together with one-year-old James Nichols, giving direct support for the brother connection between HH#98 John Wesley Nichols and HH#97 James Oren Nichols. Rebecca likewise appears in 1880 in Jones County in the household of Robert Lundy and Ester Lundy. Her later Alabama death-index entry identifies her as Mrs. Rebecca Nichols, born 14 May 1869 in Jones County, Georgia, daughter of Robert Lundy and Esther Henderson, wife of J. W. Nichols, and deceased at Birmingham on 10 December 1927. That record fits well with the Lundy family already documented in HH#97.

The older draft also carried several points that no longer hold. The marriage did not occur in Brooks County in December 1899; the direct record places it in Lowndes County in February 1898. The 1910 census does not show John in Birmingham as a grocery merchant; it still places him in Barney as a farmer. The previous parentage line naming Henderson Nichols and Mary Ann Vickers Nichols does not match the 1880 household now tied directly to John. The later record chain instead supports Thomas Nichols and Mary A. Nichols as the parental household for John and James.

John's later life can be outlined with reasonable confidence, though one piece remains secondary. Rebecca was still living in Birmingham in 1920 and in John's 1918 draft registration, then died there in 1927. Jefferson County marriage indexes show that John W. Nichols, age fifty-three, married Ella Wright on 12 May 1928. A Find a Grave memorial for John W. Nichols at Shiloh Community Church Cemetery in Hahira gives the dates 11 April 1875 and 15 July 1944. That memorial fits the rest of the sequence far better than the earlier draft's unsupported 1925 Birmingham death claim, but the actual death certificate or obituary has not yet been added to the file.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: HH#98 is directly linked to HH#97 through the 1880 Lowndes County household of Thomas Nichols and Mary A. Nichols, where John W. Nichols and James Nichols appear together as children. The household is also tied to the Lundy family through John's marriage to Rebecca Lundy. Rebecca's 1880 Jones County placement and her later death-index entry strongly support her as part of the same Robert Lundy and Esther Henderson family that also connects to Aurelia Lundy Nichols in HH#97.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • John's death date of 15 Jul 1944 and burial at Shiloh Community Church Cemetery presently rest on cemetery memorial evidence; a death certificate, obituary, or comparable direct death record would strengthen the close of the entry.
  • The 1928 marriage to Ella Wright is well supported by Jefferson County marriage indexes, but the underlying marriage record image would still be worth adding if located.
  • No child list has yet been rebuilt from direct household extracts for the later Alabama period.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched, with important corrections to the earlier draft. The household is now supported by the 1880 parental household, the 1898 marriage record, the 1900 and 1910 Brooks County censuses, the 1918 World War I draft card, the 1920 Birmingham census, Rebecca's Alabama death-index entry, and the 1928 remarriage indexes. The main remaining gap is John's direct death record.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Walter Rodgers Head 28 Georgia Farmer Charley Rountree Boarder 15 Georgia Day Laborer Farm James Harman Boarder 15 Georgia Day Laborer Farm

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census shows Walter Rodgers as a twenty-eight-year-old farmer born in September 1871, living alone except for two teenage boarders, Charley Rountree and James Harman. The surname appears in both Rodgers and Rogers forms across the record trail, but the later records point to the same man. By 1910 he appears in Barney as Walter H. Rodgers, age thirty-seven, married to Lelia, with daughter Lois, son Leo Roy, an orphan named Ernest Knight in the household, and father-in-law Isaac Merchant. The 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses continue the same family in Barney or the immediate Brooks County area and show a long farming residence there. In 1950 Walter was widowed and living with son Howell L. Rogers. Two years later the Georgia death index recorded W. H. Rogers Sr. in Brooks County, dead on 3 November 1952 at age eighty-one.

The marriage record closes the biggest gap in the household. Brooks County marriage records show that Walter H. Rogers married Lela E. Merchant on 26 November 1905, with the license issued the day before. Some later records give Walter's wife as Lelia, Leila, or Leila Estell Rogers, but the handwritten marriage certificate reads Lela E. Merchant, which fits the later family well and appears to be part of the ordinary name variation in the record set rather than a separate identity. The wife side is reinforced by the 1900 household of Isaac Merchant, where Lelia Merchant appears as a daughter, by the 1910 placement of Isaac Merchant in Walter's household as father-in-law, by records tying Isaac Merchant to Howell M. Peacock, and by later records for Merchant children including Philip Taylor Merchant.

Walter's earlier placement is also much clearer than the old draft suggested. The 1880 census includes Walton H. Rogers, age nine, in the household of Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Rogers. Walter H. Rogers's cemetery memorial later names his parents as Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires Rogers, which strongly supports that 1880 identification. The month and year of birth reported in the 1900 census, September 1871, fit the later memorial and the 1952 death index well enough to make the chain persuasive.

The children can now be followed beyond the 1900 household. The later censuses identify children including Lois, Leo Roy, Jewell, Howell, Hugh, Jewett, Margaret, Thelma, and Walter H. Rogers Jr. A 1938 Atlanta Constitution article listing boys who won forestry camp scholarships includes "Hicks Rogers, Barney," which fits the later son known as Walter Hicks Rogers Jr. A World War II draft card for Howell Lee Rogers gives Barney as his residence and birthplace and names Mrs. Lelia Estell Rogers as the person who would always know his address. A 1951 marriage announcement for Walter Hicks Rogers Jr. identifies him as son of Walter Rogers and the late Leila Merchant Rogers, confirming that Lelia had died before December 1950 and matching Walter's widowed status in 1950.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: HH#99 connects directly to the Merchant family through Walter's 1905 marriage to Lela E. Merchant and through Isaac Merchant's appearance in the 1910 household as Walter's father-in-law. The household also appears to connect to the earlier Rogers family of Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires Rogers through the 1880 Walton H. Rogers identification, though that link still rests on the combined force of census, memorial, and later vital evidence rather than one single explicit parentage record.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Other household member audit: Verify every non-nuclear household member, including in-laws, boarders, servants, laborers, uncles, grandchildren, and collateral relatives, before treating the stated relationship as part of the proved family structure.
  • Walter's death index entry and cemetery memorial align well, but the underlying death certificate would still be worth pulling for fuller detail.
  • Lelia's cemetery memorial gives a death date of 28 Mar 1947; a direct death certificate or death-index entry would tighten the close of her life in the same way.
  • The 1880 Walton H. Rogers identification is strongly supported, but a document that explicitly names Walter H. Rogers as son of Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires Rogers would make the parentage proof more direct.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household is now supported by the 1880 census, the 1900 through 1950 census chain, the 1905 marriage certificate, Walter's 1952 Georgia death index entry, cemetery memorials for Walter and Lelia, and several later records for their children. The older speculative family-network language is no longer needed. What remains are useful strengthening records, not basic identity work.

docs.title: Household #101: Russell, William
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, William Russell headed a 4-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
William Russell headed a 4-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 2 children.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William Russell Head 64 Georgia Farm Laborer Emerline Russell Wife 55 Georgia — Lizzie Russell Daughter 12 Georgia — Charley Russell Son 10 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Earlier household members: Nancy Russell, Sarah Jane Russell, Marion Russell, and William H. Russell appear in the earlier census chain
  • Second marriage: Brooks County marriage license issued 28 Feb 1882; William Russell married a woman whose given name reads as Mindia, with the surname uncertain on the surviving image and plausibly read as either Gloren or Glover; return dated 5 Mar 1882
  • Military record: William M. Russell, Brooks County, filed a Georgia Confederate indigent-soldier pension application in 1909 (GCP-036)

The 1900 Barney census shows William Russell as a sixty-four-year-old Georgia-born farm laborer with wife Emerline and two younger children, Lizzie and Charley. The household is easier to follow now because the census backbone is much firmer than the earlier entry suggested. In 1860 William appears in Brooks County with wife Nancy and children Sarah Jane and Marion. In 1870 he is in Schley County with Nancy, Sarah Jane, and William H. Russell. In 1880 he is in Colquitt County with Nancy, Sarah J., William H., and his mother Nancy Lee, whose relationship is stated directly in the household. By 1900 he is back in Brooks County, and by 1910 he remains in Barney with wife "Emly R." Russell and son Charles G. Russell. That sequence establishes a stable identity for William even though the records for his second wife remain harder to interpret.

The strongest new non-census record is the Brooks County marriage entry from 1882. It shows William Russell taking out a marriage license on 28 Feb 1882 and marrying on 5 Mar 1882. The bride's given name reads as Mindia. The surname is not secure on the available image. It has been indexed one way, but the handwriting can also be read as Glover. That uncertainty matters because the second-wife identification in the older draft went too far. The record does support a second marriage in Brooks County after Nancy disappears from the household, but it does not by itself justify a firm identification of William's later wife as Arminda Cannon.

The Cannon and Glover material is best treated as a live lead rather than settled fact. Separate records show an Arminda Cannon in 1850, then a Minda or Arminda Glover line in later census material. Those records are relevant because the 1882 surname may read Glover, but they do not yet prove that William Russell's second wife in 1900 and 1910 is the same person. The later wife appears as Emerline in 1900 and Emly R. in 1910. Those name forms could fit a broader Aramindia or Arminda pattern, but the bridge has not been proved. A Florida death-index entry for Aramindia Russell in Polk County in 1920 adds another possible lead, not a finished identification.

William's later-life circumstances are also better grounded now. The 1909 Georgia Confederate pension file for William M. Russell of Brooks County is a direct source showing that he was alive, local, and applying as an indigent soldier. That file provides much firmer support for hardship in old age than the earlier draft's interpretation based only on shifting census occupations. It also strengthens the identification of the Barney man as the same William seen in the earlier census trail.

The earlier family structure still holds in broad outline, but it needs to be stated with more care. Nancy is the documented first wife in the 1860, 1870, and 1880 households. Because William remarried in March 1882, Nancy almost certainly died or otherwise left the marriage before that date, but the present record stack does not yet show the exact event. Sarah Jane Russell is the clearest child across the early census chain. Marion Russell and William H. Russell also fit securely into the earlier household. In the later household, Lizzie and Charley are directly present in 1900, and Charles G. Russell remains with William and Emly in 1910.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The 1909 Georgia Confederate pension application for William M. Russell of Brooks County supports treating him as a Confederate veteran and provides a valuable late-life anchor. Because the current page has not yet transcribed the pension packet or tied him to a specific unit, the service note should remain limited to the documented indigent-soldier pension application until fuller military records are added.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The surname of William Russell's 1882 bride should be treated as uncertain until a clearer image, county book copy, or alternate index confirms whether it reads Gloren, Glover, or something close to one of those forms.
  • The identification of Emerline or Emly R. Russell with the Arminda Cannon or Glover line remains unproved.
  • Nancy Russell's exact death or other disappearance from the marriage has not yet been documented by death, probate, cemetery, or similar direct record.
  • The 1909 Confederate pension file should be transcribed more fully before detailed service claims are added beyond the fact of the Brooks County indigent-soldier application.
  • The Florida death-index entry for Aramindia Russell in Polk County in 1920 is a lead only until bridged to this household.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched but not source-exhausted. The census backbone from 1860 through 1910 is now strong, the 1882 remarriage is directly documented, and the 1909 Confederate pension application gives a valuable late-life anchor. The main unresolved issue is the identity of William's second wife and whether the later Emerline or Emly Russell is the same woman connected to the Cannon and Glover records.

docs.text:

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:

Ben Wingate's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Ben Wingate Head 26 Georgia Farmer Lizzie Wingate Wife 23 Georgia — Chester Wingate Son 11/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Later records: likely the same man as Jones B. Wingate in 1910, Benjamin J. Wingate in 1920, and Benjamin Wingate of the 1929 Berrien County death certificate
  • Later marriage: Brooks County marriage certificate for B. J. Wingate and Mattie Wilcox, license dated 21 Dec 1911, marriage dated 23 Dec 1911
  • Death record: Georgia death certificate for Benjamin Wingate, died 19 Jun 1929 at Nashville, Berrien County; father named as Lawrence Wingate; birthplace given as Sumter County, Georgia

The 1900 Barney census shows a young household headed by Ben Wingate, a Georgia-born farmer who owned his home. His wife was Lizzie, and their infant son Chester was born in November 1899. That census remains the anchor for the household as it appears in the Barney enumeration.

The household is clearer now because it can be followed into later records, though not every step is settled. A Valdosta Times clipping from the "Hahira Happenings" column, published 29 April 1893 and dated 26 April 1893, reports that "On Sunday last Mr. Benj. Wingate was married to Miss Lizzie Easteg" at the residence of the bride's father. The bride's surname is hard to read in the clipped image and may instead be Eastes or something close to it, but the notice is a strong fit for the 1900 Barney couple and likely preserves their marriage announcement.

The probable 1910 match is a Barney household headed by Jones B. Wingate, age 38, with wife Aima, son Clenton, and daughter Katie B. That record matters because it bridges the gap between the 1900 Barney family and the later Berrien County household, but it also introduces the main unresolved problem in the case. The wife in 1910 is not Lizzie, and she cannot be Mattie Wilcox because Ben did not marry Mattie until December 1911. The wife's name, read here as Aima, needs confirmation from the original image. The child listed as Clenton may be the same child as Chester from 1900, but that remains a plausible identification rather than a proved one.

The Brooks County marriage certificate for B. J. Wingate and Mattie Wilcox is the firmest middle record in the chronology. It shows a license issued on 21 December 1911 and a marriage on 23 December 1911. That record proves Mattie was a later wife and fixes the point that she was not the woman in the 1910 household.

By 1920 the family was in Nashville, Berrien County, where the census shows Benjamin J. Wingate, age 48, working as a merchant in a grocery store, with wife Mattie and daughters Ethel, Katie B., and Lois. This later household lines up well with the 1911 marriage record and with the family material preserved for Ethel after her marriage into the McGee family.

Benjamin Wingate's 1929 Georgia death certificate strengthens the identification further. It places his death at Nashville, Berrien County, on 19 June 1929 and describes him as a married merchant. The certificate gives his birthplace as Sumter County, Georgia, and names his father as Lawrence Wingate, though the informant did not know his mother's name. The age at death points to a birth in late January 1871, which conflicts with the January 1874 birth reported in the 1900 census. That conflict should be left visible rather than forced into a single unsupported date.

Find A Grave memorials for Benjamin Jones Wingate and Ethel L. McGee support the later Berrien County identification and the Mattie Wilcox family line, but the census, marriage, and death records remain the stronger foundation for the entry.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The 1910 wife's given name needs confirmation from the original census image; the current reading Aima may be an indexing or handwriting problem.
  • Chester Wingate in 1900 and Clenton Wingate in 1910 are a plausible match, but they should not be treated as the same person without a stronger bridge.
  • Lizzie's maiden surname in the 1893 newspaper notice is still uncertain because the clipped image is difficult to read.
  • Lizzie's fate between the likely 1893 marriage announcement and the 1910 household remains unresolved.
  • Benjamin's exact birth date remains conflicted across records: January 1874 in the 1900 census, about 1872 in later censuses, and late January 1871 by age-at-death calculation on the 1929 death certificate.
  • Benjamin's burial place has not yet been firmly documented from the records reviewed here.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched but not source-exhausted. The household now has a workable chronology from 1900 to 1929. The main remaining tasks are to clarify the 1910 wife, document Lizzie more fully, and resolve the Chester/Clenton question.

docs.text:
This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

  • Possible Pace-network newspaper references: Three 1903 "hideous monster" / "inland sea serpent" articles name Buck Pace of Barney as the first person to see the reported creature near Little River/Cecil. A 1901 Valdosta Times article on a body found in Little River also says Bailiff Pace at Barney had arrested Eli/Dave Dodson before the reported lynching. These items place Pace-named men in the Barney/Little River area, but neither article gives a first legal name, wife, child, age, or other bridge proving whether Buck Pace or Bailiff Pace was William H. Pace Sr. of this household, William H. Pace Jr. of HH#11, or another local Pace.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William Pace Head 62 Georgia Farmer Lula Pace Wife 23 Georgia — Selma Pace Daughter 5/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Property status: Farm owned free of mortgage in 1900
  • First marriage: William H. Pace and Susan Foster, married 8 Jun 1858 in Muscogee County, Georgia
  • Second marriage: William H. Pace and Lula Burns, license dated 10 Nov 1898 and marriage dated 23 Nov 1898 in Brooks County, Georgia
  • Military evidence: headstone application for William H. Pace Sr., Private, Company E, 29th Battalion Georgia Cavalry

The 1900 Barney household shows William Pace as a sixty-two-year-old Georgia-born farmer living with his much younger wife Lula and their infant daughter Selma. The census states that he owned his farm free of mortgage. Selma's age is recorded as 5/12, so the earlier draft's reading as "12-May" was wrong.

William's earlier record trail is now much clearer than the older entry allowed. In 1850 he appears in Harris County, Georgia, in the household of an older Pace family headed by a man whose given name is difficult to read in the surviving image, alongside Nancy H. Pace. By 1860 he was in Muscogee County as William H. Pace, age twenty-three, and his marriage to Susan Foster on 8 June 1858 in Muscogee County is directly documented. The 1870 and 1880 censuses place William and Susan in Muscogee County, not Brooks County, so the older timeline moved the family into Brooks too early.

The first marriage is supported by more than the marriage record alone. A 1932 death certificate for William and Susan's daughter Willie Bee Milton names her parents as William H. Pace and Susan Foster and gives Harris County, Georgia, as her birthplace. That record strengthens both the first-marriage identification and the family's earlier Harris County connection.

A Brooks County marriage license and certificate show William H. Pace marrying Miss Lula Burns in November 1898, with the ceremony performed on 23 November 1898. That record anchors the later household in 1900 and corrects the earlier draft's later date for the marriage. By 1910 William H. Pace was still in Barney with Lula, and the household included children Eula and Emmett.

The 1870 Daily Columbus Enquirer notice for the estate of Clement Pace adds useful family context. It shows William H. Pace acting as administrator in a Harris County estate sale. The clipping supports his place within the older Pace network, though it does not by itself prove the exact relationship between William and Clement Pace.

William's Confederate service now rests on firmer ground than the earlier entry showed. A military index entry points to a Georgia cavalry record, and a later government headstone application identifies William H. Pace Sr. as a Private in Company E, 29th Battalion Georgia Cavalry, buried at Gornto Cemetery in Brooks County. The application was filed by his daughter Eulalie P. Taylor, which helps tie the veteran record to the same family.

Find A Grave memorials for William Henry Pace Sr., Susan A. Pace, and Lula E. Burns Gary support the burial place, spouse sequence, and later family structure. They are useful supporting records here, especially where they line up with census, marriage, military, and death-certificate evidence. They should not carry the argument by themselves.

The Revolutionary War claim in the older entry appears to come from DAR lineage material and related derivative compilations that identify Susan Foster as daughter of John L. S. Foster and trace that line back to Sgt. John Foster of Virginia. That is enough to explain the origin of the claim, but the present record stack still supports treating it as lineage-book evidence rather than as a fully proved direct-record chain.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: William H. Pace Sr.'s Confederate service is supported by a military index entry and a government headstone application identifying him as a private in Company E, 29th Battalion Georgia Cavalry. The headstone application was filed by daughter Eulalie P. Taylor and places him at Gornto Cemetery, tying the military evidence back to this family.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• William's exact death date should be checked against a direct death record or probate record; the memorial material and the military-marker paperwork do not appear to agree perfectly on the year.
  • Susan A. Foster Pace's death should be supported by a direct death or burial record beyond memorial material.
  • Lula E. Burns Gary Pace's death should also be supported by a direct death or burial record if the entry is pushed further.
  • The exact relationship between William H. Pace and Clement Pace remains unproved from the newspaper notice alone.
  • The Buck Pace and Bailiff Pace newspaper references are useful local leads only. Do not attach either article to this household as proved family evidence unless a direct identity bridge is found.
  • The Revolutionary War descent through the Foster line should remain cautiously stated unless a fuller proof chain is assembled from direct records.
  • Selma Pace is securely present in the 1900 household as an infant, but her later life and exact parentage context have not yet been pushed further here.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched but not source-exhausted. The household now has a solid census backbone from 1850 through 1910, direct records for both marriages, a good military support record, and a child death certificate that reinforces the first family structure. The main remaining work is in death-record tightening, the Clement Pace probate context, and the deeper proof chain for the Foster Revolutionary War claim.

• Children in household: Eddie, 15, and Robert, 13
  • 1900 census notes: married about 16 years; Martha reported 4 children, 4 living

Phillip Lightsey was a Black farmer whose record trail now rests on a much firmer foundation than the older entry allowed. In 1900 he headed a Barney household with wife Martha and sons Eddie and Robert. By 1910 the family was in Fletcher, Irwin County, still with Eddie and Robert at home. In 1930 Philip was widowed and living in the Mystic household of his son Robert. His death certificate places his death in Irwin County on 27 April 1934.

The biggest correction in this entry is parentage. The older draft relied on Jasper Lightsey's household as the key kinship anchor. The better evidence is the Primus Lightsey household. In 1880 Philip Lightsey, age 32, appears in Quitman, Brooks County, as a son in the household of Primus Lightsey and Sylvia Lightsey. Henry S. Lightsey, age 16, appears there as another son. That record, together with the 1870 Primus Litsey household where Henry is present as a ten-year-old child, makes Henry Lightsey (HH#165) a proven brother of Philip. Jasper Lightsey (HH#126) still appears to belong to the wider Barney Lightsey network, but the records assembled for HH#104 do not by themselves prove the exact relationship.

Martha's identity also required correction. She was not Martha Frazier. The stronger record set shows Martha Roberts in Brooks County before her marriage. In 1870 and 1880 she appears in the household of Ephraim Roberts and Amanda Roberts. Brooks County marriage records then show a license for Philip Lightsey and Martha Roberts dated 10 January 1883 and a marriage date of 11 January 1883. That record replaces the older 1884 theory and resets the spouse identification on direct evidence.

The later records tie the family together cleanly. In 1900 Philip and Martha were in Barney with sons Eddie and Robert, and Martha reported four children born, all then living. In 1910 the family was in Fletcher, Irwin County, where the census again shows Eddie and Robert and reports four children born to Martha, with three then living. The marriage-duration figure in that census does not align cleanly with the 1883 marriage record and should be treated as approximate rather than controlling.

The death certificates strengthen both sides of the household. Philip Lightsey's death certificate names his father as Primus Lightsey and gives his mother's maiden surname as Capers, with both parents reported as South Carolina-born. Robert Lightsey was the informant. Martha Lightsey's death certificate gives her date of death as 28 December 1929 in Ben Hill County, identifies her as Martha Roberts, wife of Philip Lightsey, says she was Virginia-born, and names her father as E. Priam Roberts. Robert Lightsey was again the informant. Together with the 1930 census, these records connect the Brooks County household to the later Irwin County family and confirm that Martha Roberts is the correct spouse.

The children's picture is improved but not complete. Eddie and Robert are secure from the census trail, but two additional children remain unnamed in the current record stack. The 1910 fertility column shows that one of Martha's four children had died by that date.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Henry Lightsey (HH#165) is a proven brother through the Primus and Sylvia Lightsey household.
  • Jasper Lightsey (HH#126) remains likely kin within the Barney Lightsey cluster, but the exact relationship is still unproved here.
  • Martha Roberts ties this household into the Black Roberts network of Brooks County through Ephraim Roberts and Amanda Roberts.
  • Robert Roberts (HH#184) may connect within that Roberts network, but the degree of kinship is still unproved.
  • Octavia Roberts (HH#129) belongs to a separate White Roberts line and should not be blended into Martha's family without direct evidence.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Philip's likely 1870 appearance as Philip Letsey in the household of Charles Letsey is a good lead, but it should remain probable rather than closed until it is tied more directly to the later man.
  • The two additional children beyond Eddie and Robert still need identification from later census, death, marriage, or burial records.
  • The exact relationship of Jasper Lightsey to Philip and Henry still needs a direct linking record.
  • Martha's father is given on her death certificate as E. Priam Roberts; that should be checked against any surviving marriage, probate, or land material for the Roberts family.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household now has a solid evidentiary backbone: the Primus Lightsey household establishes Philip's parentage line and Henry connection, the 1883 marriage record establishes Martha Roberts as the wife, the 1900 and 1910 censuses carry the family from Brooks into Irwin County, and the 1929 and 1934 death certificates tie the later records back to both sides of the household. The main remaining work is in identifying the two additional children, tightening Philip's likely 1870 appearance, and proving exactly how Jasper fits into the broader Lightsey network.

docs.title: Household #105: Williams, Bryant
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Bryant Williams headed an 8-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Bryant Williams headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner, 3 children, and 3 extended-family members.

Bryant Williams's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Bryant Williams Head 35 Georgia Farmer Elizabeth Williams Wife 39 Georgia — John B Williams Son 9 Georgia — Stacy Williams Daughter 3 Georgia — Winnie Williams Daughter 1 Georgia — Jane Pike Mother-in-law 65 Georgia — Mattie Joyer Cousin 15 Georgia — Platt Joyer Cousin 14 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children in household: John B. Williams, Stacy Williams, Winnie Williams
  • Other household members: Jane Pike, mother-in-law; Mattie Joyce, cousin; Platt Joyce, cousin

This household can be followed from 1900 through 1940 with a solid census trail. In 1900 Bryant Williams appears in Barney with wife Elizabeth, three young children, Elizabeth's mother Jane Pike, and two cousins whose surname can now be read as Joyce rather than Joyer. A Brooks County marriage record shows B. M. Williams married Lizzie Pike on 22 December 1889, which fixes the Pike connection before the first census appearance. In 1910 Bryant M. Williams remains in Barney with wife Lizzie, children John B., Stacy, and Winnie D., and mother-in-law Jane J. Pike. In 1920 B. M. Williams is still in Barney with wife Lizzie, daughter Winnie Davis Williams, and mother-in-law Jane Pike. By 1930 Bryant is gone, and Lizzie P. Williams appears as a widowed head with daughter Winnie W. Waters and granddaughter Elizabeth J. Waters. In 1940 Lizzie Williams remains in Barney as a widowed head with Winnie Waters and Elizabeth Waters.

The death records fit that census arc. Georgia death index entries show Bryant M. Williams died on 21 June 1929 in Brooks County under certificate number 14660-K, and Elizabeth Williams died on 22 January 1944 in Brooks County under certificate number 4556. Find A Grave memorials place both at Camp Ground Cemetery Mount Zion Church in Morven. Elizabeth's memorial agrees with the state index. Bryant's memorial gives a different death date, so the state index is the better source unless the full death certificate shows otherwise.

The Pike side of the household is much clearer now. Jane Pike appears as Bryant's mother-in-law in 1900, 1910, and 1920, and the marriage record shows that Bryant's wife was Lizzie Pike. Jane Pike's 1923 death certificate adds the key correction. It identifies her as Jane Pike, wife of John J. Pike, but also gives her maiden name as Jane Joyce and names her parents as Jackson Joyce and Elizabeth Wells. That record directly places the Pike line inside the Joyce family network. Earlier records point in the same direction, though not all of them reconcile cleanly yet. In 1850 a sixteen-year-old Jane Joyce appears in Lowndes County in the household of James J. Joyce and Elizabeth Joyce. That is a plausible earlier record for the same woman, but the parents in that census do not fully match the death certificate and should not yet be treated as settled. In 1870 Nancy Pike appears in Brooks County in Jane Pike's household, and in 1880 Nancy E. Pike appears in Quitman in Jane J. Pike's household. That sequence suggests that Lizzie Pike may have been the same woman as Nancy E. Pike, but the point still lacks a direct linking record.

The most important correction in this entry concerns the two Joyce cousins. Mattie Henrietta Joyce and James Platt Joyce can now be identified as children of John Wesley P. Joyce and Catherine Harrington Joyce, the household treated elsewhere as HH#91. Jane Pike's death certificate explains why the two children could be described as cousins in the Bryant Williams household, because it identifies Jane herself as born Jane Joyce. That does not yet supply every intermediate generational step, but it does explain the family connection in a way the older draft could not.

Mattie can be followed forward with good confidence. In 1910 Mattie Joyce and Willie Joyce appear in Barney in the Plety Davis household, listed as nieces. In 1920 Mattie appears in Morven in the household of J. E. Elliott and Willie Elliott, listed as a sister-in-law, with Plety Davis also present as an aunt. In 1930 she appears in Brooks County as a single lodger. In 1940 she appears in Quitman as a single head of household. In 1950 she is still in Quitman, now sharing a household with brother J. Platt Joyce. Her 1952 obituary identifies her directly as the daughter of John Wesley and Catherine Harrington Joyce and names her surviving brother as J. Platt Joyce.

Platt Joyce can also be followed into adult life. A 1910 Morven census entry shows James P. Joyce as a boarder, which fits the age and place for Platt under a fuller given name. A Lowndes County marriage record shows Platt Joyce married Lellie Strickland on 26 September 1912. A July 1914 Valdosta Daily Times item places him in Quitman as a deputy sheriff. A World War I draft card for James Platt Joyce, filed in Ware County on 12 September 1918, gives his birth as 4 March 1885 and places him in Waycross as a police officer, with Jennette Joyce named as his daughter and nearest relative. A 1928 Miami city directory places James P. Joyce in Miami as a detective with wife Gertrude Joyce. A Florida divorce index entry shows J. P. Joyce and Gertrude Joyce divorced in Dade County in 1945. A 1957 obituary for James Platt Joyce then identifies him as a Brooks County native, former Miami police officer, husband of Eula Joyce, father of two daughters, and brother within the same Joyce sibling cluster already visible from Mattie's obituary. Taken together, those records make it reasonable to treat James P. Joyce and J. Platt Joyce as the same man.

The safest present reading is straightforward. HH#105 is a Barney Williams-Pike household carried from 1900 through 1940, tied to Lizzie Pike by the 1889 marriage record, tied to Jane Pike by three mother-in-law entries, and tied to the Joyce family by Jane Pike's death certificate and by the now-settled identification of Mattie and Platt Joyce as children of HH#91. The remaining uncertainties are narrower ones: whether Lizzie Pike was the same woman as Nancy E. Pike, what earlier records will identify Bryant's parentage, and what exact generational path links Jane Joyce Pike to the Joyce children living in her daughter's household in 1900.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The 1889 Brooks County marriage record directly identifies Bryant's wife as Lizzie Pike.
  • Jane Pike's repeated presence as mother-in-law strongly supports Lizzie Pike Williams as Jane's daughter or close stepdaughter.
  • Jane Pike's 1923 death certificate identifies her as born Jane Joyce, daughter of Jackson Joyce and Elizabeth Wells.
  • Nancy Pike in 1870 and Nancy E. Pike in 1880 are strong candidates for the earlier identity of Lizzie Pike Williams, but the link is not yet directly proved.
  • Winnie D. Williams in 1910 appears to be the later Winnie W. Waters in 1930 and Winnie Waters in 1940.
  • Mattie Joyce and Platt Joyce were cousins in the 1900 household and can now be identified as children of HH#91 John Wesley P. Joyce and Catherine Harrington Joyce.
  • Jane Pike's identity as Jane Joyce explains the broad cousin relationship between the Pike-Williams household and the Joyce children, even though the exact generational step still needs tighter reconstruction.
  • HH#106 Lucy Pike remains a comparison household because of surname, place, and proximity, but no exact kinship has been proved.

docs.title: Related probate records
docs.text: See the inspected probate-register entries for additional names and transactions. These are research leads; the new entries do not by themselves establish census identity, parentage, or land ownership.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Bryant Williams still needs a reliable earlier census identification before his parentage can be stated more firmly.
  • Bryant Williams still needs the full death certificate, obituary, or probate record.
  • Elizabeth Williams still needs the full death certificate or an obituary, even though the Georgia death index confirms her death date and county.
  • Lizzie Pike Williams still needs a direct record proving whether she was the same person as Nancy E. Pike of the 1870 and 1880 Jane Pike household.
  • Jane Pike still needs to be tracked through earlier Joyce records to test whether the 1850 Jane Joyce in Lowndes County is the same woman and to reconcile James J. Joyce with Jackson Joyce in the parent generation.
  • The exact generational path between Jane Joyce Pike and the children of HH#91 still needs direct proof.
  • The Plety Davis and J. E. Elliott households need closer comparison to determine whether Willie Joyce Elliott was Mattie's sister and whether Plety Davis was a maternal or paternal aunt.
  • The sequence of Platt Joyce's marriages still needs direct reconstruction, including the move from Lellie Strickland to Gertrude Joyce and later to Eula Joyce.
  • Jennette Joyce should be followed forward to determine whether she was one of the two daughters named in Platt's 1957 obituary.
  • The Miami years should be tightened with additional directory, census, or employment records.
  • Death, burial, land, and probate records for Bryant and Lizzie have not yet been fully added.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. The household now has a strong census backbone from 1900 through 1940, a direct marriage record for Bryant and Lizzie, Jane Pike's repeated mother-in-law relationship, Georgia death index entries for Bryant and Elizabeth, Jane Pike's 1923 death certificate, and a much stronger reconstruction of the two Joyce cousins. The big remaining tasks are to pull the full death records for Bryant and Elizabeth, resolve whether Lizzie Pike and Nancy E. Pike were the same woman, and locate records that define the exact Joyce-to-Pike generational link behind the 1900 cousin relationship.

docs.title: Household #106: Pike, Lucy
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Lucy Pike headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Lucy Pike headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 2 children.

Lucy Pike's listed occupation was no occupation listed.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Lucy Pike Head 32 Georgia no occupation listed West Pike Son 12 Georgia — Charley Pike Son 10 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children in household: West Pike, 12; Charley Pike, 10

Lucy Pike appears in 1900 as the head of a small Black household in Barney, Brooks County, with sons West and Charley. The census gives her as a widowed mother of two children, both living, with no occupation listed and both parents reported born in Georgia. At present that 1900 census is the only firm household anchor for Lucy as an independent adult.

One earlier record is a plausible fit. In 1880 a Lucy Pike, Black, age 10, born in Georgia, appears in Quitman in the white Jane J. Pike household and is listed as a servant with work on the farm. The same household also included William, a mulatto boy age 5, likewise listed as a servant. That Jane J. Pike is important because she is the same older Jane J. Pike who later appears in HH#105 in the 1900 Barney census as mother-in-law in the Bryant Williams household. The 1880 and 1900 records therefore show continuity of association with the same Pike household cluster across two decades. Even so, the 1880 record should still be treated as evidence of service or dependency placement, not as proof that Lucy belonged to the white Pike family line. It is useful because it places a Black child named Lucy Pike in the right county and approximate age range twenty years before the 1900 household, but the entry does not identify her parents.

The broader county Pike context matters mainly as a boundary. The 1870 Brooks County census places Jane Pike in a separate white household with Nancy Pike, showing that the Lucy and William listed with Jane in 1880 were not children already present in that household a decade earlier. The same 1870 county census also includes a separate white Pike household headed by George Pike and Alice Pike. Those records confirm that multiple Pike households were present in Brooks County before 1900, but they do not establish a direct connection to Lucy.

Nothing in the currently assembled record set safely carries Lucy forward after 1900. No later census, death record, cemetery record, or county record has yet been tied to her with enough confidence to extend the household. The same caution applies to her sons. West Pike has not yet been identified securely in later records under that exact name, and later Brooks County references to Charley or Charlie Pike appear to belong to an older man unless stronger proof shows otherwise.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The 1900 census provides the only firm household anchor for Lucy Pike as an adult head of household.
  • An 1880 Brooks County census entry for Lucy Pike, Black, age 10, in the Jane J. Pike household is a plausible earlier record, and Jane J. Pike is the same woman later appearing in HH#105 in the 1900 Bryant Williams household, but Lucy's presence there should still be read as service placement rather than family-line proof.
  • Jane Pike's household in 1870 contained Nancy Pike but not Lucy, which supports reading Lucy's 1880 presence there as later placement rather than daughter status.
  • Separate white Pike households in Brooks County, including the George Pike and Alice Pike household, show that the surname Pike in the county was not limited to one line.
  • No direct record yet connects Lucy Pike to HH#105 or to the white Joyce-Pike cluster beyond proximity of surname and place.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Lucy Pike needs a probable 1910 census candidate, if one exists, tested against age, race, birthplace, widow status, and children.
  • West Pike needs to be traced through draft registrations, marriage records, labor records, or later censuses to determine whether he remained in Brooks County or left the area.
  • Charley Pike needs the same follow-up, with special care not to merge him with older Charlie Pike records in Brooks County.
  • A Brooks County marriage record for Lucy Pike, or a death certificate for either son naming parents, would be the best route to identifying Lucy's husband.
  • Tax, labor-contract, poor-school, or court records may explain Lucy's 1880 placement in the Jane J. Pike household.
  • Cemetery, church, and funeral-home records for Barney, Morven, Quitman, and surrounding Brooks County communities should be checked for Lucy, West, and Charley.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. The household is anchored securely in the 1900 Barney census and has one plausible earlier Brooks County record in 1880, but the present evidence does not justify a stronger family reconstruction. The main cleanup point for this entry is to avoid overclaiming exhaustion. This household is not source-exhausted; it is lightly documented and still needs systematic work in county marriage, death, court, cemetery, church, school, labor, and later census records. The safest current reading is that Lucy Pike was a Black widow in Barney with two sons in 1900 and may be the same Lucy Pike who appeared as a child servant in the white Jane J. Pike household in 1880.

docs.title: Household #107: Reddick, Jake
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Jake Reddick headed a 6-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Jake Reddick headed a 6-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 4 children.

Jake Reddick's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Jake Reddick Head 40 Georgia Farmer Jane Reddick Wife 25 Georgia — West Reddick Son 3 Georgia — Mc Reddick Son 2 Georgia — Lila Reddick Daughter 2 Georgia — John Reddick Son 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children in household across the census trail: West, Mc, Lila, John or Joseph, Dola, Freddie or Frank, Emma
  • Other later household members: grandchildren Louis, Earnest, and Also Reddick; grandnephew James Gaines

Jake Reddick can be followed with good confidence from 1880 through 1920 in Brooks County. The best reading of the record set is that Jack Reddick in Quitman in 1880, Jake Reddick in Barney in 1900, Jacob Reddick in Barney in 1910, and Jake Reddick again in 1920 are the same man. The name shifts are ordinary, the county remains the same, and the household progression is coherent. He appears throughout as a farmer, and the later censuses report that he could read and write.

Janie Sharp is securely identified as his wife by the Brooks County marriage record dated 1 January 1896. After marriage she appears as Jane or Janie Reddick in the census record. Her 1920 death certificate is an important anchor. It gives her as Janie Reddick, wife of Jacob Reddick, born 30 September 1871 in Lowndes County, daughter of John Sharp and Isabella Longwood, with Jacob Reddick as informant. The same record places her death on 15 December 1920 in the Morven militia district and gives burial at a place written as Delany Cemetery. That burial reference still needs direct confirmation.

The Sharp identification is stronger than it first appeared. In 1880, Jane Sharp, age 7, appears in Grooverville in the household of John Sharp and Isabella Sharp. That is a good fit for the parents later named on Janie's death certificate. It does not finish the Longwood line, but it does give Janie a likely childhood household in Brooks County.

The children can be traced only in part. John in 1900 is very likely the Joseph Reddick found in 1910 and 1920. West in 1900 also lines up well with Westly in 1910, and that line is strengthened by the World War I draft registration for West Reddock filed at Elba, Coffee County, Alabama, on 5 June 1918. In that record he gave his birth as 30 December 1897 at Morven, Georgia, and named Janie Reddock of Barney, Georgia, as his nearest relative. That combination fits this family well and shows that one son had moved into south Alabama by 1918 while still keeping close ties to home. Freddie in 1910 is probably the Frank Reddick still in the household in 1920, but that point is not as firm as the Joseph and West identifications. Mc, Lila, Dola, and Emma remain only partly traced.

The 1920 household also shows the family entering a later stage. Jake and Janie still headed the home, but grandchildren Louis, Earnest, and Also Reddick were present, along with grandnephew James Gaines. That tells us at least one child had already formed a new family by 1920, though the present records do not show which one. Janie's death certificate, filed just after her death, also confirms that Jacob Reddick was still in Brooks County and close enough to serve as informant at the end of that year.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The household should be compared with HH#131 Harris Reddick because both were Barney-area Reddick households in 1900, though no direct kinship has been proved.
  • Janie's maiden name connects this household to the Sharp family, and her death certificate points specifically to John Sharp and Isabella Longwood.
  • The 1880 John and Isabella Sharp household in Grooverville is a strong likely early placement for Janie.
  • West Reddick's 1918 draft card shows a south Alabama migration path while preserving a direct tie back to Janie in Barney.
  • James Gaines may later connect this household to another Barney family, but no safe identification has been made yet.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Jake Reddick still needs a verified death or burial record.
  • Janie's cemetery, written as Delany on the death certificate, needs a clean identification and location check.
  • The Longwood maternal line still needs direct reconstruction.
  • Freddie in 1910 is a plausible match to Frank in 1920, but the link is not yet proved.
  • Mc, Lila, Dola, and Emma still need later records that can be tied to this family without guesswork.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household is anchored by a strong four-step census trail for Jake, a marriage record for Jake and Janie, Janie's 1920 death certificate, a likely 1880 childhood household for Janie, and a 1918 draft card that carries West into adult life. The core family structure is clear even though several children remain only partly identified and Jake's own death record has not yet been found.

docs.title: Household #108: Pinkney, Robert
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Robert Rinkney headed an 8-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Robert Rinkney headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner, 5 children, and 1 extended-family member.

Robert Rinkney's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Robert Rinkney Head 45 Georgia Farmer Harriett Rinkney Wife 40 Georgia — John Rinkney Stepson (Step Son) 19 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Jesta Rinkney Daughter 13 Georgia — Berta Rinkney Daughter 12 Georgia — Renur Rinkney Son 10 Georgia — Robert Rinkney Son 8 Georgia — Wade Rinkney Son 6 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children and household members tied to the family cluster: John Pinkney, Rosa B. Mack, Mira L. Wilson, Gertrude Busby, Robert T. Pinkney, Jessie or Jesse Pinkney

This household is clearer now than the 1900 census alone first suggested. The surname in that census was initially read as Rinkney, but the wider record trail supports Pinkney. Later records use Pinkney consistently, and the ages, place, spouse, and children fit well enough to treat the 1900 reading as a damaged rendering rather than a different family name.

Robert Pinkney can now be followed with good confidence across four censuses. In 1880 a Robert Pinkney, age 20, appears in Quitman, Brooks County, Black, single, born in Georgia, and working on a farm. In 1900 Robert appears in Barney with wife Harriet and a cluster of children under the distorted surname reading. In 1910 Robert Pinkney, age 54, is still in Barney with wife Hattie and several of the same children or their later forms. In 1930 Robert R. Pinkney, age 74, remains in Brooks County with wife Hattie. Taken together, those records support one continuous Robert Pinkney line in the Barney-Quitman area.

The marriage record is now stronger than an index citation alone. Brooks County records show Robert Pinkney and Harriet Roberts married on 26 July 1881, and the original marriage license and return support the same date. Harriet's maiden surname is reinforced again by Gertrude Busby's 1924 death record, which names her parents as Robt. Pinkney and Harritte Roberts. That is one of the best records in the file because it links the Pinkney surname, Harriet's Roberts name, and one of the 1900 children in a single direct record.

Harriet's earlier family placement is also much stronger than it was before. In 1870 a Harriet Roberts, age 8, appears in Brooks County in the household of Prince Roberts. In 1880 Harriet Roberts, age 18, appears again in Quitman in the household of Prince Roberts and Lucy Roberts. With those two censuses followed by the 1881 Brooks County marriage to Robert Pinkney, the Roberts-family identification is no longer just a loose candidate. It is now a very strong reading, though the entry still lacks one direct document that states Prince and Lucy Roberts were Harriet's parents.

The children's record trail is mixed but useful. John Pinkney appears in 1900 as Harriet's nineteen-year-old son and was likely from an earlier relationship or marriage, but he has not yet been carried forward safely. Gertrude Busby is one of the clearest lines. She appears as a daughter in the later household reconstruction, appears in a 1920 Barney household with husband John Busby, and her 1924 death record names Robert Pinkney and Harriet Roberts as parents. Robert T. Pinkney is also well anchored. He appears as a son in the later household reconstruction, his World War I draft registration gives his birth as 9 April 1892 at Barney, Georgia, and he married Fannie McBride in Brooks County in 1920. A June 1919 troop return record sharpens that line further. It identifies Robert Pinkney, serial number 1,688,785, private, 15th Service Company, 20th Engineers, departing St. Nazaire on the SS Montpelier, and names Mrs. Hattie Pinkney of Barney, Georgia, as his mother. That is strong supporting evidence that Robert T. Pinkney belonged in this household and that Harriet and Hattie were the same woman.

Jessie W. Pinkney, later Jesse Pinkney, is also a strong continuation. He appears in the later household reconstruction, gave his birth as 24 May 1896 at Barney in his draft registration, married Annie Mae Thomas in 1916, and married Lucile Palmer in 1929. The likely Jesse P. Pinkney in Brooks County in 1930 fits that path well, though the 1952 death index entry still needs a tighter proof chain. Rosa B. Mack and Mira L. Wilson are plausible daughters from the same family cluster, but their later lives have not yet been traced cleanly enough to say much more.

The same caution still applies to the rough 1900 child readings. Names that came through as Jesta, Berta, Renur, Robert, and Wade do not all map neatly onto later records, and some are probably just bad readings in a difficult image. The safer approach is to read the household through the full cluster of later records rather than forcing every 1900 given name into a fixed identity too early.

There is also a probable late-life record for Harriet. A Georgia death index entry for Hattie Pinkney shows a Brooks County death on 6 November 1939 at age 81, certificate 25428. That fits the woman who appears as Hattie in the 1930 census well enough to treat it as a strong probable match, but the full death certificate is still needed before the identification should be stated as settled fact.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Gertrude Busby's later Barney household creates a direct link from HH#108 into the Busby line.
  • Harriet's maiden name ties the household to the Roberts surname cluster in Brooks County.
  • The 1870 and 1880 Prince Roberts households give Harriet a strong earlier placement in the same county before her 1881 marriage.
  • Rosa B. Mack and Mira L. Wilson show that daughters from this household may appear in later records under married surnames.
  • The 1880 Robert Pinkney entry in Quitman and the later Barney records together support a continuous Brooks County identity for Robert.
  • The 1919 troop return for Robert Pinkney naming Mrs. Hattie Pinkney of Barney as mother strengthens the Robert T. Pinkney line and the Harriet-Hattie identification.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• John Pinkney still needs to be identified after 1900.
  • Rosa B. Mack needs a cleaner later-life trail through marriage, census, and death records.
  • Mira L. Wilson needs the same later-life reconstruction.
  • The 1952 Brooks County death index entry for Jessie Pinkney remains probable, not fully proved.
  • Harriet Roberts is now strongly placed in the Prince and Lucy Roberts households, but a direct record naming her parents would still close the point more cleanly.
  • Robert Pinkney still needs a death record, burial record, or probate record that closes the line more directly.
  • The probable Harriet or Hattie Pinkney death in Brooks County in 1939 still needs the full death certificate.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household is anchored by a strong Robert Pinkney census chain from 1880 through 1930, the 1881 Brooks County marriage record and original license-return for Robert Pinkney and Harriet Roberts, strong Roberts-family placement for Harriet in 1870 and 1880, and solid later records for Gertrude Busby, Robert T. Pinkney, and Jessie or Jesse Pinkney. The biggest remaining gaps are the later lives of Rosa and Mira, the unresolved status of John Pinkney, and direct closing records for Robert and Harriet themselves.

docs.text:

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Abe Hubbs Head 38 North Carolina Stock Cutter Annie Hubbs Wife 32 North Carolina — James Baston Stepson (Step Son) 14 Georgia — Carrie Baston Stepdaughter (Step Daughter) 13 Georgia — Sam Baston Son 6 Georgia — Alberta Baston Daughter 3 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children and stepchildren: James Baston, Carrie Baston, Sam Baston, Alberta Baston

The 1900 Barney census establishes this household clearly. Abe Hubbs, a North Carolina-born stock cutter, was living with Annie Hubbs and four children born in Georgia. The census relationship labels matter here, and the Ancestry detail pages for both Abe and Annie help fix that structure more firmly. James Baston was identified as a stepson and Carrie Baston as a stepdaughter, which strongly suggests they were Annie's children from an earlier relationship. The same detail pages identify Sam Baston as a son and Alberta Baston as a daughter rather than stepchildren. That does not by itself settle whether Sam and Alberta should be styled under Baston or Hubbs in later life, but it does strengthen the reading that they were children in Abe and Annie's own household rather than merely additional Baston stepchildren.

The later record trail is suggestive but incomplete. A man recorded as Abe Hobbs, also born in North Carolina, appears in 1910 in Colquitt County as a single man. An Abe Hobbs married Mamie Bush in Colquitt County on 23 February 1911. In 1920 an Abe Hobbs appears in Tarver District, Echols County, with children Rebecca Hobbs and Lonnie Hobbs. Those records describe a coherent later cluster, and the surname shift from Hubbs to Hobbs is plausible. Even so, no direct record has yet been found that ties the 1900 Barney Abe Hubbs household to the later Colquitt-Echols Abe Hobbs records.

That gap matters because Annie Hubbs has not been traced safely after 1900. No later record has yet been found that clearly identifies her as Annie Hubbs, Annie Hobbs, or Annie Baston in a way that can be tied back to the Barney household. The same is true for most of the children. James Baston and Carrie Baston are securely present in 1900, but neither has yet been carried forward with confidence. A later Alabama record for Carrie Bell Baston Jones, daughter of George W. Baston and Mary Etta Owens, was reviewed and excluded as a different woman. Sam Baston and Alberta Baston are also unresolved after 1900, but the census detail pages make the 1900 household reading stronger than it first appeared.

For now the household is best understood in two parts. The 1900 Barney family is secure on its own terms. The later Abe Hobbs cluster in Colquitt and Echols counties is also real on its own terms. What remains unproved is whether they belong to the same man. Until a bridging record appears, the later cluster should be treated as probable but not established continuation.

  • Rebecca Hobbs and Lonnie Hobbs may become key link points if a record names their mother or ties their father back to Brooks County.

docs.text:

  • James Baston needs a later-life trail through census, marriage, death, or military records.
  • Carrie Baston needs the same later-life reconstruction, with the excluded Carrie Bell Baston Jones kept separate.
  • Sam Baston still needs a later record that names his parents clearly and shows whether he continued under Baston or Hubbs.
  • Alberta Baston still lacks a reliable later record and may also require surname clarification in later documents.
  • The identification of 1900 Abe Hubbs with later Abe Hobbs records in Colquitt and Echols counties remains probable, not proved.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The 1900 Barney household is secure, and the census detail pages strengthen its internal structure by distinguishing James and Carrie as stepchildren while listing Sam and Alberta as son and daughter. The likely later Abe Hobbs cluster has also been identified cautiously. The main unresolved issue is the missing bridge between the 1900 Hubbs household and the later Hobbs records, along with the later identities of Annie and the children.
