docs.title: Household #110: Campbell, Ed
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Ed Campbell headed a 4-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Ed Campbell headed a 4-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 2 children.

Ed Campbell's listed occupation was Day Laborer Farm.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Ed Campbell Head 28 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Duck Campbell Wife 25 Georgia — Artmissa Campbell Daughter 8 Georgia — Calvin Campbell Son 6 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Wife in 1900: Duck Campbell, age 25, born April 1875 in Georgia
  • Children in 1900: Artmissa Campbell, age 8, and Calvin Campbell, age 6

The 1900 Barney census securely establishes Ed Campbell, wife Duck, and children Artmissa and Calvin in Brooks County. The later problem is not whether a second Campbell family existed in the same area. It did. The question is whether that later family belonged to the same Ed Campbell and, if so, whether wife Duck was the same woman later called Phoebe or Phoeby.

The later cluster is strong enough to preserve, but not strong enough to merge into the 1900 household without qualification. In 1910 Barney, Brooks County, an Edd Campbell appears with wife Phoebe and children Ida, Galvin, Lizzie E., Robert, and Anna B. In 1920, still in District 1571, Ed Campbell appears with wife Phoeby and children Robert, Anna B., Bobert Lee, and Lilly Mae, plus granddaughter Lucile. The Ancestry census detail pages for 1900, 1910, and 1920 make the conflict easier to state plainly. The 1900 detail page reports Ed Campbell born in May 1872 in Georgia, with Georgia-born parents, wife Duck born in Georgia, and children Artmissa and Calvin. The 1910 detail page reports Edd Campbell born about 1880 in North Carolina, with North Carolina-born parents, wife Phoebe born in North Carolina, and a different child set. The 1920 detail page keeps Ed and Phoeby in Barney with North Carolina birthplaces and the later child cluster. Those detail pages confirm that the 1910 and 1920 entries describe the same later family, but they also sharpen the conflict with the 1900 household.

Right now the evidence favors two wives rather than one. Duck in 1900 was reported born in April 1875 in Georgia. Phoebe or Phoeby in 1910 and 1920 was reported born about 1877 to 1882 in North Carolina. That is a meaningful conflict in given name, birthplace, and age. Ed's own reported birthplace also shifts from Georgia in 1900 to North Carolina in 1910 and 1920. The safer reading is that Duck was an earlier wife, probably the mother of Artmissa and Calvin, and that Phoebe was a later wife associated with the children in 1910 and 1920. That remains a working interpretation, not final proof.

The case is stronger on what it rules out than on what it closes. No useful Brooks County marriage hit was found on FamilySearch for Ed Campbell and Phoebe in the final targeted pass. Narrow marriage searches produced mostly irrelevant out-of-state results. No direct record was found proving Duck died between 1900 and 1910, and no direct record was found proving Duck and Phoebe were the same woman. No other source documents were located in the last pass beyond the census detail pages themselves. Some FamilySearch searches also became unreliable or intermittent, which limited extraction in the last round.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The 1910 and 1920 Campbell households in Barney and District 1571 appear to belong to the same later family cluster.
  • Calvin in 1900 may connect to Galvin in 1910, but that remains a plausible reading rather than a proved identity.
  • The Brooks County setting stays consistent across the records, which keeps the later cluster relevant even though the wife evidence conflicts.
  • The census detail pages make the birthplace conflict more explicit: 1900 gives Georgia for Ed and Duck, while 1910 and 1920 give North Carolina for Ed and Phoebe.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Duck Campbell still needs a death, burial, or other direct record between 1900 and 1910.
  • Ed Campbell still needs a marriage record to Phoebe or Phoeby if they were different wives.
  • Artmissa Campbell needs a later census, marriage, or death record.
  • Calvin Campbell and the later Galvin Campbell need a record that proves whether they were the same person.
  • Ida, Anna B., Robert, Lizzie E., Bobert Lee, and Lilly Mae all need records naming parents clearly enough to sort the 1900 household from the later one.
  • Lucile, listed as a granddaughter in 1920, may help identify one of the older daughters if a later record can be found.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. Three censuses are documented, and the central issue is now clear: whether the 1900 Duck Campbell household and the later Phoebe Campbell household represent one marriage with inconsistent reporting or two separate marriages. The census detail pages strengthen the conclusion that both household clusters are real, but they do not bridge them. The present evidence supports two probable wives, but the case still needs a direct record to settle the transition.

docs.text:

In the 1900 Barney census, J W Ingram headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
J W Ingram headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

J W Ingram's occupation is unresolved. The transcript reads “Grocer,” but the handwritten census image is difficult to read and does not clearly support either “Grocer” or “Farmer.”

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation J W Ingram Head 29 Georgia Unresolved Mary Ingram Wife 25 Georgia — Barney Ingram Son 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Child: Barney Ingram, age 1, born December 1898 in Georgia

This household is secure in the 1900 census, but its place within the larger Ingram network is still unresolved. For now it should remain separate from the better-known Berrien and Brooks County Ingram lines unless a direct record ties J. W. Ingram to a specific parent group or collateral branch.

The 1900 census gives a compact household of J. W. Ingram, wife Mary, and infant son Barney in Barney, Brooks County. The Ancestry detail page adds a few useful particulars from that same census entry: J. W. was reported as born in January 1871 in Georgia, both parents were Georgia-born, he could read and write, and he owned his house free of mortgage. The detail page also gives a marriage year of 1898, which is close to the known Brooks County marriage candidate but does not by itself prove identity. The best marriage candidate found so far is the Brooks County record showing J. W. Ingram married Mary Davis on 8 December 1897. That fits the timing of the 1900 household well, but no direct bridge record has yet proved that the Mary in the census was Mary Davis.

The leading candidate cluster remains the Berrien and Brooks County family of John Lee Ingram and Martha Ann McKinney. That line includes names worth noticing, especially Isom Barney Ingram and George Washington Ingram, because the given name Barney may reflect a family connection rather than chance. Even so, no record found so far places J. W. Ingram, born January 1871, as a documented child of John Lee Ingram and Martha Ann McKinney.

Some broader tree material has also been reviewed. FamilySearch tree work suggested an older scaffold under Guilford Ingram and, above him, Isaac Ingram and Martha Forgason. That may be useful as search guidance, but it remains tree evidence only and should not be treated as proof. A mortality-schedule entry for a John Ingram, census August 1879, born August 1838 in Georgia, also remains a plausible clue for John Lee Ingram. The fit is reasonable, but the full record has not yet been pulled and tested.

At this stage the case is defined more by what has not been proved. No documentary bridge ties J. W. Ingram of the 1900 Barney household to John Lee Ingram and Martha Ann McKinney. No clean continuation of this exact household has been found after 1900. No tax, probate, land, or heir record has yet placed J. W. Ingram inside the suspected Berrien-Brooks cluster.

  • The 1900 census detail page supports a stable profile for J. W. Ingram as a literate Georgia-born man with Georgia-born parents and a house owned free of mortgage. His occupation remains unresolved because the transcript and handwritten image do not provide a reliable reading.
  • The given name Barney may point toward the Berrien-Brooks Ingram cluster, especially the Isom Barney Ingram line, but that remains suggestive rather than proved.
  • John Lee Ingram and Martha Ann McKinney remain the leading parent candidates, though still without documentary support for J. W. Ingram.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• J. W. Ingram still needs a direct bridge to any earlier Ingram household.
  • J. W. Ingram's occupation needs further image or record research; neither “Grocer” nor “Farmer” is accepted as the final reading.
  • Mary in the 1900 household still needs proof that she was Mary Davis of the 1897 Brooks County marriage.
  • The household still needs a later census, death, burial, probate, or land record that carries J. W. Ingram forward after 1900.
  • The 1879 mortality-schedule John Ingram record still needs to be pulled in full and tested against John Lee Ingram.
  • County-level tax, probate, deed, and heir records for Brooks and Berrien remain untested enough that the family placement cannot be closed.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. The 1900 census household is secure, and the 1897 Brooks County marriage of J. W. Ingram and Mary Davis remains the best marriage candidate. The likely connection to the John Lee Ingram and Martha Ann McKinney family is still plausible, but it has not been documented well enough to merge the households.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Household partner: Will Roundtree, age 25 in 1900, sawmill laborer, born August 1874 in Georgia

This household is anchored securely in the 1900 census and remains one of the leaner entries in Volume 3. John Stroud and Will Roundtree were enumerated together in Barney, Brooks County, in dwelling and family 112. The census identifies John as head and Will as partner. That wording should be preserved. At present it is safest to read partner as a household or work relationship unless later records show something more specific.

The Ancestry detail pages add a few useful particulars from the same census entry. John Stroud was reported as single, Georgia-born, and employed as a laborer in a saw mill. He could not read or write. Will Roundtree was also single, Georgia-born, and employed as a laborer in a saw mill. Unlike John, Will was reported able to read and write. These details help define the household more clearly, but they do not extend it beyond 1900.

The main later candidate identified during research is a Willie Roundtree family in Florida. In 1910, at Lintons Mill in Jefferson County, Florida, Willie Roundtree appears with wife Daisy and children Willie, Gertrude, Washington, Pattie, Elberta, and Lee, along with mother-in-law Ella F. Simmons. In 1920, still in Jefferson County, Willie and Daisy appear again with a largely consistent child set, including Willie, Gertrude, Wash, Patsy, Berter, Leo, Daisy, Louis, and Taylor. A 1930 Sanford, Seminole County, Florida, household headed by Willie Roundtree and wife Daisy is also a plausible continuation of the same family.

The Florida records from 1910 and 1920 can be treated as one continuous Willie and Daisy Roundtree family. The child-name shifts are ordinary census variation rather than a real conflict. Washington becomes Wash, Pattie becomes Patsy, Elberta becomes Berter, and Lee becomes Leo. The question is not whether the Florida records belong together. The question is whether that later Willie Roundtree was the same man as Will Roundtree, the single sawmill laborer listed as partner in John Stroud's Barney household in 1900.

That bridge is still unproved. No direct record has yet been found tying the 1900 Barney Will Roundtree to the later husband and father in Florida. No document has been found linking John Stroud to a later Stroud household either. For now this entry should stay conservative. The Florida Roundtree family belongs in the discussion as a plausible later candidate, but it should not be merged into the Barney household as settled fact.

docs.text:
• The 1900 census securely anchors John Stroud and Will Roundtree together in Barney, Brooks County, in dwelling and family 112.
  • The census designation partner should be preserved as written, though its exact meaning remains unclear.
  • The 1910 and 1920 Willie and Daisy Roundtree households in Jefferson County, Florida, appear to belong to the same family, with the 1930 Sanford household as a plausible continuation.
  • That later Florida family remains only a candidate for Will Roundtree of Barney, not a proved continuation.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• John Stroud still needs any later census, marriage, death, burial, court, or labor record that can safely carry him beyond 1900.
  • Will Roundtree still needs a bridge record between Barney in 1900 and Jefferson County, Florida, in 1910.
  • Willie Roundtree and Daisy need a marriage record, if one survives, to help narrow place and timing.
  • Later records for Willie Roundtree should be checked for birthplace, parents, or earlier residence details that might tie him back to Brooks County.
  • Local mill, labor, court, tax, or residence records may be the best chance of connecting John Stroud and Will Roundtree after 1900.

docs.text: Further research needed. The 1900 Barney household is secure, and the later Willie and Daisy Roundtree family in Florida is a plausible but unproved candidate for Will Roundtree. No direct bridge has yet been found for either man.

docs.title: Household #113: Hunter, Dan
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Dan Hunter headed a 7-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Dan Hunter headed a 7-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 6 children.

Dan Hunter's listed occupation was Seamster.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Dan Hunter Head 33 Georgia Seamster Mary Hunter Daughter 27 Georgia — Augustus Hunter Son 8 Georgia — Ethel M Hunter Daughter 6 Georgia — Elias Hunter Son 3 Georgia — Johnson Hunter Son 2 Georgia — Mary Hunter Daughter 4/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children in 1900: Augustus, Ethel, Elias, Johnson, and infant Mary Hunter

This household has a stronger record backbone than the earlier stub suggested. The best-supported continuation is the 1910 Valdosta household of Daniel W. Hunter and wife Mary, where the ages, names, and family structure align closely with the 1900 Barney household. The best front-end marriage record is now more than an index reference. The original Brooks County marriage record shows D. W. Hunter and Mary J. Mobley, with license dated 25 September 1890 and marriage performed 30 September 1890. That record fits the 1900 couple well and is the best current identification for Mary.

The Ancestry detail pages also strengthen the census backbone. In 1900, Dan Hunter was reported born in January 1867 in Georgia, married nine years, with both parents born in Georgia, able to read and write, employed as a seamster, and owner of his home. In 1910, Daniel W. Hunter in Valdosta was again reported with Georgia-born parents, able to read and write, and living with Mary and the expected child cluster. Those details improve the continuity between the two households.

Dan Hunter can also be placed provisionally in an earlier household. In 1880, a Daniel Hunter, age 13, appears in Valdosta in the household of Harry Hunter and Julia Hunter. That remains the best current parent candidate for Dan, though it should still be treated as a leading identification rather than closed proof. The parent reading is stronger than before because Walter Hunter's 1930 Lowndes County death certificate names his father as Harry Hunter, born in South Carolina, and his mother as Julia Duncan, born in Georgia. Walter was of the right place and generation to support the reality of that parent couple in the same local Hunter line.

The child lines are uneven, but several are beginning to separate into clearer confidence tiers. Johnson Hunter is the strongest traced line. The likely chain runs from the 1900 Barney child born in April 1898 to the 1910 Valdosta household, then to the Lowndes County marriage of Johnson Hunter and Idella Jones on 4 September 1919, and later to Johnson Hunter in Orlando, Florida, including a 1942 World War II draft card giving birth date 20 April 1898 and birthplace Valdosta, Georgia. One caution remains: the later Florida line shows wife Gertrude, while the 1919 marriage is to Idella Jones. Until a divorce, death, remarriage, or other bridge record is found, that Johnson line should be treated as strong but not fully closed.

Elias Hunter is also on fairly solid ground as a likely later child in the same family. The best current reading is that the 1900 child Elias, age 3, is the same child later read in 1910 as Catrill E. Hunter. The family slot, age range, birthplace, and parent set line up well enough to make that the leading explanation.

Ethel Hunter is a good candidate for the Ethel Hunter who married Yancy Wheeler in Lowndes County on 21 March 1912. That reading is supported by the 1920 Valdosta household of Yancy and Ethel Wheeler with child Ethal May Wheeler. A later cluster of Ethel Wheeler records in Duval County, Florida, once looked promising, but those records now appear to belong to a different woman with a Simpson connection and should be excluded from this family.

Other children remain less settled. Augustus Hunter has not yet been identified securely after 1900. Infant Mary Hunter, born in April 1900, has no safe later identification yet. The likely 1910 continuation adds younger children not present in 1900, including Loamy, Maceo, Emma, Dan W. Hunter Jr., and Taft. Emma Hunter may be the woman later found in Empress, Brooks County, as wife of Jack Hunter in 1920 and 1930, but that remains plausible rather than proved. Dan W. Hunter Jr. is firmly anchored in the 1910 household, but no safe later bridge has been found, and a 1914 Lowndes County marriage for Dan Hunter and Victoria Rhea was correctly rejected as belonging to a different man.

Taken together, the strongest framework for the household is this: the 1890 Brooks County marriage of D. W. Hunter and Mary J. Mobley, the 1900 Barney household of Dan and Mary Hunter, the 1910 Valdosta household of Daniel W. and Mary Hunter, and the 1880 Valdosta placement of Daniel Hunter with Harry and Julia Hunter as the best current parent candidate. That is a solid working structure, though several child lines remain open and some of the later placements still need direct proof.

docs.text:

  • Daniel Hunter in the 1880 Valdosta household of Harry and Julia Hunter remains the best parent candidate for Dan Hunter.
  • Walter Hunter's 1930 death certificate strengthens that parent-candidate reading by naming Harry Hunter and Julia Duncan.
  • Daniel W. Hunter and Mary in 1910 Valdosta are a strong continuation of the 1900 Barney household.
  • Johnson Hunter is the strongest traced child line, though the Idella Jones to Gertrude transition still needs a bridge.
  • Ethel Hunter likely became Ethel Wheeler, but later Duval County Ethel Wheeler records should be excluded from this family.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Dan Hunter still needs a death, burial, probate, or land record that confirms his later life and family placement.
  • Mary Hunter still needs a later record confirming that she was Mary J. Mobley of the 1890 Brooks County marriage.
  • Johnson Hunter needs records that explain the shift from wife Idella Jones to later wife Gertrude.
  • Emma Hunter needs parent-naming records before she can be safely attached to the Jack Hunter household in Empress.
  • Augustus Hunter still needs broader variant searching under Gus, August, Aug, or A. Hunter.
  • Infant Mary Hunter still needs any later census, marriage, or death record.
  • Dan W. Hunter Jr. still needs a later bridge after 1910.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. The household now has a strong working structure across the original 1890 marriage record, the 1900 Barney census, the 1910 Valdosta continuation, and the likely 1880 parent household for Dan, with the Walter Hunter death certificate adding support to the Harry Hunter and Julia Duncan parent-candidate line. Several child lines are promising, especially Johnson, Elias, and Ethel, but enough gaps remain that the entry should stay open rather than be treated as closed.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Robert Stroud Head 38 Georgia Farmer Louiza Stroud Wife 36 Georgia — Milton Stroud Son 18 Georgia Farm Laborer Marietta Stroud Daughter 16 Georgia — Robert Stroud Son 14 Georgia — Margarett Stroud Daughter 11 Georgia — Martha Stroud Daughter 9 Georgia — Lula Stroud Daughter 6 Georgia — Corbit Stroud Son 3 Georgia — Carnes Stroud Son 1 Georgia — Ida Roberts Niece 15 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children in 1900: Milton, Marietta, Robert, Margarett, Martha, Lula, Corbit, and Carnes Stroud
  • Other household member: Ida Roberts, niece, age 15 in 1900

This is one of the stronger Stroud households in Volume 3. The main family line is well anchored by the 1900 census, the original 1881 Brooks County marriage record for Robert Stroud and Louisa Roberts, the 1910 census showing Robert as widowed, and the later death certificate of son Corbert Stroud naming both parents. Taken together, those records establish Robert Stroud, Louiza Roberts, and their household with good confidence.

Robert Stroud can be followed in Barney from 1900 through 1940 despite frequent spelling drift in the surname. He appears as Robert Stroud in 1900, Robert Strond in 1910, Robert Strand in 1920, Robert M. Stronel in 1930, and Robert Stroud again in 1940. The household structure remains stable enough across those records to treat them as one man. The census detail pages sharpen that continuity. In 1900 Robert was reported born in November 1861, Georgia-born with Georgia-born parents, unable to read or write, working as a farmer, and living in an owner-occupied home free of mortgage. In 1910 he was again listed as a farmer, widowed, unable to read or write, and living in an owner-occupied home free of mortgage. In 1920 he was still in Barney, again in an owner-occupied home, but was now reported able to read and write. The strongest later child line is Margaret Stroud, who appears convincingly as Margaret or Margrit Copeland in 1920, 1930, and 1940. That line helps hold the later household together.

Louiza Roberts is securely identified as Robert's wife. The 1900 census names her as Louiza. The original marriage record shows Robert Stroud and Louisa Roberts, with license dated 9 March 1881 and marriage performed 10 March 1881 in Brooks County. Corbert Stroud's 1921 death certificate gives his father as Robert Stroud and his mother as Louise Roberts, both Georgia-born. That certificate also names Margrette Copeland as informant, which further strengthens the Margaret Stroud to Copeland line inside the same family. Louiza can now be placed with good confidence in the Prince Roberts and Lucy Roberts household before marriage. She appears in 1870 in Brooks County as Louisa Roberts, age 6, in the Prince Roberts household, and again in 1880 in Quitman as 17-year-old Louisa Roberts, daughter of Prince and Lucy Roberts. The main unresolved problem is her death. Because Robert is already widowed in 1910, the best current reading is that Louiza died before that census. A later Find a Grave memorial for Louisa Roberts Stroud, said to have died 29 February 1924 and to have been buried at Sand Ridge Cemetery, cannot be accepted as this same wife without stronger proof. For now it belongs in the file only as a conflicting lead.

The child lines vary in strength. Margaret Stroud is the clearest later identification. Corbit or Corbert Stroud is also important because his death certificate reinforces the Robert Stroud and Louiza Roberts parental pair. Martha in 1900 may be the same daughter later read as Mary in 1910, but that bridge remains open. Lula appears again in 1910 but has not been traced securely beyond that point. Milton, Marietta, Robert Jr., and Carnes remain unresolved after 1900. Later censuses also add or clarify younger children and grandchildren, including Connie or Cornnice, H. McKinley, Alberta, and two grandsons whose surname reads as Homes in 1910 and Hotins in 1920. Those entries show that the family remained in Barney after Louiza disappeared from the census trail, but several of those later placements still need firmer identification.

The best current parent lead for Robert Stroud is now more limited than some earlier wording suggested. A 1870 Brooks County household headed by Margaret Stroud includes a Robert Stroud of the right age and remains a useful origin candidate. The later Find a Grave memorial for Robert Stroud Sr. repeats Henry Stroud as father and gives a death date of 17 August 1940 with burial at Sand Ridge Cemetery. That is a useful lead, but the father claim still needs original-record support before it should be treated as proved. At present, the evidence more safely supports Margaret Stroud's household as the documented 1870 placement, while Henry Stroud remains a secondary lead rather than a settled parent.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The Roberts connection is direct through Louiza Roberts and niece Ida Roberts in the 1900 household.
  • Louiza Roberts now fits well as daughter of Prince Roberts and Lucy Roberts, which places HH#114 firmly within that Roberts family network.
  • Margaret Stroud's later line into the Copeland family creates a clear connection to another Barney household network.
  • The Homes or Hotins grandsons in 1910 and 1920 may connect this household to another Barney family, but that line remains unresolved.
  • A wider Stroud-family connection, including any link to HH#112 John Stroud, remains possible but unproved.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Louiza Roberts Stroud still needs a direct death or burial record that fits Robert's widowed status by 1910.
  • The 1924 Louisa Roberts Stroud Find a Grave memorial needs independent verification before it can be attached to this household.
  • Robert Stroud still needs a death certificate, obituary, or cemetery record that confirms the 1940 death lead and any parent information.
  • Robert's parentage still needs original-record support; the 1870 Margaret Stroud household is the safest current placement, while Henry Stroud remains an unproved lead.
  • Margaret Stroud's Copeland line is strong, but the later records would still benefit from a direct parent-naming document.
  • Milton, Marietta, Robert Jr., Martha or Mary, Lula, and Carnes still need later bridge records.
  • The Homes or Hotins grandchildren need identification and parentage work.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. Robert Stroud can be followed with good confidence from 1900 through 1940, and Louiza Roberts is securely identified as his wife and as Corbert Stroud's mother. Louiza is now also well placed in the Prince and Lucy Roberts household before marriage. The main unresolved points are Louiza's death before 1910, Robert's parentage, and the still-open child and grandchild lines.

docs.title: Household #115: Rountree, Isaac
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Isaac Rountree headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Isaac Rountree headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 extended-family member.

Isaac Rountree's listed occupation was Conductor.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Isaac Rountree Head 65 Georgia Conductor Annie Rountree Wife 55 Georgia — Babe Rountree Granddaughter 5 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Other household member: Babe Rountree, granddaughter, born February 1895 in Georgia

Isaac and Annie Rountree are securely anchored in the 1900 Barney census and can be followed backward through Brooks County records with good confidence. The core census trail runs through 1870, when Isaac and Ann Rountree appear with children David, Franklin, Amy, Emma, Daniel, and James; 1880, when Isaac Rowntree and Ann Rowntree remain in Brooks County with a later child set including E. J., Isaac, Sallie A., Willie, and Dora; and 1900, when Isaac and Annie are in Barney with granddaughter Babe Rountree in the household. That gives the household a solid frame even though several family relationships inside it remain open.

The main line now under study is the branch of Frank Rountree, which can now be tied more firmly to Isaac and Annie than the earlier draft allowed. The key front-end record is the original Brooks County marriage of Frank Rountree and Maudy Stroud. The license was dated 18 January 1883 and the marriage was performed 19 January 1883. The original record strengthens the marriage itself, though the bride's given name still needs careful handling because the license reads most naturally as Maudy Stroud while the return line looks closer to Mary Stroud. That variation should be preserved rather than smoothed away.

The later records strengthen the identification of this Frank as the son of Isaac or Ike Rountree and Annie or Ann Rountree. In 1930 Frank Rountree appears in Militia District 660, Brooks County, as a 66-year-old married head of household with wife Amanda Rountree, age 64. The detail page reports that both Frank and his parents were Georgia-born, that he could read and write, that he owned his home, and that he worked on his own account doing odd jobs. The 1932 Brooks County death certificate for Frank Rountree then gives his parents as Ike Rountree and Annie Rountree, reports that he died 1 October 1932 in the Morven district, and names Robert Stroud of Barney as informant. Taken together, those records materially strengthen the case that the later Frank was the same man as Franklin from Isaac and Ann's earlier household.

The wife-name chain also becomes clearer, though not fully closed. The 1883 marriage gives a Stroud wife under the form Maudy, with the return line suggesting Mary. The 1900 household gives Amandia Rountree. The 1930 household gives Amanda Rountree. The most economical reading is that these records describe one woman under varying forms of the same name, but the file should still note the spelling problem rather than pretending it does not exist.

The Stroud connection remains the clearest outside family link in the household. Amanda Stroud, age 6 in 1870 and age 18 in 1880, appears in the Henry Stroud and Margarette Stroud household in Brooks County. She remains the strongest current candidate for the Stroud woman who married Frank Rountree in 1883 and later appears as Amandia or Amanda Rountree. That parent placement is still probable rather than fully proved, but the Robert Stroud informant line on Frank's death certificate keeps the Stroud connection active inside the same neighborhood network.

The best-documented child in the Frank and Amandia branch is still Calhoun Rountree. In 1900 he appears in their household as a farm laborer born in December 1883 in Georgia. He is the one child in that branch who is presently proved by direct census evidence. The central unresolved problem is that Amandia reported two children born and two children living in 1900, while only one child can be identified securely from the surviving evidence. That missing second child remains one of the main open questions in HH#115.

Babe Rountree, listed as granddaughter in Isaac and Annie's 1900 household, should now be handled more cautiously than in the previous draft. She is a solid household fact, but no follow-up documentation has been found for her, and no direct record yet proves her parentage. She may belong to the Frank and Amanda branch or to another child of Isaac and Annie, but the present evidence does not let her carry the argument about Amandia's missing second child.

The 1920 layer for the Frank and Amanda or Amandia branch remains open. Targeted FamilySearch work was attempted using narrowed Georgia census searches for Frank Rountree and Amanda or Amandia Rountree, but the site repeatedly returned the error message "Something Went Wrong." That should be treated as site instability on this query path, not as negative evidence against the family.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The strongest developed connection is the probable Stroud link through Frank Rountree's wife line.
  • Amanda Stroud in the Henry and Margarette Stroud household is the best current candidate for Frank Rountree's wife Maudy, Mary, Amandia, or Amanda Rountree.
  • Robert Stroud of Barney served as informant on Frank Rountree's 1932 death certificate, which keeps the Stroud connection relevant beyond the marriage alone.
  • The Rountree surname appears elsewhere in the Barney encyclopedia, including HH#119, HH#120, and HH#122, and those households may eventually connect to Isaac's line.
  • Babe Rountree's placement in Isaac and Annie's household may later connect HH#115 to another Rountree branch in the same community, but that parentage line is still open.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Franklin Rountree is now much more likely to be the later Frank Rountree, but the full bridge would still benefit from one more direct linking record across the earlier and later household forms.
  • Maudy Stroud, Mary Stroud, Amandia Rountree, and Amanda Rountree still need a full chain of records tying those names to one woman.
  • Amanda Stroud still needs direct proof that she was the daughter of Henry Stroud and Margarette Stroud and the same woman who married Frank Rountree.
  • The second child implied by Amandia's 1900 fertility report still needs identification.
  • Babe Rountree still needs parentage proof and should not be assumed to solve the missing-child problem.
  • The Frank and Amanda or Amandia branch still needs a verified 1920 census record or equivalent substitute.
  • Amanda Rountree likely died between the 1930 census and Frank's 1932 death, but that still needs direct documentation.
  • Isaac and Annie Rountree still need stronger later-life records beyond the 1900 household, especially death, burial, or probate material.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. Isaac and Annie Rountree are securely anchored across 1870, 1880, and 1900. The Frank branch is now materially stronger because the original 1883 marriage record, the 1930 Frank and Amanda household, and Frank's 1932 death certificate all reinforce the same line and support Frank as son of Ike and Annie Rountree. The biggest remaining gaps are the full wife-name chain, the identity of Amandia's second child, Babe Rountree's parentage, Amanda's death before Frank's 1932 certificate, and the still-missing 1920 layer.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
At present, this household rests almost entirely on the 1900 census, and that is the safest way to present it. Mager Williamson appears in Barney as a 31-year-old day laborer born in May 1869 in Georgia. The census detail page adds that both of his parents were Georgia-born, that he could not read or write, and that the family rented its home. His wife Emmajane Williamson was reported born in December 1869 in Georgia, could read and write, and had been married to Mager for eleven years, placing the marriage around 1889. All five children in the household were also Georgia-born.

The children named in the 1900 household were Annie, age 9; Nettie, age 5; Nora, age 3; Dollie, age 3; and Hamer, age 1. Nora and Dollie may have been twins, but the census alone does not prove that point. The 1900 record is therefore a solid baseline for the family structure, even though almost none of the household has yet been traced securely beyond that year.

Two possible later child leads have been identified, but both remain circumstantial. A 1910 Barney census entry for Annie Williams, age 19, wife of Luther Williams and mother of Lottie M. Williams, fits the age progression from Annie Williamson in 1900 and stays in the same district. Even so, no marriage record has been found that ties Annie Williamson directly to Luther Williams, so the match should remain tentative. A 1910 Morven census entry for Nettie Hoosendraft, age 16, wife of Lucious Hoosendraft, is another reasonable age-and-place match, but it too lacks a direct marriage or parent-naming record. Both leads are worth preserving, but neither is strong enough to carry the entry.

No reliable later identifications have been found for Nora Williamson, Dollie Williamson, or Hamer Williamson. No direct marriage record has been located for Mager and Emmajane themselves. The 1889 marriage year remains only a census-derived estimate. FamilySearch searches in the Georgia marriages collection for Brooks County did not produce a usable Williamson marriage for the parents or for the tentative Annie and Nettie daughter leads.

An earlier research phase incorrectly attached a death record for Mager William with spouse Mille William to this household. That should remain excluded. The surname does not match, and Mille has no sound connection to Emmajane.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• The household is securely placed in Barney in 1900, but no direct connection yet ties it to another Williamson household in the encyclopedia.
  • Annie Williams in 1910 Barney and Nettie Hoosendraft in 1910 Morven are plausible later daughter leads, but both remain unproved.
  • Nora, Dollie, and Hamer Williamson remain unplaced after 1900.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Mager Williamson and Emmajane Williamson still need a direct marriage record or other record naming both spouses together outside the 1900 census.
  • Annie Williamson still needs a marriage or death record proving whether she was the same woman as Annie Williams, wife of Luther Williams.
  • Nettie Williamson still needs the same kind of record proving whether she was the same woman as Nettie Hoosendraft, wife of Lucious Hoosendraft.
  • Nora Williamson, Dollie Williamson, and Hamer Williamson still need any reliable later-life records.
  • Mager Williamson and Emmajane Williamson still need death, burial, probate, or land records that carry the household beyond 1900.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. The 1900 census household is secure and now better defined by the census detail page, but the family has not yet been extended by direct evidence into later records. The two 1910 daughter candidates are reasonable leads, not documented identifications.

docs.title: Working conclusion
docs.text:
• The 1900 household of Mager and Emmajane Williamson is well documented with five children.
  • Two daughters, Annie and Nettie, have plausible 1910 census matches, but neither connection is verified by primary documentation.
  • No marriage records were found in the available FamilySearch Georgia collection for either the parents or the two married daughters.
  • County-level records are needed to advance this household beyond circumstantial leads.

docs.title: Household #117: McCoy, John Buck
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, John McCoy headed an 11-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
John McCoy headed an 11-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 9 children.

John McCoy's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation John McCoy Head 20 Georgia Farmer Hester McCoy Wife 29 Georgia — Joe McCoy Son 17 Georgia — Mary McCoy Daughter 15 Georgia — Arch McCoy Son 13 Georgia — James McCoy Son 12 Georgia — Reignor McCoy Daughter 10 Georgia — Hattie McCoy Daughter 6 Georgia — Johnnie McCoy Son 4 Georgia — Dollie McCoy Daughter 2 Georgia — Nina McCoy Daughter 6/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Children in household: Joe, Mary, Arch, Lorina or Rena, James, Hattie, Johnnie, and Nina McCoy

This is a well-developed household, though several child lines still need direct follow-through. The first correction is to the census extraction itself. The 1900 index apparently misreported the family as Black, but the census page and the later records consistently show John Buck McCoy and his household as White. The census page also gives John's age clearly as 40, with a June 1859 birth month.

John Buck McCoy can be followed with good confidence across the 1900 Barney household, the 1910 Barney household as a widower, the 1920 Colquitt County household with second wife Ida, and the 1935 Georgia death certificate. The death certificate gives his parents as William McCoy and Elizabeth Seay, confirms his death in Pavo, Colquitt County, and supports the same man seen earlier in Brooks County. The 1870 Lowndes County household of William and Elizabeth McCoy and the 1880 Brooks County household of William N. McCoy and E. A. McCoy provide the strongest earlier placement for John.

The evidence supports reading John Buck McCoy as the same man also described in secondary material as John Henry Buck McCoy. That fuller form appears in the Geneanet tree and fits the name pattern seen in the family, though the file should still treat tree material as support rather than primary proof. John's first wife was Hester A. Strickland, who is tied to him by cemetery and family-link evidence and is reported in compiled sources as the mother of the first child set. Her middle initial A appears consistently enough to keep. A Civil War pension file naming a John McCoy with spouse Hester A. McCoy almost certainly belongs to another man because this John was born in 1859, but the spouse name is at least consistent with the wider identification.

The 1900 household contains both well-traced and unresolved children. Lorina or Rena McCoy can be identified with fair confidence as Lorina "Rena" McCoy Shurley, born 3 December 1888 and buried at Pleasant Hill Cemetery in Berlin, Colquitt County, with compiled links naming her husband as Stephen William Shurley Sr. and placing her among the children of John Buck McCoy and Hester Strickland McCoy. That remains cemetery-level support rather than a direct-record proof, but it fits the same Colquitt County cluster seen elsewhere in this family. Johnnie can also now be read with much more confidence as John Thomas McCoy. In the 1910 Barney household he appears as John S. McCoy, age 14, son of John B. McCoy. He then fits the Brooks County marriage record for John T. McCoy and Alma Barington on 26 November 1923, the memorial for John Thomas McCoy at Oak Hill Cemetery in Quitman with birth 12 March 1897 and death 29 January 1950, and the veteran headstone application for John T. McCoy, Georgia sergeant, 269th M. P. Company, whose death date and burial place match the memorial. The Find a Grave parent links remain compiled support, but the marriage record and headstone application make John Thomas McCoy a strong identification for the HH#117 son. James L. McCoy can be carried forward with reasonable confidence through later memorial or family-link evidence, and Nina can now be identified with much greater confidence as Nina G. McCoy Croft. She appears in a clean four-census chain with husband Chester L. Croft: in Tallokas, Brooks County, in 1920; Militia District 660 in 1930; Barney in 1940; and Barney again in 1950. That line is reinforced by the Social Security Death Index entry for Nina Croft, born 13 December 1899 and dead in July 1981 with last residence in Quitman, and by the Oak Hill Cemetery memorial for Nina McCoy Croft with matching birth and death dates. A Valdosta Daily Times obituary index entry fits the same woman, but the index alone should be treated as supporting evidence rather than the backbone of the identification. The line now rests on firmer ground than earlier versions allowed. Compiled cemetery data places a James L. McCoy, born 27 April 1889 and buried at Oak Hill Cemetery in Quitman, as son of John Buck McCoy and Hester Strickland McCoy, with wife Fannie Copeland. That identification is strengthened by the 1926 Georgia death certificate for infant James Jr. McCoy of Berlin, Colquitt County, which names the child's father as J. L. McCoy, mother as Fannie Copeland, and informant as J. L. McCoy. The combination of initials, spouse name, and Colquitt County location fits well with John Buck McCoy's later family geography, making James L. McCoy a strong probable identification for the HH#117 son, though one more direct census or death record for James himself would still be ideal. Hattie McCoy can also now be identified with confidence. She married Gordon Guess in Brooks County on 22 August 1909 and appears with him in a clean census chain: as newly married Hattie Guess in Morven in 1910, as Hattie Guess in Quitman in 1920, as Hattie Guest in Valdosta in 1930, as Hattie C. Guess in Dasher in 1940, and as divorced Hattie C. Guess in Orlando in 1950. Joseph Gordon Guess's World War I draft card names his nearest relative as wife Hattie Cornelia Guess, which strongly supports Hattie's fuller form as Hattie Cornelia McCoy Guess. The 1994 Georgia death index and compiled burial record for Hattie C. Guess align with that same identity. Dolly McCoy can now be identified with similar confidence as Dolly, Dollie, or Pollie McCoy Croft. A direct Colquitt County marriage record shows Miss Dolly McCoy marrying J. P. Croft on 10 January 1915. She then appears in a stable Robinson District census chain as Pollie Croft in 1920, Dolly Croft in 1930, and Dolly McCoy Croft in 1940, when she was a widowed mother in the household of son James Clarence Croft. A 1979 obituary index for Dollie McCoy Croft of Quitman provides compiled support that fits the wider sibling cluster, though it should be used more cautiously than the marriage and census records. Archie McCoy can now be carried farther than earlier versions allowed. He appears in the 1910 Barney household as Archie McCoy, age 23, son of John B. McCoy, and he aligns well with the World War I draft registration for Archie L. McCoy of Pavo, Colquitt County, born 1 January 1887 in Georgia. The draft card, signed A. L. McCoy on 5 June 1917, shows a single white farm laborer living on Pavo Route 2 and working for Ches. Leavitt. Taken together, the 1910 household placement, exact birth date, and south Georgia location make this a strong identification, though the middle initial should remain simply L. until a fuller direct record appears. Joe McCoy can also now be identified with much greater confidence as Joseph William McCoy. The marriage record for Joseph McCoy and Lollie Chambers established the wife link, but the 1928 Georgia death certificate for Mrs. J. W. McCoy makes the fuller identification much firmer by naming her husband as Joseph William McCoy, the informant as Joseph Wm. McCoy, her father as James Chambers, and her mother as Nettie Webb. That record does not spell out Lollie's given name on its face, but the combination of husband, marriage link, Chambers parentage, and Colquitt County geography makes the identification strong. Mary McCoy can now be carried forward more cautiously as the likely Mary M. McCoy who married Anders Chambers in Brooks County. A direct Brooks County marriage license shows Anders Chambers and Mary M. McCoy licensed on 1 March 1902 and married on 2 March 1902. That record gives the needed married-name bridge and places her in the same local Chambers network seen elsewhere around this family, but it still needs a later census, death, or burial record under Mary Chambers before the identification should be treated as fully secure.

The 1910 household shows John B. McCoy as widowed in Barney with Archie, John S., Dollie, and Nina still at home. By 1920 he had moved to the Robinson district of Colquitt County and remarried Ida Mae Guess. That second household is smaller and includes Delma Semroy McCoy, recorded there as Delmer, and Bee McCoy. Later memorial and tree material extend the second family line through Everett, Betty Mae, Eula Lee, Gloria Grace, Eunice L., and Dock McCoy, though several of those children were born after the 1920 census and therefore depend on later compiled records more than on early census enumeration.

The main caution points in this entry are the unresolved children from the first marriage, the exact marriage record for John and Hester, the marriage record for John and Ida, and the need to distinguish this man from other John McCoy records in Georgia. The evidence base is good enough to call the household well researched, but not finished.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:

  • The Seay line appears in secondary material through Elizabeth Seay and her reported parents John L. Seay and Nancy A. Seay, but that grandparent layer still depends heavily on compiled evidence.
  • Hester A. Strickland ties the household into the Strickland family network of Brooks County.
  • Ida Mae Guess likely connects the later household to the Guess family of Barney, though that relationship still needs direct record support.
  • Dolly McCoy and Nina McCoy both later connect to the Croft family.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: Johnnie McCoy, age four in the 1900 household, is strongly identified with John Thomas McCoy through the 1910 household, Brooks County marriage record, cemetery memorial, and a Veterans Administration headstone application. The headstone application cites service as a Georgia sergeant in the 269th M. P. Company and gives Oak Hill Cemetery in Quitman as the burial place.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• John Buck McCoy still needs a direct marriage record to Hester A. Strickland.
  • John Buck McCoy still needs a direct marriage record to Ida Mae Guess.
  • Mary McCoy is now a strong candidate for the Mary M. McCoy who married Anders Chambers in Brooks County on 2 March 1902, but she still needs a later census, death, or burial record under Mary Chambers before the identification can be treated as secure.
  • Hattie McCoy is now well identified as Hattie Cornelia McCoy Guess, but one direct death certificate or obituary for her would still be useful beyond the death index and compiled burial record.
  • Archie McCoy is now strongly aligned with the 1917 World War I draft card for Archie L. McCoy of Pavo, born 1 January 1887, but he still needs later census, marriage, death, or burial records.
  • Anny McCoy and Fannie McCoy in the 1870 William McCoy household still need relationship proof.
  • William McCoy's parentage and earlier origins still need to be documented from records before 1870.
  • The full documentary basis for treating John Buck McCoy as John Henry Buck McCoy would benefit from one more direct record.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. John Buck McCoy is securely anchored across the 1900, 1910, and 1920 censuses and the 1935 death certificate, and his placement as son of William McCoy and Elizabeth Seay is well supported. Joseph William McCoy, James L. McCoy, John Thomas McCoy, Hattie Cornelia McCoy Guess, Dolly McCoy Croft, Nina McCoy Croft, and Archie L. McCoy are now all identified with useful follow-forward evidence, and Mary McCoy now has a plausible marriage bridge into the Chambers family though she still needs later-life confirmation. The main remaining work is in Mary McCoy, the two marriages of John himself, and the earlier McCoy parent generation.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Ida Johnson Head 34 North Carolina Farmer Hattie Johnson Wife 27 Georgia — Frank Johnson Son 2 Georgia — Walter Johnson Son 9/12 Georgia — Amanda Johnson Daughter 4 Georgia — Amanda Roberts Grandmother 69 Georgia — Bessie Roberts Niece 13 Georgia — Hubart Roberts Nephew 10 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The present evidence supports a two-census reconstruction of this household, with one later child record, but not yet a full family identification. The 1900 Barney household indexed as Ida Johnson appears to match the 1910 Barney household headed by Iley F. Johnson. The handwriting on the 1900 census appears closer to Ily than Ida, which makes the alignment with 1910 stronger than the index alone suggests. Place, spouse, and child pattern all point to the same family.

In 1900 the household consisted of a head best read as Ily Johnson, born in North Carolina about August 1865, with wife Hattie, born in Georgia about 1873, and children Amanda, Frank, and Walter. Walter was nine months old when the census was taken, so his birth belongs about September 1899 rather than 1888. The household also included Amanda Roberts, listed as grandmother, age sixty-nine, with Bessie Roberts, niece, age thirteen, and Hubart Roberts, nephew, age ten. Those Roberts relationships are important, but the records now in hand do not show whether they connect through Hattie, through the Johnson head, or through an earlier household generation.

The 1910 Barney household strengthens the continuity case. It shows Iley F. Johnson, born about 1860 in North Carolina, with wife Hattie and children Jessie, Frank, Walter, Callie, Cleveland, and Lucy. The move from owned farm in 1900 to rented farm in 1910 does not break the identification. The stronger anchors are location, spouse, and the carry-forward of Frank and Walter into the later child set.

A useful later record now extends one child forward. Jessie Easter's 1921 Brooks County death certificate gives her place of death as Barney, Militia District 1571, age twenty-six years and eight months, birthplace Brooks County, and father Iley Johnson. That makes her a strong fit for the Jessie Johnson in the 1910 household and gives direct support for reading the household head as Iley rather than Ida. The same death certificate names her mother as Jessie Johnson rather than Hattie Johnson. That conflict should be preserved as written and treated cautiously until another direct record shows whether it reflects informant error, a second name, or a different family complication not yet visible in census records.

At this stage, the household can be described as partially reconstructed but not closed. The 1900 and 1910 census households likely belong to the same family, and Jessie Easter's death certificate gives the best later confirmation now in hand. Hattie Johnson remains the clearest continuous anchor across the census records. Walter Johnson's birth should be read as about September 1899. The main unresolved problems are the missing 1920 placement, the exact relationship of the Roberts group, and the mother-name conflict raised by Jessie Easter's death certificate.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Amanda Roberts, Bessie Roberts, and Hubart Roberts likely preserve the key to Hattie's family or to an earlier Johnson-Roberts household connection.
  • The family remained in the Barney/Brooks area from 1900 to 1910, and Jessie Easter's 1921 death certificate places the same cluster in Militia District 1571.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The 1900 head is best read from the handwriting as Ily Johnson, but the indexed form Ida Johnson should still be noted in case other databases preserve that reading.
  • The household still needs a confident 1920 census identification.
  • Hattie Johnson still needs a marriage record, death record, or other direct record tying her to this same household.
  • Jessie Easter likely belongs in this family, but the death certificate's naming of mother Jessie Johnson instead of Hattie Johnson needs resolution.
  • Amanda Roberts, Bessie Roberts, and Hubart Roberts still need relationship proof.
  • Frank, Walter, Callie, Cleveland, and Lucy still need follow-forward records that confirm the 1900 and 1910 family reconstruction.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Source-exhausted online. The 1900 and 1910 Brooks County census households likely represent the same Johnson family, and Jessie Easter's 1921 death certificate gives meaningful support for the Ily/Iley reading of the head and for one child's later identity. Even so, the Roberts kinship problem, the missing 1920 census placement, and the mother-name conflict remain unresolved. Further progress likely depends on courthouse, cemetery, church, probate, tax, deed, or other local records not currently available online.

docs.title: Current findings
docs.text:
The 1900 household is secure and rests on the original census image. It does not yet carry forward into later records with confidence.

Follow-forward work has not yet produced a defensible later identification for either Daisy or Minnie. Two 1920 Valdosta candidates were reviewed during earlier work. Minnie Williams, a Black, single, twenty-two-year-old roomer and maid on South Patterson Street, remains only a loose possibility because no Brooks County tie, no connection to Daisy, and no clear path back to the 1900 household has been found. Minie Davis, a White, single, twenty-two-year-old nurse on Petters Street, can be ruled out on race and household context. No marriage record, death record, cemetery record, or later census record has yet been found that securely links back to Daisy and Minnie of this household.

Earlier review of two 1920 Valdosta candidates did not produce a defensible match, and no burial, marriage, or death record has yet closed the household. Further progress will likely depend on additional county-level records, better follow-forward evidence, or a direct later-life record for Minnie.

docs.title: Household in 1900
docs.text:
Andrew Rountree appears in Barney in 1900 as a Black farmer with the following profile: - Birth: February 1850, Georgia, USA - Occupation: farmer - Reported marriage year: 1878

His wife appears as Lucinda Rountree. - Birth: about 1852-1855, Georgia, USA

Children in the household: - Lacy Rountree, son, age 17, born about 1883 in Georgia - Elzy Rountree, son, age 16, born about 1884 in Georgia - Edward Rountree, son, age 12, born about 1888 in Georgia - Frank Rountree, son, age 4, born about 1896 in Georgia

docs.title: Current findings
docs.text:
This household can be followed with confidence across a long Brooks County census chain. In 1880, Andrew Rountree appears in Morven, Brooks County, as a Black man age 28, born about 1852 in Georgia, with wife Lucinda, age 28, stepdaughter Kate Mincay, age 12, and sons Irvin, age 2, and Simeon, age two months. That household fits the later Barney family closely in age, place, and composition.

The 1900 Barney household continues forward in 1910, 1920, and 1930 with Andrew and Lucinda or Lucindy still in Brooks County. In 1910, son Frank remained at home. By 1940, Andrew and Lucinda appear in the Barney household of Lacy Rountree, where they are identified as father and mother. That 1940 record ties Lacy securely back to Andrew and Lucinda and confirms the family remained rooted in the same community for decades.

The marriage evidence is stronger than the earlier short entry suggested. A Brooks County marriage license dated 27 January 1877 and return dated 30 January 1877 records the marriage of Andrew Rountree and Sindy Mincy. The 1880 presence of Kate Mincay as Andrew's stepdaughter strongly supports the conclusion that the woman later recorded as Lucinda was the same spouse or belonged to the same Mincy line, though the exact resolution of the Sindy/Lucinda naming difference still needs cautious handling.

Frank Rountree can also be followed into adulthood. A Georgia World War I service card identifies Frank Rountree of Barney, born about 1896 in Barney, Georgia, inducted at Quitman on 2 October 1917 at age 21 years and 8 months, and discharged on demobilization in January 1919. That record fits the youngest son in the 1900 and 1910 Andrew Rountree household.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: Andrew belongs to the same local Black Rountree cluster as HH#115, HH#119, and HH#122. The shared surname, close census geography, and long residence in Barney place these households in the same local network, but the exact kinship remains unproved.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The available evidence strongly favors treating the 1877 Andrew Rountree-Sindy Mincy marriage as the marriage of this household, but the Sindy/Lucinda naming difference should still be described carefully until a direct bridging record is found.
  • Death records, burial records, and probate or land records for Andrew and Lucinda would help close the household more fully.
  • Later records for Irvin, Simeon, Elzy, and Edward remain to be assembled into the same degree of continuity now established for Lacy and Frank.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: WELL-RESEARCHED: The household is documented through the 1877 Brooks County marriage record, the 1880 Morven census, the 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930 Barney-area censuses, the 1940 Lacy Rountree household, and Frank Rountree's World War I service card. The family continuity is strong. Remaining work centers on resolving the Sindy/Lucinda name issue with a direct bridge and locating fuller end-of-life records for Andrew, Lucinda, and several children.

docs.text:

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Household in 1900
docs.text:
George Lemon appears in Barney in 1900 as a Black farmer with the following profile: - Birth: December 1839, Georgia, USA - Occupation: farmer - Marital status: single - Literacy: could speak English, could not read or write

Nancy McLoud appears in the household as George's niece. - Birth: October 1849, Georgia, USA - Age in 1900: 50 - Relationship in 1900: niece

docs.title: Current findings
docs.text:
George Lemon is now anchored by a solid Brooks County chain from 1890 through 1920. In the 1890 Brooks County tax digest, George Lemons appears in the Tallokas district on the Freedman tax list. By 1900 he was in Barney as a single Black farmer, and he remains there in 1910 and 1920 under the surname forms Lemon, Lemons, and Lemmon. In 1910 his farm was owned free of mortgage and the household included Charlie, Katie, Columbus, Webster, and Irvin McDaniels as boarders. In 1920 he was still single, still farming, and still shown with land owned free, with Ben Fross in the household.

The strongest current pre-1890 lead for George is an 1880 Leeton, Sumter County household indexed as George Lamon. That George was a Black man of the right age, born in Georgia, and was living with wife Cheny and children Cathrine, Robert, and Henry. The match is plausible and worth keeping in the entry, but it still needs a direct bridge because the Barney man is listed as single in 1900.

The 1870 Lowndes County candidate for George is also more interesting than it first appeared. A George Lemons of about the right age appears there in a household that included Amy Lemons and Villar Rountree. That does not yet prove identity, but the age fits and the Rountree presence may matter in this Barney setting.

Nancy McLoud can now be discussed with more precision. A Lowndes County marriage record dated 8 July 1875 shows Nancy Rountree marrying Green McLeod. In 1880, Green and Nancy McLeod appear in Morven, Brooks County, with children Warren, William, and Lovie. The available evidence strongly suggests that the woman listed as George Lemon's niece in 1900 is this same Nancy, but the exact path by which she was George's niece remains unproved.

Additional McLeod records help place Nancy's household in the same regional setting. Green McLeod appears in Brooks County in 1870 and in the 1871 Tallokas district tax digest. Those records strengthen the local continuity of Nancy's married household, even though they do not by themselves identify George Lemon's parents or siblings.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
Nancy McLoud is the clearest kinship clue attached to this household. The best present reading is that she was Nancy Rountree before her 1875 marriage to Green McLeod and Nancy McLeod in the 1880 Morven household. That makes the Rountree and McLeod lines directly relevant to HH#121, but the exact documentary link between George Lemon and Nancy still has not been found.

The 1870 George Lemons candidate in a household with Villar Rountree adds another possible tie to the local Rountree network. For now, that should remain a lead rather than a stated family connection.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The 1880 George Lamon household in Sumter County is the best present earlier candidate for George, but the identification is still not proved.
  • The 1900 use of the relationship term niece for Nancy McLoud is important, but the record trail has not yet shown whether that kinship ran through a Lemon, Rountree, McLeod, or other family line.
  • Death, burial, probate, land, and later census records are still needed to close George's life after 1920.
  • Marriage records for George under Lemon, Lemons, Lemmon, and Lamon, with spouse variants Cheny, Cheney, and Chaney, remain worth searching.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: WELL-RESEARCHED: George Lemon is documented in Brooks County through the 1890 Tallokas tax digest and the 1900, 1910, and 1920 Barney censuses. A plausible 1880 Sumter County carry-back and a plausible 1870 Lowndes County candidate have both been identified, but neither is yet proved as the same man. Nancy McLoud, listed as George's niece in 1900, is now strongly supported as the same woman who married Green McLeod in Lowndes County in 1875 and appears as Nancy McLeod in Morven in 1880. The main remaining questions concern George's earlier identity, the exact kinship path to Nancy, and his death and burial.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Coleman Rountree Head 35 Georgia Laborer Farm Maggie Rountree Wife 35 Georgia — Cora Rountree Daughter 6 Georgia — Walter Rountree Son 4 Georgia — Nancy Rountree Daughter 3 Georgia — George Rountree Son 1 Georgia — Charley Rountree Cousin 17 Georgia Laborer Farm

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Household in 1900
docs.text: Coleman Rountree appears in Barney in 1900 with the following household: - Coleman Rountree, head, born May 1865 in Georgia, laborer on a farm - Maggie Rountree, wife, age 35, born in Georgia - Cora Rountree, daughter, age 6 - Walter Rountree, son, age 4 - Nancy Rountree, daughter, age 3 - George Rountree, son, age 1 - Charley Rountree, cousin, age 17

docs.title: Current findings
docs.text:
This household can now be followed much more fully than the earlier entry suggested. Coleman Rountree married Maggie Clark in Brooks County on 23 February 1893. By 1900 they were in Barney with four young children and Charley Rountree, whose relationship was recorded as cousin. The 1900 census also gives Coleman's birth month as May 1865.

Maggie's Clark-family placement is now well supported. In 1870 a Margaret Clark, age 6, appears in the Brooks County household of Fortune and Mary Clark, with Malinda Rountree also present in the home. In 1880 a Margaritte Clark, age 16, appears in Morven as daughter of Fortune and Mary J. Clark. By 1910, Mary J. Clark appears as head of household with Maggie Rountree listed as daughter and Coleman Rountree as son-in-law. That sequence ties Maggie of HH#122 back to the Clark family with good confidence.

Later censuses extend the household across several decades in Barney. In 1920, C. O. Rountree appears with a mixed household that includes son Walter, younger household members Willie and Marietta, adopted children Harry Allen and Willie Allen, grandson John B. Rountree, and granddaughter Bulah C. Hill. In 1930, Coleman O. Rountree appears in Barney as a carpenter with wife Katy. In 1940, Colman Rountree remains in Barney with wife Kate and daughter Gloria. A Georgia death-index entry for Katie Rountree, a Black woman born about 1889 who died in Brooks County on 22 June 1945 under certificate 17497, fits this later household well and strongly supports the reading that Katy or Kate was a later wife rather than a stray census variant for Maggie. In 1950, widowed Coleman appears in the household of James Shellie Godfrey and Mary Etta Godfrey, where he is listed as father-in-law. That 1950 relationship makes it very likely that Mary Etta Godfrey was another daughter of Coleman.

Several child identifications are now supported by direct records outside the census. Walter Rountree's death certificate, dated 13 April 1920 in Barney, names his parents as Coleman Rountree and Maggie Clark and gives Little River as the burial place. A later military-era record for Walter also names Coleman Rountree as his father at Route 3 Box 9, Barney, Georgia. Cora of the 1900 household is now strongly supported as the later Coraetta Rountree Wright. The Social Security Applications and Claims Index gives Coraetta Rountree Wright's birth as 26 September 1896 at Barney and names her parents as Colman Rountree and Maggie Clark.

The end of Coleman's life is partly anchored by the Georgia death index, which records Coleman Rountree, resident of Brooks County, dying on 20 November 1951 in Baldwin County under certificate 24405. The index is useful, but the full death certificate is still needed.

An earlier Coleman candidate also remains worth keeping in view. In 1870, a young Colman Rountree of about the right age appears in the household of Josiah and Delphia Rountree. That is a plausible early-life anchor, but the connection has not yet been proved with a direct bridge.

The main unresolved problem is the change from Maggie in the early household to Katy or Kate in 1930 and 1940. The later-wife reading is now much stronger. Katie Rountree's 1945 Brooks County death-index entry fits the 1930 and 1940 household well and supports a likely remarriage after Maggie's death, although the marriage record and full death certificate are still needed for direct proof.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
HH#122 belongs to the same Black Rountree cluster in Barney as HH#115, HH#119, and HH#120. The exact kinship among those households is still not documented, but the local cluster is real.

The Clark connection is now one of the strongest parts of this entry. Maggie can be placed in the Fortune and Mary J. Clark household before her 1893 marriage to Coleman, and in 1910 she appears again with Mary J. Clark as daughter.

Charley Rountree, listed as cousin in 1900, remains an important lead for linking this household to another Rountree branch already present in the Barney census. The possible connection to the Charley Rountree seen in HH#99 remains suggestive, not proved.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Coleman Rountree's full 1951 death certificate is still needed to confirm the exact death details, informant, burial, and parent field wording.
  • Maggie Clark Rountree still needs a death or burial record.
  • The record trail now strongly suggests that Katy or Kate was a later wife, probably the Katie Rountree who died in Brooks County on 22 June 1945, but a later marriage record for Coleman and Katie's full death certificate are still needed for direct proof.
  • The 1870 young Colman Rountree in the Josiah and Delphia Rountree household remains a good candidate, but not a proved identification.
  • The exact parentage links for Arthur McLeod, Harry Allen, Willie Allen, John B. Rountree, Bulah C. Hill, Marietta, and Gloria still need more direct documentation.
  • Adult records for Nancy and George Rountree would help close the family more fully.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: SOURCE-EXHAUSTED online: Coleman Rountree and Maggie Clark are now documented through their 1893 Brooks County marriage record, the 1900 through 1950 census trail, Walter Rountree's death certificate, Coraetta Rountree Wright's Social Security claims record, Maggie's Clark-family placements in 1870 and 1880, Katie Rountree's 1945 Brooks County death-index entry, and Coleman's 1951 Georgia death-index entry. The household is now well documented as a family unit, and Mary Etta Godfrey is strongly supported as Coleman's daughter by the 1950 father-in-law relationship. The later Katy or Kate household wife is now strongly supported as a second wife, probably the Katie Rountree who died in Brooks County on 22 June 1945, though the marriage record and full death certificate are still needed for direct proof. The remaining questions are no longer basic online identification problems. They center on Maggie's death, a fuller account of the younger generation, and county-level death, burial, probate, land, or marriage records that would finish the reconstruction.
