docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Charlie Isom Head 53 Georgia Laborer Saw Mill Nancy Isom Wife 52 Georgia — Edwin Isom Son 25 Georgia — Vivian Isom Son 12 Georgia — May Clayton Granddaughter 15 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Charlie Isom, head, age 53, born Dec 1846 in Georgia, laborer at a saw mill
  • Nancy Isom, wife, age 52, born about 1848 in Georgia
  • Edwin Isom, son, age 25, born about 1875 in Georgia
  • Vivian Isom, son, age 12, born about 1888 in Georgia
  • May Clayton, granddaughter, age 15, born about 1885 in Georgia

The 1900 Barney household is best read as the later Florida family of Charles N. Isom and Nancy Griffin Isom. The race label in this entry needed correction; the household is white in the census image, and the later Florida records are consistent with that reading.

The earlier Georgia trail is now much firmer than the old entry suggested. In 1860, Charles N. Isom, age 13, appears in Berrien County in the household of John and Sophia Isom. A Georgia militia reorganization census taken in Berrien County in 1864 records a Charley Isom, age 16 years 2 months, born in Georgia. In 1870, Charles Isom, 23, appears in Lowndes County with wife Nancy and children Ida and William. In 1880, Charles N. Isom, 33, appears at Valdosta with wife Nannie and children Ida, William C., John M., and Simion E. Together these records provide a workable chain from Berrien County into Lowndes County before the move to Brooks County.

Lowndes County tax and land material helps fill the gap between 1870 and 1880. A sheriff's sale notice in The Valdosta Times of 10 Mar 1877 lists 225 acres of lot 136 in the 11th district as the property of Charles N. Isom under a 1876 tax fi. fa. Additional tax digest material places Charles N. Isom in Valdosta militia district 663 in the late 1870s and early 1880s, with taxable land in the 11th district. These are continuity records rather than direct kinship proof, but they fit the census trail well.

By 1900 the family was in Barney. The schedule gives Charlie's birth month as Dec 1846 and says he and Nancy had been married 34 years. That points to a marriage about 1866, although the direct marriage record has not yet been found. The household also shows a granddaughter, May Clayton, age 15. May remains unresolved, but her age suggests that she belonged to one of the older children already present in the 1880 household, most likely through a married daughter branch rather than through the younger Florida children.

The later Florida records are strong. In 1920, Charles N. Isom appears in Plant City, Hillsborough County, age 73, with wife Nancy, 71. In 1930, he appears there again at 1304 Park Street, age 83, with wife Nancy G. Isom, 81, working as a truck farmer and marked as a Civil War veteran. Florida end-of-life records place Charles Nelson Isom's death in Hillsborough County in 1934. Cemetery evidence places him at Oaklawn Cemetery in Plant City as Chas. Nelson Isom, 1846-1934. Nancy Isom's own trail is also clearer now. The Florida death index records her death in Hillsborough County in 1937, the Tampa Tribune death notice of 10 Aug 1937 reports that Mrs. C. N. Isom, 89, died at the home of her son V. C. Isom in Plant City, and her burial is also placed at Oaklawn Cemetery.

Nancy's maiden name is now strongly supported as Griffin. A Georgia death certificate for a son of C. N. Isom names the mother as Griffin. Nancy's 1937 death notice names her brothers as W. O. Griffin of Turkey Creek and C. L. Griffin of Wauchula. Earlier Lowndes County records for Nancy Griffin in 1850 and Nancy Guffin in 1860 look like the best current candidates for her earlier life, though that part of the case is still indirect. For now, the careful reading is that Charlie's wife was Nancy Griffin, with the 1900, 1920, and 1930 census forms preserving her as Nancy or Nancy G.

Several child lines can now be followed beyond the Barney household. Vivian of the 1900 census is the later Vivian Clower Isom, born 18 Apr 1888 in Lowndes County, Georgia, later of Plant City. His draft card, later censuses, death notice, and Oaklawn burial all align, and his son Charles Jerome Isom's draft card names Vivian Clower Isom as father. Another son from the 1880 household, Simion E. Isom, can be followed as the later Simon E., Simmeon Edwin, Edwin S., or S. Ed Isom of Plant City. His 1903 marriage notice to Sallie Robinson, 1910 and later census appearances, World War I draft card, and later family records tie that branch together. These descendant lines do not solve every question in the 1900 Barney household, but they do show that the family moved into a durable Plant City cluster.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
The strongest current parentage reading is that Charlie of HH#123 was the Charles N. Isom who appears in 1860 with John and Sophia Isom in Berrien County. The later record that gives Charles's parents as John Isom and Sophia Guest or Guess fits that reading, though the exact spelling of Sophia's maiden name still needs the original document checked carefully.

The Lowndes County tax records also place Charles near John Isom and James W. Isom in the same local network. That supports a family cluster in the 11th district and militia district 663, but it is still contextual support rather than direct proof of each relationship.

The Florida branch is now clearer than before. Charles and Nancy's descendants can be followed through Vivian Clower Isom and through the Simmeon Edwin or S. Ed Isom branch, with Sallie Robinson and later children such as Ida S. Isom Jefferson and Charles Jerome Isom appearing in direct records.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: Charles Nelson Isom's current military evidence is limited to the 1930 census, which marks him as a Civil War veteran. The later Florida death and cemetery records strengthen the identity chain for the man, but no service file is yet tied to him here, so the page should avoid adding a unit or service chronology.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Obtain the full 1934 Florida death certificate for Charles Nelson Isom to confirm the exact death date, informant, burial wording, and parent field language.
  • Obtain Nancy Isom's full 1937 death certificate if possible. The death notice and cemetery record are strong, but the certificate would help close the case.
  • Look for a direct marriage record for Charles Isom and Nancy Griffin, or another early record that states Nancy's maiden name in original form.
  • Resolve the identity of May Clayton, the 15-year-old granddaughter in the 1900 household.
  • Check whether the original record behind the later parentage claim gives Sophia's surname as Guess, Guest, or another close variant.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: WELL-RESEARCHED: Charles N. Isom is now documented through the 1860 Berrien County census, the 1864 Berrien militia reorganization census, the 1870 and 1880 Lowndes County censuses, Lowndes County tax and land notices in the late 1870s and early 1880s, the 1900 Barney census, and the later 1920 and 1930 Plant City censuses. His end of life is supported by the Florida death index and Oaklawn Cemetery burial record. Nancy Isom is strongly supported as Nancy Griffin by a son's death certificate, her 1937 death notice naming Griffin brothers, and her Florida burial record. The main remaining questions concern the original marriage record, Nancy's full death certificate, the exact wording of Charles's parent fields, and the identity of May Clayton.

docs.title: Household #124: Thomas, George
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, George Thomas headed a 5-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
George Thomas headed a 5-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 3 children.

George Thomas's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation George Thomas Head 53 Georgia Farmer Louize Thomas Wife 42 Georgia — Judge Thomas Son 21 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Let Thomas Daughter 14 Georgia — Stephen Thomas Son 20 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• George Thomas, head, age 53, born Apr 1847 in Georgia, farmer
  • Louize Thomas, wife, age 42, born about 1858 in Georgia
  • Judge Thomas, son, age 21, born about 1879 in Georgia
  • Let Thomas, daughter, age 14, born about 1886 in Georgia
  • Stephen Thomas, son, age 20, born about 1880 in Georgia

The 1900 Barney household can be followed with good confidence through the next three censuses. In 1910, George Thomas appears in Barney, Brooks County, age 60, with wife Louise, 55, and daughter Lady, 26. In 1920, George Thomas appears in Dixie, Brooks County, age 77, with wife Lewise, 60. In 1930, George Thomas appears again in Brooks County district 1402, age 80, with wife Louisa, 72, on a farm on State Highway No. 38. Those records make a solid case for one long-running George and Louisa Thomas household in Brooks County.

The marriage evidence for George and Louisa is good. The Brooks County marriage record shows George Thomas and Louisa Monday, with the county record giving a license date of 30 Oct 1870 and a marriage performed 4 Nov 1870 by S. Adams. A separate index entry gives 20 Oct 1870, which is useful support for the couple and county but does not displace the fuller county record. The 1870 census also places Louisa Monday, age 16, in the household of Bright Monday in Brooks County. That remains the best current anchor for her earlier life.

George's end-of-life record strengthens the identification of the later Brooks County man. His 1937 Georgia death certificate places his death in Dixie, Brooks County, and gives his parents as Jackson Thomas and Pattie Thomas. The same certificate adds useful detail: district 1402, burial at Beulah Hill, and informant Jennie Thomas. Find a Grave places George Thomas at Beulah Hill Missionary Baptist Church Cemetery with a death date of 21 Aug 1937. Louisa Mundy Thomas is buried in the same cemetery, with a birth year of 1854 and death in Jan 1947, but her own death certificate has not yet been located.

The children are partly clearer now than in the older version of this entry. Judge Thomas of the 1900 household can be followed forward with strong evidence. His later records in Philadelphia give a birth date of 13 Sep 1879 in Brooks County, Georgia. His World War II draft registration places him at 3127 S. 83rd Street, Philadelphia, names Mrs. Mary Thomas as the contact who would always know his address, and repeats Brooks County as his place of birth. His 1959 Pennsylvania death certificate gives his father as George Thomas, names spouse Mary Thomas, and confirms the same 13 Sep 1879 Georgia birth. That does not solve every question in the Brooks County household, but it does strongly support Judge as the later Philadelphia man.

The 1910 daughter Lady Thomas is probably the same person as Let Thomas in 1900, but the evidence is still limited to census continuity. Stephen Thomas remains in the household in 1900, but no later direct record has yet been tied to him with the same confidence as Judge.

The 1880 material needs more caution than the previous entry allowed. The available 1880 Brooks County household for Geo Thomas appears to include a wife whose name reads more like Louvina or Luvina, along with children Abraham, Moses, Virginia, and Aaron. That family structure does not match the 1900 household closely enough to treat the 1880 entry as a simple spelling drift for Louisa Monday Thomas. At present, the 1880 George Thomas household should be treated as unproved for HH#124 rather than folded in as settled continuity.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
The clearest present connection is between George Thomas of HH#124 and son Judge Thomas, whose later Philadelphia records point back to a father named George Thomas and a Brooks County, Georgia birth. George's death certificate also supplies the names Jackson Thomas and Pattie Thomas as his parents, but that remains informant-level evidence until an earlier census or other direct record ties the generations together.

Louisa's connection to the Monday family is better grounded. The 1870 Bright Monday household and the Brooks County marriage record together make a strong case that Louisa Monday became Louisa Thomas, though her parentage is still not closed by direct evidence.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Look for Louisa Thomas's death certificate or another direct end-of-life record beyond the cemetery memorial.
  • Test George Thomas's reported parentage further through earlier census work or other direct records for Jackson Thomas and Pattie Thomas.
  • Try to identify later records for Stephen Thomas and for Let or Lady Thomas.
  • Keep the 1880 Geo Thomas household separate unless new evidence proves it belongs to HH#124.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: SOURCE-EXHAUSTED online: The online evidence strongly supports the George and Louisa Thomas household from 1900 through 1930, the Brooks County marriage of George Thomas and Louisa Monday, Louisa's 1870 placement in the Bright Monday household, George Thomas's 1937 death in Dixie with burial at Beulah Hill, and the forward identification of son Judge Thomas in Philadelphia. The main unresolved issues are Louisa's missing death certificate, George's earlier parentage, the later records of Stephen and Let or Lady, and whether any 1880 George Thomas household belongs to this family.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Hamilton Scraggs Head 23 Georgia Laborer Saw Mill Rainey Scraggs Wife 24 Georgia — Jane Scraggs Daughter 1 Georgia — George Scraggs Son 0 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Hamilton Scruggs, head, age 23, born Dec 1876 in Georgia, laborer in a saw mill
  • wife recorded in 1900 under a difficult reading that later records show belongs to the same Thomas-born spouse
  • children in 1900 include Jane, age 1, and George, age 0

Hamilton Scruggs can now be followed with a strong run of direct records from 1880 through his death. The 1880 Brooks County census places J.H. Scruggs, age 4, in the household of John and Jenny Scruggs. That child aligns well with Hamilton Scruggs in 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950, and the identification is reinforced by his World War I draft registration, which gives his birth date as 18 Sep 1876 in Brooks County, Georgia.

The marriage record is clearer than the older entry suggested. Brooks County marriage records show Hamilton Scruggs licensed on 22 Dec 1897 to marry Litty Ann Thomas, with the marriage performed on 23 Dec 1897. Later records show the same wife under expected census drift: Letitia, Lethia, Lethan, Letha, Lethe Ann, and Leathean. The 1900 census reading that had been treated as a separate name is best understood as another bad enumeration or indexing problem rather than evidence of a different spouse.

The household continuity after 1900 is now much firmer. In 1910, Hamilton appears with wife Lethia A. Scruggs and children including Ranie J., George, Chester A., Elbert W., Katie E., Hattie, and Monday. In 1920, the same family remains in Dixie with the wife recorded as Lethan. In 1930, Hamilton and Lethe Ann remain together with daughter Elizabeth, age 17, in the household. In 1940, Hamilton and his wife are not widowed, as the older version of this entry said. Instead, they are living in the George Sharp household as father-in-law and mother-in-law, which strongly supports the identification of daughter Elizabeth Scruggs as the later Elizabeth Sharp. In 1950, Hamilton is still in Dixie with his wife present and a granddaughter in the home.

The children's identifications are also clearer than before. The 1900 child Jane Scruggs is probably the later Ranie J. Scruggs. A Social Security claims index entry for Ranie J. Mitchell gives a birth date of 11 Sep 1898 in Brooks County and names Hamilton Scruggs as her father. That fits the age of Jane in 1900 and suggests that the 1900 name is either a bad reading of Janie or an early form displaced by the later Ranie J. usage. The same index trail also links Hamilton's wife under the form Leathean Thomas and helps tie the household to daughter Ranie later in life.

George Scruggs is present in 1900 and again in 1910, but his later record trail is still open in this entry. Elizabeth Scruggs is well supported as the woman later in the George Sharp household, though the direct marriage record still needs to be added if found. The 1920 child once read as Kaline is better treated in context with the 1930 and 1940 records as part of the Elizabeth line rather than as a separate unresolved child.

Hamilton's end-of-life trail now extends beyond the census run. A Georgia death index entry gives Hamilton Scruggs's death on 30 Nov 1956 in Brooks County, certificate number 28014. That entry fits the man still present in the 1950 census, but the full death certificate is still needed to capture parents, spouse, informant, and burial details.

The broader Scruggs family structure remains plausible but should be written more cautiously than before. The evidence supports John Scruggs and Jenny or Jinnie Miley as the parents of Hamilton and William, with William's 1939 death certificate backing that younger-child cluster. The earlier 1870 household of John Scruggs with Creasy and older children such as Amelia, Mary, George, and Joseph may reflect an earlier marriage, but that reconstruction is still an informed reading rather than a closed proof argument because direct marriage or probate evidence has not yet been added here.

A 14 Oct 1899 Valdosta Times article naming John Scruggs among the Barney-area farmers and noting a saw mill and ginnery is useful local context. Because the article predates Hamilton's mature independent household, it most likely refers to John Scruggs rather than to Hamilton.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
The strongest present connection is the one from Hamilton Scruggs back to the 1880 J.H. Scruggs in the John and Jenny Scruggs household. William Scruggs's 1939 death certificate supports the same parent pair and strengthens the placement of Hamilton in that younger Scruggs branch.

Hamilton's household is also tied forward through daughter Elizabeth, who appears as the basis for the 1940 George Sharp household connection, and probably through daughter Jane of 1900, who is likely the later Ranie J. Mitchell. Those are meaningful internal family links within the entry, even though some later marriage documentation is still missing.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Obtain Hamilton Scruggs's full death certificate for 30 Nov 1956, certificate no. 28014.
  • Look for the death certificate or burial record of Litty Ann Thomas Scruggs under her later name variants.
  • Add the direct marriage record for Elizabeth Scruggs and George Sharp if found.
  • Extend the later record trail for George Scruggs.
  • Test the earlier John Scruggs household structure further before treating the Creasy and Jenny marriages as fully proved.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: SOURCE-EXHAUSTED online: The online record set now gives a strong household chain from J.H. Scruggs in 1880 through Hamilton Scruggs in 1900-1950, supported by the 1897 marriage record to Litty Ann Thomas, the 1918 draft registration with exact birth date 18 Sep 1876, the 1940 George Sharp household connection for daughter Elizabeth, the Social Security claims evidence for daughter Ranie J. Mitchell, and the 1956 Georgia death index entry for Hamilton. The remaining gaps are the full death records for Hamilton and his wife, the direct marriage record for Elizabeth and George Sharp, the later trail for George Scruggs, and stronger direct proof for the earlier John Scruggs marriages.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Jasper Lightug Head 60 South Carolina Farmer Lucen Lightug Wife 45 Georgia — Ed Lightug Son 20 Georgia Laborer Farm

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Jasper Lightsy headed a Black farming household in Barney in 1900 with his wife Queen and their son Ed. The present evidence places him in south Georgia by 1867, when he registered to vote in Colquitt County, and in Brooks County by 1871, when he married Queen Clark and appeared on the Morven District 660 freedman tax list. The household can be followed with confidence through the 1880, 1900, and 1910 censuses, and Queen appears as Jasper's widow in Brooks County in 1930.

The records do not yet prove Jasper's exact relationship to the Primus, Philip, and Henry Lightsey branch discussed elsewhere in this encyclopedia. He belongs in the same Barney Lightsey cluster by surname, place, and timing, but that kinship remains unproved on the current direct evidence.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Queen Clark, Jasper's wife, appears to be the same woman seen in the 1870 Brooks County household of Reuben and Milley Clark, which provides a plausible pre-marriage placement for her before the 22 July 1871 marriage.
  • HH#104 establishes that Philip Lightsey and Henry S. Lightsey belong to the Primus Lightsey household. That evidence should not be extended to Jasper beyond a broader neighborhood and surname connection.
  • The 1871 Morven District 660 tax record placing Jasper alongside Price Lightsey supports Jasper's presence within the wider Lightsey cluster in Brooks County during Reconstruction, but it does not by itself prove a specific kinship tie.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Jasper's birthplace is not fully settled. The 1880 census reports Georgia, while the 1900 and 1910 censuses report South Carolina.
  • The 1900 wife-name reading "Lucen" in derivative materials is an error. The census image reads Queen, consistent with the 1871 marriage, the 1880 household, the 1910 household, and Queen's 1930 widow household.
  • No additional primary online records were located in the present evidence set for a 1920 census appearance, Jasper's death or burial, Queen's death or burial, or later land records.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Source-exhausted online. The core household has a stable direct-record spine from 1867 through 1930, and no further primary online records have been identified in the current review. Jasper's exact kinship to the other Barney Lightsey households remains unproved and should not be overstated.

docs.title: Household #127: Berryhill, John
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, John Berryhill headed a 7-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
John Berryhill headed a 7-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 5 children.

John Berryhill's listed occupation was Farmer.

Reported birthplaces span Florida and Georgia, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation John Berryhill Head 57 Georgia Farmer Welthy Berryhill Wife 52 Georgia — Thomas Berryhill Son 26 Georgia Farmer Charlie Berryhill Son 24 Florida — Susie A Berryhill Daughter 18 Georgia — John M Berryhill Son 16 Georgia — Robert Berryhill Son 12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
John Berryhill headed a white farming household in Barney in 1900 with his wife Wealthy Patrick Berryhill and five unmarried children still at home: Thomas, Charlie, Susie A., John M., and Robert. Another daughter, Priscilla, had already married Calvin Luther McKinney in 1895 and was no longer in the household. The present record set supports a strong family outline from the Civil War era into the 1920s, but it also shows that the older encyclopedia entry claimed more than the evidence would carry. This household now reads best as well documented and ready for a conservative, source-based treatment.

The strongest identity anchor for the couple is the 1867 Brooks County marriage record for John Berry Hill and W. C. A. Patrick. Later records support the reading that W. C. A. Patrick was the woman later called Wealthy Berryhill, with "Welthy" best treated as a record or transcription variant. The household can then be followed through the 1880, 1900, 1910, and 1920 censuses. John's local placement is strengthened by his 1867 Brooks County voter registration, an 1880 agricultural schedule entry in District 4, and a 1910 newspaper item about the sale of the John Berryhill farm near Barney.

John's earlier trail is stronger than it was at the start of this review, though it still needs careful wording. A Civil War service profile places a John Berryhill from Laurens County in Company C of the 2nd State Troops, with later service notes tying him to the 49th Infantry and recording a wound at the Wilderness. That compiled military material, taken with the 1867 Brooks County voter registration and the 1867 marriage, makes the 1860 Laurens County John Berryhill the best current earlier candidate. It is a solid working identification, but the compiled service profile should not be treated as the last word in place of a full service or pension file.

The newspaper trail adds useful local texture without changing the basic proof standard. In 1903 John Berryhill was named in Barney civic news as a councilman nominee. Another 1903 item about a stump-puller accident identifies him as the owner of the machine and helps place sons Charles Berryhill and John Berryhill Jr. in the same working orbit. A 1903 death notice for Charles Berryhill reports burial at Mt. Zion Camp Ground, which fits the later burial pattern seen elsewhere in the family. The 14 Oct 1899 Barney farmers notice and the 1910 farm-sale item both support John's standing as an established farm operator, but they do not by themselves justify claims about family prominence or larger economic influence.

Wealthy Berryhill's end-of-life notice is one of the most important records for the family. The Atlanta Journal of 17 Sep 1926 reported the death of Mrs. John Berryhill at home in Barney on Tuesday at age seventy-nine. The notice also said that her brother H. Wesley Patrick had died in Quitman a week earlier, and it named surviving Patrick siblings G. W. Patrick, J. E. Patrick, and Miss Emma Patrick. Most important for this household, it named surviving children as Robert Berryhill of Lakeland, W. A. Berryhill of Adel, John Berryhill of Barney, Mrs. W. F. Jones of Lakeland, Mrs. W. C. Edenfield of Barney, and Mrs. L. C. McKinney of Adel. That notice is the cleanest single source for the family's later geographic spread and for several adult child identities.

Several children can now be identified with confidence. Thomas of the 1900 household is the later Thomas Arthur Berryhill, also seen as T. A. Berryhill and Arthur A. Berryhill. His 1901 Berrien County marriage to Bettie Wingate, his 1910 and 1920 censuses, his World War I draft card giving birth date 12 Aug 1873, and his 1934 death certificate in Cook County all fit together well. The death certificate names his parents as John Berryhill and Martha A. Patrick. Because the broader household evidence points consistently to Wealthy Patrick Berryhill, Martha A. Patrick is best treated as an informant or clerk error rather than as a separate maternal identity.

Susie A. Berryhill is now firmly identified as the later Susie or Susan Edenfield, wife of W. C. Edenfield. Their 1904 Brooks County marriage is direct proof. She can then be followed through the 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses. Her obituary in the Valdosta Daily Times of 22 May 1961 is especially useful because it names son W. Ray Edenfield of Newark, Ohio, daughters Susie B. Bebout of California, Mrs. Robert Campbell of Barney, and Mrs. A. W. Hazel Victor of Tampa, and brother J. W. Berryhill of Barney. That obituary ties the Edenfield branch back into the Berryhill family in clear record language.

John M. of the 1900 household is best read as the later John Wesley Berryhill, usually styled J. W. Berryhill. He appears as a son in the parental household in 1910 and 1920, and his World War I draft card gives the fuller name John Wesley Berryhill with birth date 28 Mar 1884. Later censuses in 1930, 1940, and 1950 place him in Brooks County as a single carpenter. The Georgia death index for John W. Berryhill, who died in Brooks County on 27 Oct 1963, fits that same man. The present evidence strongly suggests that he never married and remained closely tied to the Barney home place.

Robert Berryhill is now much clearer as Robert Lee Berryhill. The 1910 census places Robert L. Berryhill in Lakeland, Florida, in the household of William F. Jones and wife Georgia, which is a strong clue that the later Mrs. W. F. Jones of Lakeland was Robert's sister Georgia. Robert's own line is then supported by his 1913 Brooks County marriage to Ethel Joyce, the 1920 Barney census, the 1930 Lakeland census, a 1952 death and funeral notice, and burial at Camp Ground. Local Barney items from March and April 1915 also support the identification of Bob Berryhill with Robert L. Berryhill. One item names Mr. and Mrs. Bob Berryhill and daughter Vivian, which matches the later Vivie Lee or Vivian L. Berryhill seen in census records.

Priscilla Berryhill can be carried forward with good confidence as the daughter who married Calvin Luther McKinney in 1895 and later appears in the 1926 widow notice as Mrs. L. C. McKinney of Adel. Georgia Jones, wife of William F. Jones of Lakeland, is also now strongly supported as a Berryhill daughter, probably the same woman listed in the widow notice as Mrs. W. F. Jones. The least settled child problem now centers on the W. A. Berryhill named in the 1926 widow notice. Because Charles Berryhill appears to have died in the 1903 stump-puller accident, W. A. Berryhill should not be treated as a later name for Charlie. The better reading is that W. A. Berryhill was another son or close family member whose exact place in the household still needs direct reconciliation.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Wealthy Berryhill's 1926 death notice firmly places this household within the Patrick sibling group through H. Wesley Patrick, G. W. Patrick, J. E. Patrick, and Emma Patrick.
  • Priscilla Berryhill's 1895 marriage links HH#127 to HH#24, the Calvin Luther McKinney household, but the evidence does not support broad social conclusions beyond the marriage itself and the later 1926 identification of Mrs. L. C. McKinney.
  • The 1910 Lakeland household of William F. and Georgia Jones, which includes Robert L. Berryhill, strongly supports Georgia Jones as another Berryhill daughter and helps explain the Lakeland branch named in Wealthy's 1926 notice.
  • Camp Ground and Mt. Zion burial references recur across the family, especially for Charles Berryhill, Thomas A. Berryhill, Robert Lee Berryhill, John Wesley Berryhill, and later Edenfield relatives.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The best current reading identifies Barney's John Berryhill with the Laurens County John Berryhill in compiled Civil War service/profile material. That material places him in Company C, 2nd State Troops, includes a later 49th Infantry note, and records a Wilderness wound. The 1867 Brooks County voter registration and 1867 marriage help bridge the identification, but the page should continue to call for a full service or pension file before treating the service profile as final.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The best current reading is that John Berryhill of Barney is the same man as the John Berryhill found in Laurens County before the war and in the compiled Civil War service profile, but a full service file or pension file would strengthen that conclusion.
  • Charles Berryhill appears to have died in the 1903 stump-puller accident, so W. A. Berryhill in Wealthy Berryhill's 1926 death notice must represent someone else; his exact identity and relationship still need direct reconciliation.
  • Priscilla Berryhill McKinney is strongly supported, but a fuller direct-record trail after marriage would still help close that branch.
  • Georgia Berryhill Jones is now strongly supported through the 1910 Lakeland household and the 1926 widow notice, but an additional direct record naming her parents would finish the case more cleanly.
  • Land, tax, probate, and burial records for John and Wealthy Berryhill would improve the household's economic and end-of-life documentation.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: WELL-RESEARCHED: John Berryhill and Wealthy Patrick Berryhill are supported by the 1867 marriage record, the 1867 Brooks County voter registration, the 1880 population and agricultural schedules, the 1900, 1910, and 1920 censuses, and Wealthy's 1926 death notice. Several children who were previously vague are now identified with strong direct evidence: Thomas Arthur Berryhill, Susie A. Berryhill Edenfield, John Wesley Berryhill, and Robert Lee Berryhill. Priscilla McKinney and Georgia Jones are both strongly supported as daughters. Charles Berryhill now appears to have been the son killed in the 1903 stump-puller accident, which means the W. A. Berryhill named in 1926 remains an unresolved identity rather than a plausible later form of Charlie. The household no longer needs inflated interpretation, but it does support a solid family reconstruction with a few remaining record-level gaps.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Serven Hall, age 19, appears alone in 1900 as a Black male farm laborer in Barney.
  • He reported a November 1880 birth in Georgia, was single, and headed his own rented house.
  • The census states that both parents were born in Georgia.
  • He could read, write, and speak English.

Serven Hall is, at present, a one-record household. The only direct evidence located for him is the 1900 federal census entry in Barney Precinct, Brooks County, Georgia. That record places him as head of household #128 on sheet 6, with no other household members present. It identifies him as a farm laborer, single, and renting a house rather than a farm.

No later or earlier record has been tied to him with enough confidence to extend his life story. Searches for him under likely variants of the given name, along with routine checks of later census schedules, marriage records, death records, draft registrations, and burial databases, have not yet produced a documented match that can be assigned to this man without guesswork.

The broader Hall presence in the 1900 Barney census is worth noting but does not, by itself, prove kinship. Other Hall households in the precinct include HH#138, headed by William Hall, and HH#140, headed by Henry Hall. William Hall's household included a son John Hall of roughly the same age as Serven, but similarity of surname, age, and place is not enough to establish a family relationship.

docs.text:

  • No confirmed marriage, death, burial, or WWI draft record has been tied to this man.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Octavia Roberts appears in Barney in 1900 as a 48-year-old widow heading a household of daughters and one granddaughter.
  • Later records tie her to the Asbell family and carry her forward into the households of her married daughters in Lowndes County.
  • The best-documented daughters are Lucy Roberts, later Lucy Zipperer, and Sallie Roberts, later Sallie Catridge and then Sally Russell.
  • Susan Roberts, Lula Roberts, and granddaughter Jessie Roberts remain only partly identified beyond the 1900 household.

Octavia Roberts was born in Georgia and appears first as Octavia E. Asbell in the 1860 and 1870 censuses. She married Stephen T. Roberts in Brooks County on 31 December 1878. In 1880 she appears in Stephen Roberts's household, though the transcription is incomplete and the census image is more reliable than the index alone.

By 1900 Octavia was a widow in Barney, Brooks County, heading household #129. The census describes her as born in September 1851, a farmer, and mother of four living children. In the same household were daughters Susan, Lucy, Lula, and Sallie, along with granddaughter Jessie Roberts.

The later family trail is strongest through Lucy and Sallie. Lucy Roberts married Charles Edward Zipperer and appears with him in Clyattville, Lowndes County, in the 1920, 1930, and 1940 censuses, then in 1950 in the household of her son Stanley Zipperer. The 1920 census is especially useful because it places Octavia Roberts in Lucy's household as mother-in-law. A 1930 death certificate for Lucy Vivian Zipperer names her mother as Lucy Roberts, which supports the Roberts-to-Zipperer identification.

Sallie Roberts married C. W. Catridge on 5 November 1905 in Lowndes County. In 1910 she appears in his household, where her mother is listed literally as Mrs. S. T. Roberts, age 61, relationship mother-in-law. By 1930 Sallie had remarried and appears as Sallie R. Russell in Florida. She continues as Sally R. Russell in later records. Her 1970 obituary names her sister as Mrs. Lucy Zipperer of Valdosta, which firmly connects the Russell woman back to the Roberts family.

The evidence for Stephen Roberts is good enough to place him as Octavia's husband, but his military career should be stated carefully. Octavia's 1927 Confederate widow's pension application says that she married Stephen Roberts on 31 December 1878 in Brooks County and that he served in Company G, 18th Georgia Infantry. Other military records for a Stephen T. Roberts are consistent with that claim, including service and prisoner-of-war material, but the widow's pension file is the clearest bridge between the soldier and this household. The same pension file says Stephen died in north Georgia in 1883.

Susan Roberts, Lula Roberts, and granddaughter Jessie Roberts remain less certain after 1900. Online records reviewed so far do not securely prove later identities for Susan or Lula, and no later record has been tied confidently to Jessie Roberts. Those individuals should therefore be left in their 1900 forms unless stronger evidence is found.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The military-service evidence for this household comes through Octavia's husband, Stephen T. Roberts. Octavia's 1927 Georgia Confederate widow's pension application says she married Stephen on 31 December 1878 in Brooks County and that he served in Company G, 18th Georgia Infantry. Other Stephen T. Roberts military records appear consistent, but the widow's pension file is the clearest bridge between the soldier and this household, so the service history should remain narrower than broad secondary summaries until the full service file is reviewed.

  • HH#129 Sallie Roberts became Sallie Catridge and later Sally R. Russell.

  • Later identities for Susan Roberts, Lula Roberts, and Jessie Roberts remain unproved.

docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Gorden Hines headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Gorden Hines headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

Gorden Hines's listed occupation was Laborer Saw Mill.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Gorden Hines Head 25 Georgia Laborer Saw Mill Jimmie Hines Wife 25 Georgia — Carrie Hines Daughter 9/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household was headed by Gordon Hiers, a sawmill laborer, with wife Jinnie and daughter Carrie.
  • Later Lowndes County records support a Gordon Hires who died at Hahira in 1920 and a widow recorded as Loca, Lockey, or Lokey Hall Hiers.
  • The older encyclopedia entry merged this family with an Augusta J. B. Hiers line. The direct records reviewed so far do not justify that merger.

The 1900 census for Barney shows Gordon Hiers, age 26, in household #130 with wife Jinnie, age 22, and daughter Carrie, age 1. After review of the census image, Jinnie is the better reading for the wife's name. The common transcription Jimmie appears to be an indexing or reading error.

A Brooks County marriage record dated 23 March 1898, with the ceremony on 27 March 1898, records the marriage of Mr. Gordon Heirs and Miss Jennie Hall. That record fits the 1900 household well. A second Brooks County marriage record, indexed to 17 October 1901, records Mr. Gordon Hires and Miss Loca Hall. The later Lowndes County records also point to a wife called Lockey or Lokey Hall. At present, the records are strong enough to connect Gordon to the later Hall-Hiers family in Lowndes County, but not strong enough to explain with confidence whether Jennie, Jinnie, Loca, Lockey, and Lokey represent one woman recorded under shifting forms or more than one wife.

Gordon's later Lowndes County trail is better anchored than the earlier entry suggested. His death certificate records Gordon Hires dying on 26 January 1920 at Hahira, Lowndes County, as a married farmer born in Brooks County. The same certificate names his father as Mitchell Hires and his mother literally as Martha Wade, and says he was buried at Shiloh Church on 27 January 1920. The age shown on the certificate reads 47 rather than 27, which fits an 1870s birth year and makes the index age of 27 unreliable.

The widow and children can be followed after Gordon's death. In 1930 Lokey Hiers appears in Hahira as a widow with children May, Gladys, Lois, and William. In 1940 she again appears as a widow in Hahira, with daughter Mae, daughter Louis Bottlier, granddaughter Peggie San Hiers, and grandson Rodney Bottlier in the household. In 1950 she appears in Cat Creek, Lowndes County, indexed as Lakery Hires, with son William Hires. A 1937 death certificate for Gladys Hires names her parents as Gordon Hires and Lockey Hall. William Mitchell Hiers's WWII draft card names Mrs. Lokey Hiers as his mother. A 1957 Valdosta Daily Times notice says Mrs. Lokey Hiers announced the marriage of her daughter, Lois Bottlier, to John A. Hicks of Valdosta.

Some parts of the former entry should be removed. The direct records reviewed here do not support folding the Augusta J. B. Hiers or John Broadus Hiers material into this Barney-Hahira household. The 1910 Augusta census shows a J. B. Hiers, age 34, a glazer in a lumber company, with wife J. L. Hiers and son E. R. Hiers. The WWI draft card and later Augusta-area records for John Broadus Hiers belong to that separate track unless a direct bridge is found. For the same reason, the four-generation lineage in the earlier entry should not be carried forward as settled fact.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The relationship between the 1898 Jennie Hall marriage and the 1901 Loca Hall marriage remains unresolved.
  • Carrie Hiers from the 1900 household has not yet been carried forward with confidence into later records.
  • The mother on Gordon's death certificate should be cited literally as Martha Wade unless stronger direct evidence proves a correction.
  • The Augusta J. B. Hiers and John Broadus Hiers records should remain separate from HH#130 unless a direct record bridges the two lines.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The 1900 Barney household, Gordon Hires's 1920 Lowndes County death, and the later Lokey Hall Hiers widow household are well supported. The wife-name sequence and any connection to the Augusta J. B. Hiers line remain unresolved.

docs.title: Household #131: Reddick, Harris
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Harris Reddick headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:

Harris Reddick's listed occupation was Illegible Mill.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Harris Reddick Head 43 Georgia Illegible Mill Mary Reddick Wife 27 Georgia — Eulail Reddick Daughter 3/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains Harris Reddick, wife Mary, and infant daughter Eulail.
  • A Brooks County marriage record dated 25 December 1898 records H. J. Reddick and Mary M. Reddick.
  • Cemetery evidence now shows that Mary M. Reddick and Eulaila Reddick were buried at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery near Pavo within a few years of the census.

The 1900 census records Harris Reddick, born March 1857 in Georgia, as a farm laborer in Barney. His household included wife Mary, born November 1872 in Georgia, and daughter Eulail, age three months, born in Georgia in March 1900. The household was rented, and both adults were reported as Georgia-born.

The marriage record for H. J. Reddick and Mary M. Reddick in Brooks County on 25 December 1898 fits the 1900 household well, but it does not by itself prove what the initials H. J. stand for. The 1900 census names the husband Harris. That makes H. J. a plausible match, but not a settled one.

New burial evidence changes the earlier reading of this household. Mary M. Reddick is memorialized at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery with dates 1872-1903, and Eulaila Reddick is memorialized there with dates 1899-1904. Those memorials align closely with the Mary and Eulail of the 1900 Barney household and make it unlikely that the family simply vanished from the record without trace. They suggest instead that Mary and the child died within a few years of the census.

The wider Reddick material supplied during this review is relevant, but it remains unresolved. Records from Webster and Randolph Counties show a related-looking line centered on H. J., Honace, or Horace Reddick, including the 26 December 1876 Randolph County marriage of Honace J. Reddick and Emma Harden, an 1880 Randolph County household headed by H. J. Reddick with wife Emma, and a 1900 Randolph County widow Emma Reddick household. A later death certificate for Dr. W. W. Reddick names parents Horace Reddick and Emma Hartten or Harden. Those records likely belong to the same broader Reddick cluster, and they may help explain the Brooks County H. J. groom, but the present evidence does not prove that HH#131's Harris Reddick was the same man as Honace or Horace Reddick of Randolph-Webster County.

The earlier ancestry discussion about eighteenth-century German immigrant Reddicks should not remain in the household entry. No direct record reviewed here bridges HH#131 to that older line.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• A direct bridge is still needed between Harris Reddick in the 1900 Barney census and H. J. Reddick in the 1898 Brooks County marriage record.
  • Mary M. Reddick and Eulaila Reddick appear to match the 1900 household strongly, but their cemetery memorials are still secondary support until backed by burial, church, or death records.
  • Harris Reddick has not been identified with confidence after the 1900 census.
  • The Webster-Randolph H. J. / Honace / Horace Reddick material should be treated as a probable related cluster, not as a proved identity merge.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Further research needed. The 1900 Barney household and the 1898 Brooks County marriage are secure, and the cemetery evidence strongly supports early deaths for Mary M. Reddick and Eulaila Reddick. Harris Reddick's pre-1900 identity and post-1900 fate remain unresolved.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains Silas Hooker, wife Mamie, and children Orbin, Nola, and Zelley.
  • A Brooks County marriage record dated 3 December 1891 records the marriage of Silas Hooker and Mamie L. Bailey.
  • Later census, draft, and death records place the same man under the names Silas C. Hooker, S. C. Hooker, and Babe Hooker.
  • A 1933 Georgia death certificate identifies S. C. Hooker as the son of G. W. Hooker and Cynthia Simmons.

The 1900 census places Silas Hooker in Barney as a sawmill laborer born in August 1868 in Georgia. His wife Mamie, born about 1876 or 1877 in Georgia, was married about nine years and was the mother of three living children. The household's three children were Orbin, Nola, and Zelley. This is the starting point for the family as it appears in Barney.

The marriage record anchors the couple before the census. Brooks County recorded the marriage of Silas Hooker and Mamie L. Bailey on 3 December 1891. Mamie fits well as the woman who appears in the 1880 Jasper J. Bailey household. The Hooker household can then be followed forward through 1910, 1920, and 1930. In 1910 Silas C. Hooker was in Lake Park, Lowndes County, with Mamie and children Olin, Nora, Zellie, Charley, and Hansel. In 1920 the family was in Cecil, Cook County, with Olin, Nora, Charlie, Hansel, Gladys, and Thelma in the home. In 1930 Babe Hooker was back in Lowndes County with Mamie, Hansel, and Thelma.

Later records help carry the children beyond the 1900 household. Orbin in 1900 fits the later Olin Hooker seen in the 1910 and 1920 censuses, the World War I draft card giving Olin Hooker's birth as 24 October 1894 at Barney, Georgia, and later Lowndes County records for Olin Cleo Hooker. Zella Hooker Sims, who died in 1928, is identified by her death certificate as a daughter of S. C. Hooker and Mamie Bailey. That record places her in the family, but it should not be used to identify her automatically with the one-year-old Zelley in the 1900 census because the death certificate gives Zella a birth date of 22 November 1900.

The pre-1900 identity chain points in the same direction. In 1870 a Clarence Hooker of the right age appears in the household of George and Cyntha Hooker in Colquitt County. In 1880 a Silas C. Hoaker of similar age appears in the George and Cynthia Hoaker household. The 1933 death certificate for S. C. Hooker names his parents as G. W. Hooker and Cynthia Simmons. Taken together, these records support treating the 1900 Barney head as the same man later recorded as Silas C., S. C., and Babe Hooker.

docs.text: • HH#133 George Hooker is strongly connected to this household. In 1880, George Hoaker and Silas C. Hoaker appear in the same George and Cynthia Hoaker household and are listed there as sons. By 1900, George and Silas appear as adjacent Hooker households in Barney.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Mamie Hooker's death and burial still need a direct record if the closing years of her life are to be stated more precisely.
  • Zella Hooker Sims belongs in the family, but her exact place in the birth order should remain cautious until a record directly aligns her with one of the census daughters.

docs.text: Complete research. The household rests on a direct marriage record, a census chain from 1900 through 1930, parental-context records from 1870 and 1880, a 1933 death certificate for Silas C. Hooker, and later records for adult children that fit the household.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains George W. Hooker, wife Lorena, and daughters Mattie, Hattie, Cinthy, and Willie.
  • A Colquitt County marriage record dated 27 September 1891 records the marriage of G. W. Hooker and Sarah Wooten.
  • Earlier census and postal records place George in the George and Cyntha Hooker household in 1870 and 1880 and identify him as the man appointed postmaster at Hempstead, Colquitt County, on 24 September 1884.
  • Later records carry three daughters beyond the 1900 household: Mattie Hooker to Mattie Rentz, Hattie Hooker to Hattie Burley, and Cinthy Hooker to Cynthia Noles.

The 1900 census places George W. Hooker in Barney as a sawmill laborer born in January 1863 in Georgia. His wife appears there as Lorena Hooker, born in July 1871 or 1872 in Georgia, and the household's four children are Mattie, Hattie, Cinthy, and Willie. Willie should be treated as a daughter because that is how the child appears in the census entry. The couple had been married about nine years, which fits the 1891 marriage record.

The marriage record anchors the household before the census. Colquitt County recorded the marriage of G. W. Hooker and Sarah Wooten on 27 September 1891. The wife's given name varies across the surviving material. She is Sarah Wooten in the marriage record, Lorena in the 1900 census, and later family material points to a Lorine or Lorena Wooten identity within the same family line. The records now support treating her as Sarah, Lorena, or Lorine Wooten Hooker, but they do not support the older claim that she came from a specific Cooper household.

George's pre-1900 identity is documented well enough to connect the Barney head to the earlier Hooker household. In 1870 he appears as a young child in the George and Cyntha Hooker household in Colquitt County. In 1880 he appears as George Hoaker in the George and Cynthia Hoaker household. A postal record then places George W. Hooker at Hempstead in Colquitt County on 24 September 1884, when he was appointed postmaster. By 1900 he was in Barney working as a sawmill laborer.

The household can be carried forward through three of the daughters. Mattie Hooker appears to be the same woman who married C. J. Ruetz or Rentz in Brooks County in 1907. She can be followed as Mattie Rentz in 1910, 1920, 1930, and 1940, and the 1940 census places Cynthia Noles in Mattie's household as her sister. Hattie Hooker is strongly supported as the later Hattie Bell Burley seen in Colquitt County in 1920, 1930, and 1940, with Social Security claims material identifying spouse Frank Burley and child Lorene Reynolds. Cinthy Hooker is strongly supported as the later Cynthia or Cintha Noles, wife of Ernest P. Noles in Cook County in 1920 and 1930 and the widowed sister living with Mattie Rentz in 1940. Willie has not been traced with confidence after the 1900 census.

The wider Hooker family context is still useful, but it should be stated carefully. George and Silas Hooker appear side by side as separate households in Barney in 1900, and the earlier Hooker household places George in a family that also included a child recorded in 1880 as Silas C. Hoaker. That makes the link between HH#133 and HH#132 plausible within the same parental household. The present entry does not need a stronger claim than that to stand on its own.

docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains John G. Scruggs, wife Martha E. Scruggs, children Robert E., Ada M., H. V., Ruby, and Eleanor, and boarder Joe Bryant.
  • John can be followed in Brooks County from the 1870 and 1880 censuses, through Morven district tax digests from 1883 through 1887, to his 1888 marriage, the 1900, 1920, and 1930 censuses, and his 1934 death certificate.
  • Martha E. Griffin Scruggs is anchored by the same marriage record, the 1900-1930 census chain, and her 1930 death certificate naming her parents as James Edwin Griffin and Ellen Judy Dorminy.
  • The household's later children are well represented in the records. Ada Moore, Horace V. Scruggs, Ruby Culpepper, Robert E. Scruggs, and Edwin Richard Scruggs all have substantial adult documentation, while Eleanor appears to have died young.

John G. Scruggs appears in 1900 as a farmer born in November 1861 in Georgia. Martha E. Scruggs appears beside him, born in August 1867 in Georgia. The census states that they had been married eleven years, which fits their Brooks County marriage on 19 July 1888. Their home in Barney included children Robert E., Ada M., H. V., Ruby, and Eleanor, along with boarder Joe Bryant. John owned the farm free of mortgage in 1900.

John's Brooks County placement starts before the marriage. In 1870 he appears as a child in the Richard and Susan M. Scruggs household. In 1880 he is still in that household, working on the farm. Tax digest records then place John G. Scruggs in Morven district 660 in 1883, 1884, 1885, 1886, and 1887, showing him as an adult in the same local area before the 1888 marriage.

The 1920 and 1930 censuses carry the household forward and show the later child set. In 1920 John and Martha were renting in Barney, with John Leon, Sam Stevens, Agness, Angus, and Arnold still at home. In 1930 John was back in an owned farm household, listed as a farmer and employer. Martha appears there as Mattie E. Scruggs, and the household also includes sons Angus and Samuel S., daughter-in-law Elsie M. Scruggs, and grandson Arnold J. Scruggs. The 1930 census therefore confirms that Mattie E. was not a second wife but the same Martha E. Scruggs seen earlier.

The death certificates close the parents' records cleanly. Martha Ellen Scruggs died in Brooks County on 31 December 1930. Her certificate gives a birth date of 15 August 1867 in Lowndes County and names her parents as James Edwin Griffin and Ellen Judy Dorminy. It also places her burial at Corinth Cemetery, Morven. John G. Scruggs died in Morven district, Brooks County, on 3 December 1934. His certificate describes him as a widowed farmer, gives a birth date of 15 November 1861, names his parents as Richard Scruggs and Margaret Horne, and places his burial at Corinth Cemetery on 4 December 1934. The two death certificates are the best direct records for the burial location.

Several children can now be stated with confidence. Ada May Scruggs married Elmer B. Moore in Brooks County on 28 July 1912 and can be followed in Morven through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses. Her 1952 obituary identifies her as a daughter of John G. Scruggs. Horace V. Scruggs married Ruth Whipple in Brooks County in June 1916, registered for the World War I draft in Brooks County, and can be followed through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses. His 1976 Macon obituary names siblings Ruby Culpepper, Reeves Suber, and Arnold Scruggs, which fits the family seen in Barney.

Ruby Scruggs married Samuel C. Culpepper in Brooks County on 22 January 1919. She appears with him in Bibb County in 1920 and 1930, as a widow in Morven in 1940, and later in Orlando in 1950. Samuel C. Culpepper's 1931 obituary states that his wife before marriage was Miss Ruby Scruggs and names their children Harold and Janet. Robert E. or Robert Edward Scruggs is tied directly to John through his World War I draft registration, which gives his birth as 14 November 1896 at Barney and names nearest relative John G. Scruggs of Barney. He can then be followed through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses and later death-index material.

Edwin Richard Scruggs is also strongly supported as a son of this household. He appears in adult records as E. R. or Edwin Richard Scruggs, with a World War I draft card, a 1920 Morven census household with wife Rosa May, a 1930 household in Lake County, Florida, and later returns to Brooks County in 1940 and 1950. A World War II draft card for James Edwin Scruggs naming Mrs. Edwin Richard Scruggs of Morven as contact supports that family unit. The sons John Leon, Sam Stevens, Angus, and Arnold are directly present in the 1920 and 1930 household records, though some of their later-life trails still deserve tighter direct-record work if the entry is ever expanded further.

The 1900 child Eleanor should be read carefully. The census gives her as a daughter born in December 1898. A cemetery memorial for Margaret Elenor Scruggs, born 28 December 1898 and died 31 August 1906, likely refers to the same child rather than to an additional daughter, but that identification still rests on secondary cemetery material rather than a preserved death record.

The strongest unresolved point in the parental generation is John's mother. The 1870 and 1880 censuses place him with Susan M. Scruggs, while the 1934 death certificate names Margaret Horne. Those records may refer to the same woman, but the entry should not flatten that difference without a direct record that bridges the names.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The identification of Eleanor in the 1900 census with Margaret Elenor Scruggs in Corinth Cemetery is likely, but it still needs a direct death or cemetery record stronger than the memorial page alone.
  • Agnes in the 1920 household is likely the later Mrs. Reeves Suber named as Horace's sister in 1976, but that later identity should be stated cautiously until it is anchored by her own marriage or death record.
  • John Leon, Sam Stevens, Angus, and Arnold all belong in the household, but fuller later-life documentation would make each child entry firmer.
  • John's mother's name remains unresolved between the Susan M. of the census records and the Margaret Horne named on his death certificate.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household rests on a direct 1888 marriage record, a census chain from 1870 through 1930 for John or the family, Morven tax digest records before the marriage, and death certificates for both John and Martha. Several children are now anchored by their own marriage, census, draft, obituary, and death-index records, though a few child identifications still need tighter direct proof.

docs.title: Household #135: Clarke, Charley
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Charley Clark headed a 3-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Charley Clark headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

Charley Clark's listed occupation was Laborer mill.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Charley Clark Head 28 Georgia Laborer mill Milia Clark Wife 28 Georgia — Memory Clark Son 6 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains Charley Clarke, wife Milia or Amelia Clarke, and son Memory Clarke.
  • The family can be followed in Barney through the 1910 census, and Amelia then appears as head of household in 1920 with nieces Connie Dasher and Blanche Dasher.
  • Their son Memory E. Clark is unusually well documented through a 1917 marriage, a World War I draft card, induction and transport records, service-death records, and later military index entries.

Charley Clarke appears in 1900 as a farm laborer born about 1871 or 1872 in Georgia. His wife is recorded there as Milia, also born about 1871 or 1872 in Georgia, and their son Memory appears as a six-year-old child born in Georgia. The household was renting in Barney. The 1900 entry establishes the three-person core household and provides the earliest firm Barney placement now in hand.

The 1910 census keeps the family together in Barney and fills out the middle part of the household's story. Charley, recorded there as Charlie or Charley Clark, was working in naval stores. Amelia was still in the home, and Memory, then about fifteen, was still with his parents. The census indicates that Charley and Amelia had been married about seventeen years and that Memory was their only child then living. The surname appears both as Clark and Clarke in the record set, but the family is stable enough across residence, age, household structure, and later military records to treat the entries as the same Barney family.

A 6 August 1910 Valdosta Daily Times article on a shooting at Barney names Charley Clark in the reported sequence that began with a fight on a South Georgia train and Clark's arrest after being put off at Barney. Because the article gives only the name and Barney setting, it should be treated as a possible later-life lead for this household head rather than a closed identification. If it does refer to this Charley Clark, it places him in a concrete public-order event only months after the 1910 census.

Memory E. Clark is the best documented member of the household. His Brooks County marriage record shows that he married Rendy James on 11 October 1917. His World War I draft card places him at Barney, gives his birth date as 25 November 1894, describes him as a single Black man working in farming, and provides a physical description. Its single-status entry conflicts with the October 1917 marriage record, so it should be used cautiously for marital status. The other details strongly identify him as the Barney resident.

The military records then provide a short but clear service chronology. A Brooks County local board record shows Memory inducted on 21 August 1918 and entrained for Camp Gordon. A Georgia service card states that he was inducted at Quitman on 22 August 1918, served as a private in Company B, 539 Engineers, and died on 11 October 1918 of lobar pneumonia. Outbound transport records place him leaving New York on 3 September 1918, and related military index material ties him to Barney or Bonney, Brooks County, to Amelia Clarke as mother or contact, and to the same October 1918 death in service. Later military compilations, including the Veterans Administration Master Index and Soldiers of the Great War, support the same basic conclusion. One small conflict remains in the birth date, which appears as 25 November 1894 on the draft card and 24 November 1894 in the VA index.

The 1920 census shows the household after Memory's death. Amelia Clark appears as head of household in Barney, with Connie Dasher and Blanche Dasher in the home and identified there as nieces. Charley does not appear with her in that census. The record supports the change in household structure, but it does not by itself show whether Charley had died, separated from the family, or was simply elsewhere when counted. The Dasher girls clearly belonged to Amelia's wider family network, though their exact parentage still needs direct proof before the relationship can be placed more precisely.

Taken together, the records support a careful reconstruction of this household. The parental household is solidly placed in Barney in 1900 and 1910, Amelia is still in Barney in 1920, and Memory's adult path from marriage to wartime service and death is well anchored. The weaker parts of the file are Charley's life before 1900 and after 1910, Amelia's life after 1920, and the later record trail for widow Rendy James Clark.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: Memory E. Clark, the son in this 1900 household, has a well-supported World War I service trail. Brooks County local-board material shows induction in August 1918, the Georgia service card places him as a private in Company B, 539 Engineers, and related military records show he died of lobar pneumonia on 11 October 1918. The only small conflict currently noted is the one-day birth-date difference between the draft card and Veterans Administration Master Index.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Charley Clarke's life before the 1900 census still needs firmer placement, including any 1880 or 1870 parental household identification.
  • Charley's disappearance from Amelia's 1920 household should not be treated as proof of death without a direct death, burial, or other closing record.
  • Amelia Clarke's later life after the 1920 census still needs a death or burial record.
  • Rendy James Clark, widow of Memory E. Clark, still needs a stronger later-life record trail after the 1917 marriage and Memory's 1918 death.
  • Connie Dasher and Blanche Dasher are called Amelia's nieces in 1920, but their parentage still needs direct documentation.
  • Memory's birth date differs by one day across records: 25 November 1894 on the draft card and 24 November 1894 in the Veterans Administration Master Index.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched for the core 1900-1920 household and for Memory E. Clark's military service, but not complete. The entry now rests on a firm three-census household trail, a 1917 marriage record for Memory, a draft card, induction and transport records, a Georgia service-death card, and later military index support. The main remaining gaps concern Charley before 1900 and after 1910, Amelia after 1920, the later life of Rendy James Clark, and the parentage of the Dasher nieces.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation John Morse Head 49 Georgia Farmer Laura Morse Wife 42 Georgia — Charley Morse Son 20 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains John Morse, wife Laura F. Morse, and son Charley Morse.
  • John can be traced backward as John Moss in Brooks County in 1870 and 1880, and the later records support treating Moss and Morse as the same man.
  • Laura is securely placed as Laura F. Olliff in the 1860 and 1870 households of Zadock and Elizabeth Olliff, and her 1940 death certificate names father Z. Oliff and mother Elizabeth Williams.
  • Later records tie this household to daughter Minnie Lee Morse Belcher, son Charles Evers Morse, and grandson Able J. Morse.

John Morse appears in the 1900 census as a forty-nine-year-old Georgia farmer renting his place in Barney. Laura, born in March 1858, had borne two children, both living, and the couple reported that they had been married twenty-three years. Their son Charley, age twenty, was still at home. The 1910 census keeps John and Laura in Barney, still farming and still renting, with the marriage length reported there as about thirty-three years.

The earlier Brooks County records support the same couple under the surname Moss. In 1880 John E. Moss and wife L. F. Moss were already established in their own household with children Minnie Lee and Charles. In 1870 a nineteen-year-old John Moss appears in the household of James and Martha Moss in Brooks County. The surname change from Moss to Morse is not unusual for this period, and the combination of age, place, wife Laura, and later children makes the identification persuasive.

Laura's side of the family is much better documented directly. In 1860 she appears as Laura F. Olliff, age two, in the Brooks County household of Zadok and Elizbeth Olliff. In 1870 she is again in the household of Zadock Olliff. Her Georgia death certificate gives her as Laura Frances Morse, born 1 March 1858, died 22 March 1940, with father Z. Oliff and mother Elizabeth Williams. The state death index gives the same death date under certificate 11517. Cemetery memorial material places both Laura and John at Oak Grove Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery.

The move from Barney to Quitman is clear in the later census trail. In 1920 John E. Morse and Laura were in Quitman, and the census states that they owned their home free of mortgage. In 1930 they were still together there with grandson Abel J. Morse in the household. By 1940 Laura had died, and the Quitman household contained widowed John Morse together with son Charley E. Morse, daughter-in-law Minnie, and grandson Fred. That 1940 arrangement helps carry the family line forward into the next generation.

The children's later records are strong enough to update the older entry in several places. Charles Evers Morse married Minnie V. Ingram in Brooks County in 1900. He can then be followed through a World War I draft card, the 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses, a 1959 Georgia death-index entry, a 1959 obituary, cemetery memorial material, and a Social Security claims entry that names his parents as John Morse and Laura Olliff or Olive. The obituary names his sister as Mrs. Minnie A. Belcher of Plant City, Florida, which supports Minnie Lee Morse Belcher as the daughter missing from the 1900 parental household. The same Charles line also clarifies the grandson in John and Laura's later home. The Social Security Applications and Claims Index entry for Able J. Morse gives his birth as 14 February 1907 at Morven and names his parents as Charles E. Morse and Minnie Ingram. That record, together with the 1930 and 1940 census placements, makes it reasonable to identify Abel as the son of Charles and the grandson living with John and Laura.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• A direct marriage record for John Morse and Laura Olliff has not yet been added to the file, even though the census trail places the marriage about 1876 or 1877.
  • A direct death certificate for John Evers Morse has not yet been added. His 1948 death date and burial are currently supported by cemetery memorial material rather than by the certificate itself.
  • The Moss-to-Morse identification is strongly supported by the census sequence and family structure, but no single bridge record has yet been found that states both forms together.
  • Minnie Lee Morse Belcher is well supported as a daughter of John and Laura through the 1880 census and Charles's 1959 obituary, but a direct record naming her parents would still strengthen the line.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household now rests on a seven-census chain for John and Laura from 1870 through 1940, direct parental-context records for Laura Olliff, Laura's death certificate and death-index entry, later records for Charles Evers Morse from marriage through death, and a Social Security claims record that names Able J. Morse as the son of Charles E. Morse and Minnie Ingram. The main remaining gaps are John's death certificate and the couple's marriage record.
