docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Jerry Castleberry Head 39 Georgia Farmer Georgia Castleberry Wife 33 Georgia — Nancy Castleberry Child 10 Georgia — Joseph Castleberry Child 9 Georgia — Idella Castleberry Child 6 Georgia — John Castleberry Child 4 Georgia — Ivy Castleberry Son 1 Georgia — Nancy Castleberry Mother-in-law 10 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains Jerry Castleberry, wife Georgia Ann Castleberry, their five children Nancy, Joseph William, Idella, John, and Ivy, and Georgia's mother Nancy Norman.
  • Georgia Ann Castleberry's 1931 death certificate names her parents as John Norman and Nancy Alderman Norman, which gives this household a direct Alderman connection on Georgia's maternal line.
  • Later records support adult identifications for at least five children from the 1900 home: Nancy Castleberry Alderman, William Joseph Castleberry, Martha Idella "Della" Castleberry Crosby, John Jerry Castleberry, and Ivey Dewey Castleberry.
  • Jerry's own parentage is still not proved to the same standard as Georgia's Norman-Alderman line, so that point should remain open.

Jerry Castleberry appears in the 1900 census as a thirty-nine-year-old Georgia farmer renting his place in Barney. He reported that he could not read or write. Georgia Ann, born in June 1864, could read and write, had borne five children, and reported that all five were living. The household also included Nancy Norman, age sixty-three, listed as mother-in-law, which provides the bridge from the Castleberry household back into the earlier Norman family records.

The marriage record places Jerry Castleberry and Georgia Ann Norman in Brooks County on 27 December 1887. That document anchors the couple before the 1900 census and fits the ages of the older children in the household. Jerry's later burial and memorial material support identifying him as Jeremiah Bryant Castleberry, born 28 March 1859 and buried at Sardis Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery after his death on 10 May 1907. The burial material is useful support, but Jerry's death still would benefit from a direct certificate or other primary death record if one can be located.

Georgia's side of the family is now much firmer than it was in the earlier version of this entry. In 1870, Georgeann Norman appears in Colquitt County in the household of John Norman and wife Nancy Norman. In 1880, the same family appears again in Colquitt County with daughter Georgia A. Norman in the home, while the wife is indexed as Rutha Norman. That 1880 given name should be treated as a record or indexing problem rather than silently normalized away, but the husband, county, daughter, and age pattern make it a strong match to the same family. Georgia Ann Castleberry's 18 April 1931 Colquitt County death certificate then names her father as John Norman and her mother as Nancy Alderman Norman. Taken together, those records support the conclusion that Georgia Ann Norman Castleberry was the daughter of John Norman and Nancy Alderman Norman.

That death certificate is the strongest direct evidence for the Alderman connection in this household. It identifies Georgia with the Norman family through her father and the Alderman family through her mother. The 1900 household therefore includes a documented maternal Alderman line. Earlier claims about founding dynasties or inherited status go beyond the evidence.

The children's later records are now strong enough to update the household in a meaningful way. Nancy Castleberry married Jim Alderman in Colquitt County on 26 December 1909. Later memorial material supports identifying that husband as James Harrison Alderman and connects the couple to daughter Ruby Alderman Ralston Moore. At the same time, Hugh James Alderman should be kept separate; his wife was Nancy White, and he should not be merged with Nancy Castleberry's husband. A 1910 census entry that appears to show a very young Nancy A. Alderman is questionable for this daughter and should not be treated as firm proof without better image review.

William Joseph Castleberry is well documented from young adulthood through death. His World War I draft registration gives his birth as 3 March 1891, residence near Omega in Colquitt County, and occupation as farming. Military service material places him in Company E, 45th Infantry, with service extending into March 1919. Later records carry him through the 1930 and 1950 censuses and to a 1971 death record. Memorial material identifies him as a son of Jeremiah Bryant Castleberry and Georgia Ann Norman Castleberry and names siblings that fit the 1900 household.

Martha Idella "Della" Castleberry can be followed through her 12 August 1917 Colquitt County marriage to Dan or Daniel E. Crosby, then through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses. A death-index entry for Martha I. Crosby, age fifty-nine, in 1951 fits her well, and Social Security claims material links Della Castleberry to husband Daniel E. Crosby and son Jerry Brogdon Crosby. Those records make her one of the more securely identified children from the 1900 home.

John Jerry Castleberry is also well anchored. He married Ida Norman in Colquitt County on 31 October 1915. A World War I draft card gives his birth as 16 May 1896, his residence on Rural Free Delivery 1 near Norman Park, and his status as married with one child. He can then be followed through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses, and later death and Social Security index records support the same identification through June 1979. A 1943 draft card for Jesse Bryant Castleberry names John J. Castleberry as father, and a 1923 child death certificate appears to tie John Castleberry and Ida Norman together in a primary-style family record.

Ivy, the two-year-old son in the 1900 household, now appears attachable to the later records of Ivey Dewey Castleberry. His World War I draft registration gives a birth date of 2 October 1898, a Colquitt County residence, and Georgia Castleberry as nearest relative. Later records place Ivey D. Castleberry in Moultrie with wife Mae, children including Gladys and Dewey, and long service as a city fireman. The 1948 Tampa Tribune notice about Gladys Castleberry, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. I. D. Castleberry of Moultrie, fits that same family. Because the 1900 census already shows Ivy as Jerry and Georgia's one-year-old son, the later Ivey Dewey chain can now be treated as the same child carried into adulthood.

This household matters because it can now be written with firmer evidence and fewer assumptions. The core structure of the 1900 family is secure. Georgia's maternal Alderman line is directly supported by her death certificate. Several children can be followed well into adulthood. What still needs restraint is Jerry's parentage and any larger social interpretation that goes beyond the records.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Georgia Ann Norman Castleberry was the daughter of John Norman and Nancy Alderman Norman.
  • Nancy Alderman Norman appears to be the same woman shown as Nancy Norman in the 1870 Colquitt County household and as the wife indexed as Rutha Norman in the 1880 Colquitt County household.
  • Nancy Castleberry married Jim or James Harrison Alderman, giving the household a second Alderman connection through the next generation.
  • John Jerry Castleberry married Ida Norman, which kept the Norman surname tied to the family in the following generation as well.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: William Joseph Castleberry, the Joseph Castleberry child in the 1900 household, has a documented World War I service trail. The current file cites draft registration and military service material placing him in Company E, 45th Infantry, with service extending into March 1919. Later death and veterans-index material carry the same adult identity into 1971.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Jerry's burial and memorial material strongly support the identification Jeremiah Bryant Castleberry, born 28 March 1859 and died 10 May 1907, but a direct death certificate or equivalent primary death record would strengthen the case.
  • Jerry's own parentage should remain open until a stronger direct record is added.
  • The 1880 census entry for John Norman's wife is indexed as Rutha Norman; the evidence supports treating her as the same woman later identified as Nancy Alderman Norman, but the name discrepancy should be acknowledged.
  • The apparent 1910 census entry for Nancy A. Alderman does not fit Nancy Castleberry's age cleanly and should not be used heavily without better image review.
  • The 1900 tax digest reference for Jerry or Jeremiah Castleberry supports adult taxable presence in the district, not land ownership by itself.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household now rests on the 1900 census, the 1887 marriage record for Jerry Castleberry and Georgia Ann Norman, the 1870 and 1880 Norman household placements for Georgia, Georgia Ann Castleberry's 1931 death certificate naming John Norman and Nancy Alderman Norman, and substantial later records for children Nancy, William Joseph, Martha Idella, John Jerry, and Ivey Dewey. The main remaining gaps are Jerry's own parentage, a stronger direct death record for Jerry, and a few points in the later Nancy Alderman trail.

docs.title: Household #138: Hall, William
docs.text:
Household #138: Hall, William

Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, William Hall headed an 8-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

Household Snapshot

William Hall headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 6 children.

William Hall's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

1900 Census Household

Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation
William Hall Head 54 Georgia Farmer
Serena Hall Wife 55 Georgia —
Ida Hall Child 30 Georgia —
Lillie Hall Child 23 Georgia —
Laura Hall Child 21 Georgia —
John Hall Child 20 Georgia —
Walter Hall Child 16 Georgia —
May Hall Child 13 Georgia —

Children and Later Trails

This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

Family Narrative

  • The 1900 Barney household contains William Hall, wife Serena Hall, and children Ida, Lillie, Laura, John, Walter, and May.
  • A longer census chain places William Hall in Lowndes County as a child in 1850 and 1860, in Brooks County as a young adult in 1870, with Serena in Brooks County in 1880 and 1900, and later in Hahira, Lowndes County, in 1910 and 1920.
  • Serena Hall is well identified as Serena Hires or Hiers through her 4 January 1870 Brooks County marriage to William Hall, her pre-marriage placement in the David Hires household, and her 1921 Lowndes County death record naming her father as David Hires and her mother as Yates.
  • The complete three-image 1907 pension packet verifies William's claimed service, Lowndes residence, farming occupation, poverty, and disabilities. It does not name his parents or biological mother.

William Hall appears in the 1900 census as a fifty-four-year-old farmer in Barney, Brooks County, with wife Serena and six children still at home. The household was marked white. William reported that he was born in October 1845, had been married thirty years, and owned his farm free of mortgage. Serena reported that she was born in October 1849, had borne nine children, and that seven were then living.

The broader record set now gives this household a workable life-course structure. In 1850, William Hall, age four, appears in Lowndes County in John Hall Jr.'s household. In 1860, a thirteen-year-old William appears again in the continuing family. This makes John Jr. William's strong-probable father, although no parent-naming record has been found. Elizabeth was nineteen in 1850 and was not the woman in John's 1840 household. Francis Pearson Hall's death certificate identifies her as Elizabeth Easter and verifies her as Francis's mother. She was John's later wife and William's probable stepmother; William's biological mother remains unresolved.

By 1870, William Hall, age twenty-one, was in Brooks County. The original Brooks County marriage return records his marriage to Serena Hires on January 4, 1870. Serena was enumerated twice that year: once with William in dwelling 779 and once under Hiers in her parents' dwelling 777. The two entries place the newly married Hall household beside David and Rebecca Hiers.

Serena can now be placed with more confidence than before. In 1860, Serena Hires appears in Brooks County in the household of David Hires. In 1870, Serena Hiers, age eighteen, appears again in Brooks County in the household of David Hiers and Rebecca Hiers. Her Lowndes County death record dated 12 June 1921 identifies her as Serena Hall, wife of W. M. Hall, and names her father as David Hires; the mother line is given as Yates in the death record and appears as Rebecca Yates in memorial material. Taken together, those records support identifying the 1900 wife Serena Hall as Serena Hires or Hiers, daughter of David Hires and a mother from the Yates family.

The 1880 census provides the first full family snapshot after the marriage. William Hall, age thirty-four, and Serena Hall, age twenty-nine, were in Brooks County with children John David, Jinnie L., Ida, Tommie A., and Laura C. By 1900, the household composition had shifted to Ida, Lillie, Laura, John, Walter, and May. Ida remained with her parents in both 1910 and 1920 at Hahira in Lowndes County. The overlap between the 1880 and 1900 households shows clear continuity, though not every child name in the two records should be silently merged without later corroboration.

William's later records are also stronger now. In 1910, William M. Hall, sixty-four, and Serena Hall, sixty, were in Hahira with daughter Ida, and the farm was again marked owned free of mortgage. In 1920, William, seventy-four, Serena, sixty-eight, and Ida, forty-nine, were still together in Hahira, and the home was again shown as owned. Those two censuses support the later Lowndes County phase of the family and show that the move out of Barney was not temporary.

The military evidence is handled separately below so the family narrative can stay focused on household movement, marriage, children, and later residence.

The household can therefore be described more securely than before, but it is not finished in every respect. The census chain from 1850 through 1920 is substantial. Serena's identity rests on her Hires household placements, original marriage return, and death certificate. William's complete pension packet supports his Confederate service claim and gives a self-reported birth date and service history, but no page names his parents or siblings. William's death, burial, biological mother, and a parent-naming record for John Hall Jr. remain unresolved.

Connections to Other Barney Families

  • Serena Hall is well supported as Serena Hires or Hiers, daughter of David Hires and a mother from the Yates family.
  • Serena's pre-marriage placement in the David Hires household ties this household into the wider Hires family cluster in Brooks County.
  • Ida Hall remained with William and Serena in both the 1910 and 1920 Lowndes County households, giving the family a clear later-life continuity point.
  • The 1900 Barney district also includes other Hall households, but no direct relationship to those households should be asserted here without stronger evidence.

Military Service

William Hall's complete three-image 1907 Georgia Confederate indigent pension packet provides the military anchor for this household. His application reports that he enlisted in April 1862 in Lowndes County in Captain H. Morgan's company of the 18th Georgia Regiment and surrendered near Petersburg, Virginia, on April 6, 1865. A witness affidavit and physicians' affidavit support the application. The packet documents his residence, farming occupation, poverty, and disabilities but names no parent, sibling, or biological mother. Its October 20, 1843 birth date conflicts with the census pattern and remains qualified.

Open Research Questions

  • John Hall Jr. is William's strong-probable father through the 1850 and 1860 census chain. William's biological mother remains unidentified.
  • Elizabeth Easter was John Jr.'s later wife and Francis Pearson Hall's verified mother. She was William's probable stepmother, not his established mother.
  • William's 1907 pension application gives a birth date of 20 October 1843, while the census trail points more toward 1845 or 1846; both should be retained until the discrepancy is resolved.
  • William's death has not yet been documented with a direct death certificate or equivalent probate-style record.
  • Burial at Old Orange Grove Church Cemetery is supported by memorial material, but the burial claim should still be treated as supporting rather than primary evidence.
  • The 1880 and 1900 child lists show continuity, but names such as John David and John, or possible spelling shifts such as Lilla and Lillie, should not be merged too aggressively without later corroboration.
  • The 1872 tax digest supports taxable presence in Brooks County, not broad claims about property scale or prosperity.

Research Status

Well-researched. The household now rests on a census chain from 1850 through 1920, the original 1870 marriage return, Serena's Hires household placements, Serena's 1921 death certificate, William's complete 1907 pension packet, and Brooks County tax material. John Hall Jr. is William's strong-probable father. Elizabeth Easter was John's later wife and William's probable stepmother. The main remaining gaps are William's biological mother, a parent-naming record for John Jr., William's death record, and stronger burial documentation.

Sources

docs.text:
William Hall headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 6 children.

William Hall's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William Hall Head 54 Georgia Farmer Serena Hall Wife 55 Georgia — Ida Hall Child 30 Georgia — Lillie Hall Child 23 Georgia — Laura Hall Child 21 Georgia — John Hall Child 20 Georgia — Walter Hall Child 16 Georgia — May Hall Child 13 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• The 1900 Barney household contains William Hall, wife Serena Hall, and children Ida, Lillie, Laura, John, Walter, and May.
  • A longer census chain places William Hall in Lowndes County as a child in 1850 and 1860, in Brooks County as a young adult in 1870, with Serena in Brooks County in 1880 and 1900, and later in Hahira, Lowndes County, in 1910 and 1920.
  • Serena Hall is well identified as Serena Hires or Hiers through her 4 January 1870 Brooks County marriage to William Hall, her pre-marriage placement in the David Hires household, and her 1921 Lowndes County death record naming her father as David Hires and her mother as Yates.
  • William's 1907 Confederate pension application provides direct evidence for his claimed service, but his exact birth year and parentage still need to be stated with care.

William Hall appears in the 1900 census as a fifty-four-year-old farmer in Barney, Brooks County, with wife Serena and six children still at home. The household was marked white. William reported that he was born in October 1845, had been married thirty years, and owned his farm free of mortgage. Serena reported that she was born in October 1849, had borne nine children, and that seven were then living.

The broader record set now gives this household a workable life-course structure. In 1850, William Hall, age four, appears in Lowndes County in the household of John and Elizabeth Hall. In 1860, a thirteen-year-old William Hall appears again in the same Lowndes County family cluster. By 1870, William Hall, age twenty-one, was in Brooks County, which fits his later adult residence there. A Brooks County marriage index then records William Hall and Serena Hires marrying on 4 January 1870. Brooks County tax-digest material places William Hall in Morven District 660 in 1872, which supports adult taxable presence in the county shortly after marriage without by itself proving land ownership.

Serena can now be placed with more confidence than before. In 1860, Serena Hires appears in Brooks County in the household of David Hires. In 1870, Serena Hiers, age eighteen, appears again in Brooks County in the household of David Hiers and Rebecca Hiers. Her Lowndes County death record dated 12 June 1921 identifies her as Serena Hall, wife of W. M. Hall, and names her father as David Hires; the mother line is given as Yates in the death record and appears as Rebecca Yates in memorial material. Taken together, those records support identifying the 1900 wife Serena Hall as Serena Hires or Hiers, daughter of David Hires and a mother from the Yates family.

The 1880 census provides the first full family snapshot after the marriage. William Hall, age thirty-four, and Serena Hall, age twenty-nine, were in Brooks County with children John David, Jinnie L., Ida, Tommie A., and Laura C. By 1900, the household composition had shifted to Ida, Lillie, Laura, John, Walter, and May. Ida remained with her parents in both 1910 and 1920 at Hahira in Lowndes County. The overlap between the 1880 and 1900 households shows clear continuity, though not every child name in the two records should be silently merged without later corroboration.

William's later records are also stronger now. In 1910, William M. Hall, sixty-four, and Serena Hall, sixty, were in Hahira with daughter Ida, and the farm was again marked owned free of mortgage. In 1920, William, seventy-four, Serena, sixty-eight, and Ida, forty-nine, were still together in Hahira, and the home was again shown as owned. Those two censuses support the later Lowndes County phase of the family and show that the move out of Barney was not temporary.

The military evidence is handled separately below so the family narrative can stay focused on household movement, marriage, children, and later residence.

The household can therefore be described more securely than before, but it is not finished in every respect. The census chain from 1850 through 1920 is now substantial. Serena's identity is much firmer through her pre-marriage Hires household placements, marriage record, and death record. William's pension file supports his Confederate service claim and gives a self-reported birth date and service history. What remains less direct is William's death, his burial, and a record that explicitly names his parents in later life rather than relying on census continuity back to John and Elizabeth Hall.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Serena Hall is well supported as Serena Hires or Hiers, daughter of David Hires and a mother from the Yates family.
  • Serena's pre-marriage placement in the David Hires household ties this household into the wider Hires family cluster in Brooks County.
  • Ida Hall remained with William and Serena in both the 1910 and 1920 Lowndes County households, giving the family a clear later-life continuity point.
  • The 1900 Barney district also includes other Hall households, but no direct relationship to those households should be asserted here without stronger evidence.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: William Hall's 1907 Georgia Confederate indigent pension application provides the military anchor for this household. The application reports that he enlisted in April 1862 in Lowndes County in Captain H. Morgan's company of the 18th Georgia Regiment and surrendered near Petersburg, Virginia, on 6 April 1865. The same application gives a birth date that differs from the census pattern, so the page should preserve that conflict rather than forcing one date.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• William's parentage is supported by the 1850 and 1860 Lowndes County census chain, but a later direct record naming his parents has not yet been added.
  • William's 1907 pension application gives a birth date of 20 October 1843, while the census trail points more toward 1845 or 1846; both should be retained until the discrepancy is resolved.
  • William's death has not yet been documented with a direct death certificate or equivalent probate-style record.
  • Burial at Old Orange Grove Church Cemetery is supported by memorial material, but the burial claim should still be treated as supporting rather than primary evidence.
  • The 1880 and 1900 child lists show continuity, but names such as John David and John, or possible spelling shifts such as Lilla and Lillie, should not be merged too aggressively without later corroboration.
  • The 1872 tax digest supports taxable presence in Brooks County, not broad claims about property scale or prosperity.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household now rests on a substantial census chain from 1850 through 1920, a Brooks County marriage index for William Hall and Serena Hires on 4 January 1870, Serena's pre-marriage placement in the David Hires household in 1860 and 1870, Serena Hall's 1921 Lowndes County death record, William Hall's 1907 Georgia Confederate pension application, and Brooks County tax-digest material placing William in Morven District 660 in 1872. The main remaining gaps are a direct death record for William, a stronger direct burial record for him, and a later record explicitly naming his parents.

docs.title: Household Snapshot

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Henry Sapp Head 70 Georgia Farmer Susan Sapp Wife 65 Georgia — Anthony Sapp Son 16 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Son: Anthony Sapp, age 16, born Mar 1884 in Georgia

Henry Sapp is securely anchored in the 1900 Barney census and can be traced through the 1880 Brooks County census, the 1870 Mitchell County census, and an 1860 Lee County household in which he appears with a wife named Sarah. The record set now supports Henry as a longtime south Georgia resident whose household changed after the Civil War, but several details in the earlier encyclopedia draft were stated too strongly and needed to be cut back.

The clearest early marriage record is the 3 February 1850 Decatur County marriage of Henry Sapp and Sarah McDonel. The 1860 Lee County census shows Henry with a wife Sarah, which likely fits that marriage, but the current file does not prove that the 1850 bride and the 1860 wife are the same woman beyond reasonable doubt. For that reason, the earlier naming of Henry's first wife as Sarah Dean should be removed.

Susan entered the household through a documented later marriage. A Dougherty County marriage record shows Susan Walden and Henry Sapp marrying on 19 December 1863. The 1870 Mitchell County census then places Henry and Susan together, along with a young Arsada Waldin. That census strongly suggests Susan had an earlier Walden marriage, but the direct marriage record for Susan Miller to Green Walden was not recovered in this pass, so Arsada is best treated as a probable stepchild rather than a fully proved one.

Henry's Confederate service is supported by military material and Susan's widow pension file. Those records identify him with Company D, 18th Georgia Infantry and show that Susan applied in Brooks County in 1911 for a widow's Confederate pension based on his service. The pension material supports the basic service claim and indicates that Henry was wounded or disabled in service, but the current evidence packet does not justify repeating older language that he was shot at Second Manassas and lost a leg unless that wording is confirmed in a direct record extract.

Henry also appears in the 24 July 1867 Reconstruction oath registration in Colquitt County, placing him in the postwar south Georgia migration path between Lee County and his later Brooks County residence. That sequence fits the census chain: Lee County in 1860, Colquitt County in 1867, Mitchell County in 1870, Brooks County in 1880, and Barney in 1900.

Anthony Sapp is better documented than the old draft indicated. The 1900 census lists him in Henry and Susan's home; the 1910 census places Susan in Anthony's household, with the original schedule indicating she was his mother despite an index transcription error calling her a daughter. Anthony can then be followed through 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 Brooks County records. His 30 November 1901 Brooks County marriage to Viola Crosby is documented, and later records show a wife Alice or Alece Sapp, indicating more than one marriage. A World War I draft registration gives Anthony a birth date of 12 October 1881, while later SSA, death-index, and cemetery material point toward 1882 or 1883. His death on 14 April 1952 is well supported, but the present records still stop short of a direct parent-naming document.

Henry's death date remains unsettled. Susan's 1911 widow pension file says he died in Brooks County on 8 January 1909, while the Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery memorial gives 16 June 1909. Until a direct death or burial record resolves the conflict, the safest reading is that Henry died in Brooks County in 1909. Memorial evidence places both Henry and Susan at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery near Pavo, but that burial placement should still be treated as secondary until matched to a direct cemetery or death record.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: Henry Sapp's Confederate service is supported by military material and Susan Sapp's 1911 Brooks County widow-pension file. Those records identify him with Company D, 18th Georgia Infantry and support the basic service claim. Older claims about a Second Manassas wound, leg loss, pension timing, and veterans-section burial should stay out unless direct record wording is added.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Henry's parentage as Janson Sapp and Jane Sapp is not proved by the current direct records and should not be stated as settled fact.
  • Henry's exact birth date is not established. The 1900 census gives Oct 1829, while later compiled sources give more precise dates that are not yet backed by a direct record in hand.
  • Henry's exact death date is unresolved: Susan's 1911 widow pension points to 8 Jan 1909, while the cemetery memorial gives 16 Jun 1909.
  • Susan's earlier marriage to Green Walden is strongly suggested, but the marriage record itself is still needed.
  • Anthony is very likely the son of Henry and Susan, but a death certificate, SSA application, or other direct parent-naming record would make that explicit.
  • Arsada Waldin in 1870 is probably Susan's child from an earlier Walden marriage, but that relationship is not yet fully documented.
  • The older claims that Henry was wounded at Second Manassas, lost a leg, received a pension beginning in 1882, and was buried in a veterans' section should stay out of the entry unless direct record text is added.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-Researched. The census chain, Henry's 1863 marriage to Susan Walden, his Confederate service, his 1867 Colquitt County oath registration, and Anthony's later life are all supported well enough to sustain the household narrative. Parentage, some earlier-family links, and Henry's exact death details remain open.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Henry Hall Head 50 Georgia Farmer Emmer Hall Wife 45 Georgia — Hubord Hall Son 12 Georgia — William Hall Son 10 Georgia — Rassie Hall Daughter 7 Georgia — Weedham Hall Son 5 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Son: Hubord Hall, age 12, born May 1888 in Georgia
  • Son: William Hall, age 10, born Apr 1890 in Georgia
  • Daughter: Rassie Hall, age 7, born Feb 1893 in Georgia
  • Son: Weedham Hall, age 5, born Jun 1895 in Georgia

Henry Hall is securely identified in the 1880 Quitman census, the 1900 Barney census, and later Appling County records. The family can be followed from Brooks County into Appling County, where Henry died in 1923 and Emma died in 1928. The household is well documented at the core level, but Henry's parentage before marriage remains unproved.

A Brooks County marriage record and surviving license return show Henry Hall and Emma Capers marrying in November 1875. The indexed record gives the date as 30 November 1875. The license image shows the ordinary issuing the license on 27 November 1875 and the return certifying that Henry Hall and Emma Capers were joined in matrimony on 30 November 1875. That record firmly identifies Emma's maiden name.

The 1880 census places Henry and Emma in Quitman with five children: Della, Sallie, Budd, Willie, and Charlie. Henry was recorded as working on a farm, and both Henry and Emma were marked unable to read and write. A separate 1880 agricultural schedule entry shows Henry engaged in farming in Brooks County, but it does not by itself prove land ownership.

By 1900 the family was in Barney, where Henry reported that he was born in May 1850 and Emma in February 1855. The household then included Hubord, William, Rassie, and Weedham. The census states that Henry and Emma had been married twenty-five years, which fits the 1875 marriage record.

Later records place the family in Baxley in Appling County. The existing household file traces Henry and Emma there in 1910 and 1920, with Emma's given name rendered in variant forms. Those later census references support the move out of Brooks County and show Henry in old age before his death in Appling County on 25 February 1923.

Emma's death certificate closes the family line more cleanly than the earlier entry did. Emma Hall, identified there as a widowed Black woman and widow of Henry Hall, died in Quitman on 5 December 1928 at about seventy-six years of age. Her father was named as Samuel Capers. The certificate also gives her burial as North End Cemetery. This record strengthens Emma's identity and ties the later widow back to the 1875 marriage.

An earlier research phase appears to have treated a 1870 Brooks County entry for a fifteen-year-old Henry Hall in the household of Alfred and Matilda Hall as if it proved Henry's parents. The current evidence does not justify that conclusion. That 1870 record may point to the same man, but without a bridging record it should remain a candidate only. The parent names reported on Henry's 1923 death record should likewise be used cautiously until the certificate is rechecked from the original image and supported by other evidence.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Possible connection to the 1870 Brooks County household of Alfred and Matilda Hall, but the identification is not proved.
  • Emma Hall's 1928 death certificate names her father as Samuel Capers, giving the Capers line a firmer footing than before.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Recheck Henry Hall's 1923 Appling County death certificate from the original image before treating the reported parents as established.
  • Confirm the literal wording of the 1910 and 1920 Appling County census entries if the household is revisited.
  • Track the 1880 children forward individually; several are still only anchored in childhood census entries.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-documented for the core household. Marriage, two key Brooks County censuses, Emma's death record, and the family's move into Appling County are supported. Henry's parentage and the full identification of all children remain incomplete.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
William Davis headed a 3-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 1 child.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William Davis Head 26 Georgia Farmer Bethenia Davis Wife 25 Georgia — Clara Davis Daughter 1 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Daughter: Clara Davis, age 1, born about 1899 in Georgia

William Davis appears in Brooks County records from his 1895 marriage through the 1927 death of his wife Bethany. The core household is well supported by the marriage record, the 1900, 1910, and 1920 censuses, Bethany's death certificate, and later records for daughter Clara.

The Brooks County marriage license and return show that Will Davis and Betheny Howell were married on 6 October 1895. Later census entries use the forms William, Will, Bethenia, and Bethany, but the records line up well enough to treat them as one family. The 1900 census states that the couple had been married four years, which is close but not exact; the marriage record should control.

In 1900 the family was in Barney, where William Davis, age twenty-six, was recorded as a farmer born in May 1874. The household included his wife Bethenia and daughter Clara. That census marked the place as owned. In 1910 the family was still in Brooks County, then in the Tallokas district, with Clara and younger son James in the home. William was again listed as a farmer, and the place was marked rented. In 1920 the family was back in the Barney area, with Will Davis, wife Bethany, and son James still together. That census also marked the place as rented.

Bethany's earlier identity is also on firm ground. In 1880, Bethany Howell was enumerated in the Dry Lake district of Brooks County in the household of Jessie Howell and Caroline Howell. Bethany's 1927 death certificate identifies her as Bethany Davis, wife of Will Davis, and names her parents as Jesse Howell and Caroline Frazier. The certificate gives her death date as 21 May 1927 in Barney, Brooks County, at age fifty.

The later record trail for Clara helps extend this household beyond the parent generation. A Brooks County marriage record shows Clara Davis married Rube Edmondson on 28 December 1914. By 1930, Clara Edmondson was a widowed head of household in Militia District 1571 in Brooks County, with children Stanley, Vally, and Ruth Edmondson, and with her brother James Davis in the household. In 1940 she was in Moultrie, Colquitt County, still widowed, with sons Walter and Willie James Edmondson and daughter Vallie Lee Jenkins nearby with young children. A Social Security Applications and Claims Index entry ties Clara Davis to spouse Ruben Edmondson and child Walter Edmondson.

William's age is not perfectly steady across the census record. The 1900 and 1910 entries point to a birth about 1874, while the 1920 entry points closer to 1868. For now, the safest wording is that he was born in Georgia, probably in the early 1870s, with May 1874 reported in the 1900 census.

An earlier attempt to connect this household to HH#104 through the Frazier surname should be dropped. Bethany's mother was Caroline Frazier, but that surname alone does not prove a link to another Barney household.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Bethany Davis was born Bethany Howell, daughter of Jesse Howell and Caroline Frazier.
  • Clara Davis married into the Edmondson family and remained tied to her Davis kin, as shown by James Davis living in her household in 1930.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• William Davis's death has not yet been pinned down with a direct death record.
  • Clara's marriage and later census trail are strong, but a direct death record for her husband Ruben Edmondson would help explain her widow status by 1930.
  • If this household is revisited, the literal wording of Bethany's 1927 death certificate can be extracted more fully for burial, informant, and cause-of-death details.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-documented for the core family. The marriage, Bethany's parentage, the three household censuses, Bethany's death, and Clara's later Edmondson records are all supported. William's death remains the main unresolved gap.

docs.text:

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Georgia Williams headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 6 extended-family members and 1 boarder, employee, servant, or other non-kin resident.

Georgia Williams's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Georgia Williams Head 49 Georgia Farmer John West Boarder 57 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Lillie Williams Niece 17 Georgia — Hubbord McCall Grandson 12 Georgia — Homer McCall Grandson 10 Georgia — Metton McCall Grandson 9 Georgia — Ila McCall Granddaughter 7 Georgia — Lulton McCall Grandson 5 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Georgia Williams was a widowed Black woman in Barney in 1900.
  • She appears again in the same community in 1910 as George A. Williams and in Homer McCall's household in 1920 and 1930 as George Ann Williams or George Williams.
  • The records consistently place her with McCall grandchildren, but the exact parent-child link between Georgia Williams and that McCall group has not been proved.
  • An 1880 Milledgeville household with Ben Williams, wife Georgia, and daughter Anna is a plausible earlier match, but the identification is not secure enough to treat as settled.

The clearest part of this household is the Brooks County census trail. In 1900 Georgia Williams, age forty-nine, born May 1851, was the widowed head of household in Barney and worked as a farmer. The household included McCall grandchildren. In 1910 she appears in Barney again as George A. Williams, still female and still living with McCall grandchildren. In 1920 she was recorded as George Ann Williams, age seventy-two, in the household of Homer McCall, where her relationship was given as grandmother. In 1930 Homer McCall's household still included George Williams, age eighty, again identified as grandmother. She was not found in Homer's household in 1940, and no death or burial record has been located.

The later McCall lines are much better documented than the bridge back to Georgia. Homer McCall can be followed forward through his 1912 Brooks County marriage to Rachel Yerby and later records. Milton or Melton McCall can be followed through his World War I draft registration, his 1921 Brooks County marriage to Lavina Harrison, later censuses, and his 1968 death record. Ila Lee McCall can be followed from Georgia Williams's household into her 1915 Brooks County marriage to Joshua Jenkins, then through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses, with a Brooks County death index entry in 1972. Those records make the McCall grandchild cluster credible, even though the missing parent link remains unresolved.

The older lead in Baldwin County should be handled carefully. In 1880 a Ben Williams household on Washington Street in Milledgeville included Ben Williams, age thirty-three, wife Georgia, age twenty-nine, and daughter Anna, age three. That record may represent the same woman later found in Barney, but the fit is not clean. The age and birthplace details do not line up neatly with the later Brooks County records, so the 1880 household is best treated as a possible earlier identification rather than a proved one.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: WELL-RESEARCHED. The Brooks County record trail from 1900 through 1930 is strong, and the later lines of Homer McCall, Milton or Melton McCall, and Ila Lee McCall Jenkins are well anchored. The main unresolved issue is the missing parent link between Georgia Williams and the McCall grandchildren, along with the unproved 1880 Baldwin County identification.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Andrew Mitchell Head 17 Georgia Farmer Annie Mitchell Daughter 33 Georgia — James Mitchell Son 11 Georgia — Nancy Mitchell Daughter 13 Georgia — Annie Mitchell Daughter 10 Georgia — Emmer Mitchell Daughter 6 Georgia — Jackson Mitchell Son 5 Georgia — Williams Mitchell Son 2 Georgia — George W Mitchell Son 9/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Census page: 14 | Lines: 16-24
  • Head: Andrew Mitchell, age 40, born Feb 1860 in Georgia, farmer
  • Wife: Annie Mitchell, age 33, born in Georgia
  • Children in household: Nancy Mitchell, George Mitchell, James Mitchell, Annie Mitchell, Emmer Mitchell, Jackson Mitchell, and Williams Mitchell
  • Later residences: Pitts, Wilcox County, Georgia; Osprey, Sarasota County, Florida; return to Pitts by 1940
  • Later death and burial evidence: Andrew died in 1945 at Pitts and was buried at New Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery; Annie died in 1942

The 1900 Barney census shows Andrew Mitchell and wife Annie with seven children in a household that can now be followed with much more confidence than the earlier draft allowed. The strongest part of the case is the long census chain. Andrew and Annie appear in Barney in 1900, in Pitts, Wilcox County, in 1910 and 1920, in Osprey, Sarasota County, Florida, in 1930, and back in Pitts in 1940. That sequence establishes a single couple moving as a family unit across four decades.

The older entry overreached on Andrew's parentage and on the claim that two different Andrew Mitchell families had been cleanly separated. The current evidence supports a narrower and safer conclusion. Andrew Jackson Mitchell, the man in HH#143, is securely identified from 1900 forward. A likely earlier appearance is the infant A. J. Mitchell in the 1860 household of Moses A. Mitchell and Winford or Winnie Mitchell, but that link still needs direct proof before it should replace all caution. The prior identification of Andrew's parents as John Mitchell and Martha H. Daniel should not stand as settled fact in this entry without a fresh direct-record review.

Annie's identity is also clearer now. Census continuity firmly places the same Annie with Andrew from 1900 through 1940. Her maiden name as King is strongly supported by later family evidence, especially records created through the lives of their children. A Social Security Applications and Claims Index entry for Annie Mitchell Hammock names her parents as Andrew Jackson Mitchell and Annie King. An 1880 Wilcox County census entry for Annie King in the household of James J. and Bettie King is a good fit in age and place. A Georgia death index entry for Annie K. Mitchell in Wilcox County in 1942 also fits the established timeline. Together these records make Annie King the best-supported identification, though the case still rests more on layered derivative evidence than on a cited marriage record naming her directly.

The children's later identities are much better developed than they were in the previous version of this entry. Nancy Mitchell is strongly supported as the Nancy who married J. W. Attaway in Wilcox County on 8 May 1904 and later appears as Nancy Attaway in Wilcox and Broward County records. James A. Mitchell is strongly identified as the son who married Mary Clark in Wilcox County on 27 September 1906 and later appears with wife-name variants Fanny, Fannie, Mae, and Fanny Mary Clark Mitchell. Annie Mitchell is the same woman later known as Annie Hammock or Annie Rosa Mitchell, with the 1970 obituary evidence tying her back to Andrew and Annie and listing matching siblings. Emmer Mitchell is strongly supported as Emma Idelia Mitchell, later Emma I. Clark and then Emma Grimes. Jackson Mitchell is strongly supported as Jackson W. Mitchell, whose military and later census records align on a birth date of 23 August 1895. Williams Mitchell is strongly supported as William David Mitchell, born 26 August 1897 at Pitts, whose 1942 draft card names Mrs. J. W. Attaway of Pitts as the person who would always know his address. George Mitchell remains the least certain of the older children, but the Thomas County man who appears as Isaac Mitchell in 1930, George I. Mitchell in 1940, and George Mitchell in 1950 fits this son well enough to treat as a strong working identification rather than a proved one.

The Florida years matter because they help connect the family branches rather than standing as an isolated migration note. Andrew and Annie's 1930 Osprey household sits in the same broader Florida orbit seen in the later records of Nancy Attaway, Emma Grimes, and William David Mitchell. That does not prove every relationship by itself, but it does make the family cluster more coherent than the earlier entry suggested.

A captioned family photograph identifying Andrew "Ander" Jackson Mitchell and Annie King Mitchell with family members adds useful family-level support. It should be treated as derivative evidence, not as a substitute for civil records, but it lines up well with the documentary picture.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • HH#148 George D. Mitchell. The present evidence points toward a likely sibling relationship between Andrew Mitchell of HH#143 and George Desheild Mitchell of HH#148. George is securely documented as a son of Moses A. Mitchell and Winiford or Winnie Mitchell. Andrew's likely earlier appearance as A. J. Mitchell in that same household makes the brother theory plausible, but it still needs a direct bridge before it should be treated as proved.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• A direct marriage record for Andrew Mitchell and Annie King should be cited before Annie's maiden name is treated as primary-record proof rather than a strong derivative conclusion.
  • Andrew's pre-1900 origin still needs a cleaner bridge. The 1860 A. J. Mitchell in the Moses A. Mitchell and Winford or Winnie Mitchell household is a good lead, not yet a finished proof argument.
  • Annie's 1942 death should be supported by a full record extract; the current reference is index-only.
  • The probable identification of son George with the later George I. Mitchell or Isaac Mitchell records in Thomas County remains short of direct proof.
  • If Andrew's 1945 death certificate is used again in future revisions, the parentage field should be checked from the original record rather than repeated from the earlier encyclopedia summary.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household is secure from 1900 forward, the long census chain is strong, and the major children can now be placed with much more confidence. The main remaining gaps are Andrew's pre-1900 origin, a direct record for Annie's maiden name, and a firmer bridge for son George.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• Census page: 14 | Lines: 25-37
  • Head: Jacob Hunter Hiers, age 45, born Feb 1855 in Georgia, farmer
  • Wife: Sallie Hiers, age 45, born Sep 1855 in Georgia
  • Children in household: Malcom, Marcus D., John, Lula, Gussie, Sallie, Eunie, Willie, Harry, Thomas, and Ruby Hiers
  • Later residence: Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia, by 1910; 119 6th Street SE, Moultrie, in 1920
  • Later death and burial evidence: Jacob died in Moultrie on 12 Jun 1925 and was buried at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery near Pavo; later burial material places Sallie there as well and gives her death as 18 Dec 1918

The 1900 Barney census shows Jacob Hunter Hiers and wife Sallie with eleven children still at home, ranging from adult sons in their twenties to Ruby, age three. The household can be followed with confidence into Moultrie, Colquitt County, by 1910 and 1920. In 1910 Jacob was still farming on the Moultrie and Quitman Road. By 1920 he was a widowed lawyer renting a house on 6th Street SE with three adult children still with him. That census sequence gives the entry its backbone and fixes the move from Brooks County to Colquitt County without needing much interpretation beyond what the records already say.

Jacob's identity is strong. The 1873 Brooks County marriage record places Jacob Hunter Hiers with Sarah or Sallie Strickland at the start of the family, the 1880 census gives an earlier household anchor, and the 1925 Colquitt County death certificate closes the line. That death record identifies his parents as Phillip Hiers and a mother from the Alderman family, which fits the broader Hiers material already associated with him. The occupation change from farmer in 1900 and 1910 to lawyer in 1920 and on the death record is unusual, but it is directly documented and does not need embellishment.

Sallie is also much clearer in the revised record trail. The marriage record identifies her as Sarah or Sallie Strickland, and the 1900 and 1910 censuses keep her in the same household with matching age, birthplace, and children. She was dead before the 1920 census, where Jacob appears as widowed. Later burial and family material place her death on 18 Dec 1918. Her mother appears to have been Jane or Jency Alderman Strickland, which means both Jacob and Sallie had Alderman mothers, but that network point should stay secondary to the direct household records.

The adult children are far better separated than they were in the older entry. James M. Hiers, the son indexed as Malcom Hines in 1900 and Jas. M. Huss in 1910, is the same man later found as James M. Hiers in Florida and Colquitt County records; his line is supported by the 1911 marriage to Ada Carlton, later census records through 1950, Social Security material giving a 21 May 1873 Brooks County birth, and a 1952 Georgia death index entry. Marcus P. Hiers is strongly documented from 1900 through 1950, with the World War I draft card giving the fuller name Marcus Phinnia or Pliny Hiers, born 28 May 1875, and the 1907 marriage record tying him to Annie Bailey. John I. Hiers is securely the son in the 1880 and 1900 households; he is probably the same man later buried as J. Irwin Hiers, but the post-1900 bridge is still thinner than for his siblings. Lula Hiers remains easier to place in the parental household than after it: she appears as Lula in 1900 and 1910 and as F. Lulu Hiers in Jacob's 1920 household, still unmarried.

The daughters are now documented with much less guesswork. Gussie, the eighteen-year-old daughter in 1900, is strongly identified as Laura Augusta or Gussie Hiers, who married Enoch Hall of HH#33 in Brooks County on 30 Dec 1900 and later appears with him across several Florida census records. Sallie V. Hiers can be followed from the parental household in 1900 and 1910 into single adult life in Tifton and Moultrie; the 1950 census still shows her never married, living with brother Harry. Eunice Hiers follows a similarly strong single-woman line from 1900 through 1950, with repeated work as a telephone operator or office bookkeeper and a 1979 Colquitt County death. Willie H. Hiers is securely the daughter who married Charlie Franklin Chitty in Brooks County on 17 Dec 1911 and later appears as Willie Chitty through the 1950 census, with a 1972 Colquitt County death record. Ruby, the youngest daughter in the 1900 household, is now strongly identified as Ruby Elizabeth Hiers Gaillard. Social Security claims material gives her birth as 17 Jan 1897 in Brooks County and names her parents as Jacob H. Hiers and Sally Strickland. She married Eugene M. Gaillard, lived in Jacksonville, Fort Pierce, and later Miami, and died in Dade County in 1954.

The younger sons are also well anchored. Harry Livingston Hiers, born 6 Jul 1891, appears in the parental home through 1920, registered for World War I as a carpenter, later worked as a salesman and tax collector, married Audrey Lucille Johnson, and died in Colquitt County on 23 Feb 1960. Probate material identifies his children Warren Royce Hiers and Mildred Hiers Moon. Thomas Watson Hiers, born 1 May 1894, can be traced from the 1900 household into a longer work migration through Quitman, Anniston, Norwood, and Smithfield. His World War I and World War II draft cards, the 1950 census, later Virginia records, and death certificate all identify the same man. He married Bessie May Wallace, worked in meat packing and plant supervision, and died in Isle of Wight County, Virginia, on 19 Dec 1964.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: • HH#33 Enoch Hall. Gussie Hiers, daughter of Jacob Hunter Hiers and Sallie Strickland, married Enoch Hall on 30 Dec 1900. That marriage creates a direct link between HH#144 and HH#33.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Sallie's reported death date of 18 Dec 1918 is supported by later burial and family material, but a full death record should be cited if one can be found.
  • John I. Hiers still needs a firmer bridge from the 1900 household to the later J. Irwin Hiers burial material before the later identification should be treated as fully proved.
  • Lula Hiers is secure in the 1900, 1910, and 1920 household trail, but her later life still needs direct end-of-life documentation.
  • If Jacob's Spanish-American War service is discussed again, it should be cited from the underlying military record rather than repeated from derivative summaries.
  • The exact wording of Jacob's mother field on the 1925 death certificate should be checked from the original certificate image whenever the parentage discussion is revisited.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The core household is strong from 1880 through Jacob's 1925 death, the Brooks County to Colquitt County move is secure, and most of the adult children can now be followed with confidence into their later lives. The main remaining gaps are Sallie's direct death record, John's post-1900 bridge, and Lula's later documentation.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Gerge Sanders Head 35 Georgia Farmer Hanna Sanders Wife 36 Georgia — Della Sanders Daughter 14 Georgia — Sallie Sanders Daughter 8 Georgia — Samuel Sanders Son 4 Georgia — Willie Sanders Daughter 1 Georgia — Lila Sanders Stepdaughter (Step Daughter) 18 Georgia — Francis Runels Granddaughter 4 Georgia — Francis Dukes Mother-in-law 50 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Household summary
docs.text:
George Sanders was recorded in the 1900 Barney census as a White farmer, age 35, born in Georgia in May 1865. His wife was Hannah Sanders, age 36. The household included children Della, Sallie, Samuel, and Willie Sanders; stepdaughter Lila Sanders; granddaughter Francis Runels; and Hannah's mother, Francis or Frances Dukes.

The current trail identifies Hannah as Hannah Dukes, who married George Sanders in Brooks County on 3 January 1884. Frances Dukes's presence in the 1900 and 1910 Sanders households is the strongest bridge tying Hannah back to the earlier Dukes family. Earlier census work places Frances with husband Samuel Dukes and daughter Hannah in Brooks County in 1870 and in Morven in 1880.

George is also linked to an earlier Sanders family in Banks County. The current entry identifies him as the George or Gerge Sanders who appears in 1870 and 1880 with parents Smith Sanders and Betty or Elizabeth Sanders. That line is plausible and useful, but it should remain tied to the census chain rather than expanded beyond the records now preserved.

Later census summaries follow George and Hannah in Brooks County in 1910, George as a widower in Lowndes County in 1920, and George with wife Anna in Gwinnett County in 1930. The later records support a broad movement pattern from Banks County to Brooks County, then to Lowndes and Gwinnett counties. They do not yet provide exact death dates for George or Hannah.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• 1870: A likely George Sanders appears in Banks County, Georgia, with parents Smith and Betty Sanders.
  • 1880: George or Gerge Sanders appears in Banks County with parents Smith and Elizabeth Sanders and siblings Mary J., Philip, Augustus, Theio, Liszy, Henry, Emma, and Cora.
  • 1884: George Sanders married Hannah Dukes in Brooks County, Georgia, on 3 January 1884.
  • 1900: George Sanders appears in Barney, Brooks County, with wife Hannah, children Della, Sallie, Samuel, and Willie, stepdaughter Lila, granddaughter Francis Runels, and mother-in-law Francis Dukes.
  • 1910: George and Hannah remain in Brooks County, with Frances Dukes again present as mother-in-law.
  • 1920: George appears in Lowndes County as a widower. The current trail reports his occupation as carpenter and his home as owned free of mortgage.
  • 1930: George appears in Gwinnett County with wife Anna. The current trail reports him as a farm laborer in a rented home.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: This household connects most clearly to the Dukes family through Hannah Dukes Sanders and her mother Frances Dukes. Frances's mother-in-law placement in both 1900 and 1910 gives the relationship more weight than a single census appearance would. The earlier Banks County Sanders identification connects George to Smith and Betty or Elizabeth Sanders, but that identification still depends on the census chain and should not be pushed beyond it without additional records.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The account was reconstructed from the encyclopedia entry and does not yet have direct record support for every claim.
  • George's death is only bounded as after the 1930 census in the current trail.
  • Hannah's death is bounded between the 1910 household and George's 1920 widowed status; no direct death or burial record is preserved here.
  • The second wife Anna is supported by the 1930 census summary, but no marriage or death record has been preserved.
  • The literacy changes across the census years should be treated cautiously. They may reflect record variation as much as actual literacy gain or loss.
  • Frances Dukes's reported age varies across the census trail and should not be forced into one exact birth year without a stronger record.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Well-researched from the current census and marriage trail; direct extracts still need to be preserved locally.
  • Strengths: The entry has a useful multi-census chain from 1870 through 1930, an 1884 Brooks County marriage, and a repeated Frances Dukes mother-in-law link in 1900 and 1910.
  • Remaining cautions: Death dates, the second marriage to Anna, and the exact strength of the Banks County-to-Brooks County identity bridge need tighter direct-record support before this can be treated as source-exhausted.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Household summary
docs.text:
Ruben Clark, also recorded as Reuben Clark, was listed in the 1900 Barney census as a Black farmer, age 66, born in Georgia in April 1834. He rented his farm. His wife was Millie Clark, age 63, also born in Georgia. The census reports that Ruben and Millie had been married for 40 years. Their 1900 household also included daughter Georgia Clark, son Rubin Clark, and granddaughters Millie Clark and Ada Clark.

The surviving record trail reaches back into Reconstruction. Reuben Clark registered to vote in Brooks County on 1 July 1867. He appears in the 1870 Brooks County census with Millie and a group of children, then in an 1871 Morven District freedman tax-list entry associated with employer W. R. Ryall. By 1880, he was recorded in Morven as a farmer with wife Millie and children still in the household. An 1880 agricultural schedule also records him in Brooks County.

The last direct record now preserved for Ruben is a likely 1910 Richmond County census household. That record lists Reuben Clark, age 73, on Waynes Bard Road with wife Sedina Clark, age 60, and grandson John T. William, age 17. It also says Reuben had been married 42 years. That creates the main unresolved problem in this entry. Sedina may be a later wife, a recording or name issue involving Millie, or a different relationship. The present evidence does not settle it.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• 1867: Reuben Clark, Black, registered in Brooks County, Election District 7, on 1 July 1867.
  • 1870: Reuben Clark, age 35, Black farm laborer, appears in Brooks County, Georgia, Quitman post office. Millie Clark, age 35, appears in the household with children Queen, Hing, Peggy, Laura, William, Mary, Thomas, and Fortune.
  • 1871: Reuben Clark appears in the Brooks County Morven District freedman tax list, associated with employer W. R. Ryall.
  • 1880: Reuben Clark, age 46, farmer, appears in Morven, Brooks County, with wife Millie and children Georgia, Reuben, Jenny, Laura, William, Mary, Thomas, Fortum/Fortune, and Charlie. The census marks Reuben and Millie as unable to read or write.
  • 1880 agricultural schedule: Reuben Clark appears in Brooks County, District 4, on 16 July 1880, OS page 47, line 3.
  • 1900: Ruben Clark, age 66, farmer, appears in Barney, Brooks County, with wife Millie, daughter Georgia, son Rubin, and granddaughters Millie and Ada. The record reports about 40 years married and rented farm status.
  • 1910: A likely same Reuben Clark, age 73, appears in Richmond County with wife Sedina and grandson John T. William. This supports a post-1900 move or late-life residence, but it does not explain what happened to Millie.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: The Clark surname appears in several Barney-area households. This entry does not yet prove a specific connection to HH#135 or to the broader Clark-Rountree network. Those remain research leads, not conclusions.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The 1910 Sedina/Sednia Clark problem remains unresolved. No direct record currently proves whether she was a second wife, a name variant for Millie, or a separate relationship.
  • Ruben's death is only bounded as after the likely 1910 Richmond County census record. No death, burial, probate, or later tax record has been found in the current source set.
  • Millie's life after the 1900 Barney census is not proved by the preserved records. A possible later connection to Anderson Clark should not be used as fact without the 1920 census image and supporting evidence.
  • No direct marriage record has been found for Ruben and Millie or for Reuben and Sedina.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Source-exhausted for currently available direct records; unresolved late-life spouse and death questions remain.
  • Strengths: The entry now rests on a direct record chain from 1867 through 1910: Reconstruction voter registration, 1870 census, 1871 freedman tax list, 1880 census, 1880 agricultural schedule, 1900 census, and 1910 census.
  • Remaining cautions: The record trail does not resolve Millie versus Sedina, Ruben's death, Millie's later life, or any specific Clark-Rountree/HH#135 connection.

docs.text:
