docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
Whitman Player headed a 4-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner, 1 child, and 1 extended-family member.

Whitman Player's listed occupation was Hostler.

Reported birthplaces span Georgia and South Carolina, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Whitman Player Head 21 South Carolina Hostler Maggie Player Wife 18 Georgia — Walter Player Son 6/12 Georgia — Charlie Taylor Brother-in-law 22 Georgia Teamster

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Household summary
docs.text:
Whitman Player was recorded in the 1900 Barney census as a White hostler, age 21, born in South Carolina in October 1878. His wife Maggie Player was age 18, born in Georgia. Their infant son Walter Player was listed as six months old, born in June 1899. Charlie Taylor, age 22, was also in the household and was recorded as Whitman's brother-in-law. The household rented a house rather than a farm.

The preserved source images now support a Georgia-centered trail after the 1900 Barney entry. Whit or Walter Player appears in Lower Fork, Lowndes County, Georgia, in 1910 and 1920; in Hahira, Lowndes County, in 1930; and in Valdosta, Lowndes County, in 1940 and 1950. This corrects the earlier encyclopedia text that placed the 1920 household in Florence County, South Carolina as a merchant household. The preserved 1920 summary instead shows Walter W. Plair, with a user-submitted correction to Walter W. Player, in Lower Fork, Lowndes County, Georgia, farming on a rented farm.

The 1880 census trail is now stronger because the full Shiloh, Sumter County, South Carolina page has been preserved along with the individual summary. Near the bottom of that page, Walter W. Player appears as an infant in dwelling/family 423/423, the D. A. Player household. James has reviewed the image and reads the wife/mother as Rosanna or Rosanne Player. A compiled Player genealogy identifies the head as Daniel Andrew Player and gives his wife as Rosa A. Long, married 11 December 1872, which is consistent with the census reading. The compiled genealogy is useful supporting evidence, but the census fact and compiled identification should remain separately stated.

Walter's World War I draft registration is now preserved directly. It names him as Walter Whitman Player, age 39, born 17 October 1878, living at Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, with nearest relative Mrs. Maggie Player. It gives his occupation as farming and was registered at the Lowndes County local board on 12 September 1918. This is the strongest preserved source for the 17 October 1878 birth date, though later death and memorial sources use 1875 or about 1876.

A World War II draft card for Lessie D. Player is also preserved. It identifies Lessie as born 18 January 1915 in Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, and names Mr. Walter Whit. Player of Valdosta as the person who would always know his address, explicitly marked as father. That record directly supports Lessie as Walter's child and gives a later Valdosta address for Walter. Index summaries now add more child-bridge support: a Social Security Applications and Claims index entry for Maggie Taylor names spouse Whitt Player and child Collis Player; a Georgia death-records index entry for Maggie Taylor names spouse W. W. Player and child Frank Player; and a Social Security Applications and Claims index entry for Walter W. Player names spouse Maggie Taylor and child Dorothy Louise Williams. These are useful links, though the underlying records would be stronger than the index summaries.

The Walter/Frank child line is now much stronger. The 1900 household summary lists the infant son as Walter Player, born November 1899. Later records follow him as W. F. Player, Walter Franklin Player, Frank Player, and Walter Frank Player. A direct Lowndes County marriage record shows W. F. Player married Beatrice Griffin on 29 October 1917. His World War I draft card names him Walter Franklin Player, born 8 November 1899, living on RFD 1 in Lowndes County, with Walter W. Player named as father and employer. The 1920 Hahira census summary shows W. F. Player, wife Beatrice, and infant son Walter E. Player at Colson Daw Mill. A Georgia death-index summary records Frank Player's death in Lowndes County on 24 February 1922, certificate 4422-D. Find a Grave memorial material places Walter Frank Player at Friendship Cemetery and gives birth as 8 November 1898, so the exact year remains a discrepancy between sources.

Maggie is identified as Maggie Player in the census records, and the Taylor connection is supported by Charlie Taylor's 1900 brother-in-law placement. The newly preserved Charlie/Charles F. Taylor trail makes that bridge much stronger: Charles F. Taylor appears as a child of John H. Taylor and Mary Taylor in Berrien County in 1880; appears as Charlie Taylor, brother-in-law, in the 1900 Whitman Player household; married Arrilla B. Roach in Berrien County on 9 April 1903; appears in 1910 Lower Fork, Lowndes County with wife Addie/Arrilla and father-in-law George W. Roach; and is followed in 1920 Cook County, 1930 Clinch County, and 1940 Du Pont, Clinch County. His World War I draft card gives his full name as Charlie Franklin Taylor, birth 26 December 1877, and nearest relative N. A. Taylor. Later index and memorial evidence now carries this same man to death: a Social Security Applications and Claims index entry names Charlie F. Taylor with spouse Narcissus A. Roach and child Sally Ruth Taylor; a Georgia death-index entry records Charlie Taylor, age 83, resident of Lowndes County, died 26 July 1961 in Baldwin County, certificate 17035; and Find a Grave memorial material places Charlie Franklin Taylor, born 26 December 1877 and died 26 July 1961, at Mud Creek Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery in Lakeland, Lanier County, Georgia. This supports identifying the 1943 death-notice brother C. F. Taylor of Dupont as the same Charlie/Charles F. Taylor who was Maggie's brother in the 1900 household.

Maggie's 1943 newspaper death notice adds stronger support for the Taylor family connection by naming one brother, C. F. Taylor of Dupont, Georgia, and one sister, Mrs. Ida Sweat of Valdosta. The notice says Mrs. W. W. Player, age 68, died at her home near Hahira on Saturday at noon, with funeral services at Old Friendship Church on Sunday afternoon. Because the notice appeared Tuesday, 9 February 1943, that Saturday corresponds to 6 February 1943. Find a Grave memorial material also places Maggie Taylor Player at Friendship Cemetery, Hahira, but it remains derivative cemetery evidence unless supported by a direct cemetery register or marker image.

Walter's end-of-life trail is supported by the Georgia death index and Social Security Death Index. The Georgia death index records Walter W. Player, White male, age 95, residence Lowndes County, death 23 January 1971 in Lowndes County, certificate number 003211. The SSDI summary lists Walter Player, SSN 255-12-9779, last residence Valdosta, Lowndes County, Georgia, death January 1971, and birth date 17 October 1875. A Find a Grave memorial places Walter Whitman Player at Friendship Cemetery, Hahira, and links Maggie Taylor Player and Nancy Wilson Player as spouses, but the Nancy Wilson spouse claim still needs a direct marriage, obituary, cemetery, or probate record before it should be treated as proved.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
• 1880: Walter W. Player, age about three months, appears in Shiloh, Sumter County, South Carolina, dwelling/family 423/423, in the D. A. Player household; the supplied summary gives roll 1247, page 258B, ED 123. James reads the wife/mother on the image as Rosanna or Rosanne; a compiled Player genealogy identifies D. A. Player as Daniel Andrew Player and his wife as Rosa A. Long.
  • 1900: Whitman Player appears in Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, sheet 8, ED 0009, family 147, with wife Maggie, infant son Walter, and brother-in-law Charlie Taylor. A separate 1900 individual summary for Walter Player gives birth as November 1899 and names father Whitman Player and mother Maggie Player.
  • 1910: Whit Player appears in Lower Fork, Lowndes County, Georgia, on Valdosta and Nashville Road, sheet 12B, ED 0117, as a farmer, with wife Maggie and children Frank, Andrew, Rosie M., and Marion.
  • 1918: Walter Whitman Player registered for the World War I draft in Lowndes County, Georgia. The card gives birth date 17 October 1878, residence Hahira, occupation farming, and nearest relative Mrs. Maggie Player.
  • 1920: Walter W. Plair/Player appears in Lower Fork, Lowndes County, Georgia, page 13A, ED 116, as a farmer, with wife Maggie and children Andrew, Rosa Mae, Marion, Lourine, Lessie D., and Hollis.
  • 1930: Whit N. Plare/Player appears in Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, page 1A, ED 0017, as a farmer, with Maggie Plare, Lessie D., Hollis, and Dorothy B. The index field says widowed, but Maggie is present in the household as wife, so the marital-status field should be treated as suspect.
  • 1940: W. W. Player appears in Valdosta, Lowndes County, Georgia, page 41A, ED 96-9, on Slomb Street, as a foreman and wage or salary worker in government work, with wife Maggie.
  • 1940: Lessie D. Player's World War II draft card names Walter Whit. Player of Valdosta as his father and gives Lessie's birth as 18 January 1915 in Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia.
  • Social Security Applications and Claims index: Maggie Taylor is listed with spouse Whitt Player and child Collis Player, supporting Collis as a child of this family.
  • Georgia death-records index: Maggie Taylor is listed with spouse W. W. Player and child Frank Player, supporting Frank as a child of this couple.
  • 1917: Lowndes County marriage record shows W. F. Player married Beatrice Griffin on 29 October 1917.
  • 1918: Walter Franklin Player's World War I draft card gives birth date 8 November 1899, residence RFD 1, Lowndes County, and names Walter W. Player as father and employer.
  • 1920: W. F. Player appears in Hahira, Lowndes County, Georgia, at Colson Daw Mill, age about 20, married to Beatrice Player, with infant son Walter E. Player.
  • 1922: Georgia death index records Frank Player's death in Lowndes County on 24 February 1922, certificate 4422-D.
  • Social Security Applications and Claims index: Walter W. Player is listed with spouse Maggie Taylor and child Dorothy Louise Williams, supporting Dorothy B. Player's married identity as Dorothy Louise Williams.
  • 1880-1961: Charlie/Charles F. Taylor is supported as Maggie Taylor Player's brother through a sequence of records: 1880 Berrien County child of John H. and Mary Taylor; 1900 brother-in-law in the Whitman Player household; 1903 Berrien County marriage to Arrilla B. Roach; 1910 Lower Fork household with father-in-law George W. Roach; 1918 World War I draft card for Charlie Franklin Taylor; 1920 Cook County household with mother Mary Taylor present; 1930 Clinch County sawmill laborer; 1940 Du Pont, Clinch County household; SSA child/spouse index naming Narcissus A. Roach and Sally Ruth Taylor; 1961 Georgia death index; and Find a Grave memorial at Mud Creek Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery. This sequence supports identifying him with the C. F. Taylor of Dupont named as Maggie's brother in 1943.
  • 1943: Mrs. W. W. Player's newspaper death notice says she died at home near Hahira on Saturday at noon, age 68, and names husband Walter W. Player, four sons, three daughters, one sister, and one brother.
  • 1950: Walter Ployer/Player appears in Valdosta, Lowndes County, Georgia, page 2, ED 92-23, on E. Savannah Ave., alone in the household. The summary lists him as married, but Maggie had died in 1943, so the marital-status field needs checking against the census image.
  • 1971: Georgia death index and SSDI records support Walter W. Player's death in Lowndes County in January 1971, with the Georgia death index giving 23 January 1971 and certificate number 003211.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
This household connects to the Taylor family through Maggie Player and Charlie Taylor's 1900 brother-in-law placement, and through the 1943 death notice naming C. F. Taylor of Dupont as Maggie's brother and Mrs. Ida Sweat of Valdosta as her sister. The supplied Charlie/Charles F. Taylor records now provide a coherent trail from the 1880 John H. and Mary Taylor household through the 1900 Whitman Player household, his 1903 Berrien County marriage to Arrilla B. Roach, later census households in Lowndes/Cook/Clinch counties, his World War I draft card as Charlie Franklin Taylor, SSA child/spouse evidence, and 1961 death/burial index evidence. It connects to the South Carolina Player line through the 1880 Shiloh, Sumter County record, where Walter appears in the D. A. Player household. Daniel Andrew Player and Rosa A. Long/Rosanna Player are the best current identifications for Walter's parents, with the compiled Player genealogy treated as supporting rather than primary evidence.

The 1943 death notice names the surviving children as Andrew Player, Marion Chester Player, Lessie Dee Player, Collis Player, Mrs. W. R. Blease of Barney, Mrs. J. T. Cain of Hahira, and Mrs. Clarence Williams of Valdosta. Lessie is directly linked to Walter by his own World War II draft card. Collis is separately linked to Maggie Taylor and Whitt Player by the Social Security Applications and Claims index. Frank is linked to Maggie Taylor and W. W. Player by a Georgia death-records index entry, and his own trail is now supported through a 1917 marriage record, 1918 draft card, 1920 household, 1922 death index, and derivative memorial summary. Dorothy B. Player's married identity is strengthened by a Social Security Applications and Claims index entry naming Walter W. Player, spouse Maggie Taylor, and child Dorothy Louise Williams. The remaining child identities are now supported by the death notice, but their individual life trails still need separate direct records.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• The full 1880 page now supports Walter's placement in the D. A. Player household. James reads the wife/mother as Rosanna or Rosanne, consistent with the compiled Player genealogy naming Rosa A. Long; a direct marriage record or independent source would further strengthen that identification.
  • A marriage record for Walter or Whitman Player and Maggie Taylor is still needed to prove the marriage directly.
  • Maggie's 1943 death is now supported by the newspaper notice, but a death certificate or cemetery register/marker image would strengthen the exact death and burial details.
  • Walter's 1971 death is supported by indexes, but the full death certificate and obituary are still needed.
  • The 1930 marital-status field conflicts with Maggie's presence in the household as wife and should be checked against the census image.
  • The 1950 marital-status field should be checked against the census image because Maggie had died in 1943.
  • Reported child lines need individual record trails, especially whether Collis and Hollis are the same person and how Mrs. W. R. Blease, Mrs. J. T. Cain, and Mrs. Clarence Williams correspond to the daughters in census records. Frank/Walter Franklin now has a much stronger trail, and Collis, Lessie, and Dorothy have additional child-link support, but underlying records and married-name bridges remain desirable.
  • Walter/Frank Player's exact birth year remains unresolved: the 1900 census summary and World War I draft card support November 1899, while the Find a Grave memorial uses 8 November 1898.
  • Reported second wife Nancy Wilson Player is currently supported only by memorial material and still needs direct evidence.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Stronger direct record trail, but not source-exhausted; marriage, full death certificates, direct cemetery evidence, Walter's obituary, independent parent-identification support, and several child-line bridges remain open.
  • Strengths: The supplied images now anchor the household in a full 1880 census page and census summaries from 1900 through 1950, correct the 1920 location/occupation error, support the 1930 Hahira identification, preserve Walter's WWI draft card, directly link Lessie D. Player to Walter as father, add a stronger Walter/Frank child-line trail and index support for Collis and Dorothy Louise Williams as children of Walter/Maggie, support Maggie's 1943 death notice, strengthen and carry forward the Charlie/Charles F. Taylor brother connection through death/burial index evidence, and document Walter's 1971 death through indexes.
  • Remaining cautions: Walter's parent identification still needs independent support beyond the Rosanna/Rosanne census reading and compiled Player genealogy; Walter's exact birth year, direct marriage proof for Walter and Maggie, direct burial proof, Walter/Frank's 1898/1899 birth-year discrepancy, complete child-line mapping, and the reported second wife remain unresolved.

docs.title: Household #148: Mitchell, George D.
docs.text:
Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, George Mitchell headed a 6-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
George Mitchell headed a 6-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 4 children.

George Mitchell's listed occupation was Farmer.

Reported birthplaces span Alabama and Georgia, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text: This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text:
Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation George Mitchell Head 42 Alabama Farmer Lacey Mitchell Wife 40 Georgia Not listed Mary Mitchell Daughter 15 Georgia Not listed Martha Mitchell Daughter 13 Georgia Not listed Rubin Mitchell Son 7 Georgia Not listed John T. Mitchell Son 5 Georgia Not listed

These ages come from the original 1900 schedule. It records Martha as born in August 1886 and age thirteen, Rubin as born in September 1892 and age seven, and John T. as born in June 1894 and age five. FamilySearch's ages fourteen, eight, and six are indexing errors. The family occupies lines 7 through 12, with George on line 7 and John T. on line 12.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: The family narrative below follows the later records located for Mary, Martha, Reuben, and John T. Mitchell. Unproved spouse or descendant links remain excluded.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
George D. Mitchell appears in the 1900 Barney census as a farmer, age 42, born in March 1858. His wife was recorded as Lacey Mitchell, age 40, born in April 1860. The children in the household were Mary, Martha, Rubin, and John T. Mitchell. The census says George and Lacey had been married about seventeen years, which fits the Wilcox County marriage record now found for George D. Michael or Micheal and Lucy Ashley on 14 December 1882. The surname in that record should be preserved as written. It is likely a clerk or spelling variant for Mitchell, but the entry should not silently normalize it.

The wife in this household appears across the record trail as Lacey, Lucy, L. A., and Lecy or Lecey Ashley Mitchell. Her birth date remains disputed. The original 1900 schedule gives April 1860 and age forty, while her photographed marker gives 27 April 1862. The 1910, 1920, and 1930 census ages generally fit an 1861 or 1862 birth better than 1860, but they are not precise enough to settle the question. The marker date is the stronger working date, with the census conflict preserved. Her Find a Grave memorial places her burial at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery near Pavo, Brooks County, and links her to the Ashley family. The Ashley parentage still needs direct-record proof, but the 1870 Wilcox County Ashley household summary and the 1882 marriage image give the wife identification much stronger support than the earlier draft had.

George's own endpoint is now well supported. His 1935 Georgia death certificate says he died on 20 April 1935 in the Barney militia district of Brooks County. It identifies him as a white married farmer, age 77 years, 1 month, and 6 days; gives his father as Mose Mitchell and his mother as Winnie Sewell; names Reuben L. Mitchell of Barney as informant; and gives burial at Bethel Cemetery on 26 April 1935. This certificate strengthens the earlier reconstruction that placed George in the family of Moses A. Mitchell and Winford or Winnie Mitchell.

The earlier census reconstruction still needs some caution. A supplied 1860 Randolph County, Alabama summary places S. S. Mitchell, age 2, in the household of Moses A. Mitchell and Winford Mitchell. A supplied 1870 Irwin County, Georgia summary places George Q. Mitchel, age 10, with inferred mother Winny Mitchel and siblings Moses W., James M., Andrew J., and Martha A. Mitchel. These records fit the family later named on George's death certificate, but the initials and full-page context still need direct review before this part of the lineage is treated as finished.

The 1880 Choctaw County, Alabama record for Geo. Mitchell should remain excluded. That man was Black, single, born about 1859 in Alabama, with Alabama-born parents, and appears to belong to a different family. The 1893 Brooks County marriage of George Mitchell and Miss Lucy Selph should also remain excluded unless later evidence proves otherwise. It conflicts with the 1882 Ashley marriage and the 1900 marriage-duration evidence.

Mary E. Mitchell, daughter of George and Lacey/Lucy, is supported in the 1900 household as age 15, born in January 1885. She married Perry D. Keine, Keen, or Keene in Brooks County in March 1907. The marriage image appears to show a license dated 18 March and a certificate dated 21 March 1907. In 1910 she appears as Mary Keen, widowed daughter in George and Lucy's household, with one child born and one living. The child Lomie Keen, age 2, appears in the same household and is best treated as Mary's child unless direct page review changes the relationship reading. Mary was back under the Mitchell surname in the 1920 and 1930 household summaries. Her death index and marker/Find a Grave material support Mary E. Mitchell, 12 January 1885 to 14 August 1943, buried at Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery, but her full death certificate or obituary would still be useful.

Martha L. Mitchell appears as a daughter in the 1900 household and later as Martha Morrow with Thomas W. Morrow. Census, death-index, and cemetery material create a coherent adult trail and support her death on 4 February 1975. A separate SSDI entry for a Martha Morrow who died on 15 February 1975 has not been connected to this family and should be treated as an unproved namesake lead. Martha's marriage image and full death record would still strengthen the entry.

Reuben Lazarus Mitchell has a strong later trail. He appears as Rubin or Reuben in the childhood census records, married Blanche or Ora Blanche Simpson in Brooks County in 1914, and can be followed in Brooks County farm households through 1950. His draft and later records support a birth date of 1 September 1893, while the original 1900 census records September 1892. The later date has the stronger personal-record trail, but the discrepancy remains. The Georgia death index, SSDI, Find a Grave, and obituary trail support his death on 15 November 1963 in Brooks County and burial at Oak Hill Cemetery in Quitman. His obituary says he was born in Wilcox County, came to Brooks County in 1900, farmed, belonged to Union Methodist Church, and was survived by his wife, several daughters, a son, sister Mrs. Martha Morrow of Barney, and brother J. T. Mitchell of Boston.

John T. Mitchell appears in the original 1900 schedule as John T., born in June 1894 and age five, and in 1910 as Tomie, age thirteen. Later records use several forms of his name: J. T., Tommy, Thomas J., and John Thomas Mitchell. His World War I draft card gives Tommy Mitchell, born 26 June 1896, with nearest relative Hattie Mitchell. The 1916 Brooks County marriage record is indexed and written as J. I. Mitchell and Hattie Gibbs, married 9 April 1916. Because the initials are not perfectly clear, the record should be cited exactly as J. I. Mitchell while explaining that the surrounding evidence points to John T. Mitchell. The 1920 through 1950 records place John and Hattie in the Brooks/Thomas County area, and the 1940 household includes father-in-law Mitch J. Gibbs, which supports Hattie's Gibbs identity. Social Security and death-index records support John T. Mitchell's death on 10 December 1968 in Thomas County, Georgia, certificate number 040711. Find a Grave places John Thomas Mitchell and Hattie Gibbs Mitchell at Boston City Cemetery. John's birth date remains unsettled. The World War I draft and Social Security records support 26 June 1896, while his marker gives 25 June 1896. The 1896 evidence is stronger than the childhood census entry, but the exact day and the two-year census conflict remain unresolved. The World War II draft card is for John Thomas Mitchell Jr., not for George's son; it is still useful because it names John Thomas Mitchell Sr. of Route 2, Barney, as the registrant's father.

George's birthplace also varies by census. The original 1880 schedule says Georgia, the original 1900 schedule says Alabama, the 1910 census says Georgia, and the 1920 and 1930 censuses say Alabama. Alabama has the stronger repeated trail, but the disagreement remains part of the record.

William A. Mitchell, age 30, appears as a nephew in George and Lucy's 1930 household. His exact relationship to George remains unresolved.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: HH#143 Andrew Jackson Mitchell was George's brother. The original 1880 Wilcox County census identifies Andrew as Winni Mitchell's son and George as Andrew's brother. The 1860 and 1870 households reinforce the earlier family chain, and George's 1935 death certificate independently names Mose Mitchell and Winnie Sewell as his parents.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Full-page images for the 1860 Randolph County, 1870 Irwin County, claimed 1880 Wilcox County, and 1910-1930 Brooks County census records.
  • Direct death certificate or image for Lecy/Lacey/Lucy Ashley Mitchell, including parentage if stated.
  • Direct Ashley-household image for Lucy/Lecy Ashley in 1870 and 1880.
  • A clearer courthouse citation or image details for the 1882 Wilcox County George D. Michael/Micheal and Lucy Ashley marriage.
  • Mary E. Mitchell's full death certificate or obituary, and direct proof for Perry D. Keine/Keen/Keene's later life and the Lomie/J. Lo? Keen or Mitchell identity.
  • Martha Mitchell Morrow's marriage image and full death record.
  • Reuben Lazarus Mitchell's full death certificate.
  • John Thomas Mitchell's full death certificate, Hattie Gibbs Mitchell's death record, and any available obituaries.
  • Direct source for George's middle name Desheild. Geneanet and tree material are useful clues but not proof by themselves.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Well-researched, but not source-exhausted.
  • Strengths: The 1900-1930 Barney census trail is coherent; George's 1935 death certificate directly names his parents; the 1882 Wilcox County marriage image now supports the Lucy/Lacey/Lecy Ashley identification; Mary, Martha, Reuben, and John T. now have substantial later-life trails.
  • Remaining cautions: Several records are still index-level or derivative. The Ashley parentage, George's middle name, early Mitchell census bridge, and some child-line details need direct-record review before the entry is final.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation William McCloud Head 27 Georgia Farmer Lula McCloud Wife 24 Georgia — Mattie McCloud Daughter 3 Georgia — Otha McCloud Son 1 Georgia — Ed Stewart Cousin 18 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Allia McLeaud Sister 25 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
William McCloud, also recorded as McLeod, McCleod, McLeaud, and Mcloud, headed household 149 in the 1900 Barney census. The 1900 enumeration gives his birth as July 1871 in Georgia and lists him as a Black farmer renting his farm. His wife was Lula Holsendolph, whose surname appears in later records with several spellings, including Holsondolph and Hosendolph. Their Brooks County marriage record names them as William McLeod and Lula Holsendolph, married on 26 December 1895.

The family can now be followed more securely than the earlier draft suggested. William appears as a child in 1880 in the John and Rose McLeod household in Morven, Brooks County, with siblings Sophie, Adaline, John W., and Mitchell. This is the best current evidence for William's parents and siblings, though the later lives of most siblings have not been traced. William appears as head of household in 1900 and 1910. In 1900, he was enumerated in Barney as William McCloud, age twenty-seven, married five years, a farmer, and a renter. The household included Lula, age twenty-four; children Mattie and Otha; Ed Stewart, listed as cousin; and Allia McLeaud, listed as sister. In 1910, William appears in Morven as William McCleod, age thirty-nine, a farmer on a general farm, with wife Lola and children Mattie L., Elther, Rufus D., Burie R., and Susie B. The spelling changes are substantial, but the ages, family structure, and Brooks County location tie the 1900 and 1910 households together.

Lula was the daughter of W. Holsondolph and Julia A. Holsondolph in the 1880 Groverville, Brooks County census, where she appears as Loula, age six. The same household included Lily, Joe, and Charlie. Later sources give her maiden name as Holsendolph or Hosendolph. A FindAGrave memorial names her parents as Joe Holsendolph and Julia Rhym Holsendolph, but the record trail has not yet resolved whether W. Holsondolph and Joe Holsendolph were the same person or whether the memorial preserves a different name tradition.

After William's death, Lula stayed in Brooks County. In 1920 she was enumerated as Lula McLeod, a widowed farmer renting a farm in Morven, with children Other, Rufus, Susy B., Blumer, John J., and Woodro Wilson. In 1930 she was a widowed farmer in Brooks County with Blinna, Jay, and Woodrow. In 1940 she was in Morven as Lula McCloud with her mother Julia Miller and sons Carl and Woodrow. In 1950 she was listed as the mother in the Quitman household of Susie B. McLeod. The Georgia death index records Lula McCloud's death on 27 December 1959 in Brooks County, certificate number 29373. Her cemetery memorial places her burial at New Macedonia Church Cemetery near Quitman.

William's exact death date has not been found. The safest statement is that he died after the 1910 census and before the 1920 census. A Georgia Death Records index entry for William Mcloud names spouse Lulla Hosendolph and child Mattie Jackson, but the available image trail appears tangled with Mattie's death certificate and does not yet provide a separate death certificate for William.

The child list remains the hardest part of this household because several names shift across records. Mattie L. McCloud / McLeod Jackson appears in the 1900 and 1910 McCloud/McLeod household. She married M. J. Jackson in Brooks County in January 1916. In 1920 she was enumerated as Mattie Jackson, wife of M. J. Jackson, with children Alma and Lawton. Her 1927 death certificate names her father as William McCloud and her mother as Lula Hosendolph, gives her death date as 28 May 1927 in Brooks County, and names tuberculosis of the lungs as the cause of death. Her burial was recorded at Morven on 29 May 1927. Her FindAGrave memorial uses the name Mattie L. McCloud Jackson and places her burial at New Macedonia Church Cemetery. A separate Mattie J. McCloud death-index entry from 1938 has been checked and is a different person; it should not be used for this household.

Otha / Elther / Other McCloud-McLeod appears as Otha in 1900, Elther or a similar spelling in 1910, and Other in 1920. The age sequence and placement in Lula's household make these likely the same son, but no later confirmed record has been tied to him. Rufus D. appears in 1910 and 1920. Burie R. appears in 1910, with no later confirmed match. Susie B. appears in 1910 and 1920, and Lula appears in Susie B. McLeod's Quitman household in 1950, supporting Susie's survival into adulthood. Blumer / Blinna appears in 1920 and 1930; the age and household placement suggest the same child, but a later direct record is still needed. John J. appears in Lula's 1920 household. Woodro Wilson / Woodrow appears in 1920, 1930, and 1940, with age variation but consistent placement in Lula's household. Carl McCloud / McLoud was born 30 June 1917 in Brooks County according to his World War II draft card; in 1940 he was in Lula's Morven household, and the draft card names Lula McLoud of Morven as the person who would always know his address.

Ed Stewart was listed in 1900 as William McCloud's cousin, age eighteen. No later matching record has been confidently identified. Allia McLeaud was listed in 1900 as William's sister, age twenty-five. She may be the Adaline McLeod who appeared as a five-year-old daughter in John and Rose McLeod's 1880 household, but that identification is not proven. For now, both should be treated as one-record relationship clues rather than fully developed connection claims.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text: The 1900 household gives two relationship clues: Ed Stewart as cousin and Allia McLeaud as sister. Both are useful, but neither has enough follow-up evidence to build a broader connection claim. Mattie McCloud's marriage to M. J. / Mayon James Jackson creates a later Jackson connection, documented by the 1916 marriage record, 1920 census, and Mattie's death certificate.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• William's exact death date and burial place remain unknown. The current evidence places his death after 1910 and before 1920.
  • A Georgia Death Records index entry for William Mcloud names spouse Lulla Hosendolph and child Mattie Jackson, but the available image trail appears tangled with Mattie's death certificate and does not provide a separate death certificate for William.
  • Lula's 1959 death is supported by the Georgia death index and cemetery memorial. Her full death certificate, certificate number 29373, would be better.
  • The W. Holsondolph / Joe Holsendolph discrepancy for Lula's father is unresolved.
  • Julia A. Holsondolph appears later as Julia Miller in Lula's 1940 household, but the intervening marriage or name-change record has not been found.
  • Several child identities still need later direct records, especially Burie R., Blumer/Blinna, John J., and Woodrow.
  • Ed Stewart and Allia McLeaud should remain notes, not full connection claims, unless later records identify them.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
Status: Partially documented; needs cleanup and targeted follow-up.

Strengths: The core couple is well supported by the 1895 marriage record, the 1900 and 1910 census records, and Mattie Jackson's 1927 death certificate. Lula's later life is now documented through the 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950 censuses, the Georgia death index, and cemetery evidence.

Remaining cautions: William's death is still not directly proven. The children's names vary enough that several should be treated as probable rather than fully resolved identities. The earlier claim that Lula disappeared after 1910 is obsolete and should not be repeated.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation George Harris Head 26 Georgia Farmer Cora Harris Wife 24 Georgia — Ruby L Harris Daughter 3/12 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
George L. Harris appears in the 1900 Barney enumeration as a young farmer with his wife Cora and infant daughter Ruby L. The household reported that George and Cora had been married two years, matching the surviving Sumter County marriage record for G. L. Harris and Cora Tomlison/Tomlinson dated 20 January 1898.

The later census trail appears to follow the same family from Barney into Quitman, Brooks County. George is enumerated as George L. Harris in 1910, 1920, 1930, 1940, and 1950, generally as a farmer or retired/unable-to-work farmer. The records show two daughters in the household line: Ruby/Rubie L. Harris and Mabel/Maybell I. Harris, later wife of Russell W. Emerson/Emmerson. In 1930 and 1940, Mabel, Russell, and their son Henry Harris Emerson were living with or near George and Cora. Ruby/Rubie moved to Winter Garden, Orange County, Florida, where the 1940 and 1950 censuses list her as an unmarried public-school educator/principal. A Florida county marriage record and the Florida marriage index place her marriage to William Fred Roper in Citrus County, Florida, on 30 December 1951. The Orlando Sentinel published the marriage notice two days later, identifying Rubie Harris as the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George Lee Harris of Quitman. Later records identify her as Rubie H. Roper of Winter Garden. She died in Orange County, Florida, on 23 January 1998 and was buried at Woodlawn Memorial Park in Gotha, Orange County.

George's earlier placement is better supported than before but still not fully resolved. The Valdosta Daily Times obituary says George Lee Harris was born in Lowndes County, Georgia, and was a son of the late Mr. and Mrs. John Harris. An 1880 Irwin County household lists George L. Harris, age eight, son of John and Liza Harris; this likely fits the obituary's father-name evidence and approximate age, but it should still be treated cautiously until a death certificate or other direct linking record confirms the mother and reconciles the Lowndes/Irwin/Brooks locality trail. Cora's 1880 Sumter County placement with W. M. and Sarah A. Tomlinson is plausible and supported by the marriage surname, but direct parentage should remain cautious until tied by a record beyond name, age, and locality.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Wife: Cora Tomlinson/Tomlison Harris.
  • Children documented in the census and obituary trail: Ruby/Rubie L. Harris Roper and Mabel/Maybell I. Harris Emerson/Emmerson.
  • Ruby/Rubie L. Harris married William Fred Roper in Citrus County, Florida, on 30 December 1951; the 1 January 1952 Orlando Sentinel notice adds the family context and Winter Garden connection.
  • Grandchild documented in the household and obituary trail: Henry Harris Emerson/Emmerson, later Lt. Henry H. Emerson.
  • Father of George: John Harris, supported by the Valdosta Daily Times obituary; possible mother: Liza Harris, based on the 1880 Irwin County census match.
  • Possible parents of Cora: W. M. Tomlinson and Sarah A. Tomlinson of Sumter County, Georgia, based on the 1880 census match and Cora's marriage surname.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• George's 25 July 1952 death in Brooks County is supported by the Georgia Death Index and by two newspaper obituaries. A full death certificate is still needed for parent fields, birthplace detail, and informant evidence.
  • The Valdosta Daily Times obituary gives the fuller survivor list: widow Cora Tomlinson Harris; daughters Mrs. Russell W. Emerson of Quitman and Mrs. W. Fred Roper of Winter Garden, Florida; and grandson Lt. Henry H. Emerson. It also says George was born in Lowndes County, was son of the late Mr. and Mrs. John Harris, moved to Brooks County as a child, was a prominent farmer, and was buried in Oak Hill after funeral services at Quitman Baptist Church.
  • Mrs. W. Fred Roper is now identified as Ruby/Rubie L. Harris by the Florida marriage records, the 1952 Orlando Sentinel marriage notice, and Ruby/Rubie's Winter Garden census, death, obituary, burial, and Social Security trail.
  • Rubie's 1998 Orlando Sentinel obituary says she was born in Barney, Georgia, moved to Central Florida in 1925, taught for Orange County schools, lived on Lakeview Avenue in Winter Garden, and was survived by Emerson nephews and a Foster niece. This fits the George Harris household and the Mabel Harris Emerson branch.
  • Cora's death is supported by the Georgia Death Index and FindAGrave marker image, but her full death certificate is still needed for parent fields and informant evidence.
  • The Social Security Applications and Claims Index hit for George Walton Harris is treated as a non-match and should not be used for this household.
  • The 1940 census race entry appears to have been recorded as Black/Negro with later corrections to White. All other listed records in this trail identify the family as White, so the 1940 entry should be noted as a discrepancy rather than used to reclassify the household.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Strong census, marriage, death-index, obituary, cemetery-marker, and Ruby/Rubie Roper trail; not source-exhausted.
  • Strengths: 1900 Barney household, 1898 marriage record, 1910-1950 census continuity, Georgia Death Indexes, FindAGrave marker images, the Valdosta/Orlando obituaries, and Ruby/Rubie's Florida marriage, census, death, obituary, burial, public-record, and Social Security trail give a coherent family line for George, Cora, Ruby/Rubie, Mabel, Russell Emerson, and Henry Harris Emerson.
  • Remaining cautions: George's mother, Cora's parentage, and the full death certificates for George and Cora need direct-record confirmation.

docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Senith Barnes Strickland is identified as Stephen's first wife in the current trail through FindAGrave, the timing of her death before the 1900 census, and William Strickland's 1944 death certificate, which names his mother as Senith Barnes and father as Stephen Strickland.
  • Della Burnes/Burns Strickland is documented before marriage in the James and Sarah Burns/Barnes household in the 1880 and 1900 censuses, then directly documented by the 1902 Brooks County marriage license/return and the 1910 census; FindAGrave and marker images support the identification as Florence Idella "Della" Burns Strickland, died 17 August 1915, buried at Hopewell Cemetery.
  • Sallie/May Strickland is documented in the 1920 census and Stephen's 1924 death record, but whether Sallie and May are the same person remains unresolved.
  • The 1860 and 1870 censuses place Stephen/Elias with Stephen S./Stephen Smith Strickland and Harriet M. Strickland. Stephen's death certificate supports the father as Steve Strickland, but the mother field reads 'don't know,' so Harriet remains supported by the childhood census trail rather than the death certificate. FindAGrave and derivative online trees identify Harriet as Harriet Mariah McClelland/McClellan Strickland, wife of Stephen Smith Strickland, and give Andrew McClelland and Mary Ann Daniel as her parents; that McClelland parentage should be treated as derivative unless a direct record is found. Stephen Smith Strickland's later marriage to Mary Scarborough is directly documented by a Colquitt County marriage license issued 29 August 1876 and marriage return dated 30 August 1876; this helps explain the later Mary Strickland household without making Mary part of Stephen Elias's maternal line. A Civil War pension index card for Stephen S. Strickland gives service in the 1st Georgia Infantry, application filed 6 September 1890 from Georgia, invalid application no. 905956; this supports the father's later identity trail but is not military evidence for Stephen Elias Strickland.
  • The possible network links to Gornto, Hiers, and Alderman families should remain tentative unless supported by direct kinship records.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• Senith Barnes Strickland's maiden name, death date, and burial are presently dependent on FindAGrave; a cemetery record, death notice, probate record, or family Bible record would strengthen this part of the entry.
  • Stephen's first marriage to Senith Barnes is still missing a direct marriage record, but William Strickland's 1944 death certificate directly names Stephen Strickland as father and Senith Barnes as mother. A derivative Ancestry compilation also names Stephen Elias Strickland and Seneth Barnes with a marriage year of 1875, but it gives Texas as the marriage state and spouse birthplace, so it should be treated as a lead rather than proof until the underlying source is identified.
  • The transition from Della Burnes to Sallie/May Strickland is not resolved. Della's death, divorce, or later whereabouts need a direct record.
  • Sallie Strickland of the 1920 census and May Strickland named on Stephen's death record may be the same woman, but this needs a marriage record, death record, obituary, or other direct link.
  • Several children and married surnames are based on FindAGrave connections. Ada's marriage to James L. Brown and Bessie's marriage to Claude Alcorn are now directly supported. Lee/Henry Lee has a high-confidence adult trail with a strong Alcorn collateral clue, and Charles/Charley now has a documented Florida trail through the 1935 Florida census, death indexes, obituary index, and cemetery evidence. Ada's later Chapman marriage, Bessie's child-line details, Lee/Henry Lee's direct parent-link proof, and Charles's parent-link proof beyond the 1900 census and derivative memorial links still need direct image review. The remaining child lines should be checked against marriage records, death certificates, obituaries, and later census records.
  • The reviewed tax page for Elias N. Strickland does not show real-estate acreage or value and should not be used as evidence of land ownership.
  • An 1880 agricultural non-population schedule for District 335, Wayne County, Georgia, lists an Elias Strickland with 8 acres of tillable land and 520 acres of woodland. This may be relevant, but it should remain tentative until tied to the same Stephen Elias Strickland by the 1880 population census, deed records, or other connecting evidence.
  • Stephen's burial at Pleasant Grove Cemetery is now supported by his 1924 death certificate. FindAGrave marker evidence also supports the burial and links him to parents Stephen Smith Strickland and Harriet Mariah McClelland Strickland, but those online family links are derivative.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Strong census, marriage, death-record, cemetery, and collateral child-line trail; not source-exhausted.
  • Strengths: The 1860, 1870, 1900, 1910, and 1920 censuses, the 1902 Brooks County marriage record, and the 1924 Georgia death record give a coherent adult identity and migration path for Stephen Elias Strickland.
  • Remaining cautions: First-marriage proof, Senith's direct death/burial evidence, Della's fate, the Sallie/May identity question, Stephen's maternal identification, and several child-to-adult links still need direct-record support. William, Ada, and Bessie now have direct marriage or parent-link evidence. Edna has a strong census/death/burial trail but still needs the underlying obituary image for the sibling list. Lee/Henry Lee and Charles/Charley now have high-confidence adult trails, but each still needs a direct parent-link record such as a death certificate, obituary text, SS-5, or probate item.

docs.text:

docs.text:
Charley Crenshaw headed a 9-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 7 extended-family members.

Charley Crenshaw's listed occupation was Farmer.

Reported birthplaces span Georgia and North Carolina, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Charley Crenshaw Head 55 North Carolina Farmer Violett Crenshaw Wife 50 Georgia — Mary Mathews Mother-in-law 76 Georgia — Guss Smith Son-in-law 23 Georgia Day Laborer Farm Arrilla Smith Stepdaughter (Step Daughter) 19 Georgia — Silvester Smith Step Granchild 3 Georgia — Gussie Smith Step-granddaughter (Step Granddaughter) 1 Georgia — Mary Smith Step-granddaughter (Step Granddaughter) 0 Georgia — Charley Brown Step-grandson (Step Grandson) 17 Georgia Day Laborer Farm

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No children are listed in this household in the 1900 census table.

docs.title: Evidence summary
docs.text:
The 1900 Barney census places Charley Crenshaw in Brooks County as a Black farmer born in North Carolina about May 1845. His wife Violett was born in Georgia about 1850, and the household was a blended one: Violett's mother Mary Mathews was present, along with Smith-surnamed stepchildren or step-grandchildren and a Brown step-grandson.

The best earlier candidate for Charley is the 1880 Wake Forest, Wake County, North Carolina household of Charles Crenshaw, a Black laborer of similar age, with wife Rachael and children Burrell, Maggie, Tabbie, and Lizzie. The name, race, age, and North Carolina birthplace make this a strong candidate, but no direct record has yet been found carrying him from Wake County, North Carolina, to Brooks County, Georgia. This should remain a leading identification, not a proven merge.

Violett's own earlier identity is also partly unresolved. Mary Mathews being listed as Charley's mother-in-law makes Mathews the strongest clue for Violett's birth family, but no independent marriage, death, or parentage record has been found proving Violett's maiden name.

The Smith cluster is clearer. Arrilla Smith is listed as Charley's stepdaughter, and the indexed 1900 census detail names Violett Crenshaw as Arrilla's mother. Guss Smith is in the household as Charley's son-in-law and is married for the same length of time as Arrilla. The best reading is that Guss and Arrilla were husband and wife, married about 1897, and that Silvester, Gussie, and Mary Smith were their children. This avoids the older overbroad assumption that every Smith-surnamed person in the household was Violett's own child.

Charley Brown remains unresolved. The 1900 indexed census detail gives him as a Black Georgia-born step-grandson in HH#152, born about October 1882, single, and working as a farm day laborer. Possible forward records include a Black Georgia-born Charley Brown in 1910 Juniper Creek, Calhoun County, Florida, age 27, single, head of household, working as a turpentine-farm chipper; a separate previously tested 1910 Norman Park candidate; a 1918 Brooks County World War I draft card naming Luginia Brown of Pavo as nearest relative; and a 1920 Morven, Brooks County, Georgia, Chales/Chaley/Charley Brown, age 37, single, boarder, working as a naval-stores laborer. These records fit the broad name, age, race, and regional pattern, but they cannot yet be proven to be the same individual and they do not prove his parentage or explain the exact step-grandson relationship.

A separate Jim/James Brown and Lugenia Brown White cluster was tested. It documents a local Brooks County Brown family, but it does not currently explain HH#152 Charley Brown's parentage. Candidate adult records for Silvester Smith and Gussie Smith were also tested; neither should be merged without parent-linked proof.

Additional Sylvester Smith documents supplied later show why the adult Silvester question remains open. One World War I draft card belongs to a married Black Sylvester Smith born in 1896 at Fort Gaines, Georgia, living in Clay County and employed by Alex Smith; that is geographically possible but not parent-linked to Guss and Arrilla. A Dade County / Coconut Grove trail belongs to a Black Sylvester Smith born about 1 August 1897 in Dublin or Laurens County, Georgia, with Lear/Lear Smith as contact; that birthplace points away from Brooks County unless another record supplies a family bridge. A 1945 Florida state census and 1950 Miami census show a Black Sylvester Smith born in Georgia about 1898, but a 1942 Dade County death index for a Black Sylvester Smith conflicts with those later census records and may represent a different man. A separate 1942 World War II draft card for a Sylvester Smith born in 1921 at Glensville/Glenville, Georgia, is too young to be the 1900 HH#152 step-grandchild.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• Direct proof linking the 1880 Wake County, North Carolina Charles Crenshaw to the 1900 Brooks County, Georgia Charley Crenshaw.
  • Violett's maiden name and parentage; Mary Mathews is a strong clue, not direct proof.
  • Any prior Smith marriage for Violett, if one existed. The Smith surname may enter the household through Arrilla's husband Guss rather than through Violett.
  • Marriage or parent-linked records for Guss Smith and Arrilla Smith.
  • Parent-linked adult records for Silvester Smith, Gussie Smith, and Mary Smith.
  • Reconciliation of the competing Sylvester Smith candidate records before any adult trail is attached to the HH#152 child.
  • Charley Brown's parents and exact relationship to the Crenshaw/Mathews/Smith household.
  • Separation of the competing Charley/Chales Brown candidate records before treating them as one adult trail.
  • The relationship, if any, between the Luginia/Lugenia Brown clue and HH#152 Charley Brown.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Well-Researched; not source-exhausted.
  • Strengths: The 1900 household structure is now clearer; the Arrilla/Guss/Silvester/Gussie/Mary Smith interpretation is source-bounded; the Wake County Charles Crenshaw candidate has been identified and held at the right confidence level; Charley Brown and Brown-cluster leads have been tested without overmerging.
  • Remaining cautions: The key identity bridge, Violett's parentage, the possible Smith marriage, and Charley Brown's parentage all remain unproved. The household should not be marked complete or source-exhausted without courthouse, image-level, or parent-linked records.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Daniel Alderman in HH#153 is best identified through a steady record chain rather than through one single naming record. He appears with Margaret/Margret/Marget J. Alderman in the 1900 Barney census, the 1910 Robinson, Colquitt County census, and the 1920 Robinson, Colquitt County census. The 1880 Colquitt County marriage record for Daniel Alderman and Margaret J. Register is the main spouse anchor. The married-years entries in 1900 and 1910 fit that marriage date.

Daniel's earlier placement is supported by the 1860 Colquitt County household of John A. Alderman and Emily S. Alderman, where Daniel H. Alderman appears as a young child. It is also supported by the 1870 Colquitt County household of John Alderman and Susannah Alderman, where Daniel appears with an overlapping sibling group. The 1860 census is the strongest direct household evidence now found for Daniel's placement with John A. and Emily S. Alderman.

Aldermans in America pp. 406-407 is useful, but it is secondary evidence. Page 406 gives John A. Alderman's dates as 25 June 1827 to April 1907 and identifies his wife as Emily Norman, born 24 March 1826, daughter of James M. Norman. Page 407 says that after Emily's death, John A. Alderman married his second cousin, Mrs. Susan Jane (Alderman) Stevenson, widow and daughter of James Alderman. It also says Susan had no children by her first husband. This supports reading Emily Norman as the mother-context for the older children and Susan Jane Alderman Stevenson as the later wife and stepmother in the 1870 household.

The same book must not be used as direct proof of Daniel's full identity. Page 406 lists child #8 as David Harrison, born 12 August 1860, and child #9 as Zilpha, born 30 June 1862. The census chain names Daniel H./Daniel, and the 1870 household also includes a separate David Alderman. The discrepancy may reflect an omission, a conflation, or an error in the book's child list. Until a direct record explains it, the entry should preserve both facts: the census record supports Daniel in the John A. Alderman household, while the book supports the Emily Norman/Susan Jane Alderman Stevenson marriage sequence.

Margaret's Register connection is stronger than several of the remaining Alderman parentage details. She appears in 1870 with Elvy Register and Louisa Register, in 1880 as Margaret Register, sister-in-law in the William and Louisa Norman household, and in 1930 as widowed Margret Alderman, sister-in-law in the William J. and Luizer/Louisa Normens household. That pattern supports Margaret J. Register Alderman as Louisa Register Norman's sister.

The 1930 widowed-Margaret record narrows Daniel's death window. Daniel was alive with Margaret in the 1920 Colquitt County census. Margaret was widowed in Brooks County in 1930. No direct death, burial, or probate record for Daniel has been found in the current research trail.

Susan Alderman, age 9 in the 1900 household, remains documented only at that anchor point. No reliable adult marriage, death, burial, or later census record has been identified for her. She may have married under an unknown surname, died young, or been missed through indexing or enumeration problems. The current entry should not assign her an adult identity without direct evidence.

A separate Daniel J. Alderman in the 1880 Nankin, Brooks County census belongs to a different Daniel Jefferson Alderman line tied to Amanda/Amanda O'Neal and Leah Studstill. That man is also present in the 1900 Quitman census as a widowed boarder with children Jacob W. and Horace, while HH#153 Daniel is simultaneously in Barney with wife Margarett and daughter Susan. The Amanda/Daniel Jefferson trail should not be merged into HH#153.

Daniel's middle initial remains unresolved. The 1860 census gives Daniel H. Alderman. The 1920 census/index and an 1898/1899 Brooks County tax-digest index point to a possible W initial. Neither source gives a full middle name. The safest form remains Daniel Alderman, with H and W treated as documented variants.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#57 Norman connection: Margaret J. Register's sister relationship to Louisa Register Norman connects this household to the Norman/Register network already documented in the Barney project.
  • Alderman network: Daniel belongs near the larger Alderman cluster represented in HH#155, HH#176, HH#178, and HH#180. The John A. Alderman household evidence remains the direct-record anchor. Aldermans in America pp. 406-407 provides secondary support for the John A. Alderman / Emily Norman / Susan Jane Alderman Stevenson family structure, with the Daniel/David Harrison child-list discrepancy preserved.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• Daniel's exact death date, death place, and burial location.
  • Margaret's exact death date, death place, and burial location after the 1930 census.
  • Daniel's full middle name.
  • Direct-record confirmation of Emily Norman/Emily S. Alderman as Daniel's mother.
  • An explanation for the Aldermans in America p.406 child-list discrepancy, where child #8 is named David Harrison rather than Daniel.
  • Whether the 1898/1899 Dan W. Alderman tax-digest entry can be tied directly to HH#153 Daniel through district, land, deed, or neighboring-property evidence.
  • A direct adult record for Susan Alderman, the daughter in the 1900 household. None has been identified in the present research trail.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Well-researched, with a completed online source-image pass for the main census and marriage chain. Not marked source-exhausted because death, burial, probate, Susan Alderman's adult identity, and some courthouse-level questions remain unresolved.
  • Strengths: Strong 1900 household anchor; direct 1880 marriage record to Margaret J. Register; consistent 1900-1920 Daniel/Margaret census trail; strong 1930 widow anchor for Margaret; Daniel Jefferson Alderman conflation separated; secondary Alderman-family context now added with clear limits.
  • Remaining cautions: Daniel's death/burial/probate trail is missing; Margaret's final record after 1930 is missing; Daniel's full middle name remains unresolved; Susan Alderman's adult identity is not found; Aldermans in America clarifies the likely Emily/Susan wife sequence but remains derivative and preserves a Daniel/David Harrison child-list discrepancy; derivative FamilySearch tree structure should be used only as a source-control checklist, not as proof by itself.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
The HH#154 head is best treated as Joe Pedleton in the 1900 Barney census, later appearing as Joe Pendleton, J. C. Pendelton, and Joseph Cury Pendleton. The identification rests on the repeated pairing with wife Ida, the same Georgia birthplace pattern, a consistent Black household context, and a migration trail from Brooks County, Georgia, into Florida.

The strongest spouse anchor is the original Brooks County marriage-license image for Joe Pendleton and Ida Donaldson. The license was issued 16 August 1897, and the marriage certificate says Joe Pendleton and Ida Donaldson were joined in matrimony on 20 August 1897 by W. M. Crittenden. This directly confirms the spelling "Joe Pendleton" in the marriage record and removes the earlier uncertainty created by the "Goe Pendleton" index variant. The 1900 census reports Joe and Ida as married for about three years, which fits this record. Ida's full later name appears in the Florida Death Index as Ida Violet Pendleton, but the current trail does not include a death certificate naming her parents.

The family remained in Brooks County through at least 1910. In 1910 Joe Pendleton was enumerated at Tallokas as a turpentine worker with wife Ida and children Georgie M., John, Annie Lee, and Ado. The 1910 Ancestry detail page also gives Georgie M. as "Georgine M Pendleton", age 9, born about 1901 in Georgia. This is the only later online documentation currently found that may relate to Morrie, the infant daughter in the 1900 household, but the name and age do not line up cleanly enough to merge them without caution. By 1920, Joe and Ida were in Parrish, Manatee County, Florida, with Lela, John, Ada, Lois, and boarder Hazel. John and Ada/Ado appear to bridge the 1910 and 1920 households, but the remaining children need separate adult-record work before their later lives can be stated confidently.

Joe and Ida were in Hillsborough County, Florida, by 1940. The 1940 census also reports their 1935 residence as Seffner, Hillsborough County. In 1950 they were in Alachua County, Florida, where Joe was enumerated as J. C. Pendelton and marked unable to work. Florida death-index evidence places Ida Violet Pendleton's death in Alachua County in May 1956 and Joseph Cury Pendleton's death in Alachua County in February 1960. James supplied the Joseph Cury Pendleton and Ida Violet Pendleton death-index images on 2 June 2026; no full Florida death certificate for either person is available online in the current trail.

Joe's exact birth year remains approximate. The 1900 census gives the most specific date, May 1875, while later censuses imply about 1872, 1871, 1874, and 1880. His parents are reported only as Georgia-born in the census trail; no parent names have been identified in the records now used.

Frank Pedleton's relationship is important but unresolved. The 1900 census calls him Joe's stepson, which means he was likely Ida's child before her marriage to Joe. That does not by itself prove Ida had a prior legal marriage, nor does it identify Frank's father. No additional online record for Frank has been found in the current trail. Morrie Pedleton appears only in the 1900 household under that name; Georgie M./Georgine M. Pendleton in 1910 is the only later online candidate presently noted, but the identification remains unresolved.

docs.text:
• Joseph Cury Pendleton's full Florida death certificate, likely requiring an offline/order request; no certificate image is available online in the current trail.
  • Ida Violet Pendleton's Florida death certificate, especially for parents, maiden name confirmation, informant, burial place, and residence.
  • Burial records, cemetery registers, funeral-home records, or obituaries for Joseph and Ida in Alachua County.
  • Earlier records for Joe/Joseph Pendleton before 1900, including a possible 1880 childhood household and parentage.
  • Earlier records for Ida Donaldson before 1897, including a possible 1880/1885/1890s Brooks County Donaldson household.
  • Clarification of Frank Pedleton's parentage and whether Ida had a prior legal marriage or another earlier relationship.
  • Later records for Frank; evidence clarifying whether 1900 Morrie Pedleton and 1910 Georgie M./Georgine M. Pendleton are the same child; and later records for Annie Lee, Ado/Ada, Lela, John, Lois, and Hazel.
  • Direct evidence for any Donaldson or Pendleton connection to other Barney households.

docs.text:
• Status: Well-researched online census trail with original marriage-license evidence. Not source-exhausted because the current entry still needs death certificates, burial records, parentage evidence, and adult records for several children.
  • Strengths: Strong 1900 household anchor; original Brooks County marriage-license image directly confirms Joe Pendleton and Ida Donaldson, with license dated 16 August 1897 and marriage performed 20 August 1897; coherent 1900-1950 Joe/Ida census trail; Florida death indexes supply later names and death months/places.
  • Remaining cautions: Death indexes are not substitutes for death certificates; parent names are unknown; burial places are unknown; Frank's father and Ida's pre-1897 status remain unresolved; no additional online record has been found for Frank; Morrie in 1900 may relate to Georgie M./Georgine M. in 1910, but this is not proven; several children have only one census appearance in the present trail.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text:
No children are listed in this household in the 1900 census table.

The Barney household is best read as the late-life household of the man recorded elsewhere as James S. G. Raymond, James S. Raymond, J. S. Raymond, Gillam Raymond, Gilham Raymond, Gilliam Raymond, Gillon Raymond, Gillam Roymond, and G. Raymond. The spellings vary enough that no single record should carry the identification by itself. Taken together, the 1850 marriage, 1852 Sumter tax digest, 1860 Sumter census, 1864 Colquitt militia census, 1867 Colquitt Reconstruction oath, 1869 Colquitt tax digest, 1870 Colquitt census, 1878-1887 Brooks/Quitman tax digests, 1880 Brooks census, and 1900 Barney census give a workable record chain for the same man and wife.

James S. G. Raymond married Mary Ann E. Philips in Sumter County, Georgia, on 10 July 1850. Ancestry image access has been confirmed for that county marriage record. The 1900 census reports that Gallnor and Mary had been married for 51 years, which fits an 1850 marriage closely enough to support the identification. A new tax-digest image also places James S. Raymond in Sumter County, District 16, in 1852. This gives the couple a second Sumter County anchor shortly after the marriage.

The 1860 Sumter County census has now been located in both Ancestry and FamilySearch. Ancestry indexes the household as J. S. Raymond, age 38, born South Carolina, farmer, with Mary A. Raymond, Matilda, A. C., and T. C. Raymond. The same record gives District 16, Sumter County, post office Americus, dwelling 646, family 653, page 447. A screenshot of the Ancestry image has been saved. This record strengthens the Sumter phase of the family and supports Matilda, A. C., and T. C. as children in the household, though T. C. remains a separate identity question because later records do not yet tie that child clearly to William Raymond.

By 1864 James S. G. Raymon was in Colquitt County in the Georgia militia census, age 41, born South Carolina. In 1867 Gillam Roymond appeared in the Colquitt County Reconstruction oath book. A newly captured 1869 Colquitt County tax digest image lists Gillam Raymond in district 1151. The 1870 Colquitt County census then enumerates Gillon Raymond, farmer, with Mary and children or likely children Louisa, Ernest, Mary, William, plus John and Matilda Mathis in the household. The 1864, 1867, 1869, and 1870 records make the Colquitt County phase much stronger than it was in the earlier entry.

By 1878-1882, tax-digest entries for Gilham Raymond place him in the Quitman/Brooks area. The 1880 census then places G. Raymond in Quitman, Brooks County, on Screen Street, working as a grocery clerk with wife M. A. and children Theodosia, Mary J., William, and Charles T. Raymond. Additional 1883-1887 Brooks/Quitman tax digest images for Gilliam/Gillam Raymond continue the Brooks County trail before the 1900 Barney enumeration. These tax records are not parentage records, but they are useful locality anchors across a period where census records alone leave gaps.

The birthplace evidence is not fully consistent. The 1860, 1864, 1880, and 1900 records point to South Carolina for Gallnor/James/Gilliam Raymond. The 1870 census gives Georgia. The 1880 census says his father was born in New York and his mother in South Carolina, while the 1900 census gives South Carolina for both parents. The safer treatment is to keep South Carolina as the best-supported birthplace while leaving his parents unidentified.

The child list is useful but still uneven. Matilda Raymond is supported by the 1860 J. S. Raymond household and by the 1870 Colquitt County household where John and Matilda Mathis are living with the Raymond family shortly after marriage. Theodosia, also found as Dockie, is supported by the 1880 Raymond household, the Brooks County marriage record for Dockie Raymond and John C. Smith, and the 1927 Georgia death record for Theadosha Smith, which names her father as Gilham Raymons and spouse as Johnnie C. Smith. Mary J., William, and Charles T. are census-supported children in 1880. Louisa and Ernest appear in 1870 but have not been traced forward. A. C. and T. C. appear in the 1860 household; their later lives are unresolved.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• Mathis connection: Matilda Raymond married John Sidney Mathis in Colquitt County in June 1870. John and Matilda were in the 1870 Raymond household shortly after marriage and later lived in Worth County. The 1900 Worth County census reports Matilda as mother of nine children, all living. A direct parent-naming record for Matilda has not been found in this pass.
  • Smith connection: Theodosia or Dockie Raymond married John C. Smith in Brooks County on 10 December 1885. Her 1927 Georgia death record, under Theadosha Smith, names her father as Gilham Raymons and spouse as Johnnie C. Smith. This is the strongest daughter-link outside the Barney household.
  • No direct connection to another Barney household has been proven from the current entry. The Mathis and Smith lines are collateral family trails rather than proved Barney-household-to-Barney-household connections.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
• Locate a full death certificate, burial record, probate file, or local death notice for Gallnor/Gilham/James/Gilliam Raymond. The current trail does not yet prove his exact death date or burial place.
  • Locate Mary Ann E. Philips Raymond after the 1900 Barney census, including death, burial, probate, or widow evidence.
  • Resolve the Georgia versus South Carolina birthplace conflict, and the father-birthplace conflict, with direct parentage, probate, land, or earlier census evidence.
  • Trace Louisa Raymond, Ernest Raymond, Mary J. Raymond, William Raymond, Charles T. Raymond, A. C. Raymond, and T. C. Raymond only where records can be tied back to this family.
  • Determine whether T. C. Raymond in 1860 and William Raymond in 1870/1880 are separate children or an enumerator/indexing problem. Current evidence does not settle it.
  • Find a direct parent-naming record for Matilda Raymond Mathis if one survives. The current case rests mainly on census placement and the nearby marriage/census trail.

docs.text:

  • Strengths: The household is now anchored by image-level evidence across the main phases of the family: Sumter County in 1850-1860, Colquitt County in the 1860s and 1870, Brooks/Quitman in 1878-1887, and Barney in 1900. The Theodosia Smith daughter-link is especially strong because her death record names father Gilham Raymons.
  • Remaining cautions: The subject's exact name form, parents, death, burial, and some child identities remain unresolved. Several later-child trails still need direct records before they should be treated as complete.
