docs.text:
1. Prince Roberts Jr.'s death record and burial remain missing after Georgia/Florida index searches.
  2. Janie Flournoy's parents need a direct record; current evidence proves her maiden name and later life but not parentage.
  3. Adult/death trails are still needed for Mary M., James F., Willie E., Simeon/Simon, and Bessie Mae Roberts. Isaac/Governor is now supported by a 1929 Georgia death record naming both parents and spouse Lola Clark.
  4. The 1910 wife name "Hannah" should be treated as an enumerator/name variant unless a separate wife is proved.
  5. The 1900 Valdosta Jane Flournoy entry is a strong candidate but should remain a likely match unless tied by address, family, or another direct record.
  6. Ancestry trees are secondary only; use them as search leads, not as proof.

docs.title: Online exhaustion update

The authenticated FamilySearch re-pass closed Isaac/Governor Roberts through a 1929 Georgia death record naming parents Janie Flournoy and Prince Roberts and spouse Lola Clark. The Frank/Prince identity remains strongly supported by the 1899 marriage and census continuity, but Janie's parents and the remaining child trails remain unclosed.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
Malory/Mallory Stewart was born about May 1850 in Georgia and appears in the 1900 Barney census with wife Lucy. Both were Black, both reported Georgia-born parents, and both were unable to read or write. The census reports that Lucy had borne no children, leaving no direct descendant trail to follow.

Two Brooks County tax-digest entries support a Brooks County presence before 1900: Mallory Stewart in the 1883-1887 digest and Malory Stewart in the 1895-1898 digest. These records place him in Brooks County across the period when no 1880 census match has been found.

A 31 March 1907 Macon Daily Telegraph item names Mallory Stewart in Macon, Georgia. That is the last known record in the current entry. Neither Malory nor Lucy has been found in 1910 or 1920 census searches, Georgia death-index searches, or the available FamilySearch tree material beyond a minimal profile.

June 14, 2026 continuation check: FamilySearch returned Winnie Ruth Ryall Beaty in the Find a Grave Index, attached to person L2CB-4TH, with birth 14 August 1900, death 17 May 1977, and burial at Pavo, Brooks County, Georgia. That narrows the Winnie adult-trail gap. The same pass found Doris Ryall in the 1920 Barney census with parents J. H. Ryall and Libbie Ryall, but no visible Doris Amy Ryall Hendrix marriage, death, burial, or later household record. John and Libbie's direct death certificate or obituary gaps also remain open.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
Discrepancies:

  1. Marriage date: The official marriage certificate is dated October 22, 1899, and the 1900 census confirms the couple married that same year. The Aldermans in America book (1957) lists November 24, 1904, while Geneanet records show September 1899. The certificate date of October 22, 1899, aligns best with the 1900 census evidence. The 1904 date in the book may reflect a church ceremony or records compiled decades after the fact from family recollection.

  2. Mother's birthplace (John's mother Edna): The 1880 census records both of John's parents as Georgia-born. The 1950 census, taken when John was 79 and living with his daughter, records his mother's birthplace as Pennsylvania. The 1950 entry likely reflects a granddaughter's secondhand information about a great-grandparent three generations removed. The 1880 census, taken when John was living in his parents' household, carries stronger evidentiary weight.

  3. Wife's name spelling: The census enumerators recorded different variants of Libbie's name across decades: "Elwin" in 1900, "Levin" in 1910, then consistently "Libbie" from 1920 onward. The Aldermans in America book uses "Lebbie," which appears to be the original family spelling. The marriage certificate and later censuses both use "Libbie," which is the form she evidently preferred in adulthood.

Alderman Family Network:

John H. Ryall married into the large Alderman family through Lebbie Alderman, daughter of Jonathan H. "Doc" Alderman (HH#176). This connects the Ryall household to several other Alderman-linked families documented in this volume: - HH#176: Jonathan H. Alderman (Lebbie's father) - HH#178: George W. Alderman (Lebbie's eldest brother) - HH#180: James Carlton Alderman (Lebbie's cousin) - HH#186: George S. Joyce (Lebbie's sister Lucy Alice Alderman married George Joyce) - HH#177: Isaac McDaniel Turner (Lebbie's sister Nancy Ellen Alderman married Isaac Turner)

The Ryall family itself connects to the broader Morven community through John's father W. R. Ryall, who appears in the 1880 census in that district with five children. The 1880 record places John among six siblings: Isaiah F., William F., Annie E., Hardy V., and Minnie Lee.

Geographic Pattern: The family moved across multiple counties over fifty years: Brooks County (1880-1900) to Berrien County (1910) and back to Brooks County (1920), then Cook County (1930-1956) before the daughters relocated to Florida. John ended his life living between his two daughters: in Lakeland, Florida with Doris Hendrick (1940) and back in Brooks County with Winnie Beatly (1950). He is buried at Sylvester Cemetery, Cook County, Georgia (FindAGrave Memorial 53995333).

docs.title: Head of Household
docs.text: George Washington Griffin - Born October 7, 1877, Georgia (per WWI draft card; FindAGrave lists February 18, 1877, a discrepancy) - Died December 11, 1961, Colquitt County, Georgia (age 84) - Buried Westview Cemetery, Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia (FindAGrave memorial 15964318) - Race: White - Occupation: Saw mill laborer, sawyer, farmer, stock clerk (varied across decades) - Parents: John Griffin (born ~1847, Georgia) and Matilda Griffin (born ~1850, Georgia)

docs.title: Parents and Siblings (1880 Census)
docs.text:
George was one of five children in the John Griffin household at House 162, Quitman, Brooks County: - Samuel Griffin (age 10, born ~1870) - Mary Griffin (age 8, born ~1872) - George Griffin (age 7, born ~1873) - Francis Griffin (age 6, born ~1874) - John Griffin (age 4, born ~1876)

The 1880 census lists George at age 7 (implying birth ~1873), which conflicts with the October 1877 birth date confirmed by the WWI draft and subsequent censuses. The parents and household location match across sources, so this is likely a census recording error rather than a different individual.

docs.title: Marriage
docs.text: George married Polly Hewit on October 22, 1899, in Colquitt County, Georgia (Ancestry marriage records, collection 4766, record 290397). The 1900 census lists his wife as "Rollie," which is an indexer misreading of "Pollie" in the original handwriting. Across later records her name appears as Pollie (1910), Kallie (1920, another enumerator variant), and Polly (1930) — all the same person.

docs.title: Three Wives
docs.text:
First Wife: Polly Hewit (married 1899 - died 1932) - Born approximately 1884, Georgia (age 16 in 1900 census) - Married October 22, 1899, Colquitt County, Georgia - Died 1932, Putnam County, Florida (Florida Death Index, collection 7338, record 5105139) - The family lived in Orange Springs, Marion County, Florida in 1930. Putnam County adjoins Marion County to the north, consistent with the family's location.

Second Wife: Annie B. Manson (married ~1935 - died 1945) - Born approximately 1867 (age 73 in 1940 census) - Died 1945 (per FindAGrave) - George returned to Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia by 1935 (per 1940 census residence inference), and appears with Annie as his wife in the 1940 census. - Child with Annie: Myrtle Bell Griffin (1913-1989), who married first Schmidt then Winter. Confirmed by FindAGrave and Social Security Applications and Claims Index.

Third Wife: Martha Griffin (married ~1945 - survived George) - Born approximately 1880 (age 70 in 1950 census) - Appears as George's wife in the 1950 census in Moultrie, Colquitt County. - George's death in 1961 means Martha likely survived him.

docs.title: Migration Pattern
docs.text: George spent his early years in Brooks County, Georgia. The family moved to Madison County, Florida by 1920, then north to Marion County (Orange Springs) by 1930. After Polly's death in 1932, George returned to south Georgia, settling in Moultrie, Colquitt County, where he remained for the rest of his life.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The 1900 census lists Arthur Chambers (age 22) as a boarder in the household. He does not appear to be related.
  • "Rollie" in 1900 and "Kallie" in 1920 are both indexer misreadings of "Pollie" (Polly Hewit). This has been confirmed by the marriage certificate and the consistent appearance of "Polly" in 1930.
  • The 1880 census age discrepancy (7 vs. the expected 2-3 given an 1877 birth) is notable but the parents and household location match, so this record is included as the same George Griffin.
  • George married three times across a 46-year span. Polly died in Florida; Annie died in Georgia; Martha survived George.
  • George's death at age 84 in Colquitt County closes a life that began in Brooks County, with the marriage to Polly in Colquitt forming a geographic bookend.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Household #195 is a sawmill boarding house in Barney Precinct, Brooks County, Georgia. Floyd Hines, age 55, is the head of household. Eight other men live with him, all listed as employees of the sawmill rather than as boarders or family members. All nine men were born in Georgia, and both of their parents were Georgia-born as well. The household sits within the industrial labor community of early 1900s Brooks County, where sawmill operations employed large numbers of Black men who often lived in group quarters near the worksite.

  • Direct death, burial, marriage, or later census records for Harry Thomas, Andrew Gates, William Wood, and Clayton Davis.
  • Better proof for William Wood and Clayton Davis, whose names are too common to separate from unrelated Georgia men without parents, spouse, employer, or county continuity.

June 14, 2026 continuation check: A targeted FamilySearch search for Floyd Hines, Black, born about 1840-1850 in Georgia, returned the 1900 Barney census record and one possible 1870 Dougherty County, Georgia Floyd Hines born about 1842. The 1870 record is only a candidate lead because it does not provide a Brooks County, family, occupation, or later-record bridge to the 1900 Barney sawmill worker. No direct post-1900 record for Floyd, Harry Thomas, Andrew Gates, William Wood, Clayton Davis, or Moses Baldwin appeared in the visible results.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• This household represents the industrial labor pattern common in post-Reconstruction South Georgia. Sawmill operations in Brooks County recruited Black men who lived in group quarters near the worksite.
  • The use of "Employee" rather than "Boarder" or "Partner" in the relationship field distinguishes this from typical boarding houses. All men appear to be direct employees of the mill operation.
  • Floyd Hines, as head of household, may have been the foreman or senior worker who managed the boarding facility. He was 55; the other residents ranged from 17 to 46.
  • Abe Gardner's subsequent marriage to Cora Rountree in January 1901 places him in Brooks County less than a year after the census enumeration. The marriage to a local woman suggests some degree of community connection despite his apparent status as a sawmill laborer.
  • The five men who have not been traced beyond 1900 (Floyd Hines, Harry Thomas, Andrew Gates, William Wood, Clayton Davis) may have moved on to other sawmill operations, which were common throughout South Georgia and North Florida during this period. Sawmill labor was highly mobile, and workers frequently relocated as operations opened and closed.
  • The Louis Raintree vs. William Rountree distinction is worth noting. Despite similar names, ages, and locations, these two men belong to different racial communities in Brooks County. Louis Raintree is Black; William F. Rountree (HH#187) is White and belongs to the Folsom-Rountree-Joyce family network.

docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Ancil Lawrence Head 49 Georgia Farmer Tirah Lawrence Wife 37 Georgia — Mohalia Lawrence Daughter 16 Georgia — Laura Lawrence Daughter 14 Georgia — William H Lawrence Son 11 Georgia — Lizzie Lawrence Daughter 9 Georgia — Missouri Lawrence Daughter 6 Georgia — Simon Lawrence Son 5 Georgia — Leola Lawrence Daughter 2 Georgia —

docs.title: Marriage and earlier household
docs.text:
The Brooks marriage return, Book B, page 398, lower entry, records Ansil Lawrance and Tira Baalam married January 15, 1880, following a January 14 license. This supplies Tira’s recorded surname at marriage; it does not name her parents. It is stronger evidence than the later index’s bracketed maiden-name suggestion.

The June 26, 1880 census, Brooks ED 4, page 50, dwelling 458/family 471, lists Ansel Lawrence, 22, and Tyre, 16, wife, with the married-during-census-year mark. The next Lawrence household has a separate number; proximity alone does not establish parentage.

The 1900 original gives Tirah December 1862, age 37, and 21 years married, with 12 children born and 8 living. The reported marriage duration differs slightly from the January 1880 return. It does not, by itself, identify every child she bore or prove her maternity for every child listed under the head.

docs.title: A possible earlier record
docs.text:
The August 16, 1870 Brooks census, page 114, dwelling/family 846, lists Ansell Walker, 12, a Black farm laborer born in Georgia, in the household headed by Norman Campbell. Samuel Walker, 16, is also listed. The 1870 schedule does not state relationships: it does not make the two Walkers brothers or identify their parents.

An Ansel Lawrence row in the Brooks 1878–1882 tax volume, Morven district 660, explicitly names Norman Campbell in the employer column. The given name, locality, compatible age in 1880 and repeated Campbell association strengthen the 1870 candidate. They do not yet prove that Ansell Walker and Ancil Lawrence were the same person, explain the surname difference, or connect either man to the John Walker named in the 1925 death certificate. The tax row’s individual year has not been securely established within the volume’s date range. A blank land field is not a deed or proof of landlessness.

The separate Harry Lawrence household immediately after Ansel and Tyre in 1880 is not assigned as Ansel’s family. Neither adjacency, shared surnames nor an employer relationship establishes kinship or a history of enslavement.

docs.title: Later household, death and burial
docs.text:
The 1920 household places Ansil and wife Tyra with Ellen, Lena, Silvester and Robert. In the 1930 original, Barney town, ED 14-16, sheet 2B, Tyre Lawrence, 68, widowed, is explicitly mother of head Missouri Davis, 35. Mary E., Sylvester and Charley M. Davis are recorded as Missouri’s children. The Sylvester in that household is not automatically the Silvester listed as Ansil’s son in 1920.

A Brooks death certificate, no. 32937, records Tyre Lawrence’s death in Barney on December 26, 1938, and burial at Rock Hill, Barney, on December 29. It describes a Black widow born in Georgia, names Robert Lawrence of Adel as informant, and gives both parents as unknown. The informant’s relationship is not stated. Name, locality, widowhood and the Robert lead support the connection to this family, but the certificate’s age 87 conflicts with the census ages; it is not used to assign an 1851 birth year. A grave marker, plot and independent burial-register confirmation remain to be located. The certificate was filed January 5, 1939, which is not the death date.

The 1925 certificate for the husband, file 6384, records April 7, 1925, Barney, wife Tyrie Lawrence, father John Walker, and mother unknown. Its age 68 differs from the 1900 age 49. It does not explain how or why the Lawrence and Walker surnames were used. An index entry under Tyrie in this collection identifies her as the deceased man’s spouse; it is not her own death record.

docs.title: Children and later trails
docs.text: The Social Security Applications and Claims index entry for Missouri Lawrence Godfrey names father Ancil Lawrence and mother Tara Bellum. It reports birth December 15, 1893, at Morven, Brooks County, and death October 27, 1988. This is a derived index of application/claim information, not an inspected original SS-5. Together with the 1930 mother-to-head statement, it supports a specific Missouri trail, distinct from her sister Mohalia.

docs.title: Missouri Lawrence, Davis and Godfrey
docs.text:
The Brooks marriage register, Book G, right-hand third entry, records Charles Davis and Missouri Lawrence married June 29, 1919, following a June 27 license. The 1920 Barney original, ED 46, sheet 16A, lists Charley Davis, 45, and Masouri, 25, wife, with his mother Henrietta and two Bradley relatives. It does not list the three children later with Missouri in 1930; this does not establish where those children were in 1920 or make Charles their father.

A stronger link to the Godfrey name is Sylvester Lawrence’s original draft card. Sylvester, born October 20, 1916, in Brooks County, names Mrs. Missouri Godfrey of Barney as his mother. The reverse dates registration October 16, 1940. His age and mother support the connection to Missouri’s 1930 son, not to Ancil and Tyra’s older son Silvester.

In the 1940 original, ED 14-19, sheet 10B, household 164, Mose Godfrey, 50, heads the household with Missouri, 36, wife. Charlie Mae, Bertha Lee, Mose Jr. and Shellie are recorded as his children; Billie McMillan is a grandson and Robert Baker a son-in-law, not the grandson shown in the index. These are relationships to the head, not independent proof of Missouri’s maternity or Mose’s biological paternity for each person.

The 1950 original, ED 14-28, sheet 7, household 45, again lists Mose—misindexed as “Thore”—with wife Missouri and Bertha Lee, Mose Jr. and Shellie James. Missouri is recorded as 60, compared with 36 in 1940 and 35 in 1930. The Georgia death index reports October 27, 1988, Lowndes County death and Brooks residence, but age 86, also inconsistent with the Social Security birth date. These disagreements remain unresolved; the original death certificate has not been inspected.

The Godfrey marriage date, the end of the Davis marriage and the original 1988 obituary remain unverified. The obituary index’s original-image link was unavailable through two routes; its extracted child list and the apparent place-name suffix “Barney” have not been adopted as family evidence.

Missouri and Mohalia are separate daughters in the 1900 original. The Missouri index does not identify Mohalia or justify merging the two. Other later child identities remain open unless a direct record establishes the connection.

docs.title: Sources still needed and research limits
docs.text:
• Original evidence resolving both spouses’ age conflicts, without choosing a convenient birth year.
  • Tyra/Tirah’s parents and a grave or burial-register confirmation at the Rock Hill named in her certificate.
  • Missouri’s original Social Security application, death certificate, Godfrey marriage and evidence for the end of the Davis marriage.
  • Separate adult trails for the other children; similar given names and household proximity are not sufficient.
  • Evidence explaining the Walker/Lawrence surname difference and a deed chain for the competing land-lot readings.

Status: Original marriage, census and death records now extend the family’s trail. Parentage, age discrepancies, some adult identities and land title remain unresolved. The earlier “source-exhausted” label is withdrawn: the preserved searches did not establish exhaustion, and this follow-up recovered additional originals. The old June 14 search-history claim has not been independently reproduced.

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text: No children are listed in this household in the 1900 census table.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Charley Thompson appears under multiple name spellings across six decades of federal census records. His surname shifted from Thompson (1900-1920) to Thomas (1930-1940) before reverting to Thompson in the 1950 census. The 1900 census provides the most reliable birth data: April 1880, Georgia, both parents Georgia-born. Later censuses show birth years ranging from 1870 to 1886, a pattern common in African American census records of this era where childhood enslavement prevented families from tracking exact dates.

The earlier narrative associated this household’s Ellen with the bride Ellen Laurence in an April 2, 1899 marriage and with Tyra in a 1910 household. Those identity links are not established by the marriage entry alone. Two distinct 1900 households contain men named Charley Thompson and wives named Ellen. The later census sequence below is retained as earlier research, not newly revalidated; the proposed death interval and child relationships depend on that continuity being confirmed.

docs.title: Candidate marriage, not an assigned household bridge (Ancestry Collection 4766, record 127489)
docs.text:
• Groom: Charley Thompson
  • Bride: Ellen Laurence
  • Date: April 2, 1899

The inspected original, printed p.128, third entry, records an April 1 license and April 2 ceremony for Charley Thompson and Ellen Laurence. The same page’s first entry records a separate June 15 ceremony with Florence Slaytor. Neither entry supplies ages, parents or a census-household identifier. Laurence is the April bride’s recorded surname; it is not yet proved as this household wife’s maiden name. - Place: Brooks County, Georgia - Race: Colored

docs.title: Census Trail
docs.text: Year Name Age Occupation Household Size Notes 1900 Charley Thompson 20 Laborer 3 Wife Ellen, son Tommie. Rents. Both illiterate. 1910 Charley Thompson 24 Sawmill laborer 4 Wife Tyra, children Ora Lee (10), Ercie (8). Years married: 13. 1920 Charley Thompson 47 Farmer 15 Wife Ellen, 10 children, 3 grandchildren. Rents. 1930 Charly Thomas 56 Farmer 14 Wife Ellen, 7 children, 2 grandchildren. Surname changed to Thomas. 1940 Charlie Thomas 70 Farmer 11 Wife Ellen (respondent, 6th grade), 2 children, 5 grandchildren. 1950 Ellen Thompson 68 — 5 Ellen widowed. 4 grandchildren. Surname reverted to Thompson.

docs.title: Children and Grandchildren
docs.text:
The household grew substantially between 1900 and 1920. By 1920, Charley and Ellen had 10 children at home plus three grandchildren. The children's names shift between census years, making precise identification difficult. Grandchildren appear consistently from 1920 onward, suggesting married daughters were leaving children with Ellen and Charley while working elsewhere.

Children identified across censuses: Tommie (1900-1920, age 19), Ora Lee (1910-1920, age 18-20), Ercie/Retha (1910-1920, age 8-18), Tira (1920, age 15), Pauline (1920, age 13), S B (1920-1930, age 12-18), Ellis (1920-1940, age 9-29), Eorca/Corey (1920-1930, age 8-16), Lilly (1920-1930, age 7-14), Charley Jr (1920-1940, age 3-23), Rubin (1920-1930, age 1-10), Robert (1930, age 9), Elbert (1930, age 7), Tyra (1940, age 30).

Grandchildren present: Ethel (1920, age 2), Frank (1920, age 0), Mattie Rountree (1920, age 0, possible Rountree family connection), Allice M/Alice Mae (1930-1950, age 0-21), Arretha/Ireatha (1930-1940, age 4-16), James (1940-1950, age 10-19), Willie (1940, age 7), Doris (1940-1950, age 6-16), Margaret Lee (1940, age 7).

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
The Thompson household illustrates several patterns common to Black families in post-Reconstruction Georgia. Surname instability (Thompson-Thomas-Thompson) reflects both the casual nature of census recording and the vulnerability of Black families to transcription errors. Birth year discrepancies spanning 16 years across six censuses suggest either the informant changed over time or census takers recorded estimates rather than asking for exact ages.

Ellen's literacy improved over her lifetime. She could not read or write in 1900 and 1930, but by 1940 she had completed the sixth grade and served as the census respondent, filling out the form herself. This suggests either personal determination or access to adult education programs in the Barney area during the 1930s.

The 1950 census shows Ellen as the head of household, widowed, age 68, living with four grandchildren. Charley died between 1940 and 1950. The surname reverted to Thompson, indicating the Thomas period was likely a transcription issue rather than a legal name change.

docs.title: Laurence Family Connection
docs.text: The candidate bride’s surname Laurence resembles the surname of Ancil Lawrence (HH#199), who lived nearby in Barney precinct. However, direct parent-child connection is unlikely: Ancil's daughter Ellen, recorded in the 1920 census at age 11, would have been born around 1909, too late to be the Ellen who married Charley in 1899. The Laurence name was present among multiple Black families in Brooks County, and any kinship between these two households remains unverified.

docs.title: Sources still needed
docs.text:
• Death record or burial place for Charley Thompson/Thomas, who died between the 1940 and 1950 censuses.
  • Death record or burial place for Ellen Laurence Thompson after the 1950 census.
  • An identity bridge assigning the April bride Ellen Laurence to this household, followed by a parent-naming record. Neither maiden name nor the proposed Ellen/Tyra equivalence is established here.
  • Adult trails for the children and grandchildren whose names shift across the 1910-1950 census sequence, especially Tommie, Ora Lee, Ercie/Retha, Tira, Pauline, S. B., Ellis, Corey/Eorca, Lilly, Charley Jr., Rubin, Robert, Elbert, and Tyra.
  • Direct evidence explaining whether the Thompson/Thomas surname shift was a recording error or a temporary family usage.

June 14, 2026 continuation check: FamilySearch returned the 1900 Charley Thompson census record and the 2 April 1899 Brooks County marriage record to Ellen Laurence. It did not return a usable Charley Thompson/Thomas death record between 1940 and 1950 in the targeted search. The high-volume Thompson/Thomas result set mostly produced unrelated men or records without an Ellen Laurence/Thompson family bridge.

docs.title: Alfred Belote of early Lowndes County, Georgia
docs.text:
Back to the Early History Profiles index

Research dossier prepared: August 18, 2026 Subject: Alfred/Alford Belote, early Lowndes County settler, taxpayer, probable Army enlistee, and reported militia officer Scope: Online and retained-source survey covering original Army, census, tax, newspaper, land, estate, genealogy, and cemetery evidence available as of August 18, 2026

docs.title: Executive finding
docs.text:
Alfred Belote was an early settler of the part of original Irwin County that became Lowndes County, Georgia. Later histories consistently group him with Lawrence Folsom, James Rountree, and Drew Vickers as the first permanent white settler families of original Lowndes. That attribution is an old and credible local tradition, but it is not a contemporary finding. The earliest fully inspectable account located is William Harden's 1913 history. Folks Huxford repeated the quartet in 1922 and supplied an 1821 date, relying chiefly on newspaper sketches by Hortense W. Baker that have not been found.[1-2]

Original records document Alfred more securely than modern family trees do. An Army enlistment register records an Alfred Belote born in Bertie County, North Carolina, who enlisted in 1814 and was discharged at Raleigh in 1815 without joining his regiment or corps. The uncommon name and compatible migration pattern make this a strong probable match, although the age conflicts with the 1840 census.[3] Federal schedules place an Alford Belote household in Lowndes County in 1830 and 1840.[4-5] Original tax pages place Alfred on 490-acre Land Lot 55, District 12, in 1830 and 1834. The 1844 digest lists an agent for Alfred's estate on the same land, proving that he had died by that return.[6-8]

Lowndes legal notices establish the death boundary and the only verified child. William D. Griffin and John Belote applied to administer Alfred's estate in a notice dated September 24, 1844. A later notice shows that the estate included real property and enslaved people. In 1851 Griffin sought guardianship of Mary Ellen Belote, explicitly called Alfred's orphaned minor daughter. Griffin and John applied for dismissal from the administration in 1851.[9-12]

Much of the usual online genealogy remains unproved or wrong. Mary Ellen is the only child directly named in a reviewed contemporary record. John is a strong probable son because he co-administered Alfred's estate and a later tribute, preserved only in a memorial transcription, reportedly calls him Alfred's son. The other people in John's 1850 household may belong to that sibling group, but the census does not state their relationships.[13-14] Ann Hodges Belote is a probable widow of Alfred, yet Huxford gives her birth as 1813. She cannot have been the mother of John, born about 1823. Martha Hendley, sometimes named as an earlier wife, is only an unsupported tree lead.[15-17]

Alfred's exact birth date, parents, complete child list, precise death date, and burial place remain unknown.

docs.title: Evidence standards
docs.text:
• Verified: read in an original image, contemporary public notice, or record that states the relationship or fact.
  • Strong probable: several specific facts support the conclusion, but no single record states the entire identity or relationship.
  • Probable: the evidence points in one direction but does not exclude a realistic alternative.
  • Secondary-supported: stated in a later history, transcription, memorial, or compiled genealogy without inspected original proof.
  • Possible: plausible and worth pursuing, but not established.
  • Unresolved: the reviewed evidence does not settle the question.
  • Contradicted: a stronger record or chronology conflicts with the claim.

Repeated public trees do not become independent proof by copying one another. Negative findings mean only that no record was found in the documented searches.

docs.title: Identity and name controls
docs.text:
The record and published-source chain uses both Alfred Belote and Alford Belote:

Form Record context Alfred Belote Army register, 1827 lottery index, tax digests, estate notices, militia roster Alford Belote 1830 and 1840 federal census indexes and original schedules Betote Alternate reading or alias written with the Army entry

The Lowndes tax and estate chain distinguishes the pioneer from later men of the same name. The uncommon name, Lowndes County continuity, tax chain, and later estate evidence make the 1830 and 1840 Alford Belote households a strong probable match to the pioneer. The conflicting adult-male age brackets prevent a verified identification. The 1844 tax entry is not a living Alfred; the manuscript explicitly lists an agent for his estate.

Later Virginia, North Carolina, and twentieth-century Alfred Belotes are excluded below.

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text: Date Event Assessment July 4, 1814 An Alfred Belote enlisted at Fayetteville, North Carolina, as a private in the 10th U.S. Infantry. Verified register entry; strong probable match to the pioneer. April 24, 1815 Discharged at Raleigh when his term expired, “without joining Regt or Corps.” Verified register wording; no battle or field service proved. 1815 Later history says Belote explored southern Irwin with Folsom, Rountree, and Vickers. Retrospective tradition; unproved. 1821 Huxford later dates the four-family move to 1821. Retrospective and unproved. April 2, 1827 Published lottery index names Alfred of Underwoods District, Irwin County, as a fortunate drawer. Verified published index; lot number disputed. August 9, 1827 Huxford lists Alfred as first lieutenant, 658th Lowndes Militia District. Strong published evidence; original commission not inspected. 1830 Federal census records Alford Belote in Lowndes with seven free white household members. Verified original schedule. 1830 Tax digest lists Alfred on 490-acre Lot 55, District 12, and a 202 1/2-acre Lee County tract. Verified original tax page. 1834 Tax digest again lists Alfred on Lot 55. Verified original tax page. 1840 Census records eleven free white household members and one enslaved woman. Verified indexed original schedule. August 29, 1842 Public land/tax KML reports an Alfred Belote plat. Derivative locator; plat not inspected. By Sept. 24, 1844 Griffin and John Belote applied to administer Alfred's estate; the 1844 tax digest lists the estate on Lot 55. Verified death boundary and estate land. February 1845 Administrators sought leave to sell Alfred's real estate and enslaved people. Verified contemporary notice. 1850 John Belote headed a seven-person Belote household in Lowndes; relationships were not recorded. Verified household, unresolved relationships. 1851 Mary Ellen Belote was called Alfred's orphaned minor daughter in Griffin's guardianship application. Verified daughter. 1851 Griffin and John applied for dismissal from Alfred's estate administration. Verified continuing administration.

docs.title: The first-four-settlers claim
docs.text:
The safest conclusion is that Alfred belonged to a four-family settlement tradition, not that a contemporary record proves the quartet's route and dates.

Harden's 1913 A History of Savannah and South Georgia is the earliest fully inspectable account found that names all four men. In a biography of Ashley Lawson and Cynthia Folsom, it says Lawrence Folsom, James Rountree, Drew Vickers, and Alfred Belote explored southern Irwin County on horseback in 1815, bought land, returned for their families, and became the first permanent white settlers of Lowndes County, especially its northern portion. It also says Alfred's land included the later village of Mineola.[1]

Harden wrote about ninety years after the event and cited no diary, deed, or public record. Its wording contains warning signs. It calls the purchases “government land,” although Lawrence Folsom's first verified tract was bought privately, and it says the men returned to Brooks County, which did not exist until 1858. The Mineola statement has not been tied to a deed or plat.

Huxford's 1922 quarterly gives the precise version: “In 1821, four settlers moved to what is now Lowndes county,” followed by the same four names and their families.[2] Huxford says his sketch depended chiefly on recent Valdosta Times articles by Hortense W. Baker. Baker's article, notes, and sources were not located.

“First permanent white settlers” is the terminology of those later histories. It describes Euro-American settlement and is not evidence that the land was previously uninhabited. The claim is also safest when applied to original Lowndes County, created from southern Irwin in 1825 and later divided.

Finding: strong for Alfred's membership in the old tradition; probable that he settled in the region by the early 1820s; unresolved for the 1815 expedition, exact 1821 family move, and Mineola land claim.

docs.title: Federal Army register
docs.text:
The original enlistment register gives an unusually detailed entry for Alfred Belote:[3]

  • private, 10th U.S. Infantry, under Colonel J. Wellborn;
  • age 21; laborer; born in Bertie County, North Carolina;
  • 5 feet 6 inches; blue eyes; fair hair and complexion;
  • enlisted July 4, 1814 at Fayetteville by Lieutenant Hill, for the war;
  • attached in the remarks to Captain H. N. Caswell's company at Raleigh;
  • discharged April 24, 1815 at Raleigh because his term expired, “without joining Regt or Corps”; reference to a pension case.

The name and geography make this a strong probable record for the Lowndes pioneer. The age implies birth about 1792-1793 and agrees broadly with the 1830 household's male age bracket. It conflicts with the 1840 schedule, where the oldest male was fifty through fifty-nine. One source may contain an age error, but the conflict cannot be solved from the records reviewed.

The entry does not prove combat duty. Its own wording says he did not join his regiment or corps.

docs.title: Lowndes militia
docs.text:
Huxford's 1948 History of Brooks County lists Alfred as first lieutenant of the 658th Lowndes Militia District, commissioned August 9, 1827. Francis Rountree appears as captain and Lewis Vickers as ensign on the same date.[18] Huxford supplies no image or item-level archive reference for the commission list.

Finding: strong published evidence for the 1827 first-lieutenant commission; the original executive or militia record remains a priority target.

docs.title: 1830 Lowndes County
docs.text:
The original schedule records "Alford Belote", household 83, stamped page 82.[4] The household contained seven free white people and no enslaved people:

  • males: three under five, one aged five through nine, and one aged thirty through thirty-nine;
  • females: one aged five through nine and one aged twenty through twenty-nine.

These unnamed children cannot be assigned to a published child list from the census alone.

docs.title: 1840 Lowndes County
docs.text:
The schedule records twelve people: eleven free white household members and one enslaved woman aged twenty-four through thirty-five.[5]

  • males: two under five, one five through nine, one ten through fourteen, two fifteen through nineteen, and one fifty through fifty-nine;
  • females: one under five, one five through nine, one fifteen through nineteen, and one thirty through thirty-nine;
  • four people employed in agriculture;
  • one white person over twenty recorded as unable to read and write.

The census does not identify Alfred's wife, children, or the enslaved woman. Her name and later fate are unknown.

docs.title: 1850 continuity
docs.text: Alfred does not appear in an age-compatible 1850 household because he was already dead. The Lowndes household headed by John Belote, twenty-seven, included Phereby, twenty-six; Henry, twenty-two; William, twenty; Eliza, eighteen; James, sixteen; and Mary E., twelve.[13] The schedule does not state relationships. John’s later obituary says he was left young in charge of many brothers and sisters, which makes a sibling group likely, but only Mary Ellen has been tied directly to Alfred.

docs.title: Land Lot 55, District 12
docs.text:
The best property chain is the 490-acre tract on Land Lot 55, District 12, Lowndes County:

  • 1830: Alfred paid tax on the full 490 acres, originally granted to Nathan Brinson.[6]
  • 1834: the digest again lists Alfred on Lot 55.[7]
  • 1844: an unnamed “Agent for Estate of Alfred Belote” returned the same 490-acre lot.[8]

This proves taxable ownership or responsibility and continuity into the estate. It does not locate Alfred's house within the lot. No deed into Alfred, deed out of the estate, estate sale, or heir conveyance was found. The public historical KML also reports Alfred on the lot in 1835, 1838, and 1840 and identifies an August 29, 1842 plat, but those underlying images were not inspected.[19]

Harden's later statement that Alfred's land included Mineola remains unproved. Lot 55's official geography can be checked in the Georgia land-lot layer, but geography alone does not prove a village claim or residence site.[20]

docs.title: Lee County lottery tract
docs.text:
The 1827 lottery index identifies Alfred of Underwoods District, Irwin County, as a fortunate drawer on April 2.[21] Ray City History Blog, citing the official-register reprint, gives Lot 125, District 25, Lee County.[22] Alfred's 1830 tax page instead lists 202 1/2 acres in District 25 as Lot 121.[6]

The two numbers must remain in conflict. The tax tract could be the lottery land with a transcription error, or a separate tract. The original official-register page and grant file were not obtained.

docs.title: Mary Ellen Belote
docs.text: Mary Ellen is Alfred's only verified child. The February 1851 legal notice calls her the orphan and minor of Alfred Belote and records William D. Griffin's guardianship application.[11] She is a strong probable match to Mary E. Belote, twelve, in John's 1850 household. Public-tree, memorial, and census evidence identifies her as the later wife of Ezekiel Parrish and Matthew Vickers; those links were not independently proved here by marriage records. Her photographed marker gives October 13, 1839 to September 28, 1908.[23-24]

docs.title: John Belote
docs.text:
John is Alfred's strong probable son. He co-administered Alfred's estate from 1844 through the 1851 dismissal application.[9,12] Tributes transcribed on John's Find a Grave memorial say he was born upward of sixty years earlier, was left young in charge of a large family of brothers and sisters, and supported them until they could support themselves. One reportedly calls him Alfred's son, but the original newspaper image was not inspected.[14] That family account fits the estate chronology and the 1850 household.

Compiled genealogy says John married Henrietta Folsom in 1851. The later census and public-tree chain supports a probable child group including Nancy/Elmore, Anthony Wain, Israel Putnam, Martha, and Joel. It also reports that Anthony married Piety Vickers and Israel married Rachel Ann Folsom. These are regional Folsom and Vickers connections, but they do not add independent proof of John's father.[16,25]

docs.title: Other proposed children
docs.text:
The remaining people in John's 1850 household are possible members of Alfred's child group, not proved children:

Person Evidence Assessment Phereby Belote, about 1824 Shared John's household; Ancestry infers spouse Role unresolved; John married Henrietta Folsom in 1851. Henry / Noah Henry Belote, about 1828 Household plus conflicting public trees Possible child; mother unproved. William Belote, about 1830 Household and public-tree claim Possible child. Eliza / Elizabeth Belote, about 1832 Household; FamilySearch gives an Elizabeth born 1837 Possible child; material birth-year conflict. James Belote, about 1834 Household; FamilySearch assigns Alfred and Ann Possible child; no parent-naming record reviewed.

The missing estate distribution, family Bible, deed recitals, church record, or guardianship file could change these grades.

docs.title: Wives and the Ann Hodges contradiction
docs.text:
Huxford's Pioneers of Wiregrass Georgia says Richard H. Burkhalter married “Mrs. Ann Hodges Belote of Lowndes County” on October 12, 1848. It gives Ann's birth as January 16, 1813 and death as May 10, 1867, and says she transferred from Friendship Church to Union Primitive Baptist on October 13, 1849. The sketch places Burkhalter and both wives at Fender Cemetery.[15] Ann's memorial repeats the dates and burial but has no marker photograph.[17]

Ann is a probable widow of Alfred based on surname, place, chronology, and later family tradition, but no reviewed marriage, estate, church, or deed record identifies her former husband.

Her birth date exposes a common public-tree error. Ann was about ten when John was born around 1823. She cannot have been John's biological mother if both dates are substantially right. WikiTree's John profile claims Alfred and Ann in prose, but its linked parent fields are blank and its census citations do not name John's parents.[16]

An Ancestry tree snippet names Martha Hendley as Henry Belote's mother and Alfred as his father.[26] No reviewed marriage, probate, deed, Bible, church, or census record supports that pairing. Martha is a possible earlier-wife lead, nothing more.

Finding: Alfred may have married more than once. Ann is a probable later wife and widow. The mother of John and the older children remains unknown.

docs.title: Parents and origin
docs.text:
Ray City History Blog says Alfred was a son of Revolutionary War soldier Noah Belote.[22] Noah's Virginia service is documented, but the reviewed bounty-land material does not connect him to Alfred.[27] A sourced WikiTree profile places Noah in Accomack and Northampton counties, Virginia, and lists Ann W., James, and Perry Leatherbury Belote as children, not Alfred.[28]

Absence from a compiled child list does not disprove another son. It does mean the parentage has not been established. No reviewed probate, Bible, deed, marriage, pension, or guardianship record names Alfred's parents.

Finding: Bertie County, North Carolina is a strong probable origin only if the Army identity match is accepted; Noah Belote as father remains unresolved.

docs.title: Death, estate, and burial
docs.text:
The earliest death boundary is clear. A notice dated September 24, 1844 says William D. Griffin and John Belote sought administration of Alfred's estate.[9] The 1844 digest already lists an agent for the estate on Lot 55.[8] The exact date of death is not stated.

A February 1845 notice says the estate included real estate and enslaved people.[10] It does not give names, counts, sale terms, or buyers. The 1840 census listed one enslaved woman, but no record establishes whether she remained in the estate or was among the people contemplated by the generic plural wording of the notice.

No will, letters, inventory, appraisal, sale bill, annual return, final return, guardian packet, heir receipt, or estate deed was located online. Lowndes's early deed books burned in the 1858 courthouse fire, and the Ordinary's office burned in 1869, which may explain some gaps.[29]

No obituary, funeral notice, cemetery register, photographed grave, or Alfred memorial was found. His burial place is unresolved.

docs.title: Public role and court activity
docs.text: The 1827 militia appointment is Alfred's only located public office. Published 1833 Lowndes grand-jury presentments do not name him.[30] No inspected legislative act, election return, justice record, court minute, road appointment, or civil suit establishes another office or civic role.

docs.title: Namesake exclusions and malformed trees
docs.text:
1. Alfred Belote, born January 22, 1810, in the Abel Belote-Dezire Egelsten family: too young for the 1814 enlistment, reported 1815 expedition, 1827 militia office, or likely fatherhood of John.[31]
  2. Geni Alfred Belote, “1809-1844,” linked to Bertie, North Carolina: the profile also carries Ann and Mary Ellen, consistent with a malformed version of the Georgia family rather than independent evidence.[32]
  3. Youmans RootsMagic Alfred, born about 1809 in “Lowndes, GA”: the place label is anachronistic because Lowndes County was created in 1825, and the birth year is incompatible with the early records.[33]
  4. Alfred Bynum Belote (1903-1924) and Alfred Thomas Belote (1927-1973): twentieth-century memorials and chronologically excluded.[34]

docs.title: Evidence grades at a glance
docs.text: Claim Grade Reason Alfred/Alford in the 1830 and 1840 Lowndes censuses is the pioneer Strong probable Uncommon name, county and tax continuity; adult-male age brackets conflict He was a member of the traditional four-family permanent white settler group Strong historical tradition Harden 1913 and Huxford 1922; no contemporary 1815/1821 proof He settled in exactly 1821 Unresolved Retrospective date only He was the 1814-1815 Army enlistee Strong probable Uncommon name, place, age, chronology; 1840 age conflict He was commissioned first lieutenant in 1827 Strong published evidence Huxford roster; original commission missing He held Lot 55, District 12 Verified Original 1830, 1834, and estate tax images His land included Mineola Unresolved Harden statement; no deed or plat proof He died by September 24, 1844 Verified Administration notice and estate tax entry Mary Ellen was his daughter Verified Contemporary guardianship notice John was his son Strong probable Co-administrator, family caretaker narrative, explicit later tribute Complete 1850 household were his children Unresolved Census states no relationships Ann Hodges was his widow Probable Surname, place, chronology, and later tradition; former husband not identified directly Ann was John's mother Contradicted Ann's 1813 birth makes her about ten at John's birth Martha Hendley was his earlier wife Possible Unsupported public-tree lead only Noah Belote was his father Unresolved No parent-naming record He died on a specific day in 1844 Unresolved Only the administration boundary is proved He was buried in a known cemetery Unresolved No memorial, marker, or register found

docs.title: Research coverage and negative findings
docs.text:
The search covered census, land, military, tax, probate, newspaper, cemetery, and published local-history sources, using Belote surname variants and associated places and relatives.

Authenticated Ancestry work covered the 1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850 federal censuses; the U.S. Army enlistment register; Georgia tax digests; the 1827 lottery index; Georgia probate; and broad military results. Original images were downloaded and reopened for the Army entry, 1830 and 1840 censuses, and 1830, 1834, and 1844 tax pages.

Georgia Historic Newspapers was searched from 1790 through 1925 for "Alfred Belote", with spelling variants and estate, guardian, obituary, militia, land, and settlement terms. The exact name produced 25 pages, all in the 1844-1845 estate or 1851-1852 guardianship/dismissal clusters. No contemporary expedition account, obituary, or funeral notice was found.

Internet Archive page images and OCR were checked for Harden and Huxford. Ray City History Blog's Alfred tag, Rountree article, land-lottery page, and grand-jury page were checked. FamilySearch public ancestor pages, WikiTree and its API, Find a Grave, Geni, Youmans RootsMagic, English Lass, and Ancestry tree snippets were used only at the level their evidence justified.

The 1941 DAR History of Lowndes County was not available in publicly inspectable full text. Hortense W. Baker's Valdosta Times sketches were not found. The original 1827 lottery register page, 1827 militia commission, 1842 plat, 1835/1838/1840 tax pages, Lot 55 deeds, estate packet, Bible, church membership record for Alfred, and grave remain unavailable.

docs.title: Best next records
docs.text:
1. Obtain the original August 9, 1827 militia commission or executive-minute entry for the 658th District.
  2. Inspect the official 1827 lottery register page and state grant to settle Lot 121 versus 125.
  3. Retrieve Alfred's August 29, 1842 plat and all surviving 1835, 1838, and 1840 tax pages.
  4. Search reconstructed deed indexes and later deed recitals for Lot 55, especially conveyances by Griffin, John Belote, Mary Ellen, Ann Burkhalter, or named heirs.
  5. Search Georgia Archives loose-name, Inferior/Superior Court, guardianship, land-grant, and county files for Alfred's estate and Mary Ellen's guardianship.
  6. Locate Hortense W. Baker's Valdosta Times pioneer sketches and determine whether she cited a family manuscript or public record.
  7. Obtain Friendship and Union Primitive Baptist records for Ann's 1849 transfer and any earlier Belote membership.
  8. Search private Bibles, cemetery surveys, and descendant papers for Alfred's wife or wives, child list, death date, and burial.

docs.title: Citation audit note
docs.text: Original images, contemporary notices, later histories, memorial transcriptions, and public trees are labeled separately. Conflicts in Alfred's age, lottery lot, wife or wives, child list, parents, death date, and burial remain visible. The dossier does not convert a repeated family-tree assertion into proof.

docs.title: Daniel McCranie Sr.: Coffee Road pioneer and early Lowndes commissioner
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: Research conclusion
docs.text:
Daniel McCranie Sr. was born about 1772, lived in Montgomery County, Georgia, by 1820, and moved into the Irwin-Lowndes frontier during the 1820s. Later county histories identify him as a Coffee Road settler and as the Daniel McCranie intended by the garbled "McCauly" in the 1825 Lowndes organizing act. Census records place the elder Daniel in Lowndes County in 1830, 1840, and 1850. A modern cemetery memorial says he died June 17, 1854, and was buried at Wilkes Cemetery in present Cook County, but no contemporary death, probate, or burial record was found online.[1-9]

The often-repeated claim that McCranie became Lowndes County's first postmaster in March 1827 is not proved by the federal records inspected here. Huxford and later writers say an office called Lowndes Court-house opened at McCranie's Coffee Road home and moved to William Smith at Franklinville in July 1828. Yet the federal Official Register as of September 30, 1827, does not list a Lowndes office, while the 1829 register directly lists Franklinville with William Smith. The local tradition may preserve a short-lived or administratively delayed office, but its exact opening date and McCranie's appointment remain unresolved.[4,10-12]

docs.title: Identity and migration
docs.text:
The 1820 Montgomery County census lists Daniel McCraney, a man aged 45 or older, with a woman of the same age class, eight younger free white household members, and two enslaved people. Two people were engaged in agriculture.[1]

In 1830, Daniel McCraney was in Lowndes County. The household contained a man and woman aged 50-59 and six younger people, with no enslaved people recorded.[2] In 1840, Daniel McCranie was 60-69, living with a woman of the same age class; the household was engaged in agriculture, and no enslaved people were recorded.[3]

The 1850 census gives the best direct age estimate: Daniel McCranie, 78, farmer, in Lowndes County, with Kittie, 46, Melvina J., 26, and Wesley, 5. The record does not state relationships.[4] Daniel's age points to birth about 1772 and connects cleanly with the earlier census sequence.

Later accounts say his first wife was Sarah McMillan and his second wife was Kittie or Kitty Paige. The 1850 household directly proves Kittie's presence, not the marriage. Sarah's identity and the second marriage are family-history and memorial claims because no original marriage record was found.[7-9]

docs.title: County organization and Coffee Road settlement
docs.text:
The act organizing Lowndes County was approved December 24, 1825. Its later printed text names Lawrence Folsom, Sion Hall, William Blair, John J. Underwood, Daniel McCranie's apparent place under the spelling "McCauly", and other commissioners charged with selecting the permanent county site.[5] Huxford identifies the intended man as Daniel McCranie.[6]

That identification is strong probable rather than literal: the printed act does not say McCranie. The cluster of named frontier residents and Huxford's interpretation make a printing or transcription error likely, but no original enrolled-act manuscript was located to settle it.

Huxford places McCranie's home on the Coffee Road, at the later Dick Hutchinson place. A modern Ray City history article narrows it to Land Lot 416 in the 9th District.[6,9] No original deed, plat, or tax entry located online ties Daniel Sr. to Lot 416. The defensible conclusion is a broad Coffee Road residence in the area that later became Cook County; the exact lot and house site remain probable at best.

An 1838 tax digest row explicitly names "Daniel McCranie Sr." and lists three 202½-acre tracts in Wilkinson County, including Lots 39 and 40 in the 11th District and Lot 263 in the 6th District.[13] This is secure evidence for the elder because the suffix appears on the row. An 1844 Lowndes tax row names an unsuffixed Daniel McCranie with 490 acres in Land Lot 314, 9th District.[14] It cannot safely be assigned to the elder: Daniel Jr. was separately active by then.

docs.title: The first-post-office claim
docs.text:
Huxford says Lowndes County's first post office was established March 31, 1827, as "Lowndes Court-house", with Daniel McCranie as postmaster at his Coffee Road home. He says it moved to William Smith and became Franklinville on July 7, 1828.[6] Ray City History gives March 27, 1827, creating a four-day conflict even among later accounts.[9]

The federal evidence is narrower:

  • The postal section of the 1827 Official Register of the United States, current to September 30, has no Lowndes Court-house or other Lowndes County office in its alphabetic southern list.[10]
  • The 1829 register directly lists "Franklinville, Ga." with "Wm Smith" and compensation of $9.06.[11]
  • The 1831 register continues the Franklinville-era federal evidence.[12]

Absence from the 1827 register does not prove the office never operated. A new office could have been omitted, short-lived, renamed, or outside the register's reporting cutoff. It does mean the exact March date and McCranie's postmastership should not be presented as verified fact. Franklinville under William Smith by September 1829 is directly proved.

The old USPS Postmaster Finder links all returned a 404 page during this research. Three identical failures triggered the anti-loop stop. No federal appointment record naming McCranie was recovered there.

docs.title: Family and same-name separation
docs.text:
The strongest early published family sketch appeared in the Tifton Gazette on March 13, 1896. Writing under the name Bohemian, the author selected “old Uncle Daniel” as head of the clan and named six sons: Malcolm, Archibald, William, Daniel, John, and Niel. He also named two daughters, Mrs. S. G. Williams and Mrs. R. N. Parrish. The article described Daniel as the first Master Mason among the family's Berrien-area pioneers.[15]

The article was written about four decades after Daniel's reported death. It is valuable because it is close to living descendants, but it is still retrospective and gives no dates or mother-child proof. A modern memorial marker lists ten children: Duncan N., Mary J., Neil, John, Daniel, Malcolm, Nancy, Archibald, William B., and Elizabeth.[7-8] The 1896 and modern lists overlap but are not identical in form, so the complete child list remains derivative.

Same-name separation is essential. An August 1840 sheriff's notice expressly levied a horse belonging to "Daniel McCranie, jr." in Griffin & Dominy v. Archibald and Daniel McCranie.[16] That record proves a younger Daniel was legally active while the elder was alive. Consequently:

  • the 1844 unsuffixed tax row cannot be assigned to Daniel Sr.;
  • an 1843 Thomas County judgment in favor of an unsuffixed Daniel McCranie cannot be assigned confidently; and
  • later estates of men styled Daniel McCranie Sr. in Dodge or Berrien County are not this pioneer without an independent identity chain.[14,17]

docs.title: Military and civic traditions
docs.text:
The Ray City account says McCranie served as a Montgomery County inferior-court justice in 1822 and that five sons supplied service or forage during the 1836 Brushy Creek campaign.[9] These are plausible leads, but the original commission and a primary roster tying the sons to those services were not found in the accessible online material. They remain unproved in this dossier.

The 1896 sketch's Masonic statement is likewise a contemporary-to-descendants tradition rather than a lodge-register extract.[15] It should be cited to that article, not repeated as an independently verified lodge fact.

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
Daniel was alive in the 1850 Lowndes census at age 78.[4] The modern Find a Grave memorial and granite marker give his death as June 17, 1854, identify Sarah McMillan as first wife, and place them in Wilkes Cemetery in Cook County.[7-8] The marker is plainly modern, not an original 1854 stone. No contemporary obituary, probate opening, estate sale, burial register, or original grave marker was located online.

The death date and cemetery are therefore probable memorial evidence. They fit the census chronology but are not independently proved.

docs.title: What is proved, probable, and unresolved
docs.text:
Directly proved or strongly documented

  • Daniel McCranie's age progression and residence in Montgomery County in 1820 and Lowndes County in 1830, 1840, and 1850.
  • A second, younger Daniel McCranie was active by 1840.
  • Daniel Sr. held the three Wilkinson County tax tracts recorded in 1838.
  • Franklinville had a federal post office under William Smith by September 30, 1829.

Strong probable or probable

  • Daniel McCranie is the commissioner intended by "McCauly" in the printed 1825 act.
  • He lived broadly along the Coffee Road in the later Cook County area.
  • The modern memorial's 1772 birth year, 1854 death, and Wilkes Cemetery placement.
  • The broad family structure preserved in the 1896 clan sketch.

Unresolved or derivative only

  • Whether he was appointed postmaster in March 1827 and the exact date or name of that first office.
  • The precise Coffee Road land lot and house site.
  • Original proof of either marriage and a complete child list.
  • Brushy Creek service by his sons, the 1822 court commission, and the Masonic priority claim.
  • A probate-grade death date or estate record.

docs.title: Enoch Hall of old Lowndes County, Georgia
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: Evidence-graded online dossier
docs.text: Subject: Enoch Hall, son of Sion Hall; early resident of original Irwin/Lowndes County and later Brooks County, Georgia Life dates: November 11, 1804–September 2, 1886, strongly supported by his photographed marker and Folks Huxford's county history; Telfair County as the birthplace remains a later family/local-history tradition Prepared: August 18, 2026 Standard: Original and contemporary records control. Later recollections, cemetery pages, and family traditions are labeled and never counted as independent proof merely because they were reprinted.

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
Enoch Hall was a farmer, mill-associated landholder, county official, state representative, and militia commander in the Morven neighborhood. His public career is much clearer than the family legends make it seem. Huxford's commission-based tables place him on the Lowndes Inferior Court from 1832 through 1837, in the Georgia House in 1838, as a militia major in 1834, and as colonel of the 81st Regiment in 1838. A preserved 1836 general-militia return identifies him as lieutenant colonel commanding the 2nd Battalion of the 81st Regiment. Hall's own July 14, 1838 letter to Governor George R. Gilmer verifies his later colonelcy directly: he signed as colonel commanding the regiment, reported raising four volunteer companies, and described plans to guard Lowndes settlements and move against Indians believed to be in the Okefenokee Swamp.[1][2][3][33]

The documentary record also ties Enoch and his father Sion to Land Lot 271. A transcription made by Huxford from the original 1831 Mount Zion deed names both men as grantors, while contemporary 1845–1846 sheriff-sale notices describe their interest in the lot and working saw and grist mills there.[2][7][8][9]

Several later stories do not survive comparison with the official chronology. Enoch did not introduce the 1858 bill creating Brooks County; Senator James West introduced and handled it. Enoch's supported legislative term was for Lowndes County in 1838, not as Brooks County's second representative. No located record proves that he was a Mexican War colonel. A Civil War soldiers index does contain a same-name "Enoch Hall" in the 11th Georgia Cavalry (State Guards), but it gives no age, residence, company, or rank with which to identify him as the older Brooks County man. His militia title was documented before the Mexican War. The Confederate claim remains possible but unproved.[25][28][29][36]

docs.title: Identity and chronology
docs.text:
This dossier concerns the Enoch Hall born in Georgia about 1804–1808, living in Lowndes County by 1840 and in the same neighborhood after it became part of Brooks County in 1858. The uncommon name, place continuity, census households, 1865 marriage, and 1886 estate bond form one reliable record chain.[10–14][19][20]

He must not be merged with Enoch Hall Pike, born in 1836; Enoch H. Hall, the son born about 1878; later Brooks County men named Enoch Hall; or an Enoch F. Hall returned in Civil War indexes. None of those identities supplies military service for the older man.[2][14][18]

Date Event Evidence judgment Nov. 11, 1804 Birth date from Huxford and the marker; Telfair County from Huxford and later family tradition Strong probable for date; strong secondary/traditional for county 1822–1824 Later accounts place Enoch's move with Sion to the Coffee Road settlement Probable period, exact year unresolved Nov. 8, 1831 Sion and Enoch conveyed Mount Zion religious-use land associated with Lot 271 Strong original-based secondary 1832–1837 Lowndes Inferior Court justice Strong compiled official evidence Sept. 3, 1834 Major, 158th Battalion, Lowndes militia Strong compiled official evidence 1836 Lieutenant colonel commanding the 2nd Battalion of the 81st Regiment on a Lowndes general-militia return Verified from the digitized manuscript May 21 / July 14, 1838 Colonel, 81st Regiment; original letter verifies command by July Verified by Hall's manuscript 1838 Lowndes County representative in the Georgia House Strong, from a near-contemporary profile and Huxford's roster; journal image not found online 1840–1880 Continuous Lowndes/Brooks census chain Verified 1845–1846 Lot 271 sheriff-sale notices; working saw and grist mills Verified contemporary evidence 1860 First wife Sarah/Sallie died during the Brooks smallpox epidemic, according to Huxford's use of Inferior Court minutes Strong compiled record evidence Nov. 23, 1865 Married Hannah E.
