Hall appointed administrator of Enoch's estate Verified manuscript

docs.title: Birth, parents, and arrival
docs.text:
The federal schedules vary from about 1805 to 1808. Huxford gives November 11, 1804 in Telfair County, and Enoch's weathered marker bears the same date. The agreement is strong, but no contemporary birth, baptism, Bible, or parental probate record was found online.[2][10–14][21]

Montgomery M. Folsom's memorial sketch, published within weeks of Enoch's death, calls him "the son of Sion Hall". Huxford identifies his mother as Bridget or "Beady" Hall. The 1831 joint deed, Lot 271 notices, adjacent 1840 households, and later testimony reinforce the Sion relationship. No birth or probate record directly names either parent. The publication-safe judgment is strong probable that Sion was his father; moderate that Bridget/Beady was his mother.[2–4][7–10]

The move date cannot be fixed to one year. Huxford says Enoch came with Sion in 1822 or 1823. Widow Hannah told a reporter in 1928 that he came in 1824 at age twenty. An 1820 Irwin County census index has the likely Sion household under the OCR form "Dian Hall", but that aggregate schedule does not name Enoch or locate the household within the enormous county. The safest conclusion is that Enoch was in the Coffee Road/Morven settlement by 1823 or 1824; the exact sequence remains unresolved.[2][26][31][34]

docs.title: Coffee Road claim
docs.text:
Huxford, the 1924 centennial account, and later retellings call Enoch an overseer in laying out the Coffee Road. No original contract, road return, pay record, or court order naming him was located. The 1822 legislation appointed John Coffee and Thomas Swain to superintend the state road. A separate July 1824 Irwin Inferior Court transcription names Sion Hall, James Allen, and Thomas Townsend to lay out a road from the Ocmulgee River to the Alapaha River; it does not name Enoch.[2][25]

Enoch may have assisted on a crew or segment without appearing in the surviving summaries, but that is not proved. Coffee Road overseer is a longstanding secondary tradition, not a verified office. The 1824 Ocmulgee-to-Alapaha order may concern a northern connector to the broader Coffee Road route, but its exact relationship to the state road remains unresolved.

docs.title: Land Lot 271, Mount Zion, the mills, and the Hall place
docs.text:
The property evidence is cumulative:

  1. Huxford printed a transcription he said he made from the original November 8, 1831 deed. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed roughly six acres associated with the existing church, camps, and burying ground to Methodist Episcopal trustees. The description begins at the west north-south line of Lot 271, District 12. The title reverted to the Halls if the land ceased to be used for worship. The destroyed Lowndes Deed Book A copy had been recorded at pages 654–655 in 1833.[2][7]
  2. An April 8, 1845 sheriff-sale notice levied Lot 271 as the property of Sion and Enoch Hall in the judgment "Drury Vickers vs Enoch Hall, Sion Hall and John Hall, securities on stay".[8]
  3. A March 10, 1846 repeat called the lot well improved and described a saw and grist mill in operation.[9]
  4. Hamilton W. Sharpe wrote in 1884 that Sion's place was occupied by his son Col. Enoch Hall, then over eighty, on Lot 271.[5]

This proves a Hall legal interest in Lot 271 and working mills on the levied property. It does not establish who built either mill, the final purchaser after levy, the full later title chain, or the exact location of the house. In 1902 Norman Campbell, an early resident, corrected a published account and placed the residence itself in adjacent Lot 270.[35] The property cluster is clear; the precise house parcel remains unsettled.

Folsom's 1886 articles associate Enoch closely with the mill and portray him talking politics and telling stories while customers waited for their meal. Huxford says he continued Sion's travelers' inn for a time. Those descriptions are plausible and locally specific, but no mill ledger, inn license, guest register, or advertisement was located. Mill association is strong; personal daily operation and the inn are secondary-supported.[2–6]

The 1844 Lowndes tax digest also indexes Enoch in Captain Blair's District. The entry confirms taxation and residence but does not, by itself, identify Lot 271 or transcribe his entire assessment.[17]

docs.title: County office and legislative service
docs.text:
Huxford's officer tables identify Enoch as a Lowndes Inferior Court justice commissioned January 18, 1832, recommissioned January 17, 1833, and serving through 1837. The same roster identifies him as Lowndes County's representative in the House for 1838.[2] Folsom wrote shortly after Enoch's death that his neighbors sent him to the legislature, without giving the county or year.[3][4]

Taken together, these are strong evidence of real public service. The underlying commission book, 1838 election return, and House journal page were not found online, so the precise table remains one step removed from the original record. The proper wording is: Huxford's commission-based roster identifies Hall as an Inferior Court justice from 1832 to 1837 and Lowndes representative in 1838; Folsom independently confirms the legislative tradition near Enoch's death.

docs.title: The Brooks County bill
docs.text:
The May 1924 centennial article says Enoch followed Sion in the legislature and introduced the bill forming Brooks County. A 1933 Hannah Hall obituary stream changed the story again, calling Sion Brooks County's first representative and Enoch its second.[24][25]

The official record contradicts both Brooks-specific versions:

  • Brooks County did not exist until December 11, 1858, nine years after Sion's death.
  • Senator James West introduced the Brooks County bill on November 4, 1858, moved its amendments, and obtained Senate passage. William A. Lane had drafted it after the Lowndes division convention.[28]
  • The 1859 official journals identify J. T. Edmondson in the House and Griffin of Brooks in the Senate, the first legislative session after the county's creation.[29]

Enoch's supported legislative service was the separate 1838 Lowndes House term. No inspected source gives him a role in drafting, introducing, amending, or passing the Brooks bill. Private support cannot be excluded, but the sponsor claim is contradicted.

docs.title: Militia command and the Indian conflicts
docs.text:
Huxford's tables give a promotion sequence: major of the 158th Battalion on September 3, 1834, then colonel of Lowndes County's 81st Regiment on May 21, 1838.[2] The digitized manuscript of a 1836 Lowndes general-militia return fills part of the interval. It identifies "Lieut Col Enoch Hall — Comd 2d Bat 81st Reg" under Colonel Henry Blair. Valdosta State's repository notes that the document was preserved through the Brooks County Historical Society and that these were general-militia returns, not active-service rosters.[33]

The decisive original is Enoch's July 14, 1838 letter from Lowndes County to Governor George R. Gilmer. He wrote that he had raised four volunteer companies to keep a constant guard between the settlements and the Okefenokee Swamp. He believed Indians were gathering there, intended to move into the swamp once provisions could be obtained, and asked for instructions. He signed "Enoch Hall Col. Comd. 81 Regt G.M." The wrapper identifies the same date and sender.[1]

That manuscript verifies his 1838 colonelcy, regiment, frontier command, and organization of four companies. The 1836 return separately verifies his lieutenant-colonel rank in the general militia. Neither item proves that he entered the swamp or fought at Brushy Creek.

docs.title: Brushy Creek and 1836
docs.text:
Huxford says Enoch served through the 1836 and 1838 campaigns. Hannah Hall's 1928 interview preserves elaborate family stories about his role at Brushy Creek, an Indian-language ability, a warning of an attack, and a battlefield exchange with Hamilton Sharpe.[2][26] The interview is valuable oral history, but it dates Brushy Creek to 1826 instead of 1836 and gives Enoch a colonel's title two years before the documented commission.

The official Brushy Creek report names John Pike, James A. Newman, Hamilton W. Sharpe, and Michael Young in command roles, not Enoch. The separate 1836 general-militia return proves that Enoch was then an 81st Regiment lieutenant colonel, but the repository description expressly warns that the return is not an active-service roster. Huxford says the campaign company rosters are lost. His 1836 general-militia command is strongly supported; active campaign service is secondary-supported; personal combat at Brushy Creek remains possible/traditional.[2][27][33]

docs.title: Mexican War and Civil War claims
docs.text:
The 1924 centennial article calls Enoch a Mexican War colonel and says he enlisted in the Confederate army at age sixty.[25] The documented 1834–1838 Georgia militia progression already explains the title "Colonel"; the authenticated searches described below did not locate a Mexican War record tied to this man.

Folsom's 1886 sketch says Enoch's sons Lyman and Boling went to the Civil War and that Boling returned with an injured leg; it does not say their father enlisted.[3][4] Huxford's Confederate roster names Lyman but not the elder Enoch.[2]

An 1864 Georgia census for reorganizing the militia lists an Enoch Hall, age fifty-five, in Brooks County. The name and place make him the probable subject despite the low age. That census enumerated men available for home defense; it does not establish enlistment or active service.[18]

The National Park Service-derived Civil War soldiers index adds an unresolved lead: an "Enoch Hall" served in the Confederate 11th Regiment, Georgia Cavalry (State Guards). The entry has no middle initial, but it also has no age, residence, company, or rank. A second result, "Enoch J. Hall" of the 13th Battalion Georgia Infantry (State Guards), is a distinct name. The exact-name 11th Regiment entry could be the elder Brooks County man, especially beside the 1864 home-defense census, but it does not establish identity.[36] Mexican War rank remains unverified. Confederate State Guard service is possible, not proved; the specific claim that Enoch enlisted at sixty still lacks an identifying service record.

docs.title: Sarah or Sallie Self
docs.text:
Huxford identifies Enoch's first wife as Sallie, daughter of Thomas Self, and their sons as Lyman and Bolen G. Hall. The 1850 schedule independently places Sarah, age thirty-four, with Enoch, Lyman, and Bolen. The 1860 schedule again places Sarah, age forty-six, in Enoch's household. "Sallie" is a familiar form of "Sarah", so the fit is close.[2][11][12]

Huxford's smallpox account, drawn from Brooks Inferior Court expenses, says Sallie Hall, wife of Col. Enoch Hall, died during the 1860 epidemic and that the county paid for her coffin and medical treatment. The original minute image was not located. No marriage record, grave marker, memorial, or probate file for Sarah/Sallie was found. Sarah/Sallie as first wife is strong probable; Self surname and Thomas Self parentage are moderate; her exact death date and burial remain unresolved.[2]

The additional Sarah Hall, twenty-three, and Nancy Hall, two, in the 1860 household must not be assigned automatically. The schedule gives no relationships. They could be Lyman's wife and child, but that remains unresolved.[12]

docs.title: Hannah Elizabeth Gornto
docs.text:
The Brooks County marriage record identifies Enoch Hall and H. E. Gornto marrying November 23, 1865. The 1870 household includes Enoch, Hannah, Sion, and infant Joel. The 1880 schedule explicitly calls H. E. Hall Enoch's wife and identifies Sion, Joel, and Enoch H. as sons.[13][14][19]

Hannah's 1933 death certificate names her as Hannah Elizabeth Hall, gives her father as Joel Gornto and mother as Mary Blair, and records burial in Hall Cemetery. The informant was her son J. L. Hall. Her contemporary obituary names the three surviving sons and repeats several family traditions assessed separately in this dossier.[23][24]

The estate evidence is even better. On December 6, 1886, Hannah E. Hall executed an administration bond after being appointed administrator of Enoch Hall's estate. The manuscript proves the estate proceeding and Hannah's role; it is not a will and does not name heirs or distribute property.[20]

docs.title: Publication-safe child structure
docs.text:
• Lyman Hall, born about 1835: in the 1850 and 1860 households; Huxford names him as a son of the first marriage. Strong probable son.[2][11][12]
  • Bolen/Bolin G. Hall, born about 1838: in the 1850 household; Huxford names him as the other first-marriage son. Strong probable son.[2][11]
  • Sion L. Hall, born about 1868: age two in Enoch and Hannah's 1870 household and explicitly a son in 1880. He later became a Barney merchant, the first recorded justice of the peace for the 1571st (Barney) District, and Barney's first mayor. Huxford's commission list begins the district with S. L. Hall on February 16, 1899, and a newspaper that November independently called him justice of the peace when his store, the post office inside it, and his legal papers burned. The mayoral evidence is explained below. Verified son; first recorded Barney-district justice of the peace and first mayor strongly supported.[2][13][14][37][38][39][40]
  • Joel L. Hall, born April 11, 1870: a two-month-old infant in 1870, explicitly a son in 1880, and living with mother Hannah in 1900. His Find a Grave page incorrectly says 1880, but the photographed marker reads April 11, 1870 and agrees with both censuses. Verified son.[13][14][22][32]
  • Enoch Hitch Hall, born about 1878: explicitly a son in 1880 and living with Hannah and Joel in 1900. Verified son.[14][22]

The list is not complete. In 1900 Hannah reported six children born and three living. Sion, Joel, and Enoch Hitch were all alive. The natural reading is that three additional children, probably of her marriage to Enoch, had died before 1900 and remain unidentified; the census does not name their father. Huxford's three-son list therefore describes the identifiable or surviving sons, not every child Hannah bore.[22]

Sion L. Hall is strongly supported as Barney's first mayor. The town charter, approved August 6, 1903, scheduled Barney's first municipal election for the first Wednesday in December 1903. Barely a month later, the January 8, 1904 Adel News reported: "Mayor S. L. Hall, of Barney, was a visitor to Adel Sunday." The original image reads S. L., although an earlier research index misread the first initial as J. A second notice on June 24 referred to "Mayor Hall of Barney." Neither notice calls Hall the first mayor or substitutes for the missing election return. Taken together, however, the charter and the two notices strongly support identifying him as the inaugural mayor. W. E. Hiers, elected in December 1905, was the next documented mayor rather than the first.[38][39][40][41]

docs.title: Farming, property, and enslaved people
docs.text:
The federal records show Enoch's changing household economy:

  • 1840: three enslaved people: one male aged ten to twenty-three, one female under ten, and one female aged ten to twenty-three.[10]
  • 1850: farmer with $2,000 in real estate; slave schedule records a woman aged twenty and a boy aged one.[11][15]
  • 1860: farmer with $1,750 in personal property; slave schedule records a woman aged thirty and boys aged eleven and nine.[12][16]
  • 1870: farmer with $1,000 real estate and $610 personal estate.[13]
  • 1880: farmer, age seventy-five, recorded as blind.[14]

The 1850 woman aged twenty and the 1860 woman aged thirty may be the same person. The 1850 infant boy may be the eleven-year-old in 1860. Those age progressions are suggestive, not proof. The schedules omit personal names. This dossier does not invent identities for the people Enoch enslaved or describe the population-schedule wealth figures as a complete estate valuation.

docs.title: Later life and character
docs.text:
Sharpe described Enoch in 1884 as over eighty and still living on Lot 271.[5] Folsom visited the neighborhood in 1886 and wrote about the old Hall house, well, mill site, Enoch's declining sight, and his habit of recognizing friends by voice. His posthumous sketch remembers a high voice, political talk, practical jokes, and phrases that became local sayings.[3][4][6]

These details are valuable as a near-contemporary portrait, but their exact source is not always stated. They should remain Folsom's recollections rather than be rewritten as documentary facts. Hannah's 1928 interview likewise records family relics she attributed to Enoch and Sion; the reporter saw the objects, but their age and chain of ownership rest on Hannah's testimony.[26]

docs.title: Death, estate, and burial
docs.text:
Enoch's photographed Hall Cemetery marker reads "COLONEL ENOCH HALL / BORN NOV. 11, 1804 / DIED SEP. 2, 1886". Huxford independently gives the same dates and says Enoch died at home near Morven. The December 6 administration bond is consistent with a September death.[2][20][21]

Two September 14 statewide briefs say he died "Thursday last", which, read literally on that publication date, would mean September 9.[30] The phrase may have been copied unchanged from an earlier weekly or local report. The photographed inscription plus Huxford's exact agreement outweigh the stale relative wording, but the conflict should remain visible. The marker inscription is verified; November 11, 1804–September 2, 1886 as the actual dates is strong probable. Death near Morven and burial in Hall Cemetery are also strong probable.

No will, inventory, appraisal, year's support, estate sale, heir petition, distribution, or final settlement was found in the authenticated Georgia Wills and Probate Records search (Ancestry collection 8635) under Enoch Hall, death 1886, Brooks County, or in the opened record's linked material. Hannah's bond proves that an estate proceeding existed, not that the surviving online packet is complete.

docs.title: Verified or strongly supported
docs.text:
• One Enoch Hall remained in the same Lowndes/Brooks neighborhood from 1840 through 1880.[10–14]
  • Sion was his father, on the combined joint-property and near-contemporary biographical evidence.[3][7–9]
  • He held an interest in Lot 271 and was associated with operating saw and grist mills.[7–9]
  • Huxford's official rosters identify him as a Lowndes Inferior Court justice and Lowndes representative in 1838; Folsom independently supports the legislative service, but not the court office.[2–4]
  • A preserved 1836 manuscript return identifies him as lieutenant colonel commanding the 2nd Battalion of the 81st Regiment; his 1838 letter proves his later colonelcy and organization of four volunteer companies.[1][33]
  • He married Hannah E. Gornto in 1865, and she administered his estate in 1886.[19][20]
  • He enslaved people in 1840, 1850, and 1860.[10][15][16]

docs.title: Probable or traditional, with limits
docs.text:
• November 11, 1804 as the birth date and September 2, 1886 as the death date near Morven.[2][21][30]
  • Telfair County as the birthplace, based on Huxford and later family tradition rather than a contemporary birth record.[2][26]
  • Bridget/Beady Hall as his mother.[2]
  • Sarah/Sallie Self as first wife and Thomas Self as her father.[2][11][12]
  • Active service in the 1836 regional Indian campaign is secondary-supported; personal combat at Brushy Creek remains possible/traditional.[2][26][27][33]
  • Work as a daily miller, continuance of Sion's inn, and the exact route/date of his move.[2–6]

docs.title: Unproved or contradicted
docs.text:
• Coffee Road overseer: repeated later, but no original road record names Enoch.
  • Brooks County bill sponsor: contradicted; James West introduced and carried the 1858 bill.[28]
  • First or second Brooks County representative: contradicted by chronology and the 1859 journals.[29]
  • Mexican War colonel: not found in the documented searches; the title is documented in Georgia militia before the Mexican War, and the failed collection probe is disclosed below.
  • Confederate enlistment at sixty: a same-name 11th Georgia Cavalry (State Guards) index entry is possible but lacks identifying details; the 1864 militia census proves enumeration for home defense, not enlistment.[18][36]
  • Complete child list: contradicted by Hannah's report of six births when only three second-family sons have been identified.[22]

docs.title: Online research coverage and limits
docs.text:
Local evidence was searched first across the Sion Hall dossier, early-settlement reports, Barney household work, retained Huxford text, memory files, newspaper result sets, deed/source extracts, and prior user corrections.

Authenticated Ancestry searches covered the 1830–1900 federal censuses, 1850 and 1860 slave schedules, Georgia marriage records, the 1844 tax digest, 1864 militia-reorganization census, Georgia probate records, and Georgia death records. The 1840–1880 population chain, 1865 marriage, and 1886 administration bond carry exact collection, record, image, and page references below. The 1870 manuscript image was reopened: it shows Enoch, Hannah, Sion/Lion, and infant Joel together; the 1870 schedule itself records no relationships, so the 1865 marriage and 1880 relationship fields control the family interpretation.[13][14][19]

Newspapers.com searches used "Enoch Hall", "E. Hall", "Col. Enoch Hall", "Colonel Enoch Hall", and combinations with Lowndes, Brooks, Morven, legislature, died, estate, Hannah, Gornto, Lyman, Boling/Bolling, Indian, militia, Mexican, and Confederate across authenticated Georgia coverage from 1800 to 1950. Georgia Historic Newspapers supplied the 1845–1846 sheriff-sale notices. The important located newspaper streams were Sharpe's 1884 recollection; Folsom's July and September 1886 articles and the September death briefs; the 1924 centennial; the 1928 Hannah interview; and Edna Cain Daniel's 1933 Hannah obituary and reprints.

The Georgia Archives File II name collection produced Hall's four-image July 14, 1838 letter. Valdosta State's South Georgia Folklife Collection supplied the digitized 1836 Lowndes general-militia return; its repository description and roster page were inspected, and the retained PDF's SHA-256 is 9bed3eca1658be51b4459eaebf2d84a8bcecea3b572a6c0a248ada2d012a9877.[33] Georgia Archives colonial/headright plat indexes also return an older Enoch Hall in Montgomery County in 1799, 1801, and 1803; those records predate the subject's birth and were excluded rather than folded into his land history.

Military searches were rerun on August 19, 2026, through authenticated Ancestry. Exact/broad searches used "Enoch Hall", birth 1804 Georgia, residence Brooks/Georgia, and the keywords "war", "Mexican War", and "Confederate". The U.S. Civil War Soldiers collection (1138) was then searched directly for Enoch Hall in Georgia; records 1816806 and 1795992 were opened. The first is the unresolved exact-name 11th Georgia Cavalry State Guards entry; the second is "Enoch J. Hall". The Civil War Pension Index (4654) was searched for Enoch Hall with Georgia residence and returned no candidate tied to Brooks County. The dedicated military-category URL and attempted Mexican War collection probe returned Ancestry page-not-found errors, so no claim of an exhaustive Mexican War collection search is made. Newspaper searches covered "Mexican", "Mexican War", "Confederate", "enlisted", and "age sixty" within the documented 1800–1950 Georgia search window. The safe conclusion is "not found in the documented search", not "no record exists".[36]

The official 1858 Brooks County act, Senate passage sequence, and 1859 House/Senate journals were checked. The public FamilySearch profile and Find a Grave pages were used only as derivative leads unless a photographed marker controlled.

"Fully researched online" here means the accessible online collections, saved subscription material, and identified leads were searched and reconciled. It does not mean every courthouse or manuscript record is digitized. The 1838 House journal/election return, original Inferior Court commissions and minutes, 1836 active-service muster/pay rolls, full Brooks estate packet, complete deed/tax chain, Hall family Bible, and named records for the people Enoch enslaved were not found online. Those are disclosed access gaps, not evidence that the records never existed.

docs.title: Best next archival work
docs.text:
1. Obtain the 1832–1838 Georgia Executive Department commission entries, 1838 House journal/election return, and original Lowndes Inferior Court minutes.
  2. Search active-service pay rolls, muster rolls, requisitions, and governor correspondence for Enoch in 1834–1838, especially Brushy Creek and the four companies mentioned in his July 1838 letter.
  3. Browse Brooks County estate volumes and loose papers from September 1886 forward for inventory, appraisal, sale, annual returns, heir petitions, and final settlement.
  4. Build the complete deed and tax chain for Lots 270 and 271, including the result of the 1845–1846 levy and the later Hall succession.
  5. Locate Sarah/Sallie Hall's marriage, 1860 death entry, coffin-payment minute, and grave; seek records identifying the three deceased children Hannah reported in 1900.
  6. Use estate, deed, church, Freedmen's Bureau, and post-emancipation labor records to seek the names of people enslaved by the Hall household.

docs.title: Citation audit
docs.text: All 41 numbered sources are cited in the body. Original records control where accessible. Reprints are grouped as single evidence streams, namesakes are separated, the people Enoch enslaved are not assigned invented names, and conflicts in the Coffee Road, Brushy Creek, Brooks County, war-service, child-list, and death-date claims remain visible.

docs.title: Francis Rountree of early Lowndes County
docs.text:
Back to the Early History Profiles index

Research completed: August 19, 2026 Geographic scope: original Irwin and early Lowndes counties, with Brooks County sources used for retrospective context, and a possible later migration to Madison/Taylor counties, Florida Controlled name: Francis Rountree Variants searched: Francis, Frances, and Frank; Rountree, Roundtree, Rowntree, Rauntree, and OCR forms including Kowntree

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Francis Rountree was a white male landholder and enslaver in early Lowndes County. His 1840 household included five people employed in agriculture, but the schedule does not assign Francis an occupation.[5][7][8][9][10][11] Georgia's 1837 official digest says the county's temporary court-and-election place was moved from Sion Hall's house to Francis Roundtree's house in 1826. Nineteenth-century recollections also place an early Superior Court term there, on property later known as part of Remer Young's farm. The official digest proves the statutory designation; actual court use rests on the retrospective accounts. The evidence does not settle which early session should be called the first Lowndes Superior Court.[1][2][3][4][12][13]

The original 1830 Lowndes census and tax records, followed by tax and census records through 1840, establish a strong continuous Lowndes identity. The household head aged from 30-39 in 1830 to 40-49 in 1840; the adult woman's age band and the younger females' age progression also fit. Tax digests place him in the districts of Captains Folsom, Godwin, Caswell, and Varner and tie him to Lowndes District 12 land lots 36, 56, 82, and 83. The records use Francis, Frances, Roundtree, Rountree, and Rowntree. Those are spelling variants, not evidence of different sexes or people.[5][6][7][8][9][10][11]

Folks Huxford's 1948 county history reports that Francis was commissioned second lieutenant in the 658th Militia District on January 17, 1827, and captain on August 9, 1827. The dates and office sequence are specific, but no original commission-book image was located online. The militia claim is therefore strong secondary evidence, not newly verified original evidence. A different index names a Francis Roundtree as a private in Whitfield's Detachment during the Florida War; nothing in that index identifies him as the Lowndes man, and it cannot be used to prove the 1827 offices.[4][18]

His origins, wife, named children, relationship to pioneer James Rountree, exact death, burial, and estate remain unresolved. A possible record chain continues to a Francis and Rebecca Roundtree in Madison County, Florida, in 1850 and to a 66-year-old Francis Roundtree recorded in Taylor County's 1860 mortality schedule as having died in December during the preceding census year, probably December 1859. The name, age-band compatibility, border geography, and household/property pattern offer a plausible match, but no located deed, probate record, or named family document bridges Lowndes to Florida. The candidate ages also conflict: fifty in 1850 versus sixty-six about nine years later. That continuation is possible, not strong probable or verified.[15][16][17]

docs.title: Identity and names
docs.text:
The controlling 1830 record is the Lowndes County household on NARA roll 19, printed page 82, Ancestry record 1850862. Ancestry indexes the handwritten entry as "Frances Kowntree [Frances Rowntree]"; the manuscript surname is difficult, but the row is the local Rountree household. A separate 1830 record for Francis Rountree in Youngs Valley, Talbot County, is a different man and is excluded from this dossier.[5][20]

The records do not support one rigid original spelling:

  • Georgia's 1837 digest prints "Francis Roundtree".[1]
  • The 1830 Lowndes census index reads "Frances ... Rowntree", while the manuscript is ambiguous.[5]
  • The 1830 tax index reads "Francis Roundtree".[6]
  • The 1834 and 1835 tax indexes read "Francis Rountree".[7][8]
  • The 1838 and 1840 tax indexes use "Frances Rowntree" or "Frances Rountree".[9][10]
  • The 1840 census index reads "Francis Rountree".[11]

This dossier uses Francis Rountree as an editorial control name because Francis is the dominant male given-name form in the official digest and census/tax chain. "Frances" must remain in the search ledger because clerks and indexers used it.

Several same-name records were rejected or separated:

  • The Talbot County household in 1830 had an adult couple, two boys, and one enslaved girl. It is not the Lowndes household, which had three girls and four enslaved people.[5][20]
  • A user-contributed Ancestry tree places a Francis Rountree born in Burke County in 1787, married to Henrietta Lester, and dead in Lowndes in 1836 while also attaching a Talbot residence. The death claim is contradicted for this subject by his original 1840 Lowndes census and tax records. The tree is a lead, not evidence.[19]
  • Later Francis/Frances/Frank Rountrees in Georgia newspapers, censuses, and cemeteries were not merged with the subject without a dated bridge.

docs.title: Court and election site
docs.text:
Lowndes County was created from Irwin County in December 1825. Oliver H. Prince's official 1837 digest gives the controlling legal summary on printed page 955:

"Courts and elections to be held at the house of Sion Hall, 1825 ... Removed to the house of Francis Roundtree, 1826."[1]

A December 5, 1826 legislative report confirms passage of a bill amending the organizing act concerning the holding of courts and elections at Sion Hall's. That report corroborates the change but does not name the destination; Prince's 1837 digest supplies Francis Roundtree's house. Neither source says that Francis was a judge, justice, clerk, commissioner, or lawyer.[1][2]

The session chronology is less certain than the legal designation:

  • Hamilton W. Sharpe wrote in 1884 that the first temporary organization and election took place at Hall's residence and that at least one Superior Court term later met at Francis Rountree's.[3]
  • Huxford reprinted William Smith's December 1880 recollection. Smith placed the first Superior Court at Sion Hall's on the first Monday in January 1827 and the next at Rountree's house in early 1828. He located Rountree's house in the old part of Remer Young's farm and said Rountree then owned the place.[4]
  • R. E. L. Folsom's 1899 historical sketch assigned the first Lowndes court to Rountree's place in 1827. A 1900 sketch and later reprints repeated related versions.[12][13][14]

These accounts were written decades after the events and disagree about date and sequence. The safest conclusion is:

Verified: Francis Rountree's house became the legally designated Lowndes court-and-election place in 1826. Strong probable: an early Superior Court term was actually held there. Unresolved: whether that term occurred in 1827 or early 1828 and whether it should be called the county's first or second Superior Court.

No online deed was found tying the site to Remer Young or supplying a land lot for the house. "Remer Young's farm" is an important retrospective location clue, not a proved title chain.

docs.title: Militia service
docs.text:
Huxford's officer table for the 658th Georgia Militia District lists:

  • "Francis Rountree, Jan. 17, 1827" among second lieutenants;
  • "Francis Rountree, Aug. 9, 1827" among captains.[4]

The sequence is plausible and the dates are exact enough to suggest that Huxford worked from commission records, but the book does not reproduce the commissions on the cited page. No original Georgia militia commission, election return, muster roll, or pay roll was found online in this project. The defensible grade is strong secondary evidence.

An Ancestry/NARA index separately lists "Francis Roundtree", private, Whitfield's Detachment, Georgia Militia, Florida War. It gives no residence, age, family, service dates, or county. It is possible that this was the same man, but the index does not prove it. It also does not corroborate the earlier captaincy because it names the soldier as a private in a different unit and context.[18]

docs.title: 1830 Lowndes census
docs.text:
The original schedule records a nine-person household:[5]

  • one white male aged 30-39;
  • one white female aged 30-39;
  • three white girls: one under five, one aged 5-9, and one aged 10-14;
  • four enslaved people: one boy under ten, two girls under ten, and one woman aged 24-35.

The census names only the household head. It does not identify the adult woman as his wife, name the three girls as daughters, or name any enslaved person.

docs.title: 1840 Lowndes census
docs.text:
The 1840 schedule records twenty people:[11]

  • one white male aged 40-49;
  • one white female aged 40-49;
  • three white girls: one under five, one aged 10-14, and one aged 15-19;
  • fifteen enslaved people: two boys under ten, one man aged 36-54, seven girls under ten, three females aged 10-23, one woman aged 24-35, and one woman aged 36-54;
  • five people employed in agriculture;
  • one white person over twenty reported unable to read and write.

The age progression strongly supports the same Lowndes household head in 1830 and 1840. It does not establish the identity or relationship of any other person.

docs.title: Tax snapshots
docs.text:
Original tax-page images were inspected. They record separate annual snapshots, not a continuous biography of the enslaved people or proof that the same individuals remained in the household:

Tax year District label Polls Enslaved people on original page Land evidence 1830 Captain Folsom 1 blank or not legible; the index's 7 is not accepted over the page one visible District 12 Lowndes entry associated with Lot 56; columns require cautious reading 1834 Captain Godwin 1 10 Lowndes District 12, Lots 56, 83, 82, and 36 1835 Captain Caswell 1 11 same four district/lot entries 1838 Captain Caswell 1 14 same four Lowndes lots plus an ambiguous fifth line that appears to concern 100 acres in Bulloch County 1840 Captain Varner 1 15 same four district/lot entries

The land columns use acreage/class or quality subdivisions that should not be flattened into simple total-acre figures. The legible raw tuples are:

  • 1834 and 1835 tax-digest entries were reviewed for the reported tracts.
  • The 1838 digest contains four relevant tract entries and an ambiguous Bulloch County line.
  • 1840: the 1834/1835 four-lot pattern returns.[7][8][9][10]

The 1834 page associates the four tracts with grantee names W. B. Lester, C. Crimm, J. Roberts, and J. Stafford and identifies Little River. Those fields help distinguish the property rows but do not prove that Rountree received the land directly from those people.

The difference between the 1840 tax total of fifteen enslaved people and the population-census total of fifteen is consistent. Earlier changes from four people in the 1830 census to ten, eleven, and fourteen in later tax years cannot be turned into a purchase history. No names, transfers, deaths, sales, hires, family connections, or individual continuity are shown.

docs.title: Land and economic position
docs.text:
The tax chain proves substantial taxable interests in four District 12 Lowndes lots by 1834 and through 1840. It does not by itself prove that his residence stood on any one of them. The court-house site might have been on one of these tracts, on property held under a different title, or at the place later remembered as Remer Young's farm. A deed chain is needed before assigning the house to a particular lot.[7][8][9][10]

The household and tax records show that Rountree farmed within an economy built on enslaved labor. The 1840 census reports five people employed in agriculture but does not identify which free or enslaved household members were counted as workers.[11]

docs.title: Family and relationship to James Rountree
docs.text:
No located original record names Francis's wife, parents, children, or siblings. The adult woman in the 1830 and 1840 households was probably his wife, but the censuses do not state the relationship or her name.[5][11]

Huxford's main text says sisters Harriet and Nancy Rountree, wives of brothers James and John McMullen, were daughters of Francis. Huxford's own corrections section reverses that statement and says they were daughters of James Rountree and Nancy Hendley. The correction controls the book's earlier claim. Harriet and Nancy therefore cannot be assigned to Francis from Huxford.[4]

No deed, probate record, Bible record, obituary, or contemporary family notice was found proving that Francis was the brother, son, cousin, or other relative of pioneer James Rountree, who died in 1834. The men shared a surname and lived in early Lowndes County; that is not kinship proof. A prior local-history sentence calling Francis James's brother is unsupported and should not be repeated.

The user-contributed Ancestry tree claim that Francis married Henrietta Lester is also unproved and appears entangled with the Talbot County namesake and the contradicted 1836 death claim.[19][20]

docs.title: Possible move to Florida and death
docs.text:
An 1850 Madison County, Florida, census record identifies Francis Roundtree, age fifty, Georgia-born farmer, with $1,000 in real estate, and Rebecca Roundtree, also age fifty and Georgia-born. The corresponding slave schedule lists twenty-one enslaved people under Francis's name.[15][16]

An indexed 1860 mortality-schedule entry records Francis Roundtree, age sixty-six, Georgia-born farmer, dying in Taylor County, Florida, in December. Mortality schedules for the 1860 census covered the year ending June 1, 1860, so this probably means December 1859, not December 1860. The original schedule was not inspected.[17]

This is a plausible candidate continuation because:

  • the 1850 age is compatible with the 1840 Lowndes 40-49 band, but the mortality index's age sixty-six about nine years later is a material conflict;
  • the name, adult-couple household, border geography, and broad property pattern are compatible;
  • Madison and Taylor counties lie just south of the Georgia border;
  • the enslaved-property scale is broadly compatible with the 1840 Lowndes record.

The chain is not verified. No located Lowndes sale deed, Florida purchase deed, tax roll, probate file, migration notice, or named relative links the Georgia and Florida households. Rebecca's relationship is indexed as inferred, not stated on the census. The 1860 mortality entry is itself a derivative index; the original mortality schedule was not inspected. Therefore:

Possible: the Lowndes man was the Francis Roundtree in Madison County in 1850 and the Francis recorded as dying in Taylor County in December during the year ending June 1, 1860, probably December 1859. Unresolved: Rebecca's maiden name, marriage, children, exact death day and cause, burial, estate, and any heirs.

docs.title: Evidence matrix
docs.text: Question Best evidence Grade Boundary Adult resident of early Lowndes original 1830 and 1840 censuses; original tax pages Verified only head is named in censuses House made court/election site in 1826 1837 official digest and 1826 legislative report Verified statutory site, not an office held by Francis Early Superior Court actually met there Sharpe 1884; Smith 1880 via Huxford; Folsom 1899 Strong probable exact first/second sequence and 1827/1828 date conflict 658th District second lieutenant and captain in 1827 Huxford's specific officer table Strong secondary original commission images not found District 12 Lots 36, 56, 82, and 83 original 1834-1840 tax images Verified taxable entries residence lot and full title chain unresolved Wife and children age-banded census households only Unresolved no names or stated relationships Kinship to James Rountree surname and proximity only Unresolved Huxford's Harriet/Nancy attribution was corrected away from Francis Move to Madison/Taylor, Florida 1850 census, slave schedule, 1860 mortality index Possible no direct Georgia-to-Florida bridge; ages conflict Death probably in December 1859 derivative 1860 mortality index for Florida candidate Possible for Lowndes subject schedule covers year ending June 1, 1860; original and identity bridge absent Burial and estate no matching verified memorial or probate file found Unresolved courthouse/manual volumes may contain records not indexed online

docs.title: Online research coverage and limits
docs.text:
The investigation began with stored Lowndes, Brooks, Rountree, Sion Hall, William Blair, John Pike, census, newspaper, and local-book evidence. It then searched authenticated Ancestry census, tax, marriage, probate, military, mortality, slave-schedule, and cemetery collections; Newspapers.com; Georgia Historic Newspapers; Internet Archive; Huxford's county history; the 1837 Georgia law digest; FamilySearch/public genealogy leads; Find a Grave; and general web results.

Searches used all controlled name variants with Lowndes, Irwin, Brooks, Burke, Talbot, Madison, Taylor, Remer Young, Sion Hall, first court, Superior Court, militia, captain, lieutenant, Florida War, Lot 56, Withlacoochee, Little River, wife, child, heir, marriage, probate, estate, administrator, death, burial, and cemetery. Newspapers.com searches covered 1800-1950. Georgia Historic Newspapers searches covered the available corpus with the same core variants. Results were adjudicated against place, age, household, date, and occupation before use.

No pre-1850 contemporary newspaper item naming the Lowndes Francis was found in the documented full-text searches. Useful newspaper accounts begin with retrospective county histories in 1884 and 1899; later reprints are not independent proof. OCR limitations remain, especially for "Frances", "Rowntree", initials, damaged columns, and unindexed legal notices.

"Fully researched online" means the accessible online collections and known leads were searched and reconciled. It does not mean undigitized courthouse and archival records were examined. The following remain unavailable or uninspected:

  • original 1825 and 1826 session-law pages behind the 1837 digest references;
  • original Lowndes Superior Court minutes or docket for 1826-1828;
  • original 1827 Georgia militia commission entries;
  • complete Lowndes deed indexes and books for the four District 12 lots and Remer Young chain;
  • Lowndes ordinary minutes, wills, bonds, inventories, sales, returns, and loose estates;
  • original Florida deeds, tax rolls, 1860 mortality schedule, probate, and cemetery records for the candidate continuation;
  • any family Bible, church record, or direct record naming Francis's wife, children, or relationship to James.

docs.title: Best next archival work
docs.text:
1. Obtain the exact 1825 and 1826 Georgia session laws cited as volume IV, pages 128, 134, and 237; transcribe the full language and effective dates.
  2. Search surviving Lowndes Superior Court dockets, minutes, writs, jury lists, and clerk papers for 1826-1828 and the James D. Shanks perjury case.
  3. Request Georgia militia commission-book images for Francis Rountree's January 17 and August 9, 1827 entries in the 658th District.
  4. Trace District 12 Lots 36, 56, 82, and 83 through Irwin/Lowndes/Brooks deeds, tax digests, plats, grants, executions, and later conveyances; separately trace Remer Young's title.
  5. Search Lowndes probate volumes and loose papers after 1840 under every surname variant, then repeat in Madison and Taylor counties, Florida, through 1865.
  6. Inspect the original 1850 Madison population and slave schedules and the 1860 Taylor mortality schedule; search adjoining households and deeds for Rebecca and named relatives.
  7. Review cemetery surveys and marker photographs in southern Georgia and Madison/Taylor counties for a matching Francis and Rebecca.
  8. Search deeds, probate inventories, bills of sale, church records, and post-emancipation records for names and family continuity of people enslaved by the household.

docs.title: Preservation and citation audit
docs.text:
The project preserves original images for the 1830 and 1840 Lowndes censuses, the 1830/1834/1835/1838/1840 tax pages, and the correct printed page 955 of Prince's 1837 digest. The initially downloaded Prince image was discovered to be printed page 986; it was moved to rejected-evidence and replaced before drafting. The Talbot County 1830 record is cited only as an excluded namesake.

The newspaper pages, Huxford pages, 1850 Florida population and slave schedules, 1860 mortality schedule, and military index card are not preserved in this evidence folder. Their links and record IDs are retained, but subscription access or another repository may be needed to reopen them. This is a real preservation gap, not a complete offline source set.

All narrative claims distinguish original/contemporary evidence, retrospective accounts, indexes, trees, and unresolved inferences. The exact first-court date, original militia commissions, family, James kinship, Florida continuity, death, burial, and probate remain open rather than being filled by assumption.

docs.title: Hamilton W. Sharpe (c. 1807–1890)
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: An evidence-based dossier on an early settler of Lowndes County, Georgia
docs.text: Research completed: August 18, 2026 Geographic scope: original Lowndes County, present Brooks County, and connected records in Tattnall and Thomas counties Name forms searched: Hamilton W. Sharpe, Hamilton Wynn Sharpe, Hamilton Sharpe, Hamilton Sharp, H. W. Sharpe, H. W. Sharp, Hamp Sharpe, Sharpe's Store, and Sharp's Store

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Hamilton W. Sharpe was an early merchant, postmaster, justice, legislator, Methodist lay preacher, militia correspondent, planter, and slaveholder in the part of original Lowndes County that became Brooks County. The record chain begins with his March 5, 1827 marriage to Jane Perry in Tattnall County and places him in Lowndes County by the 1830 census. Later accounts say he reached the Sion Hall settlement on the Coffee Road in 1826 or 1827 and opened a small log store nearby. That early-store chronology is credible local tradition, partly derived from Sharpe's own late-life recollections, but no located deed, daybook, or contemporary 1826 record proves the exact date or footprint.[2][18][20]

The postal evidence requires a distinction that earlier summaries often blur. Folks Huxford reported from Post Office Department records that Sharpe's Store opened April 2, 1828 with Hamilton as postmaster. The original federal appointment register directly inspected for this dossier begins later and proves Hamilton's January 28, 1837 reappointment when the office changed back from Magnum to Sharpe's Store. It does not independently prove the 1828 opening.[2][8]

Sharpe's place in the community is otherwise unusually well documented. Original 1836–1838 letters show him communicating with Georgia's governor about militia horses, fraudulent muster claims, and Florida-border troop rotations.[9] Census and tax records trace his household and wealth from 1830 through 1880.[4][6][10][13][14][15] His signed 1846 postal letter, contemporary newspaper uses of Sharpe's Store, his own 1884 history articles, and an 1885 character sketch show the public identity remembered locally as “Judge,” “Rev.,” “Captain,” and “Uncle Hamp.”[16][17][18][19] The titles “Judge” and “Rev.” have documentary support. “Captain” is a strong local tradition, but no commission or original roster was located.[2][9][19]

docs.title: Identity and family
docs.text:
The 1827 Tattnall County marriage register identifies the couple as Hamilton W. Sharpe and Jane Perry.[1] The recurring middle initial, Jane's continued presence, the Lowndes/Thomas/Quitman migration, and consistent occupation and age patterns join the later records into one life. The census ages vary: the 1850 entry implies birth around 1800, the 1860 entry around 1808, and the 1870 and 1880 entries around 1807. Later cemetery compilations give April 10, 1807. No original birth or baptismal record was located, so the exact date should be treated as derivative rather than contemporary.[13][14][15][21]

Online family trees and cemetery pages identify his parents as John Sharpe and Elizabeth “Betsey” Wynn. That parentage may be correct, but it was not established here by an original record. It is therefore a lead, not a proved conclusion.[21]

The 1850 Thomas County census places H. W. Sharpe and Jane in an extended household with apparent children William, Ellen, James, Jane, and Betsey Thomas. The manuscript's surname conventions are not perfectly clear. A contemporary 1867 marriage announcement independently calls Betsey Thomas the youngest daughter of “Rev. Hamilton W. and Jane Sharpe,” making her identification strong even though the census indexing is awkward.[13][22] William H. Sharpe later appears in Morven records and must not be merged with his father. A Florida probate record sometimes returned in Hamilton searches belongs to that son, whose wife was Frances A.; it is not Hamilton's estate.[23]

docs.title: Arrival, store, and the formation of Sharpe's Store
docs.text:
Huxford's 1948 history says Hamilton came from Tattnall County in 1826–1827 and built a small log store on the Coffee Road near Sion Hall's residence and inn, about a mile or more northeast of present Morven. Sharpe's own April 5, 1884 recollection likewise connected his merchant activity, Hall's settlement, the mail route, and the place-name Sharpe's Store.[2][18] An 1899 Morven history gives a more complicated merchant succession: Bradbury & Hayden began nearby in 1826, followed by Judge H. W. Sharpe and later W. H. Sharpe. These accounts confirm Hamilton's early commercial importance but do not establish one uncontested “first store” narrative.[20]

The best geographic conclusion is neighborhood-level. Sion Hall and Mount Zion were associated with Land Lot 271 in the Twelfth District, and the 1908 Brooks County map locates the Mount Zion/Camp Ground cluster there.[2][24] No located deed, plat, or map proves Hamilton owned Lot 271 or fixes his store on a particular parcel. Later derivative deed indexing points instead to Hamilton's acquisition of land in Lots 186 and 229 in the 1860s, but the underlying deed images were not available for direct inspection. Those entries remain archival leads rather than final proof.[2]

docs.title: Postal service
docs.text:
Huxford's compilation of Post Office Department records gives this sequence:[2]

  • Lowndes Court-house opened March 31, 1827.
  • Sharpe's Store opened April 2, 1828, with Hamilton W. Sharpe as postmaster.
  • The office became Magnum on April 1, 1836 under John Hall.
  • It returned to Sharpe's Store on January 28, 1837 under Hamilton.
  • James Perry became postmaster December 14, 1848; Hamilton returned August 16, 1849.
  • The office became Morven on July 21, 1853.

The original appointment register confirms the January 28, 1837 Hamilton entry.[8] Sharpe's own 1884 account apparently dated the first office to fall 1827. The conflict should not be silently harmonized: his version was written more than fifty years later, whereas Huxford said his dates came from department records.[2][18]

Sharpe's signed December 28, 1846 letter is direct evidence of his work as postmaster. Answering a complaint from the Okapilco office, he discussed postage, routes, and his handling of mail at Sharpe's Store.[16] Newspaper notices in 1848 and 1850 use “Sharp's Store” or “Sharpe's Store” as a recognized postal locality, while an 1868 notice shows the old place-name still in local use after the office had become Morven.[17]

docs.title: Public office and politics
docs.text:
Huxford's compiled office tables identify Sharpe as a justice of the peace in the 660th militia district beginning in 1827; a Lowndes Inferior Court justice beginning in 1829, again in 1838, and again in 1841; and Lowndes County's state senator in 1833. They also place him at Georgia's 1865 constitutional convention as a Brooks County delegate and list him as Brooks County treasurer for the 1883–1887 term.[2] These are specific and internally coherent, but the underlying commission books and legislative journals were not directly reopened in this project. “Judge Sharpe,” used by later writers, is consistent with his Inferior Court service.[19][20]

Sharpe's July 26, 1884 article says that during the Civil War he served as commissary for Lowndes and Echols counties and as assessor of tax in kind. This is first-person testimony, not a located appointment record.[18] An Ancestry index labeled “Civil War correspondence” links him to a Milledgeville item dated December 4, 1848—thirteen years before the war. With no image or text, that entry proves neither Civil War service nor the content of the document.[25]

docs.title: Militia and the “Captain” question
docs.text:
The Georgia Archives preserves eleven images of three original Sharpe letter groups:[9]

  • On August 3, 1836, writing from Sharpes Store, he asked Governor William Schley about compensation for horses wounded or lost at Brushy Creek.
  • On September 18, 1837, he reported what he considered false claims connected with a militia muster. The surviving cover is postmarked or addressed from “SHARPES STORE GEO.”
  • On August 9, 1838, he opposed speculative rotations of Georgia troops toward the Florida frontier.

These letters establish that Sharpe acted as a local militia organizer or liaison and had direct access to the governor. They do not state his rank. Huxford wrote that survivors later referred to captains H. W. Sharpe, C. S. Gaulden, and Michael Young, while also acknowledging that the roster was lost.[2] The 1885 Folsom sketch called him an “Indian fighter,” and a twentieth-century veterans' grave index labels him “Capt Us Army Indian Wars.”[19][21] Without a commission, pay roll, or original roster, the careful conclusion is that captain was a longstanding local and commemorative title, not a rank proved by the records inspected here.

docs.title: Mount Zion and Methodism
docs.text:
Sharpe's 1884 recollection says he served with William Blair and William Hendry—or “Hardy” in preserved OCR—on the committee that selected the Mount Zion camp-meeting site. It names him among the seven first tenters.[18] Huxford dated the first meeting to fall 1828 and quoted an 1884 Wesleyan Christian Advocate recollection that Sharpe and Rev. Howren were licensed to preach together in fall 1837.[2] That supports the later “Rev. Sharpe” usage, although no ordination record or original Advocate page was located.

The November 8, 1831 Mount Zion deed, copied by Huxford from the original before the courthouse record was lost, conveyed about six acres in Lot 271 from Sion and Enoch Hall to Methodist trustees William Blair, William Hendry, Lawrence Folsom, James J. Joyce, and William G. Hall.[2] Hamilton was not a trustee. His documented role was site committee member, first tenter, and later lay preacher or exhorter. A modern historical marker summarizes the tradition but does not supersede the deed or Sharpe's own article.[26]

The exact first-meeting wording remains unsettled. Preserved OCR of the April 12, 1884 newspaper page reads 1829 and William Hardy; Huxford's transcription reads 1828 and William Hendry. Until the original page is visually reinspected, both the year and name variation should remain disclosed.[18]

docs.title: Household, property, and slavery
docs.text:
The economic record changes substantially over Sharpe's lifetime:

  • 1830, Lowndes County: five free household members and three enslaved people.[4]
  • 1832: “Hamilton Sharp” of Blair's district drew Lot 284, Seventeenth District, First Section, in the Cherokee land lottery. A draw does not prove that he retained, occupied, or profited from the lot.[5]
  • 1835 Lowndes tax digest: three enslaved people in Captain Godwin's district.[6]
  • 1840, Lowndes County: six free people and sixteen enslaved people; seven household members were recorded in agriculture.[10]
  • 1850: the free household was enumerated in Thomas County, while a Lowndes County slave schedule assigned sixteen enslaved people to Hamilton. The separation may reflect residence or business in Thomas County alongside Lowndes property, but it does not locate a specific plantation.[11][13]
  • 1860, Thomas County: Hamilton was a farmer with $5,000 in real estate and $7,000 in personal property.[14]
  • 1870, Lowndes County: Hamilton and Jane were back in Lowndes; the schedule reports $6,000 in real estate and $5,726 in personal property. An agricultural schedule also survives, though its line was not fully transcribed in this project.[7][12]
  • 1880, Quitman: Hamilton and Jane lived on Screen Street, both reporting Georgia birthplaces for themselves and their parents.[15]

The slave schedules record age, sex, and color classifications but not names. The dossier does not convert those nameless entries into identities. The increase from three enslaved people in 1830/1835 to sixteen in 1840/1850 is direct evidence that Sharpe's commercial, farming, civic, and religious prominence rested in part on enslaved labor.[4][6][10][11]

docs.title: Later life, death, and burial
docs.text:
By 1880 Hamilton and Jane were living in Quitman.[15] In an 1886 letter, Hamilton said he was eighty and recalled shaking Lafayette's hand in Savannah in 1825; he invited the editor to the Sharpe House or “Tranquil Hall,” which he described as being kept by two old people. The letter is valuable testimony about his self-presentation and Savannah connections, but the Lafayette encounter remains an elderly man's recollection rather than an independently verified event.[27]

Compiled cemetery and veterans' records give Hamilton's death as November 4, 1890 and burial at West End Cemetery in Quitman.[21] No original death certificate existed for this period, and no probate file or contemporary obituary definitively belonging to Hamilton was located online. His exact birth date, parentage, grave military rank, and estate disposition therefore remain less secure than the census, marriage, postal, and militia evidence.

docs.title: Identity controls and rejected merges
docs.text:
• William H. Sharpe was Hamilton and Jane's son and a later Morven postmaster and merchant. The 1899 merchant succession names Hamilton and William separately.[2][20]
  • The 1866 road described from “W. H. Sharpe's” most naturally refers to William, not Hamilton. It should not be used to locate Hamilton's residence.[2]
  • The Florida probate record for William H. Sharpe and wife Frances A. is a son's record, not Hamilton's probate.[23]
  • The census spellings Hamilton Sharp and Hamelton Sharp belong to the same record chain when compared across locality, age, occupation, and Jane's presence in the later households. The 1830 aggregate does not name Jane or other household members.[4][12][15]
  • A collection title or unsourced public tree is not enough to establish military service, parentage, land ownership, or family relationships.[21][25]

docs.title: What is proved, probable, and unresolved
Proved or strongly supported
docs.text:
• Hamilton married Jane Perry in Tattnall County in 1827 and was in Lowndes County by 1830.[1][4]
  • He was directly connected to Sharpe's Store and served as its postmaster by January 1837 and again in the 1840s.[8][16]
  • He held several local and state offices reported in specific compiled office tables.[2]
  • He communicated directly with Governor Schley about militia matters in 1836–1838.[9]
  • He helped shape the Mount Zion camp-meeting tradition and later functioned as a Methodist lay preacher.[2][18]
  • He enslaved people and accumulated substantial farm and property wealth.[4][6][10][11][14]
  • He and Jane moved among Lowndes, Thomas, and Quitman during a record chain extending to 1880.[13][14][15]

docs.title: Probable but not proved by a contemporary original
docs.text:
• He arrived in the Hall settlement in 1826–1827 and opened a small log store near the Coffee Road.[2][18][20]
  • Sharpe's Store post office opened April 2, 1828 with Hamilton as first postmaster; this is Huxford's explicit summary of department records, not a register page directly inspected here.[2]
  • He was born April 10, 1807 to John Sharpe and Elizabeth Wynn.[21]
  • His local “Captain” title arose from actual command in the Indian conflicts.[2][19][21]

docs.title: Unresolved or unproved
docs.text:
• The exact location of the log store and whether Hamilton owned any part of Land Lot 271.
  • Whether the first Mount Zion meeting was in 1828 or 1829 and whether Sharpe wrote Hendry or Hardy.
  • A surviving military commission or original company roster.
  • An original birth record, a documented parent-child link to John Sharpe and Elizabeth Wynn, Hamilton's own probate file, or a contemporary obituary.
  • The names of the people he enslaved.

docs.title: Online research coverage and limitations
docs.text:
This project searched stored Barney/Lowndes research before external work, then used authenticated Ancestry collections, the Georgia Archives File II name files and county map collection, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Newspapers.com image IDs, Internet Archive, HathiTrust, the Georgia Historical Society marker database, public cemetery indexes, and image-backed local-history transcriptions. Searches covered all listed name variants combined with Lowndes, Brooks, Irwin, Tattnall, Thomas, Morven, Sharpes Store, postmaster, justice, senator, militia, Indian War, Mount Zion, Methodist, land, deed, tax, census, probate, obituary, and cemetery. Harden's 1913 South Georgia history was searched in full OCR without finding an independent Hamilton Sharpe account; that negative result prevents it from being treated as biographical support.[3]

“Fully researched online” means the accessible online record groups and identified leads were searched and reconciled; it does not mean every courthouse or manuscript record is digitized. FamilySearch was not authenticated during the final pass. The authenticated Newspapers.com session was available for much of the main research, but one independent lane had to rely on preserved result sets and exact image IDs. Some Ancestry images require a subscription. The original Mount Zion article needs a fresh high-resolution reading, and several deed, commission, tax, probate, and church records are offline or not image-accessible.

docs.title: Best next archival work
docs.text:
1. Order or inspect the original federal Post Office Department appointment pages covering April 1828 and the 1848–1850 changes.
  2. Reopen the April 12, 1884 Valdosta Times image at full resolution to settle 1828/1829 and Hendry/Hardy.
  3. Search Georgia militia commission books, pay rolls, and gubernatorial letter registers for a rank or company tied to Sharpe.
  4. Inspect Brooks County deed and tax originals for Lots 186 and 229 and search surviving land records for any Hamilton interest in Lot 271.
  5. Search Brooks County probate minutes, loose estates, and Quitman newspapers around November 4, 1890.
  6. Search Methodist conference minutes and the 1884 Wesleyan Christian Advocate for Sharpe's preaching license and reminiscence.
  7. Use estate, deed, church, and Freedmen's Bureau records to look for the names of people formerly enslaved by the Sharpe household.

docs.title: Citation audit
docs.text: All 27 numbered sources are cited in the body. Original records control where accessible. Retrospective accounts are labeled as such, source dependence is disclosed, namesakes are separated, and unresolved conflicts remain unresolved rather than being converted into fact.

docs.title: Henry Blair of Lowndes County, Georgia, and Hamilton County, Florida
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: Research scope and conclusion
docs.text:
This dossier concerns the Henry Blair who took part in the first decade of Lowndes County government, commanded county militia in the Creek conflict of 1836, and later lived in Hamilton County, Florida. The online evidence is strong enough to join those Georgia and Florida lives into one identity.

The decisive link appeared while Henry was still alive. In September 1891 a Hamilton County item described him as an eighty-eight-year-old local Methodist preacher and said he had helped organize Lowndes County, served as its first court clerk and second sheriff, and taken the county's 1830 census.[1] Censuses then trace him from Lowndes in 1840 to Hamilton County in 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880.[2-6]

Henry was born in Georgia about 1803-1805. He was in Lowndes by 1830, served as sheriff and representative, and commanded the 81st Regiment of Georgia Militia in the field at Cow Creek in August 1836. He still resided in Lowndes in 1846, but had moved to Hamilton County by 1850. There he farmed, preached, and patented federal land.[4,5,18]

Two important questions remain open. The records do not prove whether Henry was William Blair's son or brother, and they do not establish Henry's exact death date or burial place. Later sources disagree on the first question and offer only unsourced approximations for the second.[21-24]

docs.title: Identity and birth
docs.text:
The September 1891 profile is a direct identity bridge, not a modern reconstruction. Reprinted from the Jasper News, it said:

Henry Blair, a local Methodist preacher who lives in the western portion of this county, is 88 years old. He was in the organization of Lowndes county, Ga., was the first clerk of the court of that county, the second sheriff, and took the census there in 1830.

It added that he was partially deaf but otherwise hale.[1] A second newspaper reprinted the item later that month.[25]

The reported age implies birth about 1803. Census ages imply about 1805 in 1850, 1804 in 1860, 1807 in 1870, and 1804 in 1880. Every named census gives Georgia as his birthplace; the 1880 schedule says his father was born in South Carolina and his mother in Georgia.[3-6]

The best statement is therefore born in Georgia about 1803-1805. The frequently repeated exact year 1803 is compatible with the evidence but not established by a birth, Bible, or baptismal record. A 1950 article's Screven County birthplace is a useful family-history lead, not original proof.[22]

docs.title: Relationship to William and Mary Blair
docs.text:
Henry was closely tied to the older William Blair. When William died in 1840, Henry applied for administration. Henry and a younger William Blair later acted together as administrators, selling the elder man's personal property and land for creditors and heirs.[14]

None of those legal notices calls Henry a son, brother, or heir. Later accounts conflict:

  • a handwritten addendum to a 1933 Georgia Archives family letter calls Henry the elder William's brother;[21]
  • a 1950 county-history article calls Henry William's son;[22]
  • user trees commonly identify William Blair and Mary Joyce as Henry's parents, but they cite no direct parental record.[23]

Henry also served as executor of Mary Blair's estate in 1846. Her cattle, hogs, sheep, and household and kitchen property were sold at Henry's Lowndes residence. The notice does not identify Mary as his mother, sister, wife, or other relative.[17]

The age pattern makes the son tradition plausible, and Henry's estate roles show trust and proximity. Neither is kinship proof. Henry's relationship to William and Mary Blair remains unresolved, with son-versus-brother explicitly disputed.

docs.title: First Lowndes offices
docs.text:
Lowndes County was created in December 1825. A Georgia Historical Society marker says the first county officers commissioned May 29, 1826 included Henry Blair as Superior Court clerk.[8] Huxford's county-officer roster instead gives Henry's commission date as May 9, 1826 and his term as 1826-1830.[30] Hamilton W. Sharpe, an early resident writing in 1884, likewise remembered Henry as the clerk selected at the county's first election and said Henry was still living.[9]

The exact 1826 commission image was not found online, and the two later sources disagree by twenty days. The precise commission date therefore remains unresolved. Henry's status as first clerk is nevertheless strong and was also repeated in the 1891 profile published during his lifetime.[1]

The claim that Henry took the 1830 Lowndes census also comes directly from that 1891 profile.[1] The full 1830 Georgia population roll was inspected online, but a signed appointment or return identifying him as assistant marshal was not located. The statement is reported in a lifetime profile but officially unproved; it should not be presented as a verified federal appointment.

docs.title: Sheriff and legislator
docs.text:
Contemporary statewide sheriff lists published in 1832 name "Lowndes, Henry Blair". Henry's own sale notices then identify him as sheriff, including the levy of John J. Underwood's Franklinville property and a countywide sale of academy land.[10,11]

These records verify Henry's service in 1832-1833. A later office chronology extends his sheriff term through 1834, but the endpoints have not been independently proved.[22]

Henry also represented Lowndes County in the Georgia House in 1833. Contemporary election returns name Sharpe and Blair for Lowndes, while legislative reports identify "Mr. Blair, of Lowndes" as reporting a bill to extend Georgia jurisdiction over territory disputed with Florida.[30] A December report also names him among House members who signed a protest after the majority ended debate.[12] These records verify his membership and legislative activity, but the search did not establish that his jurisdiction bill passed.

docs.title: Militia command and Cow Creek
docs.text:
The original 1836 Lowndes general-militia return names Henry as colonel commanding the 81st Regiment. Enoch Hall served as lieutenant colonel; D. H. Howell as quartermaster; John Pike as paymaster; and I. S. Burnett as adjutant.[13]

That return describes the standing county militia. It is not an active-service roster. Henry's own report to Governor William Schley supplies the field evidence.[15]

Dated August 30, 1836, Henry's report says a Native party was sighted in upper Lowndes on August 24. He joined an initial pursuit, sent for Captain Levi J. Knight, and commanded about sixty or sixty-five men in an August 27 fight at Cow Creek swamp near the Ware-Lowndes line. He reported one wounded man and one killed horse among his force. He claimed two Native people killed in the field, two possibly carried into the swamp, and six prisoners, one of whom died the next day. The five survivors were sent to the Thomasville jail. He signed as "Colonel Commanding 81st Regiment, G. M."[15]

The document verifies Henry's command and what he reported. Its estimates of the Native party's size and losses are his wartime account, not independent casualty findings. A short contemporary newspaper summary confirms the basic engagement and command structure.[16]

docs.title: Household, enslavement, and Lowndes property
docs.text:
The 1840 census places Henry in Lowndes as a male aged thirty through thirty-nine. His household contained six free white people and twelve enslaved people; six people were recorded in agriculture.[2] The enslaved residents were counted by age and sex but not named: six males and six females across the schedule's age categories.

Georgia tax indexes place Henry in Lowndes in 1830, 1834, 1835, 1838, 1840, and 1844. The district labels move from Captain Pike's to Captain Godwin's, Captain Grantham's, and finally Captain Blair's.[7] Those entries establish continuity but do not, without full image transcription, prove every acreage or tax column.

Newspaper levies identify Henry's land interests:

  • In 1844, Land Lot 360 in the 12th District, 490 acres of well-improved pine land, was levied under a Lowndes Inferior Court execution. Henry pointed out the property.[20]
  • In 1848, a mortgage execution covered Lot 332, 222 acres of Lot 307, and 75 acres of Lot 333, all in the 12th District, totaling about 787 acres.[20]

The notices verify ownership or a mortgaged interest. They do not establish Henry's exact house site. The 1846 Mary Blair sale is the clearest residence statement because it places the sale at Henry's Lowndes home.[17]

Indexed searches of the Hamilton County 1850 and 1860 slave schedules returned no qualifying Henry Blair entry.[26] That is a documented negative search, not proof that he held no enslaved people after moving; schedules and indexes can omit or misread names.

docs.title: Move to Hamilton County
docs.text:
The migration can be narrowed to the mid-1840s. Henry appeared on the 1844 Lowndes tax digest and lived in Lowndes during the August 1846 Mary Blair sale.[7,17] In the 1850 Hamilton County census, his older children were Georgia-born while four-year-old Henry was born in Florida.[3]

The safest window is after August 1846 and by the 1850 census. The 1848 Lowndes mortgage sale proves continuing Georgia land interests, not continuing residence.[20]

docs.title: Wife and children
docs.text:
Henry's wife appears on original census images under several spellings:

  • "Luranah", age 38, in 1850;
  • "Laurina", age 48, in 1860;
  • "Lurany", age 55, in 1870;
  • "Lurany", age 68 and explicitly Henry's wife, in 1880.[3-6]

The name, age progression, and household continuity strongly support one woman despite normal spelling variation. A compiled genealogy calls her Lorena Beasley, and a user-created memorial uses the same name and places her at Hickory Grove Methodist Church Cemetery in Madison County, Florida.[23,24] No original marriage record or maiden-name record was found. The defensible wording is Luranah/Laurina/Lurany, traditionally Lorena Beasley.

The 1850 and 1860 schedules place James, William, Franklin, Vianah/Vienna, and younger Henry in the household with broadly compatible names and approximate ages despite normal census variation. Because those censuses did not state relationships, they are strong probable children, not directly proved from the schedules alone.[3,4]

The 1880 census provides direct relationship evidence. It identifies Robert S. Blair, age twenty-eight, as Henry's son and William H. Blair, age sixteen, as his grandson.[6] The seven-year-old William in the 1870 household is therefore strong probable to be that grandson rather than a late-born son.[5]

docs.title: Florida work, land, and post office
docs.text:
The 1850 enumerator wrote Henry's occupation as "M.P. Minister", and the 1891 profile called him a local Methodist preacher.[1,3] Together they verify a long-lived preaching role.

A 1926 Mount Zion centennial article went further, saying Henry and Hamilton W. Sharpe were local preachers who established the church at the old camp ground.[27] That claim conflicts with Sharpe's 1884 recollection and the 1831 Mount Zion deed evidence, both of which name William Blair, not Henry, on the site committee, first-tenter group, or trustee list.[9,28] Henry may have preached there, but his status as a Mount Zion co-founder is unresolved and vulnerable to William/Henry confusion.

In Florida, a federal patent issued to Henry on October 1, 1860 for land in Township 2 North, Range 12 East, Section 30, Hamilton County.[18] A Henry Blair was appointed postmaster at Bellville on July 7, 1869.[19] The appointment record does not distinguish the elder Henry from his adult son of the same name, so assigning the office to the elder is possible but unproved. The 1860 census valued the elder Henry's real estate at $600 and personal estate at $1,120; the 1870 census recorded $300 real and $150 personal estate.[4,5]

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
Henry was alive in September 1891, when the Jasper item described him as partially deaf but otherwise healthy.[1] A later family-history book says he died "circa 1891"; a 1950 article instead gives 1893.[22,23] Neither displayed source cites a death record, obituary, probate file, or grave marker.

Targeted searches of Georgia Historic Newspapers, authenticated Newspapers.com, Ancestry death and probate collections, Find a Grave, Hamilton County variants, and cemetery leads did not locate a qualifying obituary, death record, will, probate proceeding, burial register, photographed marker, or Henry Blair memorial.[29] Apparent Valdosta hits in 1893 were search false positives.

Lorena Blair's user-created memorial cannot supply Henry's burial place, and the presence of later family members at Blair Cemetery near Jennings does not place him there.[24] Henry's exact death date and burial place remain unresolved.
