docs.title: Rev. Joshua Platt of Early Lowndes County, Georgia
docs.text: A 2006 compiled genealogy identifies David Platt as a son of Rev. Joshua Platt and Amy Newell. David’s 1818 marriage and the two men’s 1820 Bulloch and later Lowndes records support the chronology and migration, but no inspected original record names David’s parents. Joshua and Amy are secondary-supported, not verified, as David’s parents.

docs.title: Research scope and conclusion
docs.text:
This report concerns the Reverend Joshua Platt whom Hamilton W. Sharpe remembered as one of the first seven tent occupants at the Mount Zion Methodist camp meeting in fall 1829. The accessible record supports a strong-probable identity chain from Bulloch County, Georgia, in 1820, through Lowndes County in 1830-1840, to Alachua County, Florida, in 1850. No single record explicitly joins all three places, so the chain is not presented as absolute fact.[2-6]

The public life is clearer than the private genealogy. Original censuses and tax digests place Joshua in early Lowndes County and document changing landholdings and enslaved labor. Sharpe's participant recollection calls him "Rev. Joshua Platt"; a later Methodist biographical register identifies him as a local Methodist Episcopal preacher and reports an 1839 deacon election.[7-14] Original Florida newspaper notices prove that a Joshua Platt of Hernando County was dead before January 27, 1855, that John Platt administered his estate, and that five unnamed enslaved people belonging to the estate were advertised for sale in January 1857. The attribution of that estate to the earlier Lowndes and Alachua man is strong probable, not directly stated in the notices.[15-16]

The often-repeated 1770 birth, Adam Platt parentage, marriages to Margaret Fussell and Amy Newell, complete child list, March 1855 death, and Williams Cemetery dates remain derivative or unproved. The March 1855 death claim is contradicted by administration notices dated January 27, 1855.[15,19-20] A photographed marker clearly reads "REV. JOSHUA PLATT", but its lower inscription is not legible enough in the preserved image to verify dates.[18]

docs.title: Identity and migration
docs.text:
The 1820 Bulloch County census index records Joshua Platt as a household head and reports five free people in all. Its extracted age fields appear to describe six people: one man forty-five or older, one man sixteen through eighteen, three girls under sixteen, and one woman twenty-six through forty-four. The preserved manuscript page is too faint to resolve that mismatch confidently. One household member was reported in agriculture. The name and place support a possible or strong-probable earlier appearance, but this conflicted household extraction is not treated as a clean identity bridge.[2]

In 1830, Joshua headed a four-person Lowndes County household: a man and woman each aged fifty through fifty-nine, a girl ten through fourteen, and a young woman fifteen through nineteen. No enslaved person was recorded.[4]

The 1840 Lowndes schedule advances the older couple by one decade. It records a man and woman each sixty through sixty-nine, one man twenty through twenty-nine, two young women fifteen through nineteen, and one enslaved Black woman aged twenty-four through thirty-five. Two household members worked in agriculture.[5]

The 1850 Alachua County, Florida, population schedule records Joshua Platt, eighty, North Carolina-born farmer, and Amy Platt, seventy-five, also born in North Carolina, in dwelling and family 92.[6] The age progression, rare exact name, occupation, household pattern, and southward movement make the Lowndes-to-Alachua identification strong probable. The census did not state relationships, so Amy is a strong-probable wife, not a relationship directly proved by the schedule.

An 1810 Duplin County, North Carolina, Joshua Platt headed a nine-person household, and an 1804 Duplin land-entry card records warrant 1485 for ten acres on a drain of Island Creek. The card says "Entered 13th Feb. 1804"; its grant-number and issue fields are blank.[1,3] Those are plausible earlier appearances, but neither record connects its Joshua to Bulloch or Lowndes. The unresolved 1820 extraction also prevents a clean household-composition comparison. These appearances remain possible, not settled.

docs.title: Namesakes and rejected mergers
docs.text:
The elder must remain separate from Joshua Platt, about twenty-two and Georgia-born, in John and Eliss Platt's Putnam County, Florida, household in 1850. That younger man continues in later Florida records as Joshua A. or Joshua Aaron Platt. Records and family trees attached to the younger man cannot be assigned automatically to the minister.[21]

Samuel Platt also headed a separate Lowndes household in 1830. Peter and John Platt appear near Joshua in census or later estate contexts, but proximity and surname do not prove their relationships.[4-5]

An 1827 Georgia land-lottery index names a Joshua Platt of Underwood's District, Carroll County, as the drawer of District 12, Lot 43 in Irwin County. That Carroll residence is not explicitly connected to the dossier subject, and Lot 43 does not appear in the minister's inspected Lowndes tax sequence. The lottery winner therefore remains unresolved rather than assigned to him.[17]

docs.title: Mount Zion and Methodist ministry
docs.text:
Hamilton W. Sharpe's "Scenes and Incidents of Our Early History", printed April 12, 1884, is the closest located narrative witness to Mount Zion's beginning. Sharpe wrote, "It was I think as early as the fall of 1829", and named "Rev. Joshua Platt" among the seven first tent occupants with William Blair, William Hendry, John Hendry, H. W. Sharpe, John Pike, and Lawrence Folsom.[7]

Sharpe wrote about fifty-five years after the event and explicitly signaled uncertainty with "I think". His original newspaper page reads 1829. Folks Huxford later printed 1828, and a modern historical marker repeats that year.[22] The dossier therefore reports fall 1829 as Sharpe's wording and preserves 1828 as a later variant.

Sharpe proves only how a participant remembered Platt: a reverend and early tenter in the Methodist Episcopal gathering. The article does not say Platt selected the site, preached the first sermon, owned the campground, or held office there. Platt is absent from Huxford's original-based transcription of the November 8, 1831 Mount Zion deed, whose trustees were William Blair, William Hendry, Lawrence Folsom, James J. Joyce, and William G. Hall.[22] He should not be called an 1831 Mount Zion deed trustee; any later trustee service is unresolved.

Harold Lawrence's 1984 biographical register gives the clearest ministerial entry: "PLATT, JOSHUA (MEC) (L) GEORGIA CONFERENCE; 1839 Deacon (E)." Lawrence defines MEC as Methodist Episcopal Church before the 1844 division, "L" as local preacher, and "E" as elected.[8] This is strong secondary evidence that Platt was a local Methodist Episcopal preacher elected deacon in 1839.

The original conference action or ordination certificate was not located. Searches of the published Methodist annual-conference minutes for 1773-1839 found no Joshua Platt appointment.[9-11] Lawrence explains that local preachers seldom appeared in printed conference minutes before 1850. The combined evidence distinguishes local ministry from an itinerant circuit appointment; no specific circuit or annual appointment has been proved.

docs.title: Taxed land and local setting
docs.text:
Original Lowndes tax digests place Joshua in the county from 1830 through 1840, but a tax return does not by itself identify a dwelling or complete deed chain.[12-14]

  • In 1830 he returned one poll, 632.5 acres of pine land and sixty acres of first-quality oak-and-hickory land, including District 12, Lot 107 in Lowndes and a Carroll County tract described as District 12, Lot 143.[12]
  • In 1834-1835, under "Joshua Plate" in one index, he returned a Lowndes tract associated with District 12, Lot 335 and a forty-acre Cherokee tract. The 1835 Cherokee district numeral is difficult to read and should not be treated as a perfected legal description.[13]
  • In 1838-1840 he returned a Lowndes tract associated with District 12, Lot 339 and another forty-acre Cherokee entry.[14]

Georgia's official land-lot GIS places Lots 107, 335, and 339 within the present Brooks County landscape.[23] That locates the taxed parcels broadly. It does not prove which tract contained his house, when title passed, or whether every acreage line represented full ownership.

No located record names Joshua as a Lowndes justice, sheriff, clerk, tax officer, legislator, militia officer, or soldier. A Savannah newspaper does place a Joshua Platt among Bulloch County grand jurors in April 1821; if the identity chain is correct, this is a strong-probable civic appearance, not a separate proof that the juror later moved to Lowndes.[24]

In June 1847, the Southern Recorder printed an equity notice in "Thomas J. S. Farr v. Joshua Platt". The Lowndes sheriff reported that Platt could not be found in the county, and the court ordered publication.[25] This directly establishes the suit and his absence when service was attempted. It does not establish permanent residence elsewhere, but it is consistent with departure before the 1850 Florida census.

docs.title: Enslaved people
docs.text:
The 1830 census records no enslaved person in Joshua's household. The 1840 census records one unnamed enslaved Black woman aged twenty-four through thirty-five.[4-5]

The 1850 Alachua slave schedule records six unnamed Black people under Joshua Platt's ownership:[6]

  • a woman aged thirty-five;
  • a man aged twenty;
  • a girl aged thirteen;
  • boys aged ten and eight; and
  • a girl aged three.

The inspected Lowndes tax rows do not supply enslaved-person counts, including the 1840 return. That difference should not be used to erase the federal census entry; tax-day and census-day records were separate instruments.[12-14]

The estate advertised five unnamed enslaved people for sale in January 1857: "Two likely young men, one girl, and two children."[16] The newspaper does not identify them or explain why the estate count was one lower than the 1850 schedule. No names or defensible person-to-person linkage can be recovered from these records.

docs.title: Family
docs.text:
Amy Platt's 1850 co-residence and similar age make her Joshua's strong-probable wife.[6] The original schedule calls her only Amy Platt. "Newell" appears in derivative trees and alternate indexing, not in the census manuscript.[19-20]

John Platt directly appears as administrator for the Hernando County Joshua in the 1855-1856 notices.[15-16] Those notices do not call him a son, and their attribution to the dossier subject is strong probable rather than explicit. Find a Grave links John Wesley Platt and Peter Platt as children, while public trees add other names.[19-20] Without an original heirs list, will, Bible, marriage record, parental probate, or relationship-bearing church record, John and Peter should not be promoted from derivative or circumstantial kinship to proved sons.

No located original record proves Joshua's parents, Amy's maiden name, an earlier wife, either marriage, or a complete child list. The popular "Joshua Adam Platt" construction is a tree label, not a name established in an original record inspected for this report.

docs.title: Death, administration, and estate
docs.text:
The Florida Peninsular of February 17, 1855, printed two notices signed by John Platt and dated January 27. One sought authority from the "Judge of the Southern Circuit Court ... sitting in Hernando County" to sell the real estate of "Joshua Platt, late of said County, deceased"; the other directed creditors and legatees of "Joshua Platt, late of Hernando County, deceased" to present authenticated claims. Both identify John as administrator.[15]

These notices prove that the Hernando County decedent died before January 27, 1855. His identification as the earlier Lowndes and Alachua man is strong probable. The notices do not give an exact date, cause, or relationship to John. They also contradict the March 1855 death attributed to this same man in derivative sources.[19-20]

On November 1, 1856, the newspaper announced a final accounting before the Hernando probate judge and a public sale at the old Hernando courthouse on the first Monday in January 1857. The sale notice offered the five unnamed enslaved people belonging to Joshua's estate.[16] An adjacent debt notice instead called Joshua "late of Hillsborough County". The newspaper itself therefore contains a Hernando/Hillsborough conflict. Because the real-estate, accounting, and sale notices use Hernando, the safest conclusion is that the estate was administered there while preserving the contrary wording.

No online will, full estate packet, inventory, heirs list, distribution, or complete deed proceeding was located. The notices prove administration and advertised actions, not that every proposed sale occurred exactly as planned.

docs.title: Burial
docs.text:
Find a Grave memorial 65687643 places Rev. Joshua Platt in Williams Cemetery near Dade City and reports 1770-1855.[18-19] The preserved marker photograph clearly shows "REV. JOSHUA PLATT". Its lower inscription is too faint to read confidently, so the image does not independently verify the dates.

The photographed marker and memorial location make Williams Cemetery a strong-probable burial identification. The exact birth and death dates remain unproved. A cemetery placement is also not proof that modern Dade City was the historical place of death.

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text:
• 1804: a possible Joshua Platt entered warrant 1485 for ten acres in Duplin County, North Carolina; the preserved card has no grant number or issue date.[1]
  • 1810: possible appearance as a Duplin household head.[3]
  • 1820: strong-probable appearance as a Bulloch County, Georgia, household head.[2]
  • April 1821: a Joshua Platt served on a Bulloch grand jury; strong probable if the identity chain holds.[24]
  • Fall 1829: Sharpe later remembered Rev. Joshua Platt among Mount Zion's first seven tenters.[7]
  • 1830: Lowndes household of four; no enslaved people; original tax return includes District 12, Lot 107.[4,12]
  • 1834-1835: tax returns associate him with District 12, Lot 335 and a forty-acre Cherokee tract.[13]
  • 1838-1840: tax returns associate him with District 12, Lot 339 and a Cherokee tract.[14]
  • 1839: Lawrence's register reports election as a local Methodist Episcopal deacon.[8]
  • 1840: Lowndes household of five free people and one enslaved woman.[5]
  • May-June 1847: sheriff could not find Joshua in Lowndes for service in an equity case.[25]
  • 1850: Joshua, eighty, and Amy, seventy-five, in Alachua County; six unnamed enslaved people.[6]
  • Before January 27, 1855: The Hernando County Joshua died; John Platt was administrator. Attribution to the dossier subject is strong probable.[15]
  • November 1856: Final accounting and a January 1857 estate sale for that decedent were announced.[16]
  • January 1857: scheduled sale of five unnamed enslaved people at the old Hernando courthouse.[16]
  • 1884: Sharpe published his Mount Zion recollection.[7]
  • 1984: Lawrence published the local-preacher and 1839 deacon entry.[8]

docs.title: Search coverage and remaining targets
docs.text:
No original birth, parental, marriage, ordination, complete child, will, estate-distribution, exact death-date, or fully legible grave-date record was found. No itinerant appointment, military service, or Lowndes public office was located. Google Books quota exhaustion and unavailable web/browser handlers restricted parts of the broad web layer; those failures mean "not found in the accessible search", not "no record existed".

The main remaining targets are:

  1. the original 1839 Georgia Conference local-deacon action or ordination certificate;
  2. complete Duplin, Bulloch, Lowndes, Alachua, Hernando, and Hillsborough deed/probate packets;
  3. an heirs list, Bible, marriage record, or church register proving family relationships;
  4. a readable high-resolution marker image or cemetery register;
  5. a complete title chain for Lots 107, 335, and 339; and
  6. a record explicitly linking the Georgia and Florida appearances.

The findings describe accessible online evidence checked through August 19, 2026. They do not imply that undigitized courthouse, church, cemetery, conference, family, or private records do not exist.

docs.title: William Folsom of old Irwin, Lowndes, and Brooks counties, Georgia
docs.text:
William Folsom of old Irwin, Lowndes, and Brooks counties, Georgia

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence-graded online dossier

Subject: William Folsom, early South Georgia settler and son of Lawrence Folsom
Life dates: born about 1795 in Georgia; died November 16, 1872, at his Brooks County residence
Prepared: August 19, 2026
Updated: October 2, 2026
Standard: Original records and contemporary newspapers control. Later county histories, compiled genealogies, collaborative trees, and cemetery pages are identified as such. Repetition among derivative sources is not treated as independent proof.

Bottom line

William Folsom was an early Irwin County resident who remained in the same general South Georgia neighborhood as county boundaries changed from Irwin to Lowndes and then Brooks. Later courthouse-based histories identify a William Folsom on Irwin County courthouse-and-jail commissions in 1823 and 1825. A published transcription of an 1845 Lowndes grand-jury list also names William Folsom, and Brooks County's first petit-jury list in 1859 includes the name. Age and location make the subject a plausible to strong-probable match in these civic records, but the records as reviewed do not identify his wife, parent, or land.[1–4]

His death is unusually well documented. Hamilton W. Sharpe's obituary says Folsom died at his Brooks County residence on November 16, 1872, in his seventy-eighth year. It describes a long-established Methodist, generous to poor people, ministers, and church causes, and says that an aged wife survived him. The complete original page appeared in the Southern Christian Advocate on February 19, 1873.[5][6]

The family structure is clearer than earlier compilations suggested, but it is not complete. FamilySearch's Pulaski County marriage record/index reports William's 1813 marriage to Elizabeth Folsom. Elizabeth's 1876 will directly calls Edith Rountree and Nancy Bradford her daughters; identifies W. R., C. W., A. C., and Ruth Ann Ryall as her grandchildren and the children of Rachel Ann Ryall; and names C. W. Ryall and William Harrell as grandsons.[7–10][34][35]

Contrary to online reports, William and Elizabeth were not buried in unmarked graves in their family cemetery, but in marked graves on their homeplace in Land Lot 520, District 9. The surviving stone is broken and weathered, but both names are visible. William's panel preserves the year 1872; Elizabeth's preserves 1877. The smaller date lines are not clear enough for a full independent transcription.[36][37]

Administration of William's Brooks County estate was secured by a $30,000 bond. William R. Ryall and Charles W. Ryall served as administrators, with West Rountree, Green Lawson, and Nicholas M. Reddick as sureties. Four administrator's deeds now prove that William died owning at least 2,080 acres: all of Land Lots 492, 519, and 521 in District 9; 120 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 491 in District 9; and all of Lot 323 in District 12. The estate sold those tracts to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree. Elizabeth's executor later conveyed her Land Lots 493 and 520 in District 9 to her daughter Edith Rountree. These deeds document a Folsom-Ryall-Rountree-Perry land network north of Barney, although William's acquisition deeds and the later Rountree-to-J. E. Moody chain remain unlocated.[11–13][38–42]

Identity and chronology

This dossier concerns the William Folsom born in Georgia about 1795, living in old Lowndes County by 1850, in Brooks County after its 1858 creation, and dying there in 1872. His age, wife Elizabeth, neighborhood, associates, 1870 household, obituary, and probate form a coherent identity chain.[5][9][14–16]

He must not be merged with Lieutenant William Folsom of Revolutionary-era Burke County; William I. Folsom, a younger Brooks County Confederate soldier; later judges or lawyers of the same name; William Folsom Ryall; or William Folsom Harrell. The surname cluster is dense, and title or location alone is not enough to transfer a record from one man to another.[7][10]

Date Event Evidence judgment
about 1795 Born in Georgia; Burke County is a compiled-family-history claim Verified for Georgia and strongly supported for approximate year from census/obituary; secondary-supported for Burke County
Dec. 11, 1813 Married Elizabeth Folsom in Pulaski County Strong indexed record evidence; FamilySearch county-marriage record/index
Dec. 13, 1823 A William Folsom named on an Irwin courthouse-and-jail commission, according to later courthouse-based history Possible to strong probable identity; original act page still required
Dec. 24, 1825 A William Folsom named on the replacement Irwin county-site commission Possible to strong probable identity; original act page still required
1845 William Folsom named on a Lowndes grand-jury list Strong secondary transcription; original newspaper page not independently inspected
1850 Lowndes County household with Elizabeth and younger household members Verified census evidence
1859 William Folsom appears among Brooks County's first petit jurors Strong compiled official evidence; same-man identity strong probable
1860 Brooks County schedule attributes one enslaved eleven-year-old boy and one slave house to Wm. Folsom Strong transcription evidence; original image needed
1870 Brooks County dwelling with Elizabeth, William Harrill, Dicy Roberts, Louis Roberts, and John Roberts Verified census evidence
Nov. 16, 1872 Died at his Brooks County residence, in his seventy-eighth year Verified by contemporary obituary
July 7, 1873 $30,000 administration bond executed Verified manuscript
Aug.–Sept. 1873 Administrators sold beef cattle and sought leave to sell land for the heirs Verified contemporary notices
Dec. 1873–Jan. 1874 Estate auctions transferred William's Brooks County lands to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree Verified original deeds
Apr.–Nov. 1874 Administrators executed deeds for LLs 492, 519, 521, part of 491, and LL 323 Verified original deeds
Feb. 5, 1878 Elizabeth's executor conveyed LLs 493 and 520/9 to her daughter Edith Rountree for $1,200 Verified original deed and will

Birth, parents, and migration

The obituary places William in his seventy-eighth year at death, implying birth between November 17, 1794, and November 16, 1795. The 1870 census gives age seventy-five, also pointing to about 1794–1795. The frequently repeated year 1797 comes from later genealogy and cemetery/tree profiles, not from a contemporary birth record. A publication-safe birth statement is about 1795 in Georgia. Burke County remains plausible but unproved.[5][7–10][16]

The 1938 Genealogy of the Folsom Family calls him the son of Lawrence Armstrong Folsom and Rachel Vickers. That Georgia section openly depends on family informants, principally Mrs. Boyd and Horace B. Folsom. FamilySearch, WikiTree, Find a Grave, and other online trees repeat the relationship. Contemporary 1849–1850 legal notices add important independent support: a William Folsom acted as executor of Lawrence Folsom's Lowndes County estate, sought leave to sell its enslaved people, and advertised estate property at James Folsom's house. The notices do not call William Lawrence's son, and the original will or probate file was not located. The executor's identity with this subject is strong probable from name, county, chronology, and family context; Lawrence and Rachel as his parents remain strong probable, not directly verified.[7–10][17][28][29]

William's migration has often been told too simply. Mrs. D. H. Purvis wrote in 1948 that he moved from Irwin County into the later Barney district in the 1830s. Yet the courthouse-commission traditions already place a William Folsom in Irwin civic affairs in 1823 and 1825, and the family genealogy assigns several children to Lowndes County before or during the 1830s. The surviving evidence supports continuous residence in the broader Irwin-to-Lowndes region, but it does not supply one exact arrival date at the later Brooks plantation.[1–3][7][18]

Public and community roles

Irwin County courthouse commissions

Folks Huxford's county history and his 1950 newspaper history say the General Assembly first appointed William Folsom, James Crum, Silloway McCall, Joshua Griffin, and Alexander McDonald as Irwin courthouse-and-jail commissioners on December 13, 1823. They apparently did not complete the work. The December 24, 1825 organizing act then named John B. F. Dixon, James Wilcox, Emanuel Knowles, William Folsom, and Elijah Beasley as replacement Irwin commissioners.[1–3]

Huxford distinguishes the 1825 Irwin appointment from the simultaneous Lawrence Folsom commission for newly created Lowndes County. The two names should not be merged: his account puts Lawrence on the Lowndes commission and William on the Irwin commission. The target William was old enough and geographically plausible, and the repeated name in the two Irwin appointments supports a single local man. Neither the original act pages nor an identifying residence, relative, or tract was recovered, however. The subject's service is therefore possible to strong probable, not verified.[1–3][30]

Jury service

A published transcription of a June 1845 Lowndes Superior Court report names William Folsom among the grand jurors at Troupville. The transcription is strong secondary evidence, but the underlying newspaper image was not independently inspected in this project. Even if the reading is correct, the report establishes only jury service, not foremanship, office, party, or a specific verdict.[4]

Huxford's transcription of Brooks County's first jury lists names William Folsom as petit juror number forty in 1859. Age, location, and prominence make the pioneer the strong-probable identity, but the list itself provides no age or residence. No record found online makes him a judge, justice of the peace, sheriff, legislator, militia officer, road commissioner, or elected county officer.[1]

Wife and children

Elizabeth Folsom

FamilySearch's Pulaski County marriage record/index reports William and Elizabeth Folsom's marriage on December 11, 1813. Their 1850 and 1870 households and the 1873 obituary continue the identity chain and establish that Elizabeth survived William. The 1938 genealogy identifies her as a distant Folsom cousin, daughter of George Folsom and Edith Penny. No inspected birth, Bible, or parent-naming record proves that ancestry.[5][7][9][14][16][34]

Elizabeth executed her will on January 28, 1876, and it was recorded August 13, 1877, disproving the genealogy's statement that she died about 1875. A memorial gives March 16, 1877. The newly supplied monument photograph visibly supports 1877, but damage and weathering prevent a confident reading of the smaller month-and-day line from this image alone. Judgment: Elizabeth as William's wife is verified, and the 1813 marriage date has strong indexed record evidence. Her George/Edith parentage is strong compiled tradition. Her death year is now verified by the photographed monument; March 16 remains probable but not independently verified from the image.[7][34–36]

Publication-safe child structure

The 1938 genealogy lists eight children. The list is useful, but it is not an heir return and should not be called complete or proved merely because modern trees copy it.[7]

  • Green Folsom: said to have died as a small boy. Compiled-family-history only. FamilySearch's Green profile points to different preferred parents, a material conflict.
  • Rachel Ann Folsom Ryall: Elizabeth's will identifies W. R., C. W., A. C., and Ruth Ann Ryall as her grandchildren and as Rachel Ann Ryall's children. The 1938 genealogy explicitly calls Rachel a daughter of William and Elizabeth, and the Ryall sons' later administration of William's estate reinforces the relationship. Because the will does not use the exact phrase “my daughter Rachel Ann,” the conservative grade is strong probable, bordering verified.[7][11][19][35]
  • Edith Folsom Rountree: Elizabeth's will directly calls Edith her daughter and the wife of West Rountree. William and Elizabeth appear as a married couple across the census chain, with no evidence of stepchildren or another marriage. Verified daughter of Elizabeth; strong-probable daughter of William.[7][11][20][35]
  • George Folsom: listed in the genealogy, but nearby men of the same name create serious confusion. The 1860 slave schedule has a separate George entry. Possible/compiled; identity and child structure unresolved.[7][21]
  • Nancy Folsom Perry Bradford: Elizabeth's will directly calls Nancy Bradford her daughter and the wife of John Bradford. The 1938 genealogy says Nancy first married a Perry, while descendant material reports a later Andrew Jackson Bradford marriage dated after the will was executed. Verified daughter of Elizabeth; strong-probable daughter of William. The Perry/Bradford spouse chronology and the will's “John Bradford” wording remain unresolved.[7][9][35]
  • Martha Folsom Harrell/Horrell: an 1892 obituary for John S. Harrell calls his late wife Martha the “youngest daughter of William Folsom, Esq.” That explicit statement, published twenty years after William's death, joins the compiled genealogy, Martha's placement in William's 1850 household, Elizabeth's identification of William Harrell as a grandson, and the younger William Harrill's presence in William's 1870 dwelling. Strong probable daughter and likely youngest daughter; the article does not identify her mother. Later sources conflict between 1861 and 1895 death dates; Elizabeth's 1876 will is consistent with an earlier death but does not prove 1861.[7][14][16][22][31][35]
  • Hardy Vickers Folsom: Hardy appears in William and Elizabeth's 1850 household; the genealogy identifies him as a son, and a Brooks County marriage record links Hardy V. Folsom and Tempy Ann Wells in 1859. Strong probable son; the census does not state relationships.[7][9][14]
  • Janie/Jane Folsom: the genealogy says James Perry's wife; FamilySearch repeats the marriage but attaches no source. Possible daughter / tree-and-genealogy claim.[7][9]

FamilySearch adds Noah Folsom, born about 1832, as another son and identifies Julia Drawdy as his wife. Noah belongs to the same local Folsom cluster, but no record found in this research names William and Elizabeth as his parents. He is therefore a possible additional son, not a ninth verified child.[9][10]

Farming, land, livestock, and wealth

The 1948 Barney history portrays “Uncle Billy” as a prominent planter near Little River who produced brown sugar for Savannah and Tallahassee and sent large cattle herds to Savannah and Charleston. It says his land later became the Rountree place owned by J. E. Moody. Sharpe's obituary independently supports a comfortable living and generous use of wealth, while the 1873 cattle notice proves that the estate owned beef cattle in Colquitt County. These points give the later account a real economic foundation, but they do not verify every production figure or annual cattle-drive claim.[5][12][18]

Four original administrator's deeds replace much of the earlier derivative land picture. William died seized and possessed of all of District 9 Land Lots 492, 519, and 521; 120 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 491; and all of District 12 Land Lot 323. The sales produced $800 from Nancy Perry for LL 492, $640 from Charles W. Ryall for LL 519 and the 120-acre portion of LL 491, $837 from West Rountree for LL 521, and $125 from West Rountree for LL 323. These deeds prove at least 2,080 acres in William's estate. They do not establish that this was his complete landholding.[38–41]

Elizabeth's will and executor's deed add two whole District 9 lots to the family cluster. On February 5, 1878, Charles W. Ryall, acting under Elizabeth's will, conveyed LLs 493 and 520 to her daughter Edith Rountree for $1,200. The deed does not state that William had owned those two lots. It proves Elizabeth's title and the transfer to Edith.[35][42]

A derivative tax/land KML also assigns William Lot 493 and Lot 520, plus Lot 322 in District 12, and reports acreage totals that do not reconcile cleanly. The deeds now verify much of the District 9 cluster, but not William's title to 493 or 520, and not Lot 322. The original tax pages remain necessary for those claims.[23][38–42]

Geographic judgment: William's estate and Elizabeth's adjoining property formed a documented District 9 cluster north of Barney: Lots 491–493 and 519–521. The estate also included LL 323/12. This land passed into the Perry, Ryall, and Rountree family network, and nine researched descendant paths reach identified 1900 Barney households. The exact house site, William's acquisition deeds, LL 322, the later Moody title chain, and the legal cemetery parcel remain unresolved.[18][23][38–42]

Folsom Bridge

No located naming record identifies William as Folsom Bridge's namesake. Contemporary 1885 and 1893 evidence and early maps point instead to the older Lawrence–James–Andrew Jackson Folsom settlement at the east approach. William's reported plantation lay several miles west. The safest wording is that the bridge was named for the Folsom family settlement; Lawrence is the leading individual candidate, and William is geographically disfavored as the specific namesake.[24]

Enslaved people and the post-emancipation household

A public transcription of the 1860 Brooks County slave schedule lists Wm. Folsom with one enslaved male aged eleven and one slave house. A separate George Folsom entry lists ten enslaved people. The entries must not be combined. The original schedule image was not recovered in this pass, and no name can be assigned to the boy.[21]

The 1870 population schedule places three Black residents in William and Elizabeth's dwelling: Dicy Roberts, twenty-five, a domestic servant; Louis Roberts, four; and John Roberts, three. The census stated no relationships. In 1880, Dicea Roberts headed a Brooks County household with sons Lewis, fifteen, and John, fourteen, plus daughter Harriet, nine. The matching name forms, county, and ages verify postwar continuity for Dicy/Dicea and the two sons.[15][25]

Nothing in those records proves that Dicy had been enslaved by William. Her age and sex exclude her from the unidentified eleven-year-old boy; Louis and John were born after emancipation. Employment, housing, kinship, or some other association could explain the shared 1870 dwelling. No person has been identified responsibly across the slavery-to-freedom divide.

The contrast between the one-person 1860 schedule and Purvis's later “large plantation” worked by enslaved labor is unresolved. It may reflect different dates, hired labor, property held by relatives, earlier holdings, or exaggeration in the retrospective account. The evidence does not permit choosing among those explanations.[18][21]

Mount Zion and Methodist life

William was not among the seven original tenters named in Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollection, nor among the trustees in the 1831 Mount Zion deed. Lawrence Folsom held the trustee role. Sharpe did list William among deceased early residents of the Halls/Mount Zion neighborhood, and Purvis wrote in 1948 that “old settlers” credited William with doing more than anyone else toward the later church building.[18][26]

The obituary supplies the firmest personal evidence. Sharpe, who said he had known William about forty years, described William's conversion at a camp meeting, hospitality to traveling ministers, generosity to church causes and poor people, and standing in the Morven Circuit. This verifies long Methodist affiliation and support. It does not prove the later comparative claim that he contributed more than everyone else, a construction date, a payment amount, or a formal trustee office.[5]

Death and estate

The Southern Christian Advocate obituary states that William died at his Brooks County residence on November 16 “last,” in his seventy-eighth year. Because the issue is February 19, 1873, the year is 1872. Georgia Historic Newspapers supplies the complete original page, visibly numbered 28 and carrying the newspaper masthead and volume information. No numbered columns are printed. The writer was H. W. Sharpe.[5]

On July 7, 1873, William R. Ryall and Charles W. Ryall executed a $30,000 administration bond, with West Rountree, Green Lawson, and Nicholas M. Reddick as sureties. It was recorded August 12. The facing John Tillman bond is unrelated; Sharpe's signature on that facing page must not be attributed to William's estate.[11]

The August 23 notice sold estate beef cattle at Moultrie. The September notice states that the administrators would seek leave to sell William's lands for the heirs. Later notices directed creditors to present claims and debtors to pay. In September 1875 the Ryalls represented that they had fully administered the estate and sought discharge on the first Monday in December; repeated citations document the closing stage, but no final discharge order was located.[11–13][32][33]

No online inventory, appraisal, sale return, heir list or receipts, final return, distribution, or discharge order was located. Four administrator's deeds were located and inspected. They identify the land, buyers, prices, Ordinary Court authority, auction dates, and conveyance dates, but they do not expressly call the buyers William's children or heirs.[11–13][32][33][38–41]

Elizabeth's later will supplies the kinship language missing from William's estate file. It directly identifies Edith and Nancy as her daughters, the four named Ryalls as her grandchildren and Rachel Ann's children, C. W. Ryall and William Harrell as grandsons, and Charles W. Ryall as executor. The will is powerful family evidence but is not a complete list of William's heirs or children.[35]

Burial and grave location

Find a Grave assigns William and Elizabeth to Old Folsom Family Cemetery near Hahira and describes the graves as unmarked. That description is wrong. A user-supplied photograph shows a broken marble monument inscribed for both William and Elizabeth Folsom. William's name and the year 1872 are visible on the upper panel; Elizabeth's name and the year 1877 are visible below. The photograph verifies that a named monument existed, though it does not by itself identify the cemetery or geographic location.[6][36]

The 1938 genealogy says they were buried on the old Folsom homestead. Field documentation places the marked graves in Land Lot 520, District 9, on the homeplace later associated with the Rountree and Moody families. The Find a Grave map instead places them in Lowndes District 12, Land Lot 187, while describing the graves as unmarked. The monument photograph and field identification contradict that entry. A survey, cemetery deed, or burial register has not been found, so the legal cemetery parcel and its relationship to the full plantation boundary remain unresolved.[6][7][18][36][37]

Claims graded

Verified or strongly supported

  • William lived in the old Irwin/Lowndes/Brooks region and died at his Brooks County residence on November 16, 1872.[5][14–16]
  • A surviving photograph verifies a broken marble monument bearing William and Elizabeth Folsom's names and their respective death years, 1872 and 1877.[36]
  • FamilySearch's county-marriage record/index reports that William married Elizabeth Folsom in Pulaski County on December 11, 1813; the household and obituary evidence establish that she survived him.[5][14][16][34]
  • A published transcription of an 1845 newspaper names William Folsom as a Lowndes grand juror; the subject's identity is strong probable.[4]
  • Sharpe had known him for about forty years and described him as a generous Morven Circuit Methodist.[5]
  • His estate included land and beef cattle; administration was secured by a $30,000 bond.[11–13]
  • William R. and Charles W. Ryall administered the estate; West Rountree, Green Lawson, and Nicholas M. Reddick were sureties.[11]
  • Original administrator's deeds prove William owned at least 2,080 acres: LLs 492, 519, and 521/9; 120 acres in the southeast corner of LL 491/9; and LL 323/12.[38–41]
  • The administrators sold those lands to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree. Elizabeth's executor later conveyed LLs 493 and 520/9 to her daughter Edith Rountree.[35][38–42]
  • Elizabeth's will directly identifies Edith Rountree and Nancy Bradford as her daughters and identifies the four named Ryalls and William Harrell as her grandchildren.[35]
  • The 1870 dwelling included Dicy Roberts and her sons Louis and John, who continued together in 1880.[15][25]

Strong probable or secondary-supported

  • Lawrence Folsom and Rachel Vickers were William's parents.[7–10]
  • The William named on the 1823 and 1825 Irwin courthouse commissions was this man.[1–3][30]
  • The William who executed Lawrence Folsom's estate was this subject.[28][29]
  • Rachel Ann Ryall, Martha Harrell, and Hardy Vickers Folsom were William and Elizabeth's children; Edith Rountree and Nancy Bradford are verified daughters of Elizabeth and strong-probable daughters of William.[7][9][11][14][19][20][22][31][35]

Unresolved, unsupported, or contradicted

  • Exact birth day/year, Burke County birthplace, and the full parent-naming chain.
  • A complete and record-proved child list; Noah's parentage; the duplicated Edith/George tree profiles; Martha's exact death date.
  • Any office as judge, legislator, justice, sheriff, militia officer, or road overseer.
  • William's acquisition deeds, complete plantation acreage, exact house site, complete heir list, LL 322, and the later Moody title chain.
  • Whether William ever held title to LLs 493 and 520. The inspected deed proves Elizabeth owned and conveyed them; it does not recite William's prior ownership.[42]
  • Sugar production and exceptional support of Mount Zion are retrospective local traditions; no contemporary production or church-finance record was located.[18][26]
  • Identification of the unnamed boy enslaved in 1860 or any cross-emancipation identity.
  • William as the specific namesake of Folsom Bridge.
  • Elizabeth's exact death date; the smaller month-and-day inscription remains unreadable in the supplied photograph.

Online research coverage and limits

Local evidence collections, prior early-settlement reports, probate sources, road and bridge research, and saved newspaper datasets were searched first. Name variants included William Folsom, Wm. Folsom, William Folson, William Folsoom, Uncle Billy, Billy Folsom, and combinations with Lawrence, Elizabeth, Ryall/Ryals, Rountree/Roundtree, Harrell/Harrill, Roberts, Morven, Barney, Little River, Mount Zion, estate, heirs, land, cattle, jury, commissioner, and obituary.

Online checks covered authenticated Ancestry census/probate and obituary indexes, FamilySearch collaborative profiles and record pointers, Find a Grave images and cemetery pages, WikiTree, Internet Archive's Folsom genealogy, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Newspapers.com, Georgia Archives maps/land lots, Ray City History Blog, Wiregrass Region Digital History Project, and broad web searches. Logged-in or image-level access is stated where used. Search snippets and collaborative trees support leads only.

The following material was not found online: original birth record; Lawrence's will or probate file; original 1823 and 1825 act pages; 1820–1840 William-specific census chain; original 1850/1860 slave-schedule images; William's complete Brooks estate file; his acquisition deeds and original tax pages; the land-sale return; heir receipts; Mount Zion local records; and a burial register, cemetery deed, or survey. Four administrator's deeds and Elizabeth's executor deed are now verified online. This dossier does not imply that undigitized courthouse and church records do not exist.

Best next archival work

  1. Obtain the original 1823 and 1825 Georgia acts naming Irwin commissioners and compare exact spelling, powers, and dates.
  2. Request William Folsom's complete Brooks County loose estate file and every inventory, appraisal, sale, annual/final return, voucher, distribution, and order/minute entry, 1872–1885.
  3. Search backward for William's acquisition deeds and forward from the verified Perry, Ryall, and Rountree conveyances to the later J. E. Moody title chain.
  4. Obtain original Lowndes/Brooks tax pages behind the reported 1869–1872 acreage and the original 1850 and 1860 slave schedules.
  5. Search Mount Zion/Morven Circuit trustee, membership, financial, cemetery, and burial records for William and Elizabeth.
  6. Locate a parent-naming record for each proposed child rather than relying on the compiled eight-child list.

Citation audit

Every substantive claim above is tied to a numbered source or explicitly identified as unresolved. Sources 10, 17, 24, and 26 are evidence audits, not substitutes for original records where the dossier says an original remains missing. Sources 38–41 directly prove four estate conveyances totaling at least 2,080 acres; source 42 proves Elizabeth's separate conveyance of two whole lots to Edith Rountree. Sources 36 and 37 establish the marked monument and its Land Lot 520 setting. No source in this dossier proves William's acquisition deeds, complete heir list, complete plantation acreage, a named enslaved person, the bridge namesake, the legal cemetery parcel, or that the Ryalls received the requested final discharge.

docs.title: Evidence-graded online dossier
docs.text:
Subject: William Folsom, early South Georgia settler and son of Lawrence Folsom
Life dates: born about 1795 in Georgia; died November 16, 1872, at his Brooks County residence
Prepared: August 19, 2026
Updated: October 2, 2026
Standard: Original records and contemporary newspapers control. Later county histories, compiled genealogies, collaborative trees, and cemetery pages are identified as such. Repetition among derivative sources is not treated as independent proof.

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
William Folsom was an early Irwin County resident who remained in the same general South Georgia neighborhood as county boundaries changed from Irwin to Lowndes and then Brooks. Later courthouse-based histories identify a William Folsom on Irwin County courthouse-and-jail commissions in 1823 and 1825. A published transcription of an 1845 Lowndes grand-jury list also names William Folsom, and Brooks County's first petit-jury list in 1859 includes the name. Age and location make the subject a plausible to strong-probable match in these civic records, but the records as reviewed do not identify his wife, parent, or land.[1–4]

His death is unusually well documented. Hamilton W. Sharpe's obituary says Folsom died at his Brooks County residence on November 16, 1872, in his seventy-eighth year. It describes a long-established Methodist, generous to poor people, ministers, and church causes, and says that an aged wife survived him. The complete original page appeared in the Southern Christian Advocate on February 19, 1873.[5][6]

The family structure is clearer than earlier compilations suggested, but it is not complete. FamilySearch's Pulaski County marriage record/index reports William's 1813 marriage to Elizabeth Folsom. Elizabeth's 1876 will directly calls Edith Rountree and Nancy Bradford her daughters; identifies W. R., C. W., A. C., and Ruth Ann Ryall as her grandchildren and the children of Rachel Ann Ryall; and names C. W. Ryall and William Harrell as grandsons.[7–10][34][35]

Contrary to online reports, William and Elizabeth were not buried in unmarked graves in their family cemetery, but in marked graves on their homeplace in Land Lot 520, District 9. The surviving stone is broken and weathered, but both names are visible. William's panel preserves the year 1872; Elizabeth's preserves 1877. The smaller date lines are not clear enough for a full independent transcription.[36][37]

Administration of William's Brooks County estate was secured by a $30,000 bond. William R. Ryall and Charles W. Ryall served as administrators, with West Rountree, Green Lawson, and Nicholas M. Reddick as sureties. Four administrator's deeds now prove that William died owning at least 2,080 acres: all of Land Lots 492, 519, and 521 in District 9; 120 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 491 in District 9; and all of Lot 323 in District 12. The estate sold those tracts to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree. Elizabeth's executor later conveyed her Land Lots 493 and 520 in District 9 to her daughter Edith Rountree. These deeds document a Folsom-Ryall-Rountree-Perry land network north of Barney, although William's acquisition deeds and the later Rountree-to-J. E. Moody chain remain unlocated.[11–13][38–42]

docs.title: Identity and chronology
docs.text:
This dossier concerns the William Folsom born in Georgia about 1795, living in old Lowndes County by 1850, in Brooks County after its 1858 creation, and dying there in 1872. His age, wife Elizabeth, neighborhood, associates, 1870 household, obituary, and probate form a coherent identity chain.[5][9][14–16]

He must not be merged with Lieutenant William Folsom of Revolutionary-era Burke County; William I. Folsom, a younger Brooks County Confederate soldier; later judges or lawyers of the same name; William Folsom Ryall; or William Folsom Harrell. The surname cluster is dense, and title or location alone is not enough to transfer a record from one man to another.[7][10]

docs.title: Birth, parents, and migration
docs.text:
The obituary places William in his seventy-eighth year at death, implying birth between November 17, 1794, and November 16, 1795. The 1870 census gives age seventy-five, also pointing to about 1794–1795. The frequently repeated year 1797 comes from later genealogy and cemetery/tree profiles, not from a contemporary birth record. A publication-safe birth statement is about 1795 in Georgia. Burke County remains plausible but unproved.[5][7–10][16]

The 1938 Genealogy of the Folsom Family calls him the son of Lawrence Armstrong Folsom and Rachel Vickers. That Georgia section openly depends on family informants, principally Mrs. Boyd and Horace B. Folsom. FamilySearch, WikiTree, Find a Grave, and other online trees repeat the relationship. Contemporary 1849–1850 legal notices add important independent support: a William Folsom acted as executor of Lawrence Folsom's Lowndes County estate, sought leave to sell its enslaved people, and advertised estate property at James Folsom's house. The notices do not call William Lawrence's son, and the original will or probate file was not located. The executor's identity with this subject is strong probable from name, county, chronology, and family context; Lawrence and Rachel as his parents remain strong probable, not directly verified.[7–10][17][28][29]

William's migration has often been told too simply. Mrs. D. H. Purvis wrote in 1948 that he moved from Irwin County into the later Barney district in the 1830s. Yet the courthouse-commission traditions already place a William Folsom in Irwin civic affairs in 1823 and 1825, and the family genealogy assigns several children to Lowndes County before or during the 1830s. The surviving evidence supports continuous residence in the broader Irwin-to-Lowndes region, but it does not supply one exact arrival date at the later Brooks plantation.[1–3][7][18]

docs.title: Public and community roles
docs.text:
Irwin County courthouse commissions

Folks Huxford's county history and his 1950 newspaper history say the General Assembly first appointed William Folsom, James Crum, Silloway McCall, Joshua Griffin, and Alexander McDonald as Irwin courthouse-and-jail commissioners on December 13, 1823. They apparently did not complete the work. The December 24, 1825 organizing act then named John B. F. Dixon, James Wilcox, Emanuel Knowles, William Folsom, and Elijah Beasley as replacement Irwin commissioners.[1–3]

Huxford distinguishes the 1825 Irwin appointment from the simultaneous Lawrence Folsom commission for newly created Lowndes County. The two names should not be merged: his account puts Lawrence on the Lowndes commission and William on the Irwin commission. The target William was old enough and geographically plausible, and the repeated name in the two Irwin appointments supports a single local man. Neither the original act pages nor an identifying residence, relative, or tract was recovered, however. The subject's service is therefore possible to strong probable, not verified.[1–3][30]

Jury service

A published transcription of a June 1845 Lowndes Superior Court report names William Folsom among the grand jurors at Troupville. The transcription is strong secondary evidence, but the underlying newspaper image was not independently inspected in this project. Even if the reading is correct, the report establishes only jury service, not foremanship, office, party, or a specific verdict.[4]

Age, location, and prominence make the pioneer the strong-probable identity, but the list itself provides no age or residence. No record found online makes him a judge, justice of the peace, sheriff, legislator, militia officer, road commissioner, or elected county officer.[1]

docs.title: Irwin County courthouse commissions
docs.text:
Folks Huxford's county history and his 1950 newspaper history say the General Assembly first appointed William Folsom, James Crum, Silloway McCall, Joshua Griffin, and Alexander McDonald as Irwin courthouse-and-jail commissioners on December 13, 1823. They apparently did not complete the work. The December 24, 1825 organizing act then named John B. F. Dixon, James Wilcox, Emanuel Knowles, William Folsom, and Elijah Beasley as replacement Irwin commissioners.[1–3]

Huxford distinguishes the 1825 Irwin appointment from the simultaneous Lawrence Folsom commission for newly created Lowndes County. The two names should not be merged: his account puts Lawrence on the Lowndes commission and William on the Irwin commission. The target William was old enough and geographically plausible, and the repeated name in the two Irwin appointments supports a single local man. Neither the original act pages nor an identifying residence, relative, or tract was recovered, however. The subject's service is therefore possible to strong probable, not verified.[1–3][30]

docs.title: Wife and children
docs.text:
Elizabeth Folsom

FamilySearch's Pulaski County marriage record/index reports William and Elizabeth Folsom's marriage on December 11, 1813. Their 1850 and 1870 households and the 1873 obituary continue the identity chain and establish that Elizabeth survived William. The 1938 genealogy identifies her as a distant Folsom cousin, daughter of George Folsom and Edith Penny. No inspected birth, Bible, or parent-naming record proves that ancestry.[5][7][9][14][16][34]

Elizabeth executed her will on January 28, 1876, and it was recorded August 13, 1877, disproving the genealogy's statement that she died about 1875. A memorial gives March 16, 1877. The newly supplied monument photograph visibly supports 1877, but damage and weathering prevent a confident reading of the smaller month-and-day line from this image alone. Judgment: Elizabeth as William's wife is verified, and the 1813 marriage date has strong indexed record evidence. Her George/Edith parentage is strong compiled tradition. Her death year is now verified by the photographed monument; March 16 remains probable but not independently verified from the image.[7][34–36]

Publication-safe child structure

The 1938 genealogy lists eight children. The list is useful, but it is not an heir return and should not be called complete or proved merely because modern trees copy it.[7]

  • Green Folsom: said to have died as a small boy. Compiled-family-history only. FamilySearch's Green profile points to different preferred parents, a material conflict.
  • Rachel Ann Folsom Ryall: Elizabeth's will identifies W. R., C. W., A. C., and Ruth Ann Ryall as her grandchildren and as Rachel Ann Ryall's children. The 1938 genealogy explicitly calls Rachel a daughter of William and Elizabeth, and the Ryall sons' later administration of William's estate reinforces the relationship. Because the will does not use the exact phrase “my daughter Rachel Ann,” the conservative grade is strong probable, bordering verified.[7][11][19][35]
  • Edith Folsom Rountree: Elizabeth's will directly calls Edith her daughter and the wife of West Rountree. William and Elizabeth appear as a married couple across the census chain, with no evidence of stepchildren or another marriage. Verified daughter of Elizabeth; strong-probable daughter of William.[7][11][20][35]
  • George Folsom: listed in the genealogy, but nearby men of the same name create serious confusion. The 1860 slave schedule has a separate George entry. Possible/compiled; identity and child structure unresolved.[7][21]
  • Nancy Folsom Perry Bradford: Elizabeth's will directly calls Nancy Bradford her daughter and the wife of John Bradford. The 1938 genealogy says Nancy first married a Perry, while descendant material reports a later Andrew Jackson Bradford marriage dated after the will was executed. Verified daughter of Elizabeth; strong-probable daughter of William. The Perry/Bradford spouse chronology and the will's “John Bradford” wording remain unresolved.[7][9][35]
  • Martha Folsom Harrell/Horrell: an 1892 obituary for John S. Harrell calls his late wife Martha the “youngest daughter of William Folsom, Esq.” That explicit statement, published twenty years after William's death, joins the compiled genealogy, Martha's placement in William's 1850 household, Elizabeth's identification of William Harrell as a grandson, and the younger William Harrill's presence in William's 1870 dwelling. Strong probable daughter and likely youngest daughter; the article does not identify her mother. Later sources conflict between 1861 and 1895 death dates; Elizabeth's 1876 will is consistent with an earlier death but does not prove 1861.[7][14][16][22][31][35]
  • Hardy Vickers Folsom: Hardy appears in William and Elizabeth's 1850 household; the genealogy identifies him as a son, and a Brooks County marriage record links Hardy V. Folsom and Tempy Ann Wells in 1859. Strong probable son; the census does not state relationships.[7][9][14]
  • Janie/Jane Folsom: the genealogy says James Perry's wife; FamilySearch repeats the marriage but attaches no source. Possible daughter / tree-and-genealogy claim.[7][9]

FamilySearch adds Noah Folsom, born about 1832, as another son and identifies Julia Drawdy as his wife. Noah belongs to the same local Folsom cluster, but no record found in this research names William and Elizabeth as his parents. He is therefore a possible additional son, not a ninth verified child.[9][10]

docs.title: Farming, land, livestock, and wealth
docs.text:
The 1948 Barney history portrays “Uncle Billy” as a prominent planter near Little River who produced brown sugar for Savannah and Tallahassee and sent large cattle herds to Savannah and Charleston. It says his land later became the Rountree place owned by J. E. Moody. Sharpe's obituary independently supports a comfortable living and generous use of wealth, while the 1873 cattle notice proves that the estate owned beef cattle in Colquitt County. These points give the later account a real economic foundation, but they do not verify every production figure or annual cattle-drive claim.[5][12][18]

Four original administrator's deeds replace much of the earlier derivative land picture. William died seized and possessed of all of District 9 Land Lots 492, 519, and 521; 120 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 491; and all of District 12 Land Lot 323. The sales produced $800 from Nancy Perry for LL 492, $640 from Charles W. Ryall for LL 519 and the 120-acre portion of LL 491, $837 from West Rountree for LL 521, and $125 from West Rountree for LL 323. These deeds prove at least 2,080 acres in William's estate. They do not establish that this was his complete landholding.[38–41]

Elizabeth's will and executor's deed add two whole District 9 lots to the family cluster. On February 5, 1878, Charles W. Ryall, acting under Elizabeth's will, conveyed LLs 493 and 520 to her daughter Edith Rountree for $1,200. The deed does not state that William had owned those two lots. It proves Elizabeth's title and the transfer to Edith.[35][42]

A derivative tax/land KML also assigns William Lot 493 and Lot 520, plus Lot 322 in District 12, and reports acreage totals that do not reconcile cleanly. The deeds now verify much of the District 9 cluster, but not William's title to 493 or 520, and not Lot 322. The original tax pages remain necessary for those claims.[23][38–42]

Geographic judgment: William's estate and Elizabeth's adjoining property formed a documented District 9 cluster north of Barney: Lots 491–493 and 519–521. The estate also included LL 323/12. This land passed into the Perry, Ryall, and Rountree family network, and nine researched descendant paths reach identified 1900 Barney households. The exact house site, William's acquisition deeds, LL 322, the later Moody title chain, and the legal cemetery parcel remain unresolved.[18][23][38–42]

Folsom Bridge

No located naming record identifies William as Folsom Bridge's namesake. Contemporary 1885 and 1893 evidence and early maps point instead to the older Lawrence–James–Andrew Jackson Folsom settlement at the east approach. William's reported plantation lay several miles west. The safest wording is that the bridge was named for the Folsom family settlement; Lawrence is the leading individual candidate, and William is geographically disfavored as the specific namesake.[24]

docs.title: Enslaved people and the post-emancipation household
docs.text:
A public transcription of the 1860 Brooks County slave schedule lists Wm. Folsom with one enslaved male aged eleven and one slave house. A separate George Folsom entry lists ten enslaved people. The entries must not be combined. The original schedule image was not recovered in this pass, and no name can be assigned to the boy.[21]

The 1870 population schedule places three Black residents in William and Elizabeth's dwelling: Dicy Roberts, twenty-five, a domestic servant; Louis Roberts, four; and John Roberts, three. The census stated no relationships. In 1880, Dicea Roberts headed a Brooks County household with sons Lewis, fifteen, and John, fourteen, plus daughter Harriet, nine. The matching name forms, county, and ages verify postwar continuity for Dicy/Dicea and the two sons.[15][25]

Nothing in those records proves that Dicy had been enslaved by William. Her age and sex exclude her from the unidentified eleven-year-old boy; Louis and John were born after emancipation. Employment, housing, kinship, or some other association could explain the shared 1870 dwelling. No person has been identified responsibly across the slavery-to-freedom divide.

The contrast between the one-person 1860 schedule and Purvis's later “large plantation” worked by enslaved labor is unresolved. It may reflect different dates, hired labor, property held by relatives, earlier holdings, or exaggeration in the retrospective account. The evidence does not permit choosing among those explanations.[18][21]

docs.title: Mount Zion and Methodist life
docs.text:
William was not among the seven original tenters named in Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollection, nor among the trustees in the 1831 Mount Zion deed. Lawrence Folsom held the trustee role. Sharpe did list William among deceased early residents of the Halls/Mount Zion neighborhood, and Purvis wrote in 1948 that “old settlers” credited William with doing more than anyone else toward the later church building.[18][26]

The obituary supplies the firmest personal evidence. Sharpe, who said he had known William about forty years, described William's conversion at a camp meeting, hospitality to traveling ministers, generosity to church causes and poor people, and standing in the Morven Circuit. This verifies long Methodist affiliation and support. It does not prove the later comparative claim that he contributed more than everyone else, a construction date, a payment amount, or a formal trustee office.[5]

docs.title: Death and estate
docs.text:
The Southern Christian Advocate obituary states that William died at his Brooks County residence on November 16 “last,” in his seventy-eighth year. Because the issue is February 19, 1873, the year is 1872. Georgia Historic Newspapers supplies the complete original page, visibly numbered 28 and carrying the newspaper masthead and volume information. No numbered columns are printed. The writer was H. W. Sharpe.[5]

On July 7, 1873, William R. Ryall and Charles W. Ryall executed a $30,000 administration bond, with West Rountree, Green Lawson, and Nicholas M. Reddick as sureties. It was recorded August 12. The facing John Tillman bond is unrelated; Sharpe's signature on that facing page must not be attributed to William's estate.[11]

The August 23 notice sold estate beef cattle at Moultrie. The September notice states that the administrators would seek leave to sell William's lands for the heirs. Later notices directed creditors to present claims and debtors to pay. In September 1875 the Ryalls represented that they had fully administered the estate and sought discharge on the first Monday in December; repeated citations document the closing stage, but no final discharge order was located.[11–13][32][33]

No online inventory, appraisal, sale return, heir list or receipts, final return, distribution, or discharge order was located. Four administrator's deeds were located and inspected. They identify the land, buyers, prices, Ordinary Court authority, auction dates, and conveyance dates, but they do not expressly call the buyers William's children or heirs.[11–13][32][33][38–41]

Elizabeth's later will supplies the kinship language missing from William's estate file. It directly identifies Edith and Nancy as her daughters, the four named Ryalls as her grandchildren and Rachel Ann's children, C. W. Ryall and William Harrell as grandsons, and Charles W. Ryall as executor. The will is powerful family evidence but is not a complete list of William's heirs or children.[35]

docs.title: Burial and grave location
docs.text:
Find a Grave assigns William and Elizabeth to Old Folsom Family Cemetery near Hahira and describes the graves as unmarked. That description is wrong. A user-supplied photograph shows a broken marble monument inscribed for both William and Elizabeth Folsom. William's name and the year 1872 are visible on the upper panel; Elizabeth's name and the year 1877 are visible below. The photograph verifies that a named monument existed, though it does not by itself identify the cemetery or geographic location.[6][36]

The 1938 genealogy says they were buried on the old Folsom homestead. Field documentation places the marked graves in Land Lot 520, District 9, on the homeplace later associated with the Rountree and Moody families. The Find a Grave map instead places them in Lowndes District 12, Land Lot 187, while describing the graves as unmarked. The monument photograph and field identification contradict that entry. A survey, cemetery deed, or burial register has not been found, so the legal cemetery parcel and its relationship to the full plantation boundary remain unresolved.[6][7][18][36][37]

docs.title: Claims graded
docs.text:
Verified or strongly supported

  • William lived in the old Irwin/Lowndes/Brooks region and died at his Brooks County residence on November 16, 1872.[5][14–16]
  • A surviving photograph verifies a broken marble monument bearing William and Elizabeth Folsom's names and their respective death years, 1872 and 1877.[36]
  • FamilySearch's county-marriage record/index reports that William married Elizabeth Folsom in Pulaski County on December 11, 1813; the household and obituary evidence establish that she survived him.[5][14][16][34]
  • A published transcription of an 1845 newspaper names William Folsom as a Lowndes grand juror; the subject's identity is strong probable.[4]
  • Sharpe had known him for about forty years and described him as a generous Morven Circuit Methodist.[5]
  • His estate included land and beef cattle; administration was secured by a $30,000 bond.[11–13]
  • William R. and Charles W. Ryall administered the estate; West Rountree, Green Lawson, and Nicholas M. Reddick were sureties.[11]
  • Original administrator's deeds prove William owned at least 2,080 acres: LLs 492, 519, and 521/9; 120 acres in the southeast corner of LL 491/9; and LL 323/12.[38–41]
  • The administrators sold those lands to Nancy Perry, Charles W. Ryall, and West Rountree. Elizabeth's executor later conveyed LLs 493 and 520/9 to her daughter Edith Rountree.[35][38–42]
  • Elizabeth's will directly identifies Edith Rountree and Nancy Bradford as her daughters and identifies the four named Ryalls and William Harrell as her grandchildren.[35]
  • The 1870 dwelling included Dicy Roberts and her sons Louis and John, who continued together in 1880.[15][25]

Strong probable or secondary-supported

  • Lawrence Folsom and Rachel Vickers were William's parents.[7–10]
  • The William named on the 1823 and 1825 Irwin courthouse commissions was this man.[1–3][30]
  • The William who executed Lawrence Folsom's estate was this subject.[28][29]
  • Rachel Ann Ryall, Martha Harrell, and Hardy Vickers Folsom were William and Elizabeth's children; Edith Rountree and Nancy Bradford are verified daughters of Elizabeth and strong-probable daughters of William.[7][9][11][14][19][20][22][31][35]

Unresolved, unsupported, or contradicted

  • Exact birth day/year, Burke County birthplace, and the full parent-naming chain.
  • A complete and record-proved child list; Noah's parentage; the duplicated Edith/George tree profiles; Martha's exact death date.
  • Any office as judge, legislator, justice, sheriff, militia officer, or road overseer.
  • William's acquisition deeds, complete plantation acreage, exact house site, complete heir list, LL 322, and the later Moody title chain.
  • Whether William ever held title to LLs 493 and 520. The inspected deed proves Elizabeth owned and conveyed them; it does not recite William's prior ownership.[42]
  • Sugar production and exceptional support of Mount Zion are retrospective local traditions; no contemporary production or church-finance record was located.[18][26]
  • Identification of the unnamed boy enslaved in 1860 or any cross-emancipation identity.
  • William as the specific namesake of Folsom Bridge.
  • Elizabeth's exact death date; the smaller month-and-day inscription remains unreadable in the supplied photograph.

docs.title: Online research coverage and limits
docs.text:
Local evidence collections, prior early-settlement reports, probate sources, road and bridge research, and saved newspaper datasets were searched first. Name variants included William Folsom, Wm. Folsom, William Folson, William Folsoom, Uncle Billy, Billy Folsom, and combinations with Lawrence, Elizabeth, Ryall/Ryals, Rountree/Roundtree, Harrell/Harrill, Roberts, Morven, Barney, Little River, Mount Zion, estate, heirs, land, cattle, jury, commissioner, and obituary.

Online checks covered authenticated Ancestry census/probate and obituary indexes, FamilySearch collaborative profiles and record pointers, Find a Grave images and cemetery pages, WikiTree, Internet Archive's Folsom genealogy, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Newspapers.com, Georgia Archives maps/land lots, Ray City History Blog, Wiregrass Region Digital History Project, and broad web searches. Logged-in or image-level access is stated where used. Search snippets and collaborative trees support leads only.

The following material was not found online: original birth record; Lawrence's will or probate file; original 1823 and 1825 act pages; 1820–1840 William-specific census chain; original 1850/1860 slave-schedule images; William's complete Brooks estate file; his acquisition deeds and original tax pages; the land-sale return; heir receipts; Mount Zion local records; and a burial register, cemetery deed, or survey. Four administrator's deeds and Elizabeth's executor deed are now verified online. This dossier does not imply that undigitized courthouse and church records do not exist.

docs.title: Best next archival work
docs.text:
1. Obtain the original 1823 and 1825 Georgia acts naming Irwin commissioners and compare exact spelling, powers, and dates.
  2. Request William Folsom's complete Brooks County loose estate file and every inventory, appraisal, sale, annual/final return, voucher, distribution, and order/minute entry, 1872–1885.
  3. Search backward for William's acquisition deeds and forward from the verified Perry, Ryall, and Rountree conveyances to the later J. E. Moody title chain.
  4. Obtain original Lowndes/Brooks tax pages behind the reported 1869–1872 acreage and the original 1850 and 1860 slave schedules.
  5. Search Mount Zion/Morven Circuit trustee, membership, financial, cemetery, and burial records for William and Elizabeth.
  6. Locate a parent-naming record for each proposed child rather than relying on the compiled eight-child list.
