docs.title: Citation audit
docs.text: Every substantive claim above is tied to a numbered source or explicitly identified as unresolved. Sources 10, 17, 24, and 26 are evidence audits, not substitutes for original records where the dossier says an original remains missing. Sources 38–41 directly prove four estate conveyances totaling at least 2,080 acres; source 42 proves Elizabeth's separate conveyance of two whole lots to Edith Rountree. Sources 36 and 37 establish the marked monument and its Land Lot 520 setting. No source in this dossier proves William's acquisition deeds, complete heir list, complete plantation acreage, a named enslaved person, the bridge namesake, the legal cemetery parcel, or that the Ryalls received the requested final discharge.

docs.title: William Hendry of Liberty and Lowndes Counties, Georgia
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: Research conclusion
docs.text:
William Hendry can be followed with strong confidence from Liberty County in 1820 to Lowndes County in 1830 and 1834. Original census and tax images, an official Georgia law, contemporary newspapers, and an estate sale establish the core of his public life. He was a Mount Zion Camp Ground trustee, served on the May 1833 Lowndes grand jury, owned land in both Liberty and Lowndes Counties, and was dead by September 23, 1840. His estate included Lowndes District 12 Land Lots 517 and 518.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

The familiar biography is less secure than that record chain. Folks Huxford, drawing on a Hendry family compilation attributed to Milton D. Wilson, says William was born in New Hanover County, North Carolina, on February 12, 1783; married Nancy McFail in Liberty County on December 7, 1807; moved to Lowndes about 1825; and died of typhoid on June 6, 1840.[9] Those details are consistent with the census, estate, and cemetery tradition, but no original birth, marriage, family Bible, death, or probate-distribution record was located online. They should be credited as family tradition, not repeated as independently proved facts.

No contemporary record located in this project gives William a middle name. The modern form “William Tillman Hendry” comes from a contributor-maintained memorial and later derivative material.[10] This dossier therefore calls him William Hendry.

docs.title: Liberty County, 1820
docs.text:
The 1820 federal census lists William Hendry in Liberty County. His household contained one male and one female age 26 through 44, five boys under sixteen, and two girls under ten, nine people in all. Three people were engaged in agriculture. No enslaved people were enumerated.[1]

The household fits the age and child pattern in the later Huxford-Wilson family account, but census tick marks do not identify a wife or children by name. The image proves a Liberty County household headed by William; it does not by itself prove the exact birth date, Nancy McFail’s identity, or the eleven-child list.

docs.title: Lowndes County, 1830-1834
docs.text:
The 1830 Lowndes census lists William Hendry with eleven free white household members and no enslaved people. The oldest male and female were each age 40 through 49. John Hendry appears in the next household on the same page.[2]

William’s 1830 tax row places him in Captain Pike’s district with one poll and no enslaved people entered. The difficult land columns include Liberty and Lowndes property and District 12 Land Lot 512. Some acreage and ownership notations are hard to distinguish, so the preserved image is more reliable than an exact modern transcription of every column.[3]

The 1834 digest is clearer. It again lists William with one poll and no enslaved people entered. His land includes District 12 Lots 517 and 512 in Lowndes County and additional Liberty County acreage. John Hendry follows him in the digest.[4] The recurring Liberty interests, adult-age pattern, surname, and move into Lowndes make the 1820 and 1830-1834 records a strong-probable chain for the same man.

docs.title: Death and estate
docs.text:
A Southern Recorder legal notice dated September 23, 1840 sought authority to sell the real estate of William Hendry, late of Lowndes County, deceased. William H. Hendry was administrator.[5] Repeated notices advertised a November 20 sale at William’s late residence of hogs, cattle, horses, household and kitchen furniture, and other movable property.[6]

The 1840 tax digest independently distinguishes the two men: it lists living taxpayer William H. Hendry and identifies him separately as administrator of the estate of William Hendry, deceased.[7] The middle initial did not refer to the elder man.

An April 13, 1841 notice advertised District 12 Lots 517 and 518 for sale at Troupville as the deceased William’s property. William H. again signed as administrator.[8] The notices prove that William died before September 23, 1840, that William H. administered the estate, and that the estate owned the two Lowndes lots. They do not state William’s exact death date or the administrator’s relationship to him.

docs.title: Home tract and location
docs.text:
The best defensible location for William’s Lowndes home is the estate tract formed by District 12 Land Lots 517 and 518. Georgia’s official land-lot GIS places the approximate lot centroids at 30.902353, -83.657136 for Lot 517 and 30.889638, -83.657372 for Lot 518.[11] The tract is in present-day Brooks County, near Mule Creek and roughly between Pavo and Quitman. That agrees with Huxford’s later description.[9]

This is a land-lot reconstruction, not an identified house footprint. The perishable-property sale was to occur at the late residence, while the later land notice names both lots, but neither notice says which lot contained the dwelling. No deed chain, survey, plat showing a house, or archaeological identification was found online.

Georgia Archives’ online headright-plat index also has five Liberty County entries under William Hendry: two 200-acre entries in 1816, 2.9 acres in 1817, 150 acres in 1818, and 196 acres on the Canoochee River in 1818.[12] They are useful leads for the Liberty-to-Lowndes man, but the index names alone do not prove that all five belong to him. Original plats, grants, and conveyances are needed before treating them as his parcel history.

docs.title: Mount Zion Camp Ground
docs.text: Mount Zion is William Hendry’s best-documented public role.

docs.title: The first tenters and the Hardy/Hendry problem
docs.text:
Hamilton W. Sharpe, a participant, wrote in 1884 that William Hendry and John Hendry were among Mount Zion’s first seven tenters. His article dates the first meeting to fall 1829.[13] That statement was made about fifty-five years later, but it is direct participant recollection and specifically names both men.

The same original page says the three-man site committee consisted of “William Hardy,” William Blair, and Sharpe. A 1941 reprint preserves “Wm. Hardy” for the committee while again naming William Hendry among the tenters.[14] Huxford later printed the committee member as William Hendry and dated the meeting to 1828.[9] The later deed and statute make Hendry’s Mount Zion leadership clear, but they do not authorize silently changing the newspaper’s "Hardy" to "Hendry". The committee identity and the 1828/1829 year remain unresolved.

Norman Campbell’s 1903 recollection broadly included William, John, Eli, and James Hendry among Mount Zion’s founders.[15] Campbell moved into the area in 1829 and admitted difficulty remembering names. A 1926 centennial account likewise placed Hendry settlers near the camp ground but warned that minor details might be inaccurate.[16] Both are useful local memory, not independent kinship proof.

docs.title: The 1831 deed
docs.text:
Huxford printed a transcription that he said he copied from the original November 8, 1831 deed. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed about six acres associated with the west line of District 12 Lot 271, including the camps, church, and burying ground, to Methodist Episcopal trustees William Blair, William Hendry, Lawrence Folsom, James J. Joyce, and William G. Hall. John Morrison proved the deed on October 3, 1832, and clerk William Smith recorded it on February 26, 1833 in Lowndes Deed Book A, pages 654-655.[17]

The courthouse copy was later lost in the fire and was not re-recorded. Huxford’s original-based transcription is strong evidence, but an image of the manuscript deed was not located.

docs.title: The 1833 incorporation act
docs.text:
The official session law gives direct proof. Section 10 incorporated “William Blair, John Jordan, William Hendry, James J. Jordan, and Randal Folsom” and their successors as the Trustees of the Mount Zion Camp Ground in Lowndes County.[18] This list differs from the deed trustees except for Blair and Hendry. The two documents served different legal purposes and need not contain identical boards.

The statute verifies William’s position without relying on Huxford or later oral history. It does not prove that every Hendry named in later founder lists was related to him.

docs.title: Civic record
docs.text:
The Georgia Times and State Rights’ Advocate printed the May 1833 Lowndes grand-jury presentments with William Hendry among the jurors and William Blair as foreman. The panel addressed road enforcement, ferry charges, county records, and poor-school funds.[19] This is direct evidence of William’s civic participation, though it supplies no age, occupation, or family relationship.

Huxford says William became a commissioner to contract for a Lowndes courthouse and jail in December 1835.[9] The official law does not print his surname that way. It names "William Henry", along with William Folsome, Jarrel Johnson, Samuel M. Clyet, Henry Strickland, John Knight, and John Lindsey, and was assented to December 23, 1835.[20] Huxford gives "Hendry" and December 28.

The printed "Henry" may be an error for Hendry, but no original bill, journal annotation, commission, or executive minute was located to prove it. William’s appointment is therefore unresolved and contradicted by the official printed text. He should not presently be called a courthouse or county-site commissioner as an established fact.

No online road petition, viewers’ return, overseer appointment, bridge contract, county road minute, or other direct record of a road role was found.

docs.title: Military claims
docs.text:
An index to War of 1812 compiled service records contains a William Hendry who served as second lieutenant in the 2nd Regiment, Pray’s Georgia Militia.[21] He is a plausible candidate because the dossier subject was in Georgia by 1820 and later family history says he served. The index supplies no age, residence, wife, or relative, however, so it does not complete the identity bridge. A second indexed William Hendry served as a private in North Carolina militia, which adds to the ambiguity.[21]

The modern cemetery marker calls the Lowndes settler a veteran of 1812.[10] That is evidence of later commemoration, not a contemporary military record. The safest conclusion is that Georgia service by a man of the same name is documented, while its assignment to this William is possible to probable, not proved.

The downloaded bounty-warrant register does not help. Warrant 996 cross-references William Samuel Hendry and the year 1806, before the War of 1812; it is not evidence for the subject.[22]

No original record was found for the reported 1807 ensign appointment or 1825 Liberty County justice-of-the-peace appointment. The 1836 Lowndes militia return does not name William among the 81st Regiment field and staff. Official Brushy Creek reports identify Captain John Pike and other commanders but do not list William, and no company roster was located.[23] William Hendry’s participation at Brushy Creek is unproved.

Huxford’s officer table lists "Wm. H. Hendry" as an ensign in 1837.[9] That is a younger man, not proof of the elder William’s service.

docs.title: Family reconstruction
docs.text:
Huxford’s Wilson-derived account calls William the third son of Robert Hendry and Ann Lee and says he married Nancy McFail in Liberty County on December 7, 1807. It lists eleven children:[9]

  1. James Edward, born September 29, 1808
  2. Eli Harrison, born September 26, 1810
  3. Harriet, born March 28, 1812
  4. Nancy Jane, born March 26, 1814
  5. Robert McFail, born February 29, 1816
  6. William Hamilton, born May 9, 1818
  7. Neil, born April 6, 1820
  8. John McFail, born July 5, 1822
  9. David Lee, born June 18, 1824
  10. Mary Winn, born July 2, 1826
  11. Elizabeth C., born December 30, 1830

The 1820 household structure fits the Wilson-derived list through that year, but the 1830 schedule is only partly consistent with it. The census has nine people below the oldest male and female, while the list supplies ten children born by the census date if all were still alive and at home, and the sex and age bands do not align exactly. The census therefore neither proves nor cleanly corroborates the full child list. No will, probate distribution, guardianship, family Bible, or original marriage return naming the whole family was located online.

William H. Hendry is a strong-probable match for the listed son William Hamilton. In 1840 he administered the estate, and an 1850 Lowndes household headed by Wm. H. Hendry, age 31, fits the reported 1818 birth year.[7][24] The estate notice itself never calls him a son.

John Hendry is likewise a strong-probable brother, not a proved one. Huxford calls him William’s brother; the two appear adjacent in the 1830 census and tax material, and the older John remained in Lowndes through 1850, when he was recorded as age 72 and born in North Carolina.[2][4][9][25] Adjacency and a compiled family account are persuasive, but no located deed, probate, Bible, or contemporary statement expressly establishes the sibling relationship.

docs.title: Death and burial tradition
docs.text:
Huxford reports that typhoid killed son Eli H. Hendry on June 4, William on June 6, and Nancy on June 27, 1840, and says they were buried on Mule Creek.[9] Find a Grave memorial 37017171 and a modern replacement marker repeat the dates and identify the burial place as Hendry Cemetery.[10]

The estate record confirms that William was dead by September 23, 1840, but no contemporary obituary, death notice, epidemic report, burial entry, or original gravestone was found. The exact dates, typhoid diagnosis, Nancy’s June death, and Mule Creek burial are strong family and cemetery tradition. The marker is modern and should not be treated as a surviving 1840 stone.

docs.title: Enslavement evidence
docs.text:
The 1820 and 1830 federal censuses enumerate no enslaved people in William’s household.[1][2] His 1830 and 1834 tax rows have no enslaved people entered.[3][4] The 1840 perishable-property notice lists livestock and household goods but does not advertise enslaved people.[6]

These records justify the narrow statement that no enslaved people appear in the inspected census and tax entries. They do not prove that William never held an interest in enslaved labor at any point in his life or through another estate or arrangement.

docs.title: What is proved, probable, and unresolved
Proved
docs.text:
• A William Hendry headed the 1820 Liberty household and the 1830 Lowndes household.
  • The Lowndes William was taxed in 1830 and 1834, with District 12 land and no enslaved people entered.
  • He was an incorporated Mount Zion trustee in 1833.
  • He served on the May 1833 Lowndes grand jury.
  • He was dead by September 23, 1840.
  • William H. Hendry administered his estate.
  • The estate owned District 12 Lots 517 and 518.

docs.title: Strong probable or strong tradition
docs.text:
• The Liberty and Lowndes records describe the same man.
  • Nancy McFail was his wife.
  • William H. was his son William Hamilton.
  • John Hendry was his brother.
  • The eleven-child Huxford-Wilson list substantially represents his family.
  • The estate tract was the general location of his home near Mule Creek.

docs.title: Unresolved or unproved
docs.text:
• "Tillman" or any other middle name.
  • Original proof of the February 12, 1783 birth and December 7, 1807 marriage.
  • Exact death date, typhoid diagnosis, and exact grave location.
  • Whether the 1884 site-committee member printed "William Hardy" was Hendry.
  • Whether the first Mount Zion meeting occurred in 1828 or 1829.
  • Whether the 1835 act’s "William Henry" was a printing error for Hendry.
  • Identity of the War of 1812 Georgia officer and any Brushy Creek service.
  • Original proof of the reported ensign, justice-of-the-peace, and road roles.

docs.title: Online research coverage and limits
docs.text:
Local project files and previously preserved books were searched first. The online search then covered Ancestry census, tax, military, marriage, family-history, and cemetery indexes; FamilySearch catalog and result leads; Find a Grave; Georgia Historic Newspapers; Newspapers.com; Digital Library of Georgia session laws; Georgia Archives plat indexes; Internet Archive; HathiTrust; Google Books metadata; and general web results. Searches used "Hendry", "Henry", "Hardy", "Hendrie", and "Hendrey" with Liberty, Lowndes, Brooks, Mount Zion, Mule Creek, estate, death, military, and family terms.[26]

The best remaining targets are the original Lowndes administrator bond and probate packet; the full Wilson manuscript; Liberty marriage, church, deed, tax, and plat records; Georgia executive commission books; the original 1835 bill and legislative journals; and a War of 1812 compiled service or pension file with residence or kinship data.

docs.title: Commerce and industry
docs.text: Barney's first municipal years remained tied to timber, rail transportation, farming, and a small business district.

docs.title: Taxable property and regional industry
docs.text:
Brooks County's 1903 tax digest listed the Barney district at $140,730 in taxable value, an increase of $17,426. The figure measures the district's tax base rather than its population, but it provides an economic baseline at the time of incorporation.

Newspaper coverage in 1905 and 1906 placed Barney & Smith in discussions of timber and railroad development around Milltown, Naylor, and Valdosta. On October 4, 1906, the Valdosta Daily Times reported that three possible Milltown-to-Valdosta routes had been surveyed for N. E. Whitehurst, manager of the Barney-Smith railway interests. The survey recorded timber and open land along each route. These reports do not establish that Barney & Smith owned the South Georgia Railway.

Edward C. Bridges's 1909 obituary supplies a personal example of the same economy. It says he moved to Brooks County nearly fifteen years earlier, settled at Barney, and worked in sawmilling with the Oglesbys before entering a wider group of lumber, grocery, hardware, banking, and naval-stores businesses.

A March 27, 1910, Atlanta Journal county profile described the South Georgia Railway from Adel through Quitman to Perry, Florida, and named J. W. Oglesby as its president and superintendent and as a central figure in the Oglesby Lumber and Manufacturing Company. Barney was one town along that regional rail-and-lumber system.

Cotton remained active as well. On August 13, 1909, the Valdosta Daily Times reported that the gins at Morven and Barney had run full time the previous day.

The naval-stores trade also continued around Barney. On December 9, 1904, the Moultrie Observer described H. D. Woolard as a naval-stores operator of Barney.

docs.title: The business district in 1908
docs.text:
A December 1908 town profile listed six general stores, a hardware and furniture business, a drugstore, a bank, a cotton gin, a meat market, a hotel, two blacksmith shops, a turpentine plant, a livery stable, a fireproof warehouse, two churches, and a school. It also counted four brick stores and a brick bank building, with two more brick buildings planned.

The correspondent estimated that Barney conducted about $150,000 in business each year and called it the largest shipping point on the South Georgia Railway between Adel and Greenville except Quitman. Those claims appeared in an argument for a better road to Valdosta and should be read as promotion. The detailed inventory, however, documents the range of businesses operating in the town.

docs.title: Stores and fires
docs.text:
On September 27 and 28, 1906, the Macon Telegraph and Valdosta Daily Times reported a fire at Walker & Moody's general-merchandise store. Fleming Bates Walker, identified in the reports as F. B. Walker, found the building filled with heat and smoke when he opened it at 6 a.m. Damage was estimated at about $1,500, most of it from smoke and water, and the cause was unknown.

On April 24, 1908, the Valdosta Daily Times reported that P. Feingold's dry-goods store, opened about two weeks earlier, had burned completely. The stock was valued at approximately $2,400, with $2,000 in insurance.

docs.title: Banking and land promotion
docs.text:
The Atlanta Journal reported on September 24, 1905, that Citizens Bank had been organized at Adel with $25,000 in capital and planned a branch at Barney. The announcement does not prove that the proposed branch opened.

A Bank of Barney was operating by June 25, 1906, when the Atlanta Georgian listed its representative among those expected at a meeting of banks associated with W. S. Witham. The paper printed the representative's initials as B. L. Long. On September 27, the same newspaper identified Ben F. Long as cashier of a bank at Barney. The December 1908 town profile confirms an operating bank and a separate brick bank building.

In February 1909, The Bankers Magazine reported, “Barney—Bank of Barney; title changed to Barney Banking Co.” A 1909-1910 Georgia business directory named W. D. Manley as president, Fleming Bates Walker as vice-president, and B. F. Long as cashier. The directory printed Walker's name as “F. B. Walker.” The evidence does not establish how the proposed Citizens Bank branch, a later-reported Bank of Adel connection, and the Bank of Barney were related. Both Bank of Barney and Barney Banking Company continued to appear in later records.

Advertisements in September 1910 promoted farms in and around the Barney district. One listed land less than a quarter mile from Barney's businesses, churches, and schoolhouse. Another promoted Brooks County roads, schools, bridges, tax rates, rising land values, and farms near Barney. These advertisements document the sales pitch used for the area, not an independent assessment of those claims.

docs.title: Community life and politics
docs.text: Newspaper notices from 1903-1910 show Barney residents traveling, worshipping, studying, organizing, and maintaining ties with Valdosta and the surrounding county.

docs.title: Church and education
docs.text:
An August 4, 1907, Macon Telegraph Adel column reported that Revs. Adams and Allaben were conducting a meeting at Barney and that about a dozen people had joined the Methodist church. The item provides a contemporary link between Huxford's 1899 organization date for the church and its later civic role.

An April 2, 1906, Atlanta Journal medical-school graduation list names Gilbert Wayne Nicholson of Barney among the Atlanta College of Physicians and Surgeons graduates in medicine.

On May 21, 1910, the Atlanta Constitution reported that Hoke Smith delivered an education address at a school-grounds picnic in Barney. Dr. S. S. Gaulden introduced him, and the newspaper said many people attended from outside the town.

docs.title: Politics and organized farm life
docs.text:
In a February 18, 1906, dispatch from Barney, Fleming Bates Walker, identified in print as F. B. Walker, wrote that fifteen men polled at his store supported Hoke Smith for governor. A 1907 Farmers' Institute picnic notice named B. Walker and W. R. Blease on the Barney district committee. In 1908, W. R. Bleas of Barney was listed on the Brooks County Democratic Executive Committee. The printed Blease and Bleas forms are retained as they appeared in the newspapers.

Barney also fielded a baseball team. On May 31, 1909, the Atlanta Georgian and News reported a game between Barney and Morven, with Barney winning 14 to 8.

docs.title: Travel, family, and daily life
docs.text:
Small notices record regular movement between Barney and Valdosta. J. S. Moody and J. H. Culpepper visited Valdosta in April 1907. S. S. Hires traveled there on business in September 1908, and T. M. Moore did the same in May 1910. Hotel lists in October and December 1909 included Barney residents A. E. Millan, A. T. Moody, and A. G. Whitehurst.

A 1909 medicine advertisement carried a testimonial signed by Mrs. J. T. Weeks and dated at Barney. On November 21, 1910, the Valdosta Daily Times reported that Elias Chancey and Alberta Simms married at the Barney home of Mr. and Mrs. D. F. Parker before moving to Valdosta.

The 1908 county map and a December newspaper profile both place a hotel in Barney. In the 1910 census, Mary Walker headed a rented First Avenue household, worked as a hotel laborer, and lived with relatives and three boarders: bank cashier Benjamin F. Long, general-merchandise salesman Hardy Ryalls, and house painter J. T. Bransom. The census links the household to hotel work and boarding, but it does not say that Walker owned or managed the hotel.

Two 1910 notices record illness and injury. James Walker of Barney, about seventeen or eighteen years old and formerly the local depot agent, died after a two-week illness described as fever and meningitis. Gordon Chambers, who lived near Barney, was seriously injured when a mule kicked him; the report also records telegram communication and family travel between Barney and Valdosta.

docs.title: The 1910 census
docs.text: The surviving 1910 census pages support individual households and occupations, including the First Avenue boarding household described above. No dependable precinct-wide population, occupation, literacy, or property total has been established from those pages. Such totals should not be stated until the full district has been transcribed and checked against the original images.

docs.title: Government and early officers
docs.text: Barney's charter called for a mayor and five councilmen, with annual elections beginning in December 1903. The surviving administrative record is thin. No continuous set of election returns, ordinances, marshal appointments, tax notices, or council minutes has been located for 1903-1910.

docs.title: Sion L. Hall, the first mayor
docs.text:
The charter scheduled Barney's first municipal election for the first Wednesday in December 1903. The election return has not been found, but two contemporary notices identify the mayor who took office afterward.

On January 8, 1904, The Adel News reported, "Mayor S. L. Hall, of Barney, was a visitor to Adel Sunday." The original page reads S. L., correcting an earlier index transcription of J. L. A second notice in the June 24 issue referred to "Mayor Hall of Barney."

Neither article uses the words "first mayor." Their dates, however, place Hall in office immediately after the charter's first scheduled election. The charter and the two notices therefore strongly support Sion L. Hall as Barney's inaugural mayor.

docs.title: The next documented administration
docs.text:
A transcript attributed to the December 16, 1905, Valdosta Times says Barney's annual municipal election was quiet and names the successful candidates:

  • Mayor W. E. Hiers
  • Councilman W. B. Greeson
  • Councilman W. E. Westbury
  • Councilman J. M. McMullan
  • Councilman Turner Folsom
  • Councilman Steve Collins

This is the only accepted full mayor-and-council slate currently documented for Barney between 1903 and 1910. It identifies W. E. Hiers as the next documented mayor after Hall. The original newspaper page has not been relocated, so the item remains an unpublished transcript in the James E. Jones collection.

docs.title: What is known about the officers
docs.text:
W. E. Hiers has not been identified as a specific person in Huxford's county history. The Hiers surname does appear among the families remembered in the older Barney district, but that does not establish the mayor's parentage or residence history.

Turner Folsom appears in the 1910 census in the household of his father, I. L. Folsom, identified elsewhere as Israel L. Folsom. Israel was a nephew of Elizabeth Folsom, wife of William "Uncle Billy" Folsom. This connects Turner to the older Little River and Folsom Bridge settlement, although the 1905 election notice remains the source for his municipal office.

The election notice prints J. M. McMullan. Huxford discusses an older McMullen family, including John and James McMullen, but no evidence presently connects Councilman McMullan to that family. The spelling difference remains unresolved.

Huxford's account of Barney Lodge No. 609 lists W. E. Westberry as a member in 1911. He may have been the W. E. Westbury named in the 1905 election notice, but no direct record has established that identity. Steve Collins is identifiable as Stephen Collins in household 001 of the 1910 Barney census. No accepted individual identification has been found for W. B. Greeson.

docs.title: Lost town records
docs.text:
Local history places Barney's city hall at the southeast corner of Main Street and First Avenue, among the brick commercial buildings on the south side of Main Street. The city hall and the building immediately east of it later burned, destroying many early town records. This was separate from the Blease building fire on the northwest corner. The loss helps explain why the charter and the 1905 election transcript survive without a fuller municipal paper trail.

The offices and powers created by the 1903 charter are described in Government and elections and Municipal powers and local needs.

docs.title: Public order and law
docs.text: Reports from 1903 to 1910 show violence in and around Barney and the town government operating alongside county law enforcement. The accounts come from white-owned newspapers and preserve their racial assumptions, so they should be read as contemporary reports rather than neutral findings.

docs.title: Perry Peeples and Ed Cook, 1903
docs.text:
On December 26, 1903, several newspapers reported that Perry Peeples, a white man, had shot and killed Ed Cook, a Black man, at Barney. The Atlanta Journal said Sheriff Connolly was summoned after reports of possible racial violence. The Atlanta Constitution reported that armed men traveled from Quitman on a special train. The Savannah Morning News followed on December 27 with "All Quiet at Barney," saying the posse found the town quiet and returned, although authorities still feared further trouble.

A separate December 22, 1905, report said Peeples had stood trial at Quitman on charges brought by some Barney citizens and the town of Barney. The newspaper said the charges failed, the defense presented no testimony beyond Peeples's statement, and the state did not substantiate its case. The article does not identify every charge or explicitly connect the trial with Cook's death. Without a court file or fuller report, the 1905 case should remain separate from the 1903 killing account.

docs.title: The killing of Tobe Robinson, 1904
docs.text:
The Moultrie Observer reported on April 15, 1904, that Curtis Webb had shot and killed Tobe Robinson Jr. at Barney after a disagreement over a horse Robinson had sold him. According to the article, Robinson abused Webb and was drawing a pistol when Webb shot him twice through the heart. Webb surrendered, was taken to Quitman, and was jailed. These details are the newspaper's account, not findings from a court record.

The article described Robinson as about 27 and Webb as 18. It also said that both men had relatives in Colquitt County and Moultrie. An editorial on another page of the same issue referred to the killing while criticizing a series of recent shootings in Brooks County. No later report or court record establishing the disposition of the case has been located.

docs.title: The Womack shooting, 1905
docs.text: On June 9, 1905, the Moultrie Observer reported violence at H. D. Woolard's turpentine place near Barney. According to Woolard's account, employee Will Womack shot his wife twice with a shotgun and then killed himself. The newspaper said Mrs. Womack was seriously wounded but expected to recover. No later report establishing her condition or identifying a court or inquest record has been located.

docs.title: The killing of “Big Kid,” 1906
docs.text:
On September 3, 1906, the Valdosta Daily Times reprinted a brief item from the Adel News. It reported that one Black man had killed another at Barney on Saturday night. The man killed was known as “Big Kid,” and Pete Crawley was arrested and accused of the crime. The item said a woman was thought to have been the cause of the dispute.

The report does not identify “Big Kid” or the woman, and no later account has been found giving the disposition of the charge against Crawley.

docs.title: The Watkins shooting, 1910
docs.text:
The Valdosta Daily Times reported another shooting on August 6, 1910. According to the article, Charley Clark fought aboard a South Georgia train, was removed at Barney, and was arrested and locked up after the conductor obtained local help. Later that night, Marshal Byrd and Mashburn went to arrest two men following a report of threats.

The ensuing gunfire killed J. W. Watkins, a Black man, near his gate and wounded two other Black men. The article said it was unknown which officer fired the fatal shot and that the other wounds were not expected to be fatal. Those statements are newspaper claims, not a court verdict, but the report names a town marshal and documents a municipal policing incident.

docs.title: Transportation and postal service
docs.text: Rail service, roads, bridges, and the post office continued to connect Barney with the surrounding district after incorporation.

docs.title: Postmasters and rural delivery
docs.text:
The U.S. Post Office Department appointment ledger gives this sequence for Barney: Thomas A. Rozier, July 26, 1897; Tobe G. Robinson, October 24, 1903; Blackmon H. Culbreth, April 18, 1904; Andrew W. Voight, May 11, 1905; Moses W. Wesberry, December 30, 1905; Thomas A. Rozier, February 20, 1906; and Paris Culpepper, February 17, 1916.

An October 24, 1903, Atlanta Journal notice independently reported Robinson's appointment, printing the former postmaster's name as Thomas A. "Roseir." The ledger supports Thomas A. Rozier, but the newspaper's spelling should remain visible.

Robinson's identity is supported by several records. The Valdosta Times reported that Tobe Robinson was killed at Barney on April 12, 1904, after a dispute over a horse trade. Six days later, the appointment ledger records Blackmon H. Culbreth as postmaster. A Brooks County estate record dated April 30 names Tobias G. Robinson as deceased and appoints Mrs. Laura J. Robinson to care for the estate. Huxford's Robinson-Wade account identifies a younger Tobias Gibson Robinson whose father lived until 1921. Together, the records make it likely that the postmaster, the man killed, and the younger Tobias G. Robinson were the same person, although the sources print different forms of his name.

Rural free delivery began at Barney on November 15, 1904. On May 10, 1905, the Atlanta Journal named Walter E. Westberry as carrier and Moses Westberry as substitute for Barney route 2. The 1908 Brooks County map marks routes 1 and 2 extending from Barney into the surrounding countryside. The evidence does not establish that both routes opened on the same day.

The primary appointment ledger does not support Edmondson's disputed sequence naming J. W. Harris and Robert Rozier as early Barney postmasters. November 1909 classified notices addressed "Rozier, Barney, Ga." support a Rozier presence in the community, but not a separate postmaster claim.

docs.title: Rail service and bridges
docs.text:
By 1904 the South Georgia Railway extended to Perry, Florida, and its northern terminal had shifted from Heartpine to Adel. Barney remained one station on the larger rail-and-timber route.

The line was vulnerable to weather. On September 29, 1903, the Valdosta Times reported that the railroad bridge across Little River above Barney had washed away. Trains continued to Barney, but through schedules to Heartpine and through mail service were delayed while crews built a replacement.

Another disruption came in January 1907, when a southbound freight train struck a coal car at Barney. Three cars and the caboose left the track. No one was injured, but traffic was delayed.

Road bridges also linked Barney with nearby counties. A July 21, 1903, report said a new bridge had been built over Reedy Creek on the Barney road and that work would next move to Wells Mill Creek. Brooks and Lowndes counties shared the expense.

docs.title: Telephone and telegraph service
docs.text:
A later court record describes how Barney residents could send telegrams in July 1909 even though the town had no telegraph office. The South Georgia Railroad maintained a private telephone line between its Barney and Quitman depots. A customer could give a telegram and payment to the Barney depot agent, who telephoned the message to Quitman for transmission by Western Union.

This was a useful relay arrangement, but it was not a public local telephone exchange. Later local history says the Quitman Telephone Company had extended lines to Barney by 1907; the first located evidence expressly describing a Barney exchange dates from after this period.

docs.title: Angus James “A. J.” Conoly: online research dossier
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed: 17 August 2026

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
A. J. Conoly was Angus James Conoly, born in Robeson County, North Carolina, in February 1864. He was a son of George Burder Conoly and Flora C. Currie Conoly and an older brother of Hector McLean Conoly. He came into the Foster, Georgia, naval-stores business in 1891, served ten years as sheriff of Brooks County, and then returned to the timber and naval-stores trade. Although his work repeatedly took him to Florida, his family home remained in Quitman.

He married Debro K. Walker in Brooks County on 5 June 1895. An original will made by her paternal uncle and guardian expands her name to Deborah Kesiah Walker; contemporary records show that she ordinarily used Debro. Her father, Isham A. Walker, was a brother of the elder Fleming B. Walker, making Debro a first cousin of Fleming Bates Walker (about 1860–1934), the Barney merchant. Their children were Samuel Stillwell “Sam” Conoly and Flora Agnes Conoly, later Mrs. Charles Henry Crandon. Angus died in Jacksonville during the night of 27–28 October 1925. Sam found him dead in a hotel room early on the 28th. His body was returned to Quitman and buried at Oak Hill Cemetery.

The identity chain is verified. The remaining death-date issue is whether the event should be recorded as 27 October, when some contemporary reports say he died, or 28 October, when he was found and the cemetery memorial dates the death. His exact birth day also rests on derivative cemetery evidence; the 1900 census independently supports February 1864.

docs.title: Identity controls and name variants
docs.text:
The following records describe one man:

  • Angus J. Conoly, age 16, son of George B. and Flora C. Conoly in the 1880 Lumber Bridge census;
  • A. J. Conley/Conoly, brother and co-investor of H. McLean Conoly at Foster in 1891;
  • Brooks County sheriff A. J. Conoly at Quitman from 1895 through 1904;
  • Angus J. Conoly, husband of Debro and father of Samuel and Agnes/Flora in the 1900, 1910, and 1920 Quitman censuses;
  • Angus James Conoly, father of Flora Agnes in her 1919 engagement announcement;
  • former sheriff and Florida naval-stores operator A. J. Conoly in the 1925 death reports.

The sources use "Conoly", "Conley", "Condley", and occasional OCR forms such as "Conloly". The family's regular spelling was Conoly. The 1919 announcement explicitly establishes the full name Angus James Conoly.

An Ancestry suggestion for five-year-old James Q. Conoly in the 1870 Lumber Bridge census is a false match. That child was in a different Black household headed by Newby and Hannah Conoly. It does not belong to Angus's record chain.

docs.title: Parents, siblings, and North Carolina origin
docs.text:
The 1880 census places Angus, age 16, in George B. and Flora C. Conoly's household at Lumber Bridge, Robeson County. His siblings in the home included Hector McL., Jane E., Mary B., Hattie C., Flora C., and William G.; Jane Currie was identified as George's mother-in-law. Ancestry records 19805080 and 14916057; NARA T9 roll 979, ED 180, p. 520C.

A 1915 family-reunion report independently names former Brooks County sheriff A. J. Conoly of Quitman, McLean Conoly of Florida, and W. G. Conoly of Waycross as George's sons. It says George and Flora had married on 20 March 1862 and raised nine children. Charlotte Observer, 28 August 1915, Newspapers.com image 616186734.

George's original North Carolina death certificate expands his name to George Burder Conoly, gives his birth at Lumber Bridge and death at Red Springs on 24 July 1923, and names James Conoly and Mary Currie as his parents. Ancestry record 323425, image S123_155-1235.

The broader Conoly kinship has been investigated separately. Original records verify George as a son of James Conoly, but no inspected original record proves that George's grandfather James and William Conoly were brothers and sons of Daniel Conoly. That older connection remains unresolved by original records and should not be presented as settled genealogy.

docs.title: Foster and the naval-stores partnership, 1891–1894
docs.text:
The earliest secure connection between Angus and Foster is the 14 November 1891 correction in the Valdosta Times. It says McNeil & Rozier sold brothers A. J. and H. McLean Conley a collective one-half interest in the Foster naval-stores business, while J. T. McNeill retained one-fourth. Newspapers.com image 889756841; the initial report is image 889756744.

This was a sale of a business interest. The notice does not convey land, identify the brothers' individual percentages, or establish that either brother owned Land Lot 227.

The Foster columns then trace the reorganized concern:

  • 2 July 1892: Thomas A. Rozier was identified with Rozier, Conoly & Company; clipping 193407281.
  • 16 July 1892: Rozier Conoly & Company continued producing naval stores despite low prices; clipping 193407600.
  • 24 December 1892: Rozier, Conoly Bros. & Company prepared for another campaign; image 889761322, clipping 193407422.
  • 3 June 1893: Rozier Conoly & Company was “doing a good business”; image 889763942, clipping 193407548.
  • 24 March 1894: the Conoly brothers' poultry operation appeared alongside the opening gum season; clipping 193408136.

The same columns add smaller but useful details. Angus traveled to North Carolina in August 1892 with a horse named Dexter McLean and prepared game-fowl yards in October 1893. Sister Katy spent part of 1893 at Foster with Angus and McLean. These reports show that the brothers lived in and helped operate the settlement rather than acting only as absentee investors.

Assessment: Angus's Foster role is verified through at least March 1894. His exact withdrawal date, individual share, and any personal ownership of Foster land remain unresolved.

docs.title: Brooks County sheriff, 1894–1904
docs.text:
Newspapers report Angus's nomination and election as Brooks County sheriff in 1894, renomination in 1896 and 1898, and continuous service for ten years. The key images are 969458858, 852590238, 889832237, 852586032, 889836688, and 969456365.

The sheriff reports show the ordinary and sometimes violent work of the office: interstate requisitions, prisoner transfers, rewards, long-running fugitive searches, and armed arrests. These items are valuable for career chronology, but they reflect the newspapers' accounts and period language. Where an article reports a confession, resistance, or justification for force, that should not be treated as an independently adjudicated legal finding unless a court record confirms it.

The 1900 census identifies Angus as the Brooks County sheriff in Quitman. He lived with wife Debro K., son Samuel S., daughter Agnes W., and mother-in-law Agnes O. Walker. It gives his birth as February 1864 and the marriage year as about 1895. Ancestry record 52867399; NARA T623 roll 181, ED 6, p. 18.

A year-end 1904 report says he retired voluntarily after ten continuous years to return to the turpentine business. It praises his vigilance and says deputy J. H. Mashburn succeeded him. Valdosta Times, Newspapers.com image 889653575. This fixes the office span more precisely than the earlier statement that he had left before February 1904: he remained sheriff through the close of 1904.

Angus also published the weekly Sheriffs' and Marshals' Record, begun about 1899 to circulate information about wanted people. The Georgia law-officers' association elected him second vice president in 1900 and made the paper its official organ; by 1902 he was first vice president and was described as its editor. Images 969466374, 879552201, 852354027, and 853119414.

One criminal allegation has a located outcome. A Lowndes County grand jury indicted Angus and several Valdosta men in 1901 over games played for cigars. He was tried on 6 February 1903 and acquitted; the follow-up says the testimony was “altogether favorable” to him. Images 889667952 and 889694165.

The political record also requires plain treatment. An 1898 report says Angus returned to North Carolina to help “free his old state from negro domination” and had been asked by his father to send a Winchester rifle amid feared election trouble. Image 889767402. A 1901 profile associated him with the special-train expedition to Wilmington during the 1898 violence, but that trip is strong probable, not independently verified by a passenger list or second contemporary source. Image 76879499.

docs.title: Marriage, household, and children
docs.text:
The Brooks County marriage record indexes "A J Condley" and Debro K. Walker as marrying on 5 June 1895. The name spelling is variant, but spouse, county, and later household records identify the couple securely. Ancestry record 125773, image 40951_294517-00023.

Two original Brooks County wills resolve Debro's expanded name and Walker kinship. John W. Walker's will calls her “my ward Deborah Kesiah Walker, daughter of the late Isham A. Walker deceased.” Joseph F. Walker's will names Fleming B. Walker as his brother and also refers to “my brothers John W. and Isham A. Walker.” The 1880 census identifies the younger Fleming B. Walker as the elder Fleming's son. Debro and Fleming Bates Walker of Barney were therefore first cousins, and the elder Fleming was her paternal uncle005782587_00074`; census record 40730106.

In 1910 the family rented 404 Johnson Street in Quitman. Angus, age 46, was an employer operating a lumber mill. The household was Debora, Samuel S., Flora A., and Agnes Walker. Ancestry record 3197464, image 31111_4327473-00344; NARA T624 roll 174, ED 17, sheet 17A.

By 1920 the family owned 611 Lafayette Street free of mortgage. Angus worked for wages as a representative of a naval-stores company. Debro, Sam, and Agnes Walker remained in the household; Flora had married and moved to Miami. Ancestry record 7316548, image 4295805-00288; NARA T625 roll 237, ED 39, sheet 6A.

The children are independently identified in the 1925 death reports:

  • Samuel Stillwell “Sam” Conoly, born about 1896, remained in Quitman and later administered both the Georgia and Florida estate proceedings.
  • Flora Agnes Conoly, born in 1898–99, married Charles Henry Crandon on 3 April 1919 and lived in Miami. Her engagement announcement names her parents as Mr. and Mrs. Angus James Conoly. Miami News, 17 March 1919, image 298374716.

Angus's original will, signed on 22 April 1920, names Debro as his wife and Sam Conoly and Agnes Conoly Crandon as his son and daughter. That original record independently settles the two-child relationship and confirms that the daughter indexed as Agnes W. in 1900 and Flora A. in 1910 was Flora Agnes Crandon. Ancestry record 1661542, image 005782588_00221, printed p. 139. The 1910 census also says Debro had borne two children and both were living.

docs.title: Bankruptcy and civil liability
docs.text:
The federal court adjudicated Angus bankrupt on 4 February 1904. A later notice says he sought discharge both individually and as a member of Rozier, Conoly & Co., direct legal-notice evidence that he personally belonged to the Foster firm. Valdosta Times, images 889681348 and 889682415.

Ed Waxelbaum, surviving partner of S. Waxelbaum & Son, opposed discharge over an unsatisfied 1895 judgment for slightly more than $225 on a homestead-waiver note. Judge Emory Speer referred the matter to the bankruptcy referee for testimony rather than deciding it at that hearing. The searched newspapers did not reveal the referee's report or final discharge order. Macon News, 30 June 1904, image 823398535. The record proves bankruptcy and a contested discharge; it does not prove misconduct or the eventual result.

A separate 1912 case involved Angus as one of the sureties on guardian I. W. Hopson's bond. A Brooks County verdict was entered for $6,028 plus interest, and the report said each bondsman was liable for the whole amount. This was surety liability, not a land acquisition. Valdosta Daily Times, 11 May 1912, image 889655311.

docs.title: Lumber, turpentine, and Florida land
docs.text:
Angus never wholly left the timber/naval-stores economy. A November 1898 report calls a Dasher-area operation “Conoly's still” (image 889767402). The 1910 census calls him a lumber-mill operator and employer. The 1920 census calls him a naval-stores-company representative.

After leaving the sheriff's office he resumed field operations in Florida. In September 1906 he was working about thirty miles below Perry when he narrowly escaped drowning in the Steinhatchee River (image 889688737).

The General Land Office issued him ten distinct Taylor County patents from 1905 through 1908. Nine fully described patents total 1,360 nominal acres; the 1905 patent FL1080__.033, document 19064, identifies township 8 south, range 9 east, section 20 but the inspected index omits the aliquot and acreage. The remaining accessions are AGS-0293-148 (160 acres), AGS-0293-150 (160), MW-0546-464 (160), MW-0546-476 (120), MW-0546-481 (160), MW-0546-496 (120), MW-0547-043 (160), MW-0547-047 (160), and 6907 (160). The complete tract table and representative BLM links are.

These patents prove federal conveyances, not continuous possession or Foster ownership. A later transaction shows the scale of the Florida operation: in September 1913 Angus, Fuller Groover, and J. R. Davis sold 11,500 acres of Taylor County land and pine timber to Producers Naval Stores Company for $85,000, reserving the cypress. The newspaper gives no parcel descriptions or allocation among the three sellers. Valdosta Daily Times, 20 September 1913, image 889662085.

The firm Groover, Conoly & Spain operated a still and convict stockade about twenty-eight miles south of Perry by 1909. Contemporary reports describe two violent escape episodes, including an armed siege after a convict broke into Angus's residence. Images 75704685, 1272299279, 1258098178, and 326430022. These reports place Angus's operation inside Florida's convict-labor system; they do not justify assigning him acts the articles attribute to guards or law officers.

By 1916 he represented Consolidated Naval Stores Company. Ocala Evening Star, image 339448571. That fits the 1920 census description of a salaried naval-stores representative and a Jacksonville directory listing him as a salesman at the Everett Hotel while his family home remained in Quitman.

The records do not support a simple permanent migration. A 1908 Robeson County social item still called him “of Quitman,” and both the 1910 and 1920 censuses place his household there. His work took him into Florida; Quitman remained the family base.

docs.title: Final accident, death, and burial
docs.text:
In early August 1925 Angus suffered a chest injury and fractured knee in an automobile collision south of Quitman. Reports say headlights from an approaching car blinded him and he struck another car. He was treated first at Madison and then at a Valdosta hospital. Valdosta Daily Times, 6 August, image 889453343; Macon News, 7 August, image 823579805; Atlanta Constitution, 9 August, image 397869830.

On the night of 27–28 October, Sam found Angus dead in a Jacksonville hotel room. The reports say Angus had appeared in his usual health the night before and had apparently died only an hour or two before he was found at about 7 a.m. They connect the recent accident to the narrative but do not give a medical cause of death. Atlanta Journal, 28 October, image 970914619; Macon Telegraph, 29 October, images 825991745 and 825991753.

The body was returned to Quitman. A Savannah obituary index records an obituary on 29 October 1925 and gives age 60. Ancestry record 25672. Find a Grave memorial 86611883 gives 6 February 1864–28 October 1925 and Oak Hill Cemetery, but the memorial has no biography and no marker image was independently verified in this pass.

The best current wording is: Angus died overnight 27–28 October 1925 and was found dead early on 28 October. The memorial uses 28 October; some contemporary copy says he died Tuesday night, 27 October.

docs.title: Probate
docs.text:
Angus signed a will on 22 April 1920 naming Debro, Sam, and Agnes Conoly Crandon. Yet the Brooks County letters issued to Sam on 7 December 1925 expressly say Angus died intestate005782590_00163`, original p. 239. The online records do not explain whether the will was rejected, never offered, revoked, or indexed out of context. That conflict is unresolved and should remain explicit.

Duval County creditor notices began on 2 March 1928, call Angus late of Duval County, and name Sam Conoly as administrator. Florida Times-Union images 1258881088, 1258881538, and 1258881754. Because the Georgia administration began in 1925, the Florida proceeding may have been ancillary administration for Florida assets, but that legal character is unresolved without the Duval case file.

docs.title: Confidence summary
docs.text: Claim Assessment A. J. was Angus James Conoly Verified Parents were George Burder and Flora C. Currie Conoly Verified Hector McLean Conoly was his brother Verified Bought into the Foster concern in 1891 and operated there through 1894 Verified Personally owned Foster land or a fixed quarter-interest Unresolved Served ten years as Brooks County sheriff, 1895–1904 Verified Married Debro K. Walker on 5 June 1895 Verified Children were Sam and Flora Agnes Verified Continued in lumber/naval stores and held Florida federal land Verified Adjudicated bankrupt in 1904, individually and as Rozier, Conoly & Co. member Verified; discharge outcome unresolved Ten Taylor County federal patents, at least 1,360 nominal described acres Verified Participated in the 1913 11,500-acre/$85,000 Taylor County sale Verified; individual allocation unresolved Died overnight 27–28 October 1925 in Jacksonville Verified Exact official death date was 28 October Strong probable, pending death certificate/marker image Duval proceeding was ancillary probate Possible, not yet proved

docs.title: Search coverage and remaining gaps
docs.text:
Local memory, Foster/McNeill/Rozier reports, saved census and newspaper data, and the prior Conoly kinship files were searched first. Fresh work directly inspected the 1880, 1900, 1910, and 1920 census chain; Brooks marriage and probate indexes with original-image links; Find a Grave; the Savannah obituary index; General Land Office hits; and Newspapers.com coverage under Angus, A. J., Conoly, Conley, Condley, sheriff, Quitman, Foster, Dasher, Perry, Jacksonville, accident, funeral, probate, lumber, turpentine, and naval-stores combinations.

The most useful remaining online or repository targets are:

  1. Angus's Florida death certificate or Jacksonville death register entry.
  2. The complete Brooks County administration pages beginning with image 005782590_00163.
  3. The Duval County probate case underlying the 1928 creditor notices.
  4. Tract-by-tract adjudication and later disposition of every Angus J. Conoly GLO patent.
  5. Brooks County deeds and tax digests for his Quitman residence, Dasher interests, and any Foster-area holdings.
  6. A photographed Oak Hill marker or sexton's register to settle the calendar death date.
  7. The federal bankruptcy file and final discharge order for the 1904 case.
  8. The Taylor County deed underlying the 1913 sale to Producers Naval Stores Company.

The general web produced no useful historical evidence beyond the subscription record repositories. No source was treated as exhaustive outside the documented queries and coverage.

docs.title: Citation audit note
docs.text: The list separates census, probate, marriage, land, directory, and cemetery records from newspaper accounts. Newspaper allegations remain attributed to the reports that published them. The General Land Office entries use accession-specific links in BLM's redesigned search system. BLM does not currently expose stable record-detail permalinks, so the full accession numbers remain part of each citation. Unresolved conflicts, including the death date, bankruptcy discharge, and signed will versus intestate administration, have not been reconciled by assumption.

docs.text:

docs.title: Identity conclusion
docs.text:
The Foster man is possibly the Archie McBryde reported at Little River Academy, Cumberland County, North Carolina, on October 1, 1891. The uncommon exact name, the five-month interval, and the Foster report's statement that he might continue to North Carolina with Theodore Byrd make this the best located candidate. They do not prove the match. [1]-[2]

Two later census-index candidates remain open: Archie McBryde, born about 1866 and living in Marion County, South Carolina, in 1900; and J. Archie McBryde, born about 1863 and living in Lee County, North Carolina, in 1910. Neither index provides a bridge to Foster, Theodore Byrd, naval stores, or the 1891 Little River notice. [3]-[4]

docs.title: What the Foster article establishes
docs.text:
The March 16, 1892 column prints the surname in OCR as "MeBryde"; project reports normalize it to McBryde. It says:

  • Archie was “temporarily staying at Foster”;
  • he was sick but able to accompany Theodore Byrd to Hahira that evening;
  • he might continue with Byrd to North Carolina. [1]

The article does not say Archie worked in naval stores. The four years of naval-stores labor belongs grammatically to Theodore Byrd. It also does not state Archie's age, home, family, employer, or reason for staying at Foster.

docs.title: Best candidate: Little River Academy, North Carolina
docs.text:
On October 1, 1891, The Fayetteville Observer reported that “Mr. Archie McBryde of Little River Academy was in town a few days last week.” This notice precedes Archie's Foster stay by about five months. [2]

The same county had a politically active Theo. Byrd in Carver's Creek by 1886 and repeatedly from 1894 through 1904. The Foster column places Archie and Theodore together and says both might travel toward North Carolina. This is a real geographic cluster, but no North Carolina source found in this pass names the two men together. [5]-[7]

Grade for the Little River identification: Possible. An additional notice saying Archie returned from Georgia, worked in naval stores, or associated with Theodore Byrd would be needed for Strong probable.

docs.title: Archie McBryde, Marion County, South Carolina
docs.text: The 1900 census index identifies an Archie McBryde born about 1866 in Marion County, South Carolina, record 59205173, image 4120568_00104. His age and Carolina residence fit broadly. No Foster or North Carolina association was found. Possible namesake; not identified as the Foster man. [3]

docs.title: J. Archie McBryde, Lee County, North Carolina
docs.text: The 1910 census index identifies J. Archie McBryde, born about 1863, in Lee County, record 163039603, image 4450009_00106. His North Carolina residence makes the record worth retaining, but the extra first initial and lack of an 1892 bridge matter. Possible candidate; not merged. [4]

docs.title: Archie McBride, Washington County, Georgia
docs.text: The 1910 census index identifies an Archie McBride born about 1868 in Washington County, Georgia. The surname spelling and Georgia residence make him worth noting, but he is roughly 150 miles from Foster and no South Georgia or North Carolina link was found. Possible namesake only. [8]

docs.title: Archie M. McBryde in Washington, D.C.
docs.text: An 1895 Fayetteville notice says Archie M. McBryde was visiting the city and then lived in Washington City. The middle initial and later residence distinguish the notice from the uninitialed Little River man; they might still be the same person, but the paper does not say so. Unresolved, not merged. [9]

docs.title: Archie McBryde in a 1919 veterans list
docs.text: A 1919 Robesonian page includes Archie McBryde in a list of Confederate veterans. If the classification applies literally, this man would have been substantially older than the census candidates born in the 1860s. The page does not connect him to Foster and may list living or commemorated veterans. Separate older candidate unless additional records prove otherwise. [10]

docs.title: Cemetery exclusions
docs.text: The exact-surname Find a Grave results located an Archie McBryde born in 1916 and Archie B. McBryde born in 1902. Both were born after the Foster event. The McBride results include an Archie born about 1870 who died in Raleigh in 1933, but no Foster, Little River, or naval-stores link appears. [11]-[13]

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text: Date Event Assessment October 1, 1891 Archie McBryde of Little River Academy visits Fayetteville Verified; best pre-Foster candidate [2] March 16/19, 1892 Archie temporarily at Foster, ill, going to Hahira with Theodore Byrd, possibly onward to North Carolina Verified Foster event [1] November 1895 Archie M. McBryde, then of Washington City, visits Fayetteville Verified; relationship to Little River Archie unresolved [9] 1900 Archie McBryde, born about 1866, indexed in Marion County, South Carolina Verified index; Foster identity unresolved [3] 1910 J. Archie McBryde, born about 1863, indexed in Lee County, North Carolina Verified index; Foster identity unresolved [4] 1919 Archie McBryde appears in a Robeson County Confederate-veteran list Verified as printed; likely older candidate [10]

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• Whether Archie was a Foster worker, visitor, contractor, or relative of an operator.
  • Why his stay was temporary and what illness he had.
  • Whether he continued past Hahira to North Carolina.
  • Whether the Little River, Marion County, Lee County, Washington City, and veterans-list references concern one person or several.
  • Archie's parents, spouse, death, and burial.

docs.text:
• Newspapers.com: stored authenticated results and the known March 1892 page were checked. Planned variants were "Archie McBryde", "Archie McBride", "Archibald McBryde", "MeBryde", "Foster", "Hahira", and "naval stores", 1880-1930. The fresh CDP search failed twice with the same connection timeout and was stopped; the access gap is disclosed.
  • DigitalNC: exact and variant surname searches with "Archie", "A. McBryde", "Little River", "Cumberland", "Lee", "Robeson", and "Theodore Byrd", chiefly 1880-1930. The productive pages are sources 2, 9, and 10. Other hits were later namesakes, female references to Mrs. Archie McBryde, or page collisions.
  • Georgia Historic Newspapers: McBryde, McBride, and separated-name searches, chiefly 1880-1930. The 1904 and 1909 McBride pages did not yield a relevant same-phrase OCR reading and were rejected.

docs.title: Census and genealogy
docs.text:
• Ancestry public indexes: exact Archie McBryde and Archie McBride, birth centered on 1865 plus or minus twenty years, census and all-category searches. The Marion, Lee, and Washington County candidates were retained but not merged.
  • Ancestry surfaced North Carolina death-index and certificate records for later men named Archie McBryde, but the public results withheld dates and relatives and the images were access-denied. No claim was drawn from them.
  • Find a Grave: exact McBryde and McBride searches nationwide and in North Carolina. Only age-excluded or unconnected candidates were found.
  • FamilySearch record details could not be inspected because the authenticated browser handler was unavailable. This remains an access gap.

docs.title: David Hiers
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed 23 August 2026

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
David Hiers, also recorded as Hires, was a South Carolina-born farmer who settled in Lowndes County, Georgia, and lived in Brooks County after its creation. He and his wife, Rebecca Yates, raised a large family in the Morven and Quitman side of the county. Their daughter Nancy J. Hires married Joseph J. "Joe" Rogers, known in family history as Joseph Jasper Rogers.

The federal censuses place David with Rebecca from 1850 through 1870. A June 1876 Brooks County order identified a David Hiers as the contractor building a bridge across a lagoon near Folsom Bridge. The contractor is highly likely to have been Rebecca's husband, but the order gives no family details. Rebecca was explicitly listed as a widow in 1880. No original record found in this search gives David's exact death date or burial place. Online trees repeat 23 January 1879, but none of the inspected tree pages supplied a source for it.

Records under David's name cover county office, politics, estate work, jury selection, and bridge construction. A county history lists him as Brooks County treasurer from 1864 through 1866. He took a Reconstruction oath in 1867, served on the county Democratic executive committee in 1872, ran for tax collector that year, applied to administer two estates in 1873, was selected for a petit-jury panel in 1874, and held the 1876 lagoon-bridge contract. The public notices do not identify his wife or children, so matching each item to Rebecca's husband is highly likely rather than certain from any single notice.

docs.title: Family and household
docs.text:
David was born in South Carolina about 1822 to 1825. His age was reported as 25 in 1850, 35 in 1860, and 48 in 1870.[1-3] Rebecca's later records place her birth about 1827 to 1830. Her recorded age of 17 in 1850 does not fit comfortably with the ages of the oldest children and should be treated as a census-age problem, not a settled birth year.

The 1850 Lowndes County household contained David, Rebecca, Nancy, William, and Mary. By 1860 the family was in Brooks County near the Tallokas post office. David was a farmer with $1,500 in real estate and $850 in personal estate. The household then contained Rebecca and children Nancy, William, Elizabeth, Serena, Beana, Georgia Ann, Laura Jane, Amanda, and infant Cincinnati.[1-2]

The 1860 slave schedule records David Hires as enslaving one unnamed sixteen-year-old female.[4] The schedule preserves no name for her. This is direct evidence of enslavement and should not be hidden inside the household's property figures.

In 1870 David and Rebecca were in Brooks County with Serine, Beann, Georgeanna, Laura, Amanda, Cincinnatus, James, Simon, and Ophelia. Three people with the Phillips surname are grouped with the indexed census entry but should not be presented as Hiers children.[3]

By 1880 Rebecca was the widowed head of a Quitman-district household. Living with her were Georgiann, Laura J., Cincinatti, James L., Simeon S., and David O.[5] Read together, the censuses support thirteen children: Nancy, William, Mary or Elizabeth, Serena, Beann, Georgia Ann, Laura Jane, Amanda, Cincinnati, James L., Simeon or Simon, Ophelia, and David O. Names and ages vary across the records. Online family trees expand James L. and David O. to James Lawton and David Lee, but those forms were not independently proved in this search.

Nancy J. Rogers's 1932 Georgia death certificate names her parents as David Hires and Rebecca Yates.[6] This original record supports the census chain independently of online family trees. Existing project notes report that Serena Hall's 1921 Lowndes County death record also names David Hires and gives her mother's surname as Yates, but this search did not recover a stable record ID or certificate image for a fresh citation. Serena's record is therefore treated as a follow-up lead rather than independent proof here.

No original marriage return was located. A derivative marriage index names David Hiers and Rebecca Yates but supplies no date or place.[8] Since Nancy was about five in 1850, the safest conclusion is that David and Rebecca were married by about 1844 or 1845. A precise marriage date remains unknown.

docs.title: Probable parents and wider Hiers family
docs.text:
FamilySearch, Geneanet, a family group sheet, and compiled family histories identify David as a son of Daniel Hiers and Nancy Hunter.[9-12] The attribution is highly likely, not fully verified. No inspected birth, marriage, probate, or Bible record directly names David's parents.

There is useful circumstantial support. David applied in September 1873 for permanent letters of administration on Daniel Hiers's Brooks County estate.[13] A submitted family group sheet also identifies David's sister Eliza as the wife of Reuben Riley Renfroe. David applied the next month to administer R. R. Renfroe's estate.[11,14] Neither newspaper notice states a relationship, and neither proves that the court granted the application. The likely father-son and brother-in-law relationships should therefore remain qualified.

docs.title: Land and place
docs.text:
David took a Reconstruction oath in Brooks County Election District 7 on 1 July 1867, and an 1871 tax entry places him in the Morven district.[15-16] These records support the same postwar locality seen in the census and later bridge order.

A compiled land-lot extraction reports several transactions in Land Lots 234 and 235, west of Folsom Bridge. It includes an F. W. Dixon conveyance to David in 1867, a David Hiers and William W. Joyce transaction in 1871, and two 7 October 1875 conveyances from David to Rebecca covering the south half of Lot 234 and 100 acres in the northwest corner of Lot 235.[17] The reported 1871 tract was bounded partly by the Quitman Road and the Widow Joyce dower line.

This land pattern fits the Folsom and Strickland road-fork environment shown by later deeds and the 1908 Brooks County map.[18] It also makes David's 1876 work near Folsom Bridge geographically sensible. The underlying Hiers deed images, book numbers, and page numbers were not preserved in the available extraction, however. These transactions are strong land leads, not image-verified deeds. A separate reported 1861 tax holding in Land Lot 513 cannot yet be assigned securely because more than one local David Hiers existed.

docs.title: County office and civic life
docs.text:
Folks Huxford's county-officer compilation lists David Hiers as Brooks County treasurer, commissioned 16 February 1864 for the 1864-1866 term.[19] This is a clear office listing. The treasurer is highly likely to have been Rebecca's husband because the older David was present in Brooks County before and after the war, but the list gives no family details.

The newspapers add a sequence of public activity:

  • On 29 June 1872, the Savannah Morning News reprinted a Brooks County Democratic meeting report that placed David Hiers on the county Democratic executive committee.[20]
  • Quitman Banner notices on 29 November, 6 December, and 20 December 1872 announced him as a candidate for Brooks County tax collector. The notices prove candidacy, not election.[21]
  • In September and October 1873, Ordinary's citations reported his applications to administer the estates of Daniel Hiers and R. R. Renfroe. Appointment, settlement, and kinship were not stated.[13-14]
  • On 23 April 1874, the Quitman Reporter listed him among petit jurors for the first week of the May term. The list proves selection, not that he was sworn or served through a trial.[22]

Together these records show county financial responsibility, political participation, estate work, and jury selection. They do not establish that David was a lawyer, that he won the 1872 election, or that either administration application was granted.

docs.title: The Folsom lagoon bridge
docs.text:
The most detailed contemporary record of David's work is a Brooks County Court order dated 20 June 1876. It called him the contractor building a bridge across the lagoon near Folsom Bridge. Morven District road commissioners Ryals, Peacock, and Dr. Hitch were directed to inspect the timber, framework, flooring, and banisters before he could receive compensation.[23]

This was a separate span across a lagoon in the Little River swamp approach. It was not the main bridge across Little River. It was also not old Hyers Bridge over Okapilco Creek on Strickland Road. No located record says old Hyers Bridge was named for David.

The order proves that construction was underway and subject to inspection. The newspaper search found no commissioners' return, acceptance certificate, or payment notice. It would be an overstatement to say that the span passed inspection or that David was paid.

docs.title: Military names and a serious record conflict
docs.text:
David's name appears in several wartime compilations, but none proves Confederate army service for Rebecca's husband. The 1864 Georgia militia reorganization census lists a 42-year-old David Hiers in Brooks County.[24] That record concerns home-front eligibility and is not an army enlistment record.

Huxford's rosters print two fatal Confederate entries for men named David Hires or Hiers. One entry says a married man born in 1825 was killed at Sharpsburg in 1862. Another says a David Hiers died in a Richmond hospital.[19] Both conflict with the verified 1870 census and 1872-1876 Brooks County record chain. More detailed online records identify at least one younger Brooks County namesake, born about 1844, who served in Company K, 50th Georgia Infantry and died in 1863.[25] David Owen Hiers, associated with Liberty County and Florida, was another separate man.

The safest conclusion is that the military indexes and later roster notes contain same-name confusion or a mistaken family attribution. No Confederate army service is assigned to Rebecca Yates's husband in this dossier.

docs.title: Death, burial, and later family
docs.text:
The 20 June 1876 bridge order is the last original record found for a Brooks County man of this name, but it does not identify the contractor's family.[23] Rebecca's status as a widow in the 1880 census proves that her husband died before that enumeration.[5] If the contractor was Rebecca's husband, as the local record chain strongly suggests, David was alive on 20 June 1876. The lower endpoint remains highly likely rather than fully verified.

FamilySearch and Geneanet trees give 23 January 1879, but the inspected pages attach no death record, obituary, probate file, cemetery record, or grave photograph to that date.[9-10] No matching Find a Grave memorial was found, and a statewide probate-index search produced no personal estate entry for the target. The exact death date and burial place remain unresolved.

Rebecca lived on in the family household. In 1900 she was living with son Sim Hires in Barney and was reported as widowed, age 71.[26] Their daughter Nancy J. Hires married Joseph J. "Joe" Rogers in Brooks County in 1866. Family history gives his full name as Joseph Jasper Rogers, while the original records reviewed so far identify him as Joseph J., J. J., or Joe. Through Nancy and Joseph, David and Rebecca were the grandparents of Dove Rogers Moody, part of the Rogers-Moody family line at Barney.[6,26]

docs.title: Evidence assessment
docs.text: Claim Assessment David and Rebecca's 1850-1870 household chain Verified Rebecca was widowed by the 1880 census Verified Rebecca's maiden name was Yates Verified through Nancy J. Rogers's death certificate The couple had thirteen children Strong, census-backed reconstruction Daniel Hiers and Nancy Hunter were David's parents Highly likely, not directly proved David and Rebecca married by about 1844-45 Highly likely; exact return not found David enslaved one sixteen-year-old female in 1860 Verified as recorded; her name is unknown David served as Brooks County treasurer, 1864-66 Office verified; family identity highly likely The 1872-1876 civic notices concern Rebecca's husband Highly likely David held land in Lots 234 and 235 Strong derivative lead; original deeds not inspected David was the Folsom lagoon-bridge contractor Work in progress verified for a man of this name; family identity highly likely The bridge passed inspection and David was paid Unresolved David built the main Little River bridge or old Hyers Bridge Unsupported David served in the Confederate army Not established; same-name records conflict David died 23 January 1879 Unverified online-tree claim David died before the 1880 census Verified Rebecca's husband was alive on 20 June 1876 Highly likely, based on the contractor identification David's burial place Unresolved

docs.title: Research coverage and remaining targets
docs.text:
The search began with the project's saved census, Barney family, Folsom Bridge, road, land-lot, and Huxford evidence. Online work then covered Ancestry census, slave schedule, Reconstruction oath, tax, probate, marriage, militia, military, Geneanet, and death collections; FamilySearch records and trees; Find a Grave; Georgia Historic Newspapers; the Georgia Archives county map; and a South Carolina family group sheet. Exact and variant searches used Hiers, Hires, Hyers, David, Rebecca, Yates, Morven, Tallokas, Quitman, Folsom, bridge, treasurer, tax collector, estate, probate, obituary, death, and burial.

The Georgia newspaper search preserved direct page links, page images, OCR, and a query ledger. It found no obituary, funeral notice, personal estate citation, bridge-acceptance report, or payment notice. Logged-in Newspapers.com and a fresh Ancestry image readback could not be completed after the browser connection failed twice. The preserved Ancestry record IDs and earlier original-image readings were retained, and no fact was inferred from the failed calls.

The most valuable remaining records are the Brooks County deed-book images for the reported 1867, 1871, and 1875 transactions; Ordinary minutes for the Daniel Hiers and R. R. Renfroe estates; county-purpose minutes for the bridge inspection and payment; and a family Bible, probate paper, tax disappearance, cemetery register, or grave marker that establishes David's death and burial.
