No reviewed ferry license, deed, or survey supplies the exact early landing coordinate.

docs.title: Completion statement
docs.text: The accessible online record has been searched across the public map KML, Georgia Archives, FamilySearch, public genealogy indexes, and the preserved newspaper/research corpus. The remaining questions depend on original local court, tax, deed, and estate pages that are not presently available through an identified public image link. No missing record has been guessed or replaced with a namesake.

docs.title: James Thomas McNeill: online dossier
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed August 17, 2026; updated August 22, 2026

docs.title: Identification
docs.text:
This dossier concerns James Thomas McNeill, born in Cumberland County, North Carolina, about April 1858. He was the Hahira and Foster-area naval-stores operator documented in south Georgia during the 1880s and 1890s and the later Wewahitchka and Indian Pass operator in Florida.

The identity chain is verified from the 1880 census, his 1890 marriage record, the 1892 Hahira profile, the 1900-1940 household sequence, and contemporary Georgia and Florida newspapers. Variant spellings and bad indexes include McNeal, McNeil, McNeill, J. T., J. S., J. Q., and James D. Mcmill. Those variants are joined here only where the household, relatives, age, birthplace, place, and occupation establish continuity.

docs.title: Conclusions at a glance
docs.text:
• Verified: His parents were recorded as J. H. McNeill and Effie McIntyre on his 1890 marriage record. No inspected original expands J. H. to John Hector.
  • Strong probable: The ten-year-old James with Effey McNeill in Black River Township in 1870 was the later James T. McNeill. His 1860 household remains unresolved.
  • Verified: He married Virginia Rhodes on January 21, 1890. She died in Franklin County, Florida, in 1905. Her middle initial was B.; the expansion Bostick is unverified.
  • Verified: His second wife was Gypsie A. Atkins, the woman indexed as Epsie, Gypsy, Gypsie, and Cyksis from 1910 through 1950. Their exact marriage date and place remain unresolved.
  • Verified: Herman and Lillian were explicitly recorded as adopted children in 1900. Ruth was recorded as a daughter, but no inspected record states whether she was biological or adopted. James Thomas McNeill Jr. is verified through the 1940 census and his draft card.
  • Verified: McNeill was a large naval-stores operator at Hahira by 1892, moved to Wewahitchka by January 1900, and remained in the Florida turpentine business for decades.
  • Most likely: The "J. T. Neill" who sold McLean Conoly a fast trotting horse at Foster in March 1892 was James T. McNeill. The initials, place, date, and association fit, but the notice does not print the full McNeill surname.
  • Verified: The "J. T. McNeal" named as Thomas A. Rozier's former partner in the 1938 will was James T. McNeill. An original 1890 Lowndes tax page places "McNeil James T" beside "McNeil and Co"; the company held 477 acres in the same Land Lots 50 and 139 later named in the will. The deed chain and the increase to 543 acres remain unresolved.
  • Verified: Contemporary newspapers used "McNeal" for James in the Indian Pass and Port St. Joe family context. They also establish a Wewahitchka Gin Company presidency in 1904, pilotage service by 1905, the known 1913 appointment, and a serious illness in February 1940.
  • Verified: Contemporary reports attributed 12,000 fenced Indian Pass acres to him in 1926 and said that he and associates controlled and operated on 11,000 Gulf-front acres in 1932. The statements describe different years and legal interests and should not be forced into one acreage total.
  • Verified: He died at his Indian Pass home on August 2, 1941, after an illness of more than two years, and was buried at Jehu Cemetery. The photographed marker's 1858-1951 ending year is wrong.
  • Unproved derivative claims: No contemporary or official source found calls him a founder of Indian Pass, names his business the Indian Pass Trading Post, or proves that it became the Indian Pass Raw Bar.

docs.title: Parents and early life
docs.text:
The 1870 census places James McNeill, age ten, and Cathrine McNeill, age seven, with Effey McNeill in Black River Township, Cumberland County. The matching township, mother, surname, and age make this James a strong-probable match. Ancestry record 22831981, image 4277209_00018.

In 1880 Jas. T. McNeill, 22, lived in the Black River household of M. McIntyre and Effie McIntyre. The census called him Effie's stepson, said he was attending school, and gave his occupation as keeping a grist mill. Ancestry record 19418011, image 4243272-00094; NARA T9, roll 960, page 357C, ED 57.

His January 21, 1890 Cumberland County marriage record names him as the son of J. H. McNeill and Effie McIntyre. It names his bride, Virginia Rhodes, as the daughter of Eley J. and Elizabeth Rhodes. Ancestry record 4562708, image 42091_329780-00648.

An Ancestry hint for two-year-old Jas. D. McNeill in 1860 belongs to a different James Duncan McNeill. It is rejected. The names John Hector McNeill and Effie McKay appear in derivative cemetery or tree material but were not established by an inspected original record.

docs.title: Georgia naval stores, roads, and Foster
Ware County and the partnership
docs.text:
A March 31, 1888 Valdosta Times report identifies McNeil & Rozier as a Ware County turpentine firm. It describes McNeil and the firm's woodsman, Connolly, pursuing a Black worker who had left the operation. McNeil shot the man in the back from about ninety yards; the report says the firm's workers had been brought from South Carolina and bound to one-year labor terms. Newspapers.com image 889632321; reprints include images 852572266 and 34091266.

The article does not give McNeil's initials. James T. McNeill's identity as that partner is therefore strong probable, supported by the business and place sequence that follows, not directly proved by the 1888 article alone.

A March-April 1888 Clinch County sheriff's notice made McNeil & Rozier judgment creditors of T. P. Jordan and levied 62 barrels of Jordan's rosin at Argyle. Images 889632317 and 889632329. This proves a debt and regional business reach. It does not place the firm's still at Argyle or make the barrels the firm's property before levy.

docs.title: Hahira and McNeill Road
docs.text:
By March 1890 newspapers placed McNeil and Rozier in the Hahira/Folsom Bridge turpentine and road network. On April 12, 1890, the Valdosta Times said J. T. McNeil had nearly completed a new road from Hahira to Folsom Bridge. Image 889794327. Later notices called it McNeill Road; Lowndes County adopted the Hahira-Folsom Bridge route as a public road in February 1897, and a circa-1910 county map labeled the corridor "McNEIL RD."

The road construction and its identification with James are verified. The record does not prove that he owned the right-of-way or that every part of the period road followed the modern alignment.

The Folsom Bridge history places McNeill's Road within the longer history of the crossing and the Foster neighborhood.

docs.title: Foster interest and J. T. McNeill & Co.
docs.text:
The November 14, 1891 correction to a Foster business report states that McNeil & Rozier sold A. J. and H. McLean Conley/Conoly a collective one-half interest in the Foster naval-stores business and that McNeill retained one-fourth. Valdosta Times, image 889756841; initial report image 889756744.

This was a business-interest transaction, not a proved land conveyance. It does not allocate the brothers' individual shares, identify the owner of the final quarter, or show when McNeill disposed of his remaining interest.

docs.title: The J. T. Neill horse notice
docs.text:
A Foster column dated March 16, 1892, says McLean Conoly bought "J. T. Neill's fast trotting horse." The source plainly prints Neill. In context, however, the seller was most likely James T. McNeill. The initials match, the transaction took place among his Foster associates only months after newspapers named him in the Foster business, and contemporary records already varied his surname among McNeil, McNeill, and McNeal. No second South Georgia man named J. T. Neill has been found in the completed search. Valdosta Times, March 19, 1892, page 1, image 889758320.

No duplicate notice has been found that expands the seller's name. The horse sale is therefore carried here as a likely McNeill naming variant, with the printed form preserved, rather than as a separate person's dossier.

An August 13, 1892 profile names James T. McNeill and "J. T. McNeill & Co." at a principal plant one mile east of Hahira. The paper valued the operation at about $30,000, suggested that it represented only half his naval-stores interests, and described him as a farmer, cattle breeder, road builder, and civic participant. Image 889759805. The profile's reference to A. Conley at McNeill's home proves association, not the legal terms of a partnership.

The follow-up adds a firmer company trail. An 1889 railroad industry report lists "McNeal" at Hahira with annual capacity of 400 barrels of turpentine and 1,600 barrels of rosin. The Hahira, date, and industry make James the strong-probable operator, although the item gives no initials. Images 825344612 and 26867424. In 1893 a team driver worked for "J. T. McNeill & Co."; in 1894 Henry B. Culbreth worked for "J. McNeil & Co." in Hahira turpentine and later died at J. T. McNeil's residence. Images 889766060, 889831644, and 889831679.

In 1904 "J. T. McNeill & Co. v. Thomas Passmore" reached Lowndes Superior Court. The company asserted a right under an 1889 lease to cut timber on 275 acres. A May 21 report initially said the plaintiff won; a May 24 correction says the defendant won. Images 889683754 and 889683819. This verifies a company-styled 1889 timber claim and litigation fifteen years later. The reports do not name Rozier, the lessor, Land Lots 50 or 139, or recording data, so they strengthen but do not finish the legal-entity chain.

A separate 1895 execution in favor of J. T. McNeil involved a two-acre Hahira parcel in Land Lot 99. Images 889834575 and 889834711. It shows creditor activity but has no demonstrated connection to the target tract.

docs.title: The Lowndes tract and the McNeal spelling
docs.text:
The original 1890 Lowndes County tax digest supplies the missing land-level connection. In Club House District 658, adjacent entries read "McNeil James T" and "McNeil and Co". The company row reports 477 acres in Land Lots 50 and 139, 12th District, valued at $1,400. Ancestry collection 1729, record 525284, original image 32306_1220706333_0005-00099.

Thomas A. Rozier's original will, dated October 26, 1938, calls "J. T. McNeal and Company" a former firm composed of J. T. McNeal and T. A. Rozier. It gives Sallie Rozier Thomas's undivided half interest in 543 acres in parts of those same two lots and district. Brooks County Record of Wills, 1918-1964, p. 230; Ancestry collection 8635, record 1205180, image 005782588_00313.

Together, the adjacent personal and company tax rows, both exact land-lot numbers, the district, the known Rozier partnership, and independent newspaper use of "McNeal" verify that the will's J. T. McNeal was James T. McNeill. The tax digest and will do not prove that the legal entity was unchanged for forty-eight years. That continuity is strong probable until the deeds or partnership papers are found.

The acreage rose from 477 in 1890 to 543 in 1938, a difference of 66 acres. No checked source explains whether the firm acquired land, corrected a survey or assessment, or changed the way acreage was counted. The difference is a title-history question, not an identity conflict.

A derivative land-lot index says Jacob Henry Croft conveyed 325 acres on the north side of Brooks County Land Lot 227, District 12, to McNeil & Rozier on October 9, 1890. The deed book, page, consideration, and original image have not been verified. The land claim remains strong probable pending the instrument.

McNeill remained associated with Hahira through the late 1890s. A January 16, 1900 notice called him formerly of Hahira and said he had moved to Wewahitchka, Florida. Images 889672128 and 889672134.

Newspaper searches under "McNeal" add several later details. The Florida Senate confirmed J. T. McNeal as a St. Joe pilotage commissioner in 1913. That notice alone names no relative or occupation, but the St. Joe location and later family-linked reports identify him as James. Florida Times-Union, May 30, 1913, image 1257958763. A 1927 item placed "J. T. McNeal and family" at Indian Pass, and a 1937 Hahira item named Mr. and Mrs. J. T. McNeal and their son James of Port St. Joe. Images 353041013 and 890575945. These family-and-residence matches directly verify "McNeal" as a contemporary spelling for James.

docs.title: Virginia Rhodes McNeill
docs.text:
The 1900 census places James and Virginia B. McNeill at Wewahitchka. James was 42, born in April 1858, and a naval-stores manufacturer. Virginia was born in May 1861; the household said they had married in 1890. Ancestry household record 33980819.

Virginia died in Franklin County in 1905. Florida death-index record 4817004, original index image VRDUSAFL1877_0106-0068. Her photographed Jehu Cemetery marker reads Virginia B. Rhodes, wife of J. T. McNeill, born in Cumberland County May 15, 1861, died August 7, 1905. Find a Grave memorial 8716041.

Find a Grave expands her middle initial to Bostick. Neither the marriage record, census, death index, nor marker spells out Bostick, so that expansion is not accepted as proved.

docs.title: Gypsie A. Atkins McNeill
docs.text:
The 1900 census places Gypsie Atkins, born July 1881, as a daughter of Joel P. and Emily V. Atkins at Wewahitchka. Ancestry record 33980835, image 4120037_00444. Joel Atkins's probate record directly names Gypsie McNeill as his child. Ancestry collection 8993, record 659476, image 005885796_00228.

The household chain verifies that Epsie McNeill in 1910, Gypsie/Gypsy in 1920 and 1930, Cyksis in the bad 1940 index, Gypsy A. in 1945, and Gypsie A. in 1950 were the same woman. Her Social Security claim gives July 25, 1881. Record 3497713.

The 1910 census says James and Gypsie had been married one year, placing the marriage about 1908-1909. No original license or notice was found. Her marker reads July 25, 1881-February 12, 1966. Find a Grave memorial 8716220. Her Port St. Joe Star obituary says she died February 12 at 3:45 p.m. in a Palatka nursing home, confirming the Florida death index's Putnam County entry. Indian Pass on the memorial is residence or community association, not her death place. Port St. Joe Star, February 17, 1966, issue.

The three-image probate result indexed under Gypsie is not her estate. It is Joel P. Atkins's will. It names wife Emily and children, gives each child five dollars, and contains no Indian Pass property or McNeill estate terms.

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
The 1900 census explicitly calls Herman McNeill, five, and Lillian G. McNeill, three, James and Virginia's adopted son and adopted daughter. Records 33980821 and 33980822, image 4120037_00443. Later censuses shorten the relationships to son and daughter; that does not undo the direct 1900 adoption wording. James's 1941 obituary again calls both adopted. It places Herman G. McNeill in Brooklyn and identifies Lillian as Mrs. H. M. Barfield of Hahira. Their birth parents remain unresolved.

Ruth McNeill appears as James and Gypsie's daughter in 1920 and 1930. Records 14621759 and 102905691. May 1936 marriage coverage says Mr. and Mrs. James Thomas McNeill announced her marriage to William Adams Walker and that James gave her away. James's 1941 obituary and Gypsie's 1966 obituary call Ruth their daughter while separately labeling Lillian and Herman adopted or foster children. This verifies Ruth's family identity and strongly supports biological-daughter status, although no birth record was found. Tallahassee Democrat, May 21, 1936, image 244759166; Florida Times-Union, May 13, 1936, image 1258719625; Port St. Joe Star issues.

James Thomas McNeill Jr. is the five-year-old boy badly indexed in 1930 and Jimmy in 1940. The 1940 census calls him James and Gypsie's son. His draft card gives birth October 1, 1924, at Indian Pass and names J. T. McNeill as next of kin. Ancestry record 12759719, image 44005_12_00024-01932.

The Barfield identities are now resolved. Mrs. H. M. Barfield was adopted daughter Lillian McNeill. Her husband's 1946 obituary calls her the former Lillian McNeal of Pensacola, and a 1948 engagement notice uses Lillian McNeill of Port St. Joe. Images 889668299, 890592039, and 826525154.

Mrs. C. L. Barfield was Blanche Rhodes, not another McNeill daughter. The 1920 census calls Blanche Rhodes, 22, James's niece14621763,40660_307913-00143, and21424729. Gypsie's 1966 obituary calls Blanche one of three nieces she reared. The February 1940 column compressed two household relationships when it called both Barfield women daughters. The June 1940 "aunts" wording reflects a family role, not a strict genealogical description for Blanche. Images890419249and890397289`.

docs.title: Florida household and business timeline
docs.text:
• 1900: James, Virginia, Herman, Lillian, and Virginia's brother George W. Rhodes lived at Wewahitchka. James was a naval-stores manufacturer and owned the home free of mortgage. Record 33980819.
  • 1901: The Valdosta Times called J. T. McNeill a large naval-stores manufacturer of Wewahitchka. Image 889668885.
  • 1904: The Wewahitchka Gin Company incorporated for $2,500 with J. T. McNeil as president. Its plans included gins and possible sawmill, rice-huller, grist-mill, and syrup equipment. Miami News, image 297547451.
  • 1905: Governor Broward appointed W. R. Shaw and J. T. McNeill of Wewahitchka as Calhoun County pilot commissioners, moving James's documented pilotage service back eight years from the 1913 confirmation. Weekly True Democrat, September 8, 1905, image 81281249.
  • 1910: At Dalkeith, James worked on his own account in naval stores. Wife Epsie/Gypsie, Herman, Lillian, and Rhodes relatives were present. The index's "Naval / Flour" occupation reading is anomalous and should not be normalized without the image. Record 150738171 for Gypsie; prior household record 2887852.
  • 1920: A bad index calls him James D. Mcmill, but the age, birthplace, wife, children, relatives, and turpentine-plant manager occupation identify James T. McNeill. Household record 14621757.
  • 1925: The McNeills' home at the Lagoon burned. The report gives no cause, injuries, insurance amount, or rebuilding details. Image 352639356.
  • 1926: A Pensacola News Journal feature called McNeill a 25-year Gulf County pioneer, attributed 12,000 fenced acres at Indian Pass to him, and described a Shetland pony enterprise of 50-75 animals. Image 352745970.
  • 1930: James, 71, was a self-employed naval-stores proprietor at Port St. Joe. He owned a $10,000 home and had a radio. Gypsie, Ruth, and the boy later verified as James Jr. were present. Household record 102905673.
  • 1932: A Tallahassee Democrat feature said McNeill first inspected the country west of Apalachicola Bay in January 1900, bought there, and made Indian Pass his home. It called him a large-scale turpentine operator and said he and associates controlled and conducted operations on 11,000 Gulf-front acres under a conservation and reforestation policy. Image 244777993.
  • 1932: On the facing page, Mrs. J. T. McNeill advertised meals, sandwiches, drinks, lodging, Texaco products, and day-and-night service at Indian Pass. Image 244778057. This directly proves a hospitality and service operation, but not the later Trading Post and Raw Bar succession story.
  • 1934: J. T. McNeill of Indian Pass was reelected a director of the West Florida branch of the Children's Home Society of Florida. Image 352638507.
  • 1937: A deed abstract records James and Gypsie McNeill conveying part of Lot 2, Section 12, Township 2 South, Range 26 East, to Maplewood Investment Company in Duval County. This verifies a transaction but not its full terms; the original deed was not inspected. Florida Times-Union, September 1, 1937, image 1258605081.
  • 1940: The man indexed as J. S./J. Q. McNeill in Gulf County was James. He was 82, born in North Carolina, married to Gypsie, and father of Jimmy, 15. He owned a $3,000 home on "McNeils Off Highway" and worked on his own account as an overseer. Record 132600936, image m-t0627-00588-00437, sheet 7A.
  • 1941: James died at his Indian Pass home on August 2 and was buried the next day at Jehu Cemetery. His obituary described him as owning several thousand acres of timberland near Indian Pass. Port St. Joe Star, August 8, 1941, issue.

The 1926 and 1932 acreage reports must remain separate. The first uses ownership language and says 12,000 acres under fence. The second says 11,000 acres controlled and operated with associates. Neither is a deed total or proof of sole fee ownership.

docs.title: The 1906 James M. McNeill probate connection
docs.text:
A Muscogee County probate citation for James M. McNeill names James T. McNeill and Ola, Clifford, Effie, and Blanche Rhodes of Wewahitchka. The citation collectively calls the listed recipients heirs at law, children of deceased heirs, or parties interested under the will. It does not assign James T. to a particular category or state his kinship.

The citation therefore verifies a legal-interest connection but not that James M. was James T.'s father, uncle, or other specific relative. Columbus Ledger, April 5-May 3, 1906, images 854810367, 854810487, 854810998, and 854789964. The original will, probate petition, service returns, and settlement are still needed.

docs.title: Death
docs.text:
James died at his Indian Pass home on Saturday, August 2, 1941, age 83, after an illness lasting more than two years. Services were held at the home Sunday, followed by burial at Jehu Cemetery near Wewahitchka. His obituary gives birth April 26, 1858, in Cumberland County and names widow Gypsie, son James, daughter Mrs. W. A. Walker, adopted daughter Mrs. H. M. Barfield, and adopted son Herman G. McNeill. Port St. Joe Star, August 8, 1941, pp. 1 and 3, issue.

The Florida death index independently records 1941 in Gulf County. Ancestry record 133861. An August 7 Hahira column says the Barfield families were called to Pensacola because of his death and attended his Sunday funeral, independently confirming the week and the "McNeal" spelling. Valdosta Daily Times, image 890424030.

The photographed marker's 1858-1951 has the right month and day in derivative memorial data but the wrong year. The obituary, state index, 1945 household, Gypsie's 1950 widow status, and a 1947 notice calling James Sr. "late" make 1951 contradicted rather than unresolved. Find a Grave memorial 8716147; Florida Times-Union image 1258886878. The original death certificate remains useful for cause, informant, and certificate details, but it is no longer needed to settle the year or date.

docs.title: Land, title, and estate limits
docs.text:
No online deed chain was found for the Indian Pass acreage. Contemporary newspaper ownership language establishes what was reported, not fee-simple title, exact parcel boundaries, or whether holdings included leases and timber rights.

No James T. McNeill Gulf County will, probate file, inventory, administrator notice, homestead proceeding, or estate deed was found. Gulf and Calhoun County official-record portals presented a Cloudflare human-verification screen or required registration, so those indexes were not fully searched. No negative inference is made from that access failure.

The strongest remaining title targets are:

  1. Lowndes County deeds, tax digests, partnership papers, and estate conveyances for McNeal/McNeil/McNeill, Rozier, and Land Lots 50 and 139, 12th District. These should explain the change from 477 acres in 1890 to 543 in 1938.
  2. The alleged October 9, 1890 Croft-to-McNeil & Rozier Brooks County deed and every forward conveyance or firm instrument.
  3. Calhoun County deeds and mortgages under McNeil/McNeill, James T., J. T., and Gypsie from 1899 until Gulf County's creation.
  4. Gulf County deeds, mortgages, tax records, business licenses, estate records, and satisfactions from county creation through 1960.
  5. James M. McNeill's complete Muscogee County probate file.

docs.title: Claims not established
docs.text:
• John Hector McNeill as father: unverified expansion of the direct record's J. H.
  • Effie McKay as mother: derivative and not established by the records inspected.
  • Virginia's middle name Bostick: unverified expansion of B.
  • Herman's and Lillian's birth parents: unresolved; later namesakes were not merged.
  • Exact James-Gypsie marriage: unresolved beyond the census estimate of about 1908-1909.
  • McNeill as the unnamed 1888 Ware partner: strong probable, not directly named by initials in that article.
  • McNeill & Rozier ownership of Argyle rosin or an Argyle still: contradicted or unsupported by the sheriff's notice.
  • Foster business interest as a land conveyance: not established.
  • Exact disposal of McNeill's retained one-quarter Foster interest: unresolved.
  • The printed "J. T. Neill" horse seller as James T. McNeill: most likely, but not independently proved by a second notice or full-name record of the sale.
  • The legal entity remaining unchanged from 1890 "McNeil and Co" to the firm described in 1938: strong probable, not proved by a formation, amendment, dissolution, or deed instrument.
  • Cause of the 477-to-543-acre change in Lowndes Lots 50 and 139: unresolved.
  • 12,000 acres in 1926 and 11,000 acres in 1932 as the same parcel total: not established.
  • Founder of Indian Pass, Indian Pass Trading Post name, and succession to the Indian Pass Raw Bar: derivative and unproved.
  • 1951 marker year: contradicted by the 1941 obituary, death index, funeral report, and later household evidence.

docs.title: Search coverage and limits
docs.text:
The investigation began with local memory, Barney/Foster research, prior McNeill reports, road research, saved newspaper JSON, land-lot work, and evidence ledgers. Three focused lanes then covered:

  • federal censuses from 1870 through 1950 and the 1935/1945 Florida censuses;
  • North Carolina marriage records, Florida death indexes, Social Security claims, probate indexes, draft records, and cemetery pages;
  • Newspapers.com Georgia and Florida titles from 1870 through 1960, with death-focused passes for 1940-1955 and 1949-1953;
  • the Florida Digital Newspaper Library's Port St. Joe Star run, including issue-by-issue 1941 searching and targeted 1966 browsing;
  • Find a Grave memorials and marker photographs for James, Virginia, and Gypsie;
  • public web results and county clerk access points;
  • stored Brooks, Lowndes, Ware, Calhoun, Gulf, Franklin, and Muscogee leads.

Name variants included James T., James Thomas, J. T., J. S., J. Q., McNeal, McNeil, McNeill, Mrs. J. T. McNeal/McNeill, Virginia Rhodes/McNeill, Epsie, Gypsie, Gypsy, Atkins, Barfield, and the principal children and associates. The McNeal addendum searched Georgia newspapers through 1945 and Florida newspapers from 1898 through 1941, plus authenticated Georgia tax-digest variants and exact firm, land-lot, acreage, and Rozier combinations.

The full 1941 local obituary and the Hahira funeral notice were found and verified. Gulf and Calhoun official-record searches were blocked by human verification or registration. FamilySearch, original Florida certificates, county marriage books, and courthouse-only probate/deed files were not fully checked. This dossier is a fully documented online pass, not a claim that every unindexed page or inaccessible courthouse record was examined.

docs.title: Best remaining record targets
docs.text:
1. Order the original Gulf County death record attached to Florida index record 133861 for cause, informant, certificate number, and other details not printed in the obituary.
  2. Obtain Virginia B. McNeill's 1905 Franklin County death record 4817004.
  3. Search Calhoun and Franklin County marriage books, about 1907-1910, for James T. McNeill and Gypsie Atkins.
  4. Retrieve James M. McNeill's Muscogee County probate packet to define the 1906 relationship.
  5. Obtain the 1889 Passmore timber lease and the 1904 "J. T. McNeill & Co. v. Thomas Passmore" Lowndes Superior Court file, then trace Lowndes deeds and post-1890 tax digests for "McNeil and Co", J. T. McNeal/McNeil/McNeill, Thomas A. Rozier, and Land Lots 50 and 139. Identify the source of the extra 66 acres and the estate conveyance after Rozier's death.
  6. Trace Brooks, Calhoun, Gulf, and Duval County deeds and business records before accepting exact acreage, title, or Raw Bar succession claims.
  7. Search adoption, guardianship, and probate files for Herman and Lillian instead of assigning birth parents from namesakes.
  8. Identify Blanche Rhodes's parents and the exact line behind the 1920 census term "niece"; do not infer it from household proximity alone.

docs.title: Citation audit note
docs.text: The list separates original and contemporary records from indexes, memorials, and derivative material. Where an article omits initials, a record is only an index, or an identification remains probable rather than direct, the dossier keeps that limitation explicit.

docs.title: Joe Rogers of the Foster neighborhood
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed: August 18, 2026

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
The "Mr. Joe Rogers" whose family lived near Foster in March 1894 was probably the later Barney farmer Joseph J. Rogers (22 August 1839-21 August 1922), husband of Nancy J. Hires. Family history gives his full name as Joseph Jasper Rogers [27]. The 1908 county map now supplies an important geographic link: it marks "J. J. Rogers Res." near the south end of Land Lot 274, about 1.5-2 miles by land-lot geometry from Foster's Land Lot 227 [5]. The map and the documented Rogers-Hires-Moody family chain make Joseph the clear leading candidate. The identification remains probable, not verified, because the 1894 newspaper gives no middle initial, spouse, child, or land lot.

No inspected original record expands his middle initial. The census, marriage, tax, death, pension, and cemetery records use Joseph J., Joe, or J. J. The dossier therefore records "Joseph Jasper Rogers" as the family's name for him while noting that "Jasper" remains unverified in the original records [6, 9, 26-27].

docs.title: What the Foster article says
docs.text: The Valdosta Times reported on 24 March 1894 that Miss Blanche Clements, who lived near Adel, had been visiting "Mr. Joe Rogers' family near Foster" [1]. It does not call Rogers a turpentine employee, place him in the settlement, or connect him to Rozier, the Conolys, or Land Lot 227. "Near Foster" is the full geographic claim.

docs.title: Why Joseph J. Rogers is the leading candidate
docs.text:
Joseph J. Rogers already had a well-established northern Brooks County household. The 1890 Brooks tax digest places him in the Morven district [2]. The original tax image, as previously reviewed for the Barney household work, records 340 acres in Land Lot 270 of the 12th district; the Ancestry index page confirms the man, year, and Morven district but omits the acreage and lot [2]. This record should not be used as evidence that he was then in the immediate Foster neighborhood. On the 1908 county map, Morven's mapped boundary enters the southern part of Land Lot 270, and the town grid lies directly along the lot's southern side [5]. The tax digest does not locate Joseph's 340 acres within the lot, and the 1908 boundary cannot be projected backward to 1890. The tax entry proves Morven-district landholding, but no more precise residence.

The 1900 census then enumerates "Joe Rodgers", born August 1839, as a farmer in Barney with wife Nancy and children Ophelia, Effie, Everett, Miles, Dove, and Willie [3, 23]. In 1910 Joseph J. Rodgers still owned a farm at Barney, free of mortgage [4].

The 1908 Brooks County map prints the exact label "J. J. Rogers Res." beside a residence marker on the road at or just north of the southern boundary of Land Lot 274 [5]. The site is in the southwest part of the lot, immediately north of Land Lot 273 and west of Lots 333 and 234. Foster's Land Lot 227 lies roughly two land-lot widths east-southeast. The road continues toward the junction in or near Land Lot 234. The map does not print "Strickland Road"; identifying this segment with the historic Strickland Road corridor depends on the separate 1907 deed language and the project's road reconstruction. The residence label is nevertheless much more specific than the dossier's earlier description of a location merely south or southeast of Barney.

This is a strong circumstantial fit: the same Joe/Joseph name, an established family, a mapped J. J. Rogers residence close to Foster, and continued residence in the Barney area. It is still circumstantial. The map dates fourteen years after the article, uses initials only, and does not identify the 1894 newspaper man.

docs.title: Hires and Moody family connections
docs.text:
Nancy J. Hires Rogers was the daughter of David Hires/Hiers and Rebecca Yates. The 1850 census places five-year-old Nancy in David and Rebecca Hiers's Lowndes County household, and Nancy's 1932 Georgia death certificate names her parents as David Hires and Rebecca Yates [20-21].

In 1876 a Brooks County notice named David Hiers as the contractor building a separate lagoon bridge near Folsom Bridge. County officials directed the Morven District road commissioners to inspect his work before payment [22]. The local contractor is a strong match for Nancy's father, but the notice gives no age, middle initial, or family detail; the same-person identification is therefore strong probable, not fully verified. The work concerned the swamp approach at the Folsom crossing, not repair of the river bridge itself.

The 1900 census directly identifies Dove Rodgers, age twelve, as a daughter in Joe and Nancy Rodgers's household [23]. By 1910 Dove was the wife of James I. Moody of Barney; the census records the couple as Jim and Dove Moody, and later cemetery evidence supplies the fuller James I. Moody identification [24-25]. This establishes the Rogers-Moody family connection independently of the 1894 Foster notice.

docs.title: Documented life of the candidate
docs.text:
• 1839: Joseph was born in Georgia. His death record gives 22 August 1839, although Ancestry's displayed birth-year field mistakenly reads 1939; age 82 and the 1850-1910 census chain show that 1839 is intended [6].
  • 1850-1860: Joseph appears with Uriah and Elizabeth Rogers, first in Lowndes County and then in Brooks County [7-8].
  • 1866: Joseph J. Rodgers married Nancy J. Hires in Brooks County on 21 October [9]. The original-image index supplies the marriage date and county.
  • 1867: A reconstruction oath places Joseph J. Rogers in Brooks County Election District 7 [10].
  • 1870-1880: Joseph and Nancy headed a Brooks County farming household. The 1880 household included children Emma, Iola, Walton H., David U., Ophelia, Havilah, and Effie [11-12].
  • 1890: The tax digest places Joseph in the Morven district [2].
  • 1894: A Joe Rogers family, not otherwise identified, lived near Foster [1].
  • 1900-1910: Joe/Joseph and Nancy were farmers at Barney [3-4].
  • 1908: The Brooks County map marked "J. J. Rogers Res." near the southern edge of Land Lot 274 [5].
  • By 1910: Their daughter Dove had married James I. Moody and lived with him at Barney [23-25].
  • 1920: J. J. and Nancy Rogers were still in the Barney district. The index places them in a household headed by "Q M Rogers", but the adult child's identity remains uncertain without inspection of the original image [13].
  • 1922: Joseph died at Barney. His Georgia death record names Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Hicks as his parents and Nancy Rogers as his wife [6]. Gornto Cemetery evidence agrees on the 1839-1922 dates [14].

docs.title: Identity conflicts and exclusions
docs.text:
1. "Jasper" is family-reported. James's family gives Joseph's full name as Joseph Jasper Rogers, but no inspected original record expands the middle initial. The family name belongs in the dossier with that provenance, not as an original-record fact.
  2. The 1894 article supplies no family bridge. Blanche Clements's name did not lead to a documented kinship with Nancy Hires Rogers or one of Joseph's children.
  3. The two land references do not carry the same geographic weight. The 1890 tax land in Lot 270 belongs to the Morven side of the district; the 1908 map even shows Morven's boundary extending into the lot's southern part. That record proves landholding but does not place Joseph near Foster. The separate "J. J. Rogers Res." label in Lot 274 is the useful Foster-proximity evidence, although it dates fourteen years after the newspaper item. Neither reference puts him inside the still settlement or Lot 227.
  4. Other Rogers lines existed. The 1900 Barney roster also contains a separate John Rodgers household. He is not a Joe/Joseph candidate, but his presence warns against treating every local Rogers reference as Joseph J.'s family [15].
  5. The 1920 index is awkward. It calls the head "Q M Rogers" and Joseph and Nancy his parents. The earlier local narrative identified the household differently. The 1920 record proves the older couple's continued Barney-area presence but should not be used to settle the adult child's identity without the original image [13].

docs.title: Reproducible search ledger
docs.text:
• Ancestry: logged-in searches covered the 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, and 1920 censuses; Brooks marriage records; reconstruction oaths; Georgia tax digests; Georgia death records; Find a Grave index; newspaper/obituary indexes; and public-tree results. Exact and variant searches used Joe, Joseph, Joseph J., J. J., Rogers, and Rodgers with Brooks, Quitman, Morven, Barney, Foster, Nancy Hires/Hiers, and 1839-1922.
  • Newspapers.com: Georgia, 1885-1900, searched "Joe Rogers", "J. J. Rogers" Brooks, "Joseph Rogers" Brooks, "Joe Rogers" Foster, and "Joe Rogers" Morven. The March 1894 Foster item was found; no second item supplied a spouse, child, middle initial, or other identity bridge.
  • Georgia Historic Newspapers: exact-name date-range search was attempted, but the returned result set ignored the range and mixed in later material.
  • FamilySearch: the exact death/place search redirected to sign-in. The Georgia death collection's Ancestry page identifies FamilySearch as the source of its extracted data, but a FamilySearch ARK was not obtained.
  • Cemetery: Find a Grave was checked directly and through Ancestry. It supports burial, dates, and the Dove Rogers-James I. Moody identification when read with the censuses, but it does not prove the 1894 Foster identity.
  • Land/probate: the 1890 tax record was inspected. No subject-indexed probate record or deed naming Foster or Lot 227 was found in the documented online search.

docs.title: Remaining proof targets
docs.text: The best remaining bridge would be an 1894-era Brooks deed, tax row, voter list, church record, school record, or local newspaper item that places Nancy, Dove, or another named member of Joseph J. Rogers's family at Foster. Blanche Clements's family correspondence or an original Quitman Free Press social item might also identify the household. Until one of those appears, Joseph J. Rogers should remain the probable leading candidate, not a settled identification. An original record expanding "J. J." to "Joseph Jasper" would separately verify the family-reported middle name.

docs.title: Katy Conoly of Foster: Flora Katharine Conoly Walker Sexton
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed: August 18, 2026

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
The Miss Katy/Kate Conoly who visited Foster in 1893 was Flora Katharine Conoly, later Flora Katharine Walker and Flora Katharine Sexton (born July 1876; died 12 November 1938). The identification is Verified. The more precise birth date of July 31 comes from the derivative cemetery memorial rather than a located birth record. [5][6][13]

The record chain does not rest on surname alone. The Foster newspaper calls Katy a sister of Angus J. and H. McLean Conoly [1-2]. In 1880, those brothers had a younger sister Flora C. Conoly, born about 1876 [3]. Her 1894 marriage record calls her "F Kattie Conoly" [4]. The 1900 census places widowed "Katie Walker", born July 1876, in H. McLean Conoly's Alabama household and explicitly calls her his sister [5]. Her 1938 death certificate names George Conoly and Flora Currie as her parents [6], matching the 1880 family.

docs.title: Foster connection
docs.text:
The Valdosta Times reported on 3 June 1893 that "Miss Katy Conoly, sister of Messrs. A. J. and H. McLean Conoly", was visiting her brothers at Foster [1]. A later Foster column reported a farewell party for her and said she and Mrs. J. T. McNeill were going to North Carolina to visit relatives [2].

Those notices document a visit and family connection. They do not show that Katy owned property, worked for Rozier Conoly & Co., or lived permanently at Foster.

docs.title: Childhood
docs.text: The 1880 Lumber Bridge census lists Flora C. Conoly, age four, as a daughter of George B. and Flora C. Conoly. Angus J., 16, and Hector McL., 13, were her brothers [3]. Her sisters Jane E., Mary B., and Hattie C. were separately named, which helps prevent a middle-name guess from swallowing several daughters into one person.

docs.title: First marriage and widowhood
docs.text:
"F Kattie Conoly", 18, married J. W. Walker, 21, in Robeson County on 7 December 1894 [4]. The initials and Kattie form connect the legal record to Flora Katharine.

By 1900, "Katie Walker", born July 1876, was widowed in Claiborne, Monroe County, Alabama. She lived with "M. L. Conoly", the census rendering of H. McLean Conoly, and was marked as his sister. Her four-year-old son John Walker was McLean's nephew. The census says she had borne two children, one living [5]. This record supplies the missing bridge between the Foster nickname, Flora's formal name, and the Walker surname.

docs.title: Second marriage and later life
docs.text:
Flora K. Walker married T. B. Sexton in Robeson County on 25 August 1909 [7]. A newspaper account called her Mrs. Flora Catherine Walker, daughter of G. B. Conoly, and named the groom Finan De Berry Sexton [8].

The 1910 census places "Floria C. Sexton" with Finan B. Sexton and fourteen-year-old "John Warker", recorded as a son [9]. In 1920, John W. Walker is correctly described as Finando B. Sexton's stepson [10]. Flora and Finander remained at Raeford in 1930 [11].

Her 1935 will record names Mrs. Flora Katherine Sexton, her husband, and son John Walker [12]. Ancestry labels 15 August 1935 as a probate date and infers death that year, but Flora lived until 1938. The date should be treated as the will's record/execution context, not her death.

Flora died in Durham on 12 November 1938, aged 62 years and three months. The state death certificate names her parents as George Conoly and Flora Currie and her spouse as Finan Bederry Sexton [6]. She was buried at Raeford Cemetery [13].

docs.title: Conflicts and namesake exclusions
docs.text:
1. Katy was Flora C., not an otherwise missing daughter. The 1894 "F Kattie Conoly" marriage, 1900 sister relationship, and parent-naming death certificate link the names.
  2. She was not Hattie C. Conoly. Hattie appears as a separate child in the 1880 household [3]. Similarity between "Hattie" and "Kattie" cannot override the later Flora records.
  3. She was not Angus J. Conoly's daughter. Angus's daughter Flora Agnes/Agnes W. Conoly was born in 1898, five years after the Foster visit [14].
  4. Unrelated Katie Walker results are excluded. Ancestry returned several women of that name. The controlling 1900 record is the one in H. McLean Conoly's household, record 34662146 [5].
  5. First husband's full identity remains incomplete. The marriage record gives J. W. Walker and the later records call Flora widowed. No death, burial, or probate record was found that safely expands his initials.
  6. Name forms vary. Records use Flora C., F. Kattie, Katie, Flora K., Floria C., Floy Catherine, Flora Katherine, and Flora Katharine. The parent, sibling, birth, marriage, son, and spouse chain resolves these variants. "Floy" is the form rendered in the death-certificate record; the document's matching parents and spouse identify the same woman. [6]
  7. The 1938 obituary index is unreliable in detail. Its automated extraction labels the subject "F. B. Sexton", misclassifies relationships, and gives an incorrect death-date field. The death certificate controls the vital facts [6, 15].

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Claim Assessment Foster's Katy Conoly was sister of A. J. and H. McLean Verified She was Flora Katharine Conoly Verified She married J. W. Walker in 1894 Verified She was the widowed Katie Walker living with McLean in 1900 Verified She married Finan/Finander B. Sexton in 1909 Verified J. W. Walker's expanded name and fate Unresolved She owned or worked at Foster Not established

The linked Ancestry marriage index is record 42440337. Its machine-extracted fields were treated cautiously; the independent county marriage record [7] controls the marriage facts.
  9. 1910 U.S. census, Quewhiffle, Cumberland County, North Carolina, Finan B. Sexton household, ED 58, sheet 4B, NARA T624 roll 1105, Ancestry record 178693172.

  13. Find a Grave memorial 41852790, Flora Katharine Conoly Sexton, Raeford Cemetery, direct memorial; Ancestry index record 15153927. Relationships are derivative unless supported elsewhere.
  14. 1900 U.S. census, Quitman, Brooks County, Georgia, Angus J. Conoly household, including daughter Agnes W., born July 1898, Ancestry record 52867402.
  15. The News and Observer, 13 Nov. 1938, p. 34, death notice/obituary extraction for the Sexton family, Newspapers.com image 651464848; Ancestry obituary-index record 831499609. Automated relationship fields are demonstrably garbled; used only as a follow-up lead.
  16. Ancestry exact-name search for Flora Katharine Conoly Walker Sexton, reproducible search.
  17. FamilySearch exact death search for Flora Katharine Sexton, North Carolina, 1938, search URL. It redirected to sign-in; no FamilySearch record page was inspected.

docs.title: Reproducible search ledger
docs.text:
• Article verification: reviewed the cited 3 June and 8 July 1893 Foster citations and retained their exact kinship and travel claims. No permanent Foster residence was inferred.
  • Ancestry: logged-in searches covered 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930 census records; Robeson marriage records; North Carolina death certificates and indexes; wills/probate; Newspapers.com marriage and obituary indexes; and Find a Grave. Searches tested Katy/Kate/Katie Conoly/Conley/Connolly, each daughter in the 1880 George and Flora household, Katie Walker with son John and brother McLean, and Flora C./K./Katharine/Catherine Walker/Sexton.
  • Newspaper follow-up: Newspapers.com searches followed the Foster visitor, both marriages, and the 1938 death. The 1909 marriage report and 1938 obituary page were opened. The obituary's automated extraction was not trusted where it conflicted with the certificate.
  • FamilySearch: the exact record search redirected to sign-in in the current browser. No ARK or original FamilySearch image was obtained.
  • Cemetery: Find a Grave was checked directly and through Ancestry. It supports Raeford Cemetery and the dates; the parentage conclusion rests on the death certificate and census, not the memorial alone.
  • Land/probate: the indexed will record was inspected. No Foster, Brooks County, or Lot 227 property record for Katy/Flora was found. Her role at Foster remains that of a documented family visitor.

docs.title: Remaining targets
docs.text: The identity itself is settled. Useful remaining records are J. W. Walker's full name and death record, the original 1894 and 1909 marriage images at full resolution, John Walter Walker's birth record, the complete will images, and a clear 1938 obituary transcription. Those could finish the family biography but are not needed to prove who Foster's Katy Conoly was.

docs.title: Theodore Byrd: online research dossier
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed: August 18, 2026 Scope: the Theodore Byrd named at Foster, Brooks County, Georgia, in March 1892

docs.title: Identity conclusion
docs.text:
The Foster man is possibly the Theodore, or “Theo.,” Byrd documented in Carver's Creek Township, Cumberland County, North Carolina, from 1886 through at least 1904. The identification is not proved.

The evidence chain is unusually specific. The Foster column says Theodore Byrd had worked four years in naval stores, obtained a four- or five-month furlough, and was leaving for North Carolina to visit friends and relatives. It also says Archie McBryde, then temporarily at Foster, might travel with him. Five months before that notice, an Archie McBryde was reported at Little River Academy in Cumberland County. North Carolina newspapers repeatedly place an exact-name Theo. Byrd in neighboring Carver's Creek, and a 1910 census index places a Theodore Byrd, born about 1860, in Cumberland County. [1]-[9]

That combination makes him the best candidate located, but no record calls the North Carolina man a naval-stores worker, names Foster, or shows him traveling with McBryde. His parents, spouse, death, and burial remain unresolved.

docs.title: What the Foster article establishes
docs.text:
The March 16, 1892 Foster correspondent reported that:

  • “Mr. Theodore Byrd” had obtained a furlough;
  • he expected to leave that afternoon for North Carolina to visit friends and relatives;
  • he intended to rest four or five months after four years of labor in the naval-stores business;
  • Archie McBryde, who was ill but mobile, planned to accompany Byrd to Hahira and might continue with him to North Carolina. [1]

The wording makes Byrd a worker or employee in the naval-stores trade, not an identified owner or partner. It does not state his job, employer, age, race, home county, or whether he returned to Foster.

docs.title: Carver's Creek public life
docs.text:
An exact-name “Theo. Byrd” appears repeatedly in Cumberland County civic records:

  • In July 1886, Carver's Creek Democrats selected him as a congressional-convention delegate. [2]
  • In July and September 1894, he was again named among Carver's Creek delegates; the September meeting elected him secretary of the township executive committee. [3]-[4]
  • In 1895 he served as an election judge. [5]
  • In 1902 he was again a Carver's Creek delegate. [6]
  • A 1904 county-expense statement paid “Byrd Theo” for election work or judicial service. [7]

These notices show an adult Theodore Byrd rooted in the same North Carolina county to which the Foster worker planned to travel.

docs.title: Census and land evidence
docs.text:
Ancestry's public 1910 index has one exact-name Theodore Byrd, born about 1860, residing in Cumberland County. The indexed image is 4449912_00104, record 20428266. The public result did not expose the household, occupation, race, or enumeration district, and the logged-in image could not be opened during this run. [8]

Land-sale notices published in 1919 and 1920 recited earlier deeds for two lots on Main Street in Linden, Cumberland County, to Theo. Byrd. The notices establish local property dealings but do not give the deed dates in the quoted text or connect the owner to Georgia. [9]-[10]

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text: Date Event Assessment July 1886 Theo. Byrd selected as a Carver's Creek convention delegate Verified for the North Carolina man [2] October 1891 Archie McBryde reported at Little River Academy, Cumberland County Verified; possible associate/geographic bridge [11] March 16/19, 1892 Theodore Byrd at Foster; four years in naval stores; departing for North Carolina Verified for the Foster man [1] 1894-1904 Theo. Byrd repeatedly active in Carver's Creek elections and party meetings Verified for the North Carolina man [3]-[7] 1910 Theodore Byrd, born about 1860, indexed in Cumberland County Verified index entry; identity with the earlier Theo. Byrd remains possible [8] 1919-1920 Land notices recite two Linden lots conveyed to Theo. Byrd Verified as printed; deed dates and later disposition unresolved [9]-[10]

docs.title: Cumberland County Theodore Byrd
docs.text: Grade: Possible; best located candidate. The exact name is uncommon in the searched record, the Foster article gives North Carolina as Byrd's destination, and the independent Cumberland sources place both Theodore Byrd and an exact-name Archie McBryde in the same county near the Foster date. Without an occupational, kinship, travel, or direct Byrd-McBryde bridge, the evidence does not justify a stronger identification.

docs.title: Theodore Byrd of Lee County, Illinois, and Webster County, Iowa
docs.text: Excluded. Ancestry's 1870 census index identifies a Theodore Byrd born about 1859 in Lee County, Illinois. The Find a Grave index gives that man as born July 23, 1858, in Lee County and dead July 9, 1896, at Moorland, Iowa. Nothing found connects him to North Carolina or South Georgia. [12]-[13]

docs.title: Theodore W. Byrd of Campbell County, Kentucky
docs.text: Excluded. Census indexes place him in Campbell County in 1860, 1870, 1880, 1910, and 1920. His continuous Kentucky chain does not fit the Cumberland County political and property record. [14]

docs.title: Later Theodore Roosevelt Byrds
docs.text: Excluded by age. The North Carolina Find a Grave search results are dominated by men named Theodore Roosevelt Byrd who were born too late to have completed four years in naval stores by March 1892. [15]

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
• Byrd's precise naval-stores employer and duties.
  • Whether his four years ran continuously from about 1888 to 1892.
  • His exact North Carolina family and the friends or relatives he intended to visit.
  • Whether the 1910 Cumberland census man and the land grantee are the same person, though the match is strong.
  • Whether Byrd returned to Foster after his furlough.
  • His death date and burial place.

docs.title: Census and genealogy
docs.text:
• Ancestry public indexes: exact Theodore Byrd, birth centered on 1860 plus or minus twenty years; census and all-category searches; North Carolina, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, and Kentucky candidates reviewed. The 1910 Cumberland record was retained as the best candidate. The logged-in record image was inaccessible during this run, so household and occupation were not claimed.
  • Find a Grave: exact Theodore Byrd in North Carolina and nationwide; no plausible nineteenth-century Cumberland memorial was found in the documented search.
  • FamilySearch public results page was checked, but record details required a working authenticated browser and were not independently inspected. This is an access gap, not a negative finding.

docs.title: Thomas Alligood Rozier: online research dossier
docs.text:
Back to the Foster Profiles index

Research completed: August 17, 2026 Subject: Thomas Alligood Rozier (3 November 1855-27 October 1938), Robeson County, North Carolina; Ware and Brooks Counties, Georgia Evidence standard: direct records and contemporary newspapers control; later books, memorials, trees, and local tradition are identified as derivative.

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
Thomas A. Rozier was Thomas Alligood Rozier, born in North Carolina about November 1855. A previously documented reading of his full Georgia death certificate gives 3 November 1855 at Lumberton, but the live Ancestry page available in this pass showed only an approximate 1856 birth year. He was a son of Simpson Rozier and a mother whose name appears as Manerva in the 1860 census index but as Maria in 1870 and Maria Carlyle in his Georgia death record. He married Sallie A. Hitch in Brooks County on 19 June 1892. Their three children were Hazel, Robert C., and Catherine or Katharine Rozier; later records identify them as Hazel Stanhope, Robert C. Rozier, and Catherine Lanneau.

Rozier was in Glenmore, Ware County, by 1886 and is the strong-probable Rozier partner in the Ware County naval-stores firm McNeil & Rozier by 1888. The grade stops short of verified because the decisive 1888 article gives neither partner's initials. From 1890 forward, the identification is direct. He signed Foster's post-office application, worked with McNeil in the Hahira-Folsom Bridge turpentine district, remained in the Foster concern after the Conoly brothers bought an interest, and signed the papers moving the post office from Foster to Barney in 1897.

His later record is broader than the turpentine story. He farmed, bred Poland China hogs, served two documented terms as Barney postmaster, offered the Edgewood tract for development, promoted Brooks County land nationally, helped organize a proposed regional railroad, served on the county board of education, and held church office. He died at Barney on 27 October 1938 and was buried in the Morven area.

The major Foster title question remains open. A derivative land index says Jacob Henry Croft conveyed 325 acres on the north side of Land Lot 227 to McNeil & Rozier on 9 October 1890. No deed book, page, recording date, image, consideration, or legal description has been found. It is a useful lead, not a verified deed citation.

This pass did locate Thomas's original will, dated the day before his death. It proves a different landholding: his undivided one-half interest in 543 acres in Lowndes County Land Lots 139 and 50, owned by "J. T. McNeal and Company", a former firm composed of J. T. McNeal and T. A. Rozier. That direct record must not be conflated with the unverified Croft deed or used by itself to identify J. T. McNeal as James T. McNeill.

docs.title: Identity and North Carolina family
docs.text:
The record chain is consistent:

  • The correct 1860 census entry is "T. A. Rozier", about age five, in North Division, Robeson County, in Simpson and Manerva Rozier's household. Ancestry collection 7667, record 41450029. The index should be checked against the original image before treating "Manerva" as a settled reading.
  • In 1870, Thomas Rozier, age fourteen, lived in Howellsville, Robeson County, with Simpson and Maria Rozier. Ancestry collection 7163, record 34465433; NARA M593, roll 1157, p. 69A.
  • No secure 1880 census entry was identified in the documented search. Same-name results in Louisiana and elsewhere were excluded.
  • The 1900 through 1930 censuses consistently place Thomas in Barney, born in North Carolina about 1855-1856.
  • Georgia death-record collection 2562, record 1031290, gives Thomas Alligood Rozier, age eighty-two, death at Barney on 27 October 1938, father Simpson Rozier, and mother Maria Carlyle.

The death record and census chain verify the full identity and parentage. The mother's given name remains unresolved between Manerva and Maria. Public trees expand the father to John Simpson Rozier and the mother to Mariah/Maria Carlisle, but those expansions are derivative unless an original record is cited. The exact 3 November date and Lumberton wording are strong probable pending renewed inspection of the full certificate image.

docs.title: Marriage, household, and children
docs.text:
The Brooks County marriage record indexes the groom as "Mr Thos A Rozie" and the bride as Sallie A. Hitch. They married on 19 June 1892; the local license was issued ten days earlier. Ancestry collection 4766, record 282614. A 2 July 1892 Valdosta Times item independently identifies Thomas A. Rozier of Rozier, Conoly & Co. as the groom and Sallie as a daughter of the late Dr. R. M. Hitch of Morven. Newspapers.com image 889759299, clipping 193407281.

The household sequence is direct:

Census Household and property details Source 1900 Thomas, 45, farmer; Sallie, 32; Hazel, 5; Robert, 3; Sallie's sister Mattie Hitch. Thomas owned the farm free of mortgage. Ancestry 7602: 52872998, ED 9, sheet 3 1910 Main Street: Thomas, 54, farmer; Sallie; Hazel H.; Robert C.; Katharine; Mattie Hitch; nephew Martin Rozier. Ancestry 7884: 3199159, ED 21, sheet 3A 1920 Thomas and Sallie owned their farm free of mortgage, with a son indexed as "K. C. Rozier" and Mattie Hitch. The son's initials conflict with the otherwise secure Robert C. identity and should not be silently corrected without the image. Ancestry 6061: 7327106, ED 46, p. 17A 1930 Main Street: Thomas and Sallie; Mattie Hitch; daughter Hazel Stanhope; grandsons Thomas and Fred Stanhope. Home value $1,000. Ancestry 6224: 19963401, ED 16, p. 2A

The children are verified through the census and later records. Some expanded middle names come from later or compiled material and should remain subordinate to the direct records:

  • Hazel Hitch Rozier Stanhope, born about 1894. A 1924 announcement says Mr. and Mrs. T. A. Rozier announced her 17 December 1923 marriage to Harry Hurst Stanhope in Washington, D.C. Atlanta Journal, 13 January 1924.
  • Robert Carlyle Rozier, born about 1896. He appears as Robert C. in 1910 and was named as R. C. Rozier in Thomas's 1935 profile and Sallie's 1958 obituary.
  • Lois Catherine/Katharine Rozier Lanneau, born about 1900. She appears as Katharine in 1910 and later as Mrs. T. F. Lanneau.

The Valdosta Daily Times reported on 24 June 1937 that Thomas and Sallie had celebrated their forty-fifth wedding anniversary at their Barney home the preceding Sunday. That agrees with the June 1892 marriage. Newspapers.com image 890575843.

docs.title: Ware County and the McNeil & Rozier firm
docs.text:
Thomas's Ware County presence is now direct. The Savannah Morning News hotel register of 2 December 1886 lists "T. A. Rozier, Glenmore, Ga." Newspapers.com image 830501568. An Ancestry tax-digest index also places Thomas A. Rozier in Glenmore District 1082 during a displayed 1881-1887 residence range, although the source citation says "Georgia Tax Digests 1890". Both labels must be retained. Ancestry collection 1729, record 6711405, linked Georgia Archives image 40881_1020705384_0416-00455.

On 31 March 1888, the Valdosta Times called McNeil & Rozier a Ware County turpentine firm. The article says McNeil and the firm's woodsman Connolly pursued and shot an unnamed Black laborer who had been recruited from South Carolina, bound for a year, and charged a debt. It is direct evidence of coercive and violent labor conditions, but it omits both partners' initials. Newspapers.com image 889632321; public reprint in the Savannah Morning News, 2 April 1888, p. 6.

A second notice says 62 barrels of T. P. Jordan's rosin at Argyle depot were levied under an execution in favor of McNeil & Rozier. Images 889632317 and 889632329. This proves a judgment debt and levy. It does not locate a McNeil & Rozier still at Argyle or make the rosin theirs before levy.

Newspapers then follow the surnames into the Hahira and Folsom Bridge district:

  • 16 March 1889: "McNeil of Hahira" among naval-stores operators, image 889789051.
  • 29 March 1890: McNeil and Rozier doing good turpentine business at Hahira; their hands worked the Folsom Bridge road, images 889794099 and 889794108.
  • 12 April 1890: J. T. McNeil nearly completed opening the road, image 889794327.
  • 24 February 1891: a reprint reports that John Clifton fatally shot Peter Armstrong at McNeil & Rozier's turpentine farm in Brooks County; the inquest returned involuntary manslaughter. Macon Telegraph, image 825352472.
  • 29 August 1891: McNeill and Rozier again had the Hahira-Folsom Bridge road worked, image 889798850.

Thomas's direct 1886 Glenmore presence makes him the best-documented and strong-probable Rozier in the 1888 firm. It does not retroactively add his initials to the article. The Ware plant's exact site, partnership formation date, and transfer of labor, leases, equipment, or accounts into Brooks County remain unresolved.

docs.title: Foster, the Conoly transaction, and firm succession
docs.text:
Thomas signed the proposed Foster/Rozier post-office location paper on 4 March 1890; the Post Office Department received it on 10 March. One proposed name was "Rozier", tied to the family, while Foster became the approved name. The postmaster appointment register records Thomas at Foster on 4 April 1890. Ancestry collection 1932, record 1630513; NARA M841, roll 22.

The 14 November 1891 Valdosta Times correction says McNeil & Rozier sold brothers A. J. and H. McLean Conley/Conoly a collective one-half interest in the Foster naval-stores business and that McNeill retained one-fourth. Image 889756841; the initial report is image 889756744. This was a sale of a business interest, not a land deed. It does not divide the brothers' half, identify the owner of the remaining quarter, or state Thomas's retained share.

The operating name then appears as Rozier, Conoly & Co. or Rozier, Conoly Bros. & Co. in 1892-1893. The marriage item directly identifies Thomas with that concern. Foster columns describe continuing turpentine production and hauling to Hahira. Clipping IDs 193407281, 193407600, 193407422, and 193407548; related images include 889759299, 889761322, and 889763942.

A 1900 Savannah Morning News report lists T. A. Rozier among Savannah Naval Stores Company stockholders at its annual meeting. The initials and career fit the Barney man, but the item gives no residence, so the identification is strong probable. Image 852595717.

No partnership agreement, dissolution instrument, or final accounting was located. Thomas's exact entry and exit dates and the disposition of the last quarter interest remain unresolved.

His 26 October 1938 will supplies direct evidence of another or surviving partnership interest. It calls "J. T. McNeal and Company" a former firm composed of J. T. McNeal and T. A. Rozier and says the firm then owned 543 acres in parts of Land Lots 139 and 50, 12th District, Lowndes County. Thomas devised his undivided half to Sallie. The record uses "McNeal", not "McNeil" or "McNeill", and describes different land from the Foster tract. It is verified as written, but the partner's full identity and the legal connection, if any, to the 1888-1891 McNeil & Rozier concern remain unresolved.

docs.title: Foster-to-Barney postal continuity
docs.text:
The postal chain is one of the best-documented parts of the dossier:

  • Foster: appointed 4 April 1890, Ancestry 1932:1630513.
  • Thomas signed the 12 February 1897 application moving the office from Foster in Land Lot 227 to Barney in Land Lot 320, three miles northwest, on the South Georgia Railroad.
  • Barney: appointed 26 July 1897, Ancestry 1932:1630564.
  • He signed a Topographer's Office questionnaire on 2 November 1897, placing the office about 175 yards west of the railroad.
  • Tobe G. Robinson was appointed "vice Thomas A. Rozier, resigned" on 24 October 1903. Atlanta Journal, 26 October 1903, image 969531602.
  • Thomas was reappointed 20 February 1906, Ancestry 1932:1630569.
  • Paris Culpepper replaced him on 17 February 1916; Atlanta Semi-Weekly Journal, 22 February 1916, image 887733697.

Thomas served two documented Barney terms, 1897-1903 and 1906-1916. Describing his service as uninterrupted would be wrong.

docs.title: Farming, livestock, land promotion, and Edgewood
docs.text:
Every census from 1900 through 1930 calls Thomas a farmer or places him on his own farm. His advertisements show a specialized livestock interest. In 1904 he sought purebred Poland China hogs. In November 1909 he offered six full-blood pigs from registered stock for $8 each or $15 per pair. Images 889652157, 889664910, and 889664935.

In August 1914, he placed a national homeseeker advertisement in the Des Moines Register: "BARNEY, BROOKS COUNTY, GA.-COME to Brooks county ... where lands are reasonable cheap. The good people here will give you a hearty welcome. T. A. Rozier." Images 129031594 and 129032073. This verifies his role as a Barney contact and land promoter, not ownership of every tract advertised.

The January 1911 Edgewood reports say Thomas offered about sixteen acres between his "commodious residence", the Methodist and Baptist churches, and the public school for a Cambridge Realty auction. Valdosta Daily Times, 19 January 1911, image 889696900; weekly reprint 889668494. Advertisements variously proposed fifty or sixty lots. No result article, buyer list, prices, deeds, or plat was found. The tract and planned auction are verified; the number of completed sales is unresolved.

Local tradition says Thomas built Barney's first house. His 1897 postal role and the documented prominent residence fit the tradition, but no located deed, tax-improvement record, construction notice, or contemporary article calls it the first house. James has identified its approximate location as 31.006130, -83.519237. That is a user-supplied geographic control, not construction-date proof.

docs.title: The Croft deed and Land Lot 227
docs.text:
The 1897 federal postal diagram directly places the existing Foster office in Land Lot 227, 12th District, and the proposed Barney office in Land Lot 320. It does not identify the owner of the Foster land or locate the still and commissary within the lot.

A derivative land-lot index says Jacob Henry Croft conveyed 325 acres on the north side of Lot 227 to McNeil & Rozier on 9 October 1890. The original instrument has not been found. There is no verified deed book, page, recording date, consideration, spouse release, metes and bounds, or image.

Thomas's 1890 Morven District tax row lists no land. Ancestry collection 1729, record 716589, image 32306_1220705227_0017-00169. That weighs against calling him the individually assessed owner at that moment, but it does not exclude firm title, a lease, a separate assessment, or an acquisition later in the year.

The deed claim is therefore a strong-probable lead only. It must not be cited as an established deed reference until the Brooks County index and deed book are inspected.

docs.title: Town, church, school, and railroad activity
docs.text:
The public record shows a range of local roles:

  • The Atlanta Journal listed Thomas A. Rozier of Barney as a Brooks County delegate in an agricultural listing on 19 April 1903, image 969502063.
  • The Valdosta Times reported on 5 December 1903 that he was among Barney's nominated councilmen. Image 889679697. Nomination is verified; election and term are not.
  • The 9 November 1935 Macon Telegraph birthday profile says he served on the board of education and was secretary-treasurer of the Baptist church. Image 826362749.
  • Huxford says he was a Methodist Church trustee in 1899 and senior warden of Barney Masonic Lodge No. 609 in 1911. Those are strong secondary claims until supported by church or lodge records.

Thomas also helped organize the Georgia, Alabama & Western Railroad Company. Late-1911 notices name him among petitioners or promoters for a proposed 150-mile line through Hahira, Barney, Pavo, Meigs, Colquitt, and Blakely. Images 889588868, 889695710, and 969949004. The state granted the charter in January 1912; images 34095609 and 970010050. By June, reports called him a director and said surveys and cost estimates had been ordered. Image 859960351. Corporate organization is verified; construction of the proposed full line is not.

docs.title: Death, burial, and probate
docs.text:
The Georgia death record establishes death at Barney on 27 October 1938. Find a Grave memorial 111534073, reopened on 17 August 2026, gives birth 3 November 1855, death 27 October 1938, and burial at Camp Ground Cemetery Mount Zion Church near Morven. The memorial links Sallie and the three children. These memorial details are derivative unless supported by a photographed marker or another direct record; the marker itself was not independently transcribed in this pass.

No clean obituary or funeral notice was found after exact and variant searches across 1935-1940. The Quitman Free Press remains an important coverage gap for October-November 1938.

Ancestry collection 8635, record 1205180, is Thomas's will, not a stray mention. The index points to Brooks County Record of Wills, 1918-1964, p. 230. The original was inspected at media image 005782588_00313.

The will is headed "Last Will and Testament of Thomas A. Rozier" and dated 26 October 1938, one day before his death. It:

  1. left burial details to Sallie;
  2. directed payment of debts;
  3. devised to Sallie his undivided one-half interest in 543 acres owned by "J. T. McNeal and Company", described as a former firm composed of J. T. McNeal and T. A. Rozier, in parts of Land Lots 139 and 50, 12th District, Lowndes County;
  4. gave Sallie all other real and personal property; and
  5. appointed Sallie executrix without inventory, appraisal, bond, or returns.

The witnesses were T. F. Lanneau, P. Culpepper, and S. M. Blease. These terms are verified from the original image. The will does not identify the full name of J. T. McNeal or explain whether this former firm was legally continuous with the earlier McNeil & Rozier partnership.

docs.title: Namesake and record exclusions
docs.text:
• Thomas A. Rozier of Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, was a different man.
  • T. A. Rozier of Bonne Terre, Missouri, was unrelated.
  • P. J. Strozier of Barney was a distinct local person; "Strozier" must not be normalized to Rozier.
  • A Louisiana-born Thomas Rozier in the 1880 census was not the subject.
  • The 1860 Pennsylvania "Thomas Roser", Ancestry 7667:4920131, was a wrong result and was excluded. The correct target is 7667:41450029.
  • "Rosier", "Rozie", and similar forms may be source spellings or OCR variants. They were accepted only when place, relatives, or record continuity established the match.

docs.title: Search coverage and limits
docs.text:
Newspapers.com searches covered 1870-1940 using Rozier's full name, initials, surname variants, associated places, relatives, occupations, and public offices.

Meaningful gaps:

  • Brooks County deed and plat indexes were not available as a fully searchable online image set. The Croft deed and Edgewood deeds remain uninspected.
  • The original will was inspected, but the loose probate packet, probate order, land deed, and later estate conveyances remain uninspected.
  • No dedicated Barney city directory was found.
  • The Quitman Free Press issue runs needed for February 1900 and October-November 1938 were not located online.
  • No clean Thomas obituary was found in the documented search.
  • The exact Ware still site, partnership agreements, final Foster shares, and partnership dissolution remain unresolved.

docs.title: Priority record requests
docs.text:
1. Brooks County grantor and grantee indexes and deed books, 1888-1905: Croft/Craft, McNeil/McNeill/McNiel, Rozier/Rosier, Conley/Conoly/Connolly, and firm forms. Retrieve the alleged 9 October 1890 instrument and trace it forward.
  2. Brooks deed and plat books, January-March 1911: Thomas and Sallie Rozier, Edgewood, and Cambridge Realty; obtain the plat, buyers, lot numbers, prices, and covenants.
  3. Brooks Court of Ordinary: obtain the loose probate packet, probate order, and any estate or year's-support papers corresponding to will-book p. 230. The will waives inventory, appraisal, bond, and returns, so some usual documents may not exist.
  4. Lowndes County grantor/grantee, deed, mortgage, and tax records: trace "J. T. McNeal and Company", J. T. McNeal/McNeil/McNeill, and T. A. Rozier in Land Lots 139 and 50, 12th District, and identify the acquisition and later conveyance of the 543 acres.
  5. Quitman Free Press: manually browse February 1900 for the reported store/post-office building item and October-November 1938 for death coverage.
  6. Georgia death certificate image: preserve the state certificate number and full informant, cause, burial, and undertaker fields.
  7. Georgia, Alabama & Western corporate file: charter packet, subscriptions, surveys, and any construction or abandonment record.
