docs.title: Charles Seymour Hawks (C. S. Hawks)
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Charles Seymour Hawks, usually printed as C. S. Hawks, was a dry-goods merchant, Civil War officer, and one of the twenty-six petitioners for the South Georgia Railroad charter. He was born at Phelps, New York, on April 18, 1841, built his first mercantile career there, and moved to Quitman, Georgia, at the beginning of 1890 after illness forced him to sell his business and property. The move was not a vague family tradition. Phelps newspapers documented the liquidation, a Savannah newspaper identified the new Quitman merchant as a man from Phelps, and his federal pension application was filed from Georgia that August.[1][2][3]

Hawks remained in Quitman for roughly seventeen years. His firm, C. S. Hawks & Co., sold dry goods, carpets, and related merchandise. He lived in a home beside the Hotel Marie, participated in local social life, and lent his name to the railroad incorporation effort in 1896. By 1908 he and his second wife, Mary Hempstone, were again spending summers in Phelps. The 1910 census found them there. Mary died in 1915, and Hawks spent his last years in Leesburg, Virginia, where he died on June 17, 1921.[4][5][6]

Identity confidence: High. The identification rests on a continuous record chain, not on initials alone. The 1880 census places Charles S. Hawks, a merchant, in Phelps. A February 1890 newspaper calls the new Quitman merchant C. S. Hawks of Phelps. The 1900 census places New York-born dry-goods dealer Charles S. Hawks in Quitman with Mary, whom he married in Virginia in 1888. Most decisively, the Civil War pension index gives the full name Charles Seymour Hawks, lists the same New York and United States Colored Troops units found in his military records, and records his August 9, 1890 filing from Georgia.[2][3][7][8]

docs.title: Phelps family and early work
docs.text:
Charles was a son of Benjamin Franklin Hawks and Hannah C. Drake Hawks. The 1850 federal census and 1855 New York census place him in their Phelps household. At nineteen, the 1860 census described him as a clerk. An 1862 Geneva directory listed Seymour Hawks as a clerk at 46 East Main Street. The use of Seymour as his calling name would continue through his military records.[9][10][11]

After the war he became a dry-goods merchant. The 1870 census placed him in Phelps with Anna E. Hawks and reported $2,500 in real estate and $7,000 in personal property. The enumerated middle initial appears as T in the index, but the household, age, occupation, and later census continuity identify the couple. New York's 1875 census and the 1880 federal census call him Charles S. Hawks and name his wife Annie E. In 1880 they lived on Main Street, where he was a merchant.[12][13][7]

An 1867 Phelps marriage notice identifies the couple as Capt. Seymour C. Hawks and Annie K. Parker of Hopewell. It both supports Parker as her maiden name and illustrates the recurring reversal of Charles Seymour's given names. The middle initial conflicts with the Annie E. found in the censuses and cemetery record. Annie died suddenly on August 29, 1883, after suffering convulsions the previous morning. A Phelps correspondent wrote that her large circle of friends would be pained by the news.[14][15]

On April 12, 1888, the widowed Hawks married Mary Hempstone in Loudoun County, Virginia. The marriage record calls him Chas. S. Hawks, age forty-six, born in New York, and a son of Benj. It gives Mary the surname Hempstone. A contemporary Phelps report said he returned from Leesburg with his bride. Later census records agree on an 1888 marriage. No child appears with the couple in the 1900 or 1910 households, and no reliable record located in this search establishes a surviving child from either marriage.[8][16][17]

Hawks was already a visible member of Phelps civic life. In September 1888 he commanded the second division of the village's annual firemen's parade. A March 1889 notice reported that Leonard E. Furner had been engaged at his store.[18][19]

docs.title: Civil War service
docs.text:
Hawks enlisted at Phelps on August 22, 1862, and mustered on September 14 as a private in Company C, 148th New York Infantry. New York's muster abstract uses the inverted form Seymour C. Hawks. He left the regiment on March 19, 1864, for a commission as first lieutenant in Company B, 38th United States Colored Troops.[20][21]

The 38th USCT service index records Seymour C. Hawks, about twenty-three, entering service in Virginia in March 1864. A compiled service profile says he was promoted to captain on March 13, 1865, and resigned on October 18, 1865. The pension index also associates him with Companies A and B of the 38th USCT, so the surviving compiled references are not perfectly uniform about the company assignment. They do agree on the man, regiment, commissioned service, and progression from the 148th New York.[3][20][21]

The 38th USCT was a Black enlisted regiment with white commissioned officers. Hawks's service therefore placed him in command roles over African American soldiers during the final phase of the war. The present research did not inspect his full compiled military service file, which the index says contains sixty-nine enclosures. Any detailed account of his battlefield movements, duties, wounds, or conduct would require that file and the regiment's original records.[21]

docs.title: The decision to move south
docs.text:
Hawks did not quietly disappear from Phelps. In November 1889 he advertised that he had decided to locate in the South and would sell his established dry-goods and carpet business, his East Main Street residence, and another house at Eagle and West Main streets. A news item published the same day said he expected to locate in Georgia soon.[22]

By January 1890 the reason was explicit. A Phelps report said that he was compelled to close his business because of poor health and contemplated a trip south to recover. His stock of dry goods, carpets, and notions was scheduled for auction beginning January 27, followed by his residence and household property. Another notice two days later said he was closing out the remaining dry goods at auction.[1][23]

The Quitman end of the journey appeared almost immediately. On February 24, the Savannah Morning News reported that Hopson & Brother were finishing two brick stores and that one would be occupied about March 1 by C. S. Hawks, "a merchant of Phelps, N.Y." This report connects the New York merchant to the man who soon appeared in Quitman records.[2]

docs.title: Merchant in Quitman
docs.text:
The 1900 federal census found Charles S. Hawks in Quitman, born in New York in April 1841 and working as a dry-goods dealer. Mary was in the household, and the census said they had been married for twelve years. They rented their home and had one boarder, Susie R. Bratton.[16]

The surviving business references are consistent with the census. A Quitman business list published in the Quitman Free Press on April 3, 1897, and reproduced by historian Folks Huxford, named C. S. Hawks & Co. under dry goods. An Atlanta Journal business list in March 1900 also included the firm. The evidence establishes a continuing dry-goods house, though it does not reveal the identities of Hawks's partners, the firm's capitalization, or its exact closing date.[4][24]

His Quitman home stood beside the three-story Hotel Marie. Fire broke out in the kitchen on April 3, 1900. Firefighters quickly brought two streams of water to bear, saved the house except for the kitchen, and held the loss to a small amount. The adjacent hotel caused considerable concern. A second report added that Mary was recovering from grip and suffered from the excitement and exertion. The reports place Hawks in an established household in the center of Quitman.[25][26]

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Huxford names C. S. Hawks among the twenty-six petitioners for the South Georgia Railroad charter in 1896. The proposed company had capital of $65,000 divided into 650 shares. Hawks's documented role is charter petitioner or incorporator.[27]

The distinction matters. Hawks does not appear in the located subscription committee, the board elected at the March 23, 1896 organization meeting, or the first officer slate. No inspected stock ledger or subscription list states how much money he invested, or even proves that he ultimately paid for shares. Incorporation shows that he joined the legal effort to create the railroad. It does not make him a director, officer, construction manager, or known large stockholder.[27][28]

His participation still fits the setting. By 1896 he had spent six years building a Quitman business. His first known store occupied a new Hopson & Brother building, and J. B. Hopson became a subscription committeeman, incorporator, director, and vice-president of the railroad. Those documented connections place Hawks within the commercial circle behind the project. They do not prove who recruited him or what private discussions led him to sign.[2][27][28]

docs.title: Community life and travel
docs.text:
Newspaper notices show that Charles and Mary entered Quitman's social life. He attended a St. Valentine Club banquet at the Hotel Marie in 1891. In 1900 Mary appeared as Martha Washington at a Young Matrons' Club costume gathering, and the couple attended other receptions and traveled to New Orleans for Mardi Gras. In 1904 Mary presented a paper on Confederate flags to the local United Daughters of the Confederacy, using miniature flags as illustrations.[29][30][31][32]

The notices also show a mobile household with durable northern ties. Charles appeared in Savannah hotel and passenger lists, including a Baltimore steamer passage in 1899. In August of that year a Rochester paper reported Charles and Mary, described as former Phelps residents then living in Quitman, visiting Dr. and Mrs. R. M. Green. Charles visited Phelps again in 1901. The couple camped with other Quitman residents at Hampton Springs, Florida, in 1904 and visited Madison, Florida, in 1905.[33][34][35][36][37]

These items are evidence of travel and social connections, not proof of a second permanent residence during the Quitman years. They do, however, help explain the later transition north. A March 1907 Quitman notice said the couple had returned from Florida and would soon leave for the summer in Virginia and other northern points. In March 1908 a Phelps paper reported that they had spent the winter in Virginia and arrived "home" to remain through the summer.[38][39]

docs.title: Return to Phelps and final years
docs.text:
The precise date when Hawks ended his Quitman business has not been located. The evidence supports a gradual, seasonal transition rather than a sharply documented departure. He was still reported from Quitman in 1907. By 1908 Phelps was again called home, and the 1910 census placed Charles and Mary on Church Street there. It indexed the surname as Harves with Hawks as an alternate, but the ages, birthplaces, marriage duration, and wife Mary make the identity secure. They owned their house free of a mortgage.[17][38][39]

Charles remained part of Phelps community life. In 1911 he and Mary Stiller Newton witnessed a wedding at St. John's Episcopal Church. This Mary was not identified as his wife, and the distinct full name should be preserved rather than collapsed into Mary Hempstone Hawks.[40]

Mary died at a Baltimore sanitarium on May 26, 1915. Her obituary called her Mollie Hawks, wife of Charles S. Hawks of Leesburg, and named several Hempstone siblings. She was buried in Union Cemetery at Leesburg. By 1920 the widowed C. S. Hawks owned a home on Market Street in Leesburg. Dorcas Hempstone, age seventy-five, lived with him and was called his sister in the census index. Because Dorcas shared Mary's maiden surname, sister-in-law is possible, but the record's stated relationship should not be silently rewritten.[5][41][42]

Virginia's death record gives Charles's full name as Charles Seymour Hawks and says he died in Leesburg on June 17, 1921. It records his birth as April 18, 1841, and names his mother as Hannah Drake. The indexed father appears as B. T. Hawks, conflicting with the repeated Benjamin F. in census, marriage, and cemetery evidence. He was buried at Union Cemetery in plot A, lot 449, site 6.[6][43]

docs.title: Evidence conflicts and limits
docs.text:
• Name order: Civil War and 1865 New York records use Seymour C. Hawks, while civilian records usually use Charles S. Hawks. The pension and death indexes give Charles Seymour Hawks and connect the forms.
  • First wife's name: The 1867 marriage notice calls her Annie K. Parker. Censuses and cemetery evidence use Annie or Anna E., so her middle initial remains in conflict.
  • Father's middle initial: Census and family records support Benjamin F. Hawks. The Virginia death index says B. T. Hawks, probably an informant or indexing error, but the discrepancy remains recorded.
  • Military company: Sources agree on the 38th USCT and commissioned service. They vary between Companies A and B. The full service file was not inspected.
  • Return north: Quitman remained the couple's reported residence through 1907. Phelps was called home in 1908 and was their census residence in 1910. No located notice gives an exact store-closing or permanent-removal date.
  • Children: No child was found in the couple's census households. That absence does not by itself prove that Hawks never had a child.
  • Railroad investment: Incorporation is established. No share amount, officer position, directorship, or operational role is established.

docs.title: Research assessment
docs.text:
The Georgia pension filing establishes the identity chain. Charles Seymour Hawks carried a distinctive pair of military units from Phelps into a pension claim filed just after his move to Georgia. Census, marriage, newspaper, and cemetery records then follow the same man from childhood to death.

The record also puts his railroad role in proportion. Hawks belonged to the group that sought the charter, but he was not found among the first directors or officers. His larger historical interest lies in the path that brought a Union veteran and former USCT officer from an established New York dry-goods business to Quitman's commercial community, where he remained long enough to join one of the town's most important development projects.

docs.title: Search ledger and access limits
docs.text:
Research conducted August 21, 2026, covered exact-name and initials searches for Charles Seymour Hawks, Charles S. Hawks, C. S. Hawks, and Seymour C. Hawks in Phelps, Ontario County, Quitman, Brooks County, Georgia, Loudoun County, and Leesburg. Variants and common OCR failures were tested in federal and state censuses, directories, military indexes, pension records, Virginia marriage and death records, cemetery memorials, Google-indexed web results, Newspapers.com, and the stored South Georgia Railroad research corpus.

Newspaper searches covered 1880 through 1940 and included combinations with Phelps, Quitman, Georgia, dry goods, merchant, railroad, death, obituary, Mary, and Mrs. C. S. Hawks. Broad searches were checked for namesakes before use. The search found no dependable obituary, business dissolution notice, railroad stock subscription, child record, or full military narrative.

The 1910 census evidence comes from the record's alternate index and the surrounding continuity evidence rather than a new manuscript transcription. The full 38th USCT service file, original South Georgia Railroad charter petition, railroad stock ledger, and local probate files were not available as inspectable online images during this research.

docs.title: Calvin Milton Hitch
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

1869-1944 | lawyer, legislator, public administrator, diplomat, banker, civic organizer, and reported railroad charter petitioner

Calvin Milton Hitch spent the first half of his career moving outward from Brooks County and the second half bringing his experience home. He began in Quitman banking and law, represented Brooks County in the Georgia House, worked for three governors and a United States senator, and served abroad for about two decades. After retiring from the Foreign Service, he returned to Quitman and helped reorganize a bank, organize the county chamber of commerce, reopen the tobacco market, and build Brooks County Hospital.[1][2][3]

Folks Huxford names Hitch among the men who petitioned for the South Georgia Railroad charter in 1896, but the original petition was not inspected. No located evidence puts him on the subscription committee, the first board, the officer slate, or the operating staff. No source found in this research states how much stock he subscribed, or even proves that he completed a stock purchase.[1][4]

docs.title: Early life and education
docs.text:
Hitch was probably born at Morven, Georgia, on July 28, 1869. The date and place appear in his Social Security claim record, and his obituary says he would have turned seventy-five on July 28, 1944. The 1900 census instead reports March 1870, while later census ages alternate between birth years of about 1869 and 1870. The Georgia death index and contemporary obituary fix his death in Brooks County on July 6, 1944.[5][6][7][13] The 1870 census places a child called Milton in the Brooks County household of Robert and Martha Hitch. In 1880, ten-year-old M. C. Hitch appears as a son of R. M. Hitch in the Morven district. The names, siblings, ages, and location make this a continuous childhood household.[8][9]

Folks Huxford identifies his parents as Dr. Robert Marcus Hitch and Martha Serena Fall. The census evidence strongly supports Robert as his father and Martha as his probable mother, but it does not itself supply either parent's full name. By 1880, R. M. Hitch's wife was recorded as A. E. Hitch, whose biological relationship to Calvin was not established in the records reviewed.[1]

The 1932 State Department register says Hitch attended Emory College from 1887 through 1889 and then attended business school. Huxford names the second institution as the Commercial College of Kentucky University at Lexington and calls him a graduate. The 1940 census reports two years of college. No diploma or institutional register was inspected, so the attendance is better documented than a specific degree or graduation year.[2][10]

docs.title: Marriage and household
docs.text:
Hitch married Ida Blanche Parrish in Berrien County. The original marriage register was inspected for this dossier. It records a license for "C. W. Hitch" and "Ida B. Parrish" on January 26, 1890, followed by a marriage return dated January 27. The entry explains why one index gives January 26 and another gives January 27. The initials do not match Calvin's usual name, but Ida's identity, the place, the date, and the later census and passport chain make the identification strong probable. Huxford's February 19 date conflicts with the original register and is not followed here.[11][12][1]

The 1900 census finds Calvin, Ida, and their son Guy boarding at 65 Capitol Avenue in Atlanta. Calvin was working as a sawyer. In 1910 he was an insurance salesman on Washington Street, with Ida and Guy still in the household.[13][14] Their son appears as Guy Hitch in 1900 and Guy H. Hitch in 1910. Huxford calls him Guy Harvard Hitch, but the middle name was not independently established from an original vital record.[1]

The overseas censuses continue the same household. In 1920 Hitch was enumerated with the United States Consular Service. The automated index assigns implausible family relationships to unrelated officials, so those labels were rejected. The 1930 census places Calvin and Ida at Basel, Switzerland. In 1940 they were back at 712 North Court Street in Quitman, where Calvin's occupation was recorded as executive manager.[15][16][10]

docs.title: Banking, law, and the legislature
docs.text:
Hitch's first documented public work was local. A March 1894 report named him to Quitman's five-member board of education for a two-year term.[17] Huxford says he read law while working at the Bank of Quitman, became its cashier in January 1895, and served as attorney for the Brooks County Building and Loan Association.[1] A January 1897 burglary report independently called him cashier of the Bank of Quitman.[18]

The most reliable description of his prosecuting office comes from federal personnel registers. The 1932 register calls him solicitor of the Brooks County Court from 1892 through 1896. Earlier editions summarize the work as prosecuting attorney for Brooks County from 1890 through 1896, while Huxford gives 1892 through 1895. His 1944 obituary elevated the title to solicitor general of the Southern Judicial Circuit, but no appointment or election record was found to support that broader office. The county-court title is therefore used here.[2][3]

Hitch served as Brooks County's representative in the 1896-97 legislature. A March 1896 report said he faced no opposition for the seat, while Huxford says he was elected that October to a two-year term. The State Department register's 1896-97 summary and Huxford's term description do not align perfectly.[19][1][2] In September 1897, the Macon Telegraph printed his detailed speech on Georgia's convict system and identified him as a member of the House penitentiary committee. The speech shows that he did more than occupy the seat: he engaged one of the legislature's most difficult policy questions and argued from his committee's inspection work.[20]

docs.title: Telephone and railroad ventures
docs.text:
Hitch participated in two local infrastructure efforts during the same period. In February 1896, he joined J. O. Bradley, Dr. E. A. Jelks, and other Quitman men in forming a stock company for a telephone system. A contemporary report said enough telephone subscriptions had been obtained to proceed. These were subscriptions to the local telephone venture, not South Georgia Railroad subscriptions.[21]

Huxford later named Hitch among the incorporators of the Quitman Telephone Company on December 7, 1896. That corporate role is consistent with the February organizing report.[1]

For the South Georgia Railroad, the evidence is narrower. Huxford includes Calvin M. Hitch among the twenty-six petitioners for the railroad charter in February 1896. The surviving organizational reports name other men to the subscription committee, the founding board, and the first officer slate. Hitch does not appear in those groups. His banking and legal background may explain why he was a plausible incorporator, but it does not prove that he performed the railroad's legal work, solicited subscriptions, served as a director, or bought a particular number of shares.[1][4]

docs.title: Georgia executive service
docs.text:
Governor Allen D. Candler appointed Hitch second executive clerk in November 1898.[22] He continued in the executive department under Governor Joseph M. Terrell. Contemporary coverage says he then left for work with Senator Augustus O. Bacon before returning to Atlanta government. On June 29, 1907, Governor Hoke Smith appointed him secretary in the executive department and warrant secretary.[23]

The work could be substantive. In 1908, Smith sent Hitch and George Tumlin to inspect the state prison farm and juvenile reformatory at Milledgeville. Their report recommended pardons or clemency for fifty-four inmates. Smith also assigned Hitch to consolidate Georgia's presidential and congressional election returns that November.[24][25]

Hitch handled political organization as well. In 1910 he directed correspondence for Hoke Smith's campaign, served as secretary of the campaign committee, and became one of the state Democratic convention's secretaries.[26] He returned as Hoke Smith's executive secretary in 1911. During a dispute over sealed gubernatorial communications, Hitch publicly argued that state senate president John M. Slaton had departed from executive-office precedent by opening them. The search found no criminal allegation, ethics charge, or personal scandal involving Hitch.[27]

A proposed move to Senator Hoke Smith's staff did not become his lasting job. By November 1911, Josiah Carter had taken the Senate post and Hitch had become Georgia manager for the Columbian Woodmen insurance organization.[28]

docs.title: Washington and the State Department
docs.text:
The federal registers give 1907 through 1910 as Hitch's period as private secretary to Senator Augustus O. Bacon. Georgia newspapers place him with Bacon by about 1905, so the exact starting year remains unsettled.[2][23] The 1913 Official Register adds a distinct position: Hitch was then a United States Senate clerk assigned to the Committee on Woman Suffrage, paid $2,100 a year.[29]

Secretary of State William Jennings Bryan appointed him assistant chief of the Division of Latin-American Affairs on July 2, 1913. Contemporary reports announced the selection just before the effective date and identified Fred M. Dearing as his predecessor.[30]

Hitch's official consular chronology can be reconstructed from the State Department's registers:

Date Appointment or assignment February 22, 1915 Appointed consul of class five and assigned to Nottingham, England September 14, 1917 Promoted to consul of class four June through October 1919 Temporarily detailed to the Department of State June 4, 1920 Promoted to consul of class three March 30, 1923 Assigned to Basel, Switzerland July 1, 1924 Appointed Foreign Service officer of class four December 17, 1925 Advanced to Foreign Service officer of class three July 24, 1930 Advanced to Foreign Service officer of class two October 9, 1930 Appointed consul general and assigned to Wellington, New Zealand

These dates come from the 1916, 1917, 1918, 1924, 1928, and 1932 registers.[2][31][32][33][34] A contemporary report said he would sail for Nottingham on March 17, 1915.[35]

Hitch remained at Nottingham through the First World War. During a 1919 visit to Washington, he described air raids in Nottingham and London and the heavy passport work that followed the armistice. The same interview said his son Guy had served as vice consul at Belfast and assisted survivors of the Tuscania disaster.[36]

His public writing reflected the years abroad. In 1923 the Atlanta Journal published his article about Nottingham and the Dorothy Vernon tradition. In 1926, while serving at Basel, he wrote an argument for strict firearms regulation based on British law.[37][38] These articles show a diplomat interpreting European institutions for a Georgia readership, although they do not establish official United States policy.

The inspected federal registers do not give Hitch's retirement date. A 1937 report said he had retired several years earlier, a 1941 family announcement called him recently retired, and an Associated Press obituary gave 1934. These accounts agree that he left the service before resuming his Quitman career, but they do not establish an exact retirement date.[39][41]

docs.title: Return to Quitman
docs.text:
Hitch returned to Quitman during a hard period for local institutions. When Citizens National Bank opened on August 25, 1934, he became executive vice president and a director, according to Huxford. The 1944 Associated Press obituary said he became executive officer after the bank-holiday reorganization and remained with the bank until his death.[1][39]

His civic work is unusually well documented because it was recognized while he was alive. In 1937 the Brooks County Kiwanis Club gave him its public-service trophy. The Valdosta Daily Times credited him with helping reorganize the national bank, leading the movement for a forty-bed hospital, helping secure a tobacco market, and organizing and presiding over the Brooks County Chamber of Commerce.[40] Reports from June 1937, when he became ill at the bank, also described Brooks County Hospital as having been built largely through his efforts.[41]

The bank, chamber, tobacco market, and hospital gave Hitch a practical use for the administrative experience he had gained in state and federal service.

docs.title: Final illness, death, and family
docs.text:
Hitch suffered a heart attack on Sunday, July 2, 1944, and entered Brooks County Hospital. He died there at 10:30 a.m. on Thursday, July 6, less than a month before his seventy-fifth birthday.[7]

The death notice named his wife Ida; son Guy; granddaughter Mrs. Frank Morrison; sisters Lula Hitch Chapman, Mrs. T. A. Rozier, Mattie Hitch, and Mrs. S. G. Etheridge; and his late father, Dr. R. M. Hitch. It said funeral services would be held in Quitman the next day, but arrangements were incomplete when the paper went to press. The follow-up funeral report and burial place were not found despite exact-name, funeral, cemetery, obituary, and adjacent-page searches. No verified Find a Grave memorial was located.[7][39]

docs.title: Evidence limits
docs.text:
• The original birth certificate, if one exists, was not located. The July 28, 1869 date comes from a government-derived Social Security record and is supported by the obituary, but the 1900 census reports March 1870.
  • The marriage register says "C. W. Hitch", not Calvin M. Hitch. The identification is strong probable from the spouse, place, date, and later household chain.
  • The State Department registers disagree with some newspapers and Huxford about the opening dates of his county prosecutor and Senator Bacon service. The conflicts are preserved rather than blended into false precision.
  • A 1902 report names a Calvin Milton Hitch among Atlanta College of Pharmacy graduates. No second record connects that graduate to this man, so it is not included as part of his education.
  • No evidence was found for a South Georgia Railroad role beyond Huxford's report that he was a charter petitioner.
  • The official retirement date, final funeral arrangements, and burial place remain unresolved.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Huxford places Hitch in the South Georgia Railroad charter group while he was a young bank cashier, lawyer, county prosecutor, and incoming legislator. No located evidence identifies him as a railroad operator. He was also involved in Quitman's telephone venture. Decades later, he applied his administrative experience to the bank, chamber, tobacco market, and hospital in Brooks County.

docs.title: Clayton Groover
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

June 1, 1829 to March 19, 1916 | farmer, merchant, Confederate sergeant, druggist, banker, mill operator, civic official, insurance investor, and railroad charter petitioner

docs.title: Identity and evidence
docs.text:
The Clayton Groover associated with the South Georgia Railroad was the elder Quitman businessman born in 1829, not Frank Clayton Groover or any of the younger men who carried Clayton as a first or middle name. His identity is verified through federal censuses from 1850 to 1910, his marriage to Floride Burney, their sons Edwin and Ledley, contemporary business reports, his full-name obituaries, and his photographed grave marker.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

The marker reads "Clayton Groover / June 1, 1829 / Mar. 19, 1916".[8] Find a Grave memorial 36045694 incorrectly transcribes the birth year as 1839. That cannot be reconciled with the marker, the 1850 census age of twenty, the 1870 census age of forty-one, the 1900 birth entry of June 1829, the 1910 age of eighty, or the obituary age of eighty-six.[2][4][6][7][9] June 1, 1829 therefore controls.

docs.title: Parents and early adulthood
docs.text:
The 1850 census placed twenty-year-old Clayton in the District 81, Thomas County household of James and Elizabeth Groover. The census did not state relationships, so Ancestry's parent labels are inferred from household position. Clayton was a farmer and had attended school during the year. Older men Redding and Thomas Groover were in the same household, along with Mary Hancock and five Adams children.[2]

Find a Grave links Clayton to James Earl Groover and Elizabeth Denmark Groover. Those parental links agree with the 1850 household, but the memorial relationships remain derivative because no birth, probate, or family Bible record was inspected.[8] Clayton's 1916 obituary independently named Dr. James Groover of Grooverville as his brother and Martha Ramsey as his sister.[9][10]

Folks Huxford's transcription of the 1860 Brooks County census lists Clayton, age thirty-one, as a merchant-clerk boarding with Mariner J. Culpepper in the new town of Quitman. The original census image was not recovered in the fresh Ancestry search, so the name and occupation remain a published transcription rather than a new image reading.[1]

Groover had already acquired a stake in the county seat. Huxford's town-lot list says "Clayton Groover, Brooks County" bought one Quitman lot for $170 on February 19, 1859.[1] His 1916 obituary called him a native of Brooks County, but Brooks did not exist until December 1858. The obituary meant the local area, not the county as a legal jurisdiction at his birth.

docs.title: Marriage and children
docs.text:
The Brooks County marriage record names Clayton Groover and Floride Burney and dates their marriage to July 16, 1861.[3] The 1900 census says they had been married thirty-eight years, a one-year difference that is ordinary for census reporting.[6]

Floride was born in Florida in November 1842. The 1900 census lists November 1842, while her marker-based memorial gives November 26, 1842.[6][11] She appears as Florida in the 1870 census and Floride in the marriage record, 1900 census, death notice, and cemetery record. These are spelling variants for the same woman.

The couple had at least two sons:

  1. Edwin A. Groover, born about 1863 or 1864. The 1870 census calls him Edwin, age six; the 1880 index renders him "E. A. Grooves", age sixteen. Later Jacksonville reports identify Edwin A. Groover as Clayton's son. He became a banker and insurance executive.[4][5][12][13]
  2. Ledley Groover, born about 1865 or 1866. He was four in the 1870 census and about fourteen in an 1882 newspaper report. The 1880 index instead gives a fourteen-year-old son as "A. S. Grooves". The original 1880 image was not inspected, so Ledley's full name and the "A. S." reading remain unresolved.[4][5][14]

Clayton's obituary said one son, E. A. Groover, survived him. That indicates Ledley had died before March 1916, but no identity-secure death or burial record was found.[9][10]

Edwin's daughter Floride was Clayton's granddaughter. Contemporary social reports repeatedly make the link. In 1903 Mrs. Edwin Groover and Miss Floride Groover visited Clayton and his wife in Quitman. In 1908 Mrs. Edwin A. Groover and Floride again visited him. A Jacksonville account that August called Clayton the young woman's grandfather and described him joining her guests.[15][16][17]

Floride Burney Groover died at Quitman early on February 9, 1905. The Valdosta report said the death was sudden and attributed it to asthma. Edwin traveled from Jacksonville for the funeral. Her photographed-marker memorial gives the same date and burial in West End Cemetery.[11][18][19] Clayton was listed as widowed in 1910.[7]

docs.title: Civil War service and Reconstruction
docs.text:
The Georgia muster-roll index records Clayton Groover in the Piscola Volunteers of Brooks County on May 9, 1861.[20] Huxford's company roster says he was elected fourth sergeant at Quitman on July 23, 1861. The unit first belonged to the 13th Georgia Infantry and became Company C of the 26th Georgia Infantry at reorganization.[1]

Huxford says Groover retired at the May 1, 1862 reorganization. A compiled soldier profile gives a muster-out date of May 8, 1862, but then adds a wound and furlough dated after that retirement. Those later notes conflict with the service boundary and may belong to another soldier or reflect a compilation error.[21] No claim about a wound or later Virginia service is adopted here. The secure finding is service as fourth sergeant from 1861 until the spring 1862 reorganization.

Georgia's 1864 militia-reorganization census listed Clayton Groover in Brooks County.[22] That list established his presence and militia eligibility, not a second period of active Confederate service. On June 20, 1867, he registered as a white voter in Brooks County's Seventh Election District under the Reconstruction Acts.[23]

A fresh exact-name search of the 1860 federal slave-schedule index returned no Clayton Groover entry. That is a documented negative index search, not proof that he never enslaved anyone. The original Brooks County schedule, tax digests, deeds, and probate records were not reviewed page by page.

docs.title: Merchant, property holder, and druggist
docs.text:
Groover's prewar merchant-clerk occupation continued into the postwar economy. The 1870 census found him in Quitman as a retail dry-goods clerk. It valued his real estate at $3,000 and personal estate at $750.[4]

Huxford says Dr. James H. McCall opened a Quitman drugstore in 1866 and took Groover into partnership about 1870. The business traded as McCall & Groover.[1] Contemporary newspapers confirm that the firm existed. A September 1873 storm unroofed its store, and a January 1876 fire report says McCall & Groover owned the building occupied by R. M. McCall and E. Ives. Their building was insured for $1,300.[24][25]

Huxford also says Quitman's first Baptist sermon was preached in a store building owned by Groover. The event belonged to the Civil War era, but the county history does not supply a deed, address, or contemporary article that would identify the building more precisely.[1]

docs.title: Banking and the Quitman mills
docs.text:
In 1878 Groover joined J. O. Morton and F. J. Spain in the private bank that preceded the Bank of Quitman. Huxford calls the concern Denmark, Groover & Company. Contemporary newspapers often print "Clayton, Groover & Co." or "C. Groover & Co." and identify it as the Quitman bank.[1][26][27] The surviving OCR and punctuation do not justify turning those forms into separate firms. What is secure is the continuity from the private banking house to the state-chartered Bank of Quitman.

The 1880 census calls Groover a banker. Floride and their two sons were in his household on Screven Street.[5] An April 1888 report says the banking firm was adding a story to its offices and rebuilding the front in pressed brick, iron, and glass.[28]

The bank also entered manufacturing. In August 1885, "C. Groover & Co." bought the Quitman mills from Jelks & Hines for $7,000. The report said the property had originally cost more than $40,000.[26] A January 1886 item called Clayton, Groover & Company bankers and said the mills were running full time with about forty employees.[27] The sources establish the purchase price, operation, and approximate workforce, but not each partner's investment or the mill's balance sheet.

The Bank of Quitman elected Groover president on February 13, 1893 after E. P. S. Denmark declined reelection before moving to Valdosta. The elected directors were Groover, F. J. Spain, Joseph Mabbett, E. A. Jelks, and R. C. McIntosh. E. A. Groover was cashier.[29]

On December 31, 1894, Clayton and Edwin A. Groover submitted resignations as president and cashier, effective immediately, but agreed to serve until January 15. The report connected the change to a proposed reduction in expenses and said the bank was prosperous, had just declared its usual semiannual dividend of 3.5 percent, and was in excellent condition.[30] Judge J. O. Morton succeeded Clayton as president. The record supports an orderly resignation, not a failure or accusation of misconduct.

docs.title: Agriculture and local development
docs.text:
Groover and his wife both appeared in the region's agricultural reporting. At the 1878 Brooks County fair, Mrs. Clayton Groover displayed 222 specimens of pickles, preserves, jellies, and marmalades made from cultivated and wild fruit.[31] In 1890 Clayton reported an acre of Japanese persimmons that brought from one to eight dollars per crate. He responded by planting another acre.[32]

In February 1890, Groover joined R. C. McIntosh and John Tillman on the committee seeking local subscriptions for a cotton compress. The committee reported that Quitman had subscribed the requested $15,000. The project then moved to negotiations with the Savannah, Florida and Western Railway.[33] The article gives Groover a verified fundraising role but does not state his personal subscription.

Quitman's council granted Groover and E. P. S. Denmark a franchise in July 1890 to install an electric-light system and furnish fifty street lights for $1,800 a year. Huxford says they did not exercise it, and the franchise reverted to the town.[1]

docs.title: Civic and political work
docs.text:
Huxford's municipal roster lists Groover as a Quitman councilman in 1876. It also identifies him as secretary of the Brooks County Democratic Executive Committee for the 1872 to 1874 term.[1] No council minutes or committee proceedings were found to show particular votes or policies.

He and Floride took part in early public organizations. Huxford names Mrs. Clayton Groover on the committee for an 1874 supper that raised money for the Ladies Memorial Association. The organization cared for Confederate graves and later became the Quitman chapter of the United Daughters of the Confederacy.[1]

Clayton was on the first board of directors of the Brooks County Library Association when it organized in 1880. Later that year he joined A. J. Rountree and Dr. Harry Mabbett on the committee for the association's two-story brick building.[1] Anniversary reports in 1912 named him as one of only three surviving members of the first board. A 1913 feature again identified Groover and G. W. Avrett as surviving founders in Quitman.[34][35]

Huxford also identifies Groover as a charter member of the Quitman Hotel Company, which developed the Hotel Marie.[1] He attended its public events, but no inspected record makes him an officer or states his subscription.

The 1882 schoolhouse incident belongs in the record because it shows a serious failure of judgment and preserves Groover's own response. A reprinted Quitman Free Press account says his son Ledley resisted punishment and tried to draw a knife. Clayton entered the school and struck teacher Sterling G. Brinkley with a cane, knocking him unconscious. Groover then signed an apology stating that he should not have attacked Brinkley in the schoolhouse and in front of the pupils. Friends of both men negotiated a settlement.[14] The apology does not erase the assault. It establishes that Groover acknowledged it.

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Groover was one of the twenty-six petitioners named in the February 1896 application for the South Georgia Railroad charter.[1][36] He does not appear on the January subscription committee, the first nine-member board elected in March, or the first officer slate. No stock ledger or subscription amount has been found.

His verified railroad role is therefore narrow: charter incorporator. His earlier banking, mill, electric-light, and cotton-compress work explains why he belonged among Quitman's development promoters, but it does not prove a railroad office or personal investment.

docs.title: Insurance work in old age
docs.text:
The 1900 census called Groover a furniture agent and showed that he owned his Quitman home free of mortgage.[6] In 1910 he lived alone at 609 Stevens Street. The census listed him as a fire-insurance agent and a Confederate veteran, and again recorded a mortgage-free home.[7]

That insurance occupation led to a new business connection with his son. On January 30, 1912, Edwin A. Groover, Clayton Groover, Ugo E. Guerrini, and J. P. Hoffman signed the proposed charter of the St. Johns Insurance Company in Jacksonville. The charter named Edwin president, Clayton vice president, and both men directors. It recorded Edwin's subscription of 950 shares and Clayton's subscription of 45 shares at $100 par value, a nominal $4,500 commitment.[37]

The charter is unusually specific, but par value is not proof of the cash amount paid on the filing date. It authorized stock payment in money, property, or services. The source proves the offices and subscription, not the form or timing of payment.

docs.title: Final years, death, and burial
docs.text:
Clayton remained socially active into his eighties. Jacksonville and Quitman reports place him with Edwin's family and granddaughter Floride, and he attended a Quitman wedding in June 1912.[16][17][38] The insurance charter shows that his business activity also continued after the Bank of Quitman years.

During his last year, Clayton lived with Edwin at 2370 St. Johns Avenue in Jacksonville. He died there at 4 p.m. on Sunday, March 19, 1916, after a short illness.[39] The body was sent to Quitman for a funeral at 10 a.m. Tuesday and burial in the family plot. The Atlanta and Macon obituaries called him one of Quitman's oldest and best-known citizens, credited him with founding the private bank that became the Bank of Quitman, and named surviving siblings Dr. James Groover and Martha Ramsey and surviving son E. A. Groover.[9][10]

The photographed marker and Find a Grave memorial place him in West End Cemetery.[8] The memorial's birth-year typo should not be repeated. The marker, census chain, and obituary age all establish 1829.

docs.title: Findings and limits
docs.text:
• Clayton Groover was born June 1, 1829 and died March 19, 1916. The photographed marker controls over Find a Grave's 1839 transcription.
  • The 1850 household and memorial links identify James and Elizabeth Groover as his parents with strong probability. A direct birth or probate record was not found.
  • He married Floride Burney on July 16, 1861. Their sons were Edwin A. and Ledley. Ledley's full name, later life, and death remain unresolved.
  • His secure Confederate service ended at the 1862 reorganization. A compiled profile's later wound and furlough notes conflict with that boundary and were rejected.
  • His career included dry-goods work, McCall & Groover, private banking, the Bank of Quitman presidency, operation of the Quitman mills, civic committees, and a late insurance venture with Edwin.
  • He was a South Georgia Railroad charter petitioner, not a verified director, officer, or stockholder.
  • No complete deed, tax, probate, will, estate, slave-schedule, bank-stock, or railroad-stock audit was available. Personal wealth, land totals, and investment amounts should not be guessed.

docs.title: Dr. Theophilus Williams Hunter
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Identity confidence: Verified.

Theophilus Williams Hunter was a Quitman physician, farmer, major landowner, school-board member, and South Georgia Railroad subscription organizer. He was born in Georgia on September 21, 1852 and died in Atlanta on December 13, 1919. He usually appeared in public records and newspapers as Dr. T. W. Hunter. His original death certificate supplies the full name, while Jefferson Medical College and the Journal of the American Medical Association independently identify him as Theophilus W. Hunter.[1-5]

docs.title: Birth, parents, and childhood
docs.text:
Hunter was a son of Abraham Hunter and Jane Bryan or Bryant. His death certificate uses Abraham and Jane Bryant. The 1860 Brooks County census lists Abram Hunter, age fifty-one, Jane, thirty, and children John M., Theophilus W., Abram B., and Virgil C. Theophilus was seven and all members of the household were Georgia-born.[1-2]

The date September 21, 1852 is supported by his photographed marker, the September 1852 entry in the 1900 census, and the age and birth day on his death certificate. Georgia is the only birthplace that can be stated without qualification. Brooks County and Quitman did not exist in 1852. Huxford's later description of Hunter as Brooks County-born may refer to the part of Lowndes County that became Brooks in 1858, but no contemporary birth record or exact land location was found. The derivative claim that he was born in Quitman is anachronistic.[1-3][6]

The parents' surname evidence also needs to remain visible. The death certificate writes Jane's maiden name as Bryant. Family and local material use Bryan. The records identify the same woman, but they do not justify silently choosing one spelling.[1]

docs.title: Schooling and medical education
docs.text:
The 1870 census places eighteen-year-old Theophilus Hunter and nineteen-year-old John Hunter at school near Jefferson in Jackson County. Their names, ages, Georgia births, and later return to the same Brooks County family make this a strong-probable match to the Hunter brothers. The schedule does not name the school.[7]

Hunter's 1919 obituary says that he graduated at the state university before receiving a medical diploma in Philadelphia. No university record was found that names his degree or attendance dates. His university education remains reported but unverified.[17]

His medical education is much firmer. Jefferson Medical College's institutional alumni roll lists "Hunter, Theophilus W., Ga., '76." Huxford's transcription of the Brooks County physicians' register gives a Jefferson Medical College diploma date of March 11, 1876. JAMA's January 1920 professional death notice again identifies Theophilus W. Hunter of Quitman as a Jefferson graduate of 1876.[4-6]

docs.title: Medicine and farming
docs.text:
The 1880 census found Hunter back in his parents' Tallokas District household. He was twenty-seven and his occupation was doctor. The schedule appears to give him a middle initial M, and Ancestry follows that reading. The single conflicting initial is outweighed by the marriage record, other censuses, medical-school records, and death certificate that use W or Williams.[8]

The 1900 Quitman census called Hunter a physician. Contemporary newspapers continued to use the title Dr. through his death. The surviving evidence does not establish a specialty, hospital appointment, public-health office, military medical service, or medical-society office. Polk's 1896 medical directory omitted him from its Quitman list, but that negative cannot overcome the county register, census, Jefferson roll, JAMA notice, and repeated contemporary identification.[4-6][10]

Medicine was only one part of Hunter's working life. An 1893 political roster described him as a farmer. The 1910 census recorded "own income," and his death certificate gave farming as his occupation. A 1911 agricultural-train report placed him among Quitman's large farmers.[1][11][20]

docs.title: Marriage and children
docs.text:
The original marriage book resolves a repeated date conflict. The license for Theophilus W. Hunter and Fannie C. Rountree was issued on November 14, 1878. The minister certified that he married them on November 17. Later family material copied the license date as the wedding date, but the original return establishes the ceremony date.[9]

The 1900 census lists four children, all then living:

  • Walter Rountree Hunter, born in September 1881, later a bank clerk and the husband of Emma De V. McCall;
  • John M. Hunter, born in October 1884;
  • Mary E. Hunter, born in June 1887; and
  • Mattie Louise Hunter, born in August 1889, later the wife of Thomas Oliver Marshall.[10-12]

The 1910 manuscript says that Fannie had borne four children and that three were living. Ancestry transcribes the last figure as two, but the original image clearly reads three. Walter, Mary, and Mattie were in the household, while John had died in 1904.[11]

John M. Hunter was killed in a street duel with Mercer Baggs at Bainbridge on February 27, 1904. Contemporary reports identify him directly as Dr. Hunter's son. At the commitment hearing, Dr. Hunter and Walter Hunter appeared as the victim's father and brother. These reports keep the event with the correct generation and distinguish John from his surviving brother.[18]

Newspaper reports place Mattie at Agnes Scott in 1906 and 1908. Her 1916 wedding report says her father gave her in marriage to Thomas O. Marshall. Fannie's 1938 death certificate and obituary identify her as Dr. Hunter's widow and confirm the surviving family chain.[12][19-20]

docs.title: Land, timber, and the 1901 sale
docs.text:
The 1890 Quitman District tax digest records Theophilus W. Hunter with 723 acres valued at $2,100. It also lists extensive Hunter family holdings on the same page. The tax entry is a dated assessment, not a complete deed history.[13]

In October 1901, Oglesby & Brother and E. C. Bridges bought Hunter's property about six miles northwest of Quitman. A Savannah Morning News report reprinted from the Quitman Free Press described about 4,500 acres and consideration above $35,000. The transfer included substantial virgin timber, productive farm land, mules, wagons, farm equipment, and supplies.[14]

A shorter report named only Oglesby Brothers and said the buyers planned a mill and tramroad to the timber tract. The fuller buyer list includes E. C. Bridges. The proposed tramroad belonged to the purchasers' timber operation and does not prove a railroad investment or operating role for Hunter.[14]

No deed image was located. The exact conveyance date, recorded acreage, land lots, deed book and page, and division of the purchase among the buyers remain unresolved. The newspapers verify the reported scale and economics, not the legal description.

docs.title: Public education and community activity
docs.text:
Huxford says the March 1894 town election placed Hunter on Quitman's school board. Contemporary reporting in March 1896 says he was already serving and was renominated with the old board. In March 1900 he appeared on the old ticket but did not finish among the five nominees. A March 1902 report again named him to a slate whose nomination was described as equivalent to election. The evidence supports service before 1896, defeat in 1900, and return in 1902, but not uninterrupted tenure.[6][15]

An 1893 political roster listed Hunter among Brooks County supporters of Clement A. Evans. That is evidence of a stated political preference, not elective office or party leadership. No inspected record establishes municipal or county office beyond the school board, a church office, fraternal membership, or medical-association office.[16]

The Baptist pastor W. M. Anderson conducted Hunter's funeral. The minister's role does not by itself prove that Hunter was a Baptist member.[17]

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Hunter helped raise subscriptions for the South Georgia Railroad. Huxford says that on January 29, 1896 he joined Mitchell Brice, Fleming Bates Walker, Silas M. Young, and a man printed as James W. Hitch on the county-at-large committee. The identity evidence makes John William Hitch the strong-probable committee member. The committee reported the required money raised five days later.[6]

His role was subscription organizing, not incorporation or governance. Hunter was not among the twenty-six charter petitioners in Huxford's list and was not among the first directors or officers in the contemporary organization report. No stock ledger, subscription amount, share count, railroad office, employment record, or construction role was found. The committee service is strong probable because it rests on Huxford's detailed retrospective account.[6][21]

docs.title: Illness, death, funeral, and burial
docs.text:
Hunter became ill in December 1919 and spent about ten days under treatment in Atlanta. His death certificate says he died at St. Joseph's Infirmary on December 13. It records arteriosclerosis and cerebral hemorrhage, with diabetes mellitus and chronic nephritis also written in the cause section. Son W. R. Hunter supplied the personal information.[1]

The Atlanta Constitution called him a prominent Quitman physician and named his wife Fannie and surviving children Walter, Mary, and Mrs. Thomas Marshall. The Atlanta Journal reported that his body reached Quitman on Sunday morning and that the funeral took place Sunday afternoon, conducted by W. M. Anderson.[17]

The death certificate orders burial or removal to Quitman. Hunter's photographed marker reads:

T. W. HUNTER M.D. SEPT. 21, 1852 DEC. 13, 1919

Find a Grave places the photographed marker in West End Cemetery. Fannie's original 1938 death certificate independently names West End Cemetery for her burial. These records make Quitman burial verified and West End Cemetery strong probable for Hunter, although no cemetery register was located.[1][3][19]

docs.title: Record conflicts and limits
docs.text:
• The full name is Theophilus Williams Hunter. The death certificate writes it in full; Jefferson and JAMA use Theophilus W. The forms Theopilus, Theophelus, and Theopheley are index or compilation variants.
  • The 1880 schedule appears to use middle initial M. The original death certificate and several independent W records control.
  • Jane's maiden surname appears as Bryant and Bryan. Both spellings are preserved.
  • The marriage license was issued November 14, 1878; the ceremony occurred November 17.
  • The 1900 census says four children born and four living. The 1910 manuscript says four born and three living, consistent with John's 1904 death.
  • Hunter was born in Georgia before Brooks County or Quitman existed. Exact birthplace is unresolved.
  • University study is reported in the obituary, but no direct university record was obtained.
  • No probate file, cemetery register, medical specialty, 1901 deed image, or railroad stock record was located in the accessible search.

docs.text: Question Finding Confidence Identity Theophilus Williams Hunter, publicly Dr. T. W. Hunter Verified Birth September 21, 1852, Georgia Date and state verified; exact locality unresolved Parents Abraham Hunter and Jane Bryan/Bryant Verified Education School near Jefferson in 1870; reported state-university study; Jefferson Medical College class of 1876 Jefferson verified; earlier institution unresolved Medical work Quitman physician by 1880 and in 1900 Verified; specialty and offices unresolved Marriage Fannie C. Rountree, November 17, 1878 Verified Children Walter R., John M., Mary E., and Mattie L. Verified Land 723 acres in 1890; about 4,500 acres reported sold in 1901 Tax acreage verified; sale scale verified as reported School board Service before 1896, defeat in 1900, return in 1902 Verified from contemporary reports; 1894 election strong probable Railroad County-at-large subscription committee Strong probable; no charter, board, office, or stock role proved Death December 13, 1919, Atlanta Verified Burial Quitman; probably West End Cemetery Quitman verified; cemetery strong probable

docs.title: Dr. Edwin A. Jelks
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

1836-1908 | Quitman physician, Confederate surgeon, civic investor, and later South Georgia Railway director

docs.title: A note about his name
docs.text:
The man usually called Edwin Augustine Jelks in local histories is securely identified in contemporary and official records as Dr. Edwin A. Jelks. His medical school, the federal censuses, military indexes, newspapers, marriage register, and gravestone use the initial but do not spell out his middle name.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8]

Two later sources disagree about what the A stood for. A detailed family biography written by Dr. E. L. Jelks and published in Folks Huxford's 1948 county history calls him Edwin Augustine Jelks. Find a Grave memorial 36063788 calls him Edwin Augustus Jelks.[9][10] No primary record located in this investigation resolves the difference. This dossier therefore uses Edwin A. Jelks in its title and treats both expansions as later claims.

This identity control matters. Edwin was not his son Edwin Briggs Jelks, his nephew and later medical partner Dr. Edwin Lamkin Jelks, or his nephew O. K. Jelks of the Bank of Quitman. He was also not the Dr. E. A. Jelks of Oviedo, Florida, whose profitable citrus acreage appeared in an 1889 newspaper report.[9][11]

docs.title: Childhood, family, and education
docs.text:
The family account gives his birth as October 1, 1836, at Hawkinsville, Georgia, to James Oliver Jelks and Mary Polhill Jelks. His gravestone independently confirms the date.[8][9] In 1850, thirteen-year-old Edwin lived in Pulaski County with I. O. Jelks, Mary Jelks, and four boys whose names and ages match brothers described by the family history. Because the 1850 census did not state household relationships, the parental identification comes from the combination of that household and the later family account.[1][9]

The family biography says the Jelkses moved to Hamilton County, Florida, while Edwin was young. A Mercer University catalogue places Edwin A. Jelks of Hamilton, Florida, among the students for 1855-1856. It confirms attendance, but not a degree.[12] The biography says Jelks taught school for two years after Mercer and began medical study at Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia in September 1858.[9]

The strongest evidence for the end of his medical training is a primary source from the Medical College of the State of South Carolina. Its annual circular for the 1859-1860 session lists "Jelks, E A" of Belleville, Florida, with L. A. Folsom as his preceptor, then names him among the graduates.[13][14] This proves that he completed the Charleston program during that session. The school's circular does not confirm every part of Huxford's story about the withdrawal of Southern students from Philadelphia, but it fits the account's basic sequence. The American Medical Association's directory of deceased physicians also identifies him as a 1860 medical graduate.[15]

By June 1860, the federal census placed twenty-three-year-old E. A. Jelks in Brooks County, Georgia, with the Tallokas post office. He was already practicing as a physician and reported $200 in personal property.[2] This identity-secure census entry conflicts with a later memorial biography that places him in Calhoun County, Alabama, that same year. A second enumeration or a namesake is possible, but the Brooks County record is the one tied clearly to the Quitman doctor.

docs.title: Building a practice in Quitman
docs.text:
The family biography says Jelks joined the practice of Dr. Henry Briggs in the young town of Quitman. The territory was broad, roads were poor, and much of a country doctor's work required travel by horse. The description is a family recollection rather than a surviving office ledger, but contemporary records support the larger picture of a long medical career.[9]

In 1870 Jelks was a physician in Quitman with real property valued at $4,000 and personal property at $1,000. His household included his wife Constance and daughter Elizabeth.[3] The 1880 census again called him a physician and placed the family at 12 Court Street.[4] In 1900 he still reported medicine as his occupation and owned his Quitman home free of mortgage.[5]

Huxford identifies Jelks as a participant in the Brooks County Medical Society formed in 1868. The same county history's physician register lists him as a Pulaski County native and an 1860 graduate of the South Carolina medical school.[16] No original society minutes were found, so the precise organizing role remains Huxford-based.

His statewide professional standing is directly documented. In April 1902 the Valdosta Times reported that Jelks, chairman of the Georgia State Board of Medical Examiners, had gone to Augusta and Atlanta to examine applicants for licenses.[17] A March 1903 report named him as the physician attending Mitchell Brice after Brice suffered paralysis.[18] These notices show that Jelks remained professionally active late in life, even if he had begun reducing the most demanding parts of his practice.

The memorial published after his death remembered him as a particularly capable surgeon and as a doctor who continued to care for poor patients. It also said Governor Allen D. Candler appointed him to the state medical examining board. The praise is valuable evidence of how Quitman remembered him, but its superlatives are eulogy, not an objective ranking.[19]

docs.title: Confederate medical service
docs.text:
Jelks entered Confederate service with the 26th Georgia Infantry. Two National Park Service indexes preserve complementary records. The regimental entry associates Edwin A. Jelks with Company C and field and staff, and shows a progression from private to surgeon. A second entry for Confederate general and staff officers shows Edw. A. Jelks entering as assistant surgeon and leaving as surgeon.[20][21]

The precise chronology comes from a later biographical register of Confederate physicians, reproduced on the Find a Grave memorial. It says Jelks enlisted as a private in the Piscola Volunteers at Quitman on July 23, 1861, was detailed as an assistant surgeon that September, received a Confederate appointment as assistant surgeon in February 1862, and was appointed surgeon in May. It also says he was paroled as surgeon of the 26th Georgia at Appomattox on April 9, 1865.[10] These details are consistent with the official rank and unit indexes, but the underlying individual service cards and parole image were not accessible. The dates should therefore be read as strong compiled-record evidence, not as a substitute for the original file.

The National Park Service's unit history says the 26th Georgia first served on St. Simons Island and at Savannah, then moved to Virginia. It fought in campaigns from the Seven Days through Cold Harbor, later served with Jubal Early in the Shenandoah Valley, and ended at Appomattox.[22] Huxford's biography places Jelks with the medical service during several of those campaigns.[9] A unit's battle history does not prove one surgeon's presence at every engagement. The safe conclusion is that Jelks served as a Confederate medical officer with a regiment that endured those campaigns.

One story from that service resurfaced in Pennsylvania newspapers in 1898. According to a modern York County history article that quotes the period reports, Jelks paid the heirs of Jacob Rudy $125 for a horse obtained near York during the Gettysburg campaign. Jelks explained that he had paid Rudy in Confederate money on June 29, 1863 and later decided that payment had not been fair. The story rests on the York newspaper correspondence and is credible as a reported act of restitution, though the original letters themselves were not located.[23][24]

docs.title: Two marriages and four children
docs.text:
A compiled Georgia marriage index records E. A. Jelks and C. D. Atkinson marrying in Camden County on November 10, 1863.[25] Huxford identifies her as Constance Atkinson, daughter of Edmund Atkinson and Sarah Elizabeth Waddell Atkinson. The 1870 and 1880 censuses place Constance or C. A. Jelks in Edwin's household.[3][4][9] The original Camden County entry was not available, so the exact date remains strong but not primary-record proof.

Edwin and Constance had four children:

  • Mary Elizabeth Jelks, born November 6, 1868, and died July 9, 1885.
  • Sarah Josephine Jelks, born July 28, 1870. She married D. A. Denmark and died in March 1940.
  • Edwin Briggs Jelks, born December 18, 1873. He married Anne Louise Felder in 1898 and died in December 1930.
  • Nellie Constance Jelks, born December 19, 1879, and died December 3, 1880.[9]

The 1880 census supports the four-child household and the children's approximate ages.[4] The exact dates come mainly from the family history. Find a Grave gives Mary Elizabeth a birth year of 1863, but Huxford's 1868 date agrees with her census age of eleven in 1880. The 1863 claim is therefore contradicted by the better evidence.

Constance died in 1890, according to Huxford.[9] The original Brooks County marriage register proves Edwin's second marriage. A license for Dr. E. A. Jelks and Miss Janie E. Sinclair was issued January 17, 1891, and the minister certified that he married them on January 20.[7]

The 1900 census found Edwin and Janie married nine years. His daughter Josephine and Alma and Willie Albritton shared their home.[5] Huxford describes Alma and Willie as Janie's orphaned nieces who became members of the household. The census called them boarders, so they should not be recast as daughters. Edwin and Janie had no children together.[5][9]

docs.title: Business and investment in a growing town
docs.text:
Jelks's life in Quitman extended far beyond his medical office. The record shows a doctor who repeatedly invested in the town's buildings, industry, utilities, and financial institutions.

In January 1880 a contemporary newspaper reported the sale of a factory property to Jelks, Mabbett, and Hines for slightly under $14,000.[26] The following year, a federal court report named E. A. Jelks and others as defendants in litigation over the Quitman Mills land.[27] These reports directly connect him to the mill property. Huxford adds that Jelks, Harry Mabbett, Joseph Mabbett, and H. B. Hines sought a charter for Quitman Mills in September 1880 with $20,000 in capital, and that Jelks served as president.[28] The presidency remains a strong secondary-source claim because the original charter and minutes were not located.

Huxford also says Jelks initially subscribed $2,000 when the cotton mill was revived in 1899, with all listed subscriptions later increased by 25 percent.[28] That would make his commitment $2,500, but the larger number is arithmetic based on Huxford's account, not an independently printed subscription amount.

Contemporary newspapers document his property development. In September 1889 Jelks had begun three two-story brick stores in Quitman. A January 1890 survey of local construction valued the three buildings at $10,000.[29][30] In June 1890 he was named as a director of the Quitman Real Estate and Investment Company, which was reported to have earned a 13 percent net return after its first year and organization expenses.[31]

His documented Bank of Quitman directorship spans fourteen years, from 1891 to 1905. Newspapers recorded his election or reelection in 1891, 1892, and 1893, and a 1905 report again listed him on the board.[32][33][34][35] Huxford's statement that he was among the bank's first directors is consistent with this pattern, though the earliest organization record was not inspected.

Jelks also helped organize new services. In February 1896 a newspaper named him among the men forming a telephone stock company in Quitman after enough customers had subscribed to make service practical.[36] Huxford later placed him among the incorporators of the Quitman Telephone Company. The county history also linked him to the first board of the Quitman Library Association and to the Hotel Marie corporation.[37] A 1912 anniversary article independently named him among the library's first directors.[38] The hotel evidence is less clean: an 1889 newspaper's OCR renders one director as "Dr. E. K. Jelks," while Huxford identifies E. A. Jelks. The likely OCR error should not be hidden.

There is no sound evidence that Edwin A. Jelks was a farmer or commercial grower. The 1889 citrus story belongs to a doctor in Oviedo, Florida.[11] His cotton-mill investments and a household garden described by Huxford do not make him a planter.

docs.title: Schools, church, politics, and civic work
docs.text:
Jelks was repeatedly chosen for Quitman's school leadership. Newspapers named him in school-board nominations in 1892, described him as a current board member in 1896, reported his successful nomination in 1900, and again placed him on the board in 1902.[39][40][41][42] This proves service by 1896 and repeated public selection across a decade. It does not prove one uninterrupted term from 1892 through 1902.

He also appeared in broader civic work. In 1873 he joined a local committee supporting an inland-water communication proposal.[43] In 1890 he served on a committee considering a $35,000 hydraulic cotton compress and was selected as a Brooks County delegate to the state Democratic convention.[44][45] The evidence shows local influence, but not a career of elective office.

The family biography says Jelks joined the Quitman Presbyterian Church on September 14, 1877 and became an elder on May 19, 1878, serving for the rest of his life.[9] These exact dates were not confirmed in church minutes. They are credible family and local-history testimony and should retain that label.

docs.title: Railroads and the South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Huxford lists E. A. Jelks among the twenty-six petitioners for the South Georgia Railroad charter in 1896.[46] No original charter petition, stock ledger, subscription book, or corporate minute book was found. Contemporary reports of the permanent organization name the first directors and officers, and Jelks was not among them.[47][48] He was also absent from the surviving reports of the January subscription committees.

The 1896 evidence supports one narrow conclusion: according to Huxford, Jelks was a charter petitioner. He was not a first director, officer, or subscription committeeman, and no stockholding or investment amount can be assigned to him from the surviving records.

A later source changes the directorship question. On April 29, 1906, the Atlanta Journal described Dr. E. A. Jelks of Quitman as a physician, capitalist, and director of the South Georgia Railway.[53] This verifies that he was identified as a director by 1906, but it does not establish when he joined the board, how long he served, or whether he owned stock.

His interest in transportation was broader than that one company. In February 1899 he called a Quitman mass meeting to order and helped explain why the town needed another railroad running south to protect its trade.[49] That was a separate proposed line, not the South Georgia Railroad.

In 1907 E. A. Jelks appeared among the petitioners for a charter for the proposed Quitman, Valdosta and Thomasville Electric Railway and Power Company.[50][51] The notices described a planned fifty-mile electric street railway. They prove participation in the petition, not that the railway was built. The listing appears to refer to the elder doctor, who was still alive, and separately names other Jelks family members where applicable.

docs.title: Final years, death, and burial
docs.text:
The family biography says heart trouble forced Jelks to stop night calls around 1895 and that he retired fully in 1904.[9] Contemporary evidence shows at least some active practice in 1903, so his withdrawal was gradual rather than abrupt.[18]

On July 28, 1908, the Valdosta Daily Times reported a telegram from Quitman: Dr. E. A. Jelks had died at 2 p.m. after about two weeks of illness. The report said he had suffered from heart trouble for years and had experienced a paralytic stroke about a year earlier. His daughter, Mrs. D. A. Denmark of Valdosta, and other relatives were present.[6]

A follow-up memorial said he was buried on July 29 before a large gathering.[19] His photographed stone at West End Cemetery in Quitman reads "E. A. Jelks, M.D.," followed by October 1, 1836 and July 28, 1908.[8][10] The stone and same-day newspaper settle the death year as 1908. The 1909 date found in some catalog and web descriptions is wrong.

The memorial portrayed him as a doctor who had grown with Quitman from its early years, a trusted adviser in civic affairs, a successful businessman, a Presbyterian elder, and a familiar friend to children and poor patients.[19] The language is affectionate and plainly local. Its value lies not in every superlative, but in the breadth of the life the town believed it had lost.

docs.title: Historical assessment
docs.text:
Edwin A. Jelks practiced medicine in Quitman for more than forty years. Outside his practice, he served on boards or committees connected with schools, banking, mills, utilities, the library, construction, and transportation proposals. Medicine remained the center of his public identity, from his 1860 graduation through his state examining-board work more than forty years later. His Confederate service carried prestige in his own era, while his investments and board work tied him to many of Quitman's development efforts.

Huxford identifies Jelks as a South Georgia Railroad charter petitioner. Contemporary organization reports show that he was not on the first board in 1896. By April 1906, however, the Atlanta Journal identified him as a South Georgia Railway director. His election date, length of service, and stockholding remain unresolved.

Later accounts disagree about his middle name. One gives the wrong state for his 1860 residence, another gives the wrong year for his daughter's birth, and several descriptions give the wrong year for his death. The census entries, medical-school circular, marriage register, military indexes, contemporary newspapers, and gravestone resolve much of the basic chronology. The original military file, first marriage entry, church records, South Georgia Railroad petition, and probate estate remain unexamined or missing.

docs.title: Evidence limits and open questions
docs.text:
• No primary record located here spells out Jelks's middle name. Augustine and Augustus are conflicting later expansions.
  • No Mercer degree is proved. The catalogue supports attendance in 1855-1856.
  • The medical-school circular proves his Charleston attendance and graduation, but the Jefferson Medical College phase still rests mainly on Huxford.
  • The original Confederate service cards and individual Appomattox parole were not accessible. Exact appointment dates come from a later compiled register.
  • No original Camden County image for the 1863 marriage was inspected.
  • No original Presbyterian membership or elder record was found.
  • No original South Georgia Railroad charter petition, subscription book, stock ledger, or company minutes were located. The 1906 newspaper verifies a later directorship as printed, but not Jelks's election date, length of service, or stockholding.
  • The Georgia Archives catalogue says its small Jelks collection includes a copy of his will, but the document is not digitized and was not inspected. No probate packet, inventory, or estate settlement was found. The catalogue also gives his death year as 1909, which the newspaper and gravestone disprove.[52]
  • West End Cemetery is supported by the memorial and a legible stone photograph, but no cemetery register was inspected.
