docs.title: Research note
docs.text: This dossier was completed August 21, 2026. Research covered the existing South Georgia Railroad collection, Huxford's county history and index, Newspapers.com, Ancestry census, military, and cemetery results, Find a Grave, public web indexes, local family material, banking and business reports, death notices, and false-match controls. Twenty-five targeted newspaper queries covered name variants, medicine, drugstores, banking, real estate, the Hotel Marie, the railroad, politics, schools, agriculture, violence, illness, death, and family. The 1850, 1870, 1880, and 1900 census households were matched; the 1860 location remains unresolved. Accessible evidence was preserved in the project package. Important gaps and conflicts are stated above rather than filled from inference.

docs.title: Judge James Oliver Morton
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

December 20, 1820 to October 16, 1911 | farmer, enslaver, Inferior Court justice, county commissioner, banker, civic organizer, and railroad charter petitioner

docs.title: Identity and evidence
docs.text:
James Oliver Morton spent most of his adult life on the southern edge of Quitman, Georgia. In public records his name appears as James O. Morton, J. O. Morton, James Morton, and, in two mistranscribed census indexes, Jas O. Martin and James O. Morten. The title "Judge" came from his service on the Brooks County Inferior Court. It did not mean that he was a Superior Court judge.[1]

Morton can be followed as the same man across the 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, and 1910 federal censuses. His age, Georgia birthplace, wife Sarah or Sallie, children Simeon and Lavinia, occupation, and Lowndes-to-Brooks residence all align.[2][3][4][5][6] Contemporary notices about his bank presidency, farm, county offices, and death match that record. No material evidence found in this search belongs to a competing James Oliver Morton in Brooks County.

docs.title: Early life, marriage, and migration
docs.text:
Morton was born in Screven County, Georgia, on December 20, 1820. The fullest local biography names his parents as Silas Morton and Sabina Archer and says that he studied in local schools and at Chatham Academy in Savannah. It also says he married Sarah Young in August 1843, then moved to the part of Lowndes County that became Brooks County in 1858.[7] Two later genealogical books agree on the 1820 birth year, 1843 marriage, Sarah Young, and the names of their children, but neither is an original civil record.[8][9]

The original marriage entry was not found in the Georgia marriage indexes searched for this dossier. The 1910 census offers useful independent support: James and Sarah reported that they had been married for 66 years, placing their marriage about 1843 or 1844.[6] The precise August 1843 date therefore rests on the local biography and family-history compilations.

In 1850 the Mortons lived in Lowndes County. James was 29, Sarah 24, Simeon 6, and Lavinia 3. Morton was a farmer with $5,000 in real estate.[2] In 1860, after Brooks County was created, the same family lived near Tallokas. His census entry reported $15,000 in real estate and $22,915 in personal property.[3]

docs.title: Household and children
docs.text:
James and Sarah had two known children. Simeon L. Morton was born about 1844, and Lavinia Calhoun Morton about 1847.[2][3] Huxford's family sketch says Simeon joined the Savannah Volunteer Guards and was killed in the final fighting around Richmond. That statement was not confirmed in a compiled military service record during this search, so it should be treated as a family-history claim rather than a settled military fact.[7]

Lavinia married Henry Gray Turner, who became a Georgia legislator, congressman, and judge. The 1870 household shows Lavinia and Henry Turner living with her parents, along with their children James and infant Henry.[4] James and Sarah were alone in their 1880 household.[5] In 1910, both were still at their home on Nankin Road. James was 89 and Sarah 85.[6]

Sarah's family was central to Morton's move and community standing. A newspaper account after the 1911 death of Sarah's sister Lavinia Young described the Young, Morton, and Avera families as early neighboring settlers whose original homes remained occupied. The article rounded Morton's age upward, but its account of the family cluster agrees with the censuses and local history.[10]

docs.title: Land, wealth, and slavery
docs.text:
Morton's antebellum prosperity depended in substantial part on enslaved labor. The 1850 slave schedule lists seven people enslaved by James O. Morton: three males, ages 30, 22, and 20, and four females, ages 16, 16, 13, and 12.[11] By 1860 the schedule lists 24 people, ranging from infancy to age 50.[12] The schedules record age, sex, and color, but not names. No names for these 31 schedule entries were recovered.

The rise in his reported wealth tracks that expansion. His real estate increased from $5,000 in 1850 to $15,000 in 1860, while the 1860 census assigned $22,915 to personal property, a category that included the monetary valuation of enslaved people.[2][3] The local family sketch describes the farm as land cleared with "the labor of a few slaves." The federal schedules show that phrase understates the size of the forced-labor operation by 1860.[7][11][12]

Morton also appears on the September 11, 1850 federal agricultural schedule in Lowndes County. The online index identifies the schedule and page but does not transcribe the acreage, livestock, or production columns, so those figures are not claimed here.[13] In 1870, after emancipation and the Civil War, the census reported $14,000 in real estate and $3,000 in personal property. His household included two Black farm laborers, Matthew Young and Paul Colson.[4]

His plantation remained active outside Quitman. An 1891 report placed it three miles from town.[14] An 1890 Quitman tax-list index identifies Morton and reports 20 employees, but the underlying columns were not transcribed in the online record.[15] The farm was still a large commercial operation after emancipation. The surviving records do not explain its labor contracts, wages, tenancy, or living conditions.

docs.title: County government and the title "Judge"
docs.text:
Morton first held public office in Lowndes County. Huxford's office list places him on that county's Inferior Court from 1855 to 1859.[16] When Brooks County was organized, Governor Joseph E. Brown commissioned the first justices on December 11, 1858. Morton, John J. Pike, and James T. Robeson had served in Lowndes and continued in the new county. The Brooks minutes place Morton in court on January 15, 1859.[1]

The best term reconstruction is more precise than the broad summaries printed after his death. Morton served from 1859 until 1861. He was elected again on January 10, 1861 but declined the new term, and Isaac Johnson took the seat on March 27. Morton returned on April 3, 1866 to complete William Hudson's unexpired term and served until 1868.[1] A 1911 obituary said he served only the first two years, while another said he served "throughout the sixties." Neither captures both terms.[17][18]

The Inferior Court handled much of the county's daily administration. One surviving example authorized Morton in August 1860 to have a bridge built across the Okapilco at the old Stage Bridge.[19] He also served as foreman of the grand jury in February 1866 and November 1870.[20]

Brooks County created a five-member Board of Commissioners in 1881. Morton was appointed to the first board and became its first chairman. He served from September 1881 until 1885, when he resigned and F. J. Spain was recommended for the vacancy.[21][22] This office, like the Inferior Court, put him directly into county finance and infrastructure rather than ordinary private litigation.

docs.title: Civil War record and its limits
docs.text:
Morton's wartime record is not simple. An 1886 local retrospective said that when the Piscola Volunteers organized under their flag, Morton was first lieutenant. It dated that organization to June 1, 1861.[23] Huxford's military chapter gives a different chronology, placing the company's formation in July and its muster on July 23 as Company I, 26th Georgia Infantry. Morton does not appear on the final company roster printed there.[24]

The same county history does identify him as adjutant of the 81st Battalion, Brooks County militia, commissioned March 4, 1862. Huxford cautioned that the militia records were incomplete.[25] No compiled Confederate service record for Morton was found in the reviewed material. The supportable conclusion is that he held local military responsibilities and was associated with the Piscola Volunteers at their early organization, but his service in the final Confederate company roster is unproved.

His home front activity is clearer. At an August 10, 1861 meeting, Morton joined the committee that recommended a special county tax for destitute soldiers' families.[26] He was later chosen for a county committee that procured provisions for the army.[27] A disturbing 1864 newspaper report also identified enslaved people on Morton's and neighboring plantations among those punished after authorities alleged an insurrection plot. The account says confessions were extracted under the lash. It reflects both the violence of slavery and the local wartime system Morton helped govern.[28]

docs.title: Agriculture and community institutions
docs.text:
Farming remained Morton's main occupation throughout the census record.[2][3][4][5] In March 1869 he helped organize the Brooks County Agricultural Society and became its first president. The society promoted improvements in farming, gardening, household production, and agricultural education.[29] He later served as master of the Quitman Grange, which won the best general Grange display at the 1877 Thomasville fair.[30]

A detailed 1878 fair report shows Morton experimenting with crop methods. From one and a half acres he reported 90 bushels of non-rusting oats, followed by 300 bushels of sweet potatoes. He had sown the oats on January 14 and fertilized them with 25 bushels of cottonseed. He also displayed corn from the 1877 crop and explained that excluding light from a tightly closed crib prevented weevil damage.[31]

Morton chaired the Brooks County Fair Association as it developed a permanent local fair in 1901. A 1900 meeting thanked him for attending every session and helping manage the exhibition, and Huxford identifies him as the permanent association's first president.[32][33]

His civic work extended beyond agriculture. He was one of the directors selected when the Brooks County Library Association organized on January 31, 1880.[34] He served as a Quitman Academy trustee and joined the 1893 conveyance of academy property to the city school board.[35] In 1889 he became a director of the Quitman Hotel Company and served with R. C. McIntosh and J. C. McDonald on the committee that planned the Hotel Marie.[36][37]

Morton also participated in commerce and local industry. He was a partner in W. Hudson & Company, a general merchandise firm formed in 1869, and was among the early directors of the Quitman Factory venture.[38] In March 1897, Quitman's largest recorded fire destroyed property belonging to him. Newspapers estimated his loss at $2,000 with $800 insurance. Two days later, his teams were clearing damaged machinery and he was preparing to rebuild in brick.[39][40]

In 1904 a local report identified Morton as a stockholder in Quitman's new long-staple cotton mill. He marked the start of operations by feeding the first cotton into its picker.[41] His public work and private investments repeatedly met in projects meant to expand Quitman's economy.

docs.title: Bank of Quitman
docs.text:
Morton's longest business association was with the Bank of Quitman. In 1878 he joined Clayton Groover and F. J. Spain in the private bank Denmark, Groover & Company. It was reorganized under a state charter as the Bank of Quitman in 1888, with Morton among the first directors.[42] When Clayton Groover and cashier E. A. Groover resigned in January 1895, Morton became president and Jeff Davis became cashier.[43]

He remained president until his death. A 1905 profile reported capital of $100,000, surplus and undivided profits exceeding $67,000, deposits above $389,000, and loans of $428,589.95. It credited $112,000 in dividends since organization.[44] A 1911 report gave capital of $100,000 and surplus of $140,000. It emphasized the bank's farm-loan policy and the directors' weekly Thursday meetings, held without salaries.[45]

That 1911 story called the 90-year-old Morton 96 and declared him the oldest bank president in the United States. October obituaries variously called him the oldest or second-oldest. No national banking census was found to prove either ranking.[17][18][46] The age error and disagreement make the national distinction unsafe. What is well supported is that he remained an active bank president into his nineties.

The Atlanta Constitution reported that he worked at the bank as late as the Thursday before his death.[17] A more colorful Valdosta account said he signed papers without eyeglasses, told his driver he probably would not return, and set aside his funeral expenses before going to bed. That account also misstated his age, so its personal details should be read as contemporary remembrance rather than verified verbatim fact.[46] On November 5, the directors elected longtime vice president S. S. Rountree to succeed him.[47]

docs.title: Railroad roles
docs.text:
Morton's direct place in the South Georgia Railroad was limited but real. He was one of the 26 men named in the February 1896 charter petition.[48] No checked source places him on the January subscription committee, the first board elected in March, or among the original officers. No stock ledger or subscription amount for him has been found. It is safest to call him a charter petitioner, not an operating officer or proven stockholder.

He later took a documented role in the connected West Coast Railway. Morton attended its December 1900 stockholders' meeting at Greenville, Florida, with Henry G. Turner, F. J. Spain, R. C. McIntosh, S. S. Rountree, and Florida participants. The planned line would run from Greenville toward Perry and the Gulf coast and work closely with the South Georgia Railway.[49] The report proves that Morton took part as a West Coast Railway stockholder. It does not enlarge his office in the South Georgia Railroad itself.

docs.title: Final years, death, and burial
docs.text:
The 1910 census found James and Sarah on Nankin Road, owning their home free of mortgage. The occupation field is poorly transcribed, but the employer and Bank of Quitman entries make the intended occupation clear.[6] A September 1911 newspaper described him as still active and living in the family's longstanding home.[10]

Morton died at his home just south of Quitman at about 11 p.m. on Monday, October 16, 1911. He was 90 years old and two months short of his 91st birthday. The Atlanta Constitution reported that he had been ill only a few days. His wife Sarah and daughter Lavinia Turner survived him.[17] This corrects older secondary summaries that placed his death in September or made him 91 or 92.

The funeral was held at the residence and conducted by the Rev. C. A. Campbell of First Presbyterian Church. Morton was buried in West End Cemetery in Quitman.[17] The Find a Grave index agrees on the birth date, death date, cemetery, wife, daughter, and father, but the contemporary funeral report is the stronger evidence for death and burial.[50] No civil death certificate, probate file, original cemetery register, or will was inspected.

Morton helped organize Brooks County and spent half a century in its public and private institutions. He experimented with crops, ran a bank, supported schools and civic projects, and joined railroad promotion. He also built much of his early wealth through enslaved labor and exercised authority within a slave society. Any honest account of his place in Brooks County has to hold those facts together.

docs.title: Open questions and research limits
docs.text:
• No original marriage register was found. August 1843 is supported by later family histories and broadly by the 1910 marriage-duration answer.
  • A targeted 1900 census index search did not identify James and Sarah Morton. Their documented presence in 1880 and 1910 leaves that one census-year residence unresolved.
  • The slave schedules do not name the people Morton enslaved. Deeds, probate records, labor contracts, and Freedmen's Bureau material were not located in the accessible online sweep.
  • The 1850 agricultural schedule was identified, but its image columns were not transcribed. The 1890 tax index's "20 employees" field was not verified against the original digest image.
  • No compiled military service record confirms service in the final Piscola Volunteers roster. The local-company retrospective and militia record support a narrower wartime role.
  • No evidence was found for the national rank claimed for Morton among elderly bank presidents.
  • No Bank of Quitman stock ledger or South Georgia Railroad subscription ledger was found.

docs.title: James W. Hitch: printed-name correction
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

There is no separate dossier for a Brooks County commissioner or South Georgia Railroad organizer named James W. Hitch. The strongest available evidence identifies the man in those records as John William Hitch of Morven.

Folks Huxford printed "James W. Hitch" in his county-commissioner roster and subscription-committee account. His own index assigns the commissioner page to John W. Hitch, and his errata changes the railroad director's first name from James to John. Contemporary reports call the commissioner and director "J. W. Hitch". The complete evidence, confidence rulings, biography, and sources are in the John William Hitch dossier.

Rev. James W. Hitch of Waycross was a real but younger namesake. He was not the Brooks County official or railroad man discussed here.

docs.title: James Wood Oglesby Jr.
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

James Wood Oglesby Jr. was a son of South Georgia Railway president James Wood Oglesby Sr. He served as an Army officer during World War I, became railway general manager by December 1919, and sat on the board by 1925. A 1939 obituary identified him as vice president and general manager.[1-7]

He must not be confused with his brother Wilbur Oglesby. Wilbur was acting superintendent and then superintendent before leaving for Army service in 1917. James Jr.'s documented management career began after Wilbur's 1918 death.[2][5]

docs.title: Family and identity
docs.text:
The 1908 Men of Mark in Georgia biography of James Sr. names four sons: James, Pope, Wilbur, and Hugh. It does not give James Jr.'s birth date. No birth certificate or original census image was inspected for this dossier, so his exact birth date remains unresolved.[1]

On February 16, 1918, James married Juanita Bullard Oglesby at Vancouver, Washington. She was the widow of his first cousin Zenas Wise Oglesby Jr. A contemporary report identifies the groom as James Wood Oglesby, an Army lieutenant, and the son of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Oglesby of Quitman. That relationship and wartime setting keep him distinct from both his father and Wilbur.[4]

Huxford says James and Juanita had one daughter, Martha Elizabeth, who married Norman Traverse Slater. That family detail is probable, but no birth, marriage, or census record for the daughter was inspected.[8]

docs.title: World War I
docs.text:
An August 1917 report said James had been accepted into the Emory Hospital unit and appointed first sergeant in its quartermaster department. It also said he was above draft age and had previously failed a physical examination when trying to enlist. An October report said he would go to France with the Emory unit.[2][3]

By February 1918 he was a lieutenant on the Pacific coast and was obtaining fir timber for Army airplanes. Huxford later said he volunteered on September 19, 1917, and served for the duration as a first lieutenant and captain. The contemporary reports verify his enlisted and commissioned service. The precise promotion chronology remains dependent on Huxford until the military file is inspected.[4][8]

docs.title: Railway management
docs.text:
The first located contemporary report of James Jr. as general manager dates to December 23, 1919. It lists James Sr. as president and James Jr. as general manager, with C. T. Tillman as secretary-treasurer, C. F. Cater as auditor, C. H. Myers as general freight and passenger agent, R. H. Rives as superintendent, and W. M. Leverette as trainmaster.[5]

That roster matters because it separates the jobs. James Jr. was general manager, while Rives held the superintendent title. Wilbur's earlier superintendent service does not belong to James Jr.

A February 1920 Atlanta Georgian report nevertheless called Capt. J. W. Oglesby Jr. the railway's superintendent while naming him to the Brooks County Salvation Army advisory committee.[9] The title conflicts with the detailed December 1919 roster. It may describe a short-lived change, overlapping duties, or loose newspaper usage. Without board minutes or an annual report, the conflict cannot be resolved and both reports should remain visible.

At the November 1925 annual meeting, stockholders elected James Jr. to a six-member board with James Sr., Roderick C. McIntosh, Samuel S. Rountree, Charles T. Tillman, and C. F. Cater. The meeting report named James Sr. president, McIntosh vice president, and Tillman secretary-treasurer. It did not name James Jr. first vice president.[6]

Huxford calls James Jr. general manager and first vice president. The 1939 obituary calls him vice president and general manager. Those sources support later vice-presidential service, but the exact date he received that title has not been found.[7][8]

docs.title: Other business and civic work
docs.text:
Huxford identifies James Jr. as president of the West Coast Lumber Company and the Steinhatchee Development Company. No corporate filing, annual report, or contemporary business notice was inspected to confirm the dates, so those offices remain probable.[8]

The 1939 Valdosta Daily Times obituary also said he had served as president of the Brooks County Chamber of Commerce. It is the only located source for that specific office. The obituary reported his death and described him as an Army officer during World War I, as well as vice president and general manager of the railway.[7]

docs.title: Death
docs.text: The Valdosta Daily Times published its obituary on November 20, 1939. The underlying death certificate, cemetery register, grave marker, and funeral report were not inspected. The obituary establishes that his death had occurred by publication, but this dossier does not assign an exact death date or burial place without a stronger record.[7]

docs.title: Evidence summary
docs.text: Claim Finding James Jr. and Wilbur were different sons of James Sr. Verified. Contemporary reports give them separate Army and railroad careers. James Jr. served during World War I. Verified. Contemporary reports follow him from the Emory unit to commissioned service. He was general manager by December 1919. Verified. A contemporary operating roster names him. A 1920 newspaper called him superintendent. Verified as printed, unresolved as a corporate title. It conflicts with the detailed 1919 roster. He was a director by November 1925. Verified. The annual-meeting report names him on the board. He later became vice president. Verified by 1939 obituary; strong probable earlier. The appointment date remains unknown. He was first vice president. Probable. Huxford supplies that precise title, but the 1925 meeting report does not. He led lumber and development companies. Probable. Huxford is the located source. He served as Brooks County Chamber of Commerce president. Verified as reported in his 1939 obituary. No chamber minutes were inspected.

docs.title: Research limits
docs.text: No original birth record, census image, military personnel file, railway board minutes, corporate filings for the lumber and development companies, chamber minutes, death certificate, funeral notice, cemetery register, or grave marker was inspected. His exact birth and death dates and burial place remain unresolved.

docs.title: James Wood Oglesby Sr.
docs.text: Back to the Railroad Organizers index

docs.title: Online research dossier
docs.text: Prepared August 19, 2026

docs.title: Identity verdict
docs.text:
The South Georgia Railway figure was James Wood Oglesby Sr., usually printed as J. W. Oglesby. He was born at Marietta, Georgia, on May 11, 1857, and died at his home in Quitman on November 8, 1930.[1][17][18] His long presidency is verified by contemporary corporate reporting. The 1908 Men of Mark sketches describe him as the largest individual shareholder and say that he and his older brother Zenas Wise Oglesby held family majority control. Those ownership claims are strong probable, not verified from a stock ledger, and they do not make James the railroad's sole owner or sole builder.[1][4][7]

This identification is verified. Contemporary records distinguish him from:

  • James Wood Oglesby Jr., his son, who entered railway management and was usually marked "Jr." in records involving both men;
  • Zenas Wise Oglesby, his brother, business partner, railway superintendent, and director;
  • J. J. or Joe J. Oglesby, another brother, who appears in a 1897 Barney injury report and a 1914 death notice.[1][3][5]

James Wood Oglesby Sr. Portrait and signature from Men of Mark in Georgia, volume 4, pp. 341-344, via Internet Archive.

docs.title: Main findings
docs.text:
• A Georgia marriage index resolves his marriage to Martha Elizabeth “Bessie” Cobb as May 14, 1878, not 1877.[2]
  • The railroad corporation elected James president in March 1896. Its board included nine men, including James, Zenas, J. J. Oglesby, and prominent Quitman investors.[4]
  • The first Heartpine-Quitman line most likely opened in March 1897. Later biographies that call it complete in 1896 are one year early.[6][20][21]
  • The often-repeated claim that the Greenville extension opened in 1898 is contradicted. Newspapers in March 1900 still described Quitman as the terminus and the Florida extension as planned work; specialist history dates the Greenville opening to October 1901, and the 1903 Georgia Railroad Commission report shows the route operating to Greenville.[8][9]
  • James's banking position is proved by federal records: the First National Bank of Quitman, national charter 7994, had $100,000 capital and listed J. W. Oglesby as president in both 1906 and 1910.[10][11]
  • Contemporary reporting confirms his major lumber, railway, resort, and public-service activity. Some biographical superlatives and unnumbered patent claims remain unverified.[1][12][13]
  • The Georgia Death Index and a November 9 Associated Press obituary resolve his death as November 8, 1930. Huxford and Find a Grave are wrong in giving November 18.[17][18][19]
  • His burial in Oak Hill Cemetery, Quitman, is verified by contemporary funeral coverage and a photographed marker. The marker gives only the years 1857-1930.[18][19]

docs.title: Origins and early work
docs.text:
The best detailed early-life source is the 1908 fourth volume of Men of Mark in Georgia. It identifies James as a son of cotton-gin manufacturer Thomas I. Oglesby, says the family traced its ancestry to Scotland, and gives James's Marietta birth date as May 11, 1857. The adjacent biography of Zenas names their mother as Elizabeth Johnson Wood. James was still a child when his father died, and the biography says he had common-school education before entering work.[1]

The source is contemporary, specific, and useful, but it is also promotional biography. Birth and parentage are therefore strong probable, not equivalent to an inspected birth, Bible, probate, or church record. Huxford's 1948 Brooks County history repeats much of the account and calls James the youngest of six sons, but Huxford is demonstrably wrong on both the marriage year and death date. Its uncorroborated family details must be used cautiously.[3]

Men of Mark says James and Zenas worked in cotton-gin manufacturing before concentrating on lumber. It credits James with two cotton-machinery inventions and says the brothers obtained patents. No safely attributable patent numbers were located in this search. The cotton-gin work is strong secondary evidence; the patent claim remains unverified.[1]

The move south followed timber. The brothers established a sawmill at Heartpine, near Adel, then expanded their operations into Brooks County and North Florida. The exact chronology in later biography is not fully reliable, but the resulting business network is well documented by 1890s newspapers and by James's 1908 company-office list.[1][7]

docs.title: Marriage and household
docs.text:
James married Martha Elizabeth Cobb, commonly called Bessie. The Georgia marriage index identifies J. W. Oglesby and M. E. Cobb in Bartow County, record 728186, with source image identifier 40660_303194-00401. An exact-date search returns the record for May 14, 1878, and the index agrees exactly with Men of Mark. Huxford gives May 14, 1877 and is contradicted.[1][2][3]

The couple had four sons:

  1. James Wood Oglesby Jr., later a railway general manager and first vice president;
  2. Robert Pope Oglesby;
  3. Wilbur Oglesby, railway superintendent before military service and his 1918 death in France;
  4. Hugh Oglesby.[1][3][14][18]

Huxford identifies nephew Henry Lumpkin as a foster son. That detail was not independently established from an original household or guardianship record.[3]

Original census images for 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930 were not inspected. This dossier therefore does not claim a verified census household chain, residence-by-residence chronology, or census-based wealth figures.

No located evidence proves that James personally enslaved anyone. He was eight years old when slavery legally ended. No original slave schedule, parental probate inventory, deed, or tax record was inspected that would prove or disprove enslavement by his parents. The answer for the parental household is unknown; wealth and location are not evidence.

docs.title: Lumber and related businesses
docs.text:
James's 1908 biography names him as:

  • president of the Oglesby Lumber and Manufacturing Company at Quitman;
  • president and a large shareholder of the Inter-State Lumber Company at Perry, Florida;
  • a director and large shareholder of the Perry Naval Stores Company;
  • the largest shareholder of the West Coast Lumber Company;
  • a director of Jacksonville naval-stores factor West-Flynn-Harris Company;
  • a director and shareholder of the Atlantic and Gulf Cotton Mills at Quitman;
  • an owner of farm land and Quitman real estate.[1]

The company offices are strong evidence because the account was published during his life and contemporary newspapers independently place him in lumber and railroad operations. Exact production capacities, stock percentages, acreage, and claims such as “one of the largest” remain biographical assertions unless supported by operating records.[1][7][13]

An 1898 mill-operators' meeting places J. W. Oglesby among Georgia lumbermen negotiating railroad loading rules. In March 1899 the Atlanta Constitution reported that an Oglesby mill at Barney was cutting railroad-car standards, that James had acquired timber east of Barney, and that a logging line was being built toward it. That ties his timber acquisition, mill production, and private tram construction directly to the South Georgia Railway corridor.[7]

An August 1899 newspaper said the brothers acquired roughly 200 acres along the railroad within Quitman and planned a railroad-car manufacturing plant expected to employ at least 500 people. The report proves a well-developed plan. No located source proves that the factory was completed, so it must not be listed as an operating Oglesby company.[7]

docs.title: Organization and first operation
docs.text:
On March 23, 1896, South Georgia Railroad stockholders accepted the charter, adopted bylaws, and elected a nine-member board. The directors included F. J. Spain, J. W. Hopson, J. W. Oglesby, J. G. McCall, Z. W. Oglesby, R. C. McIntosh, A. J. Rountree, J. J. Oglesby, and J. W. Hitch. The board elected James president, Hopson vice president, John Tillman treasurer, and Zenas superintendent.[4]

That evidence rules out the one-man-founder story. James was the president and central public figure, but the corporation had multiple directors, local investors, and an operating role for Zenas from the beginning.

Later technical histories date incorporation to March 6, 1896 and opening of the 27.5- or 28-mile Heartpine-Quitman line to March 1897.[20][21] Contemporary 1897 reports identify J. W. Oglesby as president, Barney as a station, and Oglesby mills at Heartpine and Barney. They also say James and H. G. Turner traveled to Washington to seek federal mail service for the railroad.[5][6]

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text:
Men of Mark calls James president and largest shareholder in the South Georgia and West Coast lines. The adjacent Zenas sketch says the brothers held equal interests in several ventures and together owned a majority of the railroad stock. The defensible conclusion is:

James was president and largest individual shareholder; James and Zenas together held Oglesby-family majority control.

Calling James the sole owner or saying the brothers were the only owners is unsupported.[1]

docs.title: Florida expansion and corporate form
docs.text:
The Greenville timeline needs correction. In March 1900 James publicly discussed a future extension from Quitman toward Greenville and Tampa. Reports still described the operating railroad as the 28 miles between Heartpine and Quitman. The line therefore was not already at Greenville in 1898, as Men of Mark and Huxford later claimed.[8]

RailGa dates the Greenville opening to October 1901. The Georgia Railroad Commission's 1903 report then lists a Heartpine-Greenville route, with Quitman at mile 29 and Greenville at mile 51, and gives 38.69 miles within Georgia.[9][20]

The later structure consisted of the Georgia company and Florida's West Coast Railway. South Georgia leased West Coast, and both used the operating style South Georgia & West Coast on equipment and in public usage. TapLines cautions that the combined style was not necessarily a separately incorporated company. The line reached Perry in 1904, and the northern endpoint moved from Heartpine to Adel. South Georgia absorbed West Coast in November 1923.[20][21]

Mileage varies by date and endpoint. Contemporary and later sources give totals from about 76 to 88 miles. Those figures should not be forced into one timeless number.[13][20][21]

docs.title: Hampton Springs
docs.text:
The railway and related-company structure met at Hampton Springs. TapLines says South Georgia bought Inter-State Lumber Company's five-mile Perry-Hampton Springs logging railroad on March 1, 1915 for $26,343. Because James was president and a large shareholder of Inter-State, the transaction moved a related lumber line into the railway system. The branch ended service in February 1929 and was removed in 1931.[1][21]

The Florida Railroad Commission's official 1929 route table lists the line through Perry to Hampton Springs and gives 44.41 Florida miles from the state line to the resort terminus.[23]

docs.title: Banking, resorts, and proposed ventures
docs.text:
Federal bank records verify a major office that family histories sometimes state without proof. The U.S. Comptroller of the Currency listed the First National Bank of Quitman, charter 7994, with $100,000 capital, J. W. Oglesby as president, and H. L. Young as cashier in 1906. The 1910 report still lists Oglesby and Young in those positions.[10][11]

James also bought and improved White Sulphur Springs near Gainesville, Georgia. A long 1907 newspaper feature describes hotel, cottages, baths, roads, landscaping, recreation, and water-system improvements under his ownership. Its tone is promotional, but ownership and the broad improvement campaign agree with later business reporting and his obituaries.[12][13][18]

At Hampton Springs, the Oglesby interests connected resort development to rail access. The evidence establishes common ownership, a hotel and resort operation, and a railway branch. It does not prove that resort profits financed railway construction.[1][21]

James and James Jr. also joined a 1907 charter petition for the proposed Quitman, Valdosta and Thomasville Electric Railway and Power Company. The petition proves participation in the proposal, not completion of a fifty-mile electric system.[7]

docs.title: Management and succession
docs.text:
James remained president until death. Zenas served as superintendent and director until his death in January 1915. The board then appointed James's son Wilbur superintendent; a contemporary report said Wilbur had already been acting superintendent for more than a year.[7]

After Wilbur entered military service and died in France in 1918, James Jr. became general manager. A 1919 report lists James Sr. as president and James Jr. as general manager. The 1925 annual meeting again elected James Sr. president and James Jr. a director.[7][13]

In 1926 James announced a tentative arrangement under which the Seaboard Air Line might lease and later purchase the South Georgia, subject to Interstate Commerce Commission approval. The Quitman general offices denied that a sale had already occurred. No transfer followed. Describing Seaboard as having acquired the line in 1926 is false.[7]

Later specialist histories say Brooks-Scanlon acquired the South Georgia and Live Oak, Perry & Gulf operations in 1946, Southern Railway bought them in 1954, and the South Georgia merged into the Live Oak, Perry & South Georgia Railway in 1971. Those dates are useful succession context, but the original sale and merger instruments were not inspected in this project.[20][21][24]

docs.title: War work and public activity
docs.text:
An October 1917 report says three of the Oglesbys' four sons were in military service, James served on the executive committee of the Georgia State Council of Defense, and Martha was active in Red Cross work. Wilbur was identified as railway superintendent and James Jr. with the Emory Hospital unit.[14]

In June 1918 James was elected vice chairman of an interstate association advocating a St. Marys-to-St. Marks canal.[15] A September 1918 report listed him among four Brooks County delegates to a Democratic state gathering. These records prove civic and party participation, but no located article shows him seeking elective office.[7]

James also used newspapers to argue public policy. In 1909 he contended that hostile regulation discouraged private railroad investment. In 1925 he urged reduced cotton acreage and criticized federal crop estimates, arguing that increased production harmed growers.[16] These are evidence of his economic views, not proof that his prescriptions were correct.[7]

Huxford says Governor Hugh M. Dorsey commissioned him lieutenant-colonel and aide-de-camp during World War I. No commission was located online, so the title remains secondary-source only.[3]

No contemporary source located in the documented search proves a particular church membership. Men of Mark says he leaned Methodist but was not a member in 1908. His 1930 funeral involved Baptist, Presbyterian, and Methodist ministers. That ecumenical service does not establish denomination.[1][19]

docs.title: Wilbur memorial gift
docs.text: James made a substantial gift to Brenau College in memory of Wilbur. Contemporary 1930 obituaries give $10,000. Huxford gives $20,000. The gift is verified, but the amount is unresolved until Brenau trustee, building, or accounting records are checked.[3][18]

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
James died at his Quitman home on Saturday night, November 8, 1930, after several weeks' illness. The Georgia Death Index identifies James W. Oglesby in Brooks County, record 387197, and exact-date testing isolates November 8. Newspapers dated November 9 carried the same Associated Press report from Quitman announcing the death, surviving widow, sons James Jr., Pope, and Hugh, and Monday burial at Oak Hill Cemetery.[17][18]

The Valdosta Daily Times funeral report of November 11 describes large regional attendance. Baptist minister C. W. Henderson conducted the service with Presbyterian minister J. D. Gillespie and Methodist minister W. F. Smith; burial followed in Oak Hill.[19]

The grave photograph reads "J. W. OGLESBY / 1857-1930" and names "MARTHA ELIZABETH COBB / WIFE OF / J. W. OGLESBY / 1860-1939". It does not show exact dates.[22]

The later November 18 date in Huxford and Find a Grave is contradicted by the state death index and contemporaneous report. November 8 should control.[3][17][18][22]

docs.title: Claims audit
docs.text: Claim Verdict James Wood Oglesby was South Georgia Railway president. Verified. Contemporary corporate reports from 1896 through 1925 and his 1930 obituary agree. James alone founded, built, or owned the railway. Overstated. He was president and largest individual shareholder; James and Zenas held family majority control; a multi-member board governed the company. The line was completed in 1896. Probably one year early. 1896 was the organization/construction year; March 1897 is the best opening date. The Greenville extension opened in 1898. Contradicted. It was still proposed in March 1900; October 1901 is the best opening date. South Georgia & West Coast was always one incorporated company. Misleading. The name described joint operation during South Georgia's lease of West Coast. James owned Inter-State Lumber outright. Not proved. He was president and a large shareholder. The planned 1899 railroad-car plant employed 500 people. Not proved. The source describes a proposal and forecast, not a completed factory. James held cotton-machinery patents. Unverified. Contemporary biography makes the claim but supplies no patent numbers. Seaboard acquired the South Georgia in 1926. False. The announced transaction was tentative and dependent on ICC approval; it was not completed. James gave Brenau $10,000 or $20,000. Gift verified; amount unresolved. Contemporary obituaries say $10,000, Huxford says $20,000. James died November 18, 1930. False. The state index and next-day report establish November 8. James was Methodist. Unresolved. In 1908 he leaned Methodist but was not a member; the funeral used ministers from three denominations. James personally enslaved people. No evidence located. He was a child before emancipation. Parental enslavement remains unknown because original slaveholding records were not inspected.

docs.title: What remains unresolved
docs.text:
• An original birth, family Bible, baptismal, or parental probate record for the May 11, 1857 birth and parentage;
  • the original Bartow County marriage image behind index record 728186;
  • original census images and a verified household chain from 1860 through 1930;
  • original stock ledgers and exact ownership percentages for the railway and related companies;
  • patent numbers, if any, for machinery attributed to James or Zenas;
  • original charter, lease, merger, and sale instruments for the complete corporate sequence;
  • Brenau records resolving whether the Wilbur memorial gift was $10,000 or $20,000;
  • a documented church membership;
  • original parental slave schedule, probate, deed, or tax evidence;
  • a complete personal litigation history. No personal case was found in the documented newspaper search, but that is not proof none existed.

docs.title: Research coverage
docs.text:
The project searched stored Barney/Oglesby research first, then online newspapers, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Internet Archive books, Georgia and Florida railroad-commission reports, U.S. Comptroller of the Currency reports, Ancestry indexes, FamilySearch access routes, Find a Grave and cemetery images, RailGa, TapLines, HawkinsRails, and bounded general-web queries. Names, initials, relatives, companies, railroad titles, towns, resorts, litigation terms, civic roles, and obituary variants were used.

The dossier is based on records available in the accessible online collections and does not claim an exhaustive search of undigitized archives. Original census and marriage images were not inspected.

docs.title: John Goldwire McCall
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

John Goldwire McCall (January 18, 1836-December 3, 1921) was a lawyer, judge, farmer, public official, educator, Baptist lay leader, businessman, and railroad promoter in Quitman, Georgia. He served as Brooks County ordinary, mayor of Quitman, judge of the City Court of Quitman, and a Brooks County member of the Georgia House. He was also a founding director of the South Georgia Railroad and remained on its board after the road opened.[1-8]

John Goldwire McCall. Portrait and signature from Men of Mark in Georgia, volume 5, published in 1908.

docs.title: Name and identity
docs.text:
The full name is secure. Contemporary biographies, his death notice, and his marker identify him as John Goldwire McCall or John G. McCall. The titles Captain, Judge, and Doctor all appear in the record. Captain referred to his Confederate rank, Judge to his civil offices, and Doctor to Mercer's honorary LL.D. He was not a physician.[1-5]

He must be kept separate from two close relatives:

  • Dr. James H. McCall, his brother, was a physician, druggist, banker, and South Georgia Railroad charter petitioner.
  • John Francis McCall, his son, was also a lawyer and appears in later Quitman records as John F. McCall.[1][3][6]

This distinction matters most in the railroad record. Contemporary reports elected J. G. McCall to the first board, while Huxford's charter-petitioner list names James H. McCall. The brothers did not hold the same founding role.[6-8]

docs.title: Family and early years
docs.text:
McCall was born in Screven County on January 18, 1836, the oldest child of Francis Stephen McCall and Ann Dopson McCall. The family moved through Telfair County before settling in 1845 about eight miles south of the future Quitman. The area was then part of Lowndes County; Brooks County was created in 1858.[1][3][4]

Francis McCall was a planter who also operated a grist mill and blacksmith shop. Huxford says the household belonged to Concord Baptist Church and names thirteen children. Those details describe the parental farm. No slave schedule, deed, or probate record inspected for this dossier establishes whether John personally enslaved anyone in his own right.[3]

John married Rosa Elizabeth Bobo of Glenville, Alabama, in January 1867. Two lifetime biographies disagree by one day: one gives January 30 and the other January 31. Later family history calls her Rosella Elizabeth. She was a daughter of Dr. Virgil Bobo and Sarah Hanson Black Bobo.[1][2][3]

The family record and the 1921 death report identify five surviving children:

  • Rosa Lena, also printed Rosa Lee or Rosalena, who married John O. Lewis;
  • Rachel Black, who married Charles F. Cater;
  • Nonnie Bobo McCall, who did not marry;
  • John Francis McCall, whose later marriages are recorded in the family history; and
  • Edna Floride McCall, who married Albert L. Tidwell.[1-4]

One 1908 biography says six children had been born and five were living. No inspected source names the child who died, so the complete six-child birth list remains unresolved.[2]

docs.title: Union University and the Mercer degree
docs.text:
McCall studied at Union University in Murfreesboro, Tennessee. University catalogues list J. G. McCall, A.M., first as an adjunct professor of languages and mathematics and then as professor of Greek and Hebrew. A lifetime biography says he graduated in 1858, pursued additional work in French, German, and Syriac, and received the A.M. degree. These records establish his education and faculty work before the Civil War.[1][9-11]

Huxford says he graduated with highest honors and mastered seven languages. A separate 1908 biography says he graduated with second honor. The catalogues do not settle the class rank, so neither claim should be preferred as fact. The sources do agree that he received advanced classical and language training and taught at Union before leaving for military service.[2][3][9-11]

Mercer University conferred an honorary LL.D. on McCall. An 1895 biography dates the degree to 1894, and an 1899 Baptist Convention roster already printed his name with the degree. The honorific Doctor in later sources refers to this degree.[1][12]

docs.title: Confederate service
docs.text:
McCall joined Company K, 50th Georgia Infantry, as first lieutenant on March 4, 1862. Huxford's roster records a severe facial wound at Funkstown, Maryland, on July 10, 1863, his election as captain on July 31, and transfer to the Invalid Corps on December 2, 1864.[3]

The lifetime accounts say he fought in the Virginia and Maryland campaigns, including Second Manassas, Fredericksburg, Antietam or Sharpsburg, and Gettysburg. During the retreat after Gettysburg he commanded infantry and artillery guarding a bridge over Antietam Creek. A bullet shattered his lower jaw. He survived but lost part of the bone and later wore a metal plate.[1-3]

Huxford adds that Dr. George Todd, Mary Todd Lincoln's brother, operated on him. That detail was not confirmed in a wartime medical record. The company, ranks, dates, wound, and later disability are well supported; the surgeon's identity remains a family-history claim.[3]

docs.title: Law and the courts
docs.text:
After returning home disabled, McCall became Brooks County ordinary. The county roster dates his commission to February 16, 1864, and his service through 1868. He studied law during that term. A May 1867 report concerning a professional visit to Berrien County proves that he was practicing by then.[3][13]

He remained at the Quitman bar for the rest of his working life. A June 1866 memorial for four Brooks County lawyers killed in the war bears his name with Henry G. Turner, William A. Lane, William B. Bennet, James H. Hunter, and Carey W. Styles. Much later, William H. Long worked in his office before joining S. S. Bennet.[3]

Governor Hoke Smith appointed McCall judge of the City Court of Quitman in January 1908 after William B. Bennet resigned. He received a full four-year appointment that July and served through 1912. A 1911 report shows him sitting by designation in Douglas when the local judge was disqualified.[14-16]

Huxford's family sketch also calls him a County Court judge, but its office roster lists William B. Bennet as County Court judge throughout the relevant period and lists McCall only for the City Court. No primary record found for this dossier supports a County Court term. That part of the family sketch is contradicted.[3]

docs.title: Elections and public office
docs.text:
McCall's first countywide office began during the war. After four years as ordinary, he lost the April 1868 Reconstruction election to James L. Beaty, 667 to 366. The result ended his term but not his public life.[3]

He was mayor of Quitman in 1889, 1890, and 1891. A January 1890 report says he was elected without opposition while voters approved the new graded-school system. He also ran for the state Senate in 1886 but Brooks County chose Thomas Livingston.[3][17-18]

McCall represented Brooks County in the Georgia House during the 1919-20 term. He resigned in April 1920 because of age and poor health, and Burton L. Weston succeeded him. This was House service, not a state Senate term.[19-22]

McCall was active in Democratic politics and temperance work. Huxford says he drafted an unsuccessful local dispensary bill after Brooks County supported the 1896 Bush temperance proposal. The bill did not become law.[3]

docs.title: Schools and educational government
docs.text:
McCall's work in public education began long before the graded-school campaign. He served as a Quitman Academy trustee in the 1870s. When Brooks County organized its Board of Education in 1872, the board elected him president. Huxford's roster dates that presidency from 1872 through 1880.[3]

In January 1890 he won the mayoralty on the same ballot that approved Quitman's public graded-school system. Voters then elected him to the first city Board of Education, and the board chose him as president. He was reelected in 1892 and 1894. These records show that he helped move Quitman from a mix of academy and private-school arrangements into a municipal system.[3][17][23]

Huxford also calls him a co-founder and trustee of Norman Junior College. That role is plausible and fits his wider educational work, but no dated founding record inspected here establishes his exact part.[3]

docs.title: Baptist and Mercer work
docs.text:
McCall and his wife belonged to Quitman Baptist Church. He served as church clerk and Sunday school superintendent and taught a Bible class for at least fifty years. A 1914 article reported a church observance of his fiftieth year as a teacher. Huxford later gave the tenure as more than sixty years, but the 1921 obituary again said fifty. The safe conclusion is that the teaching began during or soon after the Civil War and continued for at least half a century.[3][24-25]

He served as moderator of the Mercer Baptist Association and as a vice president of the Georgia Baptist Convention. The convention elected him to the latter office in 1899 and also placed him on a committee dealing with mob violence and criminal-law reform.[3][12][26]

His longest institutional connection was with Mercer University. Contemporary reporting identifies him as a trustee by the 1890s and as president of the board during the first decade of the twentieth century. He took part in presidential searches and board reorganization, resigned after thirty-four years of service in 1915, and later returned to the board. At his death, Mercer reported that he had served ten years as board president. The university also held a $1,000 John G. McCall scholarship for students.[25][27-30]

docs.title: Agriculture, business, and community projects
docs.text:
McCall practiced law but also farmed and remained active in agricultural organizations. He signed the March 1869 call to organize the Brooks County Agricultural Society and served as secretary pro tem at its second meeting. Later reports place him in state agricultural meetings, and Huxford calls him a vice president of the State Agricultural Society.[3][31]

The Quitman Hotel Company elected him its first president in 1889. The company built the Hotel Marie at Screven and Washington streets. He also joined the first board of Merchants & Farmers Bank in 1891, became vice president in 1893, and was president in 1895. His brother Dr. James H. McCall, not John, was the bank's first president.[3][32-33]

In 1899 McCall chaired the campaign to reopen and enlarge Quitman's cotton mill. Huxford records his initial $1,000 subscription and says the listed subscriptions were later raised by 25 percent. The family sketch calls him a mill director, though no corporate minute book was found to fix his term.[3]

His public record included views that should not be softened by later praise. A 1908 biography quoted him advocating race legislation that recognized what he called Anglo-Saxon superiority. That was an explicit white-supremacist position. The same sketch presented him as a firm supporter of religious education and constitutional government. Both positions belong to the record.[2]

docs.title: Railroad promotion
docs.text:
McCall promoted rail connections well before the South Georgia Railroad was organized. In February 1885 he helped lead a Brooks County convention seeking a branch from Quitman to Monticello, Florida. In January 1886 he chaired the Quitman delegation that met Savannah, Florida and Western Railway officials about the proposal. The reports document negotiation and advocacy, not construction of the line.[34-36]

South Georgia Railroad stockholders met on March 23, 1896, accepted the charter, adopted bylaws, and elected J. G. McCall to the first nine-member board. He was a director, not one of the first executive officers. The old board, including McCall, was reelected in 1899. A 1911 annual-meeting report probably records another reelection, though the printed initials are shortened.[6-8][37-38]

John was not the documented charter petitioner. Huxford's petitioner list names his brother James H. McCall, then separately names John on the first board. Without the missing original petition, the two roles should not be exchanged.[3][6-8]

In February 1899 McCall joined Frank J. Spain and Joseph Mabbett on a committee investigating a possible railroad southward from Quitman. In 1907 he also joined the petition for the proposed Quitman, Valdosta and Thomasville Electric Railway and Power Company. Neither record proves that the proposed extension or electric line was built.[39-43]

No stock ledger, share certificate, subscription amount, resignation, or complete board minute book was found for his South Georgia Railway service. The supported chronology is founding director in 1896, verified director again in 1899, and strong probable board service in 1911.[6-8][37-38]

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
McCall attended church on Friday, December 2, 1921, and appeared to be in his usual health. He was found dead in bed the next morning when he did not answer for breakfast. The local dispatch and his marker establish December 3 as the date of death. He was eighty-five.[4-5][25]

The funeral took place at Quitman Baptist Church on December 4. The surviving children named in the death report match the family history. His marker in West End Cemetery reads "Capt. John G. McCall LL.D. / Jan. 18, 1836 - Dec. 3, 1921".[3-5]

The Macon Telegraph said he died late Friday night, which points to December 2, while the local dispatch says he was found dead on the morning of December 3 and his marker uses December 3. The local report and marker control. One line in the Macon notice also printed John J. McCall, but the Quitman setting, Mercer service, degree, Bible class, son, and scholarship make clear that it concerned John G. McCall.[4-5][25]

docs.title: Record conflicts and limits
docs.text:
• Marriage date: January 30 or January 31, 1867. The two lifetime biographies differ by one day.
  • Wife's name: contemporary accounts favor Rosa Elizabeth; Huxford uses Rosella Elizabeth.
  • Children: five surviving children are verified; a 1908 biography says six were born, but the deceased child is unnamed.
  • Union class standing: one source says highest honors, another second honor. The catalogues do not settle the point.
  • Military surgery: the service and wound are secure; Dr. George Todd's role remains a later family-history claim.
  • Court service: City Court judge is verified. The County Court claim is contradicted by Huxford's own roster.
  • Mercer chronology: long trusteeship and ten years as board president are secure, but the exact dates of every board term remain incomplete.
  • Railroad: founding and later board service are documented; stock ownership, subscription amount, final term, and an executive office are not.
  • Property: the evidence shows farming and a 240-acre tract sold near Quitman, but no complete deed or probate chain was assembled.

docs.title: Confidence summary
docs.text: Question Finding Confidence Identity John Goldwire McCall of Quitman Verified Birth and death January 18, 1836-December 3, 1921 Verified Parents Francis Stephen McCall and Ann Dopson Verified from two lifetime or family accounts Marriage Rosa Elizabeth Bobo, January 1867 Verified broadly; exact day disputed Children Five named surviving children; one additional deceased child reported Survivors verified; complete birth list unresolved Education Union A.M. and prewar faculty service Verified; class rank disputed Military service Company K, 50th Georgia; first lieutenant, captain, facial wound, Invalid Corps Verified Legal career Quitman lawyer by 1867; City Court judge, 1908-1912 Verified County Court judgeship Later family-sketch claim Contradicted by the office roster Public office Ordinary, mayor, and Georgia House member Verified School work County and city education-board president Verified Baptist and Mercer work Bible teacher, denominational officer, Mercer trustee and board president Verified broadly Business Hotel Company president, bank director and officer, cotton-mill promoter Strong probable to verified by dated local records Railroad Founding director in 1896 and director in 1899 Verified; 1911 reelection strong probable Burial West End Cemetery, Quitman Verified by photographed marker and county history

docs.title: Research note
docs.text: This dossier was completed August 21, 2026. Research covered the existing South Georgia Railroad collection, Huxford's county history and office rosters, Union University catalogues, two lifetime biographies, Georgia's official legislative register, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Newspapers.com, Find a Grave and the photographed marker, Mercer and Baptist reporting, and prior McCall family research. The source review covered 1855 through 1921 and kept the lawyer and railroad director separate from his physician brother and lawyer son. Conflicts that change a historical claim are stated above rather than silently resolved.

docs.title: John Tillman
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

John Tillman (April 4, 1845 to August 6, 1899) was a Quitman merchant, hardware and farm-supply dealer, planter, county commissioner, Baptist lay leader, Confederate veteran, and the first treasurer of the South Georgia Railroad. He was not among the charter petitioners or first directors identified in the surviving evidence. The first board elected him treasurer on March 23, 1896, and by April 1899 he was serving as secretary and treasurer.[1-2][16-19]

The name requires care. Judge Joseph Tillman, John’s sons Charles Thomas and Joseph Bruce Tillman, and several earlier or later men named John Tillman had separate careers. The railroad treasurer is securely identified because his contemporary obituary joins the railroad office, Quitman hardware business, Baptist membership, and former county chairmanship in one account.[14-15]

docs.title: Family and early years
docs.text:
Tillman’s marker gives April 4, 1845 as his birth date. Folks Huxford places his birth in Tattnall County and identifies his parents as Joseph Isaiah Tillman and Casandra C. Everett Tillman. John was reportedly one month old when his father died. His mother later moved the family to Thomas County, where her brother Josiah Everett lived.[1-2]

Huxford names John’s full siblings as Eliza Everett, Casandra, and Joseph Isaiah Tillman, with James M. and Henry Tillman as paternal half-brothers. This is a coherent compiled family account, but no original birth, probate, or census image inspected for this dossier independently proves the whole household.[1]

Huxford says John entered Mercer University at Penfield at age fifteen and belonged to the Phi Delta Literary Society. The Civil War interrupted his studies, and he did not return after the war. No Mercer matriculation register, contemporary catalog entry, or society roll naming him was located, so the Mercer account remains strong probable rather than verified.[1]

No original 1860, 1870, or 1880 census image was located for this dossier. Household composition, census occupation wording, property values, and residence on each enumeration date therefore remain unverified by census.

docs.title: Confederate service
docs.text:
The safest military identification is John Tillman of Quitman in the Piscola Volunteers. Huxford’s company roster places that unit as Company I, 26th Georgia Infantry. It records Tillman’s enlistment on July 23, 1861 and reenlistment on May 1, 1862.[1]

Huxford’s separate family sketch gives August 2, 1861 as the enlistment date and says Tillman served without a wound, was paroled in April 1865, and then held the rank of second sergeant. Those details were not independently closed with the compiled service file, parole, or pension packet. The roster and biography agree that he served with the Piscola Volunteers, but they conflict on the enlistment date and only the later sketch supplies his ending rank.[1]

His Find a Grave biography labels the unit Company C, 29th Georgia Cavalry. That conflicts with Huxford’s roster and should not be treated as settled without the original military records. Confederate service with the Piscola Volunteers is strong probable. The exact regiment throughout the war, the August date, second-sergeant rank, and April 1865 parole remain unresolved at the original-record level.[1-2]

docs.title: Marriages and children
docs.text:
Tillman first married Mary Lawson Wyche. Huxford gives December 23, 1868 as the wedding date and identifies her parents as John S. and Hannah MacIntyre Wyche of Cherry Lake, Florida. Mary’s memorial links John as her husband, gives 1844 to 1871, and includes a marker photograph, but no original marriage image was found.[1][3]

An original Brooks County bond dated July 5, 1873 records Tillman as the court-appointed trustee for Mary Lawson Tillman and her children under a deed from John S. Wyche. It proves that fiduciary appointment, not that Tillman practiced law.[26]

Their first son, John Tillman Jr., was born November 22, 1869 and died July 28, 1870. Charles Thomas Tillman was born June 5, 1871. Mary died on November 2, 1871, shortly after Charles’s birth. The relationships and dates are strong probable from the compiled history and cemetery network.[1][3]

An original Thomas County marriage-book image verifies Tillman’s second marriage. The license for John Tillman and C. M. Gaulden was issued November 28, 1873. Minister C. D. Campbell married them on November 29, and the record was entered February 27, 1874. The record proves Thomas County, not specifically Thomasville.[4]

Huxford identifies the bride as Charlie Gaulden, daughter of Rev. Charles S. Gaulden and Charlotte LeSueur Gaulden. Her memorial uses Charlie Mary Gaulden Tillman and gives April 7, 1847 to March 2, 1925.[1][5]

John and Charlie’s children were:

  • Ela Groover Tillman, who married James L. Key of Atlanta;
  • Joseph Bruce Tillman, who married Carrie Denmark; and
  • Marie Tillman, who married Herbert Rhodes.[1]

Charles Thomas and Joseph Bruce later became prominent in Quitman business. Charles also held later railroad offices. Those careers belong to the sons and should not be assigned to John.[1][25]

docs.title: Merchant and hardware dealer
docs.text:
In 1866 Tillman joined J. B. Creech and his brother-in-law M. J. Culpepper in Culpepper, Creech & Company, general merchants. Huxford calls him the managing partner. The partnership dissolved January 1, 1871, and Tillman continued the business under his own name.[1]

Contemporary advertising shows the range of that business. A January 1873 advertisement offered plows, steel farm tools, cotton seed, cotton planters, and guano distributors. In 1877 his store advertised dry goods, boots, shoes, hats, hardware, crockery, plows, and farming implements.[7-8]

Huxford says Tillman sold the non-hardware stock to W. T. Gaulden & Company in March 1883. He then concentrated on hardware, building supplies, and farm equipment. Huxford’s 1889 and 1897 business lists identify his hardware store, and a February 1890 report says he was extending the building and installing a glass and iron front.[1][10]

The 1885 bird’s-eye map of Quitman lists "John Tillman, Hardware" in its business references. The map is useful evidence of the store’s presence, though it is not a business ledger or property survey.[9]

An 1896 national feature described Tillman as one of three wealthy Quitman agricultural-implement dealers. It said he owned a plantation and quoted him on the importance of a practical cotton-picking machine. The article proves plantation ownership and the implement trade, but gives no acreage, legal description, crop schedule, or labor record.[12]

The November 1897 Quitman fire threatened Tillman’s building, but the contemporary reports place it among the structures saved. His August 1899 obituary called his operation the largest hardware business in Quitman. That was the newspaper’s contemporary assessment, not an audited market ranking.[13-15]

After John’s death, Joseph Bruce bought the other heirs’ interests and continued the hardware company. Charles Thomas developed a separate record in railroads, lumber, banking, education, and civic work. A 1910 profile discussed both sons and the old family business, but it does not prove that John held their later offices.[1][25]

docs.title: Manufacturing, hotel, agriculture, and local development
docs.text:
Tillman had corporate treasury experience before the railroad. Huxford identifies him as treasurer of the Brooks County Manufacturing Association when it reorganized Quitman’s cotton factory in 1875. The association and the later South Georgia Railroad were separate companies.[1]

He was one of the charter members of the Quitman Hotel Company in May 1889. The company developed the Hotel Marie. Tillman was not listed among its first directors or executive officers, so charter membership should not be expanded into management.[1]

In February 1890 he joined Clayton Groover and R. C. McIntosh on a committee raising Quitman’s requested $15,000 subscription for a cotton compress. The report does not state Tillman’s personal investment or prove that the project became affiliated with the railroad.[11]

The surviving record supports a merchant-planter with interests in manufacturing and community development. It does not supply a complete deed chain, farm acreage, probate inventory, bank account, or personal investment schedule. No evidence found identifies him as a bank officer or director.[1][12]

docs.title: Town and county service
docs.text:
Huxford’s municipal tables place Tillman among Quitman’s town commissioners in 1870, councilmen in 1875 and 1876, and councilmen again in 1882. The 1876 result is independently visible in the local newspaper’s election report. The complete minute books were not inspected, so the year-by-year municipal record is strong probable.[1][6]

The November 1880 grand jury recommended Tillman for the proposed Brooks County Board of Commissioners. The General Assembly created the board in 1881 and named him to it. He served from 1881 through 1894.[1]

Tillman became chairman in 1887 after the service of James O. Morton and Clayton R. Denmark. Huxford says he held the chair until resigning in 1894 and spent considerable time supervising the courthouse-remodeling contract. The 1899 obituary independently remembers him as a former chairman, but no complete set of board minutes was reviewed for this dossier.[1][14-15]

No evidence found places Tillman in the Georgia House, Georgia Senate, a state constitutional convention, or statewide office. Judge Joseph Tillman and other public figures of the same surname must not be merged into his record.

docs.title: Baptist and civic work
docs.text:
Tillman was a Quitman Baptist deacon by September 1878, when he was assigned to open a Mercer Baptist Association discussion about churches meeting their obligations to pastors. In October 1886 he was named among Quitman’s delegates to the association.[20-21]

Huxford says he served for years as senior deacon and Sunday school superintendent and sometimes represented the association at the Georgia Baptist Convention and the state convention at the Southern Baptist Convention. The deacon and superintendent claims fit the contemporary record. The higher-convention service was not closed with dated delegate lists.[1]

His civic activity ranged beyond business and officeholding. In 1873 he joined a local committee supporting an inland waterway proposal. After a Black school was burned in 1885, Tillman spoke at a biracial public meeting that condemned the attack and supported a plan for a replacement school on ten acres within Quitman. The report does not say he donated the land or signed the later petition. His home also hosted a literary club meeting in April 1886.[22-24]

These episodes establish participation in local civic life. They do not support a claim that Tillman held a school-board office, personally funded the school, or led the waterway project.

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
John Tillman was not one of the twenty-six charter petitioners named by Huxford. He also was not among the nine first directors named in two contemporary reports. His name appears separately in the officer slate elected by those directors.[1][16-17]

South Georgia Railroad stockholders met at Quitman City Hall on March 23, 1896, accepted the charter, adopted bylaws, and elected the board. The directors then chose James W. Oglesby as president, John W. Hopson as vice president, John Tillman as treasurer, and Zenas W. Oglesby as superintendent. The Savannah and Atlanta reports independently verify Tillman as the first treasurer.[16-17]

In April 1899 the directors reelected the existing officers. The report calls Tillman secretary and treasurer, showing that his title had expanded by then. Huxford says he remained treasurer until his death and had become a stockholder when the company was organized.[1][18]

The stockholder claim is strong probable, not verified. No stock certificate, subscription entry, stock ledger, payment record, share count, or voting percentage was found. Election as treasurer does not by itself prove ownership.[1]

Tillman died on Sunday, August 6, 1899. Four days later the directors held a called meeting and appointed his eldest surviving son, Charles Thomas Tillman, as treasurer. This verifies that John still held the office at death. Continuous service between the dated elections is strong probable because no complete annual minute series was located.[14-15][19]

No evidence found names John Tillman as a South Georgia Railroad director, president, vice president, superintendent, general manager, or charter petitioner. Those are distinct roles, several of which later belonged to his son Charles or to other organizers.[1][16-19]

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
Tillman died in Quitman on August 6, 1899 after an illness of several months. The newspaper reported dropsy, a historical term for fluid accumulation, as the cause. It should not be converted into a modern diagnosis without medical records.[14-15]

The obituary called him fifty-three, but his marker dates make him fifty-four. The date-specific marker and Huxford agree, so the obituary’s age is contradicted.[1-2][14-15]

The funeral was held at Quitman Baptist Church, with Rev. W. B. Bennet and Rev. R. D. Harris of Thomasville officiating. The local dispatch said Quitman’s business houses closed during the services. Tillman was buried in West End Cemetery, where his photographed marker reads "BORN APRIL 4, 1845" and "DIED AUGUST 6, 1899".[2][14-15]

docs.title: Record conflicts and limits
docs.text:
• Birth and death: the marker and Huxford agree on April 4, 1845 and August 6, 1899. The obituary’s age fifty-three conflicts with those dates.
  • Census: no original 1860, 1870, or 1880 image was located. Household and property details are not census-verified.
  • Mercer: attendance and Phi Delta membership come from Huxford. No contemporary Mercer record naming him was located.
  • Military: Piscola Volunteers service is well supported. Huxford’s roster and family sketch conflict on the enlistment date, while the memorial gives a different regiment. Original service and pension files remain unchecked.
  • First marriage: Mary Lawson Wyche and the family are well supported by Huxford and linked memorials, but the exact marriage date lacks an inspected original record.
  • Second marriage: C. M. Gaulden, Thomas County, November 29, 1873 is verified by the original marriage-book image.
  • Business: the merchant, hardware, farm-supply, and plantation record is supported. No complete ownership, acreage, employee, or probate account was assembled.
  • Public office: town and county roles are supported. No state legislative, judicial, or banking office was found.
  • Railroad: first treasurer, 1899 secretary-treasurer, and service at death are verified. Stockholding is strong probable. No director, president, or charter-petitioner role is supported.
