docs.title: Mitchell Brice
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Mitchell Brice was born in Georgia on December 14, 1840, according to the date preserved by the Brice family history and his cemetery memorial. He died in Quitman on March 7, 1903. Census records place him at Tallokas from childhood through the end of his life. By the 1890s he had interests in farming, timber, turpentine, a sawmill, a store, racehorses, and land. He also served as a county commissioner, helped raise subscriptions for the South Georgia Railroad, and later sat on its board.[1][2][3]

The exact birth date is not established by a civil record. The 1850 census, which gives his age as nine, and the 1900 census, which gives December 1840 as his birth month, support the year and month. The day comes from later sources.[1][4][5]

docs.title: Parents and childhood at Tallokas
docs.text:
The 1850 census places nine-year-old Mitchell in Thomas County with Francis and Elisabeth Brice and six other Brice children. The 1860 census follows the family into newly created Brooks County: Mitchell, nineteen, was living at Tallokas with Francis, Elizabeth, David J., Timothy W., and Martha Brice. The schedules did not record family relationships, but the matching household, ages, and locations establish a continuous family group.[4][6]

Folks Huxford identifies Mitchell's parents as Francis Brice and Elizabeth Murphy. He says they moved from Duplin County, North Carolina, in 1833 and settled at Tallokas. The 1850 and 1860 households support the parents' names and Tallokas residence. The 1880 census reports Mitchell's parents as North Carolina natives, while the 1900 census reports Georgia. That conflict leaves Huxford's migration account plausible but not independently proved, and neither census establishes Elizabeth's maiden name.[1][4][5][6][13]

The 1850 slave schedule names Francis Brice as the owner of five enslaved people: three males, ages twenty-four, twenty, and fifteen, and two females, ages forty-three and eighteen. Mitchell was nine and living in his parents' household. The record documents enslavement by Francis. It does not establish that Mitchell personally owned those five people or later inherited them. A usable 1860 Brooks County slave-schedule entry for the family was not recovered.[7]

An original Brooks County Reconstruction oath records Mitchell Brice on June 29, 1867. The evidence located in this research does not establish Confederate military service. A militia enrollment or postwar oath should not be turned into a claim that he served in the Confederate army.[8]

docs.title: First marriage and the Lyman Hall case
docs.text:
In April 1870, newspapers reported that Brice shot and killed Lyman Hall at the Alderman and Brice store near Scruggs Mill. The initial report withheld details because an investigation was underway. Brooks Superior Court later tried Brice for voluntary manslaughter. After a trial lasting more than two days, the jury found him not guilty on May 20. The surviving reports establish the killing, charge, trial, and acquittal. They do not explain what happened inside the store or why the jury acquitted him.[9][10]

The next month, Brooks County issued a marriage license to Mitchell Brice and K. M. Walker. The original record gives June 15, 1870, as their marriage date. The 1870 census was taken on July 25. It places Mitchell with a fourteen-year-old woman whose first name is difficult to read; both were marked as married in June. Ancestry indexes her as "Tissy" and labels her as a child, but the marriage entry and later records make her identification as Keziah Walker strong. Her exact age remains less certain because the census and later reported birth date differ by about a year.[11][12]

The 1880 census names Mitchell's wife as Kisiah M. and their eight-year-old son as David J. An original will supplies the family links that the census does not state. John W. Walker called Kiziah M. Brice his sister, David James Brice his nephew, and Mitchell Brice his brother-in-law. He appointed Mitchell as executor and as guardian for David and another minor nephew.[13][14]

Huxford and cemetery memorials give Keziah's life dates as February 4, 1855, to January 26, 1882, and David James Brice's as February 13, 1872, to June 24, 1894. David reportedly died unmarried. No readable marker image or civil death record was recovered for either person, so the exact dates rest on derivative sources.[1][15]

docs.title: Farming, labor, turpentine, and credit
docs.text:
A December 1875 account said Osburn Bird had worked as a farm laborer on Brice's place. This confirms that Brice employed farm labor by then, but the article does not identify the acreage or crops.[16]

Huxford says Brice inherited Tallokas Plantation after his father's death in 1878, added adjoining land, and operated farms, a sawmill, and a general store. Those details are not equally secure. Contemporary reporting confirms the general business profile, while the inheritance and acreage claims still depend on Huxford because no deed chain or estate inventory was recovered.[1]

Huxford also says Brice bought the Hilton turpentine still in 1882. A newspaper reported that Brice's turpentine still in Quitman burned on November 28 of that year, causing an estimated $1,000 loss. The cause was unknown. The paper mentioned suspicion of arson but reported no finding. The timing confirms that Brice was operating a still in 1882, though it does not identify the seller.[17]

Mortgage and sheriff's-sale notices show that Brice extended secured credit. An 1888 notice concerned 245 acres in Berrien County; an 1889 notice listed two mules and a wagon as collateral in Lowndes County. These records prove individual secured debts. They do not establish a general lending business.[18]

An 1890 Lowndes County tax digest lists Mitchell Brice as the owner of 100 acres in Folsom District, returned by another person. The uncommon name and nearby location probably point to the Tallokas man, but the entry contains no household or residence information.[19]

docs.title: Party activity, post office, and county government
docs.text:
At a Brooks County Democratic meeting in July 1876, Brice represented Tallokas on the committee that proposed delegates to the state convention. The meeting also elected him and J. M. Williams to the county Democratic executive committee for Tallokas. This was a party role, not county office.[20]

A federal register records Brice's appointment as Tallokas postmaster on December 4, 1882. In May 1903, a newspaper announced John P. Clower's appointment in place of Mitchell Brice, deceased. The register and the later notice together resolve the identity.[21]

Brice served on the Brooks County Board of Commissioners from 1892 to 1900. A contemporary January 1895 report names him with the other four commissioners. Huxford's family sketch says Brice chaired the board during the 1892 and 1893 courthouse remodeling. Huxford's official roster contradicts that statement: it names John Tillman as chairman through 1894 and S. S. Rountree afterward. No surviving minute found in this search resolves the discrepancy. Brice's commission service is verified; the chairmanship and direct responsibility for the remodeling are not.[1][22]

docs.title: The 1894 killings and Brice's public response
docs.text:
In December 1894, white mobs killed Black laborers in the area around Brice's plantation. Newspaper accounts identify several victims as his tenants and preserve his response. Brice rejected reports of an armed Black uprising, said the victims were innocent of the alleged conspiracy, and said most of the armed white party came from Colquitt County. The county commissioners, including Brice, issued a resolution condemning the killings and calling for prosecution.[22][23]

The same reporting attributed a sharply different allegation to John Simmons: that Brice treated Black workers as though they were still enslaved and whipped them rather than send them to the chain gang. No court record or independent finding was located to confirm that accusation. It remains an attributed allegation, not an established fact.[23]

docs.title: Second marriage and children
docs.text:
An original Brooks County entry records Brice's marriage to Mattie E. Edmondson on March 14, 1895. A contemporary newspaper announced the marriage that month. Huxford calls her Martha Elizabeth Edmonson but spells her father's surname Edmondson. The records therefore preserve both spellings rather than settling on one.[1][24]

The 1900 Tallokas census places Mitchell, age fifty-nine, with Mattie E., age thirty, and Henry T., age two. It says Mitchell and Mattie had been married five years. The handwritten surname is Brice, but Ancestry indexes the family as Buice.[5]

Later sources identify two sons of this marriage. Mitchell Brice Jr., born in 1896, died in 1899. Henry Turner Brice was born in May 1898 and survived his father. Huxford gives May 2 as Henry's birthday, while his cemetery memorial gives May 5. The census confirms May 1898 but does not settle the day. Henry later chaired the Brooks County Commission and the Georgia Board of Corrections.[1][15]

docs.title: Horses, store, and the Barney tram road
docs.text:
Brice's involvement with racehorses is documented beyond the family history. In April 1897 a newspaper said he owned several fine horses and planned to spend $1,000 improving the Quitman track for carnival races. A June report called him a high-class sportsman with a string of racehorses and named one horse, Little Baltick, that had raced in Savannah. Huxford says Brice bred horses at Tallokas and raced in cities including New Orleans, Jacksonville, St. Louis, Atlanta, and New York. The contemporary reports confirm serious involvement with horses and racing, but not every venue in Huxford's list.[25][26]

Brice described his retail operation in an 1898 testimonial advertisement. He said his nephew A. B. Williams had kept his books and later took charge of "my store." The praise in the advertisement is promotional, but Brice's statement directly confirms the store and Williams's management role.[27]

The clearest link between Brice's business and Barney appeared in an October 1899 Valdosta Times profile. It said he operated a tram road about seven miles west from Barney to his large lumber mills and turpentine still. This was a private industrial tram serving his woods operation. The source does not make it part of the South Georgia Railway main line, identify its western terminal, or fix the route on a modern map.[3]

A 1901 Moultrie Observer item reported that Brice sold land near Hempstead to a Mr. Griffin of Irwin County and planned a fifty-acre Elberta peach orchard. The full name, date, and regional business profile probably identify the Tallokas man. The item itself does not mention Tallokas or Barney, and no follow-up report was found to show that the orchard was planted or harvested.[28]

docs.title: Railroads
docs.text:
Brice backed two railroad efforts. In June 1892, a contemporary report said that he and John W. Hopson each subscribed $2,000 toward a proposed line between Quitman and Moultrie. The search did not establish that this version of the project was completed.[29]

Huxford places Brice on the county-at-large subscription committee formed on January 29, 1896, to raise Quitman's half of the cost of the Adel-to-Quitman railroad. Five days later, the committee reported the required money raised. Brice was not one of the twenty-six named charter petitioners and was not elected to the first board in March. Two contemporary reports, published on March 30 and April 4, 1899, later named him among the South Georgia Railway directors. The April 4 report corroborates the March 30 account.[1][30]

The evidence supports a precise description: Brice helped organize local subscriptions and later became a director. It does not establish how much he personally subscribed in 1896 or make him one of the original incorporators.

docs.title: Convict leasing
docs.text:
Brice participated in Georgia's county misdemeanor-convict leasing system. In 1897 he bid $5 per month for each of ten Colquitt County prisoners, with D. J. Devane appointed as guard. A 1900 report said Brice held county contracts and operated a convict camp in Brooks County. That report came from rival lessee Ed McRee during a business dispute, so McRee's criticism of Brice's management requires attribution and is not treated here as an official finding.[31][32]

A 1903 Thomas County report independently confirms the business relationship. The county had previously hired its misdemeanor prisoners to Brice for $8 per person per month. After his death, his executors did not bid because they were winding up his affairs. Bell Lumber Company received the new contract at $11.50. The sources establish the use of leased convict labor. They do not identify every work site, describe daily conditions, or resolve the separate allegations about Brice's treatment of Black workers.[33]

docs.title: Final illness, death, and estate
docs.text:
On February 28, 1903, the Thomasville Times-Enterprise reported that Brice had suffered paralysis and was in precarious condition. He died in Quitman on March 7. The Savannah Morning News gave pleuropneumonia as the immediate cause, described his timber interests and Quitman property, and said he left a widow and one son. Burial took place at Tallokas on March 8.[2][34]

The paralysis report and the later cause of death are not necessarily contradictory. One describes a serious event a week before death; the other names the illness associated with his death. No civil death certificate was located.

On April 6, Mattie E. Brice posted a guardian's bond for Henry Turner Brice, identified in the original record as the minor and orphan child of Mitchell Brice, deceased. This is direct evidence for the surviving mother and son. A will-book index points to a Mitchell Brice entry on page 21, but the actual will pages and estate inventory were not recovered. No claim about the will's provisions can yet be made.[35]

The cemetery memorial identifies his burial place as Bethel Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery near Pavo. The contemporary obituary says Tallokas and another report says Bethel Church. Together they support the cemetery identification, though no readable marker image was recovered in this research.[2][15]

docs.title: What the record supports
docs.text:
Mitchell Brice's identity can be followed from his parents' Thomas County household in 1850 through Tallokas censuses, marriages, probate records, business reporting, county service, and his 1903 death. His documented railroad role was important but limited: he helped raise local subscriptions in 1896 and later served as a director. He was not one of the named incorporators or a member of the first board.

The fuller record is less tidy than the older county sketch. Brice publicly condemned the 1894 killings of Black laborers, yet other sources place him inside the coercive labor system of his time through county convict leasing and preserve an unverified accusation about his treatment of Black workers. Both parts belong in an honest account.

Several questions remain open. No direct bank ledger confirms Huxford's claim that Brice owned stock and served as a director in early Quitman banks. The commission-chairmanship claim conflicts with Huxford's own roster. The exact inheritance and land chain, the 1860 slave schedule, the original 1896 subscription report, the complete racing record, the death certificate, and the actual probate file still require archival work.

docs.title: Namesake control
docs.text: This Mitchell Brice died in 1903. He is not the Mitchell Brice convicted in Valdosta in 1902 for killing Tom Canidate. He is also not the schoolboy associated with Sparks in 1902 and 1903, his son Mitchell who died in childhood, or his grandson Dr. Mitchell Brice, born in 1920. A newspaper hit that contains only the name is not enough to merge any of those people with the Tallokas planter.[15][36]

docs.title: Norman Campbell Hendry
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

January 2, 1857 to September 7, 1938 | farmer, merchant, school trustee, and probable South Georgia Railroad incorporator

docs.title: The “Neal C.” correction
docs.text:
Folks Huxford's 1948 county history prints “Neal C. Hendry” in its 1896 railroad petition list and again in an 1897 general-merchandise list.[1] No separate Neal C. Hendry has been found. The evidence instead points to Norman Campbell Hendry, usually written N. C. Hendry.

The identification is strongly probable rather than verified because the original railroad petition and the April 3, 1897 Quitman Free-Press page have not been located. Even with that limit, the chain is unusually specific. Norman C. Hendry was a Brooks County taxpayer before his 1885 marriage, lived in Quitman, worked as a dry-goods dealer, owned a plantation near Morven, served on Quitman's school board, and appears repeatedly as N. C. Hendry in contemporary newspapers. A 1904 report gives his full form as Norman C. Hendry.[2] Wedding announcements for two daughters spell out Norman Campbell Hendry.[3][4]

Huxford's own book supports the correction. Its family chapter identifies Norman Campbell Hendry as a son of Neal and Margaret Campbell Hendry. Elsewhere the book says telephone service reached N. C. Hendry's farm by 1907. Only the railroad and merchant passages expand the initials to “Neal C.”[1][5] The most likely explanation is that Huxford expanded an N. C. source form incorrectly.

This distinction matters because Norman's father was a prominent man in his own right. The elder Neal Hendry died in 1892, four years before the railroad charter petition. He was the Brooks County commissioner, Farmers' Alliance Warehouse director and manager, and political figure found in the 1880s and early 1890s.[6][7] Those offices belong to the father, not to Norman.

docs.title: Parents and childhood
docs.text:
Norman was born January 2, 1857. His original Georgia death certificate names his parents as Neal Hendry and Margaret Campbell and gives his birthplace as Taylor County, Florida.[8] The birthplace is not completely settled. Find a Grave says Lowndes County, Georgia, while some family trees say Brooks County. The certificate is the closest original record, but it was completed eighty-one years after the birth.

The census record follows the family across the Florida-Georgia border. In 1860, three-year-old “Nomand C. Hendry” lived with Neal and Margaret in Taylor County, Florida.[9] By 1870, fourteen-year-old Norman was in their Brooks County household.[10] The 1880 census placed Norman C. Hendry, age twenty-two, with Neal and Margarette in Quitman. It explicitly called him their son.[11]

The elder Neal had been born in Liberty County in 1820 and married Margaret Campbell at Morven in 1844. Huxford lists seven children: William Eli, Sarah Catherine, Alexander Campbell, Neal Wesley, John Gardner, James Edward, and Norman Campbell.[6] A 1916 newspaper account independently called Neill Hendry the father of the then-living N. C. Hendry of Quitman.[12]

That family had several men named Neal or Norman. Norman's brother Neal Wesley Hendry died in 1887, and Neal Wesley's son Neal W. Hendry Jr. was born in 1880. Neither man fits the initials, age, household, wife, property, and civic record attached to N. C. Hendry. They remain important namesake controls, but they do not explain the railroad-era evidence as well as Norman does.

docs.title: Marriage and household
docs.text:
Norman C. Hendry married Mattie, or Martha Jane, Townsend in Mitchell County on December 30, 1885.[13] Huxford gives December 29, one day earlier. The county marriage record controls the date.

The couple had three daughters:

  • Sarah Nona, born November 30, 1886, who married Cuthbert Powell Grady
  • Tecoah, born December 15, 1888, who married Macon banker Charles Blackwell Lewis
  • Ida Belle, born January 12, 1892, who married Joseph Winfred Harner

The 1900 census found Norman, Mattie, Nona, Tecoah, Ida Belle, and Mattie's brother Henry P. Townsend in Quitman. Norman was a dry-goods dealer and owned the family home without a mortgage.[14] The 1910 census, despite indexing the surname as Hudry, placed the family at 204 Clay Street. Norman was a retired merchant. The household included Martha, Tecoah, Ida Belle, Nona and Cuthbert Grady, Martha's mother Ann E. Townsend, and her brother Henry.[15]

Contemporary family notices reinforce that census chain. In 1907, Mr. and Mrs. Norman Campbell Hendry announced Nona's engagement to Cuthbert Powell Grady.[3] In 1910, they announced Tecoah's marriage to Charles Blackwell Lewis.[4] In 1913, they announced Ida Belle's engagement to Joseph Winfred Harner.[16] A 1911 notice that placed Mrs. N. C. Hendry with her mother, Mrs. Townsend, independently bridges the initials to Norman's wife.[17]

In 1920, Norman was listed as a farmer at the Clay Street home with Mattie, the Gradys, and grandson Norman H. Grady.[18] No secure 1930 census match was found in the documented exact and variant searches.

docs.title: Merchant and property owner
docs.text:
Norman was in Brooks County's property-tax records by the mid-1880s. Ancestry indexes Norman C. Hendry in local tax digests from 1883 through 1887.[19] The digest images were not fully transcribed for acreage or valuation, so the entries establish taxable property, not its precise size.

An 1894 Atlanta report referred to “N. C. Hendry, of Hendry & Hendry.”[20] The surviving paragraph does not identify the other partner or describe the firm's trade. Huxford's transcription of the April 3, 1897 Free-Press business list calls “Neal C. Hendry” a general-merchandise dealer.[1] The 1900 census's dry-goods occupation fits that business. By 1910 he called himself a retired merchant.

Farming remained a substantial part of his life. The 1904 Atlanta Journal said Norman C. Hendry and his family would spend several weeks at their plantation home.[2] Other reports locate the country home near Morven or Kennedy, on or close to the South Georgia Railroad.[21] In 1903, Governor Joseph M. Terrell appointed N. C. Hendry as one of Brooks County's delegates to the Georgia Farmers' Congress.[22]

The plantation appeared in a detailed auction advertisement in May 1926. The ad placed it ten miles from Quitman, fourteen miles from Valdosta, and two miles from Morven. It described cultivated tracts with woodland, water, tenant houses, barns, and two main dwellings, with the sale beginning at the Kennedy place on the South Georgia Railroad.[23] These were the seller's promotional claims, not an independent appraisal. They do show the scale and location of the property being broken into smaller farms.

Norman also owned town property. The censuses say the Quitman home was owned free of mortgage in 1900, 1910, and 1920.[14][15][18] In 1912 he sold the house, then bought it back from J. P. Malloy later that year and returned to Quitman.[24] The surviving notices do not provide a street description, deed book, price, or complete title chain.

docs.title: Public schools and civic work
docs.text:
Quitman voters placed N. C. Hendry on the city school board in 1900. A contemporary election report names him with S. S. Bennet, E. A. Jelks, S. S. Gaulden, and Jeff Davis.[25] In 1906, Quitman's mass meeting again nominated Hendry to the school board, and the report said the incumbent board was being returned without opposition.[26] The evidence therefore supports service across more than one term, although exact starting and ending dates and any officer title remain unknown.

His other public roles were more limited. Governor Terrell's 1903 Farmers' Congress appointment recognized him as a Brooks County agricultural representative.[22] In 1915 he was drawn for the federal court's traverse jury at Valdosta.[27] Neither item amounts to elective office.

Norman should not be called a county commissioner. The Neal Hendry who served from 1883 until his death in 1892 was his father.[6][7] The same rule applies to the elder Neal's place on the Brooks County Alliance Warehouse board and his appointment as warehouse manager in 1891.

docs.title: Church and community life
docs.text:
The Hendrys were closely connected to Quitman's Methodist community. Their daughters' marriages were held at the Methodist Episcopal Church, and Norman hosted several Methodist ministers during the 1908 South Georgia Conference.[4][16][28] When the congregation honored departing pastor Guyton Fisher in 1918, N. C. Hendry was chairman of the board of stewards.[30] In 1930, the First Methodist Church again elected him to its board of stewards.[29] These reports provide direct evidence of church membership and governance late in his life.

Social columns followed family visits, weddings, and guests for decades. Those notices are useful because they keep the same N. C. Hendry tied to Mattie Townsend and the three daughters. They should not be mistaken for evidence of a separate public office.

docs.title: The South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Huxford names “Neal C. Hendry” among twenty-six petitioners for the South Georgia Railroad charter in 1896. The proposed capital was $65,000 in 650 shares.[1] The original petition, Secretary of State charter file, subscription book, stock ledger, and corporate minutes were not located online.

The March 23, 1896 organization meeting is independently documented. Stockholders accepted the charter, adopted bylaws, elected nine directors, and chose the first officers. Hendry was not on the first board or officer slate.[31] No evidence places him on the earlier subscription committee, right-of-way committee, or construction staff.

The safe conclusion is narrow: according to Huxford, N. C. Hendry, who was very likely Norman Campbell Hendry, was a charter petitioner. His merchant and plantation interests give a sensible reason to support the line, but motive cannot substitute for a record. No source found states his number of shares, payment, engineering work, or later management role.

The line did matter to his property. Huxford says the Quitman Telephone Company extended service to N. C. Hendry's farm by 1907.[5] The 1926 plantation sale began at a place on the South Georgia Railroad.[23] Those later connections do not prove an operational railroad role.

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
Norman died in the Morven, or 660th militia, district of Brooks County at 7:30 p.m. on September 7, 1938. His Georgia death certificate records myocarditis, with senility as a contributing condition. It calls him a married farmer, names Neal Hendry and Margaret Campbell as his parents, and records burial at Oak Hill Cemetery on September 8.[8]

The next day's Macon Telegraph reported that Norman C. Hendry had died near Quitman on Wednesday night. It named his wife as the former Mattie Townsend of Camilla and listed their three daughters, Mrs. Charles B. Lewis, Mrs. C. P. Grady, and Mrs. J. W. Harner. The funeral was set for Friday morning, September 9.[34] The notice independently confirms the death date and the family identification.

Two later sources disagree. The photographed marker says September 8, apparently using the burial date, while Huxford gives September 15.[6][32] The original death certificate is the best evidence and controls this dossier. The marker remains valuable for the cemetery placement and for showing how the one-day conflict arose.

No fuller contemporary obituary was found in the documented online newspaper searches. Norman's probate indexes were located, but the underlying files were not fully transcribed.[33] No estate value should be inferred from the plantation, town home, or probate index alone.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Norman Campbell Hendry spent most of his adult life between Quitman and the family's country property near Morven. He worked in dry goods and general merchandise, farmed, owned substantial rural and town property, served on the city school board, represented Brooks County at a farmers' congress, and sat on the Methodist board of stewards.

The railroad connection survives through a flawed name. Huxford's “Neal C.” is best understood as an incorrect expansion of N. C. Hendry, whose contemporary full name was Norman Campbell Hendry. That correction is graded strong probable because the life record fits in every material respect and the elder Neal was already dead. It remains short of verified until the original charter petition or another independent shareholder record is found.

docs.title: Open questions and research limits
docs.text:
• The original South Georgia Railroad petition and the April 3, 1897 Quitman Free-Press business page were not located. They are needed to determine whether the source printed N. C. or Neal C.
  • Norman's birthplace remains conflicted. The death certificate says Taylor County, Florida; derivative sources give Lowndes or Brooks County, Georgia.
  • The original tax digest images, deed indexes, probate packets, and any will or estate inventory were not fully examined.
  • No secure 1930 census household or contemporary 1938 obituary was found.
  • The other member of Hendry & Hendry and the firm's exact business history remain unresolved.
  • The railroad share count, subscription amount, and any later stock ownership are unknown.

docs.title: Roderick Chilly McIntosh
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Roderick C. McIntosh (October 27, 1855-July 17, 1926) spent most of his life in Quitman, Georgia. Original census, death, and probate records identify him as the son of Roderick McIntosh and Bathsheba McMillan, the husband of Cora B. Lewis, and the father of Lewis E. McIntosh, Cora B. Vaughn or Vaughan, and Roderick C. McIntosh Jr. The records follow him from a fourteen-year-old in his mother's Quitman household in 1870 to a merchant, planter, bank director, mayor, and long-serving South Georgia Railway officer.[2-7][9][12-13][17][19][21-22][27][33]

The middle name is not spelled consistently. Huxford uses "Chilly," the death certificate reads "Chilli," the will heading reads "Chili," and derivative indexes and cemetery material add other variants. This dossier uses "Chilly" in the title because it is the familiar local form, but it does not treat the spelling as uniform.[1][7][9][34]

docs.title: Family and childhood
docs.text:
The 1870 census places fourteen-year-old Roderick in Quitman with Bersheba McIntosh and several other McIntoshes. The schedule does not state their relationships. His 1926 death certificate identifies his parents as Roderick McIntosh, born in North Carolina, and Bathsheba McMillan, born in Georgia, which secures the mother-son link that the census alone cannot prove.[2][7]

Huxford says the elder Roderick died in 1857 and that Bathsheba moved the family to Quitman in 1861, where she acquired the old Quitman Hotel. That 1948 account remains the source for the move and hotel story because no secure 1860 household or deed was located in the documented search.[1][35]

Huxford also says Bathsheba, her daughters, and an enslaved woman named Harriet worked at the hotel during the Civil War. No 1857 estate record or 1860 slave schedule was inspected for this project. The evidence does not establish who legally held Harriet, and it gives no basis for assigning ownership to Roderick, who was a small child.[1][35]

docs.title: Marriage and children
docs.text:
The 1880 census records R. C. McIntosh, age twenty-five, as a Quitman merchant with wife C. B. and their ten-month-old son, L. E. The 1900 schedule identifies the household as Roderick C. and Cora B. McIntosh with children Lewis E., Cora B., and Roderick C. McIntosh. The 1910 and 1920 schedules continue the family in Quitman.[3-6]

A compiled Virginia marriage entry says Roderick C. McIntosh and Cora B. Lewis married in Albemarle County on November 14, 1878. The 1900 census independently reports a marriage in 1878, but the original Virginia return was not inspected. The date and county are therefore strongly probable. "Cora B. Lewis" is verified by Roderick's death certificate; the expanded name "Cora Barksdale Lewis" comes from derivative family material.[7][8]

Roderick's will names his three children as Lewis E. McIntosh, Mrs. Cora B. Vaughn, and Roderick C. McIntosh Jr. The July 1926 death reports spell the daughter's married surname Vaughan, so both forms are preserved as a source spelling conflict.[9][33] Cora survived her husband. The Georgia death index and FamilySearch record agree that Mrs. Cora B. McIntosh died in Brooks County on June 13, 1934.[10]

docs.title: Merchant, property owner, and planter
docs.text:
The original censuses trace McIntosh's occupations from merchant in 1880, to grocery dealer in 1900, hardware merchant in 1910, and planter in 1920. His death certificate calls him a retired businessman.[3-7]

Georgia tax-digest indexes also place Roderick or R. C. McIntosh in Brooks County through the documented business years. Because the saved files show index results rather than original schedules, they support name-and-place continuity but not unverified details about property or employees.[11]

Contemporary reporting gives the business more shape. In 1893, R. C. McIntosh & Co. was described as a large hardware and grocery concern, with his brother-in-law John O. Lewis as a member of the firm.[15] An 1897 fire report identifies a store building belonging to McIntosh among the commercial property threatened by fire, but it supplies neither a value nor a legal description.[16]

McIntosh also took part in local development efforts. He served on committees seeking a hydraulic cotton compress in 1890, chaired the 1899 meeting that organized Quitman's Board of Trade, and helped draft the new body's rules.[14][18] These records prove committee work, not ownership of every project promoted.

Later reports describe his farming operations. In 1916 he sold 142 bales of cotton from the 1914 and 1915 crops for $8,000 and was said to have built a farm warehouse in 1914.[26] A 1924 report says McIntosh Farms slaughtered 120 hogs averaging about 300 pounds. One OCR rendering says 800 pounds, but the parallel report supports 300.[30] In February 1926, McIntosh sold a nine-acre East Quitman tract for $10,000 after roughly forty years of ownership. The accounts disagree on whether he held it for forty or forty-four years.[32]

These examples establish substantial commercial and farming activity. They do not establish his total acreage, net worth, complete property holdings, or ownership percentages in family or corporate enterprises.

docs.title: Bank, hotel, telephone, and other companies
docs.text:
McIntosh was elected to the first Bank of Quitman board in January 1889 and was reelected in 1891. Newspaper profiles continued to list him as a director in 1905 and near his death.[13][20][33] Figures published for the bank describe the institution, not McIntosh's personal wealth.

Huxford identifies McIntosh with the Quitman Hotel Company, Quitman Telephone Company, Interstate Lumber Company, Building and Loan Association, and a cotton-mill subscription. The new research did not inspect each original corporate charter, minute book, or stock ledger. Those Huxford-based roles are strongly probable unless a specific contemporary record is cited.[1][35]

One later role is independently clear. A 1919 regional business survey identifies him as president of a transfer company that moved freight from the Atlantic Coast Line and South Georgia depots.[29]

docs.title: Mayor and public work
docs.text:
An 1886 artesian-well advertisement is signed "R. C. McIntosh, Mayor, Quitman, Ga." and directly verifies his mayoral office that year.[12] Huxford's municipal tables also place him on the council in several years during the 1880s, but city minutes were not inspected and no complete office-by-office chronology has been established.[1][35]

McIntosh participated in several later public projects. He represented Brooks County in highway-routing efforts in 1910 and 1911, served on Quitman's school bond commission and building committee in 1912, and joined W. J. Powell in conveying a Screven Street lot to the federal government for the new Quitman post office in 1913.[23-25] The post-office report proves joint conveyance, not the share held by either seller.

In 1918 he served on Brooks County's executive committee for the Fourth Liberty Loan campaign.[28] A 1925 report places R. C. McIntosh and John O. Lewis at First Presbyterian Church when their overcoats were stolen, providing direct, if incidental, evidence of his Presbyterian association.[31]

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad and related railways
docs.text:
Huxford names McIntosh as one of four men assigned to solicit Quitman subscriptions on January 29, 1896, and as one of the charter petitioners. The original meeting report and charter petition were not inspected in this project, so those two roles remain strongly probable rather than verified.[1][35]

His founding-board role is verified. The March 24, 1896 Savannah Morning News reported that stockholders elected R. C. McIntosh to the South Georgia Railroad's first board.[17] He was reelected in 1899, and in February 1900 the board elected him vice president after J. W. Hopson disposed of his holdings.[19][21]

Later contemporary records repeatedly identify him as a director and vice president. The evidence includes business travel with railway officers in 1903, company descriptions in 1906 and 1910, reelection in 1911, and another reelection as director and vice president of the South Georgia & West Coast Railroad in November 1925.[22][27][31] His 1926 death reports still called him a railway vice president.[33]

He also became vice president of the West Coast Railway when it was organized at Greenville, Florida, in December 1900, and he joined the published 1907 charter petition for the Quitman, Thomasville & Valdosta Railway and Power Company.[21][22] These were related but distinct enterprises. The surviving evidence does not give his share count or original South Georgia Railroad subscription, and it should not be compressed into a claim that every office was held without interruption.

docs.title: Will and estate plan
docs.text:
McIntosh signed his will on June 17, 1926, one month before his death. It names his wife, Cora B. McIntosh, and their three children. He appointed Cora and Roderick Jr. as executors.[9]

The will directed that the estate remain together for ten years unless specified family conditions intervened. It asked the managing executor to consult S. S. Rountree, J. W. Oglesby, and C. T. Tillman, and expressed McIntosh's wish that Roderick Jr. succeed him in corporate directorships and other positions of trust. It also names his sister Mattie McIntosh, cousin Katie Comfort of Boston, son-in-law B. L. Vaughn, and servants Rebecca Jones and Arthur Thomas.[9]

The relevant will is on the McIntosh portions of images 164, 165, and 166 in the Brooks County will book. Image 167 continues Nancy Becton's will and is not McIntosh evidence. No probate petition, letters testamentary, inventory, appraisement, land schedule, or executor accounting was located in the saved research.[9][35]

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
Roderick died at home in Quitman at 3:30 p.m. on July 17, 1926. His original Georgia death certificate gives chronic myocarditis as the primary cause, with diabetes mellitus and uremia contributing. Newspaper reports mention recent pleurisy, but that report of his preceding illness does not replace the certified cause.[7][33]

The certificate says he was buried at Oak Hill Cemetery on July 18. A Valdosta follow-up independently reports Oak Hill burial and names the clergy and pallbearers.[7][34] An index points to Find a Grave memorial 78221283, but neither the memorial page nor the marker photograph was inspected for this review.[36]

docs.title: Conflicts and identity controls
docs.text:
The death certificate fixes his birth at October 27, 1855, and the 1900 census gives October 1855. Huxford gives 1856. The original certificate controls, with Huxford's one-year difference retained as a conflict.[1][4][7]

His father's birthplace also conflicts. The 1880 census and death certificate say North Carolina; the 1900, 1910, and 1920 schedules say Georgia. North Carolina is better supported because the earlier census agrees with the son-informed death certificate, but the disagreement remains unresolved.[3-7]

The 1920 schedule uses "Jr." for the sixty-four-year-old head of household. His age, wife Cora, son Lewis, and continuous Quitman identity show that the record concerns the elder Roderick, not his son born in 1888.[6]

The Haralson County 1892 marriage of "Chillie McIntosh" and Calia Alman is a different man. The Quitman subject was already married to Cora, and the county, spouse, and chronology do not fit.[37] Articles about the Creek leader Chilly McIntosh, the Revolutionary-era Roderick McIntosh, and R. C. McIntosh Jr. were also excluded.[35]

docs.title: What remains unresolved
docs.text:
The documented search did not locate a secure 1860 household, the original Virginia marriage return, the complete probate administration, a railroad stock ledger, corporate minute books, a complete farm acreage record, original tax-schedule images, or a cemetery register. Online newspaper coverage cannot be called exhaustive because of OCR and collection limits.[35]

No surviving record inspected here proves that the family occupied one unchanged house throughout their Quitman years. Census addresses change among Screen, Jefferson, and Johnson streets, and renaming or renumbering has not been proved.[3-6]

docs.title: Confidence summary
docs.text:
• Verified: identity; October 27, 1855 birth; July 17, 1926 death; parents; wife as Cora B. Lewis; three children, with the daughter's married surname spelled Vaughn in the will and Vaughan in death reports; Quitman residence from 1870 through 1920; census occupations; original will; 1886 mayoral office; first Bank of Quitman board; 1896 railroad board election; later documented railway offices; certified cause of death; Oak Hill burial.
  • Strong probable: November 14, 1878 Albemarle County marriage; Cora's full middle name as Barksdale; 1896 subscription-committee and charter-petitioner roles; Huxford-based corporate and municipal details not independently matched to original records.
  • Unresolved: secure 1860 location; exact legal form and extent of household slaveholding; unchanged-house tradition; total property and acreage; railroad investment; full corporate and city-office chronology; complete probate administration; original cemetery documentation.

docs.title: Sources

docs.title: Samuel Stevens Rountree
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Samuel Stevens Rountree (March 25, 1855-October 29, 1952) spent eighty-seven years in Quitman and more than seven decades in its business life. He began in his father's general store, led a regional wholesale grocery company and the Suwannee Stores chain, served the Bank of Quitman as director, vice president, president, and chairman, and held long runs of municipal and county office. He also became a director, president, and chairman of the South Georgia Railway.[1]

A contemporary Florida Times-Union obituary reports that Rountree died at his Quitman home on the morning of October 29, 1952. That account and a same-day Atlanta brief agree, so the October 20 date printed in a separate statewide list was an error.[36][37]

It also gives his railroad career firmer boundaries. Rountree appears in Huxford's 1896 charter-petitioner list but not on the verified first board. He was a director by March 1899, president by 1939, and chairman in October 1945. Huxford's statement that he succeeded James W. Oglesby in 1930 is strong probable because the actual 1930 election notice or minutes have not been found.[1][8][32][33][35]

docs.title: Edgefield family and move to Quitman
docs.text:
Rountree was born in Edgefield District, South Carolina, to Andrew Jackson Rountree and Sarilla Stevens Rountree. The 1860 census places five-year-old Samuel with his parents and siblings in Edgefield. The family is badly indexed as "Ranndtrer", but the names, ages, and later household continuity identify them.[2]

The family moved to Quitman in 1865, when Samuel was ten. A June 1866 collection notice proves that Samuel Stevens, A. J. Rountree, and W. D. Rountree had left South Carolina by then. Quitman's 1866 business record lists Stevens & Rountree as dry-goods dealers. Huxford says Andrew took over the concern the following year.[1][3]

The 1870 census places Samuel, fourteen, in Andrew and Sarilla's Quitman household with Fannie, Daniel, Mattie, Bartow, Walter, and Edward. In 1880, twenty-four-year-old S. S. Rountree was still in his parents' Screven Street household. These records establish the same family across the interstate move and separate Samuel from unrelated Rountree families in Georgia.[4][5]

Andrew's recorded will is the strongest family document. Signed November 29, 1893, it named Samuel as a son, residuary heir, and executor. The other surviving children were Fannie R. Hunter, Daniel M. Rountree, Mattie E. Dukes, J. B. Rountree, and Edward N. Rountree. Walter J. Rountree, present in the earlier censuses, had died in 1882. The will permitted the executors to continue Rountree & Co. for as long as five years if most of the children agreed.[6]

The will calls Daniel "Daniel M. Rountree"; census and newspaper records identify him as Daniel W. or Daniel Webster Rountree. That middle-initial conflict remains. A ten-year-old Lillie appeared in the 1880 household without a stated relationship. No second record inspected here proves that she was Samuel's sister.[5][6]

docs.title: Schooling, marriage, and household
docs.text:
Huxford says Samuel attended the old Quitman Academy and other local schools before studying at Eastman Business College in Poughkeepsie, New York. A detailed 1948 profile independently says he chose an Eastman business course at eighteen, returned directly to Quitman, and went to work for his father. No college register or diploma was located, so the education is strongly supported rather than original-record verified.[1][7]

He married Minnie Lewis on February 12, 1890. Huxford identifies her as a daughter of John G. Lewis of Scottsville, Virginia. Minnie's 1939 obituary independently calls her the former Minnie Lewis of Scottsville and says she had married Samuel forty-nine years earlier. The exact February date rests on Huxford because the original marriage return was not found.[1][8]

The 1900 census places Samuel and Minnie in the home of his sister Fannie and her husband, Dr. Theophilus W. Hunter. Samuel's widowed mother Sarilla was there as well. The index calls Samuel a boarder and omits a spouse link, but the full household places Minnie beside him. In 1910, Samuel appears as a Quitman household head with Minnie L. Rountree.[9][10]

No inspected record names a child. None appears with them in the 1900 or indexed 1910 households. Minnie's obituary names her husband and siblings but no child, while Samuel's 1952 obituary says four nieces and four nephews survived him. A childless marriage, or at least no surviving children, is strong probable. It is not fully verified without Samuel's will, probate distribution, or an original census child-count field.[8-10][38]

Minnie died December 4, 1939. Her Find a Grave memorial supplies the fuller name Minnie Clayburn Lewis Rountree and an August 10, 1867 birth date. Those details are derivative. Contemporary Lewis-family records use several spellings of Clayburn or Clayborne, so Minnie's middle-name spelling should remain memorial-supported rather than treated as an original-record fact.[8][39]

docs.title: Merchant and executor
docs.text:
The 1948 profile says Samuel worked for his father for five years. When another businessman offered to finance a concern Samuel would manage, Andrew gave his son an interest and renamed the firm A. J. Rountree & Son in 1878. Huxford gives the same general succession.[1][7]

A February 1896 newspaper report called Rountree & Co. Quitman's oldest mercantile firm, announced Andrew's retirement, and said S. S. Rountree would continue the business. This contemporary report corrects the 1948 profile's implication that the name changed only after Andrew's death. Andrew died January 21, 1898, not in 1899 as the profile states.[11][12]

Samuel and Daniel served as their father's executors. The 1948 article said Samuel was still administering real property held in Andrew's estate fifty years later, including the family home in Quitman and Atlanta residential property. The will verifies the original executorship, but the later estate holdings have not been reconstructed deed by deed.[6][7]

docs.title: South Georgia Grocery Company and Suwannee Stores
docs.text:
The grocery company's exact starting year has a small conflict. An April 1903 report said the South Georgia Grocery Company had been organized recently and was already operating. A 1905 promotional account called it established in 1902. Huxford and the 1948 profile give 1903. The best description is that it was organized in late 1902 or early 1903.[7][13][14]

By June 1909, the company had $20,000 capital and occupied a concrete warehouse 300 feet long and 80 feet wide beside the South Georgia and West Coast Railroad. It dealt in groceries, tobacco, flour, hay, grain, feed, and provisions; employed traveling salesmen; maintained a 1,000-bale cotton warehouse; and traded across southwest Georgia and north Florida. The article names S. S. Rountree as president.[15]

The business kept expanding. It began a new brick-and-concrete office and warehouse near the Atlantic Coast Line depot in 1924. A May 1925 report valued the completed property at $50,000 and noted branch houses in Georgia and Florida. The company added wholesale dry goods in 1927.[16-18]

Huxford says manager S. J. Faircloth led the development of the Suwannee Stores chain after 1910. By 1947 it had 133 stores and 573 employees. The 1948 profile says South Georgia Grocery owned the chain and that Rountree held controlling interests in the parent company, Capital City Grocery Company of Tallahassee, and Rountree Grocery Company of Americus.[1][7]

The 1952 obituary instead locates Rountree Grocery Company in Thomasville. No charter or corporate directory was found to resolve Americus versus Thomasville. The evidence verifies Rountree's presidency, the regional wholesale concern, and ownership of Suwannee Stores, but the affiliate's city remains unsettled.[36]

docs.title: Bank of Quitman
docs.text:
Rountree attended the November 1888 meeting that led to the incorporated Bank of Quitman. Huxford describes the bank as the successor to a private concern begun in 1878, while the state bank received its charter on December 26, 1888. The two dates describe different stages rather than rival founding claims.[1][19]

He was a director by February 1892. Huxford dates his vice presidency to 1891, and contemporary reports place him in that office in 1898, 1905, 1909, and early 1911.[1][20-23]

After Judge James O. Morton died, the directors unanimously elected Rountree president on November 5, 1911. The report called him the county's best credit man and said he had been vice president for fifteen years. That rounded figure conflicts with Huxford's 1891 start, but the election itself is direct contemporary evidence.[24]

Rountree remained president until February 12, 1945, when H. W. Stubbs succeeded him and Rountree became board chairman. Huxford supplies the exact transition date; the 1948 profile independently confirms that Rountree was still chairman and went to the bank daily despite failing eyesight. The 1952 obituary describes a thirty-year presidency, while the dated record gives a little more than thirty-three years.[1][7][36]

docs.title: Manufacturing, telephone, farm, and hotel interests
docs.text:
Rountree was elected a Quitman Compress Company director on July 8, 1890, and vice president later that month. Huxford says he became president of the Quitman Manufacturing Company when Atlantic & Gulf Mills was reorganized in 1914 and retired when majority control was sold in February 1920. The 1948 profile independently confirms that he had served as the mill company's president.[1][7][25]

The telephone chronology contains a real conflict. Huxford names Rountree among the Quitman Telephone Company's December 7, 1896 incorporators and says the first system was built in 1896-1897. The 1948 profile calls him a founder but says the company introduced Quitman's first telephone service in 1906. The 1952 obituary says he organized and led the company for years. The charter-era date and Huxford's construction account make service by the late 1890s better supported; the 1906 statement should not be repeated as settled fact.[1][7][36]

His agricultural holdings were substantial. A Brooks County deed dated December 8, 1894, conveyed 510 acres in District 12, Lots 376 and 377, to A. J. and S. S. Rountree. The official land-lot map places the tract about ten miles north of Quitman, matching 1898 newspaper references to S. S. Rountree's farm. The 1948 profile says his later farm reached 1,500 acres, so he acquired or operated more land than the single identified deed covers.[26]

After the Hotel Marie burned in 1926, Rountree became an incorporator and director of the Community Hotel Corporation that built the General Quitman. Huxford identifies the corporation, the January 15, 1927 charter, the directors, and the new hotel's cost and dimensions. The underlying corporate petition was not independently inspected for this dossier.[1]

docs.title: Quitman council and Brooks County commission
docs.text:
Rountree served repeatedly on Quitman's governing body. Huxford lists him as a councilman in 1878 and 1879 and as an alderman across the annual or paired terms from 1881 through 1903. Newspaper spot checks place him on the successful ticket in 1884 and again in 1900. Other contemporary election reports name him in 1886, 1890, 1892, 1894, 1896, 1898, and 1902.[1][27][28]

The record should not be flattened into one uninterrupted term because some reports describe nominations treated as equivalent to election. It does establish long and repeated service. Huxford's mayoral table does not name him, and no checked newspaper made him mayor.[1]

The county record is equally substantial. Huxford lists him as a Brooks County commissioner in 1892-1900 and 1902-1915, with chairmanships in 1894-1900 and 1903-1915. The one-year 1902/1903 difference between the member and chairman tables appears to be a transition or compilation discrepancy.[1]

A December 1894 report directly names Rountree chairman of the five-member board. The commissioners condemned recent murders and abuse of Black residents, called for prosecution, and disputed parts of an earlier newspaper's description of a race riot. Both parts of the resolution matter: the board denounced the violence while also contesting the press account's scale and characterization.[29]

A February 1911 county profile again identifies Rountree as commission chairman. The contemporary reports verify the office at both ends of the two periods; Huxford's compiled table supplies the full runs.[23][29]

docs.title: Hospital work, church gifts, and library bequests
docs.text:
Rountree chaired a February 26, 1916 mass meeting that raised more than $5,000 toward a proposed city-county hospital. In 1940 he created a $50,000 charitable trust for Brooks County Hospital patients unable to pay. A February 1941 editorial confirms the fund and says the hospital could draw $1,000 of principal plus interest each year for fifty years. Huxford estimated that about 150 patients had benefited by 1948.[1][30][31]

After Minnie's death, Rountree gave $16,000 to the Quitman Presbyterian Church as her memorial. His 1952 obituary also reports that he gave the old library building to the Baptist church as a memorial to his mother and made bequests to the Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist churches and the Brooks County Library.[1][36]

These gifts do not settle his own denomination. His parents were Baptists and Minnie was Presbyterian, but no reviewed source explicitly states Samuel's church membership.[1][8]

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad and Railway
docs.text:
Huxford lists S. S. Rountree among the 26 applicants for the South Georgia Railroad charter in 1896. The original charter petition and subscription book have not been found. His petitioner role is therefore strong probable rather than original-record verified.[1]

He was not one of the nine directors elected at the March 23, 1896 permanent organization. The contemporary report names James W. Oglesby as president, John W. Hopson as vice president, John Tillman as treasurer, and Zenas W. Oglesby as superintendent. It is important not to turn a petitioner into a founding director.[32]

Rountree joined the board later. The March 1899 annual-meeting report names him among nine reelected directors. This is the earliest direct board evidence found, although it does not give his first election date. A 1925 report independently places him on the board years later.[33][34]

Huxford says Rountree was a stockholder and director when James W. Oglesby died in 1930 and then succeeded him as president. A December 1939 report directly calls Rountree president of the South Georgia Railway, Bank of Quitman, and South Georgia Grocery Company. The presidency is verified by 1939; the 1930 succession remains strong probable without the election notice or minutes.[1][8]

In October 1945 the railway elected R. C. Brooks president and J. J. Parrish vice president and general manager, with S. S. Rountree as board chairman. That report directly verifies his final railway office.[35]

Rountree also joined other transportation proposals. In April 1904 he served on a five-man Quitman committee investigating a rail connection involving the Nashville & Sparks and Pinebloom roads. In 1907 he was one of the published applicants for the Quitman, Valdosta and Thomasville Electric Railway and Power Company, a proposed fifty-mile street railway and power concern. The repeated legal notice proves the application. It does not prove a granted charter, paid subscription, construction, or operation.[40][41]

docs.title: Death and burial
docs.text:
Rountree died at home in Quitman on the morning of Wednesday, October 29, 1952. The Florida Times-Union published a detailed Quitman obituary the next day. A separate Atlanta Journal brief printed on October 29 says he died Wednesday at age ninety-seven. Its statewide list gives October 20, but that entry conflicts with both the same-page brief and the fuller next-day report. October 29 controls.[36][37]

The obituary reviews his bank, grocery, telephone, railroad, and charitable work and says four nieces and four nephews survived him. No funeral-service report, burial notice, or probate announcement was located in the saved newspaper corpus.[36][38]

Find a Grave memorial 36072263 places him in West End Cemetery and links him to Andrew, Sarilla, and Minnie. Its family-plot photograph confirms a Rountree enclosure but does not show a readable Samuel inscription in the images inspected. West End burial is strong probable, not verified by a burial register or readable marker.[38]

docs.title: Research limits
docs.text:
The documented search covered local project files; memory and evidence logs; Huxford's county history; 1860-1910 census records; Andrew Rountree's recorded will; FamilySearch; Ancestry; Find a Grave; Georgia Historic Newspapers; authenticated saved Newspapers.com corpora; business, bank, municipal, county, railroad, church, hospital, death, and burial terms; and five broader web searches. Name forms included Samuel Stevens Rountree, Samuel S. Rountree, S. S. Rountree, Roundtree, and family, place, office, and business combinations.

Not found in the documented online search: original birth or baptism record; Eastman enrollment or diploma; original 1890 marriage return; original images and complete household fields for 1910-1940; Samuel's will or probate file; readable grave marker or burial register; original South Georgia Railroad charter petition, stock book, or complete minutes; exact first railway board date; 1930 presidential-election minutes; full grocery, bank, telephone, manufacturing, hotel, county, church, or hospital records; grocery-company charter; hospital trust instrument; or a funeral report.

docs.title: Silas Morton Young
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Identity confidence: Verified.

Silas Morton Young was a Brooks County farmer, landowner, turpentine operator, merchant, banker, school-board president, postmaster, and railroad organizer. Friends called him Bully Young. He was born in Georgia on April 3, 1850 and died at his home near Nile on August 25, 1911. Huxford places his birth in Lowndes County, where the census found him as an infant before Brooks County existed. That county identification is strong probable rather than proved by a contemporary birth record. Original census, marriage, tax, postmaster, and cemetery records establish the identity behind the initials S. M. Young.[1-10]

Silas Morton Young. Portrait attached to Find a Grave memorial 211690535 by memorial contributor Kris. The memorial does not identify the original photographer or owner.

docs.title: Parents and childhood
docs.text:
The 1850 census lists him as the infant Silas "Yeung" in Lowndes County with Matthew and Emily Young and four older children. By 1860 the family was in the newly created Brooks County, where the index gives Silas contradictory age readings. The household continuity and later records identify him as the same child born in 1850.[1-2]

Huxford identifies his parents as Matthew Young and Emily Morton. Emily was a sister of James O. Morton, an early Brooks County official and banker. An 1870 legislative report also names James O. Morton as an executor settling with the minor Silas M. Young. A 1911 obituary says Young was reared by an uncle printed as Judge J. O. Martin, then calls that man Judge Morton in the next clause. The internal conflict and the family evidence point toward Morton, but the wording is not clean enough to treat the obituary as independent proof of the uncle's name. The county history traces both families much farther back, but those extended lines depend on compiled genealogy. This dossier treats the parents and local household chain as verified while leaving the earlier ancestry secondary.[10][22]

The original 1870 census places twenty-year-old Silas Young in the Quitman district. He worked as a farm laborer and reported $1,600 in personal property. He had not yet married.[3]

docs.title: Marriage and children
docs.text:
The original Brooks County marriage book corrects a long-repeated date. The license and minister's return both say that Silas M. Young and Ivey L. Johnson married on October 19, 1871. Huxford prints October 17. The original record controls.[4][10]

The 1880 census writes the household head as S. J. Young, and the index follows that form. His age, location, occupation, wife I. L., and children Mary A., Emily A., James A., Henry L., and infant B. identify the household as Silas Morton's. The middle initial is an enumerator error or aberrant rendering, not evidence of another man.[5]

Huxford names eight children: Mary Araminta, Henry Lane, Silas Morton Jr., Sarah Lavinia, William Briggs, Rachel Aleph, Emily Anna, and James Otis. The 1900 and 1910 censuses independently place William Briggs, Morton, Rachel, and Sarah or Lavinia in the household. The two children absent from the later schedules, Emily Anna and James Otis, reportedly died young.[7-8][10]

The 1911 obituaries name six surviving adult children. That does not contradict the eight-child family list. It reflects the deaths of Emily and James before their father.[22]

docs.title: Building the farm
docs.text:
Huxford says Young first bought a small farm, sold it in 1878, and then bought 1,000 acres about six miles north of Quitman. He added adjoining land and eventually held about 2,500 acres. A contemporary 1887 hailstorm report independently placed his farm about seven miles north of Quitman.[10-11]

The original 1890 Morven District tax digest supplies the first firm acreage figure. It records Silas M. Young with 2,000 acres valued at $8,000 and town property valued at $500. The entry appears to record ten farm hands, although its land-lot numerals need a closer archival reading before they are quoted.[6]

The 1900 census calls him a farmer who owned his farm free of mortgage. In 1910 he was a farmer and employer, again on a mortgage-free farm. A February 1911 county profile reported 2,000 acres in one body at Niles and another 500 acres at Morven. Huxford's total, the tax digest, and the newspaper can be reconciled as dated or rounded descriptions, but none should be treated as an exact deed inventory at death.[7-8][21]

The 1908 Brooks County map gives the home plantation a firmer location. It marks Young ownership in Land Lots 356, 357, and 381, with another Young tract in the northwest part of Lot 355. Lot 357 is labeled "Young (Timber)". The map places "S. M. Young Res." in the southwest corner of Lot 356, west of the Adel-Quitman Road and just north of Springhill School. These are map labels, not surveyed deed boundaries, so the map does not prove the exact acreage within each lot.[24]

docs.title: Farming, turpentine, and horses
docs.text:
Young's work extended beyond ordinary row-crop farming. An 1888 report placed a turpentine operation on his farm. In November 1890, two newspapers identified the turpentine still of S. M. Young & Co. about eighteen miles north of Quitman. The reports prove the firm and the operation but do not name the other partner or partners.[11]

An 1892 farming report credited him with cultivating sixty acres to the plow through improved methods and machinery. The figure describes a reported work rate, not the size of the farm.[13]

Horses were another interest. A newspaper used the nickname Bully Young in 1890 when reporting that his mare won a 350-yard race against a horse backed by Mitchell Brice. Later that year he joined J. W. Hopson, Brice, S. S. Rountree, L. T. Creech, and Fuller Groover as an incorporator of the Brooks County Trotting Association.[11-12]

docs.title: Banking and mercantile work
docs.text:
Young was elected a director of the Merchants and Farmers Bank at its February 4, 1896 annual meeting. Huxford's bank chronology also places him on the board in 1893. The state bank became the First National Bank of Quitman in 1905, and Young's 1911 obituary calls him a First National director. The later directorship is verified as reported, but no surviving board list found in this search fixes the date of his return or continuation after nationalization.[10][14][22]

He also entered the mercantile trade. In October 1896, D. R. Creech & Son filed mortgages that included one in Young's favor. The following day's report said the firm had sold its general-merchandise stock to him. The newspapers do not say how long he operated the business.[16]

Huxford's transcription of the Quitman Free Press business list for April 3, 1897 names "S. M. Young, Farm-supplies." This dated business listing identifies him as a farm-supplies dealer rather than only a planter who bought supplies.[17]

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Young helped organize the South Georgia Railroad but was not one of its first directors. Huxford places him on the county-at-large subscription committee appointed January 29, 1896. The committee covered the countryside while A. J. Rountree, Frank J. Spain, R. C. McIntosh, and John W. Hopson worked in Quitman.[15]

Huxford also names S. M. Young among the twenty-six petitioners for the charter. The first board and officer slate did not include him. No original charter petition, stock ledger, or subscription book was found online, so the committee and petitioner roles remain strong probable from the county history. His subscription amount, share count, right-of-way work, and any later railroad investment are unresolved.[15]

docs.title: Agricultural and political activity
docs.text:
Young took part in county agricultural organizing. In October 1900 he successfully moved that district committees be allowed to hire canvassers with teams to collect products for the Brooks County exhibit. This was practical organizing work, not an honorary listing.[18]

In 1897 he served on an advisory board for Valdosta's Harvest Celebration and Horse Swappers Convention. In June 1908, delegate lists identify S. M. Young of Nile among the Brooks County delegates to the state convention that nominated Joseph M. Brown for governor. These reports document public and political participation but not elective office.[20]

docs.title: School board and Masonry
docs.text:
The 1911 Macon obituary identifies Young as a member of the Brooks County Board of Education. Huxford's office roster is more precise: it places him on the board from July 1893 until his death and names him president for 1908-09. The roster is detailed secondary evidence because the original board minutes were not available online.[10][22]

Huxford also says Young belonged to Sholto Lodge No. 237, Free and Accepted Masons. No membership return or lodge record naming him was located in the accessible online sources. The affiliation is strong probable rather than independently verified.[10]

docs.title: Postmaster and the place-name problem
docs.text:
The federal postmaster register names Silas M. Young as postmaster at Nile, Brooks County, appointed August 13, 1903. Huxford gives the same date. Ancestry's derivative index says August 15, and an Atlanta Journal notice published on August 15 says he replaced Charles A. Crocker, who had resigned. The newspaper establishes the announcement date, not the appointment date. The original register controls.[19]

The newspapers sometimes place Young at Spain, Nile or Niles, and Morven. The evidence points to one person:

  • Young farmed north of Quitman by 1887.
  • A 1903 convention list used Spain as his post-office address.
  • The federal register and later newspapers place his postmastership and home at Nile.
  • The 1911 profile separates a 2,000-acre Niles tract from 500 acres at Morven.[11][19][21]

Spain was an address used in 1903, Nile was his post office and home area, and Morven referred to a district or separate holding. The records do not provide surveyed boundaries among the settlement, post office, militia district, and individual tracts.

Oliver B. Rogers received the Nile appointment in January 1912. A contemporary notice said he replaced Young, deceased. That supports Young's tenure until death, though it does not identify who handled the office during the five-month vacancy.[23]

docs.title: Illness, death, and burial
docs.text:
The Valdosta Daily Times reported on August 26, 1911 that Young had died the previous evening after a serious illness. It called him Bully Young, placed him in the Nile district, and estimated his age at about sixty-five. The next day's Macon Telegraph named him Silas Morton Young, gave his age as sixty-one, and said he died after cancer and several operations. The age of sixty-one agrees with the 1850 birth record and cemetery marker.[1][9][22]

The Macon report described a 2,000-acre plantation, while the February profile reported 2,000 acres at Niles plus 500 at Morven. The obituary may have counted the home plantation or rounded the estate. A probate inventory was not found, so the dossier preserves both figures.[21-22]

His photographed marker in Oak Hill Cemetery reads:

SILAS MORTON YOUNG APRIL 3, 1850 AUG. 25, 1911

Huxford says Ivy died March 15, 1931 and was buried there with him. Her original death certificate or marker was not inspected in this investigation.[9-10]

docs.title: Namesake control
docs.text:
The elder Silas must be separated from his son, usually called S. Morton Young or Silas Morton Young Jr. The younger man's residence burned in 1924, and he was murdered in 1926. Those events do not belong to the father's lifetime. A Find a Grave derivative record gives the son's birth as 1892, but the 1900 and 1910 censuses place his birth about 1882-83. The census evidence controls unless the son's own original vital record proves otherwise.[7-10]

The 1924 fire appears to connect the son to the father's mapped home. The Macon Telegraph called the burned residence a large country seat, a beautiful home for generations, and placed it eight miles from Quitman. The younger Silas was still in his father's household in 1910. Taken together with the 1908 residence label, this makes it strongly probable that the house marked in the southwest corner of Land Lot 356 later became the son's home and burned in 1924. The article does not give a land-lot number, so the identification remains strong probable rather than verified.[8][24-25]
