Method The project compares voter registers, censuses, pensions, compiled service records, military indexes, newspapers, cemetery material, and family records. A service claim must connect the soldier to the Barney-area person through identifying facts such as age, residence, family, occupation, or a direct pension or newspaper statement. “Research underway” means the current evidence is not strong enough to publish a service conclusion. It does not prove that the person did or did not serve.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
The project compares voter registers, censuses, pensions, compiled service records, military indexes, newspapers, cemetery material, and family records. A service claim must connect the soldier to the Barney-area person through identifying facts such as age, residence, family, occupation, or a direct pension or newspaper statement.

“Research underway” means the current evidence is not strong enough to publish a service conclusion. It does not prove that the person did or did not serve.

docs.title: Jesse Chambers
docs.text:
Jesse Chambers 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 Jesse Chambers was the young mechanic from the Barney neighborhood who married Nellie Bennett in Berrien County on March 17, 1898. 
 Barney connection  The contemporary marriage notice places Chambers in the Barney neighborhood. A Brooks County voter registration dated May 12, 1898, independently places him in the county soon after the marriage. 
 Census and civil record  The 1900 census records Jesse, wife Nellie, and daughter Osa Lee in Berrien County. The household and marriage record explain why he does not appear in the Barney enumeration. 
 Military review  Born about 1871-1873, Chambers was not Civil War eligible. No later military service was proved. 
 Evidence limits  The 1900 census gives a January 1871 birth, while the voter registration implies 1873. The discrepancy does not affect the spouse, marriage, and county chain. 
 Sources    1900 census, FamilySearch    Brooks County voter registration, FamilySearch

docs.title: Jeremiah Walton Folsom
docs.text:
Jeremiah Walton Folsom 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 Rev. J. W. Folsom of the Barney reports is identified as Jeremiah Walton Folsom, born about September 1855 in Georgia. 
 Barney connection  A Brooks County voter registration dated May 11, 1898, and contemporary reports of his Barney picnic and former Barney-district notary service connect him to the district. 
 Census and civil record  The 1860 Brooks census records Jeremiah W. Folsom. The 1880 Quitman census records J. Walton Folsom in the B. J. and Sarah E. Folsom household. In 1900 J. W. Folsom was a minister in Valdosta with wife M. C. and their children. 
 Family and settler connections 
 Jeremiah belonged to the Randal Folsom branch of the early Lowndes and Brooks County Folsom family. The reported line is: 
   Lawrence Folsom   →  Randal Folsom  →  Berry Jones Folsom  and Sarah Ellen Wilson →  Jeremiah Walton Folsom . 
 The 1860 and 1880 censuses directly place Jeremiah in Berry J. and Sarah E. Folsom's household. The earlier Berry-to-Randal-to-Lawrence line comes from the 1938  Genealogy of the Folsom Family . Local land, tax, church, and newspaper records independently establish Lawrence, Randal, and Berry in the region, but no reviewed original probate or deed names every parent-child step. The line above is therefore census-verified for Jeremiah and Berry and secondary-supported for the two earlier generations. 
  William Folsom , associated with the old Folsom plantation north of Barney, was reported as Randal's brother. On that evidence, William was Jeremiah's great-uncle, and William's daughter Edith Folsom Rountree was Jeremiah's first cousin once removed. These collateral relationships carry the same compiled-genealogy limitation. 
 Berry Jones Folsom was one of the trustees named in the 1856 Salem Methodist Church conveyance. Jeremiah's appearances in Barney records continued a family connection with Salem Church, Mount Zion, Little River, and the Folsom Bridge settlement neighborhood. 
 Military review  Born in 1855, Folsom was a child during the Civil War. No military service was proved. 
 Evidence limits  The FamilySearch Family Tree profile supplies expanded dates and names but has no attached sources. The census and voter records control this identification. 
 Sources    1900 census, FamilySearch    Brooks County voter registration, FamilySearch    1860 Brooks census, FamilySearch    1880 Quitman census, FamilySearch    Genealogy of the Folsom Family, revised 1938, vol. 2, pp. 866-869    Lawrence Folsom dossier    William Folsom dossier

docs.title: E. D. Ponder
docs.text:
E. D. Ponder 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 E. D. Ponder was the Brooks County coroner who conducted the 1901 inquest north of Barney. The 1880 census and repeated county tax entries establish him as a Quitman resident born about 1833. 
 Barney connection  Ponder's appearance in the Barney report arose from his county office. He was not a missing Barney householder. 
 Census and civil record  The 1880 Quitman census records E. D. Ponder with wife F. Ponder and their children. Repeated Brooks County tax entries preserve the same initials and locality. 
 Military review  An exact-name Georgia Confederate pension index in Brooks and Wilkinson counties confirms veteran status. The unit is not established by the index entry alone. 
 Evidence limits  The original pension images and compiled service record have not been inspected. His unit, enlistment, and discharge details therefore remain unresolved. 
 Sources    1880 Quitman census, FamilySearch    Georgia Confederate pension index, FamilySearch    Brooks tax digest, FamilySearch

docs.title: James Perry Peeples
docs.text:
James Perry Peeples 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Strong probable 
 The Perry Peeples named in Barney-area reports is strongly identified as James Perry Peeples, a Quitman stock dealer. The newspapers use Perry rather than James, so the identification remains strong probable rather than verified. 
 Barney connection  In February 1899, Peeples recognized S. L. Hall's stolen horse in Quitman and telephoned Barney. A separate December 1903 report names Perry Peeples in the shooting of Ed Cook at Barney. These reports establish repeated contact with Barney, not residence there. 
 Census and civil record  The 1900 census places James P. Peeples in Quitman with wife Emma and sons Herbert and Charley. The same family appears in 1910 under a badly corrupted index entry. No Peeples household appears in the Barney enumeration. 
 Military review  No military service was proved in the documented identity-linked searches. 
 Evidence limits  The newspapers do not print James. A contemporary record explicitly calling the Quitman stock dealer James Perry Peeples would make the identity verified. 
 Sources    Valdosta Times, February 7, 1899    1900 census, Ancestry record 52866146    1910 census, Ancestry record 3620720    Find a Grave memorial 11848016

docs.title: Michael Phillip Brogan
docs.text:
Michael Phillip Brogan 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 Michael Phillip Brogan was the man called White Brogan in the 1898 Barney wedding reports. The marriage year, spouse, later census records, occupation, and family record establish the identity. 
 Barney connection  The May 1898 reports describe White Brogan and Ida Bullard or Ballard as Barney people who married in Valdosta. The couple's stay at Barney was temporary or ended before the 1900 census. 
 Census and civil record  Michael and Ida May Brogan lived in Warrior, Colquitt County, in 1900 and 1910. Michael worked as a bookkeeper in the lumber or sawmill business. They were living in Ashburn by 1920. 
 Military review  Civil War service was impossible. No Spanish-American War service was proved in the documented search. 
 Evidence limits  The census ages imply a birth about 1868, while his cemetery memorial gives December 25, 1877. The age conflict remains unresolved but does not weaken the spouse, marriage-year, occupation, and household chain. 
 Sources    Savannah Morning News, May 26, 1898    1900 census, Ancestry record 8572096    1910 census, Ancestry record 3281901    1920 census, Ancestry record 86066770    Find a Grave memorial 92437975

docs.title: Ida May Bullard Brogan
docs.text:
Ida May Bullard Brogan 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 Ida May Bullard Brogan was the bride called Miss Bullard in one 1898 report and Ida Ballard in another. Later family and census records consistently support Bullard as her maiden surname. 
 Barney connection  The wedding reports place Ida in the Barney social circle when she married White Brogan at Valdosta in May 1898. She was not a missing Barney householder in 1900. 
 Census and civil record  Ida May and Michael Brogan lived in Warrior, Colquitt County, in 1900 and 1910 and in Ashburn in 1920. Their later family record identifies children Mildred, Michael Jr., Verna, and Davis. 
 Military review  No military or nursing service was alleged in the source or proved in later records. 
 Evidence limits  The original marriage return has not been inspected. Bullard is supported by later records, while Ballard is preserved as the conflicting newspaper form. 
 Sources    Savannah Morning News, May 26, 1898    1900 census, Ancestry record 8572096    1920 census, Ancestry record 86066770    Find a Grave memorial 92437964

docs.title: George Washington Prine Jr.
docs.text:
George Washington Prine Jr. 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 George Washington Prine Jr. was the G. W. Prine Jr. whose sudden death at Barney was reported in September 1898. 
 Barney connection  The reports say Prine died of heart failure at his Barney home on September 3, 1898. His remains were buried at Sparks, and the notices said he left a wife and four children or four little girls. 
 Census and civil record  Prine died before the 1900 enumeration, which explains the absence of a Prine household. The 1870 census and cemetery record identify him as a son of George Washington Prine. 
 Military review  Born in 1863, Prine was too young for normal Confederate service. He died during the Spanish-American War, and no service was proved. 
 Evidence limits  The memorial lists wife Catherine 'Cattie' Stalvey and five children, including an infant. That compiled family count does not exactly match the newspaper's four-child wording. 
 Sources    Tifton Gazette, September 9, 1898    Valdosta Times, September 13, 1898    Find a Grave memorial 52550971

docs.title: Robert Paxson
docs.text:
Robert Paxson 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Strong probable 
 Robert Paxson is strongly identified as the 1899 smallpox victim associated with Barney's milling economy and as a brother of Charles Dorothus Paxson. 
 Barney connection  A sequence of August and September 1899 reports uses Paxson, Paxon, and Paxton. The Atlanta report calls the patient R. Paxton and names C. D. Paxton as his brother. The broader Macon sequence supplies Robert. 
 Census and civil record  Robert died before the 1900 census. Charles Dorothus Paxson headed Barney household 197, providing the local family bridge. Robert's own age and complete civil record have not been recovered. 
 Military review  No service was proved. Robert's age is unknown, so same-name military records cannot be graded reliably. 
 Evidence limits  The identification rests on the unusual surname, brother C. D., event sequence, and Barney mill context. A death, probate, cemetery, or family record explicitly joining Robert and Charles would make it verified. 
 Sources    Atlanta Constitution, August 18, 1899    Charles D. Paxson household dossier

docs.title: Janie Joyce
docs.text:
Janie Joyce 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Strong probable 
 Janie Joyce, who died near Barney in September 1901, is strongly identified as the daughter of John Wesley P. Joyce and Catharine V. Harrington Joyce recorded in 1880 as infant Rachel J. Joyce. 
 Barney connection  The death notice calls Janie the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John Joyce and says she was buried at the old camp grounds near Morven. A cemetery record gives April 24, 1880 to September 28, 1901. 
 Census and civil record  The 1900 census records Jannie Joyce, born April 1880, as a niece in A. T. Cook's Valdosta household. The 1880 Brooks census records John and Catharine Joyce with one-month-old Rachel J. Joyce, whose age matches an April 1880 birth. 
 Military review  No military-service allegation applies to this civilian identity. 
 Evidence limits  The evidence does not explain whether Janie was a middle name, nickname, or later-used name for Rachel J. The exact birth timing and parent bridge are strong, but the unexplained name change prevents a verified grade. 
 Sources    Valdosta Times, October 5, 1901    1900 census, Ancestry record 9190737    1880 census, Ancestry record 8270331    Find a Grave memorial 53434676

docs.title: Jason W. Kendrick
docs.text:
Jason W. Kendrick 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Strong probable 
 Jason W. Kendrick is the strongest candidate for the J. W. Kendrick who served on the 1901 Will Dodson inquest jury. 
 Barney connection  The original newspaper names J. W. Kendrick as one of six jurors. It gives no age, occupation, or residence and does not connect him explicitly to the Hall & Kendrick business. 
 Census and civil record  J. W. Kendrick married Ruth F. Pike in Brooks County on January 3, 1894. In 1900 Jason Kendrick, born January 1872, lived with wife Ruth in Militia District 660. The shared wife, marriage duration, initials, and county identify Jason as the man using J. W. Kendrick. 
 Military review  Born in 1872, Kendrick was not Civil War eligible. No later service was proved in searches linked by Brooks County, wife Ruth, or birth year. 
 Evidence limits  No jury minute, business record, or newspaper item explicitly expands the juror's initials to Jason. The match is therefore strong probable. 
 Sources    Valdosta Times, May 21, 1901    Brooks County marriage, Ancestry record 282849    1900 census, Ancestry record 52857314

docs.title: Minnie A. McKinnon
docs.text:
Minnie A. McKinnon 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Strong probable 
 Minnie A. McKinnon is strongly identified as the Hahira teacher who went to Barney for the 1899–1900 school term. 
 Barney connection  The Valdosta Times said the school east of Barney would be in Miss Minnie McKinnon's hands. The Atlanta Constitution reported that Miss McKinnon of Hahira had gone to Barney to take charge of a school. 
 Census and civil record  The 1900 census records Minnie A. McKinnon in Hahira and Minnie McKennan in Dixie, Brooks County. Both entries give February 1873 as the birth month and year. The exact name, Hahira origin, and Barney-area presence strongly favor one woman enumerated twice. 
 Military review  No military-service allegation applies to this civilian teacher. 
 Evidence limits  The duplicate-enumeration and household relationship have not been joined by an original teacher license or family record. She is not Minnie Adelia Culbreth; the women had different ages, households, and teaching periods. 
 Sources    Valdosta Times, October 14, 1899    Atlanta Constitution, October 16, 1899    Hahira census, Ancestry record 9196556    Dixie census, Ancestry record 52870348

docs.title: Minnie Adelia Culbreth
docs.text:
Minnie Adelia Culbreth 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 Minnie Adelia Culbreth was the daughter and school assistant named with Professor Blackman Hawley Culbreth in Barney reports from 1901 and 1902. 
 Barney connection  The October 1901 report says Professor Culbreth and his daughter Minnie opened the Barney school. A July 1902 report again places Professor Culbreth at the school. 
 Census and civil record  The 1900 Berrien County census records teacher Blackman Culbreth, wife Adelia, and daughter Minnie A. Culbreth, age twenty. Name, father, occupation, age, and chronology establish the identity. 
 Military review  No military-service allegation applies to this civilian teacher. 
 Evidence limits  The available research establishes her identity and teaching role but does not yet reconstruct her complete later life.

docs.title: Lula S. Collingsworth Hall
docs.text:
Lula S. Collingsworth Hall 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified identity; strong probable school reference 
 Lula S. Collingsworth Hall was the wife of John Byron Hall in Barney household 46. She is the strong-probable identification for Huxford's private-school teacher Mrs. J. B. Hall. 
 Barney connection  John B. Hall and Lula S. Collingsworth married in Bibb County in June 1896. A contemporary announcement independently described Lula as a schoolteacher. The couple later lived at Barney. 
 Census and civil record  John and Lula Hall appear together in Barney in 1900 and remain identifiable in later Brooks County censuses. Lula's 1930 death certificate names John as her husband and Thomas M. Collingsworth and Sarah C. Maddox as her parents. 
 Military review  No military-service allegation applies to Lula. No service was proved for John Byron Hall. 
 Evidence limits  Lula's civil identity is verified. A surviving Barney teacher license or direct school notice is still needed to prove that Huxford's Mrs. J. B. Hall was Lula rather than relying on the unique local married-name match and her known teaching occupation. 
 Sources    John and Lula Hall household dossier    Savannah Morning News, February 14, 1904

docs.title: Isom Barney Ingram
docs.text:
Isom Barney Ingram 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Strong probable 
 Isom Barney Ingram is strongly identified as the I. B. Ingram who appeared in a 1903 Barney business report. 
 Barney connection  The report uses I. B. Ingram. The local farmer was commonly recorded as Isom Barney or Barney Ingram, producing the B. I./I. B. initial-order conflict that prevents a verified grade. 
 Census and civil record  The 1900 census records him as Benny Ingram, age thirty-five, farmer, in Barney household 168. The household and later local research establish the civil identity even though the newspaper initials are reversed. 
 Military review  Born about 1864, he was too young for ordinary Confederate service. No later service was proved. 
 Evidence limits  A deed, tax entry, business record, or second newspaper using I. B. for Isom Barney Ingram would resolve the initial-order problem. 
 Sources    Isom Barney Ingram household dossier

Elias P. S. Denmark 
  Back to the contemporary-reports table  
  Identity grade:  Verified 
 Elias P. S. Denmark was the Valdosta attorney and public speaker identified as E. P. S. Denmark in the 1902 Barney school program. 
 Barney connection  The April 1902 program lists Denmark as a visiting education speaker. His appearance was civic and educational; it does not make him a Barney resident or a missing census householder. 
 Census and civil record  Denmark belonged to Valdosta's legal and public community. His absence from the Barney household enumeration is expected because the newspaper describes a visit for the school program. 
 Military review  No military service was found or alleged in the source. He belonged to the post-Civil War generation. 
 Evidence limits  This dossier documents the identity and Barney appearance. A fuller professional biography would require separate legal-directory, obituary, and court-record research. 
 Sources    Valdosta Times school-program reporting

docs.title: Public Analysis
docs.text:
The 1900 census captures Barney just before incorporation, with 992 people in 201 households. Household size ranged from 1 to 13 people, with an average of 4.9 people per household. The record shows a working sawmill, railroad, farm, mercantile, and turpentine community tied together by kinship, boarding arrangements, and labor networks.

The relationship counts show why household pages matter: the census includes children, spouses, extended kin, boarders, employees, servants, and neighbors whose later records often explain how Barney families connected across surnames. Age and name readings remain tied to the source notes on the household pages where the encyclopedia flags uncertain handwriting or later-record conflicts.

docs.title: James Rountree
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: Online research dossier
docs.text: Prepared: August 18, 2026 Subject: James Rountree, early settler of southern Irwin and original Lowndes County, Georgia Research purpose: Identify the man later counted among Lowndes County's first four permanent white settlers; test that tradition against original records; and document his family, land, household, public role, death, estate, and connection to later Brooks County and Barney families.

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
James Rountree was an early South Georgia landowner whose record trail runs from Pulaski County into the portion of Irwin County that became original Lowndes County in 1825. An original 1820 census image places his household in Pulaski County. Reported deed-book citations say he bought Irwin County Land Lots 497 and 516, District 9, in 1821. The deed images were not available for fresh inspection, so those purchases remain precise, high-value leads rather than fully reverified facts.[1-4]

The claim that Rountree, Lawrence Folsom, Drew Vickers, and Alfred Belote were Lowndes County's first four settlers is a genuine local-history tradition, but not a contemporary 1821 finding. The earliest fully inspectable source found that names all four is William Harden's 1913 history. It says they explored southern Irwin County in 1815 and later returned with their families as the first permanent white settlers of Lowndes, especially its northern portion. Folks Huxford repeated the quartet in 1922 and supplied an 1821 settlement date, relying chiefly on then-recent newspaper sketches by Hortense W. Baker that have not been located.[5-6]

Earlier newspapers show that the tradition was already circulating. An 1888 Valdosta Times reminiscence called Rountree the builder of the first house in Lowndes County, while an 1890 article said an elderly formerly enslaved woman named Clara had come to the county with its first settlers as a person enslaved by him.[7-8] Those recollections strengthen the tradition's age, but they were published more than fifty years after Rountree's death. An 1899 county sketch gave a conflicting chronology, naming Washington Joyce's 1824 place as the first white settlement in present Lowndes County.[9]

The careful conclusion is that James Rountree was one of four men repeatedly identified in old local histories as the first permanent Euro-American settler group of original Lowndes County. His presence in the region by the early 1820s is strongly supported, but the exact 1815 expedition and 1821 family migration remain unverified. “First permanent white settlers” is the later sources' terminology; it does not mean the land was previously uninhabited and should not erase the Native peoples who occupied South Georgia before American settlement.[5-6]

James married Nancy Hendley in Pulaski County on March 6, 1823, as shown by the original license and return.[10-11] Contemporary newspapers establish that he was murdered on March 26, 1834, while camped on the Thomasville-Tallahassee road in Leon County, Florida. A Lowndes estate-administration notice followed in July.[12-17] His likely birth year, parents, first wife's identity, complete child list, final burial place, and estate distribution are not established by original records located online.

docs.title: The pioneer and his name forms
docs.text:
The records use several spellings: James Rountree, Roundtree, Rowntree, and Rauntree. Place, date, associates, and family context—not spelling alone—control the identification. The subject of this dossier is the adult Pulaski County householder of 1820, Nancy Hendley's husband in 1823, the early Lowndes juror of 1833, and the Lowndes resident killed in Florida in 1834.[1,10-17]

Later genealogies commonly give his life span as about 1787 to March 26, 1834 and call him a Burke County son of William F. Rountree and Rachel. No birth record, Bible entry, baptism, probate record, or parent-naming deed was found to verify the year, birthplace, or parents. The original 1830 census cannot settle his age because the entry long indexed as James is actually Jesse Townsend.[18-20]

docs.title: People who must not be merged with him
docs.text:
• James Lester Rountree (1823-1905), usually identified as his son, lived long after the pioneer died.[21-22]
  • James Rountree Folsom (1831-1896) was a different man in the related Folsom family.
  • Francis Rountree, enumerated separately in Lowndes County in 1830, may have been related, but the census states no relationship.[19]
  • Later Brooks and Lowndes County Rountrees cannot be attached to the pioneer by surname alone.

The middle name Lester should not be assigned to the pioneer. It belongs securely to the younger James in later records and appears for the elder James only in derivative online trees.

docs.title: Source lineage
docs.text:
Harden's 1913 county biography is the earliest fully inspectable source located that names the quartet. It says James Rountree, Lawrence Armstrong Folsom, Drew Vickers, and Alfred Belote explored southern Irwin County in 1815, obtained land, returned for their families, and became the first permanent white settlers of Lowndes County.[5]

Huxford's 1922 quarterly names the same four families but dates their move to 1821. The article says its information came chiefly from Hortense W. Baker's Valdosta Times historical sketches. No Baker article, interview notes, or earlier manuscript was located, so the sharper 1821 date cannot be treated as original evidence.[6]

The 1888 Valdosta Times reminiscence predates both books and says the first house in Lowndes County was built by James “Roundtree” on land later owned by West and James. It does not name the quartet or date the construction.[7] The 1890 Clara article likewise places Rountree among the first settlers, but its principal subject was Clara's life, not a formal county chronology.[8]

R. E. L. Folsom's 1899 sketch conflicts with the quartet chronology by identifying Washington Joyce's 1824 home and ferry as the first white settlement in present Lowndes County.[9] Geography explains part of the disagreement: original Lowndes was much larger than today's county. The conflicting accounts still show why a precise “first” ranking cannot be proved from the later narratives alone.

Finding: strong for an old and repeated tradition; probable for Rountree's permanent settlement in the region by the early 1820s; unresolved for the 1815 scouting trip and exact 1821 household move.

docs.title: Origins, land, and migration
docs.text:
A modern synthesis preserving Robert Jeffries's research reports that Rountree bought Telfair County Lots 318 and 319, District 14, on June 27, 1808; appeared in the 1811 Pulaski tax digest with land in several counties and four enslaved people; and held 405 acres and eight enslaved people in 1818. The cited deed and tax images were not obtained, so these entries remain reported abstracts.[3]

The original 1820 census establishes a James Rountree household in Pulaski County.[1-2] Jeffries's abstracts then place “James Rountree of Pulaski County” in two Irwin County purchases:

  • March 6, 1821: Land Lot 497, District 9, from Kinchen P. Tyson of Jones County for $220, reported as Irwin Deed Book A, page 27.
  • October 16, 1821: Land Lot 516, District 9, from Joseph Barr of Franklin County for $200, reported as Irwin Deed Book A, page 25.[3-4]

These exact citations make the deeds reproducible courthouse targets. They support an early move toward original Lowndes, but they do not by themselves prove when James built a house or brought his family. His March 1823 Pulaski marriage shows that he retained an active connection there after buying the Irwin land.[10-11]

The 1830 Lowndes tax digest reportedly taxed James for Lots 451, 497, and 516, District 9, with his home plantation on Lots 497 and 516.[3] The digest image was not located. The lots lie in old Lowndes County, not the later town of Barney; their relevance to Barney is genealogical through descendants, not because James lived in the future town.

docs.title: 1820 Pulaski County census
docs.text:
The original image shows James Rountree as the head of a Pulaski County household. The clearest fresh reading of the column marks is:

  • one free white male age 26-44;
  • one free white male under ten;
  • three free white females under ten;
  • no adult free white female;
  • nine enslaved people: two males under 14, two males 14-25, three females under 14, one female 14-25, and one female 26-44;
  • six people engaged in agriculture; fourteen people total.[1-2]

Published and derivative readings sometimes give ten enslaved people. Ancestry also exposes a duplicate or misaligned index entry that produces a different total. Because the original image's tightly spaced tally marks are difficult and the derivative indexes conflict, nine is the best fresh image reading, not an unquestionable total. The dossier preserves the disagreement rather than silently choosing the most repeated number.[1-3]

The absence of an adult white woman is consistent with the family tradition that James's unidentified first wife had died by 1820. It does not prove widowhood or name the four children.

docs.title: 1830 census correction
docs.text:
A derivative Lowndes census transcription long printed household 257 as “James Rowntree - 4 M, 7 F.” High-resolution inspection of the original NARA schedule shows that the name is Jesse Townsend, not James Rountree.[18-19] The supposed 1830 James household must be removed from the evidence chain.

The original schedule does show Francis Rountree at household 84, but it gives no relationship to James.[19] James's absence as a clearly identified head remains unexplained. Tax evidence, if the original digest is obtained, may clarify whether he was omitted, counted elsewhere, or represented under a damaged or misread name.

docs.title: Clara
docs.text:
The 1890 Valdosta Times article about “Auntie Clara” said she came to Lowndes with the first settlers while enslaved by James Rountree. After his death, the article said, she was “hired” by one of his daughters, whose married name appears in the OCR as Mrs. Linton. Clara later went to Palatka, Florida, after emancipation, bought land and an orange grove, and was described as independent in her eightieth year.[8]

This account is important because it remembers an enslaved person as an individual rather than only a census tally. It is still a late newspaper recollection; Clara's full name, the daughter's identity, and the exact wording of the faint original article need further verification. The apparent daughter “Mrs. Linton” also does not fit the standard compiled child lists and must not be forced into them.

docs.title: Unidentified first wife
docs.text: No marriage record or name was found for James's first wife. Later family reconstructions assign five children to her: John, Harriet, Nancy, Weston W., and Henrietta. They usually explain the four young children in the 1820 household by saying John died before enumeration. The census names nobody, and no located estate or guardianship record proves that reconstruction.[1-3]

docs.title: Nancy Hendley
docs.text:
The original Pulaski County marriage license and return are clear. The license authorized the marriage of James Rountree and Nancy Hendly on March 5, 1823; W. B. McGehee, justice of the peace, solemnized it on March 6, 1823.[10-11]

This corrects two derivative errors. Some indexes turn March 6 into May 6, and a 1976 compiled family article gives 1811. The original record controls.[10-11,23]

Later accounts identify Nancy as a daughter of William Hendley and give her birth as April 22, 1793. The marriage record does not name her parents. Children commonly assigned to James and Nancy are James Lester, Annie B., and Georgia Ann. Their placement is repeated across compiled genealogies and collaborative profiles, but no complete estate distribution or guardianship packet was found naming all of them.[21-23]

The 1976 family article is especially cautionary: it gives James's death as 1837 and his marriage as 1811, both contradicted by contemporary or original evidence. Its child list is useful as a research lead, not proof.[23]

docs.title: Civic record
docs.text: Direct newspaper reprints of the 1833 Lowndes County grand-jury presentments include James Rountree among the jurors.[24-26] This is the strongest located proof of a public role. No reliable evidence was found that he held elected office, militia rank, church trusteeship, or War of 1812 service. Those roles should not be borrowed from the other early settlers.

docs.title: Murder on the Tallahassee road
docs.text:
James Rountree was killed in Leon County, Florida, on the night of March 26, 1834. The contemporary reports form a short but coherent chain:

  1. The Georgia Courier of April 4 reported that a Mr. Rountree's body had been found near the Georgia line and that robbery was suspected.[12]
  2. The Southern Recorder of April 16 named him as James Rowntree, a Lowndes County resident. It said he was murdered at night while camped on the road from Tallahassee to Thomasville and that three Black men were suspected, one already apprehended.[13]
  3. The Georgia Constitutionalist of April 18 said Florida's governor offered $200 and Tallahassee citizens another $200 for two fugitives charged with the murder.[14]

These reports verify the death, general place, travel route, and reward. They do not prove the suspects' guilt. They also do not say that James was returning from salt works, despite that detail in later retellings.

A later historical quotation from an 1837 Tallahassee Floridian item names Joe and Crittenden and gives robbery as the supposed motive.[27] The original 1837 newspaper page was not located. Later accounts connect the killing to Florida's Regulators and vigilante violence; those retrospective narratives should not be treated as a proved trial record.[28]

No conviction, acquittal, execution, pardon, or complete court file was found. The safest account stops where the contemporary evidence stops.

docs.title: Estate, death date, and burial
docs.text:
The Federal Union published a Lowndes legal notice on July 23, 1834, stating that James McMullin had applied for letters of administration on the estate of James Rountree, deceased. William Smith, clerk of the court of ordinary, had issued the notice July 8; it was repeated through August.[15-17]

The notice verifies that James was dead and that administration was being opened. It does not name a widow, children, land, enslaved people, creditors, or distributees. No full probate packet, inventory, appraisal, sale, guardian return, or final distribution was located online.

The contemporary death date is March 26, 1834.[12-14] Find a Grave and Ancestry's derivative memorial index repeat a Tallahassee-area death but provide no photographed marker or cemetery register for James.[29] His burial place remains unresolved.

docs.title: Connection to later Brooks County and Barney families
docs.text:
The best-supported route is:

"James Rountree (d. 1834)" → "Weston/West W. Rountree (about 1815-1895)" → "Henrietta Elizabeth Rountree Joyce and other children" → later Brooks County and Barney Rountree/Joyce households.

The critical first step is now strong probable. A transcription of West Rountree's February 15, 1895 Tifton Gazette obituary explicitly calls James his father and says West and his brother James lived on their father's Lowndes place. The same obituary names West's daughter Mrs. Elizabeth Joyce and sons James W., George F., Noel L., William F., and Hardy V. Rountree.[30] The original newspaper image has not been obtained, so the transcription cannot yet carry a fully verified grade.

The 1850 Lowndes census independently places Weston with Eda/Edith and children Henrietta E. and James W.[31] This supports the household structure, while later records identify Henrietta Elizabeth as the wife of William Washington Joyce. Their descendants connect directly to the Joyce family around Barney. William F. Rountree also appears among successful farmers near Barney in the 1899 town profile.[9,30-31]

Thus James is a strong-probable ancestor of the later Barney Rountree-Joyce cluster. The missing controlling document is James's own probate, guardian, or parent-child deed naming Weston.

docs.title: Conflicts and cautions
docs.text:
1. Birth and parents: about 1787, Burke County, William F. Rountree, and Rachel all come from later genealogies, not located original proof.[3,23,29]
  2. First-settler date: Harden gives an 1815 exploration; Huxford gives an 1821 move; neither cites a contemporary record.[5-6]
  3. 1820 slavery count: the original image is difficult; the best fresh reading is nine, while published accounts say ten.[1-3]
  4. 1830 census: the alleged James entry is Jesse Townsend. Any dossier or tree using “4 males, 7 females” for James should be corrected.[18-19]
  5. Marriage: March 6, 1823 is original-record proof; May 6 and 1811 are derivative errors.[10-11,23]
  6. Children: the standard lists are reconstructions. No located estate record names a complete set, and the 1890 Clara article creates an unresolved daughter-name conflict.[8,21-23]
  7. Murder: contemporary sources prove the death and accusations, not guilt, trial outcome, a salt-works destination, or later vigilante narratives.[12-14,27-28]
  8. Burial: no verified grave or marker was found.[29]
  9. Barney connection: strong probable through Weston's 1895 obituary transcription; James's own probate remains the missing direct link.[30-31]

docs.title: Research coverage and negative findings
docs.text:
The investigation began with stored Barney, Lowndes, early-settler, genealogy, land-lot, census, and newspaper research. It then used two independent research lanes: genealogy/official records and newspapers/local history. Name variants included Rountree, Roundtree, Rowntree, Rauntree, and “Jas.” paired with Pulaski, Irwin, Lowndes, Telfair, Burke, Nancy Hendley, Weston, Francis, Lots 497/516, probate, jury, murder, grave, and Tallahassee.

Fresh logged-in Ancestry work inspected the 1820 census, the 1823 marriage, a 1834 tax-index entry, the Find a Grave index, and a 1976 compiled family-history image. Internet Archive supplied original federal schedules and the Harden and Huxford volumes. Georgia Historic Newspapers supplied direct 1833-1834 newspaper pages. Newspapers.com supplied the 1890 and 1899 Valdosta Times images; the 1888 item was available only through a public transcription. FamilySearch, WikiTree, Find a Grave, Ray City History, Georgia Archives, and JSTOR were used for record leads and derivative continuity, with their limits stated.

No original image was obtained for the 1808 Telfair deeds, 1811/1818 Pulaski tax digests, 1821 Irwin deeds, 1830 Lowndes tax digest, 1895 Weston obituary, James's probate packet, a grave marker, or a court disposition in the murder case. No verified military, church, officeholding, or War of 1812 record was found.

docs.title: Best next records
docs.text:
1. Obtain Irwin Deed Book A, pages 25 and 27, and verify the grantors, dates, consideration, recording dates, witnesses, and exact lot descriptions.
  2. Inspect the original 1811/1818 Pulaski and 1830/1834 Lowndes tax digests, including enslaved-person columns and estate timing.
  3. Locate James's Lowndes probate/administration packet, inventories, sales, guardian returns, and final distribution. This is the best route to his children and the names of enslaved people.
  4. Obtain the February 15, 1895 Tifton Gazette image for West Rountree's obituary.
  5. Search Leon County and territorial Florida court, jail, reward, governor, and clemency files for Joe, Crittenden, and the unnamed third suspect.
  6. Identify Hortense W. Baker's Valdosta Times sketches and determine whether she used family papers, interviews, or an earlier manuscript.
  7. Reopen the 1890 Clara article at full resolution and trace Clara and the apparent Mrs. Linton in Palatka records.
  8. Search for a cemetery register, grave survey, or contemporary burial reference for James.

docs.title: Citation audit note
docs.text: Original records, contemporary reports, later recollections, compiled genealogy, collaborative profiles, and modern memorials are labeled separately. Repetition does not turn a later tradition into independent proof. The 1830 census error, 1820 tally conflict, uncertain parentage, incomplete child proof, unadjudicated murder accusations, missing probate, and unresolved burial remain visible rather than being silently harmonized.

docs.title: Lawrence Folsom
docs.text: Back to the Early History Profiles index

docs.title: Online research dossier
docs.text: Prepared: August 18, 2026 Subject: Lawrence Folsom, early settler of southern Irwin and original Lowndes County, Georgia Research purpose: Identify the man later called Lawrence Armstrong Folsom, test the tradition that he belonged to Lowndes County's first four settler families, and document his land, family, public, religious, and community record without merging him with later Folsoms.

docs.title: Bottom line
docs.text:
Lawrence Folsom was among the earliest documented settlers in the part of southern Irwin County that became Lowndes County in 1825. The first original record located for him is a recorded deed dated November 27, 1823. Newman Pounds sold Lawrence Folsom of Irwin County all 490 acres of Land Lot 187, 12th District, for $268. The deed was recorded December 31, 1823.[1-3]

The familiar claim that he was one of Lowndes County's first four settlers is supported as an old local-history tradition, not as a proved 1821 event. The earliest inspectable quartet account found is William Harden's 1913 county biography. It groups Lawrence with James Rountree, Drew Vickers, and Alfred Belote, says they explored the region in 1815, and calls their families the first permanent white settlers of Lowndes, especially its northern portion.[4] Folks Huxford's 1922 quarterly gives the sharper date of 1821, but credits much of its information to then-recent newspaper sketches by Hortense W. Baker whose underlying article and sources were not located.[5] “First permanent white settlers” is the later sources' Euro-American settlement terminology; it is not evidence that the land was previously uninhabited.

The safest conclusion is that Lawrence was one of four men repeatedly identified in early twentieth-century histories as the first permanent settler group of original Lowndes County. His early presence is independently verified by the 1823 deed and by his appointment as a county-site commissioner in December 1825. The exact 1815 scouting trip and 1821 family migration remain unverified.[1-5]

The contemporary records reviewed call him Lawrence Folsom. The identification with the later-named Lawrence Armstrong Folsom, husband of Rachel Vickers and ancestor of the local Folsom family, is strong probable rather than strictly verified because no reviewed original record uses the middle name. His likely life span is about 1772-1775 to April 11, 1842, but the exact birth year and birthplace remain disputed.[4,6-10]

docs.title: Contemporary Lawrence and the later middle name
docs.text:
The identity chain is persuasive:

  • The 1823 deed names Lawrence Folsom of Irwin County and places him on Lot 187 east of Little River.[1-3]
  • A public transcription of the 1830 Lowndes census lists a Lawrence Folsom household with three males and three females.[11-12]
  • Later local and family histories consistently describe Lawrence Armstrong Folsom as the Burke-to-Pulaski-to-Lowndes migrant who married Rachel Vickers, settled near Little River, and died in Lowndes.[4,6-10]
  • A contemporary 1893 account says James Folsom inherited his father's lands and that James's children later divided them. The 1938 genealogy identifies James as Lawrence's youngest son, creating a strong, though partly derivative, land-and-family chain.[8,13]

No inspected deed, census entry, legislative record, or church deed gives Lawrence the middle name Armstrong. The dossier therefore uses Lawrence Folsom for original-record claims and treats Lawrence Armstrong Folsom as the strong-probable later identification.

docs.title: Namesakes and related men
docs.text:
Lawrence must be kept separate from:

  • William "Uncle Billy" Folsom, a son in the compiled genealogy who became a large landholder west of Little River.[8]
  • Randal or Randall Folsom, another early local Folsom and later public figure.[8]
  • James Folsom, the son who reportedly inherited Lawrence's lands.[8,13]
  • Elijah, John, Maston, and other Folsoms appearing in the 1830 census and later histories.[8,11]

Shared surname, neighborhood, or land use is not enough to merge these men.

docs.title: What the sources actually say
docs.text:
Harden's 1913 A History of Savannah and South Georgia is the earliest fully inspectable source located that names the quartet. In a biography of Ashley Lawson and his wife Cynthia Folsom, it says Lawrence Armstrong Folsom, James Rountree, Drew Vickers, and Alfred Belote explored southern Irwin County in 1815, acquired land, returned for their families, and became "the first permanent white settlers of Lowndes county, more especially of its northern portion."[4] Two details warn against reading it literally: its statement that they acquired “government land” conflicts with Lawrence's verified private purchase from Newman Pounds, and its statement that they returned to Brooks County uses a county name that did not exist until 1858.

Huxford's 1922 South Georgia Historical and Genealogical Quarterly states that the same four men and their families moved in 1821 and were the first settlers of what it called the present county of Lowndes. The article says its data came chiefly from Hortense W. Baker's recent Valdosta Times sketches. No direct 1821 record or Baker source note was found.[5]

These sources preserve a credible early-settlement tradition, but they were written roughly ninety years after the events. The 1823 deed is the earliest original proof located for Lawrence in the region.[1-5]

docs.title: Conflicting 1899 chronology
docs.text:
R. E. L. Folsom's 1899 Valdosta Times "Historic Sketch of Lowndes County" gives a different sequence. It calls Washington Joyce's 1824 home and ferry the first white settlement in present Lowndes County and places Drew Vickers and Lawrence Folsom next.[14] That account conflicts with Lawrence's verified November 1823 land purchase.

The geographic wording explains part, but not all, of the disagreement. The quartet tradition makes the most sense for original Lowndes County, which was much larger than today's county. The 1899 sketch explicitly discusses present Lowndes and Joyce's east-bank settlement at the later Miller Bridge. Even so, the conflict shows that none of the later narratives should be treated as a precise arrival calendar.

Finding: strong for the existence and membership of the tradition; probable for permanent settlement in the early 1820s; unresolved for the 1815 trip and exact 1821 arrival.

docs.title: Origins, marriage, and children
docs.text:
Elizabeth Knowles Folsom's 1938 Genealogy of the Folsom Family identifies Lawrence as a son of William Folsom and Sally Armstrong. It says he was born in Burke County, while preserving another informant's statement that he was a North Carolina native. The book gives his birth only as about 1775; modern collaborative profiles usually use 1772. No contemporary birth or parent-naming record was found.[8-10]

The same genealogy says he married Rachel Vickers, daughter of Jonathan Vickers, in Burke County, and gives her death as December 18, 1849, in Lowndes County. Huxford reportedly described Rachel as Drew Vickers's sister, but other researchers have not independently confirmed that relationship. The marriage is strong probable; Rachel's precise parentage and her relationship to Drew remain derivative.[7-10]

The 1938 genealogy lists eight children: William, Randal, John, Elijah, Maston, Cynthia, Elizabeth, and James.[8] Harden's 1913 account lists nine: William, John, Maston, Randall, James, Elijah, Cynthia, Rachael, and Betsy.[4] Collaborative online trees also disagree and sometimes duplicate children. The dossier does not flatten these into a definitive list.

The cleanest working reconstruction is the 1938 eight-child list, labeled compiled and conflict-aware. James receives stronger contextual support from the 1893 inheritance article, although that article itself does not name his father.[8,13]

docs.title: Migration and household evidence
docs.text:
The 1938 genealogy says Lawrence moved from Burke County to Pulaski County in 1808 and later to Lowndes County.[8] The 1913 history adds the 1815 exploration narrative.[4] Both are retrospective.

The first firm date is November 27, 1823, when Lawrence was described as a resident of Irwin County in the Lot 187 deed.[1-3] Lowndes County did not yet exist; it was created from Irwin on December 23, 1825.[5,15]

The public 1830 census transcription lists Lawrence Folsom - 3 M, 3 F.[11] It compresses the original schedule to sex totals and does not preserve age columns or household-level enslaved-person details. The NARA microfilm is freely available online, but it has no usable text layer and Lawrence's exact image was not identified during this investigation.[12] The transcription confirms a household only at a derivative level.

The derivative land/tax KML places Lawrence in District 12 Lot 182 in 1830, 1834, 1835, 1838, and 1840, and Lot 187 in 1830, 1834, 1835, and 1838. It places Drewry Vickers on Lot 187 by 1838/1840 and James Folsom on Lots 182 and 187 in 1844.[16] The Lot 187 deed is original-record proof; the tax years and Lot 182 remain derivative until their digest images are inspected.

docs.title: The Lot 187 deed
docs.text:
FamilySearch DGS 008032657, images 50-51, preserves the recorded instrument. Newman Pounds of Gwinnett County sold Lawrence Folsom of Irwin County all 490 acres of Land Lot 187, 12th District, for $268. The deed was executed November 27, 1823 and recorded December 31. It says Pounds's state grant was dated November 17, 1823. John Durham and W. B. McGehee, J.P., witnessed it; Pounds signed by mark.[1-3]

A clerk's note says the instrument was transcribed from Book B, pages 65-66, on February 7, 1827. This corrects three derivative errors: the grantor was Newman, not Norman, Pounds; the deed date was November 27, not December 27; and the state grant date was November 17, not November 7.[1-3]

Lots 182 and 187 lie east of Little River in the later Folsom Bridge neighborhood. The deed proves Lawrence's ownership of Lot 187, not the exact footprint of his house.[16-17]

docs.title: Folsom Bridge caution
docs.text:
No contemporary source says the bridge was named for Lawrence. His verified and indexed landholdings, together with the later family-land chain through James Folsom's children, make the surrounding Folsom settlement the strongest geographic source of the name.[13,16-17]

The Folsom Bridge history brings together the settlement, naming, map, road, and bridge evidence.

The defensible conclusion is that the bridge probably took its name from the Folsom family settlement. Lawrence is the leading individual candidate, but the namesake remains unresolved.

docs.title: County-site commissioner
docs.text:
Lowndes County was created December 23, 1825. A separate organizing act approved December 24 appointed Lawrence Folsom, Sion Hall, William Blair, John J. Underwood, and Daniel McCranie to select a public site for the new county. Elections and courts were to remain at Sion Hall's house until a site was chosen.[15]

This appointment shows that Lawrence was an established public figure by the county's creation. No reviewed source shows that he later served as sheriff, clerk, Inferior Court justice, legislator, tax officer, or county surveyor.

docs.title: Mount Zion
docs.text:
Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 reminiscence names Lawrence among the seven first tenters at Mount Zion, with William Blair, William Hendry, John Hendry, Rev. Joshua Platt, Sharpe, and John Pike. The newspaper OCR reads the first meeting's year as 1829, while Huxford's later transcription reads 1828. The original image needs a close visual read before selecting between them.[18]

Lawrence's trusteeship is firmer. Huxford printed a transcription he said he made from the original November 8, 1831 deed. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed about six acres on Land Lot 271, including the existing camps, church, and burying ground, to Methodist Episcopal trustees William Blair, William Hendry, Lawrence Folsom, James J. Joyce, and William G. Hall. The title reverted if the property ceased to be used for worship. The county copy was lost in the courthouse fire and was never re-recorded.[15,19]

Finding: verified through Huxford's original-based transcription that Lawrence was a Mount Zion trustee in 1831; strong for his participation among the first tenters, with the exact year unresolved.

docs.title: Militia and community logistics
docs.text:
A letter written by Lasa Adams in 1893 and published in the Valdosta Times in 1895 recalled 1836 militia operations near Little River. Adams said men were sent to tell Capt. Jonathan C. Hawthorn to come down and draw supplies at Lawrence Folsom's place.[15] The account shows that the farm was established and capable of provisioning militia in the region. It does not prove that Lawrence held military command or a formal quartermaster office.

A separate later claim says Lawrence was commissioned an ensign in the Burke County militia on January 23, 1799.[7] The underlying commission was not located. If correct, this was peacetime Georgia militia service. No War of 1812 record, pension, or bounty-land file for Lawrence was found, so he should not be described as a War of 1812 veteran.

docs.title: Death, estate, and burial
docs.text:
The 1938 genealogy gives Lawrence's death as April 11, 1842, says he left his farm to youngest son James, and places both men in a family burial lot on the farm. These statements are attributed to family informant Mrs. Boyd and lack a will-book citation or marker transcription.[8]

A FamilySearch collaborative-profile note reportedly says Lawrence's will was probated in 1850 with William Folsom as executor. No will, probate index entry, letters testamentary, inventory, appraisal, return, or executor deed was located online. The eight-year gap after the stated death and proximity to Rachel's reported 1849 death make the story possible but not record-proved.[9]

The missing estate record may not survive, but this investigation did not locate a record-loss inventory establishing what happened to Lawrence's specific probate papers. Until a private copy, later deed recital, loose file, or church paper is found, statements about the devise must remain attributed to the 1938 genealogy.

Find a Grave memorial 64843909 gives 1772-April 11, 1842 and cites Old Folsom Family Cemetery near Hahira.[10] The accessible memorial text did not expose a marker image. The cemetery name and date are useful derivative evidence, not original grave proof.

docs.title: Evidence grades

docs.title: Conflicts and cautions
docs.text:
1. Birth: sources range from about 1772 to about 1775 and conflict between Virginia, Burke County, Georgia, and North Carolina.[4,8-10]
  2. Middle name: Armstrong appears in later histories, not in the reviewed contemporary records.[1,11,15,19]
  3. Settlement date: the 1913 history gives an 1815 exploratory trip; the 1922 history gives an 1821 family move; neither has been verified from an original record.[4-5]
  4. 1899 contradiction: R. E. L. Folsom placed Lawrence after Washington Joyce's 1824 settlement, while Lawrence's deed is dated 1823.[1,14]
  5. Children: the 1913 and 1938 lists differ, and collaborative trees add more conflicts.[4,8-9]
  6. Tax years: the public KML lists Lawrence on Lot 182 through 1840 but on Lot 187 only through 1838; the digest images remain unverified.[16]
  7. Estate: no original will or probate file was found, and the fate of Lawrence's specific probate papers is unknown.[8-9]
  8. Burial: the family-lot and Old Folsom Family Cemetery descriptions may refer to the same place, but no photographed marker or contemporary burial register was reviewed.[8,10]
  9. Slavery: the 1830 transcription omits household-level enslaved-person columns. This dossier does not assign Lawrence a specific number without the original schedule or tax image.[11-12]

docs.title: Research coverage and negative findings
docs.text:
This investigation searched stored Barney, Folsom Bridge, Coffee Road, Mount Zion, road, genealogy, census, and newspaper evidence before broader online sources. The name forms included "Lawrence Folsom", "Laurence Folsom", "L. Folsom", and "Lawrence Armstrong Folsom", with Rachel Vickers, the proposed children, Lots 182/187, commissioner, trustee, militia, will, probate, cemetery, and first-settler terms.

The online source ladder included original FamilySearch deed images, NARA's 1830 census roll, Georgia Archives custody records, official Georgia land-lot data, Internet Archive books and OCR, Genealogy Trails, Newspapers.com image IDs, Find a Grave, FamilySearch public and previously reviewed signed-in profile data, Ray City History Blog, Georgia Historical Society, and public catalog records.

The managed logged-in browser timed out twice while attempting fresh Ancestry access; under the anti-loop rule the source was not retried. Existing project notes from prior signed-in FamilySearch and Ancestry work were used only with that provenance disclosed. The underlying Hortense W. Baker newspaper sketch, the original 1799 militia commission, exact 1830 census image, original Mount Zion manuscript, 1895 Lasa Adams page ID, Lawrence's will/probate papers, and a photographed grave marker were not located. These are access or survival gaps, not proof that the records never existed.

docs.title: Best next records
docs.text:
1. Lowndes tax digests for 1830, 1834, 1835, 1838, and 1840: inspect every Lawrence entry, including acreage, valuation, polls, enslaved people, and adjoining owners.
  2. NARA 1830 census image: manually browse roll 19 to identify Lawrence's exact schedule page and full age/slavery columns.
  3. Georgia Archives legislative copy: obtain the December 24, 1825 organizing act image naming the county-site commissioners.
  4. Probate and later deed reconstruction: search surviving loose papers, post-fire indexes, private Folsom papers, and James/Andrew J. Folsom deeds for a recital of Lawrence's will or heirs.
  5. Mount Zion and Methodist archives: look for the original trustee deed, membership books, cemetery register, and first-meeting date.
  6. Burke County militia commissions: verify or reject the January 23, 1799 ensign claim.
  7. Hortense W. Baker's Valdosta Times sketches: identify the article Huxford used and determine whether she cited an earlier manuscript or family informant.
  8. Old Folsom Family Cemetery: obtain a site survey or marker photographs testing whether the cemetery can be tied to Lots 182/187 and the Lawrence-James landholdings.

docs.title: The Folsom Family
docs.text:
The Folsom Family¶

The Folsom surname appears in several early Lowndes County and Barney-area families. The surviving evidence does not support treating every Folsom as part of one proved line. This page keeps the documented branches separate and explains where the proposed links remain unproved.

Elijah Folsom: a traditional candidate¶

Elijah Folsom remains a traditional early-settler candidate. Folks Huxford wrote that he came to the territory of present Brooks County in 1824 or 1825, but no contemporary record inspected for this audit identifies Elijah's household, land, or residence there.

Elizabeth Knowles Folsom's 1938 genealogy gives the following reconstruction:

William Folsom + Sally Armstrong → Lawrence Folsom + Rachel Vickers → Elijah Folsom + Nancy Morrison → Green, Martha, Jackson, Elizabeth, Macon, and Elijah.

That is the strongest compiled theory, not a proved lineage. No inspected parent-, spouse-, or child-naming original establishes the Elijah links. The proposed six children remain unresolved individually, and the reported move to Florida lacks a county, date, and original record.

Elijah identity controls¶

At least three people must remain separate unless new records connect them:

  1. the proposed early-settler Elijah;
  2. the younger Elijah whom the 1938 genealogy calls his unmarried son; and
  3. the much later Elijah identified as the father of Ella Dee Folsom, born in 1902.

The claimed 1832 Georgia Land Lottery draw for Carroll County Lot 255 is not used as evidence. No page, draw category, residence, stable identifier, or identity bridge to the proposed pioneer has been recovered.

The Lawrence and William branch¶

Lawrence Folsom is independently documented by an 1823 Irwin County deed and a later Lowndes County record chain. Those records establish Lawrence's presence; they do not prove that Elijah was his son.

The separate William Folsom and Elizabeth Folsom branch has a stronger original-record trail. Elizabeth's will identifies Edith Rountree as her daughter and names Rachel Ann Ryall's four children. Estate deeds document land passing through the Ryall, Rountree, Perry, Joyce, Pounds, Ingram, and Jones families. Those descendants reached Barney, but no inspected record joins their branch to Elijah generation by generation.

Known 1900 Barney descendants¶

The following nine paths were already documented from the 1900 Barney census. The recent parent-child steps are supported by census, marriage, death, or comparable records. The earlier Lawrence-to-William step remains supported by compiled genealogy and circumstantial records rather than a parent-naming original.

Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones¶

Lawrence Folsom → William Folsom → Rachel Ann Folsom Ryall → William Raiford Ryall → Annie Elizabeth Ryall Jones
Secondary-supported.

Charles Wesley Ryall¶

Lawrence Folsom → William Folsom → Rachel Ann Folsom Ryall → Charles Wesley Ryall
Secondary-supported.

Cora Ella Rountree Pounds¶

Lawrence Folsom → William Folsom → Edith Elizabeth Folsom Rountree → James Wesley Rountree → Cora Ella Rountree Pounds
Secondary-supported.

The Priscilla Jane and Israel Lee branch¶

The best documented Barney surname branch runs through Priscilla Jane Folsom and Israel Lee Folsom. The 1880 census directly identifies Priscilla as Israel Lee's mother. Household continuity makes Priscilla the strong-probable wife of Ebenezer Folsom, although no original marriage record has been located.

The proposed relationship between the older Ebenezer and pioneer Israel Folsom remains secondary-supported. No reviewed record joins this branch to Elijah.

The Barney census also contains Folsom households that cannot yet be placed safely. The 1920 schedules include F. B. Folsom and Israel Lee's household, while several 1930 groups remain unreconciled. Shared surname and proximity are not enough to assign them to Elijah or another pioneer line.

Other early Folsoms¶

Pennywell, pioneer Israel, John, Thomas, Ebenezer, and several men named William appear in early regional records. They remain separate identity controls unless a relationship-naming record connects them. The proposed Lawrence-and-Rachel sibling group—William, Randal, John, Elijah, Maston, Cynthia, Elizabeth, and James—is secondary-supported by compiled genealogy rather than proved by inspected originals.

Jesse Folsom does not supply a South Georgia bridge. The identifiable Jesse in the 1938 genealogy was born in New Hampshire in 1817 and lived there. No distinct South Georgia Jesse was found in the documented local searches.

Evidence grades¶

  • Traditional / unresolved: Elijah's reported 1824–1825 arrival in future Brooks County.
  • Secondary-supported / possible: Lawrence and Rachel as Elijah's parents; Nancy Morrison as his wife; the reported move to Florida.
  • Secondary-supported as a compiled group; unresolved individually: Green, Martha, Jackson, Elizabeth, Macon, and the younger Elijah as their children.
  • Unsupported; rejected as current evidence: the unlocated 1832 Carroll County Lot 255 assertion.
  • Unresolved: any generation-by-generation connection between Elijah and a documented Barney Folsom branch.

What would settle the open questions¶

The most useful missing records are Lawrence and Rachel's probate or distribution papers naming children; an original record naming Elijah with Nancy or one of the six proposed children; a county-specific Florida record; and child-specific Alabama, Georgia, or military records that identify parents or close associates. The complete 1832 lottery entry would also be needed before the Lot 255 claim could be reconsidered.

Sources¶

  1. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), chapter 4, pp. 29–33.
  2. Elizabeth Knowles Folsom, Genealogy of the Folsom Family, rev. ed., vol. 2 (1938), printed pp. 867 and 872, Internet Archive scan.
  3. 1880 U.S. census, Quitman, Brooks County, Georgia, ED 4, p. 319D, dwelling 658, P. J. Folsom household.
  4. Brooks County deed and probate records summarized in the linked Lawrence, William, Priscilla Jane, and Ebenezer profiles.

Latest surname-audit findings

The documented core is Joel Gornto and Mary Blair through their children Hannah Elizabeth Gornto Hall and William Blair Gornto Sr. Hannah’s son Sion L. Hall headed Barney household #7. William Sr. and his son William Jr. headed households #15 and #14.

Nathan Gornto’s administration of Joel’s estate proves association, not fatherhood. No inspected record names Nathan as Joel’s father. Martha Jane Gornto Dean and Emma Gornto Pace are verified Gornto-born Barney residents, but their parents remain unresolved.

Mary Blair’s proposed parents were early settler William Blair and his reported wife Mary Joyce. That link remains secondary-supported and probable. The earliest explicit parentage statement located is an unsourced 1999 compiled genealogy, and later accounts are not demonstrably independent. Original records identify Joel’s wife as Mary Blair; none inspected gives her the middle name Joyce.
