Final assessment

Surviving records provide more than Drew Vickers’s name on a pioneer list. They trace a North Carolina-born man of the Revolutionary generation from Montgomery County to the old Irwin–Lowndes frontier, where he farmed, enslaved people, held property, and pursued claims in court. An 1889 local biography remembered his stock raising, hunting, and distribution of seed cane to neighbors.

The evidence does not establish his exact birth or death dates, parents, complete list of children, burial place, or probate history. The 1815 expedition and 1821 migration appear only in later accounts; the 1845 death date and 1833 grand-jury claim conflict with direct records. These limits should remain explicit.

docs.title: Executive finding
docs.text:
Drewry “Drew” Vickers was an early settler of the part of original Irwin County that became Lowndes County, Georgia. Later histories consistently include him among the county’s first four permanent white settlers. The earliest located account that could be examined directly is William Harden’s 1913 history; Folks Huxford repeated the attribution with an 1821 date in 1922. This is a secondary-supported traditional attribution. No located contemporary record proves the quartet claim, the reported 1815 scouting expedition, or an exact 1821 family move.

Contemporary records nevertheless provide a substantial outline of his life. A Drury Vickers was a fortunate land-lottery drawer from Montgomery County in 1820. A probable identity chain traces a man of this name from Montgomery County that year to Lowndes County in 1830, 1840, and 1850. Newspapers document old-Irwin land, Lowndes Superior Court judgments, and a transaction connecting Drew with Lewis Vickers between 1833 and 1848. In 1850, Drew was about seventy-four, born in North Carolina, farming in Lowndes County, and living with Sarah Vickers. The census and slave schedules establish that he enslaved people in 1820, 1830, and 1850.

His exact death date is unknown. The frequently copied 1845 date is false for this man because he appears in the 1850 census and in an 1848 court notice. No probate file, death notice, cemetery register, or photographed grave marker was found. The defensible conclusion is that he died sometime after the 1850 enumeration.

docs.title: Evidence standards used in this dossier
docs.text:
• Verified: read in an original or indexed-original image, or in a contemporary newspaper page.
  • Strong probable: supported by several compatible records, but identity or interpretation still requires an inference.
  • Secondary-supported: stated in a later history, transcription, memorial, or compiled genealogy with useful detail but no inspected original proof.
  • Unresolved: plausible, but the evidence located online does not establish it.
  • Contradicted: inconsistent with a stronger original record.

Negative findings mean only that no record was found in the documented searches. They do not prove that a record never existed.

docs.title: Identity and name variants
docs.text:
The early records use several spellings:

Form Record context
Drury Vickers 1793 militia-roll transcription; 1820 land-lottery list; 1820 census alternate reading; 1833 tax sale; 1845-1846 court notices
Drewey Vickers 1820 census indexing
Drewy Vickers 1840 census and land/tax indexing
Drew Vickers 1830 and 1850 censuses; 1848 court notice; later histories
Drewry Vickers Later genealogies, memorials, and land-index references

The name, geography, age, and chronology make these records a coherent probable identity chain. No located record calls the pioneer Andrew Vickers, and “Drew” should not be expanded to Andrew. No evidence supports a first initial J; the subject named in the historical sources is Drew or Drury Vickers.

Several later men had the same or similar name. In particular, Florida probate and Indian War records belong to a Drewry Vickers born about 1820, not to the North Carolina-born pioneer who was already about seventy-four in 1850. A Drew Vickers born about 1831 in the 1860 Berrien County census and William Drew Vickers and other later Hahira-area men must also be kept separate.

docs.text:

docs.title: Was he one of Lowndes County’s first four settlers?
docs.text:
Later histories consistently include Drew among the four settlers, but no located contemporary record proves the quartet claim or fixes its date. The appropriate grade is secondary-supported traditional attribution; the exact group, permanence, geography, and dates remain unproved.

William Harden’s 1913 A History of Savannah and South Georgia is the earliest located account that could be examined directly and names the quartet. In a biography of the Folsom family, Harden says Lawrence Folsom joined James Rountree, Drew Vickers, and Alfred Belote on an 1815 exploration. It says the men invested in government land, returned for their families, and became the first permanent white settlers of Lowndes County, especially its northern portion. Harden gives no contemporary citation for the expedition.

Folks Huxford’s 1922 county sketch supplies the familiar precise date: “In 1821, four settlers moved to what is now Lowndes county.” He names Rountree, Folsom, Vickers, and Belote with their families. Huxford said his account relied chiefly on recent Valdosta Times sketches by Hortense W. Baker. Those underlying sketches were not located.

Two earlier local accounts complicate the chronology:

  • An 1889 biography says Drew settled his “Coffee county road” lot in 1824.
  • R. E. L. Folsom wrote in 1899 that Washington Joyce established the first white settlement in present Lowndes County at the Miller Bridge crossing in 1824, and that Drew Vickers and Lawrence Folsom came next.

These statements are not necessarily irreconcilable. “Original Lowndes,” “present Lowndes,” an exploratory trip, a legal land entry, and permanent occupation can refer to different events and geographies. They do show why an unqualified claim that all four families permanently settled present-day Lowndes in 1821 goes beyond the evidence now available.

The safest wording is:

Drew Vickers was one of the four men traditionally credited as the first permanent white settler group in northern original Lowndes County. Contemporary evidence places Drury Vickers in the regional record by 1820 and securely in Lowndes County by 1830; the reported 1815 expedition and exact 1821 family migration come from later histories.

docs.title: Origin, age, and migration
docs.text:
The 1850 census is the best age-and-origin evidence found. It records Drew at about seventy-four and born in North Carolina, implying a birth around 1776. The public image is readable but not ideal, so 1776 should remain an approximate year, not an exact birth date. No birth, baptism, or parental record was located.

The 1889 profile agrees on North Carolina and says he came to Georgia soon after the Revolutionary War. The 1793 Washington County militia transcription is geographically compatible with that account. By 1820 he was enumerated in Montgomery County, while a court transcription may place him on an Irwin County jury panel that same year. He was in Lowndes by the 1830 census.

The records do not reveal whether the apparent Montgomery/Irwin overlap reflects a recent move, differing civil boundaries or registrations, or two men. The later record chain strongly favors one pioneer moving through the south-central Georgia frontier, but it should not be treated as a single-record proof.

docs.title: Sarah Vickers
docs.text:
The 1850 population schedule places Sarah Vickers, about sixty and born in North Carolina, immediately with Drew in the same household. This is direct proof of co-residence and strong evidence that she was his wife. The census does not state relationships or maiden names.

Find a Grave, WikiTree, and other compiled genealogies call her Sarah Elvington or Yelvington. No inspected marriage record, deed, Bible, probate, or death record gives that maiden name. Therefore:

  • Sarah as Drew’s wife: strong probable.
  • Sarah Elvington/Yelvington as her full identity: secondary-supported, not independently verified.

docs.title: Proposed children
docs.text:
Public genealogies commonly list Lewis, Nancy, Henry, and Matthew Vickers; some add Benjamin. No located probate distribution, Bible, deed, guardianship record, or parent-naming vital record proves the complete child set.

Proposed child Best evidence located Assessment
Lewis Vickers A modern account of the 1827 land lottery calls Lewis Drew’s son. The 1848 sheriff’s notice says Lewis pointed out property in a judgment held by Drew. Strongest proposed child, but still not directly proved as a son.
Nancy Vickers Fuquay Repeated in WikiTree and compiled genealogy. Secondary-supported only.
Henry Vickers Linked in WikiTree and Find a Grave. Henry’s 1859 Brooks County estate record, as inspected, does not name Drew. Plausible, unresolved.
Matthew Vickers Repeated in compiled genealogy; appears in the broader Vickers network. Secondary-supported only.
Benjamin Vickers Appears in some reconstructions but not all child lists. Possible and disputed.

The 1889 profile says William and Drew Vickers, then living on the old “Coffee county road” lot, were the pioneer’s grandsons. This is useful family testimony, but it supplies no intermediate parent.

docs.title: Proposed parents and sibling
docs.text:
Modern trees sometimes identify Joshua Vickers as Drew’s father. The 1793 militia transcription lists Joshua immediately after Drury in Captain Parrott’s Company, but it states no relationship. Joshua could have been a father, brother, cousin, or unrelated same-surname neighbor. Drew’s parents remain unknown.

Huxford called Rachel Vickers Folsom Drew’s sister. A 1938 Folsom genealogy instead called Rachel a daughter of Jonathan Vickers. No reviewed original record names Drew and Rachel as children of the same parent. Their proposed sibling relationship remains unresolved.

The line Drew → Henry Vickers → Edna Vickers Ryall is not proved at its oldest link. Edna’s death record separately identifies Henry Vickers and Linnie Bradford as her parents, but no located original record makes that Henry a son of Drew. The dossier does not present Drew as a proved direct ancestor of the Barney families through Henry.

docs.title: 1820 Montgomery County
docs.text:
The census records Drewey Vickers, with Drury as an alternate reading. The indexed original schedule reports twelve people: seven free white household members and five enslaved people. The free household consisted of one male forty-five or older, two males aged ten through fifteen, two males under ten, one female aged twenty-six through forty-four, and one female aged ten through fifteen. The enslaved people were recorded only by age and sex, not by name.

This record proves neither the names of Drew’s family members nor the later compiled child list.

docs.title: 1830 Lowndes County
docs.text: The census records Drew Vickers in Lowndes County with fifteen people total, seven of whom were enslaved. The schedule does not name other free or enslaved members of the household.

docs.title: 1840 Lowndes County
docs.text: Ancestry indexes Drewy Vickers in Lowndes County and supplies original image identifiers. The original-image locator was independently confirmed. Because the columns could not be read reliably at the available resolution, no exact 1840 household or slavery total is asserted here.

docs.title: 1850 Lowndes County
docs.text:
The population schedule records Drew at about seventy-four, Sarah at about sixty, both born in North Carolina, and Drew as a farmer. The image appears to value his real estate at about $2,000, but that figure should be confirmed from a full-resolution scan before being quoted as exact.

The separate slave schedule visibly contains five consecutive enslaved-person entries under Drew’s name. The people were not named, and the available public image was not clear enough for a responsible age-by-age transcription.

docs.title: 1820 lottery
docs.text: The Georgia Journal lists Drury Vickers under Montgomery County among fortunate drawers in Georgia’s 1820 land lottery. This proves a successful draw but does not identify the parcel on the newspaper page.

docs.title: District 13 land in old Irwin
docs.text:
A 1833 Thomas County sheriff’s notice gives the strongest directly inspected land description. It levied on Drury’s 490-acre Lot 389 in the 13th District of original Irwin, then Thomas County, for his 1833 tax. Ownership or taxable responsibility is established; personal residence on the lot is not.

A public historical KML separately says a state grant issued to Drewry Vickers of Montgomery County on November 11, 1830, for Lot 397 in District 13. The relevant placemark is headed “LL 397. LD 13. Vickers.” The official Georgia land-lot layer identifies the parcel as feature ID 103844, object 423625, a 490-acre original-Irwin lottery lot now in Thomas County. The grant image was not inspected, and Lot 397 must not be confused with the newspaper-proved Lot 389.

docs.title: Lowndes-area lots
docs.text:
The public KML places Drewy or Drewry Vickers in Lowndes tax lists or a plat involving Lots 179, 181, 182, 187, and 188 from 1830 through 1844. The relevant placemarks are headed “LL 181, 188. LD 12. Vickers,” “LL 187. LD 12. Vickers,” and “LL 179, 182. LD 11. Vickers.” They report:

  • appearances on Lots 181 and 188 in 1830 and 1838;
  • an August 30, 1844 plat associated with those lots;
  • appearances on Lot 187 in 1838 and 1840;
  • appearances on Lots 179 and 182 in 1840.

The index has a material internal conflict: its heading calls Lots 181 and 188 part of District 12, while detailed text calls them District 11. Both districts contain lots with those numbers. Find a Grave repeats the District 12 version without citing a deed. The lot and district cannot be settled from those derivatives alone.

Tax-list placement can show a taxable interest without proving fee-simple ownership or residence. No inspected deed proves that Drew acquired Lawrence Folsom’s interest in Lot 187. The original tax digest pages, 1844 plat, state grant, and later deed recitals are priority records.

docs.title: Courts and civic activity
docs.text:
The newspaper record shows Drew as an active creditor in Lowndes Superior Court:

  • In 1845 and 1846, sheriff’s-sale notices enforced a judgment in Drury Vickers v. Enoch Hall, with Sion Hall and John Hall as securities on stay. The levied property was Lot 271, District 12; the 1846 notice described a working saw and grist mill.
  • In 1848, another notice enforced Drew Vickers v. Asabell Rentfroe against the Rentfroe place. Lewis Vickers pointed out the property.

These notices prove participation in civil litigation as a judgment creditor. They do not disclose the underlying debts or disputes.

A modern transcription says Drew was selected for Irwin County’s first petit-jury panel in September 1820. It also says the panel was not called when court met the following March, so this is selection rather than proof that he heard a case.

One modern local page claimed Drew served on the 1833 Lowndes grand jury. The published roster does not name him. That claim is contradicted and should not be repeated.

No record was found showing Drew as a justice, sheriff, legislator, commissioner, militia officer, or church trustee.

docs.title: Militia service
docs.text:
An online transcription titled “Muster Rolls for Washington County, GA 1789–1793” lists Drury Vickers and Joshua Vickers consecutively in Captain Parrott’s Company in 1793. Washington County then covered territory later organized into counties including Montgomery, where a man of the same name appears in 1820. The identification is geographically and chronologically plausible.

Because the page is a modern transcription and supplies no original muster image or archive call number, the service is secondary-supported and unverified. It does not establish an officer’s rank, a pension, War of 1812 service, or a relationship between Drury and Joshua.

docs.title: Farming, stock raising, and the sugar-cane story
docs.text:
The 1889 Valdosta Times life sketch, as reprinted in the Savannah Morning News, says Drew was the first white man to settle on the “Coffee county road” and that he introduced sugar-cane cultivation to the neighborhood. It recounts that Hartwell Mitchell, moving toward Thomas County, stayed overnight and gave Drew “a dozen cane for seed.” The article separately says Mitchell had obtained seed at St. Marys. Drew banked the cane, planted it in spring, and later supplied neighbors.

The article describes early wooden roller mills and cane juice boiled in wash-pots. It also calls Drew a farmer and stock raiser, describes his hunting habits and old-fashioned clothing, names “Handy” as the leader of his dog pack, and says he kept tame deer and wild turkeys. According to the story, he kept gold and silver money in gourds in his kitchen loft and remained alert for thieves.

This is the earliest located narrative devoted to Drew. As a retrospective local account, it does not prove that he was the first person to grow sugar cane locally.

docs.title: Death, estate, and burial
docs.text:
The last verified life record is the 1850 census. No age-compatible Drew, Drewry, Drewy, or Drury Vickers was found in the 1860 federal census. The available 1860 matches belong to younger namesakes.

The 1889 profile says Drew “lived to be near 100 years old.” That recollection is not enough to calculate a death year, especially without an exact birth date. It may explain later genealogical estimates, but it does not override the absence of a death or probate record.

No Georgia probate file, will, administration, estate distribution, obituary, funeral notice, church burial record, or cemetery register for the pioneer was found in the documented online searches. Find a Grave places him in Vickers Cemetery near Hahira, gives no death date, and has no grave photograph, marker transcription, or plot evidence. That placement remains derivative.

The correct conclusion is:

  • Born: about 1776, North Carolina — supported by the 1850 census; exact date unproved.
  • Died: after the 1850 census — exact date and place unresolved.
  • Burial: Vickers Cemetery is a plausible tradition, not verified by a marker or register.
  • 1845 death claim: contradicted by direct records.

Lowndes County’s early record losses matter. Pre-1858 deed books were destroyed, and the Ordinary’s office burned in 1869. Those losses may explain the missing direct land and probate trail, but surviving court minutes, state grants, tax digests, loose papers, and later deed recitals may still contain evidence.

docs.title: Claims and confidence summary
docs.text:

docs.title: Namesake exclusions
docs.text:
The following records were deliberately excluded from the pioneer’s biography:

  • Florida probate and Indian War records for a Drewry Vickers born about 1820.
  • The 1860 Berrien County Drew Vickers born about 1831.
  • Drew R. Vickers, born 1854 and died 1924.
  • William Drew Vickers and twentieth-century Hahira or Barney men.
  • Records for Andrew Vickers without independent proof that Andrew was an alias of Drury.

These exclusions prevent the most serious error in the public search results: extending the pioneer’s life with records belonging to a younger Florida namesake.

docs.title: Research coverage and negative findings
docs.text:
This investigation reviewed prior local research first, then searched the following online record groups:

  • federal population and slave schedules;
  • Ancestry census, probate, military, and non-population indexes and available images;
  • Georgia Historic Newspapers, including exact-name searches across variant spellings;
  • Newspapers.com for the 1899 settlement account;
  • Internet Archive page images and OCR for Harden and Huxford;
  • public Georgia land-lot mapping and a historical Lowndes land/tax KML;
  • Find a Grave and Vickers Cemetery;
  • WikiTree and other compiled genealogy leads;
  • Ray City History Blog’s Drew/Drury, lottery, court, and early-settlement pages;
  • the archived Washington County militia-roll transcription.

No contemporary record of the alleged 1815 expedition or exact 1821 family migration was located. The Hortense W. Baker sketches behind Huxford’s account were not found. No original 1793 muster image, 1820 Irwin jury minute image, Georgia probate for Drew, death notice, obituary, church record, cemetery register, or photographed marker was found. Exact newspaper searches were complicated by OCR reading “Drew” as a verb, and some subscription images were available only at limited resolution.

docs.title: Final assessment
docs.text:
Surviving records provide more than Drew Vickers’s name on a pioneer list. They trace a North Carolina-born man of the Revolutionary generation from Montgomery County to the old Irwin–Lowndes frontier, where he farmed, enslaved people, held property, and pursued claims in court. An 1889 local biography remembered his stock raising, hunting, and distribution of seed cane to neighbors.

The evidence does not establish his exact birth or death dates, parents, complete list of children, burial place, or probate history. The 1815 expedition and 1821 migration appear only in later accounts; the 1845 death date and 1833 grand-jury claim conflict with direct records. These limits should remain explicit.

docs.title: George Alderman (about 1797–after 1880)
docs.text:
George Alderman (about 1797–after 1880)

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Identity and arrival

This page concerns the older George Alderman who lived with Nancy Carlton Alderman and remained in the Lowndes and Brooks County area. He must be kept separate from the younger George Alderman, husband of Mary “Polly” Newton, who moved to Bradford County, Florida.

The older George was a regional resident by 1830. His exact arrival year is unknown. Folks Huxford's later roster gives 1829, while Aldermans in America has been summarized as 1826 or 1827. No contemporary arrival record located in this research settles the difference.[1][2]

Census and family

The 1850 Lowndes County census places George, about 53, and Nancy, about 47, with a household that included Jonathan H. Alderman. In 1880, George, age 85, and Nancy, age 75, lived in Jonathan's Brooks County household. The schedule identifies them as Jonathan's father and mother.[3][4]

That 1880 relationship field directly establishes George and Nancy as Jonathan's parents. George's relationship to William Alderman is strong probable from the 1850 household reconstruction and compiled family material, but no reviewed probate or other parent-naming record states it.[2][3]

Brooks County land records

The original Brooks County deed indexes contain five entries for George Alderman:

  1. Daniel J. McLeod to George Alderman, warranty deed, Book A, page 239; instrument dated December 6, 1854; 490 acres in Land Lot 210, District 9.
  2. Samuel Moore to George Alderman, warranty deed, Book A, page 241; instrument dated June 24, 1850; 245 acres in Land Lot 59, District 15.
  3. George Alderman to William Alderman, warranty deed, Book C, page 786; instrument dated November 21, 1859; six acres in Land Lot 491, District 9.
  4. George Alderman to John Blair, warranty deed, Book D, page 92; instrument dated August 4, 1873; 220 acres in Land Lot 57, District 15.
  5. George Alderman to Amy Alderman, warranty deed, Book E, page 444; instrument dated October 9, 1878; 194 acres in Land Lot 490, District 9.[5][6]

These are deed-index entries, not the recorded deeds. They do not supply complete boundaries, consideration, residence statements, witnesses, reservations, or family relationships. Amy Alderman cannot be identified from the index entry alone.

Connection to Barney

The six-acre conveyance in District 9 Land Lot 491 places George in the north-of-Barney land cluster later associated with the Folsom and Alderman families. Together with compiled family evidence placing his farm about four miles north of Barney, the deed strengthens the local connection. It does not prove that George lived on those six acres or owned land inside the later town.[2][5]

Public offices and namesakes

Huxford's office lists and other local references name a George Alderman, but the two men overlap in the regional record. The younger George has previously been associated with the tax-collector entry. No public office should be assigned to the older George without a record that distinguishes him by age, spouse, residence, or land.

Death and estate

Compiled sources give February 14, 1797, and April 11, 1882, as George's birth and death dates. No contemporary death record, probate entry, Bible image, obituary, or photographed marker was inspected for this page. The 1880 census proves only that he was living when the household was enumerated.[4]

Qualified 1900 Barney descendant paths

  • Jonathan Howell Alderman — the 1880 census identifies George and Nancy as his parents.
  • George Washington Alderman — later census and death evidence connects him through Jonathan.
  • James Carlton Alderman — later records identify William as his father; George's relationship to William remains strong probable.

See the evidence grade for each generation.

What remains unresolved

  • George's exact arrival year and complete child list
  • the full text and title chains of the five indexed deeds
  • the location of his residence
  • his estate, exact death date, and burial
  • public offices or road and church references that cannot yet be separated from the younger George

Sources

  1. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948, arrival roster and county, road, and church references, HathiTrust catalog record.
  2. Jennie Alderman Park, Aldermans in America (1957), southern-family entries; compiled genealogy.
  3. 1850 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, George Alderman household; original image and reconstruction preserved in the Barney census project.
  4. 1880 U.S. census, Morven district, Brooks County, Jonathan H. Alderman household; George and Nancy recorded as parents.
  5. Brooks County Grantor Index A–K, FamilySearch images, George Alderman entries, locally preserved image 269, displayed page 87.
  6. Brooks County Grantee Index A–K, FamilySearch images, George Alderman entries, locally preserved image 167, displayed page 185.

docs.title: Nathan Gornto
docs.text:
Nathan Gornto¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision¶

Nathan Gornto was a verified supplemental early settler. Census evidence places him in Lowndes County in 1830 and 1840. A published commission list identifies him as a justice of the peace for the 659th, or Nankin, District beginning in 1834. The 1860 Brooks County census records Nathan “Gronto,” about eighty, with Easter in the Tallokas area.

Relationship to Joel Gornto¶

Nathan and Joel's widow, Mary, administered Joel Gornto's estate with the will annexed. That proves association, not fatherhood. No inspected will, deed, Bible, guardianship, census relationship, or vital record names Nathan as Joel's father.

The complete Barney Gornto audit therefore keeps Nathan → Joel unresolved. Public trees and later surname histories repeat the father-son claim, but no independent parent-naming source has been found.

Barney relevance¶

Nathan belongs in the broader future-Brooks context. Joel's documented descendants reached Barney through Hannah Elizabeth Gornto Hall and William Blair Gornto Sr., but that bridge does not extend backward to Nathan unless the missing Nathan-to-Joel link is proved.

Sources¶

  • 1830 and 1840 U.S. censuses, Lowndes County, Nathan Gornto households.
  • Folks Huxford, published Lowndes County justice-of-the-peace list.
  • 1860 U.S. census, Tallokas post office, Brooks County, Nathan “Gronto” household.
  • Joel Gornto estate administration bonds and inventory warrant, 1861.

docs.title: Early record and arrival tradition
docs.text:
Nathan Gornto was an early regional settler who was still living in the Tallokas area in 1860. Folks Huxford places him in original Irwin County in 1820 and says that he moved into the future Brooks County area when Coffee Road opened in 1823. The census trail supports early regional residence but does not independently prove the 1823 move.[1]

The 1830 and 1840 federal indexes place Nathan in Lowndes County. Their original schedule rows have not received a complete column-by-column transcription for this project.[2][3]

docs.title: The 1860 Tallokas household
docs.text:
The 1860 Brooks County census lists Nathan Gronto, age 80, born in North Carolina, with Easter, age 79, at Tallokas. Their ages imply births about 1779–1781 but do not establish exact years.[4]

Easter was probably Nathan's wife. Later accounts call her Easter Burnett, but no inspected marriage record, Bible, deed, probate paper, or other original record confirms the Burnett surname.

docs.title: Justice of the peace
docs.text: Huxford's compilation of county officers lists Nathan in the 659th, or Nankin, District. It gives a commission beginning July 9, 1834, and another beginning January 14, 1841.[1] The original commission book or election return has not been inspected. The service is strong secondary evidence and places Nathan in the Nankin district network, not in Barney itself.

docs.title: Joel Gornto's estate
docs.text:
Joel Gornto's will was dated October 20, 1860. Nathan and Joel's widow, Mary, petitioned for probate. Administration bonds dated January 3 and March 4, 1861 name Mary and Nathan as principals, and the inventory warrant identifies them as administrators with the will annexed.[5][6][7]

These records prove Nathan's role in Joel's estate. They do not identify Nathan as Joel's father. An administrator could be a relative, creditor, or trusted associate. The proposed father-son relationship remains unproved and is not required for the published Joel-to-William Gornto paths.

docs.title: Land and Barney connection
docs.text:
No deed or tax record inspected for this page fixes Nathan's land. Later Brooks County deed-index entries for Nathan L. Gornto belong to a younger man. Joel's estate inventory lists part of Land Lot 274, but that record concerns Joel's property, not Nathan's.[7]

Nathan's direct connection to Barney remains unresolved. A proposed line through Joel reaches later Barney households only if the unproved Nathan-to-Joel relationship is accepted, so Nathan is not presented here as a proved Barney ancestor.

docs.title: Death, burial, and estate
docs.text: Later accounts give 1861 as Nathan's death year. The March 4, 1861 administration bond proves that a Nathan Gornto was living then. No inspected death notice, grave image, estate filing, or probate record establishes Nathan's death date or burial place.

docs.title: What remains unresolved
docs.text:
• the exact 1823 move into the future Brooks County area
  • full transcriptions of the 1830 and 1840 households
  • Nathan's land and exact residence
  • Easter's maiden name
  • Nathan's relationship to Joel Gornto
  • Nathan's death, burial, and estate
  • a direct land or institutional connection to Barney

docs.title: Sion Hall (c. 1784–1849)
docs.text:
Sion Hall (c. 1784–1849)

Back to the Early History Profiles index

An evidence-based dossier on an early settler of original Irwin and Lowndes counties, Georgia

Research completed: August 18, 2026
Geographic scope: original Irwin County, original Lowndes County, and the Hall–Mount Zion neighborhood north of present Morven in Brooks County
Name forms searched: Sion, Sian, Zion, Lion, Simon, Sim, and Dian Hall; Hall's and Halls

Conclusion

Sion Hall was in original Irwin County by 1820. Later accounts place his move to the Coffee Road neighborhood north of later Morven in 1823 or early 1824. Georgia law designated his house as the temporary Lowndes County court-and-election place in 1825, then moved those functions to Francis Roundtree's house in 1826. The law also made Hall's house the 1829 justice-court place for Captain Pike's district. These records prove that Hall's home was an early public center. They do not prove that Hall was a judge, justice, military captain, or legislator.[1][2][3][4][19][20]

Hall and his son Enoch held an interest in Land Lot 271, District 12. Their 1831 Mount Zion deed and 1845–1846 sheriff-sale notices tie them to the lot; the 1846 notice describes operating saw and grist mills there. Later accounts place Hall's home, travelers' lodging, mill, grave, and Mount Zion campground in the same small neighborhood. A credible 1902 correction says the residence itself stood in adjoining Lot 270. The property cluster is clear, but the house footprint is not.[4][5][6][7][8]

The family record is thinner. Census records trace Hall from Irwin in 1820 to Lowndes in 1830 and 1840. An indexed Telfair County entry records his 1817 marriage to Elizabeth Coaker. Nineteenth-century and later sources identify Colonel Enoch Hall as his son, but no located probate or Bible record establishes a complete family. Claims about Sion's parents, three wives, all children, exact birth date, and exact death day remain derivative or unresolved.[9][10][11][12][13][14]

Identity and namesakes

The record chain concerns the older Sion Hall who headed households in original Irwin County in 1820 and Lowndes County in 1830 and 1840. The unusual name, county continuity, public-site records, Hall family land, and the later Enoch Hall accounts point to one man. Census indexes obscure him as "Dian Hall" in 1820 and "Sim Hall" in 1830. The original 1830 schedule was inspected and reads "Sion Hall".[9][10][11]

He must not be merged with Sion L. Hall, a grandson born about 1868, or with his son Enoch Hall, John Hall, or other Hall men in the neighborhood. A 1925 obituary says Lottie Hall was Sion's niece and identifies her father as John Hall. That later account supports an older John Hall as Sion's brother, but it gives no suffix and supplies no original parentage source. The relationship remains secondary-supported and probable.[25] Later honorifics such as "Hon." and "Judge" are not office records. No located document proves that Sion held judicial office, served in the militia, or sat in the legislature.[1][2][15]

Origins, marriage, and family

The modern Hall Cemetery marker gives the years 1784–1849. Find a Grave adds North Carolina as the birthplace, November 14 as the death date, and Enoch Hall and Nancy Ann Jackson as parents. Those details may be correct, but the photographed marker does not contain them and the memorial cites no original birth, Bible, probate, or death record. The safest birth description is about 1784, place unproved.[13]

Three Ancestry collections report that Sion Hall married Elizabeth "Coaker" in Telfair County on April 27, 1817. The entries probably descend from the same county record, so they count as one line of evidence, not three independent confirmations. The original marriage-book image was unavailable. "Coaker" should remain the record spelling; "Coker" is a later variant.[12]

Folks Huxford's sketch of Colonel Enoch Hall identifies Enoch, born in Telfair County in 1804, as the son of Sion and Bridget "Beady" Hall. An 1886 profile independently calls Enoch "the son of Sion Hall", without naming his mother. This makes the father-son relationship strong. Bridget's identity as Enoch's mother rests on the later compiled sketch rather than a located birth or marriage record.[4][14]

Find a Grave, FloridaRoots, public trees, and family stories expand the family considerably. They name Bridget or Beady Hall, Elizabeth Coker or Coaker, and Polly or Pollie Morrison as wives; identify Sion's parents as Enoch Hall and Nancy Jackson; and offer varying child lists. FloridaRoots candidly says its compiler had not done much Hall research. No original record found in this project proves the alleged Bridget or Polly marriages, an 1816 separation, Sion's parentage, or a complete list of children. These are research leads, not a publication-safe pedigree.[13][16]

Presence in original Irwin County

Huxford identifies Sion as an 1820 Irwin County householder. The matching federal census index appears as "Dian Hall": eighteen people in the household, eight of them enslaved. The original image was not reopened, so the name identification and totals are strong probable rather than fully image-verified.[4][9]

A published transcription of Irwin court records says Sion was drawn for the first petit-jury panel at the September 21, 1820 Superior Court. The court met at David Williams's house on Lot 147, District 4. The account says the panel was selected for the next term but was not called in March 1821. This distinction matters: Sion's jury selection does not make his home the first Irwin court site.[17]

A second court-record transcription says that in July 1824 the Irwin Inferior Court appointed Sion Hall, James Allen, and Thomas Townsend to lay out a road from the Ocmulgee River to the Alapaha River. The original minute images were not located for either item, so both remain strong secondary evidence.[18]

The Coffee Road settlement date

The census and jury evidence place Sion somewhere in the large original Irwin County by 1820. They do not place him on Lot 271. The move to the Coffee Road neighborhood is remembered in two versions:

  • Huxford says Hall moved when the Coffee Road opened in 1823.[4]
  • The Valdosta Times stated in 1899 that Hall first cut timber in the area on January 20, 1824; a 1900 account gives 1824 without the exact day.[19][20]

No located 1823 or 1824 deed, tax entry, diary, or road record settles the difference. The defensible conclusion is that Hall moved within original Irwin County to the Coffee Road settlement in 1823 or early 1824. January 20, 1824 is a precise but unsourced retrospective claim.

Hall's house as the temporary Lowndes public center

Lowndes County was created from Irwin on December 24, 1825. Georgia's official 1837 digest summarizes the relevant laws:

"Courts and elections to be held at the house of Sion Hall, 1825 ... Removed to the house of Francis Roundtree, 1826."[1]

A contemporary legislative report from December 1826 confirms passage of the amendment concerning courts and elections at Sion Hall's. One House-column rendering says "Levi Hall", but the Senate report and official digest identify Sion. The same digest says that in 1829 Hall's house was designated as the justice-court place in Captain Pike's district. "Captain Pike's district" identifies the militia district; it is not Sion's rank.[1][2]

Huxford says the 1825 act appointed Lawrence Folsom, Sion Hall, William Blair, John J. Underwood, and Daniel McCranie to select the permanent county site. The exact session-law page naming the commissioners was not located, so the commissioner list is strong secondary evidence rather than a newly verified original.[4]

The date of the first Lowndes Superior Court remains unsettled. A 1900 retrospective places it at Hall's in spring 1826. Huxford quotes William Smith's 1880 recollection that it met there on the first Monday in January 1827. The latter date sits awkwardly beside the 1826 law moving courts and elections to Roundtree's. Original court minutes or a docket are needed. It is safe to say that Hall's house was the statutory temporary site and hosted early county business; it is not safe to assign one exact first-court date.[1][4][20]

Later accounts describe a large double-pen hewn-log house used for court, lodging, and meals, with some jurors deliberating outdoors. The earliest detailed version located is Montgomery M. Folsom's 1885 travel-history account. An 1886 Atlanta profile repeats its distinctive details and is probably derivative; it should not be counted as independent confirmation.[14][21]

Several later histories mistakenly call Hall's house the site of Irwin County's first court. That claim is contradicted by the court-record transcription placing the 1820 Irwin court at David Williams's house. The Lowndes and Irwin claims must remain separate.[17][20]

Land Lots 270 and 271, Mount Zion, and the mills

The Georgia land-lot service places Lot 271 in the Twelfth District of original Irwin, now Brooks County. The map proves the lot's location, not Hall ownership.[22]

The Hall interest in Lot 271 rests on three cumulative lines of evidence:

  1. Huxford printed a transcription he said he made from the original November 8, 1831 deed. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed about six acres connected with camps, church, and burying ground to Methodist Episcopal trustees. The description begins at the west north-south line of Lot 271. The lost Lowndes Deed Book A copy had been recorded at pages 654–655 on February 26, 1833.[4]
  2. An April 1845 sheriff-sale notice levied Lot 271 as property of Sion and Enoch Hall to satisfy a Lowndes Superior Court judgment in "Drury Vickers vs Enoch Hall, Sion Hall and John Hall, securities on stay".[5]
  3. A March 1846 repeat calls Lot 271 well improved, with a saw and grist mill in operation. This proves operating mills on the levied Hall property by 1846. It does not prove who built or personally ran them.[6]

Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollection placed Enoch at the Hall center on Lot 271. The 1908 Brooks County map later marked Mount Zion/Camp Ground and a J. L. Hall residence in that lot.[3][8]

The house itself may have stood next door. In 1902 Norman Campbell, an early resident, corrected a published account and said the first-court residence stood on Lot 270. Lots 270 and 271 adjoin, and a home, mill, campground, burying ground, and larger plantation need not occupy one lot. The best present conclusion is: Hall's court house, lodging place, mills, and Mount Zion campground formed a compact Coffee Road neighborhood at or adjoining Lot 271; Hall's Lot 271 interest is proved, but the residence footprint and its placement in Lot 270 or 271 remain unresolved.[7]

Inn, merchant activity, and local tradition

Huxford says Sion kept a public inn on the Coffee Road, lodging twelve to fifteen travelers, and that Enoch continued it after Sion's death. The nineteenth-century court narratives support a large house that lodged officials and travelers. No tavern license or guest register was found, so "public inn" is strongly supported but not proved by a business license.[4][21]

Sharpe wrote in 1884 that he was "merchantising at Mr. Sion Hall's" when he helped establish an early mail route and Sharpe's Store. This proves merchant activity at the Hall settlement, but it does not show who owned the stock, store, or building. Later claims that Sion owned the store or that his brother John ran a liquor bar remain possible and unverified.[3]

The 1885 account described old mill sills and a dam near the former Hall home and repeated a comic story about the slow grist mill. The writer expressly declined to vouch for the story's authenticity. The physical mill claim is consistent with the 1846 sale notice; the anecdote remains folklore.[6][21]

Census households and slavery

The federal census indexes give the following household totals:[9][10][11]

Year Indexed name and county Total household Enslaved people Evidence boundary
1820 "Dian Hall", Irwin 18 8 Strong probable identification; original image not reopened
1830 "Sim Hall", Lowndes 8 3 Original schedule inspected; manuscript name reads Sion Hall; totals retained from index
1840 "Sion Hall", Lowndes 14 4 Index verified; original image not reopened

These schedules do not name wives, children, or enslaved people. They support only numerical statements. No names or relationships can be reconstructed from the aggregate entries.

The decline from eight enslaved people in 1820 to three in 1830 and four in 1840 is real at the indexed-household level, but the schedules do not explain transfers, sales, deaths, hiring, residence changes, or household composition. No estate inventory was found to connect particular individuals to Hall at his death.

Death, burial, and probate

Huxford gives Sion's death year as 1849. The modern Hall Cemetery marker also reads "SION HALL / 1784-1849". Find a Grave supplies November 14, 1849, but that day does not appear on the photographed stone and no contemporary notice or probate record was found. The year is strong; the exact date is unresolved.[4][13]

The earliest located burial descriptions are from 1885 and 1886. They place Sion's grave under large trees or in a grove by his mill creek. Together with the Hall Cemetery memorial, they make burial in the Hall home-and-mill neighborhood near Morven strong probable. They do not establish that the modern marker occupies the exact original grave.[14][21]

Searches found no will, administration, inventory, estate division, obituary, death notice, or administrator advertisement. The Ancestry Georgia wills-and-probate index displayed no Lowndes County result for Sion, but that was a name-index search, not a page-by-page review of county volumes. Newspapers.com searches for 1840–1870 also produced no death or estate notice. These are documented negatives, not proof that no estate proceeding existed.

Public roles that are proved, probable, or unsupported

Proved or strongly supported

  • Irwin petit-jury panel selection in 1820, from a published court-record transcription.[17]
  • Irwin road commissioner in 1824, from a published court-record transcription.[18]
  • Member of the 1825 Lowndes public-site commission, from Huxford's specific act-based account.[4]
  • His house's statutory use for Lowndes courts and elections in 1825–1826 and as a justice-court place in 1829.[1][2]
  • A legal/property interest with Enoch in Lot 271 and operating saw and grist mills on the levied property by 1846.[4][5][6]

Unsupported or contradicted

  • Judicial office. The court met at Hall's house; no record found makes Hall a judge or justice.
  • Militia rank or Indian-war service. No commission, muster, pay roll, pension, bounty file, or roster naming this Sion was located.
  • Legislative service. The May 1924 centennial article says Sion "was a member of the Legislature" and that Enoch "followed him"; it does not name a county, office, or term. Service for Lowndes County sometime between its creation in 1825 and Sion's death in 1849 is therefore chronologically possible, but no election return, legislative roster, or official journal located in this project proves it. Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollection instead names William A. Knight and Benjamin Sermons as Lowndes County's first legislative delegation, so Sion was probably not one of the county's first legislators. Three derivative September 1933 articles changed the story by calling the elder Sion Brooks County's first representative and Enoch the second. That version is impossible: Sion died in 1849, nine years before Brooks County was created.[3][4][13][23][24]
  • A Hall-owned store, liquor bar, or licensed tavern.
  • A personal 1820 land-lottery draw. Lot 271's survey history and Hall's 1820 census presence do not establish how he acquired the property.

Evidence summary

Verified or strong

  • Sion Hall was in original Irwin County by 1820 and in Lowndes County in 1830 and 1840.[9][10][11]
  • His house was the legally designated temporary Lowndes court-and-election site.[1][2]
  • He and Enoch held an interest in Lot 271, which had operating saw and grist mills by 1846.[4][5][6]
  • Enoch was his son.[4][14]
  • An 1817 Telfair County marriage entry names Sion Hall and Elizabeth Coaker.[12]
  • Sion died in 1849 and was remembered as buried near the Hall home and mill.[4][13][21]

Probable or moderate

  • The move to the Coffee Road/Lot 271 neighborhood occurred in 1823 or early 1824.[4][19][20]
  • Bridget or Beady was Enoch's mother.[4]
  • Hall's large house functioned as a public inn or travelers' lodging place.[4][21]
  • The current Hall Cemetery memorial identifies the original burial neighborhood.[13][14][21]
  • An older John Hall was Sion's brother, based on the 1925 obituary identifying Lottie Hall as Sion's niece and John Hall's daughter.[25]

Unresolved

  • Exact birth date and place; parentage; every spouse and child.
  • Whether the Coffee Road move occurred in 1823 or on January 20, 1824.
  • Whether the residence stood in Lot 270 or Lot 271.
  • The exact first Lowndes Superior Court date.
  • Exact death day, probate, estate distribution, and exact grave continuity.
  • Tavern or store ownership, military service, judicial office, and legislative service.

Online research coverage and limits

The project searched stored Brooks/Lowndes research first, then used authenticated Ancestry census, marriage, probate, and cemetery collections; Newspapers.com; Georgia Historic Newspapers; Internet Archive; Georgia Archives maps; the state land-lot service; Huxford's county history; public FamilySearch profile pages; Find a Grave; and selected image-backed local-history transcriptions. Searches used the listed name variants with Irwin, Lowndes, Brooks, Morven, Coffee Road, Mount Zion, Lot 270, Lot 271, court, election, jury, road, commissioner, mill, inn, tavern, store, militia, marriage, death, probate, estate, and cemetery.

"Fully researched online" means the accessible online groups and known leads were searched and reconciled. It does not mean all courthouse or manuscript records are digitized. The 1820 and 1840 census images, original 1817 marriage entry, original Irwin jury and road minutes, exact 1825 and 1826 session-law pages, Lowndes probate volumes, and tax/deed chains for Lots 270 and 271 remain uninspected or unavailable. FamilySearch record images required authentication or were blocked, and some Ancestry and Newspapers.com links require subscriptions.

Best next archival work

  1. Inspect the original Irwin Superior and Inferior Court minutes for the 1820 jury panel and July 1824 road order.
  2. Locate the original Georgia session laws of December 24, 1825 and November 30, 1826, including the commissioner list and exact court-removal language.
  3. Review Lowndes Inferior Court ordinary minutes, wills, bonds, inventories, appraisements, annual returns, and loose estates for 1848–1855, including filings under Enoch or another administrator.
  4. Trace Lots 270 and 271 through tax digests, deeds, plats, execution files, and the Vickers judgment to identify acreage, the sheriff-sale purchaser, the mill, and the house site.
  5. Search tavern licenses, merchant licenses, daybooks, and court expense accounts for Hall's inn and any store.
  6. Search Georgia militia commission books and 1836 rosters before assigning Hall any rank or service.
  7. Obtain a cemetery survey, church burial register, or older grave record for the Hall home-and-mill neighborhood.
  8. Use probate, deeds, church records, and later labor or Freedmen's Bureau records to look for names of people enslaved by the Hall household.

Citation audit

All 25 numbered sources are cited in the body. Contemporary and original records control where accessible. Later recollections, compiled histories, and family pages are labeled by type; repeated narratives are not counted as independent proof. The 1823/1824, Lot 270/271, first-court-date, family, and probate conflicts remain open.

A credible 1902 correction says the residence itself stood in adjoining Lot 270. The property cluster is clear, but the house footprint is not.[4][5][6][7][8]

The family record is thinner. Census records trace Hall from Irwin in 1820 to Lowndes in 1830 and 1840. An indexed Telfair County entry records his 1817 marriage to Elizabeth Coaker. Nineteenth-century and later sources identify Colonel Enoch Hall as his son, but no located probate or Bible record establishes a complete family. Claims about Sion's parents, three wives, all children, exact birth date, and exact death day remain derivative or unresolved.[9][10][11][12][13][14]

docs.title: Identity and namesakes
docs.text:
The record chain concerns the older Sion Hall who headed households in original Irwin County in 1820 and Lowndes County in 1830 and 1840. The unusual name, county continuity, public-site records, Hall family land, and the later Enoch Hall accounts point to one man. Census indexes obscure him as "Dian Hall" in 1820 and "Sim Hall" in 1830. The original 1830 schedule was inspected and reads "Sion Hall".[9][10][11]

He must not be merged with Sion L. Hall, a grandson born about 1868, or with his son Enoch Hall, his brother John Hall, or other Hall men in the neighborhood. Later honorifics such as "Hon." and "Judge" are not office records. No located document proves that Sion held judicial office, served in the militia, or sat in the legislature.[1][2][15]

docs.title: Origins, marriage, and family
docs.text:
The modern Hall Cemetery marker gives the years 1784–1849. Find a Grave adds North Carolina as the birthplace, November 14 as the death date, and Enoch Hall and Nancy Ann Jackson as parents. Those details may be correct, but the photographed marker does not contain them and the memorial cites no original birth, Bible, probate, or death record. The safest birth description is about 1784, place unproved.[13]

Three Ancestry collections report that Sion Hall married Elizabeth "Coaker" in Telfair County on April 27, 1817. The entries probably descend from the same county record, so they count as one line of evidence, not three independent confirmations. The original marriage-book image was unavailable. "Coaker" should remain the record spelling; "Coker" is a later variant.[12]

Folks Huxford's sketch of Colonel Enoch Hall identifies Enoch, born in Telfair County in 1804, as the son of Sion and Bridget "Beady" Hall. An 1886 profile independently calls Enoch "the son of Sion Hall", without naming his mother. This makes the father-son relationship strong. Bridget's identity as Enoch's mother rests on the later compiled sketch rather than a located birth or marriage record.[4][14]

Find a Grave, FloridaRoots, public trees, and family stories expand the family considerably. They name Bridget or Beady Hall, Elizabeth Coker or Coaker, and Polly or Pollie Morrison as wives; identify Sion's parents as Enoch Hall and Nancy Jackson; and offer varying child lists. FloridaRoots candidly says its compiler had not done much Hall research. No original record found in this project proves the alleged Bridget or Polly marriages, an 1816 separation, Sion's parentage, or a complete list of children. These are research leads, not a publication-safe pedigree.[13][16]

docs.title: Presence in original Irwin County
docs.text:
Huxford identifies Sion as an 1820 Irwin County householder. The matching federal census index appears as "Dian Hall": eighteen people in the household, eight of them enslaved. The original image was not reopened, so the name identification and totals are strong probable rather than fully image-verified.[4][9]

A published transcription of Irwin court records says Sion was drawn for the first petit-jury panel at the September 21, 1820 Superior Court. The court met at David Williams's house on Lot 147, District 4. The account says the panel was selected for the next term but was not called in March 1821. This distinction matters: Sion's jury selection does not make his home the first Irwin court site.[17]

A second court-record transcription says that in July 1824 the Irwin Inferior Court appointed Sion Hall, James Allen, and Thomas Townsend to lay out a road from the Ocmulgee River to the Alapaha River. The original minute images were not located for either item, so both remain strong secondary evidence.[18]

docs.title: The Coffee Road settlement date
docs.text:
The census and jury evidence place Sion somewhere in the large original Irwin County by 1820. They do not place him on Lot 271. The move to the Coffee Road neighborhood is remembered in two versions:

  • Huxford says Hall moved when the Coffee Road opened in 1823.[4]
  • The Valdosta Times stated in 1899 that Hall first cut timber in the area on January 20, 1824; a 1900 account gives 1824 without the exact day.[19][20]

No located 1823 or 1824 deed, tax entry, diary, or road record settles the difference. The defensible conclusion is that Hall moved within original Irwin County to the Coffee Road settlement in 1823 or early 1824. January 20, 1824 is a precise but unsourced retrospective claim.

docs.title: Hall's house as the temporary Lowndes public center
docs.text:
Lowndes County was created from Irwin on December 24, 1825. Georgia's official 1837 digest summarizes the relevant laws:

"Courts and elections to be held at the house of Sion Hall, 1825 ... Removed to the house of Francis Roundtree, 1826."[1]

A contemporary legislative report from December 1826 confirms passage of the amendment concerning courts and elections at Sion Hall's. One House-column rendering says "Levi Hall", but the Senate report and official digest identify Sion. The same digest says that in 1829 Hall's house was designated as the justice-court place in Captain Pike's district. "Captain Pike's district" identifies the militia district; it is not Sion's rank.[1][2]

Huxford says the 1825 act appointed Lawrence Folsom, Sion Hall, William Blair, John J. Underwood, and Daniel McCranie to select the permanent county site. The exact session-law page naming the commissioners was not located, so the commissioner list is strong secondary evidence rather than a newly verified original.[4]

The date of the first Lowndes Superior Court remains unsettled. A 1900 retrospective places it at Hall's in spring 1826. Huxford quotes William Smith's 1880 recollection that it met there on the first Monday in January 1827. The latter date sits awkwardly beside the 1826 law moving courts and elections to Roundtree's. Original court minutes or a docket are needed. It is safe to say that Hall's house was the statutory temporary site and hosted early county business; it is not safe to assign one exact first-court date.[1][4][20]

Later accounts describe a large double-pen hewn-log house used for court, lodging, and meals, with some jurors deliberating outdoors. The earliest detailed version located is Montgomery M. Folsom's 1885 travel-history account. An 1886 Atlanta profile repeats its distinctive details and is probably derivative; it should not be counted as independent confirmation.[14][21]

Several later histories mistakenly call Hall's house the site of Irwin County's first court. That claim is contradicted by the court-record transcription placing the 1820 Irwin court at David Williams's house. The Lowndes and Irwin claims must remain separate.[17][20]

docs.title: Land Lots 270 and 271, Mount Zion, and the mills
docs.text:
The Georgia land-lot service places Lot 271 in the Twelfth District of original Irwin, now Brooks County. The map proves the lot's location, not Hall ownership.[22]

The Hall interest in Lot 271 rests on three cumulative lines of evidence:

  1. Huxford printed a transcription he said he made from the original November 8, 1831 deed. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed about six acres connected with camps, church, and burying ground to Methodist Episcopal trustees. The description begins at the west north-south line of Lot 271. The lost Lowndes Deed Book A copy had been recorded at pages 654–655 on February 26, 1833.[4]
  2. An April 1845 sheriff-sale notice levied Lot 271 as property of Sion and Enoch Hall to satisfy a Lowndes Superior Court judgment in "Drury Vickers vs Enoch Hall, Sion Hall and John Hall, securities on stay".[5]
  3. A March 1846 repeat calls Lot 271 well improved, with a saw and grist mill in operation. This proves operating mills on the levied Hall property by 1846. It does not prove who built or personally ran them.[6]

Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollection placed Enoch at the Hall center on Lot 271. The 1908 Brooks County map later marked Mount Zion/Camp Ground and a J. L. Hall residence in that lot.[3][8]

The house itself may have stood next door. In 1902 Norman Campbell, an early resident, corrected a published account and said the first-court residence stood on Lot 270. Lots 270 and 271 adjoin, and a home, mill, campground, burying ground, and larger plantation need not occupy one lot. The best present conclusion is: Hall's court house, lodging place, mills, and Mount Zion campground formed a compact Coffee Road neighborhood at or adjoining Lot 271; Hall's Lot 271 interest is proved, but the residence footprint and its placement in Lot 270 or 271 remain unresolved.[7]

docs.title: Inn, merchant activity, and local tradition
docs.text:
Huxford says Sion kept a public inn on the Coffee Road, lodging twelve to fifteen travelers, and that Enoch continued it after Sion's death. The nineteenth-century court narratives support a large house that lodged officials and travelers. No tavern license or guest register was found, so "public inn" is strongly supported but not proved by a business license.[4][21]

Sharpe wrote in 1884 that he was "merchantising at Mr. Sion Hall's" when he helped establish an early mail route and Sharpe's Store. This proves merchant activity at the Hall settlement, but it does not show who owned the stock, store, or building. Later claims that Sion owned the store or that his brother John ran a liquor bar remain possible and unverified.[3]

The 1885 account described old mill sills and a dam near the former Hall home and repeated a comic story about the slow grist mill. The writer expressly declined to vouch for the story's authenticity. The physical mill claim is consistent with the 1846 sale notice; the anecdote remains folklore.[6][21]

docs.title: Census households and slavery
docs.text:
The federal census indexes give the following household totals:[9][10][11]

Year Indexed name and county Total household Enslaved people Evidence boundary
1820 "Dian Hall", Irwin 18 8 Strong probable identification; original image not reopened
1830 "Sim Hall", Lowndes 8 3 Original schedule inspected; manuscript name reads Sion Hall; totals retained from index
1840 "Sion Hall", Lowndes 14 4 Index verified; original image not reopened

These schedules do not name wives, children, or enslaved people. They support only numerical statements. No names or relationships can be reconstructed from the aggregate entries.

The decline from eight enslaved people in 1820 to three in 1830 and four in 1840 is real at the indexed-household level, but the schedules do not explain transfers, sales, deaths, hiring, residence changes, or household composition. No estate inventory was found to connect particular individuals to Hall at his death.

docs.title: Death, burial, and probate
docs.text:
Huxford gives Sion's death year as 1849. The modern Hall Cemetery marker also reads "SION HALL / 1784-1849". Find a Grave supplies November 14, 1849, but that day does not appear on the photographed stone and no contemporary notice or probate record was found. The year is strong; the exact date is unresolved.[4][13]

The earliest located burial descriptions are from 1885 and 1886. They place Sion's grave under large trees or in a grove by his mill creek. Together with the Hall Cemetery memorial, they make burial in the Hall home-and-mill neighborhood near Morven strong probable. They do not establish that the modern marker occupies the exact original grave.[14][21]

Searches found no will, administration, inventory, estate division, obituary, death notice, or administrator advertisement. The Ancestry Georgia wills-and-probate index displayed no Lowndes County result for Sion, but that was a name-index search, not a page-by-page review of county volumes. Newspapers.com searches for 1840–1870 also produced no death or estate notice. These are documented negatives, not proof that no estate proceeding existed.

docs.title: Public roles that are proved, probable, or unsupported
Proved or strongly supported
docs.text:
• Irwin petit-jury panel selection in 1820, from a published court-record transcription.[17]
  • Irwin road commissioner in 1824, from a published court-record transcription.[18]
  • Member of the 1825 Lowndes public-site commission, from Huxford's specific act-based account.[4]
  • His house's statutory use for Lowndes courts and elections in 1825–1826 and as a justice-court place in 1829.[1][2]
  • A legal/property interest with Enoch in Lot 271 and operating saw and grist mills on the levied property by 1846.[4][5][6]

docs.title: Unsupported or contradicted
docs.text:
• Judicial office. The court met at Hall's house; no record found makes Hall a judge or justice.
  • Militia rank or Indian-war service. No commission, muster, pay roll, pension, bounty file, or roster naming this Sion was located.
  • Legislative service. The May 1924 centennial article says Sion "was a member of the Legislature" and that Enoch "followed him"; it does not name a county, office, or term. Service for Lowndes County sometime between its creation in 1825 and Sion's death in 1849 is therefore chronologically possible, but no election return, legislative roster, or official journal located in this project proves it. Hamilton W. Sharpe's 1884 recollection instead names William A. Knight and Benjamin Sermons as Lowndes County's first legislative delegation, so Sion was probably not one of the county's first legislators. Three derivative September 1933 articles changed the story by calling the elder Sion Brooks County's first representative and Enoch the second. That version is impossible: Sion died in 1849, nine years before Brooks County was created.[3][4][13][23][24]
  • A Hall-owned store, liquor bar, or licensed tavern.
  • A personal 1820 land-lottery draw. Lot 271's survey history and Hall's 1820 census presence do not establish how he acquired the property.

docs.title: Verified or strong
docs.text:
• Sion Hall was in original Irwin County by 1820 and in Lowndes County in 1830 and 1840.[9][10][11]
  • His house was the legally designated temporary Lowndes court-and-election site.[1][2]
  • He and Enoch held an interest in Lot 271, which had operating saw and grist mills by 1846.[4][5][6]
  • Enoch was his son.[4][14]
  • An 1817 Telfair County marriage entry names Sion Hall and Elizabeth Coaker.[12]
  • Sion died in 1849 and was remembered as buried near the Hall home and mill.[4][13][21]

docs.title: Probable or moderate
docs.text:
• The move to the Coffee Road/Lot 271 neighborhood occurred in 1823 or early 1824.[4][19][20]
  • Bridget or Beady was Enoch's mother.[4]
  • Hall's large house functioned as a public inn or travelers' lodging place.[4][21]
  • The current Hall Cemetery memorial identifies the original burial neighborhood.[13][14][21]

docs.title: Unresolved
docs.text:
• Exact birth date and place; parentage; every spouse and child.
  • Whether the Coffee Road move occurred in 1823 or on January 20, 1824.
  • Whether the residence stood in Lot 270 or Lot 271.
  • The exact first Lowndes Superior Court date.
  • Exact death day, probate, estate distribution, and exact grave continuity.
  • Tavern or store ownership, military service, judicial office, and legislative service.

docs.title: Online research coverage and limits
docs.text:
The project searched stored Brooks/Lowndes research first, then used authenticated Ancestry census, marriage, probate, and cemetery collections; Newspapers.com; Georgia Historic Newspapers; Internet Archive; Georgia Archives maps; the state land-lot service; Huxford's county history; public FamilySearch profile pages; Find a Grave; and selected image-backed local-history transcriptions. Searches used the listed name variants with Irwin, Lowndes, Brooks, Morven, Coffee Road, Mount Zion, Lot 270, Lot 271, court, election, jury, road, commissioner, mill, inn, tavern, store, militia, marriage, death, probate, estate, and cemetery.

"Fully researched online" means the accessible online groups and known leads were searched and reconciled. It does not mean all courthouse or manuscript records are digitized. The 1820 and 1840 census images, original 1817 marriage entry, original Irwin jury and road minutes, exact 1825 and 1826 session-law pages, Lowndes probate volumes, and tax/deed chains for Lots 270 and 271 remain uninspected or unavailable. FamilySearch record images required authentication or were blocked, and some Ancestry and Newspapers.com links require subscriptions.

docs.title: Best next archival work
docs.text:
1. Inspect the original Irwin Superior and Inferior Court minutes for the 1820 jury panel and July 1824 road order.
  2. Locate the original Georgia session laws of December 24, 1825 and November 30, 1826, including the commissioner list and exact court-removal language.
  3. Review Lowndes Inferior Court ordinary minutes, wills, bonds, inventories, appraisements, annual returns, and loose estates for 1848–1855, including filings under Enoch or another administrator.
  4. Trace Lots 270 and 271 through tax digests, deeds, plats, execution files, and the Vickers judgment to identify acreage, the sheriff-sale purchaser, the mill, and the house site.
  5. Search tavern licenses, merchant licenses, daybooks, and court expense accounts for Hall's inn and any store.
  6. Search Georgia militia commission books and 1836 rosters before assigning Hall any rank or service.
  7. Obtain a cemetery survey, church burial register, or older grave record for the Hall home-and-mill neighborhood.
  8. Use probate, deeds, church records, and later labor or Freedmen's Bureau records to look for names of people enslaved by the Hall household.
