docs.title: Archibald Strickland
docs.text:
Archibald Strickland's connection to the future Brooks County area rests on strong secondary evidence. Folks Huxford's account of Bethel Primitive Baptist Church names Archibald and Luander Strickland among the congregation's organizing members in 1826 and identifies Archibald as a deacon. The original minute book has not been inspected.

The original 1820 Tattnall County census records Archibald with three boys ages 10–15. Simpson and Simeon Strickland were each about fourteen and fit that household structure. A later Ray City History Blog account explicitly identifies Simpson as a son of Archibald and Luander and Simeon as Simpson's brother. An original 1826 Lowndes deed independently places Simpson and Simeon together as witnesses. Taken together, the evidence supports the father-and-sons reconstruction as secondary evidence, but no inspected original record states the relationships.

The 1850 Ware County census names Archibald, age 64, born in North Carolina, with $300 in real estate. A five-year-old Archibald appears in the same household and must remain a separate person. The elder Archibald's precise death and estate remain unresolved, and the surviving online Ware deed series begins too late to settle them.

No Strickland in the canonical Barney census pages is presently connected to Archibald through Simpson or Simeon. The identified Barney households belong to separate reconstructed branches.

docs.title: John Hall
docs.text:
John Hall¶

Lowndes County records distinguish two adult John Halls by 1840. The older household head was born between 1791 and 1800. The younger man, written as John Hall Jr. on the original census schedule, was born about 1812–1814. The suffixes distinguish the men but do not by themselves prove that they were father and son.

John Hall Sr.¶

Folks Huxford's Morven postmaster list identifies John Hall Sr. as postmaster beginning April 1, 1836. An 1841 sheriff's-sale notice separately calls him “John Hall Sen'r” and places his residence on 343 acres in District 12, Land Lot 270. Huxford also reports a John Hall commissioned second lieutenant of the 660th District in 1831. John Sr. is the better chronological candidate, but the original commission has not been inspected.

A 1925 obituary says Lottie Hall was a niece of Sion Hall and identifies her father as John Hall. This explicitly makes that John a brother of Sion. Chronology favors John Sr., but the obituary supplies no suffix or original parentage source. John Sr. as Sion's brother is therefore secondary-supported and probable, not verified.

John Hall Jr.¶

John Jr.'s 1840 household contained a man and woman ages twenty to twenty-nine and three boys under five. In 1850 and 1860, the continuing Lowndes household included William Hall at the expected age. This makes John Jr. William M. Hall's strong-probable father, although no inspected record states the relationship directly.

Elizabeth was nineteen in 1850 and was not the woman in John Jr.'s 1840 household. Francis Pearson Hall's 1938 Georgia death certificate names his parents as John Hall and Elizabeth Easter. The census also places Roxanna, Instant, and Sarah Easters in John and Elizabeth's 1850 household. Elizabeth Easter was John Jr.'s later wife and Francis's verified mother. She was William M. Hall's probable stepmother; William's biological mother remains unresolved.

Militia and land records¶

The original 1836 Lowndes general-militia return lists an unsuffixed John Hall as a private in the 660th District. John Jr., then about twenty-two to twenty-four, is the stronger candidate. The manuscript does not distinguish him from John Sr., and a militia return is not proof of active Creek War service.

An 1845 legal notice names John Hall with Enoch and Sion Hall as securities in Drury Vickers v. Enoch Hall. It verifies association, not kinship. Later deed transcriptions use John Hall's millpond as a boundary and report an 1877 conveyance from “heirs of John Hall” to Rebecca Hall. The original deed images are not available online, the heirs are unnamed in the transcription, and a separate William G. Hall had held the relevant Lot 132 in the 1840s. Those deeds cannot yet be assigned safely to John Sr. or Jr.

Evidence status¶

  • Verified: two adult John Hall households in 1840; John Sr.'s 1841 Lot 270 residence; John Jr.'s continuing 1850–1870 household.
  • Strong probable: John Jr. was William M. Hall's father.
  • Secondary-supported/probable: John Sr. was Sion Hall's brother.
  • Unresolved: John Sr. as John Jr.'s father; William's biological mother; the 1831 officer and 1836 private identities; the heirs in the 1877 Lot 132 deed.

docs.title: Simeon Strickland
docs.text:
Simeon Strickland was in South Georgia by 1826. A Lowndes County deed executed that June was witnessed by Simeon and Simpson Strickland. In 1837 Simpson swore that he had seen Simeon sign the instrument. The deed verifies that the two men were personally associated, although it does not call them brothers.

The original 1830 Thomas County census names a household head whose surname is best read as Stricklen, and the original 1850 Lowndes schedule names Simeon Strickland, age 44, a Georgia-born farmer. Later district records place him as a justice of the peace in the 659th, or Nankin, District in 1832–1833. That placement is strong secondary evidence pending inspection of the underlying commission or court record.

The Ray City History Blog identifies Simeon as Simpson's brother and both men as sons of Archibald and Luander Strickland. Archibald's 1820 Tattnall County household contained three boys ages 10–15, which fits the proposed family, and the 1826 deed independently places Simeon and Simpson together. The relationship is secondary-supported, not verified, because no inspected original record names them as brothers or sons.

No Strickland in the canonical Barney census pages is presently connected to Simeon or Simpson. The 1900 Stephen Elias Strickland household and the 1920 Shelley Lee Strickland household trace to other reconstructed branches.

docs.title: Ebenezer Folsom
docs.text:
Ebenezer Folsom was living in Lowndes County by 1840. The original census schedule names a household head indexed as “Ebenezer Tolsom,” with Ebenezer Folsom supplied as an alternate reading. Ten years later, the original Lowndes County census clearly records Ebenezer J. Folsom, a thirty-three-year-old Georgia-born farmer, in a household with Priscilla J. Folsom and seven younger residents.

Land records place him more precisely. A deed dated November 21, 1859 conveyed Ebenezer G. Folsom 245 acres in District 12, Land Lot 259, then in Brooks County. Another deed records Ebenezer G. Folsom conveying fifty acres in November 1859. The deed indexes establish his presence in Brooks County, although the recorded instruments still need to be opened and transcribed.

The 1860 Brooks County census records E. J. Folsom, age forty-three, with Priscilla J. and a household that continues the 1850 family. The schedules therefore verify Ebenezer J. and E. J. as the same man. The deed indexes use the middle initial G, and later cemetery and family sources call him Ebenezer George Folsom. His complete name should remain qualified until an original record resolves the difference.

An 1861 Brooks County deed-index entry independently names Priscilla Jane Folsom as the grantee of 485 acres in District 13, Land Lot 106. Later tax and deed indexes document her property record, and the 1870 census records Jane as head of the continuing household. These records verify her full married name and independent landholding. The maiden surname Rogers remains secondary-supported because no inspected original record supplies it or names her parents.

A 1938 Folsom genealogy identifies Ebenezer as a son of George Folsom and Edith Penny and a brother of Thomas, Israel, Pennywell, and Elizabeth Folsom. That reconstruction is secondary-supported because no inspected original record names the parents. The same body of evidence, combined with the census household chain, makes Ebenezer the strong-probable father of Israel Lee Folsom, the later Barney farmer and railroad promoter.

Ebenezer now qualifies as a supplemental early settler through his 1840 and 1850 census record. The 1859 deeds place him more precisely in Brooks County. They do not place his home at the later Barney townsite; his documented Barney connection runs through his son Israel Lee.

docs.title: Priscilla Jane Folsom
docs.text: Priscilla Jane Folsom was living in Lowndes County by 1850. That census records Priscilla J., about thirty, in Ebenezer J. Folsom's household. The 1860 Brooks County census continues the same family as E. J. and Priscilla J. Folsom with their children, including four-month-old Israel. Neither census states household relationships.

docs.title: Land and household record
docs.text:
A Brooks County deed index gives her full name in an official contemporary record. Nathan S. McCall conveyed 485 acres in District 13, Land Lot 106 to Priscilla Jane Folsom by warranty deed dated January 15, 1861. The index establishes the parties, property, date, and recording reference. The underlying deed text has not been inspected for its consideration or other terms.

By 1870, Jane Folsom headed the continuing Brooks County household. The 1880 census identifies P. J. Folsom as Israel L. Folsom's mother, directly verifying that relationship. Tax and deed indexes also document her as a Brooks County property holder during the 1870s and 1880s.

The 1900 Quitman census records Jane Folsom as widowed and reports that she had borne eleven children, four of whom were living. It gives her birth as January 1826. That conflicts with the derivative cemetery dates of February 14, 1820, to August 17, 1903, so her exact birth date remains unverified.

docs.title: Name and family assessment
docs.text:
The census chain and land record verify the identity Priscilla Jane Folsom. The 1880 census verifies that she was Israel Lee Folsom's mother. Her identification as Ebenezer Folsom's wife is strong probable from the continuous household record, but no original marriage license or return has been located.

The maiden surname Rogers is secondary-supported by cemetery and compiled family material. Every official record inspected in this study names her as Folsom. No inspected deed, estate paper, guardianship bond, census entry, or marriage record names her parents or connects her to James Rogers, Thomas F. Rogers, Uriah Rogers, Isaac J. Rogers, or Joseph J. Rogers.

Priscilla belongs on the supplemental early-settler and family-bridge roster because she was individually named in Lowndes County by 1850 and later held land in Brooks County. Her exact arrival year and any direct residence in the later Barney townsite remain unproved.

docs.title: Evidence assessment
docs.text:
• Priscilla Jane Folsom: verified.
  • Mother of Israel Lee Folsom: verified.
  • Wife of Ebenezer Folsom: strong probable.
  • Rogers maiden surname: secondary-supported.
  • Parents and connection to the other Rogers families: unresolved.
  • Exact 1820–1903 dates: derivative and not original-record verified.

docs.title: Thomas F. Rogers
docs.text:
Thomas F. Rogers was present in old Lowndes County by 1844. The original tax digest lists him in Captain Blair's District with 163 acres in District 12, Land Lot 199. James Rogers returned another 163 acres in the same lot on the preceding line, and Uriah Rogers followed Thomas in the tax list. Those entries establish a Rogers land cluster in the territory later included in Brooks County. They do not state how the men were related.

The 1850 census indexes Thomas as “Thomas F. Rogen,” a thirty-year-old North Carolina-born farmer with $400 in real estate. Nancy and five younger residents appear in the household, but the schedule does not identify their relationships. A later county history included Thomas among the families living at Troupville and named him as a serving Brooks County grand juror in November 1859.

A Brooks County deed index supplies a second land anchor. Thomas F. Rogers conveyed 245 acres in District 12, Land Lot 259 to Ebenezer G. Folsom by warranty deed dated November 21, 1859. The index verifies the parties, date, acreage, lot, district, and recording reference. It does not identify Ebenezer as a relative or mention Priscilla Jane Folsom.

Thomas therefore qualifies as a supplemental early settler through the original 1844 tax entry. His exact arrival year is unknown. The shared Lot 199 entries and the later Rogers-to-Folsom deed make a family or close-associate connection plausible, but the relationship between Thomas, James, Uriah, and Priscilla remains unresolved.

Thomas died before February 1865. His estate records identify Mary Rogers as one of his heirs, while later guardianship bonds concern several orphan children. Melissa A. J. Rogers is individually clear. Aaron, Phebe A., and William Rogers are strong-probable readings from the 1868 bond and the 1860 household. Later bond names require further handwriting review.

A Mary Rogers married Thomas McLoney in Brooks County on October 4, 1866. Mary Maloney became Melissa's guardian in January 1867 and appears with Thomas Malony in Quitman in 1870. These records make the two Mary identities strong probable, but they do not state Mary's exact relationship to Thomas F. Rogers. The evidence does not justify calling her his widow.

docs.title: Uriah Rogers
docs.text:
Uriah Rogers was established in the future Brooks County area by 1844. The original Lowndes County tax digest places him in Captain Blair's District immediately after James Rogers and Thomas F. Rogers. James and Thomas each returned 163 acres in District 12, Land Lot 199. Uriah returned a poll but no land.

The 1830 Thomas County census and the 1850 Lowndes County census provide a strong-probable household chain for the older Uriah. The 1850 schedule records him as a 43-year-old North Carolina-born farmer with $800 in real estate. Elizabeth Rogers and nine younger household members follow him, although that census does not state their relationships.

The shared surname and consecutive tax entries show a local Rogers network, not a family tree. No inspected record establishes Uriah's relationship to James Rogers, Thomas F. Rogers, Isaac J. Rogers, or Priscilla Jane Rogers Folsom.

The underlying Brooks County deeds have now been inspected. Uriah sold District 12, Land Lot 513 property to Joseph J. Rogers in 1868 and to Robert Milton Rogers in 1873. Both were cash sales using ordinary warranty language; neither deed states a relationship. Joseph's status as Uriah's son is verified by the previously inspected death certificate. Robert Milton's placement in Uriah's 1860 household, combined with the 1873 conveyance, makes him a strong-probable son, but not an original-record-verified son. John W. Rogers witnessed both transactions, while Francis R. Rogers witnessed Joseph's deed and Ashley Uriah Rogers witnessed Robert Milton's deed.

The James Rogers estate deed identifies Ann Rogers as James's widow, Thomas F. Rogers as administrator, and Isaac J. Rogers as the highest bidder for estate land. It does not call Thomas or Isaac a relative. Thomas's later estate records prove that Mary Rogers was one of his heirs and identify several minor children, but they supply no bridge to Uriah. Mary is strong probable as the Mary Maloney who married in October 1866 and became guardian of Thomas's orphan child Melissa in January 1867. Her exact relationship to Thomas remains unresolved. Uriah therefore belongs on the supplemental early-settler roster, while his connection to the James-Thomas-Isaac branch and to Priscilla remains unresolved.

docs.title: Israel Lee Folsom
docs.text:
Back to the Railroad Organizers index

Israel Lee Folsom (April 11, 1860-February 4, 1926) was a Brooks County farmer and plantation operator whose adult life became closely tied to Barney. He appears in the local record as a cotton producer, a promoter of two railroad ventures, and one of the community's substantial landholders. His full name and life dates are verified through a continuous census and family record, his original marriage entry, a contemporary obituary, an original probate bond, and the inscription on his grave marker.[2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9][23][24][25]

Huxford lists “I. L. Folsom” among the twenty-six men who petitioned in 1896 for the charter of the South Georgia Railroad.[1] The petitioner was strongly probably Israel Lee Folsom. The identification is supported by his age, Brooks County residence, farming interests, later Barney residence, and later service as a director of another proposed railroad. It is not graded verified because the known charter list gives only initials, and the original petition or signature page was not found online.

docs.title: Identity and parents
docs.text:
Folsom was born in Brooks County on April 11, 1860. The federal census taken that year records Israel Folsom, four months old, in the household of E. J. and Priscilla J. Folsom near the Tallokas post office. The schedule did not state family relationships, but the household, age, county, and later records establish a strong continuity.[2]

The household head was Ebenezer Folsom. A 1938 genealogy identifies Ebenezer and pioneer Israel Folsom as brothers, which would make the pioneer Israel Lee’s uncle. That older relationship is secondary-supported; the two Israels were different men.

In 1870, “Isreal” Folsom, age ten, lived in Quitman with Jane Folsom and the same family group.[3] The 1880 census makes the relationship explicit. Israel L. Folsom, age twenty, was recorded as the son of P. J. Folsom in Quitman. He was single and working as a farm laborer.[4]

These records verify Priscilla Jane Folsom as his mother. An 1861 deed-index entry independently verifies her full married name, and the 1900 census records her as widowed with eleven children born and four living. Cemetery and family-history sources expand his parents' names to Ebenezer George Folsom and Priscilla Jane Rogers Folsom.[26] The father's expanded name and the mother's Rogers surname remain derivative rather than original-record verified. The 1900 census reports Priscilla's birth as January 1826, so the exact 1820–1903 cemetery dates also remain unverified.

The grave marker supplies the middle name that the census and railroad sources leave abbreviated. It reads “Israel Lee Folsom” and gives April 11, 1860, and February 4, 1926.[25] The photographed inscription verifies the name and dates. Family links attached to the cemetery memorial remain derivative unless independently supported.

docs.title: Marriage and children
docs.text:
Israel L. Folsom married Ann C. Walker in Brooks County on December 11, 1884. The date and names appear in the original county marriage book.[5] Later census schedules identify her variously as Ann, Ann C., and Annie. “Civility,” the middle name used by cemetery sources, was not found in an original record inspected for this dossier, so she is called Ann C. Walker here.

The 1900 census records Israel as a farmer who owned a mortgaged farm. It gives April 1860 as his birth month and year and says he and Ann had been married fifteen years. Their household included Turner, Fleming Bates, Jane, Benjamin, and Cora.[6] Ann's fertility columns were recorded as six children born and six living. That conflicts with the contemporary report of a daughter's death in 1895, and the household itself lists only five children. The 1900 fertility count cannot be accepted as exact.

By 1910 the family was living on First Avenue in Barney. Ancestry's primary index calls the head H. L. Folsom, but the original schedule reads I. L. Folsom. He was a farmer and employer. Ann C. reported that they had been married twenty-five years and had nine children, eight of whom were living. The household listed Turner W., Fleming B., Sarah J., Benjamin, Cora L., Manor B., A. J., and I. L. Jr.[7] The marriage duration was rounded. The original marriage entry fixes the wedding date in December 1884.

The eight children accounted for in the census sequence were Turner Walker, Fleming Bates, Sarah Jane, Benjamin Franklin, Cora L., Manor B., Allen James, and Israel L. Jr. Contemporary newspaper reports identify the missing child as a daughter, although they do not give her name or age. On the morning of July 21, 1895, Israel walked out to inspect one of his farms a few miles east of Quitman. One of his little girls tried to follow him. He told her to remain at a tenant's house, but she continued after him. When Israel returned and learned that she had gone on, he searched and found her drowned in a nearby branch. The report supposed that she had fallen from a log while trying to cross.[29]

The 1910 census later reported nine children born and eight living, while the census sequence accounts for the other eight children. Despite the faulty 1900 count, the 1910 total and the contemporary death report strongly identify the girl who drowned in 1895 as the ninth child. A derivative cemetery memorial calls her “Unknown daughter Folsom,” gives the same death date, and assigns her to Camp Ground Cemetery, but it displays no marker photograph or original burial record.[30] Her name, exact age, and burial place therefore remain unverified, and no separate funeral notice was found.

In 1920, I. L. Folsom was still farming at Barney. He owned his farm free of mortgage and worked as its manager on his own account. Annie and sons Ben, Manor, A. J., and I. L. Jr. remained in the household.[8]

Turner Walker Folsom's original Georgia death certificate later named his parents as I. L. Folsom and Annie Walker.[9] That certificate verifies the parent-child relationship. It belongs to Turner, not Israel, and is not evidence of Israel's own cause of death.

docs.title: Farming and property
docs.text:
Folsom's first substantial newspaper appearance came in March 1896, the same month the South Georgia Railroad organized. Fire destroyed his large barn near the Brooks-Lowndes county line. One account called him an energetic and prosperous young farmer. Reports listed about 700 bushels of corn, 3,000 bundles of fodder, hay, ground peas, mules, a horse, a cow, and hogs among the losses. The gate had apparently been saturated with oil, and arson was suspected. The loss was uninsured and estimated at several thousand dollars.[10][11]

The Barney cotton reports show the scale of his later farming. In August 1906, I. L. Folsom, printed once as Folsome, brought Barney's first bale of new cotton to market. It weighed 510 pounds.[13][14] Two years later, eight bales were ginned at Barney in one day, six of them belonging to Folsom.[16] These reports show that he was a significant producer. They do not establish that he owned the gin.

Another fire struck property at Barney in April 1908. A brief report said three houses associated with Folsom, E. Jones, and R. P. Pinkey were destroyed, and that Folsom's loss was partly insured.[15] The compressed account appears to assign one house to each man. It does not support a claim that Folsom owned all three.

In January 1917, Israel Folsom of Barney attended a Sea Island cotton growers' convention in Valdosta. Growers were deciding whether long-staple cotton remained viable as the boll weevil spread through the region.[20] His attendance places him among the commercial planters dealing directly with the crop crisis.

The clearest description of his agricultural scale appeared in 1923. The Americus Times-Recorder said he operated several large plantations, was held in high esteem, and was guarding about 200 bales of cotton at his Barney home amid threats connected with the prosecution of his son's killer.[22] The article verifies substantial plantation operations and a large cotton holding at that moment. It does not supply acreage, deeds, tenant lists, or an estate valuation.

docs.title: South Georgia Railroad
docs.text:
Huxford's county history lists I. L. Folsom among twenty-six petitioners for the South Georgia Railroad charter in 1896. The proposed capital was $65,000 in 650 shares.[1] Huxford separates the petitioners from the nine first directors and four officers. Folsom appears only in the larger petitioner list.

A contemporary report of the March 1896 organization meeting confirms the first directors and officers but does not reproduce all twenty-six petitioners.[12] Folsom was not on that first board and held no listed office. No source found online gives his subscription amount, share count, right-of-way contribution, or later participation in the company.

The identification of the petitioner as Israel Lee Folsom is strong probable. The case rests on a specific combination: an adult farmer named Israel Folsom was prominent in Brooks County at the time of the petition; the census chain places Israel L. continuously in the county; later schedules place I. L. at Barney; and contemporary reports show the Barney man promoting another railroad. No competing Brooks County adult with the same initials and profile emerged from the search. Still, the initials-only charter list leaves a small evidentiary gap that should not be hidden.

docs.title: Georgia, Alabama and Western Railway
docs.text:
Folsom's later railway role is directly documented. In June 1912, several newspapers named I. L. Folsom of Barney as a director of the proposed Georgia, Alabama and Western Railway Company. Its planned route ran through Hahira, Barney, Pavo, Meigs, Colquitt, and Blakely toward Dothan, with an intended eastward extension toward Brunswick. The directors authorized surveys and cost estimates.[17][18][19]

This directorship is verified as printed and shows that Folsom remained interested in transportation development sixteen years after the South Georgia Railroad petition. The reports describe the company's officers and directors as prominent business men and expected stockholders, but they do not state Folsom's investment. The 1912 project was a separate corporation. It cannot be used to turn his 1896 petitioner role into an unrecorded South Georgia Railroad board seat or office.

docs.title: Barney community and family notices
docs.text:
Newspaper social columns add small but useful checks on the household. In August 1913, Mrs. I. L. Folsom and sons Ben and Manor returned to Barney after visiting near Quitman. A September notice recorded I. L. Folsom making a business trip to Adel.[27][28] These notices agree with the 1910 and 1920 family schedules.

In October 1914, Turner Folsom of Barney was injured when his gun discharged. The report identified him as a son of I. L. Folsom.[21] The item supplies contemporary support for the relationship later stated on Turner's death certificate.

The same evidence does not establish a store, bank office, elected post, or named partnership for Israel. No reliable online source found in this search placed him in those roles.

docs.title: Turner Folsom's killing
docs.text:
Turner Folsom was shot and killed in July 1923. Contemporary reporting described the encounter as a dispute involving Max Jordan, a tenant or farm worker associated with the Folsom and McGill plantation network.[22] Later that year, while Jordan awaited trial, Israel Folsom told authorities that witnesses were being threatened. The claim of intimidation was his allegation and should remain attributed to him.

The coverage is important for Israel's biography because it directly identifies Turner as his married son, places Israel at Barney, and describes the scale of the family's plantation and cotton interests. It also explains why the 1923 articles devote unusual attention to Israel's property and standing in the community. Trial follow-up appeared in November, but the accessible reports do not provide a complete court file or final appellate record.[22]

docs.title: Death, probate, and burial
docs.text:
Folsom suffered a stroke on Sunday, January 31, 1926, and died at his Barney home on Thursday morning, February 4. The Valdosta Daily Times called him a prominent citizen and wealthy farmer. He was sixty-five by the dates on his marker, although the obituary called him sixty-six.[23][25]

The obituary named his widow and seven surviving children: Mrs. Grady Hendrix, Mrs. T. H. Byrd, F. B. Folsom, B. F. Folsom, Manor Folsom, A. J. Folsom, and I. L. Folsom Jr. Turner had died in 1923. The funeral was set for February 5 at Camp Ground Church near Morven, where Folsom was buried.[23]

On April 5, 1926, the Brooks County Court of Ordinary appointed Ann C. Folsom administratrix of I. L. Folsom's estate. The original administrator's bond survives.[24] It verifies the widow's legal role and closes the identity chain, but it does not reveal the estate inventory, land descriptions, debts, heirs' distributions, or final value.

His marker at Camp Ground Cemetery reads “Israel Lee Folsom / Apr. 11, 1860 / Feb. 4, 1926.”[25] The inscription agrees with the census birth month and year, the obituary's death date, and the probate sequence.

docs.title: Evidence assessment
docs.text:
1. The Barney farmer is verified as Israel Lee Folsom. The 1860-1920 censuses, original marriage record, family record, obituary, probate bond, and grave inscription form a continuous identity chain.
  2. His marriage to Ann C. Walker and eight surviving children in 1910 are verified. Contemporary reports identify the ninth child as a young daughter who drowned in 1895, but they do not give her name or age. The 1900 fertility count conflicts with that death and is treated as a census error.
  3. His career as a farmer and substantial plantation operator is verified in broad outline. Exact acreage, title history, cotton production totals, and estate value were not found.
  4. His identity as the I. L. Folsom named in the 1896 South Georgia Railroad charter petition is strong probable, not verified. The published list uses initials only, and the original petition was not located.
  5. He was not named among the South Georgia Railroad's first directors or officers. No later South Georgia board service or stockholding was found.
  6. His 1912 directorship in the Georgia, Alabama and Western Railway Company is verified. That proposed railway was separate from the South Georgia Railroad.
  7. The full name Ebenezer George Folsom for Israel's father is strong probable. Israel's mother, Priscilla Jane, is verified through the census chain.
  8. A possible 1881 coroner-jury reference was rejected from the narrative because surviving reprints conflict between I. L. and L. L. Folsom and provide no identifying bridge.

docs.title: Open questions and limits
docs.text:
• The original 1896 South Georgia Railroad charter petition, signatures, subscription book, stock ledger, and corporate minutes were not located online.
  • No source found online states Folsom's South Georgia Railroad share count or establishes later service as a company director or officer.
  • No complete deed chain, plantation map, tax series, farm ledger, tenant ledger, or cotton account was found.
  • The probate index and administrator's bond were located, but the estate inventory, returns, distributions, and final settlement were not.
  • The 1895 reports identify the ninth child as a young daughter and describe her drowning, but they do not give her name, exact age, burial place, or a funeral notice.
  • The 1900 census says six children had been born and all six were living, which conflicts with both the 1895 drowning and the five children listed in the household. The later 1910 count of nine born and eight living fits the drowned daughter and the eight surviving children.
  • The father's expanded name, Ebenezer George Folsom, remains strong probable because the 1860 record was indexed E. J.
  • The reports do not establish ownership of a Barney cotton gin, a named commercial partnership, a bank office, or an elected public position.
  • A possible 1881 coroner-jury service cannot be assigned to him because contemporary reprints conflict on the juror's initials.

docs.title: Search coverage
docs.text:
Research covered the local Barney and South Georgia Railroad files, Huxford's county history, newspaper corpora, and stored census references. Online work covered the federal censuses for 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910, and 1920; Brooks County marriage and probate collections; Georgia death records; cemetery evidence; Georgia Historic Newspapers; preserved Newspapers.com searches and direct image pages; the Internet Archive copy of Huxford; and broad exact-name web searches. Two July 1895 reports document the daughter's drowning.

Search variants included "I. L. Folsom", "I L Folsom", "I. L. Folsome", "Israel Folsom", "Israel L. Folsom", "Israel Lee Folsom", "Ann C. Folsom", "Annie Folsom", and "Turner Folsom", combined with Barney, Brooks County, Quitman, Morven, railroad, railway, director, farmer, plantation, cotton, fire, court, death, funeral, obituary, probate, and cemetery. Namesakes were rejected unless a record supplied the correct age, Brooks County or Barney location, Ann or the children, farming profile, or known railroad role.

Original images were inspected for the 1884 marriage, 1910 and 1920 censuses, Turner's death certificate, the 1926 administrator's bond, and Israel's marker. No claim is made that unindexed courthouse, corporate, plantation, or church records were searched.

docs.title: Household #94: Hires, Sim
docs.text:
Household #94: Hires, Sim

Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Sim Hires headed a 5-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

Household Snapshot

Sim Hires headed a 5-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 2 extended-family members and 2 boarders, employees, servants, or other non-kin residents.

Sim Hires's listed occupation was Farmer.

Reported birthplaces span Georgia and South Carolina, pointing to movement into Barney or family formation across county or state lines.

Newspaper and Public-Record Trail

This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

1900 Census Household

Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation
Sim Hires Head 34 Georgia Farmer
Rebecca Hires Mother 71 Georgia —
Ellen Hayes Cook 71 Georgia Cook
John Blecten Boarder 16 South Carolina Farm Laborer
Will Giles Boarder 25 Georgia no occupation listed

Children and Later Trails

No child-tracking items are open for this page because the 1900 table lists no children in the household.

Family Narrative

Rebecca Yates Hiers, Sim’s mother, now has a separate evidence-graded profile. Original deeds document the family’s Brooks County land, and the 1900 census verifies Rebecca in Sim’s Barney household. Her identification as a daughter of William Yates remains strong probable rather than verified.

The census chain James supplied is strong enough to place this household much more securely than the earlier draft did. In 1870, Simon Hiers, age 3, appears in Brooks County in the household of David Hiers, age 48, and Rebecca Hiers, age 42. In 1880, Simeon S. Hien, age 15, appears in Quitman in the household of Rebecca Hien, age 53, with siblings that match a Hiers-Hires family cluster already visible elsewhere in Brooks County records. By 1900, Sim Hires is a single farmer in Barney, born in April 1866, owning his farm free of mortgage while living with his mother Rebecca and taking in boarders.

The later censuses continue the same man in Barney. In 1910, Sim S. Hires, age 42, is a married farmer in Barney with wife Georgia Hires, age 24, and the census states they had been married for zero years. James's newly supplied Brooks County marriage record now anchors that transition directly: S. S. Hires married Georgia Blease, with the license issued and the marriage performed on 6 April 1910. The handwritten return supports Blease as the bride's surname, which fits the record better than the census form Hires. In 1920, S. S. Hires, age 52, still appears in Barney as a married farmer with wife recorded as Georgit Hires, age 34. In 1930, Simeon S. Hiers, age 63, is again in Brooks County, now divorced, living on a farm with Georgia Smith, age 75, identified as his sister. In 1940, Sim S. Hiers, age 73, appears in Barney as a widowed farmer, still with Georgia Smith, now age 86, again identified as his sister.

These records make several things clear. First, the 1870 and 1880 censuses support Sim as the son of David Hiers and Rebecca Hiers, with Rebecca remaining the key parental anchor after David disappears from the household by 1880. Second, the 1910 marriage record identifies the younger wife as Georgia Blease rather than a same-surname Hires bride, which removes the earlier confusion created by the census index. Third, the younger wife of 1910 and 1920 is not the same person as the older Georgia Smith seen in 1930 and 1940; the ages are too far apart, and the later censuses explicitly label Georgia Smith as Sim's sister. Fourth, the household shows long continuity in Barney farming life from at least 1900 through 1940, even though Sim's marital status changes from single to married, then divorced, then widowed.

The newspaper trail now gives that census backbone more local texture. The Valdosta Times of 14 October 1899 named Sim Hires among the successful farmers around Barney, which places him in that farm community just before the 1900 census. A useful marriage-era anchor then appears in the Valdosta Daily Times of 16 April 1910. In OCR form, the notice reads substantially: "Mr. S. S. Hires, a well-known citizen of Brooks county, drove up to the home of Mr. W. R. Blease near Barney and took Miss Georgia Blease for a ride in his buggy. The couple drove over to Quitman and were married in the parlor of the ... hotel by Rev. W. T. Gaulden." The hotel word is fuzzy in the marriage notice OCR, but James's additional newspaper clippings make the likely reading much firmer: Quitman newspaper references from 1892 and 1902 clearly show the long-established Hotel Marie in town, and the 1910 OCR string reads close to "Marie" rather than a different name. I would therefore read the marriage notice as placing the ceremony in the parlor of the Hotel Marie, while still noting that the original clipped OCR is imperfect. The newspaper independently supports the 6 April 1910 marriage record, confirms the bride as Georgia Blease, places her at the home of W. R. Blease near Barney, and shows the marriage was socially reported in the local press.

The later newspaper items fit the same household well. The Jeffersonian of 19 August 1915 printed a Barney letter signed "Georgia V. Hires"; that item probably belongs to Sim's wife, but because the clipping alone does not independently tie the signer to him, I would treat it as probable contextual support rather than as a hard identification record. The Macon Telegraph of 21 July 1917 described "Mrs. S. S. Hires, living near Barney, in Brooks County" as an extensive home canner who had already put up roughly 1,000 cans of tomatoes, 250 cans of berries, and 156 cans of beans, with peaches still to finish, from less than an acre of land. That report fits the 1910 and 1920 household well and gives a rare period glimpse of Georgia Hires's work within the farm economy. By 20 August 1921, the Macon Telegraph also placed "S. S. Hires" among the temporary committee members at the Adel meeting that organized a potato growers association, which supports his continued role in regional agricultural life. James's newly supplied Greenville News obituary for Warren R. Blease, who died in 1957 at age 93 near Barney, along with the Brooks County legislative list showing Warren R. Blease in repeated terms, makes it very likely that the "W. R. Blease" of the 1910 marriage notice was Warren R. Blease. Blease the strongest current identification for Georgia's father, but the father-daughter relationship should still be treated as awaiting direct census or vital-record confirmation rather than as fully closed. Hires at Gornto Cemetery in Brooks County also looks promising as a likely later-life match, but I would still keep that as a likely identification until the death and burial records are checked directly against the census chain.

The one part of the older entry I would still leave unresolved is the boarder written as John Blecton in 1900. James's later comparison work usefully narrows the problem but does not close it. Becton appears as a sixteen-year-old farm laborer born in Georgia to Georgia-born parents, and a likely continuation of that same man appears in 1910 in nearby Hickory Head as John J. Becton line strongly enough that the Barney boarder should remain unidentified rather than being absorbed into that nearby Becton trail.

HH#94 clearly belongs to the same Brooks County Hiers-Hires family cluster represented elsewhere in the encyclopedia. Hien, age 15, appears in Quitman in the household of Rebecca Hien, age 53, with siblings that match a Hiers-Hires family cluster already visible elsewhere in Brooks County records. The later censuses continue the same man in Barney. In 1910, Sim S. Hires, age 42, is a married farmer in Barney with wife Georgia Hires, age 24, and the census states they had been married for zero years. Becton appears as a sixteen-year-old farm laborer born in Georgia to Georgia-born parents, and a likely continuation of that same man appears in 1910 in nearby Hickory Head as John J. docs.text:
Household #100: Rodgers, Joe

Back to the 1900 Census & Household Index

In the 1900 Barney census, Joe Rodgers headed an 8-person household. The table below preserves the exact names, relationships, ages, birthplaces, and occupations recorded for the household.

Household Snapshot

Joe Rodgers headed an 8-person household in the 1900 Barney census with 1 spouse or marital partner and 6 children.

Joe Rodgers's listed occupation was Farmer.

All listed household members were reported as born in Georgia.

Newspaper and Public-Record Trail

This section flags public-record leads separate from the census table. The detailed discussion stays in the family narrative, research status, and source citations below.

1900 Census Household

Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation
Joe Rodgers Head 60 Georgia Farmer
Nancy Rodgers Wife 54 Georgia —
Ophelia Rodgers Daughter 24 Georgia —
Effie Rodgers Daughter 20 Georgia —
Everett Rodgers Son 16 Georgia —
Miles Rodgers Son 14 Georgia —
Dove Rodgers Daughter 12 Georgia —
Willie Rodgers Daughter 9 Georgia —

Children and Later Trails

This section is reserved for later-life child evidence. No later spouse, death, burial, obituary, probate, separate household, or descendant-line identification has been added here yet from direct records.

Family Narrative

The 1900 Barney census shows Joseph J. "Joe" Rodgers as a sixty-year-old farmer born in August 1839, with wife Nancy and six younger children still at home: Ophelia, Effie, Everett, Miles, Dove, and Willie. That household sits in the middle of a long local record trail. Joseph appears in 1850 in Lowndes County and in 1860 in Brooks County in the household of Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Rogers. The 1866 Brooks County marriage record then joins him to Nancy J. Hires. By 1870 he appears as a married head of household with Nancy and young children; by 1880 the family includes Walter and Oriphelia and the infant Effie; by 1910 Joseph and Nancy are still in Barney with daughter Willie; and by 1920 they are in the household of daughter Effie and son-in-law J. I. Moody. Joseph's 1922 death certificate gives his birth date as 22 Aug 1839 and names his parents as Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Hicks. Nancy's 1932 death certificate gives her birth date as 18 Oct 1845 and names her parents as David Hires and Rebecca Yates.

The marriage record is now direct rather than inferred. Brooks County marriage records show Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires obtaining a license on 18 October 1866 and marrying on 21 October 1866, with the ceremony performed by B. H. Martin, J.P. That original record fixes the couple in Brooks County immediately after the war. A Brooks County reconstruction oath dated 28 Jun 1867 places Joseph J. Rogers in Election District 7, providing another early postwar residence record.

Nancy's side of the household is better documented than the old entry suggested. In 1850 she appears as five-year-old Nancy Hiers in the Lowndes County household of David Hiers and Rebecca Hiers. Her 1932 death certificate later names her parents as David Hires and Rebecca Yates, which strongly supports that 1850 placement. The same death certificate shows that Nancy died at Barney on 29 Jun 1932 and was buried at Gornto Cemetery. Her obituary in The Tampa Tribune reported that she died in her sleep at the home of her daughter Mrs. J. I. Moody in Barney and listed surviving sons and daughters spread across Georgia and Florida.

Joseph's side is also much firmer than the older draft allowed. The 1850 and 1860 census placements in the Uriah Rogers household are reinforced by Joseph's 1922 death certificate, which names his parents as Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Hicks. An 1868 Brooks County deed records Uriah's cash sale of land to Joseph. The deed does not state that Joseph was his son; the death certificate is the controlling parentage evidence. A Brooks County tax digest for 1890 places Joseph J. Rogers in the Morven district and shows him taxed on 340 acres in land lot 270 of the 12th land district. That digest does not prove every detail of his farm history, but it does show him as an established landholding farmer before the 1900 census. A separate 1871 tax digest lists Mrs. Nancy Rogers in the Tallokas district, which is useful as an early county-presence record, though the available image does not support a firmer property claim for her row.

The collateral Rogers search found no inspected record connecting Joseph's branch to James Rogers, Thomas F. Rogers, Isaac J. Rogers, or Priscilla Jane Folsom. Shared surname, proximity, and land associations are not treated as proof of kinship.

The household's children can be followed well enough to tighten the family picture without leaning on guesswork. Later records and memorials connect Joseph and Nancy to children including Emma Arilla, Ida, Walter H., Ophelia, Harri[a]t/Harvinia, Effie, Everett M., Dove, Willie, and likely others who had already left home before 1900. Nancy's obituary is especially helpful for the later family cluster because it names Mrs. J. I. Moody as the daughter in whose home she died and also names surviving children in Palmetto, Wauchula, Zolfo, Alachua, Morven, Adel, and Barney. A Confederate service profile for a Joseph J. Rogers of Brooks County, with enlistment in 1862 and parole at Thomasville in 1865, likely pertains to this man, but that military identification should remain tied to the service profile unless the full underlying record or pension file is pulled.

Connections to Other Barney Families

Nancy’s mother now has a separate Rebecca Yates Hiers profile. The William Yates-to-Rebecca link is strong probable, while Rebecca-to-Nancy is verified.

HH#100 connects directly to the Hires family through Nancy J. Hires, whose 1850 census placement and 1932 death certificate identify her as daughter of David Hires and Rebecca Yates. That likely makes her a sibling of Sim Hires in HH#94, though the cleanest proof for that relationship still comes from the shared parentage pattern rather than one explicit sibling statement. HH#100 also connects to HH#99 through son Walter H. Rogers, whose later household appears separately in Barney.

Military Service

The current file gives a likely Confederate-service lead for Joseph J. Rogers of Brooks County, showing enlistment in 1862 and parole at Thomasville in 1865. That profile probably pertains to the Barney household head, but the page should keep it as a likely identification until the compiled service record or pension material is reviewed.

Open Research Questions

  • Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The likely Confederate service profile for Joseph J. Rogers should be backed by the compiled service record or pension material before it is treated as firm military biography.
  • The obituary survivor list is valuable, but a few names are blurred enough in OCR that they should be checked against the image before every married surname is treated as settled.
  • Deed or probate records could sharpen the property history and child list, but the basic household identity no longer depends on them.

Research Status

Well-researched. The household is now supported by Joseph's 1850 and 1860 census placements with Uriah Rogers, Nancy's 1850 placement with David Hires, the 1866 marriage certificate, Joseph's 1867 reconstruction oath, the 1870 through 1920 census chain, Nancy's 1871 tax-list appearance, Joseph's 1890 tax digest entry, both death certificates, Nancy's obituary, and burial support from the Gornto Cemetery memorials. The older network-heavy framing can be retired; the main remaining work is record tightening, not basic identification.

The 1900 Barney census shows Joseph J. "Joe" Rodgers as a sixty-year-old farmer born in August 1839, with wife Nancy and six younger children still at home: Ophelia, Effie, Everett, Miles, Dove, and Willie. That household sits in the middle of a long local record trail. Joseph appears in 1850 in Lowndes County and in 1860 in Brooks County in the household of Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Rogers. The 1866 Brooks County marriage record then joins him to Nancy J. Hires. By 1870 he appears as a married head of household with Nancy and young children; by 1880 the family includes Walter and Oriphelia and the infant Effie; by 1910 Joseph and Nancy are still in Barney with daughter Willie; and by 1920 they are in the household of daughter Effie and son-in-law J. I. Moody. Joseph's 1922 death certificate gives his birth date as 22 Aug 1839 and names his parents as Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Hicks. Nancy's 1932 death certificate gives her birth date as 18 Oct 1845 and names her parents as David Hires and Rebecca Yates.

The marriage record is now direct rather than inferred. Brooks County marriage records show Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires obtaining a license on 18 October 1866 and marrying on 21 October 1866, with the ceremony performed by B. H. Martin, J.P. That original record fixes the couple in Brooks County immediately after the war. A Brooks County reconstruction oath dated 28 Jun 1867 places Joseph J. Rogers in Election District 7, providing another early postwar residence record.

Nancy's side of the household is better documented than the old entry suggested. In 1850 she appears as five-year-old Nancy Hiers in the Lowndes County household of David Hiers and Rebecca Hiers. Her 1932 death certificate later names her parents as David Hires and Rebecca Yates, which strongly supports that 1850 placement. The same death certificate shows that Nancy died at Barney on 29 Jun 1932 and was buried at Gornto Cemetery. Her obituary in The Tampa Tribune reported that she died in her sleep at the home of her daughter Mrs. J. I. Moody in Barney and listed surviving sons and daughters spread across Georgia and Florida.

Joseph's side is also much firmer than the older draft allowed. The 1850 and 1860 census placements in the Uriah Rogers household are reinforced by Joseph's 1922 death certificate, which names his parents as Uriah Rogers and Elizabeth Hicks. An 1868 Brooks County deed records Uriah's cash sale of land to Joseph. The deed does not state that Joseph was his son; the death certificate is the controlling parentage evidence. A Brooks County tax digest for 1890 places Joseph J. Rogers in the Morven district and shows him taxed on 340 acres in land lot 270 of the 12th land district. That digest does not prove every detail of his farm history, but it does show him as an established landholding farmer before the 1900 census. A separate 1871 tax digest lists Mrs. Nancy Rogers in the Tallokas district, which is useful as an early county-presence record, though the available image does not support a firmer property claim for her row.

The collateral Rogers search found no inspected record connecting Joseph's branch to James Rogers, Thomas F. Rogers, Isaac J. Rogers, or Priscilla Jane Folsom. Shared surname, proximity, and land associations are not treated as proof of kinship.

The household's children can be followed well enough to tighten the family picture without leaning on guesswork. Later records and memorials connect Joseph and Nancy to children including Emma Arilla, Ida, Walter H., Ophelia, Harri[a]t/Harvinia, Effie, Everett M., Dove, Willie, and likely others who had already left home before 1900. Nancy's obituary is especially helpful for the later family cluster because it names Mrs. J. I. Moody as the daughter in whose home she died and also names surviving children in Palmetto, Wauchula, Zolfo, Alachua, Morven, Adel, and Barney. A Confederate service profile for a Joseph J. Rogers of Brooks County, with enlistment in 1862 and parole at Thomasville in 1865, likely pertains to this man, but that military identification should remain tied to the service profile unless the full underlying record or pension file is pulled.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
Nancy’s mother now has a separate Rebecca Yates Hiers profile. The William Yates-to-Rebecca link is strong probable, while Rebecca-to-Nancy is verified.

HH#100 connects directly to the Hires family through Nancy J. Hires, whose 1850 census placement and 1932 death certificate identify her as daughter of David Hires and Rebecca Yates. That likely makes her a sibling of Sim Hires in HH#94, though the cleanest proof for that relationship still comes from the shared parentage pattern rather than one explicit sibling statement. HH#100 also connects to HH#99 through son Walter H. Rogers, whose later household appears separately in Barney.

docs.title: Military Service
docs.text: The current file gives a likely Confederate-service lead for Joseph J. Rogers of Brooks County, showing enlistment in 1862 and parole at Thomasville in 1865. That profile probably pertains to the Barney household head, but the page should keep it as a likely identification until the compiled service record or pension material is reviewed.

docs.title: Open Research Questions
docs.text:
• Parentage audit: Keep head-of-household and spouse parentage as unresolved unless a cited direct record names the parents or the entry explains the census chain supporting the identification.
  • Child census audit: Continue direct-record tracking for each child named in the 1900 household where later census, marriage, death, burial, obituary, or other parent-link proof is not already cited above.
  • The likely Confederate service profile for Joseph J. Rogers should be backed by the compiled service record or pension material before it is treated as firm military biography.
  • The obituary survivor list is valuable, but a few names are blurred enough in OCR that they should be checked against the image before every married surname is treated as settled.
  • Deed or probate records could sharpen the property history and child list, but the basic household identity no longer depends on them.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Well-researched. The household is now supported by Joseph's 1850 and 1860 census placements with Uriah Rogers, Nancy's 1850 placement with David Hires, the 1866 marriage certificate, Joseph's 1867 reconstruction oath, the 1870 through 1920 census chain, Nancy's 1871 tax-list appearance, Joseph's 1890 tax digest entry, both death certificates, Nancy's obituary, and burial support from the Gornto Cemetery memorials. The older network-heavy framing can be retired; the main remaining work is record tightening, not basic identification.

docs.title: Ashley Lawson
docs.text:
Ashley Lawson

Back to the Early History Profiles index

District and land record

Ashley Lawson was present in Lowndes County's 660th District by 1836, when an original general-militia return listed him as a private. The return establishes district residence and militia eligibility, not active Creek War service.

Folks Huxford later assigned Ashley an 1824 or 1825 arrival. William Harden's 1913 descendant biography says Ashley was born in 1810 and came south with his father, John Lawson. If so, Ashley would have arrived as a child in a parental household. No contemporary record proves that date.

A reconstructed 1849 deed abstract places Ashley on District 9 land that later became part of Cook County. Later abstracts place him in District 12 transactions, but they do not locate his home at the future Barney townsite.

Family

A reconstructed 1867 deed names Cynthia Lawson as Ashley's wife and Hardy V. Lawson and Irvin Lawson as their children. Harden identifies Cynthia as Cynthia Folsom, daughter of Lawrence Armstrong Folsom, and Ashley as a son of John Lawson and Rachel Green. Those two generational links remain secondary-supported because no inspected original record names Cynthia's parents or Ashley's parents.

Harden also said John Lawson first settled land in what became the Barney district. That is useful family context, but it does not prove Ashley's own residence at Barney.

Evidence assessment

  • Roster: supplemental early settler, verified in the 660th District in 1836.
  • Ashley and Cynthia as spouses: supported by the reconstructed 1867 deed.
  • Hardy V. and Irvin as children: supported by the same deed.
  • Cynthia's Folsom parentage and Ashley's descent from John Lawson: secondary-supported.
  • Direct Barney residence: not proved.

Sources

  1. Lowndes County, Georgia, 81st Regiment Georgia Militia, 1836 general-militia return, Ashley Lawson, private, 660th District; Valdosta State University Archives item 10428/1219.
  2. William Harden, A History of Savannah and South Georgia, vol. 2 (1913), pp. 862–865.
  3. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), pp. 29–33.
  4. Wiregrass Region Digital History Project, reconstructed Lowndes County deed-book abstraction, Ashley Lawson entries dated 1849–1880.
  5. Elizabeth Knowles Folsom, Genealogy of the Folsom Family, vol. 2 (1938), Georgia branch; compiled corroboration only.

docs.title: Jared Johnson
docs.text:
Jared Johnson

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Local record

Jared Johnson was established in the part of Lowndes County that later became Brooks County by 1837. Reconstructed deed indexes place him on District 12 land in Lots 492, 394, and 436 between 1837 and 1841. The original 1840 census contains a Lowndes household read as Jared Johnson. The deed entries are useful locators, but the recorded instruments have not yet been inspected.

A row formerly assigned to Johnson in the 1830 census actually reads Jared Singleton. It is not evidence for Johnson. His traditional 1824 or 1825 arrival date also remains unproved.

Bethlehem Church

Folks Huxford's account of Bethlehem Primitive Baptist Church identifies Johnson as an early deacon, twice-elected clerk, and an 1836 association delegate. Huxford wrote that Johnson moved to Florida and died on October 16, 1844. These claims appear to come from the church minutes, but the original minute-book images have not been inspected.

The reported move needs clarification because Lowndes records continue through 1841. No spouse, child, Florida record, or direct connection to the later Barney townsite has been proved.

Evidence assessment

  • Roster: supplemental early settler.
  • Present by: 1837, based on the reconstructed deed index.
  • Original household anchor: 1840 census.
  • Church roles and death: strong secondary evidence.
  • 1830 census claim: rejected; the household head was Jared Singleton.

Sources

  1. 1840 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, manuscript p. 77; Ancestry collection 8057, record 1792315, image 4411334_00479.
  2. 1830 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, stamped p. 79; Ancestry collection 8058, record 1850779, image 4409522_00156; used to reject the Jared Singleton row as a Johnson record.
  3. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), pp. 29–30 and 309–311.
  4. Reconstructed Lowndes deed index, Jared Johnson entries for District 12 Lots 492, 394, and 436.

docs.title: William G. Hunter
docs.text:
William G. Hunter

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Land and public record

William G. Hunter was established in the future Brooks County area by 1838. A reconstructed Lowndes deed abstract records District 12 transactions involving Hunter that year, and Folks Huxford's militia-officer transcription lists Wm. G. Hunter as captain of the 790th, or Tallokas, District on August 27, 1838.

Later deed entries track Hunter in Lowndes County and on Land Lot 491. A 1855 settlement involving William G. Hunter and Mary Hunter supports Mary as his wife or former wife, although the underlying record should be inspected before its terms are quoted more precisely. The repeated middle initial, District 12 land, militia office, church work, and later Brooks County appointment make one continuing William G. Hunter identity strong probable from 1838 through 1861.

Church and county service

Huxford's transcription of Bethlehem Primitive Baptist Church records names Hunter as pastor during several terms between 1839 and 1854 and places him in the 1854 presbytery that ordained James J. Renfroe. The original church minute book has not been inspected.

Brooks County's Inferior Court appointed Hunter to the courthouse building committee on April 6, 1859. Huxford reports that he resigned on July 16, 1861. The court-minute images remain to be inspected.

Evidence assessment

  • Roster: supplemental early settler with strong land and public-office support.
  • Present by: 1838.
  • Traditional 1826 arrival: unverified.
  • Parents, children, death, probate, and direct Barney residence: unresolved.

Sources

  1. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), pp. 29–33, 56, 69–70, 86, and 307–311.
  2. Wiregrass Region Digital History Project, reconstructed Lowndes County deed-book abstraction, William G. Hunter entries dated 1838, 1844, 1853, and 1855.
  3. C. E. Hightower, Lowndes County, Georgia Deed Book A and Other Records, identified reconstructed-record source; original deed images not inspected in this review.

docs.title: William Yates
docs.text:
William Yates

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Identity and early record

William Yates was established in the Lowndes–Thomas border region by 1840 and later became a Brooks County landowner. A locally preserved tax index places him in District 12, Land Lot 463 by 1835, but the original tax page has not been inspected. Folks Huxford's claim that he arrived in 1824 or 1825 also remains secondary evidence.

Census indexes trace an elder William, born about 1807 or 1808, from Lowndes County in 1840 through Thomas County in 1850 and Brooks County in 1860 and 1870. A separate William R. Yates, born about 1838, was already an adult by 1860. Records for the younger man, including likely Civil War service, should not be assigned to the pioneer without a direct identity bridge.

Washway, mill, and estate

An 1869 road notice placed “William Yates' Wash Way” on the Quitman–Tallokas Road. Notices in 1875 called the site Yates Mill and described the road over the mill dam and a bridge across the mill wasteway. The records establish a Yates road-and-mill landmark in northern Brooks County, but they do not place William at the later Barney townsite or connect the site to modern Yates Road.

William died before August 3, 1874. Owen Yates and James W. Yates were appointed temporary administrators. Both are strong-probable sons based on earlier household associations, but the bond states no relationship.

The October 1874 inventory valued William's estate at $12,073.80 and names Owen as administrator. It contains no heir list. Estate vouchers show that William owed David Hiers $1,496.96 on a November 1, 1873 note; Owen paid the balance in February 1875. A store account also charged purchases for “Mrs Hiers” and “Miss Hiers” to William. Another note explicitly calls Catharine Smith “my daughter,” verifying her relationship while leaving Rebecca's unstated.

Rebecca Yates Hiers

Rebecca Yates Hiers is William and Elizabeth's strong-probable daughter, not a verified daughter. Rebecca fits the only girl age 10–14 in William's 1840 household and was already married before the named 1850 household. On May 13, 1864, Owen Yates sold Rebecca's husband, David Hiers, about 580 acres for $3,000. The original deed is an ordinary cash sale and states no relationship.

On October 27, 1875, David conveyed Rebecca four adjoining tracts totaling about 545 acres for $2,500. Earlier compiled work incorrectly described this as four deeds dated October 7. The original record is one deed dated October 27 and does not identify Rebecca as David's wife or William's daughter.

Rebecca's daughter Nancy J. Hires married Joseph J. Rogers, creating a documented Hiers–Rogers line into Barney. The proposed William-to-Rebecca link is supported by chronology, household composition, land dealings, and estate associations, but no inspected record explicitly names Rebecca as William's daughter or heir.

Evidence assessment

  • Roster: supplemental early settler, strong probable identity.
  • Antebellum regional residence: well supported.
  • 1835 Lot 463 ownership: derivative lead; original tax page needed.
  • Catharine Smith as daughter: verified by William's note.
  • Owen and James W. as sons: strong probable.
  • Rebecca as daughter: strong probable, not verified.
  • Direct residence at Barney: not proved.

Sources

  1. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), early-settler, jury, political, lodge, and family sections.
  2. 1840–1870 federal census entries for the elder William Yates in Lowndes, Thomas, and Brooks counties.
  3. Quitman Banner, August 27, 1869, road notice naming William Yates' Wash Way.
  4. Quitman Reporter, August 26 and November 11, 1875, Yates Mill road and bridge notices.
  5. Brooks County administrator bonds for William Yates, August 3 and October 5, 1874.
  6. Owen Yates to David Hiers deed, May 13, 1864.
  7. David Hiers to Rebecca Hiers deed, October 27, 1875.
  8. William Yates inventory and appraisement, October–November 1874.
  9. William Yates estate vouchers, 1873–1875: Hiers accounts and note and additional vouchers.
  10. Nancy J. Rogers death certificate, 1932, naming David Hires and Rebecca Yates; Brooks County marriage return for Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires, October 21, 1866.

docs.title: Rebecca Yates Hiers
docs.text:
Rebecca Yates Hiers

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Household and family

Rebecca Yates Hiers is documented in Lowndes and Brooks counties from 1850 through 1900. The 1850 census reports an implausible age of seventeen for Rebecca because daughter Nancy was already five. Later censuses place Rebecca's birth about 1827–1830.

Two daughters' death records independently preserve her Yates surname. Nancy J. Rogers's 1932 death certificate names David Hires and Rebecca Yates as her parents. Serena Hall's 1921 death record names David Hires and a mother surnamed Yates. Nancy married Joseph J. Rogers in Brooks County on October 21, 1866.

By 1880, Rebecca was the widowed head of a Quitman-district household. In 1900, she was living in Barney with her son Sim Hires. Her death date and burial place remain unknown.

Land records

On May 13, 1864, Owen Yates sold David Hiers Lot 233 and ninety acres of the east half of Lot 274—about 580 acres—for $3,000. The deed states no relationship.

David's transfer to Rebecca was previously reported incorrectly as four deeds dated October 7, 1875. The original record is one deed dated October 27, 1875. For $2,500, David conveyed four adjoining tracts totaling about 545 acres: 245 acres in the south half of Lot 234, 100 acres in the northwest corner of Lot 235, 125 acres in the northeast corner of Lot 273, and 75 acres in the southeast corner of Lot 274. The deed describes the property as the place where David lived. It conveys the land to Rebecca and her heirs but does not identify her as his wife or state any family relationship.

Proposed Yates parentage

Rebecca was a strong-probable daughter of William and Elizabeth Yates, but the relationship is not verified. She fits the only girl age 10–14 in William's 1840 household and was already married before William's named 1850 household. Owen Yates—William's strong-probable son—dealt directly with David Hiers in 1864.

William's 1874 estate vouchers strengthen the family-network case. They include purchases for “Mrs Hiers” and “Miss Hiers” and a $1,496.96 debt to David Hiers, paid by administrator Owen Yates in February 1875. The inventory contains no heir list, however, and no inspected record calls Rebecca William's daughter. A separate note explicitly calls Catharine Smith “my daughter,” showing that relationship language was preserved when it appeared.

Barney connection

Rebecca has documented connections to two Barney households through her daughters. Nancy Jane Hires married Joseph J. Rogers on October 21, 1866, and the Rogers family appears in Barney's later record. Serena Hires married William M. Hall on January 4, 1870; William and Serena were enumerated as Barney household #138 in 1900. Rebecca herself was enumerated in son Sim Hires's Barney household that year.

Rebecca's motherhood of Nancy is verified by Nancy's death certificate. Serena's death certificate names David Hires and a mother surnamed Yates, while Nancy's certificate supplies the full name Rebecca Yates; Serena's identification as Rebecca's daughter is therefore strong probable rather than parent-naming verified. Only the earlier William-to-Rebecca link remains strong probable rather than verified.

Evidence assessment

  • Rebecca's Yates surname: verified through two daughters' records.
  • Marriage to David Hiers: verified by the continuing household and land record; exact marriage date unknown.
  • Daughter of William and Elizabeth Yates: strong probable, not verified.
  • Mother of Nancy J. Hires Rogers: verified.
  • Barney residence in 1900: verified.
  • Death and burial: unresolved.

  2. 1850–1900 federal census entries for David, Rebecca, and their continuing Hiers/Hires household in Lowndes and Brooks counties.
  3. Nancy J. Rogers death certificate, 1932, naming David Hires and Rebecca Yates; Serena Hall death record, 1921, naming David Hires and mother Yates.
  4. Brooks County marriage return, Joseph J. Rogers and Nancy J. Hires, October 21, 1866.
  5. Brooks County marriage return, William M. Hall and Serena Hires, January 4, 1870; 1900 U.S. census, Barney precinct, Brooks County, household 138.
  6. Owen Yates to David Hiers deed, May 13, 1864.

docs.title: Alexander Campbell
docs.text:
Alexander Campbell

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, indexed official-record continuity from 1830 to 1850; Morven/future-Brooks placement strong. The reported 1826 or 1827 arrival remains secondary.

Evidence

Prior census audits identify Alexander Campbell as a Lowndes household head in 1830, 1840, and 1850. A fresh Ancestry search confirms an indexed 1850 Lowndes record for an Alexander Campbell born in Scotland around 1777. The original 1850 image was not reinspected in this cohort, so household members and exact ages are not adopted from the index alone.

A contemporary grand-jury presentment, reproduced by the Ray City History Blog, lists Alexander Campbell among the Lowndes jurors. The blog labels the proceeding as May 1833 but reproduces a footer with a conflicting June 12, 1832 date. The list supports local public activity while the exact publication date remains unsettled until the original newspaper page is inspected.

Huxford and later derivative accounts identify Alexander's wife as Flora Morrison, say both came from the Isle of Skye, place the family near Sharpe's Store/Morven after about 1827, and identify Margaret Campbell—wife of Neal Hendry—as a daughter. These details are coherent with the indexed census chain and later Hendry family material. They remain secondary-supported because no inspected marriage, probate, Bible, or deed names the relationships.

Family and identity controls

  • Flora Morrison as wife: secondary-supported.
  • Margaret Campbell Hendry as daughter: secondary-supported.
  • Norman Campbell and other proposed children require their own parent-naming or household bridge.
  • The Lowndes household must remain distinct from same-name Campbell families elsewhere.

Barney relevance

Morven and the 1833 county activity place Campbell in the future-Brooks regional network. No residence at the later Barney townsite is proved.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1830, 1840, and 1850 schedules; original grand-jury publication; immigration/naturalization evidence; Flora's marriage or probate; Alexander's estate; and the Margaret Campbell–Neal Hendry marriage and parentage evidence.

Sources

  1. Ancestry census index search, Alexander Campbell, born about 1777 Scotland, 1850 Lowndes County, accessed October 4, 2026.
  2. Ray City History Blog, “Lowndes Grand Jury of 1833,” June 9, 2018: https://raycityhistory.wordpress.com/2018/06/09/lowndes-grand-jury-of-1833/
  3. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), early-settler and Hendry family sketches.
  4. Early-settler master audit, ES-037, preserved local research.

docs.title: James McLeod
docs.text:
James McLeod

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early Lowndes settler, census-index anchored by 1830; future-Brooks institutional placement secondary-supported. The reported 1826 arrival remains unverified.

Evidence

The prior roster audit reported no census household for James McLeod. A fresh Ancestry search located an indexed James McLeod household in Lowndes County in 1830. This corrects the earlier search gap, but the original schedule has not yet been opened and transcribed. The index establishes a usable locator, not a complete identity chain.

Folks Huxford's Bethlehem Primitive Baptist Church narrative identifies James and Jemima McLeod in the charter-member group, reports that James was commissioned a lieutenant in the 659th District in 1827, and says he was licensed to preach in 1836. These claims place him in institutions associated with the future-Brooks area, but the underlying commission and original church minutes remain uninspected.

No secure marriage, deed, probate, later census, or death record was located that identifies Jemima's maiden name, names children, or distinguishes this James from other McLeods. The Lowndes 1830 index and the Huxford institutional narrative are mutually compatible, but they do not by themselves prove that every claim concerns one man.

Family and identity controls

  • Jemima as wife: secondary-supported by the church narrative.
  • 1830 household head and the church/militia figure: strong possible same man, pending the original census and another dated identity bridge.
  • No parents or children are established.

Barney relevance

The reported 659th District commission and Bethlehem affiliation provide a secondary-supported future-Brooks connection. No Barney-townsite residence or descendant bridge is proved.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1830 schedule; locate the 1827 commission; seek original Bethlehem minutes, Lowndes deeds and tax digests, marriage and probate records, and later residence or death evidence.

  2. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), pp. 29–34, 56, 309–311.
  3. Early-settler master audit, ES-041, preserved local research.

docs.title: John Lawson
docs.text:
John Lawson

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, verified as a Lowndes grand juror by 1833 through a contemporary-record transcription and indexed as a household head in 1840. The traditional 1823 arrival and exact Barney-district land remain secondary-supported.

Evidence

The previous audit left John Lawson as a traditional candidate with no secure civil identity. Two leads materially improve that assessment.

First, a Lowndes grand-jury presentment reproduced from a contemporary Milledgeville paper lists John Lawson among the jurors. The article describes the term as May 1833, while the reproduced footer carries a conflicting June 12, 1832 date. The original newspaper image has not been inspected, so the event is best stated as service by 1833 with the date conflict disclosed.

Second, a published 1840 Lowndes census transcription lists a John Lawson household with two males and one female. The entry appears near Simpson Strickland and Daniel Lawson. This supplies a specific household locator, but the original census image remains uninspected and proximity does not prove kinship.

William Harden's 1913 descendant biography says John was born about 1783 in North Carolina, first lived in Laurens County, settled land in what became the Barney district, later moved to Colquitt County, married Rachel Green, and had Eliza, Ashley, Greene, and Daniel. The same source explicitly identifies Ashley as John's son. These family and land claims are secondary-supported, not verified by an inspected deed, probate, Bible, or parent-naming record.

Family and identity controls

  • Rachel Green as wife: secondary-supported.
  • Ashley, Eliza, Greene, and Daniel as children: secondary-supported.
  • John as father of Ashley: secondary-supported, consistent with Ashley's chronology but not original-record verified.
  • Daniel Lawson's nearby 1840 entry is an association, not proof of sonship.

Barney relevance

Harden explicitly places John's land in the later Barney district. Because no tract, lot, deed, or plat was supplied, this is a secondary-supported Barney connection, not verified title or residence at the townsite.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1840 census image, original grand-jury publication, Laurens/Irwin/Lowndes/Colquitt deed indexes, tax digests, Rachel Green marriage evidence, probate and cemetery records, and a tract-level test of the Barney-district claim.

Sources

  1. Ray City History Blog, “Lowndes Grand Jury of 1833,” reproducing a contemporary presentment: https://raycityhistory.wordpress.com/2018/06/09/lowndes-grand-jury-of-1833/
  2. Genealogy Trails, “1840 Lowndes County Georgia Census,” later transcription.
  3. William Harden, A History of Savannah and South Georgia, vol. 2 (1913), pp. 862–865.
  4. Ashley Lawson dossier and deed evidence, preserved local research.
