docs.title: Melus or Milus Thigpen
docs.text:
Melus or Milus Thigpen

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, original-record verified in Lowndes County by 1826; future-Brooks church placement strong. The traditional 1826 arrival date should be stated as presence by 1826, not arrival in that year.

Evidence

The earliest inspected original is the June 16, 1826 deed from Miles or Milus Thigpen to John Hendry for 200 acres in District 12, Land Lot 515. Simpson and Simeon Strickland witnessed the conveyance, and Simpson proved it in 1837. The surviving copy supports the spelling Milus; later sources also use Melus.

An Ancestry census search locates Milus Thigpen in Captain Hutchinson's District, Warren County, Georgia, in 1820 and Melus Thigpen in Lowndes County in 1830. A later published transcription counts one male and five females in the 1830 household. The 1820-to-1830 migration is coherent, but the original census images were not reinspected in this cohort.

Folks Huxford's church reconstruction places Thigpen as a minister at Union by August 12, 1826, an organizing member of Bethel Primitive Baptist Church, and ordained in 1828. It identifies Sarah Whaley as his wife, reports seven children, and gives his death as January 1839. These are strong secondary claims; the original church minutes, probate, and named child list were not located online.

Family and identity controls

  • Sarah Whaley as wife: secondary-supported.
  • Seven reported children: secondary-supported as a group, not reconstructed individually here.
  • The 1820 Warren and 1830 Lowndes households: strong-probable continuity based on name, chronology, and migration; original image comparison remains needed.
  • Later Thigpen families must not be attached to this household from surname alone.

Barney relevance

The 1826 land transaction and Bethel/Union church accounts place Thigpen in the early future-Brooks institutional corridor. No direct Barney-townsite residence or descendant chain was proved.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1820 and 1830 census images, Bethel and Union minutes, marriage evidence for Sarah Whaley, probate or administration around 1839, and land-title records for Lot 515.

Sources

  1. Lowndes County deed, Miles/Milus Thigpen to John Hendry, June 16, 1826; Brooks County Deed Book A copy: https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C9BZ-3S7Z-K
  2. Ancestry census index, Milus Thigpen, 1820 Warren County and Melus Thigpen, 1830 Lowndes County, accessed October 4, 2026.
  3. Genealogy Trails, “1830 Lowndes County Georgia Census,” later transcription.
  4. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), early-settler and church narratives.

docs.title: Simpson Strickland
docs.text:
Simpson Strickland

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, verified in Lowndes County by 1826; future-Brooks association strong. No exact arrival year is proved.

Evidence

An original deed copied into Brooks County Deed Book A records a June 16, 1826 conveyance from Miles or Milus Thigpen to John Hendry. Simpson Strickland and Simeon Strickland witnessed it. On July 23, 1837, Simpson swore that he saw Thigpen execute the deed and saw Simeon sign. This is direct proof that Simpson was in Lowndes County and personally associated with Simeon by 1826. The deed does not call them brothers.

The 1830 Lowndes census index and a later published transcription each identify a Simpson Strickland household. The transcription counts three males and three females, but the original schedule image was not reinspected in this cohort. An indexed 1850 Lowndes household and an indexed 1860 Brooks household identify a Simpson born about 1806–1807 in South Carolina. Those entries fit the same man, but the original schedules remain a follow-up target.

A later local-history account reports that Simpson served on the 1833 Lowndes grand jury, was commissioned captain of the 790th District in 1834, married Mary Wooten in 1829, and was a son of Archibald and Luander Strickland and brother of Simeon. The explicit kinship claim agrees with Archibald's 1820 Tattnall household and the 1826 deed association, but no inspected original names Simpson's parents or calls Simeon his brother. The family reconstruction remains secondary-supported.

A deed index places Simpson on 580 acres in District 12, Lots 233 and 274, which he conveyed in 1858. This is a reproducible land locator in territory that became Brooks County. The underlying deed text still needs inspection.

Family and identity controls

  • Simpson Strickland and Mary Wooten: secondary-supported; original marriage not inspected.
  • Simpson and Simeon Strickland: secondary-supported brothers; original-record association verified.
  • Simpson as son of Archibald and Luander: secondary-supported.
  • Later Simpson S. and Simpson J. Stricklands must remain separate unless a record supplies an identity bridge.

Barney relevance

Simpson's land and militia activity place him in the broader future-Brooks corridor. No record located in this cohort proves residence at the later Barney townsite or descent to a canonical Barney census household.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1830, 1850, and 1860 schedules; the reported 1829 marriage; the 1834 commission; Brooks/Lowndes Deed Book A, pp. 88–89; and any estate or cemetery record.

Sources

  1. Lowndes County deed, Miles/Milus Thigpen to John Hendry, executed June 16, 1826, proved by Simpson Strickland July 23, 1837; Brooks County Deed Book A copy, FamilySearch image: https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C9BZ-3S7Z-K
  2. Ancestry census index searches, Simpson Strickland, 1850 Lowndes and 1860 Brooks, accessed October 4, 2026.
  3. Genealogy Trails, “1830 Lowndes County Georgia Census,” later transcription of a DAR county history.
  4. Ray City History Blog, “Lowndes Grand Jury of 1833,” June 9, 2018: https://raycityhistory.wordpress.com/2018/06/09/lowndes-grand-jury-of-1833/

docs.title: Evidence assessment
docs.text: Supplemental early settler, verified in Lowndes County by 1826; future-Brooks association strong. No exact arrival year is proved.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
An original deed copied into Brooks County Deed Book A records a June 16, 1826 conveyance from Miles or Milus Thigpen to John Hendry. Simpson Strickland and Simeon Strickland witnessed it. On July 23, 1837, Simpson swore that he saw Thigpen execute the deed and saw Simeon sign. This is direct proof that Simpson was in Lowndes County and personally associated with Simeon by 1826. The deed does not call them brothers.

The 1830 Lowndes census index and a later published transcription each identify a Simpson Strickland household. The transcription counts three males and three females, but the original schedule image was not reinspected in this cohort. An indexed 1850 Lowndes household and an indexed 1860 Brooks household identify a Simpson born about 1806–1807 in South Carolina. Those entries fit the same man, but the original schedules remain a follow-up target.

A later local-history account reports that Simpson served on the 1833 Lowndes grand jury, was commissioned captain of the 790th District in 1834, married Mary Wooten in 1829, and was a son of Archibald and Luander Strickland and brother of Simeon. The explicit kinship claim agrees with Archibald's 1820 Tattnall household and the 1826 deed association, but no inspected original names Simpson's parents or calls Simeon his brother. The family reconstruction remains secondary-supported.

A deed index places Simpson on 580 acres in District 12, Lots 233 and 274, which he conveyed in 1858. This is a reproducible land locator in territory that became Brooks County. The underlying deed text still needs inspection.

docs.text:
• Simpson Strickland and Mary Wooten: secondary-supported; original marriage not inspected.
  • Simpson and Simeon Strickland: secondary-supported brothers; original-record association verified.
  • Simpson as son of Archibald and Luander: secondary-supported.
  • Later Simpson S. and Simpson J. Stricklands must remain separate unless a record supplies an identity bridge.

docs.text: Simpson's land and militia activity place him in the broader future-Brooks corridor. No record located in this cohort proves residence at the later Barney townsite or descent to a canonical Barney census household.

docs.title: Henry Rowell
docs.text:
Henry Rowell

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, verified in the future-Brooks 659th District by 1836 and strongly supported there by 1832 office and 1834–1836 church evidence. His household and family remain unresolved.

Evidence

The original 1836 Lowndes general-militia return lists Henry Rowell as a private in the 659th District. This proves district presence but is not evidence of active wartime service.

Huxford's militia-officer compilation lists Henry Rowell commissioned ensign of the 659th District on October 15, 1832. His Bethlehem church history identifies Henry among the probable charter members and as church clerk beginning in June 1836. The original commission and church minutes were not inspected.

The same church reconstruction lists Cyntha Rowell and James Rowell separately. It does not call Cyntha Henry's wife or James his relative. Those relationships remain unresolved.

Identity and family controls

  • Henry in the 1832 officer list and 1836 militia return: strong probable same man.
  • Cyntha Rowell as wife: unresolved.
  • James Rowell as brother or other relative: unresolved.
  • No secure census household or probate identity was established.

Barney relevance

The 659th District and Bethlehem Church belonged to the broader future-Brooks area. No record proves residence at the later Barney townsite.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1832 commission, original Bethlehem minutes, census schedules, deeds, marriage records, and probate.

  2. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948, militia-officer list and Bethlehem church history.

docs.title: James Newton
docs.text:
James Newton

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, strongly anchored in the Bethel community by 1836 and in an original 1850 household. The reported 1827 arrival and 1830 Thomas County identity remain unverified.

Evidence

Huxford's abstract of Bethel Primitive Baptist Church records identifies James Newton as church clerk from 1836 through 1845. The church stood in the territory that became Brooks County, giving Newton a direct future-Brooks institutional anchor. Huxford also lists James Newton as Lowndes County Superior Court clerk from January 10, 1854, through 1856. Neither underlying church minutes nor the original commission were inspected in this cohort.

The original 1850 Lowndes census schedule identifies James Newton, age 51, born in North Carolina, as a farmer. Jemima, age 40, and eight younger Newtons were in the household, along with Stephen Knowles. The census does not state relationships, so Jemima remains strong-probable as James's wife and the younger Newtons remain household members rather than automatically proved children.

A deed extraction for Rachel Newton's 1847 conveyance to “Isaac James Newton, her son” describes adjoining land on the south as James Newton's. This is a useful District 12 land association but does not identify Rachel's relationship to James. Later extracted transactions to a James Newton concern District 15 and cannot be assigned to this man without further identity work.

Identity and family controls

  • James Newton and Jemima: strong probable spouses, based on household placement and later secondary accounts.
  • Elizabeth, Mary Ann, Isaac F., Damaris, Nancy P., William G., James H. P., and Jemima Newton: household members; probable children, not parent-naming verified.
  • The James Newton adjoining Rachel Newton's Lot 466 tract: strong possible identity.
  • The traditional 1827 arrival and reported 1830 Thomas census entry: secondary/index leads, not inspected originals.

Barney relevance

Bethel's location and the District 12 land boundary place James Newton in the future-Brooks area. No record proves residence at the later Barney townsite.

Remaining targets

Inspect the reported 1830 Thomas census entry, original Bethel minutes, Superior Court commission, District 12 deeds, and probate or estate material.

  2. 1850 United States census, Lowndes County, Georgia, James Newton household; FamilySearch locator MZYY-PVG.
  3. Lowndes deed extraction, Rachel Newton to Isaac James Newton, Book D, p. 180, recorded February 29, 1848.

docs.title: James Rowell
docs.text:
James Rowell

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, verified on future-Brooks land by 1828. His church service is strongly supported by later abstracts; his family and relationship to Henry Rowell remain unresolved.

Evidence

An original deed copied into the later Brooks records shows Daniel Rowe of Crawford County conveying District 12, Lot 393 to James Rowell of Crawford County on December 13, 1828. The deed was recorded October 5, 1832. This directly anchors James to land that later lay in Brooks County, although it does not prove when he took up residence there.

Huxford's Bethel history names James as a delegate in 1827 and says he was elected deacon in July 1828 but declined. The Bethlehem history lists James Rowell and wife Sarah among the probable charter members, calls James a deacon, and records their dismissal by letter on November 12, 1842. These are detailed secondary abstracts; the original church books were not inspected.

A deed extraction records James Rowell of Lowndes County mortgaging most of Lot 393 to Francis Jones on July 1, 1842, while reserving the southeast 75 acres and a cemetery. This supplies continuity on the same tract, but the underlying deed image remains a target.

Identity and family controls

  • Sarah Rowell as James's wife: secondary-supported, explicitly stated in the Bethlehem abstract.
  • James and Henry Rowell: relationship unresolved.
  • Cyntha Rowell: relationship unresolved; shared church membership and surname are insufficient.

Barney relevance

Lot 393 was in District 12 within the future Brooks County area. No evidence places James at the later Barney townsite.

Remaining targets

Inspect original Bethel and Bethlehem minutes, the 1842 mortgage, census schedules, probate, and any record connecting or separating James, Henry, and Cyntha Rowell.

Sources

  1. Daniel Rowe to James Rowell, December 13, 1828, recorded October 5, 1832, Deed Book A, pp. 596–597; FamilySearch ARK https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-C9BZ-3S7D-V
  2. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948, Bethel and Bethlehem church histories.
  3. Lowndes deed extraction, James Rowell to Francis Jones, July 1, 1842, Book C, p. 295.

docs.title: Jeremiah Wilson Sr.
docs.text:
Jeremiah Wilson Sr.

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler, strongly anchored on future-Brooks land and later verified as Brooks County's first surveyor. His reported 1831 arrival and older parentage remain secondary-supported.

Evidence

A deed extraction records Jeremiah Wilson Sr. conveying 300 acres in District 12, Lot 431 to “Jeremiah Wilson Jr., his son” on February 3, 1849. This is the cohort's clearest original-record kinship statement, although the underlying deed image still needs inspection. Another extraction records Jeremiah Wilson conveying District 12, Lot 355 to Israel Folsom in 1846.

Huxford's family account identifies Jeremiah as a son of Capt. James Wilson, husband of Elizabeth “Bettie” Lucas, and father of seven named children. It places the family in Lowndes County about 1831 and their home about four miles northwest of Quitman. Those family details remain secondary-supported except for the deed's explicit father–son statement concerning Jeremiah Jr.

County-history extracts and court material identify Jeremiah as a surveyor. The Brooks Inferior Court paid him $136.50 on May 3, 1859, for surveying and laying out Quitman. That work is verified as a public act, but it postdates the antebellum settlement anchor.

Identity and family controls

  • Jeremiah Wilson Jr. as Jeremiah Sr.'s son: verified in a deed extraction; underlying image pending.
  • Elizabeth Lucas as wife and Capt. James Wilson as father: secondary-supported.
  • Margaret Louise, Eliza Ann, Emily Jane, Mary Ann, Sarah Ellen, and Silas: secondary-supported children.
  • Jeremiah Sr. must be kept separate from his son in census, deed, and office records.

Barney relevance

Lots 355 and 431 and the reported home northwest of Quitman establish a future-Brooks connection. No record proves residence at the later Barney townsite.

Remaining targets

Inspect the 1849 father-to-son deed, original census schedules, probate, Mexican War service, and the records underlying his Lowndes surveyor tenure.

Sources

  1. Lowndes deed extraction, Jeremiah Wilson Sr. to Jeremiah Wilson Jr., Book D, p. 322, recorded March 16, 1850.
  2. Lowndes deed extraction, Jeremiah Wilson to Israel Folsom, Book D, p. 34, recorded May 4, 1846.
  3. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948, Wilson family account and Quitman beginnings.

docs.title: Ezekiel Selph
docs.text:
Ezekiel Selph

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler; verified Lowndes household head in 1830 and strong-probable future-Brooks land associate by 1843–1847. The original 1830 schedule names Ezekiel Selph in Lowndes County, and the original 1840 schedule is indexed and visually consistent with an Ezekiel Selph household. A deed extraction uses Ezekiel Selph's corner as a boundary in District 12, Lot 466, a parcel later in Brooks County. The traditional 1829 arrival remains unverified.

Two generations must remain separate

The adult household head in 1830 and 1840 cannot be the Ezekiel Selph aged thirteen in Elizabeth L. Selph's 1850 household. The latter was born about 1837. The age difference verifies that at least two generations are represented.

The older man is the roster subject. The younger Ezekiel appears with Elizabeth L., Thomas, John, Charnic, William, Jackson, Polly Ann, and Freeman Selph in household 81 in 1850. That schedule gives no relationships. Elizabeth may have been the older man's widow and the younger residents may have been their children, but the census does not prove either proposition.

Census trail

The original 1830 Lowndes schedule, stamped page 79, clearly names Ezekiel Selph. The preserved 1840 Lowndes schedule, manuscript page 195, is indexed to “Ezekel Selph”; its row is visible, although a complete header-aligned demographic transcription remains unfinished. Huxford's census table also treats Ezekiel as a household head in both years.

The 1850 original schedule verifies a separate younger Ezekiel, age thirteen, in Elizabeth L. Selph's household. FamilySearch indexes his birthplace as Georgia, while an independent image-only reread recorded Alabama. That birthplace conflict should remain open; it does not affect the generational separation.

Land and future-Brooks geography

A reconstructed Lowndes deed dated December 25, 1843 and recorded March 13, 1845 describes 200 acres in the southwest corner of District 12, Lot 466, running east to Ezekiel Selph's corner. A second deed dated November 3, 1847 again bounded the east side of the conveyed portion by Ezekiel Selph. These references make the older Ezekiel a strong-probable landholder or adjoining occupant in future-Brooks territory. The underlying instruments have not been inspected, so exact ownership and residence remain qualified.

Family and later records

No inspected marriage, probate, guardianship, or deed names Elizabeth L. as the older Ezekiel's wife or the 1850 residents as their children. The younger Ezekiel married Margaret Parkerson in Bibb County on October 17, 1864 according to FamilySearch marriage indexes. An 1880 Worth County record indexes an Ezekiel born about 1837 with wife Mary and children Love, Charles, and Ellefair. The Margaret-to-Mary spouse difference and postwar movements require more evidence before treating the records as one continuous biography.

Conflicts and limits

  • Arrival: Huxford's 1829 date is retrospective and unverified.
  • Generation: older 1830/1840 head and younger 1850 child are verified as different people.
  • Elizabeth L.: possible widow of the elder, but unresolved.
  • 1850 household: co-residence does not prove parentage or sibling relationships.
  • Birthplace of younger Ezekiel: Georgia in the FamilySearch index; Alabama in an image-only reread.
  • Future-Brooks geography: deed-boundary extracts are strong locators, but the original instruments remain uninspected.
  • Barney connection: no direct residence at the later Barney townsite or descendant path to a documented Barney household was proved.

Public-ready summary

An older Ezekiel Selph was a Lowndes County household head in 1830 and 1840. Deed descriptions from the 1840s place an Ezekiel Selph boundary at District 12, Lot 466, in territory later included in Brooks County. He must not be confused with the thirteen-year-old Ezekiel living in Elizabeth L. Selph's 1850 household. Elizabeth may have been the older man's widow, but no inspected record states that relationship or identifies the younger residents as their children. The traditional 1829 arrival date therefore remains secondary and unverified.

Sources and reproducible gaps

  1. 1830 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, stamped p. 79; NARA M19, roll 19; Ancestry collection 8058, record 1850791, image 4409522_00156; preserved original schedule.
  2. 1840 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, manuscript p. 195; Ancestry collection 8057, record 1792464, image 4411334_00489; preserved original schedule, complete row transcription pending.
  3. 1850 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Division 53, household 81; Ancestry collection 8054, record 18779178, image 4193244-00467; preserved original schedule.
  4. FamilySearch census record for younger Ezekiel, MZYT-X4Q; linked household record citation MZYT-XW1.
  5. Lowndes deed reconstruction: Jeptha Newton to William B. Newton, Book C p. 480; Rachel Newton to Isaac James Newton, Book D p. 180; both use Ezekiel Selph as an eastern boundary at Lot 466.
  6. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia, pp. 29 and 33.
  7. FamilySearch Georgia marriage indexes, Ezekiel Selph and Margaret Parkerson, October 17, 1864, Bibb County; original image not inspected.
  8. FamilySearch 1880 census index, Ezekiel Selph household, Worth County; continuity from the 1850 youth remains unproved.

docs.title: Ivy Simmons
docs.text:
Ivy Simmons

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler; locator-anchored in future-Brooks territory. The original 1830 census schedule names Ivy Simmons in Lowndes County. Reconstructed Lowndes deed entries associate Ivey/Ivy Simmons with District 12, Lot 173 in 1844 and Lots 523 and 307 in 1847–1854; those parcels later lay in Brooks County. His reported 1826 arrival should not be repeated as fact.

Identity and chronology

The original 1830 Lowndes schedule, stamped page 88, contains a legible Ivy Simmons household. The original 1840 schedule is preserved and indexed to Ivy Simmons on manuscript page 237, though a complete header-aligned household transcription has not been accepted. FamilySearch also indexes an Ivey Simmons, born about 1798 in North Carolina, in Lowndes County in 1850. These records support one adult Lowndes identity across 1830–1850, but the full household continuity still needs image-level comparison.

Huxford gives two incompatible migration statements. His dated roster says Simmons came to future Brooks territory in 1826, while a later family sketch says he lived in Montgomery County and moved to the Lowndes area that became Brooks County about 1840. Neither date is independently proved. The narrow public conclusion is that Simmons was in Lowndes County by 1830 and held future-Brooks land by 1844.

Public and military role

Huxford's militia-officer compilation identifies Ivy Simmons as the first major of the 158th Battalion, commissioned January 29, 1830. This is strong secondary evidence, not an inspected commission. The 1830 household independently confirms an adult Ivy Simmons in the county that year.

Land and future-Brooks geography

The preserved Lowndes deed reconstruction supplies three reproducible land anchors:

  • James McMullen to Ivey Simmons, February 5, 1844, District 12, Lot 173, 3,500 dollars, Deed Book C, p. 408.
  • James M. Wilkinson, sheriff, to Ivey Simmons, January 6, 1847, District 12, Lot 523, Deed Book D, pp. 92–93.
  • Ivy Simmons to Leary Stanley, May 17, 1854, 220 acres in the southeast section of District 12, Lot 307, Deed Book E, pp. 479–480.

An 1848 sheriff's-sale notice also advertised interests in District 12, Lots 332, 307, and 333 under a mortgage execution in favor of Ivy Simmons against Henry Blair. This verifies a substantial legal and land association in the future-Brooks district, but not residence on each parcel.

Family claims

Huxford names Piety Joyce, daughter of Henry Joyce of Montgomery County, as Ivy's wife. The same compilation identifies Mary Simmons, wife of Benjamin Johnson Jr., and Rachel Simmons, later wife of Dr. Henry Briggs, as Ivy's daughters. These links are secondary-supported because the located census, deed, and newspaper records do not state the relationships. A later descendant path through Mary and granddaughter Ivy Johnson is likewise derivative until each generational link is independently proved.

Death and burial

FamilySearch's Find a Grave index gives 1798–1855 and Providence Community Church Cemetery near Morven. This is a cemetery-index lead, not inspection of a marker image or death record. No probate file was located in the preserved local evidence.

Conflicts and limits

  • Arrival: 1826 and about 1840 conflict; neither is verified.
  • Major's commission: strong secondary evidence only; original commission uninspected.
  • Piety Joyce and daughters Mary/Rachel: explicit compiled relationships, coherent but not parent- or marriage-record verified.
  • Barney connection: future-Brooks land association is strongly supported by reproducible deed locators, but the underlying instruments remain uninspected and no direct residence at the later Barney townsite or direct institutional effect on Barney is proved.
  • Census detail: the names and county are secure for 1830; complete demographic transcription for 1830 and 1840 remains unfinished.

Public-ready summary

Ivy Simmons was a Lowndes County household head by 1830. A reconstructed deed entry associates him with District 12 land in territory later included in Brooks County by 1844. A county-history compilation identifies him as the first major of the 158th Battalion and names Piety Joyce as his wife, but the underlying commission, deed, and a relationship-naming marriage or probate record have not been inspected. Conflicting county-history statements place his arrival in either 1826 or about 1840, so no exact migration date should be assigned.

docs.title: James T. Robeson
docs.text:
James T. Robeson

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler; original-census anchored in Lowndes County by 1850 and strongly located in future Brooks County by public office and residence evidence. The original 1850 schedule names James T. Robeson, age 36, a Georgia-born farmer, in Division 53 of Lowndes County. Huxford’s office tables place him on the Lowndes Inferior Court from 1857 to 1859 and among the justices continued into newly created Brooks County for 1859–61. A county-road abstract locates his dwelling north of Bethel Church and calls him “late” by February 20, 1865.

The traditional 1834 arrival year remains a retrospective county-history claim, not a proved date.

Original census household

The retained original 1850 image clearly shows James T. Robeson, age 36, farmer, born in Georgia, heading household 63. Sarah, age 40, and several younger people follow him. The schedule predates relationship columns; it does not label Sarah as his wife or any younger resident as his child. Huxford later identifies Sarah Gibson as James’s wife and Delilah Robinson/Robeson as their daughter. Those links are coherent with the household and later Wilson records, but remain secondary-supported until a marriage, estate, Bible, deed, or other relationship-naming original is found.

Public office and residence

Huxford’s Lowndes officer table gives James a January 12, 1857 commission and a 1857–59 term on the Inferior Court. Its Brooks County narrative says James T. Robeson, John J. Pike, and James O. Morton were serving Lowndes when Brooks was created and were authorized to continue in the new county. The Brooks officer table dates James’s new commission to December 11, 1858 and his term to 1859–61. Huxford also quotes an 1873 historical account praising the first Brooks Inferior Court and names James among its five members.

A county-road abstract dated February 20, 1865 begins at an old road north of “the late James T. Robeson’s dwelling,” then runs by or near Bethel Church toward Pleasant Hill Church. This supplies the clearest future-Brooks residence description and establishes that James had died by that date. It does not establish his exact death date.

Family claims

Huxford’s Wilson genealogy says Delilah Robinson, born September 26, 1829, was a daughter of James T. and Sarah (Gibson) Robinson or Robeson, and married Jeremiah Wilson Jr. on April 6, 1848. The spelling variation is explicit in the source. Later census work independently establishes Delilah as Jeremiah’s wife and the mother in their continuing household, but no inspected original names James and Sarah as her parents.

Accordingly:

  • Sarah Gibson as James’s wife — secondary-supported; Sarah’s 1850 co-residence is original, but the census states no relationship.
  • Delilah as their daughter — secondary-supported; explicit compiled parentage, coherent with place and chronology, but no parent-naming original inspected.
  • Jeremiah Wilson Jr. as Delilah’s husband — secondary-supported here from the compiled marriage statement and later household continuity; the original marriage return was not inspected in this lane.

An automated Brooks deed-index extraction has an 1871 entry involving “heirs of James T. Robinson,” District 13, Lot 173. The OCR is flagged for human verification and the spelling/identity bridge is incomplete, so it is retained only as a probate/deed lead.

Identity and spelling controls

James appears as Robeson in the original 1850 census and official-history tables, while Huxford’s Wilson genealogy says Robinson “or Robeson.” The two spellings may refer to the same family in these specific records, but unrelated Robinsons and later James T. Robinsons are not merged. The 1871 heirs entry cannot control identity without inspection of both index images and the underlying deed.

Place and Barney relevance

James’s residence near Bethel and his service in the first Brooks County government make him an important future-Brooks and early Brooks County figure. No record inspected here places his home at the later Barney townsite, shows ownership in Barney’s land lot, or proves a generation-by-generation descendant link to a Barney household. His profile should therefore describe regional public service, not direct Barney founding.

Conflicts and reproducible gaps

  1. Arrival: 1834 is Huxford’s later statement only.
  2. Birth: the 1850 age implies about 1814; no birth or baptismal record was found.
  3. Marriage and children: explicit only in compiled genealogy; the census itself states no relationships.
  4. Death: “late” by February 20, 1865 is supported; an exact date, cemetery inscription, probate opening, and estate distribution were not found.
  5. Office records: exact commission dates are preserved in Huxford’s transcription; underlying gubernatorial commissions and complete court minutes were not inspected in this lane.
  6. Web coverage: the live web/browser research endpoint was unavailable. Negative findings are limited to the accessible local census, deed, court, county-history, marriage, probate, cemetery, and newspaper corpus.

Public-ready profile copy

James T. Robeson

The original 1850 census places James T. Robeson in Lowndes County as a 36-year-old Georgia-born farmer. Later county records and histories place his home north of Bethel Church, in territory that became Brooks County in 1858. A road entry dated February 20, 1865 referred to the “late James T. Robeson,” showing that he had died by then.

James also helped govern the new county. A county officer compilation places him on the Lowndes Inferior Court from 1857 to 1859 and records his continuation as one of Brooks County’s first Inferior Court justices for 1859–61. The exact 1834 arrival date repeated in the county history has not been independently verified.

A later Wilson family account identifies Sarah Gibson as James’s wife and Delilah Robinson or Robeson as their daughter. Delilah married Jeremiah Wilson Jr. The 1850 census supports the household setting, but it did not record relationships, and no inspected marriage, estate, Bible, or deed names Sarah as James’s wife or Delilah as his daughter. Those family links therefore remain secondary-supported.

James’s residence and public service make him a documented figure in the future-Brooks region. No direct connection to the later Barney townsite has yet been proved.

Sources and reproducible gaps

  1. 1850 U.S. census, Division 53, Lowndes County, Georgia, household 63, James T. Robeson; Ancestry collection 8054, record 18779040, image 4193244-00463; original schedule inspected.
  2. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (Quitman, 1948), arrival and census lists, Lowndes and Brooks Inferior Court tables, first-court narrative, road abstracts, and Wilson genealogy, especially printed pp. 29–33, 63, 71, and 574–575.
  3. Brooks County deed universal-index extraction, 1871, “heirs of James T. Robinson,” Book C, p. 597, District 13, Lot 173; automated paired OCR flagged for human verification. Original index rows and deed not inspected.
  4. Priority targets are the underlying gubernatorial commissions and court minutes, the 1871 heirs deed, a probate/estate distribution, a marriage or Bible record, and an original Delilah–Jeremiah marriage record.

docs.title: John O’Steen
docs.text:
John O’Steen

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment

Supplemental early settler; strong future-Brooks case by 1835, with the 1840 household still awaiting an original-schedule reading. Folks Huxford’s published transcription places John O’Steen as captain of the 659th militia district on December 11, 1835. The 659th was the Nankin district, territory later included in Brooks County. Huxford also lists a John O’Steen as a Lowndes County household head in 1840, and the surviving census index supplies an exact image locator. These independent civil and census locators are enough for the supplemental roster, but the traditional 1828 arrival year is not independently proved.

Identity controls

The records do not support treating every John O’Steen as one man.

  • The 1831 federal official register names John Osteen as postmaster at Waresboro, Georgia. Waresboro was in Ware County, not the future-Brooks Nankin district. A later move is possible, but no record found in this pass bridges the postmaster to the 1835 militia captain.
  • Huxford’s officer list names John O’Steen as captain of the 659th District on December 11, 1835.
  • The 1840 Lowndes census index identifies a household head indexed as John Ostna, with Osteen and O’Steen supplied as alternate readings. The original frame, Ancestry image 4411334_00477, was not preserved and independently read in this pass.
  • Huxford separately lists John H. O’Steen as ensign of the 659th District on April 22, 1844. The middle initial matters. No inspected source proves that the captain and ensign were the same man; the 1844 officer may be a younger relative or an unrelated namesake.

The older project audit described John as a justice of the peace in 1844–45. The officer table inspected here instead records John H. O’Steen as ensign in 1844. Until an underlying commission or court record is inspected, the justice-of-the-peace statement should not be published as fact.

Household and family

No spouse, child, parent, sibling, or estate heir has been established from an inspected relationship-naming record. The 1840 census can describe only age-and-sex categories even after its image is recovered; it cannot by itself name a wife or children. Younger Civil War-era and later John O’Steens must remain separate unless a dated generational bridge is found.

Place and Barney relevance

The 659th/Nankin district is a direct future-Brooks regional anchor. It does not prove residence at the later Barney townsite, ownership in Barney’s land lot, or influence on the later town. John should therefore be presented as an early settler of the surrounding future-Brooks area, not as a founder of Barney.

Conflicts and limits

  1. Arrival: Huxford says 1828; no contemporary record inspected here establishes that year.
  2. Office: the 1835 captaincy and 1844 ensign appointment are retrospective transcriptions of official appointments; the underlying commissions were not inspected.
  3. 1840 census: exact indexed locator recovered, but the original handwritten row remains unread in the retained evidence.
  4. Namesakes: John Osteen at Waresboro in 1831, John O’Steen in Nankin in 1835/1840, and John H. O’Steen in 1844 are not merged.
  5. Land/probate: no responsive original deed, tax, probate, marriage, cemetery, or newspaper record was located in the accessible local corpus. The live web/browser search endpoint was unavailable in this pass, so this is not a comprehensive negative search.

Public-ready profile copy

John O’Steen

John O’Steen belongs on the supplemental early-settler roster because a published militia-officer transcription places him in the 659th, or Nankin, district by December 1835. That district lay in the part of Lowndes County later included in Brooks County. A separate census locator identifies a John O’Steen household in Lowndes County in 1840, although the original handwritten row still needs an independent reading.

The exact year of his arrival is less certain. A later county history says he came in 1828, but no contemporary record inspected for this profile proves that date. The records also contain more than one potentially relevant John: the 1831 federal register names a John Osteen as postmaster at Waresboro, while an 1844 officer list names John H. O’Steen as ensign in Nankin. No record yet proves that either was the 1835 captain.

John’s spouse, children, land, and estate remain unresolved. His documented importance is regional: he was associated with the future-Brooks Nankin district, but no direct connection to the later Barney townsite has been established.

Sources and reproducible gaps

  1. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (Quitman, 1948), early-settler list, census table, and 659th District officer table, printed pp. 29–33 and officer appendix.
  2. 1840 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, John Ostna index entry; Ancestry collection 8057, record 1792273, image 4411334_00477. The locator is accepted; the handwriting is not yet independently transcribed.
  3. Register of All Officers and Agents, Civil, Military, and Naval, in the Service of the United States (1831), post-office table, Waresboro, Georgia, John Osteen. Identity with the Nankin officer is unresolved.
  4. No underlying 1835 or 1844 commission, original 1840 row image, deed, tax entry, probate packet, or parent-naming record was accessible for inspection. Those are the priority targets.

  • Huxford separately lists John H. O’Steen as ensign of the 659th District on April 22, 1844. The middle initial matters. No inspected source proves that the captain and ensign were the same man; the 1844 officer may be a younger relative or an unrelated namesake.

The older project audit described John as a justice of the peace in 1844–45. The officer table inspected here instead records John H. O’Steen as ensign in 1844. Until an underlying commission or court record is inspected, the justice-of-the-peace statement should not be published as fact.

docs.title: Household and family
docs.text: No spouse, child, parent, sibling, or estate heir has been established from an inspected relationship-naming record. The 1840 census can describe only age-and-sex categories even after its image is recovered; it cannot by itself name a wife or children. Younger Civil War-era and later John O’Steens must remain separate unless a dated generational bridge is found.

docs.title: Place and Barney relevance
docs.text: The 659th/Nankin district is a direct future-Brooks regional anchor. It does not prove residence at the later Barney townsite, ownership in Barney’s land lot, or influence on the later town. John should therefore be presented as an early settler of the surrounding future-Brooks area, not as a founder of Barney.

docs.title: Conflicts and limits
docs.text:
1. Arrival: Huxford says 1828; no contemporary record inspected here establishes that year.
  2. Office: the 1835 captaincy and 1844 ensign appointment are retrospective transcriptions of official appointments; the underlying commissions were not inspected.
  3. 1840 census: exact indexed locator recovered, but the original handwritten row remains unread in the retained evidence.
  4. Namesakes: John Osteen at Waresboro in 1831, John O’Steen in Nankin in 1835/1840, and John H. O’Steen in 1844 are not merged.
  5. Land/probate: no responsive original deed, tax, probate, marriage, cemetery, or newspaper record was located in the accessible local corpus. The live web/browser search endpoint was unavailable in this pass, so this is not a comprehensive negative search.

docs.title: John O’Steen
docs.text:
John O’Steen belongs on the supplemental early-settler roster because a published militia-officer transcription places him in the 659th, or Nankin, district by December 1835. That district lay in the part of Lowndes County later included in Brooks County. A separate census locator identifies a John O’Steen household in Lowndes County in 1840, although the original handwritten row still needs an independent reading.

The exact year of his arrival is less certain. A later county history says he came in 1828, but no contemporary record inspected for this profile proves that date. The records also contain more than one potentially relevant John: the 1831 federal register names a John Osteen as postmaster at Waresboro, while an 1844 officer list names John H. O’Steen as ensign in Nankin. No record yet proves that either was the 1835 captain.

John’s spouse, children, land, and estate remain unresolved. His documented importance is regional: he was associated with the future-Brooks Nankin district, but no direct connection to the later Barney townsite has been established.

docs.title: Fleming Bates
docs.text:
Fleming Bates

Assessment

Fleming Bates qualifies as a supplemental early settler. His name is legible on the original 1830 Lowndes County census, stamped page 88. The demographic columns have not been fully transcribed, but the household-head reading is secure.

A rerecorded Lowndes deed supplies a future-Brooks land locator. Acting through a sheriff's sale, Fleming Bates conveyed District 12, Lot 435 to William Smith for $21 on July 14, 1830. The instrument was recorded in 1837. The record establishes Bates's legal association with the lot; the underlying execution and title history need further study before describing him as an ordinary voluntary seller.

Huxford's Bethel pastor table places Bates at the church from 1827 through 1830. This makes the traditional 1826 migration plausible, but the original minutes have not been inspected and no contemporary record states the arrival year. His wife, children, later residence, and death remain unresolved.

Identity controls

  • The 1830 census head and sheriff-deed party are consistent in name, county, and date.
  • The church role remains based on a later transcription.
  • No spouse or child should be assigned without a relationship-naming record.

docs.title: James McMullen Jr.
docs.text:
James McMullen Jr.

Assessment

James McMullen Jr. is a supplemental early-settler candidate with a generational conflict. His name is legible on the original 1830 Lowndes schedule at stamped page 82, entry 108. That verifies a James McMullen household but does not distinguish the older James Jr. from every later namesake.

Three original deed locators place James McMullen on future-Brooks land. Enoch Hall sold him District 12, Lot 173 in December 1836 and part of Lot 174 in September 1836. James Taylor conveyed another portion of Lot 174 to James McMullen in November 1836. In 1844, James McMullen sold Lot 173 to Ivey Simmons for $3,500. These transactions establish a substantial local landholder but do not state his parents, spouse, or generation.

Huxford identifies James Jr. as William McMullen's brother and Rebecca Fain's husband. The same sketch identifies a younger James—William's son—as Harriet Rountree's husband. Three separate 1850 census candidates survive in Lowndes and Thomas counties, so none can be assigned to the 1827 settler without a deed, probate, marriage, or household bridge.

Identity controls

  • The 1830 household is verified; assignment to the older James Jr. is strong probable, not direct proof.
  • The 1836–1844 landholder may be that household head, but no relationship language appears in the extraction.
  • The younger James, husband of Harriet Rountree, remains separate.

docs.title: William Jones
docs.text:
William Jones

Assessment

William Jones qualifies as a supplemental early settler. The original 1830 Lowndes County census names his seven-person household near several people independently associated with the future-Brooks roster. The schedule does not identify which of the three males was the household head, and it does not prove Huxford's 1828 arrival date.

An original rerecorded deed adds a precise association: William Jones witnessed Daniel Rowe's December 13, 1828 sale of District 12, Lot 393 to James Rowell. Lowndes tax entries index William Jones in Captain Burnett's District in 1834 and 1835; James's readings place both returns on Lot 393. The repeated lot supports continuity, although the manuscript land columns remain user-verified readings rather than a new independent transcription.

Two original deeds prove that a William Jones of Lowndes County acquired a one-third interest in District 15, Lot 106 in 1843 and sold it in 1848. Those deeds do not connect that man explicitly to the 1828 witness or the 1830 household. A separate 1856 marriage-contract deed concerns William Jones and Martha Hunter, widow of Hardee Hunter; it should not be assigned to the earlier man without an identity bridge.

Huxford's Bethlehem account names William and Elizabeth Jones in the church community in 1834. The original church minutes have not been inspected, so Elizabeth's relationship and the church role remain secondary-supported.

Identity controls

  • The 1830 household, 1828 witness, and 1834–1835 taxpayer form a strong-probable local identity cluster.
  • The 1843–1848 deed party may be the same man, but the deeds do not bridge the identities.
  • The 1856 William Jones–Martha Hunter instrument and later Valdosta-area Jones records remain separate.
  • No exact arrival year or direct Barney residence is proved.
  • A dedicated test against the documented Barney Jones line found that Malachi Jones's father was Thomas Jones, not this William. Malachi is chronologically compatible with the unnamed male age 20-29 in William's 1830 household, but no record identifies him there or establishes William as an uncle, cousin, or other relative.

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Roster and Barney relevance

  • Roster: supplemental; original-record anchored by 1828–1830.
  • Barney relevance: broader future-Brooks context. Lot 393 and Bethlehem lie in the wider settlement history, but no direct effect on Barney is proved.
  • Jones-family bridge: none proved. William as Malachi's father is contradicted; any collateral relationship remains unresolved.

Barney Jones line test

The documented Barney line runs from Thomas Jones and Matha Denmark through Malachi Jones, M. Franklin Jones, and Edgar Jelks Jones. William Jones is not named in that chain. Malachi's age is compatible with the unnamed male age 20–29 in William's 1830 household, but the census names no relationship. William as Malachi's father is contradicted; an uncle, cousin, or other collateral relationship remains unresolved.

  2. Daniel Rowe to James Rowell, December 13, 1828, Lowndes Deed Book A, pp. 596–597; rerecorded image, FamilySearch ARK 3:1:3Q9M-C9BZ-3S7D-V.
  3. Lowndes County tax digests, 1834 and 1835, Captain Burnett's District; Ancestry records 3476533 and 3526004. Lot 393/12 is a user-verified manuscript reading.

  6. Walter C. Jones biographical sketch, A History of Savannah and South Georgia (1913), identifying Thomas Jones as Malachi Jones's father.

docs.title: William McMullen
docs.text:
William McMullen

Assessment

William McMullen qualifies as a supplemental early settler with an identity qualification. Ancestry supplies an exact 1830 Lowndes locator, but the schedule pixels did not load during the preserved review. Two 1840 candidates—one in Lowndes and one in the Swaines area of Thomas County—must remain separate until their rows and household marks are read.

Huxford's McMullen sketch identifies the older William as born about 1782, husband of Lavinia Fain, brother of James McMullen Jr., and father of John and a younger James. Those relationships are secondary-supported because no probate, Bible, marriage, or parent-naming deed has been inspected.

The 1836 Lowndes militia return contains more than one William McMullin entry. The names establish McMullen men in the county's militia-age population but do not identify which entry belongs to the older William. They do not prove active Creek War service.

Identity controls

  • The proposed older William must remain separate from William R. McMullen and later namesakes.

docs.title: Cornelius English
docs.text: Cornelius English ¶ Assessment ¶ Cornelius English qualifies as a supplemental early settler . The original 1830 Lowndes County census names his household, and the original 1836 general-militia return places a Cornelius English in the 659th District. The militia record proves district association, not active wartime service. The 1840 census contains two Cornelius English households, one identified as junior. No inspected deed, probate, tax record, or other original source yet proves how the two men were related or which household belonged to the father of Matthew Joseph English. An 1849 sheriff notice names Cornelius English with Barbary English and Nathan Lindsay but does not state their relationships. Back to the Early History Profiles index Roster and Barney relevance ¶ Roster: supplemental; original-record anchored by 1830 and 1836. Barney relevance: secondary-supported descendant bridge. The later generations are supported by census and parent records, but the Cornelius-to-Matthew link still rests on compiled genealogy. Direct Barney residence: none proved for Cornelius. Descendant bridge to Barney ¶ The best-supported reconstruction is: Cornelius English and Abigail Allbritton → Matthew Joseph English → John Cornelius English → Andrew James English of Barney. The 1860 Madison County, Florida, census records M. J. English, a 21-year-old Georgia-born planter, with Flora M. English and two-year-old William H. English. A Civil War profile identifies him as Matthew Joseph English, records his marriage to Flora Blanton on February 19, 1857, and reports that he was killed at Sharpsburg on September 17, 1862, while serving in Company D, Fifth Florida Infantry. After Matthew's death, Flora returned to her Blanton family. The 1870 Taylor County census places Flora and nine-year-old John English in James A. Blanton's household. In 1880, John C. English is explicitly identified as Flora's son. The 1900 census places Flora in John's household with his wife and children, including Andrew J. English. Andrew later became the railroad agent at Barney. His Social Security parent record independently names John C. English and Elizabeth C. Eakins as his parents. The later chain is well supported, but the first link is not yet verified by an original parent-naming record. Two compiled genealogies identify Matthew as the son of Cornelius English and Abigail Allbritton, and Huxford separately reports Abigail's marriage to Cornelius. No inspected probate, deed, Bible, guardianship, marriage, or estate record names Matthew as their son. The complete bridge is therefore secondary-supported , not fully verified. The other A. J. English ¶ The A. J. English once considered as a possible father of John C. English was Andrew J. English, born about 1835 in Georgia. He remained in Brooks County, lived alone in 1860, and reported himself single in both 1880 and 1900. Those records make him a separate local man and remove him as the leading candidate for Flora Blanton's husband. docs.title: Henry Dean
docs.text:
Henry Dean

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision

Supplemental early settler; verified household presence by 1830 and strong future-Brooks land evidence. A preserved 1830 Lowndes census transcription reports Henry Dean's four-person household, and the 1840 transcription reports a nine-person household. Reconstructed Lowndes deed locators place him on District 12 Lots 492 and 436 in 1838–1841. Huxford's officer table identifies Henry Dean as first lieutenant of the 790th District on January 12, 1836; the underlying commission was not inspected.

Identity and household

Henry remains separate from John Dean and William E. Dean. The 1830 household was reported as three males and one female; the 1840 household as six males and three females. Those totals do not identify a wife or children. No parent-naming, marriage, probate, or Bible record was found in the documented search.

Land

The reconstructed deed index supplies a coherent chain:

  • Jared Johnson to Henry Dean, District 12, Lot 492, March 21, 1838, $50; Book C, p. 198.
  • Henry Dean to John Bryan, the same lot, February 12, 1841, $300; Book C, p. 199.
  • Jared Johnson to Henry Dean, 245 acres in the east half of Lot 436, July 12, 1841, $300; Book D, p. 111.
  • Henry Dean to Frances A. Griffin, the same 245 acres, December 15, 1841, $300; Book D, p. 112.

These locators strongly place Henry in the future-Brooks land record, but the recorded instruments have not been inspected for legal descriptions, witnesses, or family language.

Barney relevance

Broader future-Brooks context; no direct Barney influence proved.

Remaining work

Inspect the four deeds and the original 1830/1840 schedules; identify Henry's spouse and children through marriage, probate, church, or Bible evidence; inspect the 1836 commission.

docs.title: James E. Hendry
docs.text:
James E. Hendry

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision

Supplemental early settler; strong household and family-network case. Huxford's Hendry sketch identifies James Edward Hendry, born September 29, 1808, as the eldest son of William Hendry and Nancy McFail. It says he married Lydia Carlton in Thomas County in 1829, lived for several years in present Brooks County, and appears there in the 1830 census before moving to Thomas County and later Florida.

Kinship chain

  • William Hendry + Nancy McFail → James Edward Hendry: secondary-supported.
  • James Edward Hendry + Lydia Carlton: secondary-supported.
  • Lydia as daughter of Judge John Carlton: secondary-supported.

The compiled claims are explicit and mutually coherent, and independent online family histories repeat them. No original marriage or parent-naming instrument was inspected. Lydia must not be assigned to Thomas Carlton merely because she shared the surname; the reviewed sources identify her father as John Carlton.

Original and near-contemporary anchors

  • A future-Brooks household list places James in the 1830 Lowndes census.
  • A January 1841 newspaper notice names James E. Hendry administrator of Eli H. Hendry's Thomas County estate. Administrator status proves the legal role, not kinship.
  • A reconstructed deed locator places James E. Hendry in a January 9, 1839 transaction involving about 490 acres and Lot 562; the OCR district and counterparties require inspection before geographic use.

The family sketch reports eleven children, a move near Tampa in 1851, and James's death in Thomas County on January 3, 1852. Those details remain compiled-family evidence unless supported separately.

Barney relevance

Secondary-supported family bridge to the later railroad-era Brooks network; no direct Barney residence proved.

Huxford's Hendry family sketches identify James Edward Hendry and Neal Hendry as sons of William Hendry and Nancy McFail. Norman Campbell Hendry was Neal's son. On that compiled evidence, James was Norman's paternal uncle. The James-to-Neal relationship is secondary-supported because no inspected parent-naming original has yet established both men as William and Nancy's sons.

The Neal-to-Norman link is stronger. Norman's original death certificate names Neal Hendry and Margaret Campbell as his parents, and the 1860, 1870, and 1880 census trail places Norman in their household; the 1880 schedule explicitly calls him their son. Norman Campbell Hendry was a Brooks County merchant, farmer, school-board member, and the strong-probable N. C. Hendry named as a South Georgia Railroad charter petitioner. His business and plantation interests connected him to the railroad serving Barney.

This bridge does not establish that the later Black Hendry or Henry families enumerated at Barney descended from James, Neal, or Norman. No biological, formerly enslaved, labor, or surname-association link to those households has been proved.

Remaining work

Inspect the 1829 marriage, the 1830 schedule, the 1839 deed, and probate/estate material; seek original records naming William and Nancy as parents of both James and Neal and naming John Carlton as Lydia's father.

Sources for the later bridge

  1. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), Hendry family sketches identifying James and Neal as sons of William Hendry and Nancy McFail and Norman as Neal's son. These are compiled family histories.
  2. Georgia death certificate, Norman Campbell Hendry, September 7, 1938, naming Neal Hendry and Margaret Campbell as his parents; Ancestry collection 2562, record 1008248.
  3. 1860 Taylor County, Florida; 1870 Brooks County, Georgia; and 1880 Quitman, Brooks County censuses following Norman in Neal and Margaret Hendry's household. The 1880 schedule explicitly identifies Norman as their son.
  4. Norman Campbell Hendry profile and railroad-petitioner identity analysis: https://www.barneyga.com/railroad-people/neal-c-hendry/

docs.title: John Dean
docs.text:
John Dean

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision

Supplemental early settler; verified regional household tradition with a strong secondary family identification. Huxford's Allbritton sketch says Jane Allbritton married John Dean in Laurens County in 1812 and that the couple moved to Lowndes County about 1830, settled in present Brooks County, and left descendants. Census-derived household lists place a John Dean in the relevant 1830–1850 sequence. The underlying marriage and census images were not inspected in this pass.

Identity and kinship

Jane Allbritton was reported born in 1795, a sister of Matthew Allbritton. The exact chain is therefore:

John Dean — spouse claim — Jane Allbritton

Current grade: secondary-supported. The compiled account states the marriage explicitly and is chronologically coherent, but no original marriage entry, Bible, deed, or probate record naming the couple was inspected.

John remains separate from Henry Dean and William E. Dean. No record reviewed proves they were related.

Public office

Huxford's 790th District table lists John Dean for a justice-of-the-peace term beginning January 23, 1833. The table provides a strong official lead in the future-Brooks Tallokas district, but the underlying commission was not inspected.

Barney relevance

Broader future-Brooks context; no direct Barney influence or descendant bridge proved in the reviewed evidence.

Remaining work

Inspect the Laurens marriage book, original 1830–1850 schedules, the 1833 commission, and Dean probate/deed records naming Jane or their children.

docs.title: Thomas Carlton
docs.text:
Thomas Carlton

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision

Supplemental early settler; household continuity supported, family unresolved. The 1830 Thomas County household list and the 1840 Lowndes census transcription each name Thomas Carlton in territory associated with future Brooks County. The 1840 transcription reports a household of six males and five females.

Identity controls

Thomas must remain separate from John Carlton, Rev. Peter Carlton, Hardy Carlton, William Carlton, and the other Carlton household heads in Thomas and Lowndes counties. No deed, probate, marriage, or parent-naming record reviewed identifies Thomas's wife or children.

The James Hendry family material identifies Lydia Carlton as a daughter of Judge John Carlton, not Thomas Carlton. Thomas therefore receives no Hendry family bridge on surname evidence alone.

Geography

The 1830 Thomas and 1840 Lowndes placements support a regional household trail, but the original schedule rows and an exact land locator are still needed before assigning one continuous identity or a specific future-Brooks tract.

Barney relevance

Broader future-Brooks context; no direct Barney influence proved.

Remaining work

Inspect both census schedules; search Thomas/Lowndes deeds, taxes, marriage, and probate records; distinguish every same-name or same-generation Carlton before reconstructing a family.

docs.title: William Holloway Jr.
docs.text:
William Holloway Jr.

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision

Supplemental early settler; strong probable identity across household, church, and land records. Huxford's Edmondson sketch identifies Elizabeth Edmondson, born 1801, as wife of William Holloway Jr. A derivative Holloway family account gives William's birth as May 5, 1802, and their marriage as January 17, 1825. Census-derived lists place William Holloway households in the 1830, 1840, and 1850 Thomas-side future-Brooks record, but William Sr. and Jr. must be separated on the original schedules.

Church and community

Bethel's compiled history lists William Holloway Jr. as church clerk in 1835–1836. It separately says William Holloway and William Newton were elected deacons in September 1856. The later entry probably concerns the younger William, but the minutes were not inspected and the name lacks a suffix.

Sharpe's 1884 historical series names William Holloway among the residents near Mount Zion. This supports community context but is retrospective.

Land

A reconstructed deed index records John Edmondson of Lowndes County conveying District 12, Lot 510 to William Holloway of Thomas County on February 20, 1855, for $200; Book E, pp. 600–601. The exact party is compatible with William Jr. and the Edmondson family network, but the original deed has not been inspected for relationship language. A later 1863/1867 deed-index entry involving Everett Solomon and William Holloway at Lot 445 may concern another or later William and remains unassigned.

Kinship

  • William Holloway Jr. + Elizabeth Edmondson: secondary-supported.
  • Elizabeth as daughter of Isaac Edmondson: secondary-supported in the reviewed family histories.
  • John Edmondson to William Holloway deed: association only; the transaction does not prove kinship without the instrument.

Barney relevance

Broader future-Brooks, Bethel, and Mount Zion context; no direct Barney influence proved.

Remaining work

Inspect the 1830–1850 schedules, 1825 marriage, Bethel minutes, 1855 deed, and probate/estate records for both William Sr. and Jr.

docs.title: Household #155: Alderman, Mitchell Enoch
docs.text: In the 1900 Barney census, this household was headed by Mitchell Alderman and included 4 people. The census summary records the head's listed occupation was Farmer, 1 spouse or marital partner, 2 child or stepchild.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
A good way to read this page is to start with Mitchell Alderman (age 30, born in Georgia, listed as Farmer). That placed the household in the farm economy around Barney, where land, crops, livestock, kin labor, and seasonal work shaped daily life as much as the town's railroad and stores did.

The household was not just the head's name. In 1900 it included spouse or marital partner Georgia Alderman; children Shelton Alderman and John F Alderman. Those names are the starting point for the later family, labor, marriage, migration, and neighborhood trails below.

Every listed person in this household was reported as born in Georgia, which makes the page a local-family snapshot unless later records show movement into or out of Barney.

docs.title: Newspaper and Public-Record Trail
docs.text:
The expanded research below already preserves these public-facing leads for this household:

  • This resolves the 1930 granddaughter question toward John F. rather than Shelton, though a birth, delayed-birth, death, or obituary parent-naming record would still be stronger.
  • Verify Shelton Madison Alderman and John Franklin Alderman with birth, death, obituary, SS-5, delayed birth, or other records naming parents.
  • Corroborate Geraldine Alderman's parentage with a birth, delayed-birth, marriage, death, obituary, or other parent-naming record.

docs.title: 1900 Census Household
docs.text: Name Relation Age Birthplace Occupation Mitchell Alderman Head 30 Georgia Farmer Georgia Alderman Wife 30 Georgia — Shelton Alderman Son 9 Georgia — John F Alderman Son 6 Georgia —

docs.title: Children and Later Trails
docs.text:
The household table above already lists the children present in 1900: Shelton Alderman, John F Alderman.

Where a child's adult trail is not identified here, the gap is intentional. The page should wait for a marriage, death, cemetery, obituary, probate, later census, or other direct record before naming a later spouse or descendant line.

Mitchell E. Alderman and Georgia Crosby were married in Colquitt County, Georgia, in 1889. The Ancestry marriage detail previously used for this entry gave 25 December 1889, while FamilySearch search results for the same Georgia Crosby / M. E. Alderman marriage cluster show 1889, 5 December 1889, and 28 November 1889 variants. The marriage is therefore solidly placed in Colquitt County in 1889, but the exact day should be tied to the best inspected image rather than harmonized silently. The 1900 census places Mitchell and Georgia in Barney District, Brooks County, with Shelton and John F. Alderman in the household. The checked 1900 Barney census report says Mitchell and Georgia had been married ten years, broadly matching the 1889 marriage record cluster, and records Shelton and John F. as sons. Earlier cleanup wording that called them stepchildren was erroneous and has been removed.

The household can be followed after 1900 in Colquitt and Brooks County records. In 1910, Mitchell and Georgia were in Robinson District, Colquitt County, with Madison S. and John F. in the household. Mitchell was recorded as working in a turpentine factory and owning his farm free. In 1920, Mitchell and Georgia were again in Robinson District, with no children in the household. In 1930, they were in Brooks County with granddaughter Geraldine, age seven, and boarder Loma Mitchell. The 1930 census says Mitchell could not read or write, which conflicts with the 1900-1920 literacy entries and may be an enumerator or informant difference. A 1940 Barney District census detail page places Geraldine Alderman, age 17, as daughter in the John F. Alderman household; FamilySearch independently indexes that 1940 result with parents John F. Alderman and June P. Alderman. This resolves the 1930 granddaughter question toward John F. rather than Shelton, though a birth, delayed-birth, death, or obituary parent-naming record would still be stronger.

The original death certificates now strengthen the death, parent, and burial evidence for both spouses. Georgia died 29 May 1937 at Edmondson-Brannen Hospital in Moultrie, Colquitt County, Georgia. Her certificate gives her birth date as 21 March 1871, birthplace as Brooks County, Georgia, parents as Adam Crosby and Lucy Griffin, both born South Carolina, and burial at Wesley Chapel, Berlin, Georgia, on 30 May 1937. The informant was J. F. Alderman of Barney, Georgia. Georgia's 1880 childhood census household also places her as a daughter of Adam J. Crosby and Lucy Crosby in Robinson District, Colquitt County, with Elizabeth, Isam T., William, Christiana, and Augustus Crosby in the same household. FamilySearch also surfaces an Augustus Lee Crosby death result naming Adam Crosby and Lucy Griffen Crosby as his parents, strengthening Augustus as Georgia's sibling in the Adam/Lucy Crosby cluster.

Mitchell died 29 December 1938 at Barney, Brooks County, Georgia. His certificate gives his birth date as 20 November 1868, birthplace as Colquitt County, Georgia, occupation as farmer, parents as John Alderman and Susie Stevens, and burial at Wesley Chapel, Pavo, Georgia, on 31 December 1938. The informant was Frank Alderman of Barney, Georgia. These certificates are direct support for the parent and burial details. FindAGrave screenshots supplied by James list John Franklin Alderman and Shelton Madison Alderman as children and list Crosby/Alderman relatives; the child links align with the checked 1900 Barney census report, though the memorial family links remain derivative leads until matched to direct parent-naming or sibling-proof records.

docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
• HH#153 Daniel Alderman: If HH#153 Daniel was John A. Alderman's son by Emily Norman, Daniel and Mitchell were probable half-brothers, not half-uncle and nephew. The census trail supports Daniel in John A.'s family context, but Aldermans in America calls the relevant child David Harrison. The relationship remains strong probable with that conflict explicit.
  • Alderman family cluster: Mitchell belongs in the broader Alderman cluster that includes HH#153, HH#176, HH#178, and HH#180, but the exact kinship paths should be cited from direct records where possible and from Aldermans in America only as secondary support.
  • Crosby-Alderman double marriage: Georgia Crosby's brother Augustus L. Crosby reportedly married Mitchell's sister Martha/Mattie J. Alderman. James did not locate the marriage certificate in this pass, but a Social Security Applications and Claims Index detail page for Mattie J. Alderman names spouse Augustus L. Crosby and child Dennis Wilson Crosby. This supports the couple as a collateral clue, but it is not a marriage record and should not be used to prove the exact marriage date or the full sibling network by itself.

docs.text:

The checked 1900 Barney census report and derivative family sources call them sons; direct parent-naming records would strengthen, not reverse, that reading.
  • Verify Georgia Crosby's full sibling list from additional direct census, marriage, probate, or death records rather than relying on Geneanet, FindAGrave family links, or the Social Security Applications and Claims Index collateral clue alone. Her parents, Adam Crosby and Lucy Griffin, are directly supported by her death certificate, and the 1880 census directly places Georgia in Adam and Lucy's household with several likely siblings.

  • Cemetery-marker photographs or cemetery register entries would still be useful corroboration, but the original death certificates now directly support Wesley Chapel burial for both Mitchell and Georgia.
  • Corroborate Geraldine Alderman's parentage with a birth, delayed-birth, marriage, death, obituary, or other parent-naming record. The 1930/1940 census chain points to John Franklin Alderman as her father, but a direct parent-naming record would be stronger.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text:
• Status: Source-researched, not complete.
  • Strengths: The household has a solid direct-record core: 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930, and Geraldine-linked 1940 census trail; Colquitt County marriage record; and original Georgia death certificates for both Mitchell and Georgia.
  • Remaining cautions: Shelton and John F. are recorded as sons in the checked 1900 Barney census report, so the earlier children-as-stepsons caution was erroneous and should not be preserved. Direct parent-naming records for the two sons would still strengthen the file. Much of the sibling, half-sibling, grandparent, and extended Alderman lineage depends on Aldermans in America, Geneanet, and FindAGrave rather than direct records. Georgia Crosby's parents are now supported by her death certificate and 1880 childhood census household, but her full sibling reconstruction still needs follow-through across later direct records.

Spouse: Jonathan "Doc" Howell Alderman (1847-1924). Lists 16 children with variant names. Source: Ancestry.com Public Member Trees.

Book Reference: "Aldermans in America" (1957).

Jonathan H. Alderman appears as entry 15-2-14 in the genealogical work "Aldermans in America" by Jennie Alderman Park (1957). The numbering system traces his lineage:

  • 15 = Daniel Alderman (1774-1857), David Sr.'s eldest son → stayed in North Carolina
  • 15-2 = George Alderman (1797-1882), Daniel's son → moved to Georgia 1826
  • 15-2-14 = Jonathan H. Alderman (1847-1924), George's 14th and youngest son

The book lists 16 children for J.H. and Amy Ann, provides full birth/death dates and spouse names for each, and records that J.H. "was also in the ranks with Lee" during the Civil War. Three of George Alderman's sons died in Confederate service: William (killed by shell at Rappahannock, August 1862), Daniel H., and David J.

Correction: earlier research incorrectly described George, William, and Timothy as "three founding brothers." David Alderman Sr. (1749-1831) is the patriarch. Daniel (Col 15), William (Col 26), and Timothy (Col 27) are David's sons, making them brothers. George (15-2) is Daniel's son, making him their nephew, not their brother.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
George Washington Alderman (age 35, farmer) - Born 18 August 1864, Brooks County, Georgia - Died 22 December 1935, Douglas, Coffee County, Georgia - Buried Douglas City Cemetery, Coffee County, Georgia - Parents: Jonathan Howell Alderman and Amy Ann McKinney - Book ID: 15-2-14-1 in Aldermans in America; first child of Jonathan Howell Alderman

Isabel "Belle" Coulter Alderman. - Born 23 October 1863, Brooks County, Georgia - Died 3 June 1934, Douglas, Coffee County, Georgia - Buried Douglas City Cemetery, Coffee County, Georgia - Parents: John A. Coulter and Sena Ann Saffold; the Saffold parentage is supported by Isabel's death record, while full-name detail comes partly through Find a Grave/Geneanet.

George Washington Alderman was the first child of Jonathan Howell Alderman and Amy Ann McKinney. The book "Aldermans in America" (1957) assigns him book ID 15-2-14-1, tracing his lineage as David Sr. (1749-1831) to Daniel (Col 15) to George (15-2) to Jonathan H. (15-2-14) to George Washington (15-2-14-1). The SAR application for Jonathan H. Alderman (SAR #90614, filed Nov 6, 1963) lists "George Washington Alderman" as a child, with father George Alderman and mother Nancy Carlton for Jonathan, and spouse Amy Ann McKinney.

George's middle name "Washington" appears on his death certificate and FindAGrave memorial. Census records use "George" (1870), "George W." (1880), "Geo" (1900), "Geo W" (1910), "Georg W" (1920), and "Geo W" (1930). The 1920 enumerator or indexer rendered the surname as "Aulderman," a variant that also appears in HH#176's 1920 census for Jonathan H.

Isabel Coulter's maiden name appears with spelling variants: "Colter" in 1870 and 1880 censuses, "Coulter" on her death record, FindAGrave, and Geneanet. The marriage certificate indexes her as "Belle Colter." FindAGrave and Geneanet agree on the full name "Isabelle Belle Coulter."

Wife's Family: The Coulters.

Isabel Coulter's parents were John A. Coulter and Sena Ann Saffold. The 1870 census records John Colter (30) and Ann Colter (32) with children Isabella (6), William (5), and Ella (3) in Brooks County. The 1880 census records John (40) and Elizabeth (33) with children Isabella (16), William (14), Ella (12), David J. (9), and James (7) in Dry Lake, Brooks County.

The name discrepancy between "Ann" (1870) and "Elizabeth" (1880) for Isabel's mother is resolved by the death record, FindAGrave, and Geneanet. The death record lists mother as "Saffold." FindAGrave gives "Ann C. Coulter." Geneanet provides the full name as "Sena Ann Saffold." The census variants are explained: "Ann" in 1870 captures her middle name; "Elizabeth" in 1880 is either a different enumerator's error or a nickname. Her actual name was Sena Ann Saffold.

An 1889 Brooks County sheriff sale notice (documented in HH#153's notes) lists land adjoining "John Alderman, John Coulter, Dan Alderman, and John Copland." The appearance of John Coulter alongside Alderman landholders places the Coulter and Alderman families as neighbors in Brooks County, which explains the 1881 marriage between George W. Alderman and Isabel Coulter.
