docs.title: Connections to Other Barney Families
docs.text:
George W. Alderman sits at the center of the Alderman family cluster in Barney:

  • HH#176 Jonathan Howell Alderman (Source-Researched): George is Jonathan's first child (book ID 15-2-14-1). The SAR application for Jonathan H. Alderman lists "George Washington Alderman" as a child. George's death certificate names "J H Alderman" as father and "Annie McKinney" as mother, independently confirming the identity of J.H.'s wife Amy Ann McKinney ("Annie" = diminutive of "Ann").

  • HH#177 Isaac McDaniel Turner (Source-Researched): Isaac married Nancy Ellen Alderman, George's sister (book ID 15-2-14-8, child #2). Nancy E. Alderman, age 13 in the 1880 J.H. Alderman household, is the same Nancy Ellen who married Isaac Turner. George is Isaac's brother-in-law.

  • HH#171 Mary Turner (Source-Researched): Mary's daughters Mollie and Nancy Orelia married Alderman men, creating a Turner-to-Alderman link independent of Isaac's marriage. Isaac Turner (HH#177) is Mary's son.

  • HH#175 Charlie W. Turner (Well-Researched): Charlie is Isaac's younger brother, both sons of Job and Mary A.R. Turner.

  • HH#153 Daniel Alderman (Well-Researched): This Daniel, born about 1860, is not elder Daniel Alderman (1774-1857), George Alderman's reported father. HH#153 Daniel probably belongs to the William C. → John A. branch, but the compiled genealogy calls the relevant child David Harrison. His exact relationship to George Washington remains secondary-supported and unresolved at that link.

  • HH#155 Mitchell Enoch Alderman (Source-Researched): Mitchell's death certificate names John Alderman and Susie Stevens as his parents. The compiled genealogy places John A. under William C. Alderman, making Mitchell part of a collateral branch. The exact common ancestry with George Washington remains secondary-supported rather than directly verified.

  • HH#144 Jacob Hunter Hiers (Cross-Volume, Complete Research): Phillip Hiers married Mary "Polly" Alderman, daughter of William Alderman (Col 26). This connects the Hiers family to the same Alderman network.

  • The Coulter-Alderman neighborhood: The 1889 Brooks County sheriff sale notice (documented in HH#153's notes) lists land adjoining John Coulter and John Alderman. This John Coulter is Isabel's father. The families lived near each other in Brooks County, which explains the 1881 marriage of George W. Alderman and Isabel Coulter.

docs.title: Research Notes
docs.text:
1. Marriage date conflict: The Ancestry marriage certificate image shows 4 Dec 1881. Geneanet records 24 Dec 1881. The Ancestry image is the primary source; the Geneanet date is from a community tree and may reflect a transcription error.

  2. Death date conflict (George): The death certificate gives Dec 22, 1935. FindAGrave gives Dec 21, 1935. One-day discrepancy; the death certificate is the official record.

  3. 1930 census marriage age: George's "age at first marriage" of 29 conflicts with all other evidence. The 1900 census says married 18 years (marriage ~1882, age ~18). The 1910 census says married 28 years (marriage ~1882). The actual marriage was Dec 4, 1881, when George was 17. The 1930 entry of 29 appears to be an enumerator error.

  4. Isabel's mother name variants: 1870 census "Ann," 1880 "Elizabeth," death record "Saffold," FindAGrave "Ann C. Coulter," Geneanet "Sena Ann Saffold." Resolved: her name was Sena Ann Saffold. The 1870 enumerator recorded her middle name; the 1880 "Elizabeth" is likely an error or nickname.

  5. Children count: The 1900 census records Isabel as mother of 8 children born, 6 living, but only 3 appear in census records. The other 5 children may have died young or left the household. Further research in Coffee County, where the family moved after 1910, might locate additional records.

  6. George's middle initial in 1880: The 1880 census records "George T. Alderman" rather than George W. This is likely an enumerator error, as all other records use W. or Washington.

  7. Child-count reconciliation: Isabel's 1900 census reports 8 children born and 6 living, but only Annie, Louis Cleveland, and William Brinson are documented in the current entry. Direct records are still needed for the other children or for a corrected interpretation of the 1900 child count.

  8. Adult trails for children: Louis Cleveland Alderman Sr. has a direct adult/death trail through SAR, draft, census, Find a Grave, and death-index records. William Brinson is now tied to the household through the 1910 "Brenson" child entry and later Coffee County records. Annie now has a direct Brooks County marriage record to J. Calvin McAlester / McAllister, but her later death trail remains unresolved.

docs.title: Research Status
docs.text: Source-researched, not source-exhausted. Six federal censuses (1870-1930), a marriage record, two death records, two FindAGrave memorials, and two Geneanet entries document George Washington Alderman and Isabel Coulter Alderman from childhood through death. George is confirmed as the first child of Jonathan H. Alderman (HH#176) through the book "Aldermans in America" (15-2-14-1), the SAR application of Jonathan H. Alderman (which lists George Washington Alderman as child), and the 1870/1880 censuses where George appears in J.H.'s household. The Coulter family's physical proximity to the Alderman family in Brooks County is independently corroborated by an 1889 sheriff sale notice listing land adjoining John Coulter and John Alderman. The remaining work is child-count reconciliation and direct adult/death trails for all children implied by Isabel's 1900 child count.

docs.title: Household #180: Alderman, James Carlton
docs.text: In the 1900 Barney census, this household was headed by James Alderman and included 9 people. The census summary records the head's listed occupation was Farmer, 1 spouse or marital partner, 7 child or stepchild.

docs.title: Household Snapshot
docs.text:
A good way to read this page is to start with James Alderman (age 24, born in Georgia, listed as Farmer). That placed the household in the farm economy around Barney, where land, crops, livestock, kin labor, and seasonal work shaped daily life as much as the town's railroad and stores did.

The household was not just the head's name. In 1900 it included spouse or marital partner Martha Alderman; children Enoch Alderman, Newton Alderman, Florence Alderman, Joseph Alderman, James Alderman, Brooks Alderman, and Essie Alderman. Those names are the starting point for the later family, labor, marriage, migration, and neighborhood trails below.

Every listed person in this household was reported as born in Georgia, which makes the page a local-family snapshot unless later records show movement into or out of Barney.

docs.title: Family Narrative
docs.text:
James Carlton Alderman (age unknown in 1900, Farmer) - Born 12 February 1851, Coffee County, Alabama (per Geneanet and death certificate; 1860 census says Alabama, 1870 says North Carolina, 1900 says Georgia — the weight of evidence favors Alabama) - Died 26 February 1925, Barney, Brooks County, Georgia (age 74) - Buried Sardis Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery, Berlin, Colquitt County, Georgia - Occupation: Farmer (owned farm free of mortgage in 1900; farm laborer in 1870) - 1899 newspaper context: A 14 Oct 1899 Valdosta Times article names Jim Alderman among the Barney-area farmers, providing a contemporary local reference consistent with James Carlton Alderman's 1900 farming household. - Death Certificate: Georgia (parents listed as William Alderman and Cathern Wells)

  • Father was William Alderman (1824-1864), died during the Civil War era, approximately age 40. Son of George Alderman (1797-1882) and Nancy Carlton (1803-1887) per the 1957 book Aldermans in America.
  • Mother was Catherine Wells (1821-1891). The death certificate lists her maiden name as Wells; census records showed her under the Alderman surname after marriage. She lived 27 years beyond William's death.
  • Paternal grandparents were George Alderman (1797-1882) and Nancy Carlton (1803-1887), documented in Aldermans in America as the 15-2 family line. George was born in Duplin County, North Carolina, moved to Bulloch County, Georgia in 1826, and settled near Pavo in Brooks County. Three of George's sons died in the Confederate Army.

Martha Ann Baker. - Born 20 February 1856, Palatka, Putnam County, Florida (per Geneanet; census records say Georgia; FindAGrave says Colquitt County, Georgia) - Died 27 March 1918, Colquitt County, Georgia (age 62) - Buried Sardis Primitive Baptist Church Cemetery, Berlin, Colquitt County, Georgia (same as James) - Married 7 January 1880, Colquitt County, Georgia (marriage certificate confirms; 1900 census lists marriage year as 1876, which does not match the certificate) - FindAGrave Memorial: 88925343 (via Ancestry collection 60525)

  • Father was Absalom Baker (appearing as Absolom in 1870 census, age 62). Born approximately 1808. In the 1860 census he was age 51, listed in Colquitt County with wife Martha and six children.
  • Mother was Martha Ann Mims (1831-1912). Geneanet lists her as Martha Ann "Annie" Mims. This connects the Baker family to the Mims family network documented in HH#172 and HH#173.
  • Maternal grandparents were Joseph W. Mims (1782-1870) and Elfira Martin (1793-1876).

Seven children are directly documented in the 1900 household: Enoch, Newton, Florence, Joseph, James, Brooks, and Essie. Earlier text treated Hattie and Sidney as documented children, but the June 2026 FamilySearch/Ancestry pass did not find direct records for either one. Hattie remains a Geneanet-only lead, and Sidney remains a FindAGrave-child-list lead unless a direct birth, death, burial, or census source is found.

  1. Enoch Alderman (b. 4 November 1881). Head of his own household by 1920, with James living as a widower in Enoch's home. Wife Viola Wingate; later marriage lead to Alphia Neling in 1926.
  2. Newton Alderman (25 Sep 1882-14 Oct 1966). Direct Ancestry search found 1900/1910/1920/1930/1940/1950 census leads, 1910 Brooks County marriage lead, WWI draft card naming relative Mary Alderman, Georgia Death Index, SSDI, and Find a Grave.
  3. Sidney Florence Alderman Harris (4 Dec 1883-29 Oct 1957). Married William L. Harris, 8 January 1909, Brooks County. A Georgia death record for child Thomas Jay Harris names parents William L. Harris and Florence Alderman.
  4. Joseph "Joe" Alderman (12 Jan 1885-10 Jun 1960). NUMIDENT names parents James C. Alderman and Martha A. Baker; later census/death/burial records place him in Cook County.
  5. James Alderman Jr. (6 Apr 1888-11 Dec 1977). Supported by 1900/1920/1930/1940/1950 census trail, WWI draft/service records, SSDI, Georgia death index, VA master index, and FindAGrave.
  6. Brooks Alderman (25 Dec 1891-3 Aug 1973). Direct Ancestry search found 1900/1910/1920/1940/1950 census leads, WWI draft/service records, Veterans Administration/BIRLS records, SSDI, Georgia Death Index, and Find a Grave.
  7. Essie Alderman Simmons (18 Nov 1893-31 Jul 1939). Supported by 1900/1910 census entries, Brooks County marriage to L. N. Simmons on 22 June 1916, and FindAGrave.

docs.text:
• HH#176 Jonathan Howell Alderman (Source-Researched): Jonathan H. Alderman (15-2-14 in the book) is the brother of James's father William. This makes James Carlton the nephew of Jonathan H. and places him in the Alderman founding family line.

  • HH#178 George W. Alderman (Source-Researched): George W. is the son of Jonathan H. Alderman, making him James Carlton's first cousin. George's wife Isabel Coulter and James's wife Martha Baker were neighbors in the Barney precinct.

  • HH#153 Daniel Alderman (Well-Researched): This younger Daniel, born about 1860, is not the elder Daniel Alderman (1774-1857) who was the reported father of George Alderman. HH#153 Daniel probably belongs to the separate William C. Alderman → John A. Alderman branch, but the compiled genealogy calls the relevant child David Harrison. The two Daniels must remain separate.

  • HH#155 Mitchell Enoch Alderman (Source-Researched): Mitchell's death certificate names John Alderman and Susie Stevens as his parents. The compiled genealogy places John A. under William C. Alderman, a different William from James's father. Mitchell and James belong to collateral branches of the same compiled Alderman family; the shared upper ancestry remains secondary-supported.

  • HH#144 Jacob H. Hiers (Source-Exhausted): James's sister Mary Wright Alderman (1859-1949) married into the Hiers family per the Aldermans in America book, connecting HH#180 to the Hiers household cluster.

  • HH#172 James D. Johnson / HH#173 George A. Johnson (both Source-Researched): The Mims family connection comes through Martha's mother Martha Ann "Annie" Mims. Joseph W. Mims (1782-1870), Martha's maternal grandfather, belongs to the same Mims family as Sidney L. Mims who married James C. Johnson (parents of James D. and George A. Johnson). This connects HH#180 to the Johnson-Mims line documented in HH#172 and HH#173.

docs.title: Audited family structure
docs.text:
The Alderman references in this project fall into three principal branches of the family reconstructed in Aldermans in America. The oldest links remain secondary-supported because no inspected original record yet names all of David Alderman and Jemima Hall's relevant children.

  • Daniel branch: Daniel Alderman → George Alderman → Jonathan Howell Alderman and William Alderman. Jonathan was the father of George Washington Alderman. The younger William and Catherine Wells were the parents of James Carlton Alderman.
  • Thomas branch: Thomas Alderman and reported sons James and Timothy. No direct descendant of this branch has been matched to a Barney household.
  • William C. branch: William C. Alderman → John A. Alderman → Mitchell Enoch Alderman and probably the Daniel Alderman in household #153.

The Daniel in household #153, born about 1860, was not the elder Daniel Alderman born in 1774. If the younger Daniel was John A. Alderman's son, he and Mitchell Enoch were probable half-brothers. The compiled genealogy instead calls the relevant child David Harrison, so that placement remains strong probable rather than verified.

Several references remain unplaced: the two James Alderman households in 1830, the two adult Timothy Aldermans in 1850, Susan Alderman after 1900, Hattie and a possibly duplicate Sidney in James Carlton's reported child list, the unidentified Mrs. Alderman who visited Douglas in 1908, Mrs. Mannie Alderman, Mrs. Hollis Alderman, and Frank Alderman, the informant on Mitchell's death certificate.

The full audit contains 60 controlled people or surname references. That is a research-control count, not a claim that all 60 represent separately proved individuals.

docs.title: 1908 visit to the Tomlinson family
docs.text:
A 6 September 1908 Douglas social column reported that an unnamed “Mrs. Alderman of Barney” was visiting Mrs. W. H. Tomlinson. Ancestry records identify the hostess as Sarah Jane Creed Tomlinson, wife of Elder William Henry Tomlinson. Sarah's 1880 census entry names her as the daughter of Darling Creed and Sarah Creed, and a 1849 Thomas County marriage record identifies her mother as Sarah Ann Alderman Creed.

The visit therefore had an Alderman-family context, but the article does not identify the Barney visitor or state her relationship to Sarah. Isabel “Belle” Coulter Alderman is the strongest circumstantial candidate because she later lived in Douglas. Amy Ann McKinney Alderman, Martha Ann Baker Alderman, Georgia Crosby Alderman, and several younger Barney wives also remain possible. No specific household assignment is justified yet.

Sources: The Macon Telegraph, 6 September 1908, page 6; Ancestry collections 7602:8515720, 7884:146860917, 4766:20062976, 6742:7441712, and 4766:1056782; Find a Grave memorial 33601687; research/tomlinson-alderman-ancestry-20260713.md.

docs.title: Dennis Adams: an unresolved early identity
docs.text:
Dennis Adams: an unresolved early identity¶

Dennis Adams remains a traditional early-settler candidate, but the surviving records do not support one continuous biography. At least an elder deceased landholder and later adult namesakes must be kept separate.

What the 1829 record proves¶

A Lowndes County deed transcription/locator records a conveyance to the heirs of Dennis Adams for land lot 402 in District 12 in 1829. The wording makes it strong probable that Dennis was dead by the transaction date. The original instrument has not been inspected.

The probable family¶

Cason Adams's 1911 obituary identifies his father as Dennis Adams and names Cason's siblings as Joshua, Lasa, Dennis, Caswell, Irene Dees, Sallie Rogers, Jane Dallis, and Rachel. The father in this family account and the man represented by heirs in the 1829 transcription are strong probable to be the same man, but no inspected original directly joins the obituary's child group to lot 402.

Sarah Adams appears in reconstructed tax material for lots 402 and 403 from 1830 through 1844. She is a possible-to-strong-probable wife or widow of the elder Dennis. Lasa Adams's 1852 disposal of lot 402 makes him a strong-probable son or estate successor. Both relationships remain short of verified.

Why the 1836 story fails as written¶

Huxford's retrospective account places Dennis Adams's arrival in 1836. That date cannot describe the elder Dennis personally if his heirs received land in 1829. It may refer to a younger Dennis, another family movement, or an error in the tradition.

Later Dennis Adams controls¶

Adult men named Dennis Adams appear in controlled Echols and Lowndes County transactions executed from 1861 through 1866. Some were recorded later, through 1884; those recording dates do not prove that Dennis was alive in 1883 or 1884. The records do not bridge back to the elder estate family. They are retained as separate identity controls rather than folded into one profile.

Barney connection¶

No Adams descendant line has been proved into Barney. Four Adams entries formerly generated from Barney census summaries were transcription and household-boundary errors in the 1900 and 1940 originals. The audited corpus therefore provides no verified Adams household to trace backward.

Current status¶

Traditional/unresolved. The transcription's “heirs of” wording makes it strong probable that the elder Dennis was dead by the September 12, 1829 transaction date; the original deed is uninspected. He is strong probable to be the father named in Cason Adams's obituary, while Sarah and Lasa are evidence-supported but unproved estate-family links. His parents, exact death place, complete child group, and any connection to later men named Dennis remain unresolved.

See the full Adams surname audit for the branch map and Barney census corrections.

Source notes¶

Remaining gaps¶

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
Roster status: traditional/unresolved. Huxford's claimed 1836 arrival conflicts with an 1829 deed to the heirs of a deceased Dennis Adams.

Barney relevance: none proved.

docs.title: Evidence and conflict
docs.text:
A Lowndes deed extract records David Ingram of Decatur County conveying District 12, Lot 402 to the heirs of Dennis Adams of Lowndes County on September 12, 1829, recorded December 4, 1829, in Deed Book A, p. 248. The legal description places the transaction in land later associated with Brooks County. The wording proves that one Dennis Adams was deceased by the transaction date and that the grantees were called his heirs. It does not name them or state their exact relationships.

Huxford's later roster says Dennis Adams arrived in 1836. That date cannot describe the already-deceased man represented by heirs in 1829. The roster may refer to a younger Dennis, preserve a faulty date, or conflate generations.

Numerous later deeds name a Dennis Adams in Echols and Lowndes Counties during the 1860s. Those records belong to a later adult unless an explicit bridge proves otherwise. They cannot be used to reconstruct the deceased 1829 landholder.

docs.title: Barney surname bridge test
docs.text: No Adams surname household appears in the 1900 Barney roster, and no descendant chain from the unnamed 1829 heirs to a Barney resident was found. Lot 402 is a future-Brooks geographic anchor for the estate family, not proof of influence on Barney.

docs.title: Sources and gaps
docs.text:
1. Lowndes County deed transcription/extract, David Ingram to heirs of Dennis Adams, District 12, Lot 402, September 12, 1829, Deed Book A, p. 248.
  2. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), retrospective 1836 arrival roster.
  3. Later Lowndes deed extracts for Dennis Adams, 1861–1884; retained as a separate later identity group.

The original 1829 deed, the names of the heirs, Dennis's probate, and any parent-child bridge to a later Dennis remain unlocated or uninspected.

docs.title: Edward Clinton Dukes (1810–1855)
docs.text:
Edward Clinton Dukes (1810–1855)

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Conclusion

Roster status: supplemental early settler, verified in future-Brooks territory by 1840.

Barney relevance: broader future-Brooks context. No genealogical bridge to the later Barney Dukes households is proved.

Evidence

The original 1840 population schedule names Edward C. Dukes in Grooverville, Thomas County, an area later included in Brooks County. The original 1850 Lowndes County schedule names Edward C. Dukes, age thirty-eight, Georgia-born farmer, with real estate valued at $3,000. The household includes Nancy Dukes and children beginning with Martha Ann R., Elizabeth J., Caroline C., and John W. The schedule records co-residence, not relationships.

Folks Huxford's later county history identifies Edward as Edward Clinton Dukes, born January 6, 1810, in Liberty County; husband of Nancy Hodges; son of John Taylor Dukes; and father of twelve children. Huxford also places him as militia captain in the Grooverville district in 1836–1837, justice of the peace there in 1841–1845, and justice of the peace in the 790th/Tallokas District from 1840 to 1853. These biographical and office claims are explicit but remain secondary-supported unless the underlying commissions and family records are inspected.

Edward Clinton must remain separate from his son Edward Taylor Dukes (1846–1920). Probate material concerning the E. C./Edmund Dukes estate names orphan children and guardians, but it does not connect the estate family to Eli and Hulda Dukes or to Frances Dukes in the later Barney census.

Two-direction Barney bridge test

The early line was traced forward through Huxford's reported children and the preserved E. C./Edmund estate group. The Barney surname occurrences were traced backward from Eli and Hulda Dukes and from Frances Dukes, mother of Hannah Dukes Sanders. No parent-child chain reaches Edward Clinton. Eli and Hulda were Black landholding farmers, and the inspected probate instruments for the white E. C./Edmund family do not name them. A biological, formerly enslaved, labor, or surname-association relationship is possible but unproved.

Sources and gaps

  1. 1840 U.S. census, Grooverville, Thomas County, Georgia, p. 301, Edward C. Dukes household; preserved original image 4411224_00620.
  2. 1850 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, Division 53, dwelling/family 61, Edward C. Dukes household; preserved original image 4193244-00463.
  3. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), Dukes sketch, pp. 451–453.
  4. Brooks County probate records cited on the Eli Dukes household page; those instruments distinguish the E. C./Edmund estate group but state no connection to Eli or Hulda.

The original office commissions, marriage record, and a complete probate distribution remain uninspected.

docs.title: Thirteenth early-settler cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover Edward Clinton Dukes, Mills or Miles M. Brinson, Dennis Adams, Jacob Bryan, and the unresolved Joseph Kinsley/John Kinsey identity. Edward Dukes is verified in future-Brooks territory. The other profiles preserve geographic or identity limits rather than treating countywide office, Lowndes residence, or similar names as proof of future-Brooks settlement.

The update also corrects two traditional claims: a 1829 deed to Dennis Adams's heirs conflicts with his reported 1836 arrival, and the 1829 officer and land records name John Kinsey rather than Joseph Kinsley. No direct Barney family bridge is proved for this cohort.

docs.title: Full Alderman surname audit
docs.text:
The Alderman family page and the Barney household profiles for Mitchell Enoch, Jonathan Howell, George Washington, and James Carlton Alderman now reflect a 60-reference surname audit. The revised family map separates the Daniel-to-George, Thomas, and William C.-to-John A. branches and keeps unresolved people and name variants unplaced.

The audit corrects two older conflations. The Daniel Alderman in household #153, born about 1860, was not James Carlton Alderman's great-grandfather; that ancestor was the elder Daniel Alderman born in 1774. If the younger Daniel was John A. Alderman's son, Daniel and Mitchell Enoch were probable half-brothers, not half-uncle and nephew. Their shared upper ancestry with the other Barney Alderman branches remains secondary-supported because it still depends on the 1957 compilation Aldermans in America.

docs.title: Eleventh early-settler cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover Henry Dean, John Dean, James E. Hendry, Thomas Carlton, and William Holloway Jr. Dean, Carlton, and Holloway belong to the broader future-Brooks context. The profiles preserve unresolved spouse, child, land, and namesake questions.

James E. Hendry has a secondary-supported family bridge to Norman Campbell Hendry and the later railroad-era Brooks network. The James-to-Neal sibling link rests on compiled Hendry family history, while Neal-to-Norman is verified by Norman's death certificate and census household evidence. No genealogical bridge is proved to the later Black Hendry or Henry households enumerated at Barney.

docs.title: Cornelius English descendant bridge
docs.text:
One new evidence-graded profile

A new Cornelius English profile follows the best-supported line through Matthew Joseph English and John Cornelius English to Andrew James English, the later Barney railroad agent. Census and parent records support the later generations. The Cornelius-to-Matthew link remains secondary-supported because no inspected original record names Matthew as the son of Cornelius and Abigail Allbritton, and the two 1840 Cornelius households remain unseparated.

docs.title: Ninth early-settler cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover William Jones, Fleming Bates, William McMullen, James McMullen Jr., and James Burnett. Jones, Bates, and the McMullens are classified in the broader future-Brooks context. Burnett remains a traditional unresolved candidate because the 1829 James S. Burnett record cannot be joined safely to the later James H. Burnett household claim.

The William Jones profile also records the dedicated Barney-family test. The documented line descends through Thomas Jones and Malachi Jones; no relationship between that family and the Lowndes William Jones has been proved.

docs.title: Eighth early-settler cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover John O’Steen, James T. Robeson, Ivy Simmons, Ezekiel Selph, and Elias Roberts. O’Steen, Robeson, Simmons, and Selph are classified as broader future-Brooks settlers. Roberts remains a traditional candidate because no contemporary record yet places him securely in the future county.

The profiles preserve the unresolved points, including the separate John H. O’Steen identity, conflicting Simmons migration dates, two generations of Ezekiel Selph, and the unproved Tallokas connection for Elias Roberts.

docs.title: Early History profiles reorganized by Barney relevance
docs.text:
The 67 Early History profiles are now divided into three evidence-based groups: 20 people with direct Barney-area influence or a documented family or settlement bridge, 36 broader future-Brooks settlers, and 11 traditional or unresolved candidates.

Every entry now separates roster status from Barney relevance. This preserves the wider county history without implying that every regional settler lived at Barney or influenced the town directly.

docs.title: Seventh early-settler cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover James Newton, James Rowell, Jeremiah Wilson Sr., Henry Rowell, and William Newton. An original 1828 deed verifies James Rowell's ownership of District 12, Lot 393. The original 1836 militia return places Henry Rowell in the 659th District, while the 1850 census anchors the later James and William Newton households. Jeremiah Wilson's District 12 deeds and later survey work establish his future-Brooks record.

The profiles preserve the unresolved points. Neither of the two 1830 Thomas County William Newton households can yet be assigned safely to the later Lowndes man. James and Henry Rowell are not treated as relatives, Cyntha Rowell's relationship to Henry remains unknown, and the traditional Newton and Wilson arrival dates remain secondary rather than verified.

docs.title: Sixth early-settler cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover Simpson Strickland, Melus or Milus Thigpen, James McLeod, Alexander Campbell, and John Lawson. An original 1826 deed verifies Simpson and Thigpen in Lowndes County and places Simpson with Simeon Strickland. A fresh census search supplies a 1830 Lowndes locator for James McLeod, while a contemporary-record transcription and an 1840 census locator strengthen John Lawson's civil identity. Alexander Campbell's indexed census trail extends from 1830 through 1850.

The profiles keep later family and institutional claims qualified. Simpson's kinship to Simeon and Archibald, Thigpen's church and family history, McLeod's commission and Bethlehem roles, Campbell's wife and daughter relationships, and Lawson's family and Barney-district land remain secondary-supported until parent-naming, deed, probate, church, or other original records are inspected.

docs.title: Hall family identity and parentage update
docs.text:
Four evidence-based profile revisions

The John Hall profile now separates John Hall Sr. from John Hall Jr. The older man is documented as Morven postmaster and at District 12, Lot 270; the younger man's 1840–1870 household chain makes him William M. Hall's strong-probable father. Francis Pearson Hall's 1938 death certificate identifies John Jr.'s later wife as Elizabeth Easter and verifies her as Francis's mother. Her age and the earlier household structure show that she was William's probable stepmother, while William's biological mother remains unresolved.

William M. Hall's Barney household page now incorporates the original 1870 marriage return, Serena Hires Hall's duplicate 1870 enumeration beside her parents, and all three pages of William's 1907 pension packet. The pension confirms his service history, residence, occupation, poverty, and disabilities but names no parents. The William G. Hall page now explains why his 1840s ownership of Lots 132–133 prevents the later “heirs of John Hall” deed from being assigned safely without the original instrument and title chain. Sion Hall's page treats John Sr. as his secondary-supported probable brother, based on a later obituary rather than original parentage proof.

docs.title: Fifth early-settler cohort and Yates–Hiers update
docs.text:
Six new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover Jared Johnson, William Hancock, William G. Hunter, Ashley Lawson, William Yates, and Rebecca Yates Hiers. The Johnson page corrects a former 1830 census attribution: the household head was Jared Singleton. Hancock’s first-sheriff identification remains strong secondary evidence because the original election and census records have not been inspected. Hunter and Lawson are anchored in the future-Brooks area by land, militia, church, and public records with their unresolved family claims kept qualified.

Original deeds correct the Yates–Hiers land record. Owen Yates sold David Hiers about 580 acres in 1864. David’s later conveyance to Rebecca was one $2,500 deed dated October 27, 1875—not four deeds dated October 7—and covered about 545 acres. William Yates’s 1874 inventory was valued at $12,073.80. Estate vouchers document purchases for Mrs. and Miss Hiers and a $1,496.96 debt to David Hiers, but no heir list or parent-naming statement identifies Rebecca as William’s daughter. That relationship remains strong probable, while Rebecca’s 1900 residence with son Sim Hires in Barney and her daughter Nancy’s marriage to Joseph J. Rogers are documented.

docs.title: Joshua and David Platt family evidence
docs.text:
Two evidence-based profile revisions

A 2006 compiled genealogy identifies David Platt as a son of Rev. Joshua Platt and Amy Newell. David's 1818 Bulloch County marriage and the two men's appearances on the same 1820 Bulloch census page and later in Lowndes County support the chronology and migration. No inspected original record names David's parents, so both profiles grade the relationship as secondary-supported rather than verified.

docs.title: Priscilla Folsom and Rogers evidence update
docs.text:
One new profile and five evidence-based revisions

A new Priscilla Jane Folsom profile follows her from the 1850 Lowndes household through her 1900 widowed household in Quitman. An 1861 deed-index entry verifies her full married name and independent Brooks County landholding. The page identifies her as Israel Lee Folsom’s verified mother while keeping Rogers as a secondary-supported maiden surname and her exact birth and death dates unresolved.

The Ebenezer and Israel Lee Folsom pages now reflect that distinction. The Uriah Rogers, Thomas F. Rogers, and Joseph J. Rogers pages incorporate the inspected deeds, estate records, marriage, and guardianship evidence without treating land associations as kinship. No inspected record connects Priscilla or Joseph’s branch to the James–Thomas–Isaac Rogers group.

docs.title: Rogers, Hall, Platt, and Strickland cohort
docs.text:
Five new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover Uriah Rogers, John Hall, David Platt, Simeon Strickland, and Archibald Strickland. Original records place Uriah in the future-Brooks area by 1844, John in the 660th District in 1836, and David in Lowndes County in 1830. David’s precise future-Brooks location remains unproved.

The Strickland profiles incorporate the authenticated deed and census follow-up. An 1826 Lowndes deed verifies that Simpson and Simeon Strickland witnessed the same transaction, while a later affidavit records Simpson’s knowledge of Simeon’s signature. A secondary local history identifies them as brothers and sons of Archibald and Luander Strickland; Archibald’s 1820 household fits that reconstruction, but no inspected original record names the relationship. No canonical Barney census household is presently connected to Simpson or Simeon.

docs.title: Folsom household cohort and Thomas F. Rogers
docs.text:
Seven new evidence-graded profiles

New profiles cover John, Elijah, Pennywell, pioneer Israel, Thomas, and Ebenezer Folsom, together with Thomas F. Rogers. The update corrects Pennywell’s death to July 15, 1836, removes the unsupported claim that he was Lawrence Folsom’s son, and identifies his reported sibling relationship to Elizabeth Folsom as secondary-supported. Pioneer Israel remains separate from Israel Lee Folsom of Barney. Ebenezer’s household chain supplies the collateral bridge between them.

The original 1844 Lowndes tax digest verifies Thomas F. Rogers with 163 acres in District 12, Land Lot 199. James Rogers returned another 163 acres in the same lot, and Uriah Rogers appears on the following line. The cluster and Thomas’s 1859 deed to Ebenezer Folsom strengthen a Rogers association, but they do not establish Priscilla Jane Folsom’s parents or exact relationship to the three men.

The John and James Groover profiles now explain the family's collateral connection to Barney. Compiled Groover family evidence places Sarah Reiser Groover as a daughter of Charles Groover, the reported brother of John Sr.; a 1913 biographical sketch names Sarah as the mother of M. Franklin Jones. The Jones chain into Barney is well documented, while Sarah's parentage and the older Groover sibling link remain identified as strong secondary evidence.

Five new early-settler profiles examine John Groover Sr., James Groover, Canneth or Kenneth Swain, Morgan G. Swain, and Matthew Allbritton. The original 1830 census verifies the Groover and Allbritton county residences described in their profiles. Conflicting arrival dates, same-name households, the Canneth/Kenneth identity, Morgan's parentage and early land, and every claimed direct connection to Barney remain qualified where the surviving records do not settle them.

docs.title: Seventeen early-settler profiles reviewed
docs.text:
Three five-person reviews and a two-subject follow-up cover George Alderman, Nathan Gornto, Drewry Vickers, Sion Hall, William Blair, William Alderman, Ely Webb, Joel Gornto, Alfred Belote, Willis King, Daniel McCranie Sr., Francis Rountree, Washington Joyce, Abraham Hunter, William Smith, the Jose/Joe Bryant–John Bryan identity question, and William G. Hall. The revised profiles separate original records from later tradition and state plainly when an arrival date, family relationship, land claim, or direct connection to Barney remains unproved.

The latest additions document William Alderman in Lowndes County by 1833, Joel Gornto’s 1836 militia office and 1860 probate, and Alfred Belote’s census and land-tax trail. They also treat Ely Webb’s relationship to Malinda Webb Chambers as strong probable and Willis King’s reported 1823 move as a relocation theory rather than his first arrival in the county.

The third review confirms that Daniel McCranie Sr., Francis Rountree, Washington Joyce, and William Smith already have publication-ready profiles. A new Abraham Hunter profile follows his probable move from Screven County to Lowndes County after 1830 and explains why the surviving chronology conflicts with the traditional 1823 settlement date.

The follow-up revises the Jose Bryant page without merging Jose or Joe with John Bryan. It adds John’s reconstructed District 12 deed locators while explaining why the apparent 1824 instrument is not yet verified residence evidence. A new William G. Hall profile documents his 1830–1844 tax trail, Mount Zion trusteeship, and 1836 militia office. Hall’s reported 1824–1825 arrival and any direct residence in Barney remain unproved.

docs.title: Amos Emanuel and the proposed Little River ferry
docs.text:
New profile

A new Amos Emanuel profile brings together the 1827 ferry bill, Senate vote, census trail, Lowndes County tax entry, 1838 militia record, and later Ware County household. The page does not call him a verified ferry operator: the bill is absent from the published session laws, no record proves that the ferry opened, and Emanuel's land has not been tied to Miller Bridge, Folsom Bridge, or another crossing. It also identifies “Amos Enoch Emanuel” and “Martha Elizabeth Jones” as unverified names found in public family trees.

docs.title: William and Elizabeth Folsom original deeds
docs.text:
Expanded original-record profile

The William Folsom dossier now incorporates four administrator's deeds proving at least 2,080 acres in his estate. The deeds identify District 9 Land Lots 492, 519, and 521, 120 acres of Lot 491, and District 12 Lot 323, together with the purchasers and auction prices. A separate executor's deed records Elizabeth Folsom's conveyance of District 9 Lots 493 and 520 to her daughter Edith Rountree. The Early Settlers and Folsom family pages now explain how these land transfers and Elizabeth's will connect the Folsom, Ryall, Rountree, and Perry families north of Barney. William's acquisition deeds, complete acreage, and the original 1867 road record remain unresolved.

docs.title: Wider early-settler verification
docs.text:
Research update

The Early Settlers section now reports the results of an independent review of eighty additional roster names. A digitized 1836 Lowndes County general-militia return supplies narrow district and rank evidence for fourteen named men, while federal official registers place Hamilton W. Sharpe at Sharpe's Store by 1829. The update also states what the review did not prove: no newly inspected census image verified a named household from the wider roster, and traditional arrival dates remain attributed to their retrospective sources.

The review preserved identity safeguards for same-name people and separate generations. It did not promote possible matches, surname associations, or reel-level census references into verified biographies.

docs.title: Expanded early-settler descendant crosswalk
docs.text:
New family connections

The Families & Connections section now documents 22 residents of the 1900 Barney census through 29 graded paths to eight early settlers. New pages establish three qualified George Alderman lines and two Joel Gornto lines. The Swain and Strickland proposals remain under research: an 1858 guardianship record supports Thomas E. B. Swain as Stephen Swain's father, but the Morgan G. Swain generation remains unproved, and no reviewed record connects Stephen Smith Strickland to the earlier regional Strickland families.

docs.title: Folsom settler-descendant link
docs.text:
New family connection

Jeremiah Walton Folsom's dossier now traces his reported line to early settler Lawrence Folsom and links to the Lawrence and William Folsom dossiers. The page separates the census-supported father-son relationship from the earlier generations supplied by compiled genealogy, for which no parent-naming original has been reviewed at every step.

docs.title: FamilySearch review of eleven contemporary-report identities
docs.text:
Research correction

An authenticated FamilySearch review verified Rev. J. W. Folsom as Jeremiah Walton Folsom through Brooks County census and voter records. It also established the broader civil record of county coroner E. D. Ponder and found his exact-name Confederate pension index. Jesse Chambers received an independent Brooks County voter-registration bridge. Eight other identities remain possible because no record securely joined them to the Barney reports.

docs.title: Contemporary-report dossiers and military review
docs.text:
New research

The 1900 census page now links individual dossiers for all 15 people whose identities are verified or strong probable. Possible and unresolved identities remain unlinked. A military-record audit also corrected Joseph J. Oglesby's status: near-contemporary and county-history accounts establish his Confederate service, although his detailed company, rank, and Macon shop assignment still await original military records.

docs.title: Original-record research on unresolved contemporary-report names
docs.text:
Research correction

Original-record searches strengthen two identities. The 1901 inquest juror J. W. Kendrick is probably Jason W. Kendrick of Brooks County, and the 1899 teacher Minnie McKinnon is probably Minnie A. McKinnon of Hahira. Eighteen names remain unresolved after census, marriage, tax, court, school, business, newspaper, and military checks. The revised table records the strongest available finding without assigning same-name records that lack a Barney connection.

docs.title: Joyce and Culbreth second-round research
docs.text:
Research correction

New census, cemetery, and military records strengthen Janie Joyce as a daughter of John Wesley P. Joyce and verify Minnie Adelia Culbreth as Blackman Hawley Culbreth's daughter. They also correct Blackman's birth year to 1847 and establish his Confederate service in North Carolina units.

docs.title: Hall cluster second-round research
docs.text:
Research correction

A second review separated the Hall references into at least two families. Mrs. J. B. Hall is now verified as Lula S. Collingsworth Hall. The 1899 merchant belongs to the older household-1 J. F. Hall family, while the railroad conductor remains unresolved. Frank Henry Hall is the leading candidate for the early merchant Frank Hall, but direct Barney business evidence has not been found. Mrs. Frank Hall and the 1901 juror George P. Hall remain unresolved. No Hall military service was proved.

docs.title: Contemporary reports reconciliation
docs.text:
Research correction

The 44 people named in contemporary reports but previously left unmatched were reviewed individually. The revised census page now distinguishes verified, strong probable, possible, and unresolved identities and explains which people lived outside the Barney district or died before the census. Later military follow-up established Confederate service for Blackman Hawley Culbreth and Joseph J. Oglesby.

docs.title: Hope and Jack Croft dossiers
docs.text:
New research

The Hope Croft dossier brings together the 1887 Stonewall Academy reports, the community resolution requiring the Croft family to leave, census evidence for Hope's likely identity as Abba or Abner Croft, his probable adult record as George A. Croft, and the younger namesake killed near Barney in 1922. The proposed connection to the 1885–1886 Morven-area fires remains unproved.

The revised Jacob Henry “Jack” Croft dossier covers his family, Confederate service and amputation, Brooks County farm, Land Lot 227 conveyance, removal from the community, second marriage, later life, and estate. It also corrects the geography: Croft's tract belonged to the Morven district during his residence, before the McNeil & Rozier company village developed there.

docs.title: Initial website release
docs.text:
Site update

The first public edition was published at barneyga.com. Research currently extends through 1910, with later material included where it helps explain Barney's roads, bridges, railroads, and community sites.

The launch edition included:

  • New research: expanded accounts of early settlement, Mount Zion, county formation, early roads, Folsom Bridge, and the communities along Little River.
  • New research: separate histories of the South Georgia Railway, the Tallokas-to-Barney tram, the Valdosta, Moultrie and Western, and the proposed Georgia, Alabama and Western Railroad.
  • New research: reorganized coverage of Barney before incorporation, the 1903 charter, early municipal government, commerce, postal service, community life, and public order.
  • Correction: the earlier 1910 census totals were withdrawn after a systematic extraction error was identified. Household information is used only where it has been checked, and a page-by-page reconstruction is underway.
  • New images: historical maps, photographs, restored images, and clearly labeled AI-generated reconstructions were added throughout the site.

docs.title: William E. Dean - Early Families of Barney, Georgia
docs.text: William E. Dean ¶ Back to the Early History Profiles index Decision ¶ Supplemental Brooks-area settler with a strong-probable family bridge to Barney. The 1860 Brooks County census places Robert Dean, age 10, in William E. Dean's household. A later Dry Lake tax record lists Robert D. Deen directly below William E., and R. D. Dean married Martha J. Gornto in Brooks County in 1880. Robert later headed Barney household #95. Family and identity ¶ The combined age, place, tax, and marriage evidence makes William E. Dean Robert's strong-probable father. The relationship is not verified: the 1860 census has no relationship column, and no probate, death certificate, Bible, deed, or guardianship record names William as Robert's father. The 1870 household requires separate treatment. The young man recorded with William and Dillilah or Delilah Dean is Daniel Dean , age 19, not Robert. Daniel may have been Robert under another given name, a brother, or another relative. The record does not prove Robert Daniel Dean , so Daniel remains unplaced. William E. Dean is also kept separate from the earlier Henry Dean and John Dean. No evidence reviewed proves that the three men were related. Barney bridge ¶ Strong probable family bridge: William E. Dean → Robert Dean → Robert and Martha Dean's 1900 Barney household. Robert and Martha's verified household included Anna, Katie, Ida, and William. Martha, Ida, and William remained together at Barney in 1910. The Robert D. Deen who lived with Eliza in Florida in 1910 is not treated as the same man; his age and reported first marriage conflict with the Barney record. Remaining work ¶ Find a parent-naming record for Robert or Daniel. Identify Dillilah or Delilah's maiden name. Locate William's death and estate records. Determine whether Daniel and Robert were the same person or separate relatives. Test any new evidence connecting William to Henry or John Dean. Sources ¶ 1860 U.S. census, Brooks County, Georgia, William E. Dean household, including Robert Dean, age 10; Ancestry collection 7667, record 10755406, image 4211371_00055 . 1870 U.S. census, Nankin district, Brooks County, Georgia, William and Dillilah Dean cluster, including Daniel Dean, age 19; Ancestry collection 7163, record 3670229, image 4263363_00016 . Brooks County tax digest, Dry Lake district, volume covering 1872–1877, Deen Robert D. directly below Deen Wm E. ; Ancestry collection 1729, record 2724864, image 40141_1220705227_0748-00445 . Brooks County marriage return, R. D. Dean and M. J. Gornto, married December 16, 1880; Ancestry collection 4766, record 184569, image 40951_294515-00633 . 1900 U.S. census, Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, Robert and Martha Dean household #95. 1910 U.S. census, Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, Martha J. Dean household.

docs.title: Zachariah Fletcher - Early Families of Barney, Georgia
docs.text: Zachariah Fletcher ¶ Back to the Early History Profiles index Decision ¶ Supplemental early settler, verified in the future-Brooks 660th District by 1836. The original Lowndes County militia return names Zachariah Fletcher as a private in that district. The return establishes his district association; it does not prove active Creek War service. Land and family ¶ An 1846 deed involving District 12, Land Lot 244 names Mary Fletcher as Zachariah's wife. An 1850 deed concerning District 11, Lot 297 explicitly identifies A. Z. DeKalb Fletcher, Samuel Fletcher, and Jeremiah Fletcher as his sons. The second tract lay outside the future-Brooks area, but its relationship language makes it important family evidence. Compiled genealogies also assign William Lofton Fletcher and John Wesley Fletcher to Zachariah and Mary. Those additional parent-child claims remain secondary-supported because no inspected original record names them as sons. The surviving 1840 census locator is compatible with Zachariah, but the handwritten row has not received a controlling independent transcription. A former 1850 candidate is not used as evidence because the surname may read Frederick rather than Fletcher. Barney connection ¶ No descendant bridge to Barney has been proved. Cleve Fletcher, a Black lodger enumerated at Barney in 1910, cannot be connected to Zachariah's white antebellum household or to the three sons named in the 1850 deed. The shared surname alone is not evidence of kinship. Sources ¶ Lowndes County general-militia return, 660th District, 1836; Valdosta State University Archives, item 10428/1219. Lowndes County deed extract, Book E, p. 108, October 22, 1846, Zachariah and Mary Fletcher, District 12, Lot 244. Lowndes County deed extract, Book C, p. 635, April 21, 1850, naming A. Z. DeKalb, Samuel, and Jeremiah Fletcher as Zachariah Fletcher's sons. 1840 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, preserved household locator; Ancestry image 4411334_00481 . 1910 U.S. census, Barney, Brooks County, Georgia, Cleve Fletcher entry.

docs.title: Angus Morrison - Early Families of Barney, Georgia
docs.text: Angus Morrison ¶ Back to the Early History Profiles index Decision ¶ Supplemental future-Brooks settler with a documented place-based connection to Barney. Angus Morrison, born about 1819, later served as Brooks County's first ordinary in 1858–1859 and returned to the office in later terms. Compiled county history identifies him as the son of Daniel Morrison and Catherine McCrimmon and the husband of Louisa Pike. Those family relationships remain secondary-supported. The traditional claim that Angus arrived as a teacher in 1834 is retrospective and unusually early: he would have been about fourteen. It should not be treated as a verified arrival date. Compiled land history places him on District 12, Lot 362, but the underlying deed has not been inspected. The Morrison home at Barney ¶ A June 25, 1937, Valdosta Daily Times article places the old Angus Morrison home at Barney. William Arthur Webb and Mary Morrison returned there for their fiftieth wedding anniversary, held in the room where they had married. The paper described the house as nearly a century old, built from hand-hewn timbers, and occupied in 1937 by Daniel A. Morrison. The newspaper directly establishes the historic home's Barney location and identifies Mary Morrison Webb. It does not state Mary's exact relationship to the pioneer Angus. The place connection is therefore verified, while the complete family descent through Mary and Daniel A. remains secondary-supported. Identity cautions ¶ Later records name Angus Morrison Jr. and other men of the same name. A 1913 deed cannot be assigned to the 1819–1873 pioneer. Catherine's reported maiden surname McCrimmon is also kept separate from McCranie. Sources ¶ Valdosta Daily Times , June 25, 1937, p. 8, report of the Webb anniversary and Morrison reunion at the old Angus Morrison home; Newspapers.com image 890575852 . Folks Huxford, compiled Morrison family sketch and Brooks County settlement account, pp. 507–509. Brooks County officer summaries identifying Angus Morrison's service as ordinary beginning in 1858.

docs.title: Nathan Hodges - Early Families of Barney, Georgia
docs.text:
Nathan Hodges¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision¶

Nathan Hodges was a qualified supplemental early settler. The original 1830 Lowndes schedule contains a household head read or indexed as Nathan Hoages, with Hodges supplied as an alternate. The county, page, and row are secure, but the surname still warrants a second handwriting review.

Collateral bridge to Barney¶

Huxford's compiled Hodges genealogy identifies Nathaniel Hodges and Joseph Hodges as sons of Joshua Hodges and Ann Raiford. The same reconstruction identifies James Carr Hodges as Joseph's son. James's strong-probable son Robertson or Robinson L. Hodges later headed Barney household #8.

Under that reconstruction, Nathan was Joseph's brother and James Carr's uncle—not James's father or a direct ancestor of Robinson. This is a secondary-supported collateral bridge. No inspected probate, Bible, deed, or comparable parent-naming original verifies the Joshua-to-Nathan-and-Joseph generation.

Huxford also identifies Martha Whittington as Nathaniel's wife. That relationship remains secondary-supported. The traditional 1828 arrival date is retrospective and unverified.

Sources¶

  • 1830 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Nathan Hoages/Hodges household.
  • Folks Huxford, early-settler roster and compiled Hodges family sketches.
  • 1850 U.S. census, Lowndes County, James C. Hodges household.
  • 1860 U.S. census, Brooks County, J. C. Hodges household.
  • 1900 U.S. census, Barney, Brooks County, Robinson L. Hodges household #8.

docs.title: James C. Hodges - Early Families of Barney, Georgia
docs.text:
James C. “James Carr” Hodges¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision¶

James C. Hodges was a verified supplemental early settler with a strong-probable descendant bridge to Barney. The 1840 and 1850 Lowndes censuses anchor his household, and an 1859 deed-index entry places him in District 12. His reported 1838 arrival remains retrospective.

Family¶

The 1850 household included Sarah A. Hodges and Lafayette, Adeline, Robertson, Joseph J., Mary, Margaret, and Martha. The census did not state relationships. Huxford's compiled family sketch identifies James as James Carr Hodges and Sarah as Sarah Ann Newton.

The 1850 and 1860 censuses place Robertson or Robinson L. Hodges in James's continuing household. Huxford explicitly calls Robinson their son. The census continuity makes James Carr → Robinson L. strong probable, although no inspected original parent-naming record states the relationship.

Barney bridge¶

Robinson married Mary J. Stephens in 1861 and later headed Barney household #8. Their household is documented through the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses. Their son Joseph E. continued at Barney in 1910 as Joe E. Hodges with wife Lola and children Roddie, Vida, and Thomas J.

The compiled upper genealogy places James under Joseph Hodges and makes Nathaniel Hodges Joseph's brother. That collateral Nathan-to-Barney bridge is secondary-supported, not original-record verified.

Sources¶

  • 1840 and 1850 U.S. censuses, Lowndes County, James C. Hodges households.
  • Brooks County deed index, 1859, James C. Hodges, District 12 land.
  • 1860 U.S. census, Brooks County, J. C. Hodges household.
  • Brooks County marriage record, Robinson Hodges and Mary J. Stephens, January 22, 1861.
  • 1900 U.S. census, Barney household #8; 1910 U.S. census, Barney Hodges households.
  • Folks Huxford, compiled Hodges family sketches.

docs.title: Elijah Folsom
docs.text:
Elijah Folsom¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision¶

Elijah Folsom remains a traditional early-settler candidate. Folks Huxford included him among people who came to the territory of present Brooks County in 1824 or 1825, but no contemporary record inspected for this profile confirms that date or identifies his home within old Lowndes County.

Family tradition¶

Elizabeth Knowles Folsom's 1938 genealogy identifies Elijah as a son of Lawrence Armstrong and Rachel Vickers Folsom. It says he married Nancy Morrison, moved to Florida, and had children named Green, Martha, Jackson, Elizabeth, Macon, and Elijah. The account is useful as a research lead, but no inspected marriage, census, deed, probate, or death record proves the reconstruction or distinguishes every member of the family from same-name people.

The younger Elijah whom the genealogy lists as a son must remain separate from the proposed pioneer. A much later Elijah identified as the father of Ella Dee Folsom also belongs to another generation.

The wider Folsom surname audit also tested Elijah's proposed family against the documented Barney branches. Elijah's forward line stops at the unproved six-child group. The documented Barney surname branch runs backward through Priscilla Jane and Israel Lee Folsom, while separate William-and-Elizabeth descendants reach Barney through Ryall, Rountree, Joyce, Pounds, Ingram, and Jones families. No reviewed record joins either branch to Elijah generation by generation.

Unsupported lottery claim¶

An older site draft stated that Elijah drew Lot 255 in the 8th District of Carroll County in the 1832 Georgia Land Lottery. No page, draw, residence, or stable record locator has been recovered, and no evidence ties that drawer to this Elijah. The assertion is not used here as proof of his residence, migration, family, or landholding.

Evidence status¶

  • Secondary-supported tradition: the 1824–1825 arrival; Lawrence and Rachel as parents; Nancy Morrison as wife; the six-child list; and a later move to Florida.
  • Unresolved: the original household, exact land, family links, Florida destination, death, burial, and any direct Barney connection.
  • Rejected as current evidence: the unlocated 1832 Carroll County Lot 255 assertion.

Sources¶

  1. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), chapter 4, pp. 29–33.
  2. Elizabeth Knowles Folsom, Genealogy of the Folsom Family, rev. ed., vol. 2 (1938), printed pp. 867 and 872, Internet Archive scan.

docs.title: Thomas S. Swain
docs.text:
Thomas S. Swain¶

Thomas S. Swain was a Telfair County public official, road superintendent, ferry proprietor, surveyor, livestock owner, and enslaver. Georgia's official 1823 report identifies him as one of the two men appointed to supervise the Alapaha-to-Florida road that became the southern part of Coffee Road. He spent his later years at Jacksonville on the Ocmulgee River and died in 1840.[1][2]

Swain left a thinner paper trail than his fellow superintendent, General John Coffee. No personal correspondence, will, obituary, military record, or authenticated portrait was located online. Even so, official reports, statutes, newspapers, census material, estate notices, and a photographed grave marker allow much of his public and economic life to be reconstructed. They also show where the record stops.

Identity¶

The road superintendent was Thomas S. Swain of Telfair County. The controlling evidence is Georgia's 1823 legislative report, which says an executive order of December 24, 1822 appointed "General John Coffee and Thomas S. Swain Esqrs. of the county of Telfair" to superintend the road.[1]

Later records follow the same man through a distinctive combination of name and place. Georgia authorized Thomas S. Swain to establish an Ocmulgee River ferry on his own land opposite Jacksonville in 1831. A sheriff's notice records a judgment in his favor in 1838. Estate notices then identify Thomas S. Swain as a deceased Jacksonville resident with Ocmulgee land and property spread across Telfair and Irwin counties.[5][8][9]

The evidence does not support merging every Thomas Swain in early Georgia with him. A later Telfair debtor of that name was alive in 1856, sixteen years after this man's estate opened. An Emanuel County legislator listed only as "Swain" in 1827 has not been identified. Canneth or Caneth Swain of Thomas County was a different man; the later Kenneth form remains an unresolved possible match for Canneth.[17][18]

Relationship to the Thomas County Swains¶

No inspected record proves a family connection between Thomas S. Swain and Canneth or Caneth Swain. One compiled reconstruction would make them first cousins: Thomas as a son of Job Swain, Canneth as a son of an older Stephen Swain, and Job and Stephen as brothers in Richard Swain's family. That is possible, secondary-supported theory—not a documented pedigree. The required Thomas-to-Job and Canneth-to-Stephen links lack inspected parent-naming originals, and compiled accounts conflict over the identity of Canneth's proposed father.[13][21]

The later Barney branch can be followed back with confidence only to Thomas E. B. Swain's minor son Stephen M., named in a located 1858 guardianship entry. Identifying that minor as Barney's Stephen W. Swain is strong probable despite a middle-initial conflict. The next generation is only possible, and no inspected record joins the Barney branch to Thomas S., Canneth, or Morgan G. Swain.[22]

Birth, migration, and family¶

A modern grave memorial with a photographed marker gives Swain's life dates as 1784 to 1840. The marker establishes the traditional birth year, but no birth, baptism, family Bible, or other contemporary birth record was located. A FamilySearch profile places his birth in Bertie County, North Carolina, and names Job Swain and Susanna Smith as his parents. The public sources attached to that profile do not prove either claim, so his birthplace and parents remain unresolved.[12][13]

Julian Williams's Jacksonville history says Swain came from Warren County, Georgia, about 1808. That account was written long after the event and no migration deed or tax sequence was found online. It is useful local history, not direct proof.[14]

Rebecca Swain served with Mitchell G. Willcox as administrator of Thomas's estate from 1840 into the 1840s. Family and cemetery sources identify her as Rebecca Pridgen, his wife, who lived about 1795 to 1865. No marriage entry was inspected. The relationship is strongly supported by the combined estate, family, and cemetery evidence, but the contemporary notices call her administratrix rather than widow.[9][12][15]

The number of their children is not settled. A Telfair County family history says Thomas and Rebecca had six. The current FamilySearch tree attaches seven. Susannah, Martha, Elizabeth, and Mark have the strongest support from family histories, marriage indexing, linked memorials, and their placement with the family. Thomas Jr., Stephen, and Josiah appear in the online tree but were not tied to Thomas by an original record inspected for this project. A complete child list should wait for the probate distribution, family Bible, or comparable record.[12][13][15]

Telfair County public service¶

Swain held county office before the road project. An official resolution approved December 7, 1812 appointed Thomas Swain a justice of the Telfair County Inferior Court, replacing one removed justice and one who had resigned. Inferior Court justices handled county judicial and administrative business, including roads, ferries, estates, and local government.[3]

The name, county, public standing, and chronology fit the later road superintendent. Because the 1812 resolution omits the middle initial, it is best read as very strong identity evidence rather than an entirely self-proving link.

A local history also places Swain on the Telfair Inferior Court in 1814 and says he later conveyed Jacksonville's old courthouse lot to Methodist Episcopal trustees in 1834. The attached deed image requires a FamilySearch sign-in and was not inspected, so the land gift remains a well-supported local account rather than a verified deed finding.[14]

Coffee Road¶

Georgia approved the road measure on December 23, 1822. It authorized the governor to appoint two suitable people to supervise a road beginning at or near Cunningham's Ford on the Alapaha River. The route was to pass through specified Irwin and Early County land districts and continue to the Florida line near the Ochlocknee River. The state appropriated $1,500. The statute did not name the two appointees.[4]

The next year's official legislative report supplies the names and dates. It says Governor John Clark appointed General John Coffee and Thomas S. Swain of Telfair County on December 24, 1822. Work began in August 1823 and ended November 15. The committee described nearly ninety miles of road, plus about seven additional miles needed to reach a suitable Alapaha crossing, several small bridges, a larger bridge over a stream whose printed name is difficult to identify, and four ferry flats.[1]

The report does not explain how Coffee and Swain divided the fieldwork. It says Coffee received the full $1,500 appropriation. The governor's order supplied no instructions, contract, performance bond, or accounting method. Legislators therefore could not judge the work or determine how the money had been spent, and they ordered a detailed report within six months.[1]

The accounting remained unresolved in the next published report. In 1824 Coffee sent the governor a letter and accounts, but the legislative committee said they still did not show enough about the work or the manner in which it had been completed. The legislature asked the governor to investigate. The report does not accuse Coffee or Swain of stealing money, and it does not say funds were missing. It shows an inadequately documented public project. No separate report from Swain or final settlement was located online.[6]

Coffee Road later came to mean a longer corridor extending north toward the Ocmulgee. The 1822 state project began at the Alapaha, not at Jacksonville or Swain's Ferry. A published transcription of Irwin County minutes says county officials appointed Sion Hall, James Allen, and Thomas Townsend in July 1824 to lay out the northern Ocmulgee-to-Alapaha segment. Nothing located online shows that Swain supervised that separate extension.[7]

Twentieth-century Georgia historical markers repeatedly name Coffee and Swain as the road's superintendents. Those markers preserve the correct names, but the 1823 official report is the earlier and stronger source.[16]

Swain's Ferry and Jacksonville¶

Legislative reporting in 1830 described a proposal allowing Thomas S. Swain to establish a ferry on his own land opposite Jacksonville. The enacted measure appeared in the 1831 passed-act list as an authorization for Thomas S. Swain to establish a ferry across the Ocmulgee River.[5]

This is the best evidence for the origin of the name Swain's Ferry. It does not prove that a chartered ferry was operating during the 1823 road work. The authorization came eight years later. An earlier informal crossing is possible, but no ferry license, bond, deed, or court entry was located to establish one.

The middle initial appears as L or J in a few newspaper renderings. The 1823 official report, the 1831 passed-act list, the 1838 court notice, and the 1840 estate notices use S. That repeated form in the stronger sources controls.[1][5][8][9]

Surveying and other possible records¶

Georgia Archives metadata identifies Thomas S. Swain as the surveyor of Cherokee County, Section 3, District 5, from May 15 through June 13, 1832. The name and initial match, and the timing is compatible with the Telfair man. The field notebook metadata does not give the surveyor's residence or another identifier, so this assignment remains probable rather than certain.[19]

A Telfair election report from 1831 says Thomas J. Swain received six votes for district surveyor and lost to John Fitzsimons. The J may be a printing error, or the candidate may have been another man. It cannot safely be used to prove or disprove the identity of the Cherokee surveyor.[20]

No verified militia commission, War of 1812 service, pension, bounty-land file, or muster roll was located for Thomas S. Swain. He should not be assigned a military rank. The title "Esquire" in the 1823 report indicates civil standing, not military office.[1]

Land, livestock, and business¶

By the end of his life Swain ran a large regional livestock operation. A sale notice dated April 15, 1840 advertised between five hundred and six hundred cattle at John Willis's place in Irwin County, between one hundred and two hundred at Woodson Willcox's place in Telfair County, and about two hundred at Jacksonville. The estate also held sheep, horses, and other stock.[9]

Later notices advertised property at Swain's Jacksonville residence: three horses, three mules, a yoke of oxen, about eight hundred bushels of corn, a two-horse wagon, blacksmith tools, household and kitchen furniture, and farming equipment. His real estate included the western half of Telfair Land Lot 269 and all of Lot 321, about 429.9 acres on the Ocmulgee River.[10]

A June 1838 sheriff's notice records an Irwin Superior Court execution in favor of Thomas S. Swain against Angus Finlyson and William Bradford. The notice does not explain the underlying debt, but it documents Swain's business activity beyond Jacksonville shortly before his death.[8]

Estate administration continued for years. Rebecca Swain and Mitchell G. Willcox were still seeking authority to sell estate land in 1849. The long administration is consistent with the size and geographic spread of the property, though the notices do not explain the delay.[11]

Slavery¶

Swain was an enslaver. An 1840 administrator's notice said fourteen enslaved people belonging to the estate would be hired out for the following year. The notice does not name them, give their ages, or preserve their family relationships.[10]

A Telfair family history reports that Sarah Pridgen sold an enslaved person to Swain on February 13, 1819 for his daughter Susannah. The original instrument was not accessible online, so that transaction should remain attributed to the family history rather than presented as an independently inspected deed.[15]

The public 1830 census image identifies Thomas S. Swain as a Telfair County household head, but the accessible image did not provide a reliable complete slave-schedule count for this research. No names or additional numbers should be inferred. The probate inventory, appraisement, hire records, sale bill, and estate division are the best remaining sources for recovering the identities and family ties erased by the newspaper notices.[13]

Death and burial¶

Thomas S. Swain died before April 8, 1840. On that date Telfair clerk James H. McCall issued a citation on the application of Rebecca Swain and Mitchell G. Willcox for letters of administration. A later sale notice dated April 15 also calls Swain deceased. No obituary, funeral notice, medical account, or exact death date was located.[2][9]

Find a Grave memorial 86291771 includes a photograph of a marker reading Thomas S. Swain, 1784-1840, in Swain Family Cemetery at Jacksonville. The memorial and marker give strong support for the burial place and life years. No cemetery register, church record, or contemporary burial record was found, so the exact dates and original placement of the marker remain unverified.[12]

Portrait search¶

No authenticated likeness of Thomas S. Swain was found. The search covered Wikimedia Commons, Library of Congress Prints and Photographs, the Digital Library of Georgia, Georgia Archives, Internet Archive metadata, Georgia Historical Society marker pages, Find a Grave, family-history pages, and general web indexes.

Because Swain died in 1840, any photograph would require unusually strong provenance from the earliest years of American photography. No portrait, miniature, silhouette, engraving, or family-owned image located in this search could be tied to him. Images of General Coffee, unrelated men named Thomas Swain, or a generic pioneer should not be used as his likeness.

Evidence assessment¶

Claim Grade Reason
Thomas S. Swain of Telfair County supervised the Alapaha-to-Florida road with General John Coffee Verified Georgia's official 1823 report names both men, their county, and the appointment date.
The 1822 statute itself named Coffee and Swain False The statute authorized two gubernatorial appointees but did not print their names.
Swain personally received or controlled the $1,500 appropriation Not proved The 1823 report says Coffee received the money.
Swain supervised the later Ocmulgee-to-Alapaha extension Not proved The available 1824 county-minute transcription names Hall, Allen, and Townsend.
He was the Thomas S. Swain later associated with Jacksonville and the ferry Strong probable Exact name, county, chronology, Ocmulgee land, and regional activity align.
A chartered Swain's Ferry was operating in 1823 Not proved The located authorization dates to 1831.
He was a Telfair Inferior Court justice Strong probable Official 1812 appointment matches name, county, standing, and chronology but omits the middle initial.
He performed the 1832 Cherokee survey Probable Exact name and initial; archival metadata does not state residence.
He held military rank or served in the War of 1812 Unresolved No qualifying military record was located.
He was born in 1784 Strong marker evidence Grave marker and derivative family records agree; no contemporary birth record found.
He was born in Bertie County to Job Swain and Susanna Smith Unresolved Public tree claims were not supported by an inspected original record.
Rebecca Pridgen was his wife Strong probable Estate, cemetery, and family evidence agree; no marriage record inspected.
He and Rebecca had exactly six or seven children Unresolved The principal derivative sources conflict.
He owned Ocmulgee land and a large livestock operation Verified Contemporary estate and land notices describe the assets.
His estate held fourteen enslaved people Verified Contemporary administrator's notice advertises their hiring.
He died before April 8, 1840 Verified Dated administration citation.
He was buried in Swain Family Cemetery Strong marker evidence Memorial includes a photographed marker; no burial register found.
An authenticated portrait survives Not found Institutional, memorial, publication, and general searches produced no verified likeness.

Research limits¶

The documented search covered stored Barney and Coffee Road research; Georgia's published acts and legislative reports for 1812, 1822, 1823, and 1824; Georgia Archives and Digital Library of Georgia records; Georgia Historic Newspapers; available Newspapers.com material; the 1830 federal census record; FamilySearch public records and trees; Find a Grave; Internet Archive; Library of Congress; Wikimedia Commons; Georgia Historical Society markers; Telfair family histories; cemetery compilations; and general web indexes.

Not located online were Swain's birth or baptism record; proof of his parents; marriage record; family Bible; complete deed and tax sequence; the original December 24, 1822 executive order; road contract, vouchers, payroll, survey, or final settlement; Swain's correspondence; ferry license or bond; original 1832 surveyor appointment; military file; full probate packet; named inventory and hire records for the enslaved people; obituary; exact death date; cemetery register; or authenticated portrait.

Those gaps do not weaken the official proof of Swain's road appointment, his Telfair County identity in 1822, his Jacksonville estate, or the scale and character of his property. They do require caution about his origins, complete family, precise role in the road work, ferry operations before 1831, military service, and exact burial history.

Sources¶
