docs.title: Willis King (1792–1857)
docs.text:
Willis King (1792–1857)¶

Willis King appears in later county history as an early Irwin and Lowndes County resident. The detailed record locators are promising, but several of the underlying originals still need inspection.

What the records show¶

Folks Huxford identifies King as an Irwin County citizen selected to help conduct the county's first election in 1819. Huxford also places him on the first superior-court grand jury in 1820 and in the 1820 Irwin County census. Those precise references make his presence in Irwin by 1820 strong probable, but the original act, court record, and census image have not yet been inspected.

The same history says King moved into the territory that later became Brooks County in 1823, after the Coffee Road opened. Because he was apparently already elsewhere in Irwin County, 1823 should be read as a proposed relocation south, not his first arrival in the county.

Preserved deed and minute-book references identify an 1837 conveyance from Solomon Walker to Willis King, a conveyance from King to George Folsom, and Nancy King's 1857 dower application as Willis's widow. Huxford places the main plantation on Lots 25 and 26, District 14. The original deeds, dower record, plantation title chain, and estate inventory remain to be read.

The deed locators are geographically specific. Solomon Walker conveyed District 12, Lot 435 to Willis on May 15, 1837 (Deed Book B, p. 25), and Willis later conveyed the west half of District 12, Lot 268 to George Folsom (Deed Book A, p. 91). Both lots fall in present-day Brooks County. Nancy King's October 19, 1857, dower locator explicitly calls her Willis King's widow and covers Districts 12 and 15 (Superior Court Minutes Book A, pp. 49–51). These records upgrade Willis to a locator-anchored future-Brooks landholder; the uninspected originals prevent a stronger title-chain claim.

Connection to Barney¶

King belongs to the wider settlement history of land that later became Brooks County. No complete descendant chain, land record, or institutional record presently connects him directly to Barney.

Evidence status¶

  • Strong probable: presence in Irwin County by 1820; Nancy was his widow; death in 1857.
  • Secondary-supported: plantation on Lots 25 and 26 and the estate details reported by Huxford.
  • Relocation theory: the 1823 move into future Brooks County.
  • Unresolved: direct Barney influence, the complete land chain, and the original estate inventory.

Sources¶

  1. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948, Willis King profile and early county-organization sections, pp. 497–498.
  2. Lowndes County Deed Book B, p. 25, Solomon Walker to Willis King, May 15, 1837.
  3. Lowndes County Deed Book A, p. 91, Willis King to George Folsom, west half of Land Lot 268, District 12.
  4. Lowndes County Superior Court Minutes Book A, pp. 49–51, Nancy King's 1857 dower application.

docs.title: Elias Roberts
docs.text:
Elias Roberts¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Evidence assessment¶

Traditional early-settler candidate; regional residence verified, future-Brooks residence secondary-supported but unresolved.

The original 1830 household predates Huxford's 1834 arrival date. The safest reading is that Elias was a regional resident by 1830; the later date may describe a move into a narrower locality or may be inaccurate.

An original 1830 Thomas County census schedule contains a household headed by Elias Robert; Ancestry indexes the surname as Roberts. An 1840 index and preserved schedule image place Elias Roberts in Swaines, Thomas County. These records verify a Thomas County household sequence, not residence within the territory that became Brooks County.

The strongest future-Brooks claim is retrospective. Huxford wrote that Elias arrived in 1834 and that his son Hezekiah Roberts was born in the Tallokas district of old Lowndes County in 1840. If accurate, the Tallokas birthplace would place the family in territory later included in Brooks County. No birth, baptism, deed, tax page, or other contemporary record inspected in this pass independently confirms that statement.

Elias should remain on the traditional/candidate roster rather than the verified supplemental roster until an original record bridges the Thomas County household to Tallokas or another future-Brooks location.

Identity and census trail¶

1830 Thomas County¶

The original schedule at stamped page 27 names Elias Robert. The literal reading is verified; adding the final s is an indexed normalization. Household demographic marks were not accepted as a reconstructed family because they have not received the required header-aligned transcription and independent reread.

This is the earliest inspected record attributable to the candidate. It conflicts with a literal reading of Huxford's claim that Elias “came” in 1834 unless that date meant movement into the future-Brooks portion rather than arrival in the broader region.

1840 Thomas County¶

Ancestry locates Elias Roberts in Swaines, Thomas County, manuscript page 323, and the original schedule image is preserved. The name/index locator is usable; a complete demographic transcription remains pending. Swaines is not, by itself, proof of Tallokas or future-Brooks residence.

1850 Thomas County namesakes¶

The original District 81 frame contains two separate entries rendered Eleas Roberts: a younger man about 28 and an older man about 60. The older man is chronologically compatible with the 1830 household head, but the shared page and age alone do not establish continuity. The younger man could be a son, another relative, or unrelated. Neither household may be merged with the pioneer without distinguishing evidence.

Family claims¶

Hezekiah Roberts¶

Huxford explicitly called Hezekiah a son of Elias and said Hezekiah was born in Tallokas in 1840. This is secondary-supported, not original-record verified. No inspected census relationship, death certificate, probate record, family Bible, or deed names Elias as Hezekiah's father.

Other possible household members¶

Earlier audit work identified Elizabeth E. and Sherrod E. Roberts as possible household or family candidates. No inspected record in this pass establishes their relationship to Elias. They remain unresolved and should not appear as children or spouse in public copy.

Elias's wife has not been identified from an inspected original record.

Tax, land, deed, marriage, and probate findings¶

  • FamilySearch record 6C12-N7SL indexes an Elias Roberts tax assessment in Georgia, but the captured detail supplies no year, county, district, land lot, acreage, or image reading. It proves only that an indexed tax entry exists; it cannot locate this Elias.
  • A Brooks County universal-index OCR pair associates an “Elias Roberts” with a deed recorded in 1921 and an instrument date OCR'd as 1827. The century-scale recording anomaly and unverified handwriting make it unsafe for this identity. It was not used as pioneer evidence.
  • No parent-naming deed, marriage, will, administration, guardianship, cemetery marker, or contemporary newspaper item was located in the accessible stored evidence and bounded online searches for Elias.
  • No inspected land or tax record places Elias in a named future-Brooks district or lot.

Conflict analysis¶

  1. 1834 arrival versus 1830 census: the original 1830 Thomas County household predates Huxford's arrival date. The 1834 date may refer to movement into a narrower locality, may concern another Elias, or may be inaccurate. It is not independently verified.
  2. Thomas County versus Tallokas: the 1830 and 1840 records are Thomas County records; the Tallokas claim is retrospective. The two claims can coexist only if the family changed residence or the county attribution obscures a boundary-area movement. No inspected record supplies that bridge.
  3. 1850 namesakes: two Elias/Eleas Roberts entries on the same Thomas County frame prevent a safe single-line reconstruction.

Barney and Brooks County relevance¶

No direct Barney-townsite residence, landholding, church office, road duty, or public role has been proved for Elias. His relevance rests on Huxford's placement of son Hezekiah's 1840 birth in Tallokas and Hezekiah's later prominence in western Brooks/Pavo. That is meaningful local tradition but does not independently establish Elias's own future-Brooks residence.

Public-ready profile copy¶

Elias Roberts¶

Elias Roberts belongs on the traditional early-settler research list, but his exact local trail remains unsettled. An original 1830 census schedule records Elias Robert as a Thomas County household head, and an 1840 index places Elias Roberts in Swaines, Thomas County. Two Elias or Eleas Roberts entries appear in Thomas County in 1850, and no inspected deed, tax page, probate file, or family record connects either man to Tallokas. The safest conclusion is that Elias was a documented regional resident by 1830 and a traditional future-Brooks settler candidate. Promotion to the verified supplemental roster requires a contemporary record locating him in Tallokas or elsewhere inside the future Brooks County boundary.

Research coverage and remaining targets¶

Searched: preserved local research files; the original 1830 and preserved 1840 census images; the original-image review notes for the two 1850 candidates; Huxford's Brooks County history; the FamilySearch tax capture; Brooks deed-index data; and exact-name web queries for Elias and Hezekiah with Thomas, Lowndes, Tallokas, deed, and probate terms.

Remaining decisive targets:

  1. the original tax-digest image behind FamilySearch 6C12-N7SL, with year, county, district, and adjoining taxpayers;
  2. a complete header-aligned transcription and independent reread of the 1830 and 1840 households;
  3. independent reconstruction of both 1850 Elias households;
  4. a deed, tax, road, church, court, or probate record locating Elias in Tallokas or another future-Brooks district;
  5. an original record naming Hezekiah as Elias's son.

docs.title: Amos Emanuel and the 1827 Little River ferry proposal
docs.text:
Amos Emanuel and the 1827 Little River ferry proposal¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Latest audit conclusion¶

The Georgia Senate's 43–20 vote is verified, but the bill's absence from the official 1827 session laws strongly contradicts enactment. The 1830 tax image lists Emanuel only as a single poll in Captain Studstill's District and supplies no land description. No exact Amos Emanuel deed appears in the reviewed Lowndes index. The evidence therefore proves neither an operating ferry nor an exact crossing, and the proposal cannot be assigned safely to Joyce's Ferry, Miller Bridge, Folsom Bridge, or another site.

What the record proves¶

Amos Emanuel was a Lowndes County resident named in an 1827 bill for a ferry across Little River where Coffee Road crossed the river. Senator Duncan Blair introduced the measure. The Georgia Senate amended it and passed it 43–20 on November 14, 1827.[1][2]

The published 1827 session laws do not contain the bill. Their roads, bridges, and ferries index also omits it.[3] No record located in this research shows that the House passed the measure, that the governor approved it, or that Emanuel opened the ferry. He should therefore be described as the proposed ferry proprietor, not as a verified ferry operator.

The proposed crossing¶

The newspaper report placed the ferry on Emanuel's land where Coffee Road crossed Little River.[1] It did not give a land lot, adjoining owner, distance, or other detail that fixes the site.

Two later crossings are central to the local road history. Washington Joyce's ferry is associated with the later Miller Bridge, while a separate body of evidence places the early Coffee Road corridor near the later Folsom Bridge. Emanuel's tract has not been tied to either crossing. Until a deed, plat, tax land return, road record, or the original bill supplies a location, the site remains unresolved.

Identity and movement¶

The Amos Emanuel named in the bill is strong probable as the man found in a sequence of South Georgia records from 1820 through 1850. The uncommon name, compatible household, Lowndes County residence, and later militia service support the identification, but the census ages do not align perfectly.

  • 1820: Amos Emmanuel headed a Montgomery County household of five. Two household members were engaged in agriculture.[4]
  • 1830: Amos Emanuel headed a seven-person household in Lowndes County.[5]
  • 1830 tax digest: He appeared under “Single Polls in Capt. Studstill's District” and paid one poll. The entry lists no land, acreage, district, lot, watercourse, or value.[6]
  • 1838: Folks Huxford's transcription of state records lists Amos Emanuel as a private in Captain Levi J. Knight's Lowndes County company, which served from August 15 through October 15.[7]
  • 1840: An Amos Emanuel headed a Ware County household in District 719.[8]
  • 1850: Amos Emanuel, age 55, was recorded as a Georgia-born farmer in Ware County with Martha, 60, and five other household members.[9]

The 1830 census places Amos in the forty-to-forty-nine age range. The 1840 and 1850 records instead imply birth around 1790–1795. An enumeration error could explain the difference, but the Montgomery–Lowndes–Ware chain remains strong probable rather than verified.

Household and Martha¶

The 1850 Ware County census is the only original record located here that names Martha. It lists her in Amos's household at age 60 but does not state relationships. She was probably his wife. The unnamed adult women in Amos's 1820, 1830, and 1840 households fall within age ranges generally compatible with Martha, though the censuses do not prove that they were the same woman.[4][5][8][9]

Public family trees call her Martha Elizabeth Jones and call Amos “Amos Enoch Emanuel.” No inspected marriage record, deed, probate file, death record, Bible record, or other original source confirms Martha's middle or maiden name, Amos's middle name, or either person's parents. No reliable connection has been established between Martha and a particular Jones family in Montgomery, Lowndes, Ware, or the Barney area.

Joyce and Folsom associations¶

The census records place Amos near members of a broader Joyce migration group. Henry Joyce appeared eight households before Amos Emmanuel in Montgomery County in 1820. The 1840 Ware County sequence placed Amos among Cornelius, Michael, and Henry Joyce, with Asa Emanuel adjacent.[4][8] Census order shows proximity, not kinship, shared land, or ferry succession. None of these entries names Washington Joyce.

No reviewed census, tax, military, probate, deed, family-history, or newspaper record connects Amos with William Folsom, Lawrence Folsom, or another member of the Folsom family.

Newspaper findings¶

A Georgia newspaper search for 1820–1860 used Emanuel, Emmanuel, Emanual, and Manuel spellings. The 1827 ferry report was the only located item that clearly concerned the Lowndes County man.[1] An 1846 Early County list also named an Amos Emanuel, but it contained too little identifying information to connect him with the Lowndes and Ware County resident.

A later online history reports that the Ware County sheriff seized seven cattle belonging to Amos Emanuel on July 2, 1844, to satisfy court debts. The original newspaper notice has not been preserved and inspected for this project, so that statement remains an unverified lead.

What remains unresolved¶

  • Whether the House passed the ferry bill or why the measure did not appear in the session laws
  • Whether Emanuel ever opened or operated a ferry
  • The land lot and exact location of his 1827 tract
  • Whether the proposed site corresponded to a later named crossing
  • Whether the Montgomery, Lowndes, and Ware records all concern the same man
  • Martha's maiden name, parents, and relationship to local Jones families
  • Amos's death date, burial place, and estate record

Sources¶

  1. Weekly Telegraph (Macon), November 27, 1827, p. 2, report of Duncan Blair's ferry bill and Senate passage; Newspapers.com image 823537670.
  2. Journal of the Senate of the State of Georgia (1827), pp. 21, 28, 36, 42, 59–60, Internet Archive.
  3. Acts of the General Assembly of the State of Georgia (1827), published session laws and index, Digital Library of Georgia.
  4. 1820 U.S. census, Montgomery County, Georgia, p. 62, Amos Emmanuel, NARA M33 roll 9; Ancestry record 1480766.
  5. 1830 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, p. 86, Amos Emanuel, NARA M19 roll 19; Ancestry record 1850986.
  6. 1830 Lowndes County tax digest, Captain Studstill's district, single-poll list, Amos Emanuel; Ancestry collection 1729, record 3440981, image 40141_1220705227_0567-00028.
  7. “Indian War Troops of 1838,” South Georgia Historical and Genealogical Quarterly 1, no. 1 (January 1922), p. 6, roster transcribed by Folks Huxford from Georgia capitol records.
  8. 1840 U.S. census, District 719, Ware County, Georgia, p. 134, Amos Emanuel, NARA M704 roll 52; Ancestry record 1855293.
  9. 1850 U.S. census, Division 89, Ware County, Georgia, dwelling and family 422, p. 116b, Amos and Martha Emanuel, NARA M432 roll 86; Ancestry record 16036802.

docs.title: William Hancock
docs.text:
William Hancock¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Decision¶

William Hancock was a verified regional settler in Lowndes County by 1830. The original federal census names him on stamped page 90. He is also strong probable as the William Hancock whom later accounts identify as the county's first sheriff, although no original election return, commission, bond, or court minute has been located.

Census and sheriff tradition¶

The 1830 Lowndes County schedule lists William Hancock at handwritten row 312. The record verifies his name and county residence but does not state an occupation, identify household members, or place his home in the part of Lowndes County that later became Brooks County.

Hamilton W. Sharpe wrote in 1884 that Hancock was elected sheriff at Lowndes County's first election, held at Sion Hall's residence. Folks Huxford later assigned Hancock sheriff terms beginning in May 1826 and January 1830. The same name, county, and period make the census householder and the reported sheriff a strong-probable match. The identity is not verified without a contemporary office, family, or land record that joins them.

Limits and Barney relevance¶

Huxford's 1824–1825 arrival date remains retrospective. The census does not establish future-Brooks residence, and no inspected record places Hancock at Barney. A reported continuation into Columbia County, Florida also remains unresolved because no age, family, land, probate, or migration record links a Florida man to the Lowndes householder.

The reviewed Lowndes deed index contains no exact William Hancock entry that locates his home in future Brooks County. Hancock remains a verified regional settler and strong-probable sheriff, not a proved future-Brooks resident. See Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved.

Evidence status¶

  • Verified: a William Hancock household in Lowndes County in 1830.
  • Strong probable: the 1830 householder was the reported first sheriff.
  • Secondary-supported: sheriff terms beginning in 1826 and 1830; arrival in 1824 or 1825.
  • Unresolved: original office records, exact residence, family, land, Florida continuation, and any direct Barney connection.

Sources¶

  1. 1830 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, stamped p. 90, handwritten row 312, William Hancock, NARA M19, roll 19; Ancestry collection 8058, record 1851091, image 4409522_00178; Internet Archive viewer frame.
  2. Hamilton W. Sharpe, early Lowndes history series, 1884, naming William Hancock at the first county election.
  3. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948 (1948), pp. 26 and 29–30.

docs.title: Census and sheriff tradition
docs.text:
The 1830 Lowndes County schedule lists William Hancock at handwritten row 312. The record verifies his name and county residence but does not state an occupation, identify household members, or place his home in the part of Lowndes County that later became Brooks County.

Hamilton W. Sharpe wrote in 1884 that Hancock was elected sheriff at Lowndes County's first election, held at Sion Hall's residence. Folks Huxford later assigned Hancock sheriff terms beginning in May 1826 and January 1830. The same name, county, and period make the census householder and the reported sheriff a strong-probable match. The identity is not verified without a contemporary office, family, or land record that joins them.

docs.title: Limits and Barney relevance
docs.text:
Huxford's 1824–1825 arrival date remains retrospective. The census does not establish future-Brooks residence, and no inspected record places Hancock at Barney. A reported continuation into Columbia County, Florida also remains unresolved because no age, family, land, probate, or migration record links a Florida man to the Lowndes householder.

The reviewed Lowndes deed index contains no exact William Hancock entry that locates his home in future Brooks County. Hancock remains a verified regional settler and strong-probable sheriff, not a proved future-Brooks resident. See Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved.

docs.title: Evidence status
docs.text:
• Verified: a William Hancock household in Lowndes County in 1830.
  • Strong probable: the 1830 householder was the reported first sheriff.
  • Secondary-supported: sheriff terms beginning in 1826 and 1830; arrival in 1824 or 1825.
  • Unresolved: original office records, exact residence, family, land, Florida continuation, and any direct Barney connection.

docs.title: David Platt
docs.text:
David Platt¶

David Platt was an early Lowndes County household head. His name is legible on the original 1830 federal census, and an 1840 index supplies a plausible later household locator. Those records establish regional residence but do not place his home within the part of Lowndes County that became Brooks County.

A 2006 compiled genealogy identifies David as a son of Rev. Joshua Platt and Amy Newell. Original records support the chronology: David married Mary Rowe in Bulloch County in 1818, Joshua and David headed separate households on the same Bulloch census page in 1820, and both later lived in Lowndes County. None of those original records names David's parents, so the father-son relationship remains secondary-supported rather than verified.

Folks Huxford listed Platt among the settlers arriving in 1824 or 1825 and among the justices appointed to the first Lowndes County Inferior Court on May 29, 1826. The original appointment or court minute has not been inspected. The arrival period and office therefore remain secondary-supported rather than verified from the underlying records.

Platt belongs in the wider early-Lowndes story. His status as a settler of the future Brooks County area remains qualified until a land lot, tax district, deed, or court record supplies a more precise location.

A deed locator records David and Peter Platt conveying a District 11 grist mill and improvements to James D. Shanks (Deed Book A, p. 625). District 11 is not a future-Brooks locator. Joshua Platt's District 12 land cannot be assigned to David without a record proving the relationship and transfer. See Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved.

docs.title: William Smith of Franklinville, Troupville, and Valdosta
docs.text:
William Smith of Franklinville, Troupville, and Valdosta¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Latest geography audit¶

The reviewed deed index contains a sheriff sale to a William Smith for District 12, Lot 435 in 1830 and later District 12 transactions. Because William Smith is a high-frequency name, two William Smith household heads appear in 1840, and no inspected instrument identifies the buyer as the clerk or postmaster, those parcels cannot be assigned to this profile. Smith remains a verified regional official with an unresolved future-Brooks residence and no proved direct Barney role.

See Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved for the shared comparison and recommendations.

Research scope and conclusion¶

This dossier concerns the William Smith born in North Carolina about 1797-1800 who settled at Franklinville in early Lowndes County, served as a court clerk and postmaster, kept Tranquil Hall at Troupville and Valdosta, and died in Valdosta on February 1, 1882.

The identity is unusually well anchored for an early Lowndes settler. Smith wrote his own account of the county's first courts in 1880. His original 1882 obituary then joined that witness to Franklinville, the clerkship, Troupville, Tranquil Hall, Valdosta, his wife, and his two sons. An Atlanta reprint confirms the contemporary circulation of the death account.[12] Federal registers, court notices, censuses, and slave schedules independently support the same chain.[1-11]

The evidence also corrects or narrows several familiar claims. Smith was signing as Superior Court clerk by an 1828-era dateline, earlier than Huxford's 1830 commission date. He was Franklinville postmaster by September 30, 1829, but the often-repeated July 7, 1828 appointment was not recovered from an original federal record. The precise location of his Franklinville land, the full office chronology, his wife's formal given name, his probate, and his exact burial place remain unresolved.[6,13-17]

Birth, migration, and first-hand recollection¶

The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses consistently place Smith's birth in North Carolina and imply birth about 1797-1800.[3-6] His original obituary says he was born in North Carolina in 1797 and died in his eighty-fourth year.[9]

Smith's own letter in the Valdosta Times appeared on December 11, 1880. Newspapers.com's metadata assigns the image to December 18, but the photographed masthead clearly reads December 11; the printed issue controls. Signing "W. S.", Smith recalled the first Lowndes Superior Court at Sion Hall's house in January 1827, the next court at Francis Rountree's, and the severe cold. He closed by saying that after the 1828 term he rode eight miles to his "lonely domicile at old Franklinville, where we had settled but a short time before".[1]

The initials alone would be insufficient. The obituary identifies William Smith as the Franklinville settler who later wrote the first-court account, and Hamilton W. Sharpe's participant history names Smith as Franklinville's first settler.[9][18] That makes Smith's authorship and the basic settlement chain verified.

Early households and the 1840 namesake problem¶

The 1830 Lowndes census lists a William Smith household with a man aged 30-39, a woman 20-29, three boys under ten, and three other adult men. It records no enslaved people.[2] The head's age and place fit the subject, but the common name and unstated relationships make this a strong probable, not verified, assignment.

Two Lowndes households were indexed under Wm Smith in 1840. The page 249 household is the stronger match. Its head and adult woman were both 40-49, matching the later William and Mary; it included three adolescent boys and other residents. Two enslaved people were counted: one boy under ten and one woman aged 24-35. The page 238 namesake had a man 30-39, woman 20-29, and boy under five, with one person in agriculture and no enslaved people.[2]

The later evidence says Smith had sons William and Henry, but it does not name every person in either early household. The page 249 household is therefore strong probable, while page 238 is retained as a same-name control.

Wife and sons¶

The named census sequence is consistent:

  • In 1850 William, age 50 and a hotelkeeper, lived with Mary Smith, 50, Charles S. Rockwell, 28, Mary E. Rockwell, 18, and William Ashley, 26.[3]
  • In 1860 William, 60, was a hotelkeeper and postmaster at Troupville. Mary Smith, 59, Laura Smith, 9, and Mary Smith, 7, shared the household.[4]
  • In 1870 William, 73, kept a hotel at Valdosta. Mary N. Smith, 72, Laura C. Smith, 19, Mary N. Smith, 16, and five other residents shared the dwelling.[5]
  • In 1880 William, 80, was a retired hotelkeeper at Valdosta. The continuation page explicitly identifies his wife, age 80. Her written middle initial appears to be "P"; Ancestry indexes it as "A".[6]

The pre-1880 schedules do not state relationships. The Rockwells, Laura, and younger Mary cannot be labeled daughters or grandchildren merely because they shared the household.

The original 1882 obituary directly identifies two sons, William and Henry, both of whom had died after the Civil War leaving families. It says William Jr.'s family had all died, while Henry's widow, four children, and one or two grandchildren survived. No original birth, marriage, or probate record was found for either son.[9]

William's wife presents a real naming conflict. The censuses call her Mary and Mary N.; the 1880 image appears to read Mary P., while Ancestry indexes Mary A. A January 1892 Valdosta death notice calls her "Mrs. Polly Smith", identifies her as Uncle Billy Smith's widow, and says she was a sister of David Hutchinson of Adel.[10] The age, place, widowhood, and unique husband identification make Mary and Polly the same woman with strong confidence and establish her Hutchinson family connection.

An original January 1870 Tranquil Hall advertisement is signed "WM. SMITH / MARGET SMITH".[19] "Marget" may represent Margaret, a nickname, a printing error, or a different person involved in the hotel. No marriage or Bible record settles the issue. The safest wording is: Smith's wife was recorded as Mary during 1850-1880 and as Polly at death; the advertisement's Marget Smith remains an unresolved conflict. The modern form "Mary Hutchinson Smith" is plausible, but her full legal name has not been proved.

Court service¶

The earliest contemporary clerk evidence conflicts with Huxford's later office table. A mortgage-foreclosure rule printed March 7, 1829 ends with Smith's certification of a May 5, 1828 Lowndes Superior Court minute, followed by "WILLIAM SMITH, Cl'k. Sup. Court, Lowndes county" and a "June 21" dateline. The year is not printed beside June 21, but the twelve-month publication sequence makes June 21, 1828 the strong-probable reading.[13]

A July 1831 equity extract again carries Smith's Lowndes Superior Court clerk signature.[14] In March 1832 he certified an Inferior Court estray extract as "c. i. c." In June 1833 he certified the Lowndes grand-jury presentments; his name appears as clerk, not as a juror.[15]

By 1835 Smith was signing probate notices as "c. c. o.", clerk of the Court of Ordinary. The same issue also shows him acting as administrator of John Sutton. Further signed Lowndes probate notices continue through the 1830s and 1840s.[16]

Huxford's officer table begins Smith's Superior Court clerk term on January 20, 1830 and assigns Henry Blair through 1830. Sharpe wrote shortly after Smith's death that Smith had been elected clerk in 1827.[11,17] The records prove Smith's service by the 1828-era dateline, but they do not show whether Huxford recorded a later commission or recommission. The exact Blair-to-Smith handoff, election, and commission sequence remains unresolved rather than neatly disproved.

Smith's obituary says he had more than once been Ordinary and had held the office about 1868-1870. That later elected service was not independently reconstructed. The antebellum signatures prove clerk work in ordinary business, not every later term as elected Ordinary.[9]

Franklinville post office¶

The federal Official Register lists Smith at Franklinville on four reporting dates:

Register date Entry Compensation
September 30, 1829 "Franklinville, Ga. / Wm Smith" \$9.06
September 30, 1831 "Franklinville, Ga. / Wm. Smith" \$16.67
September 30, 1833 "Franklinville, Ga. / William Smith" \$26.96
September 30, 1835 "Franklinville / William Smith" \$28.08

These are direct federal records and verify Smith as postmaster by September 30, 1829 through the September 30, 1835 reporting date.[7] They do not prove that he served continuously between every register date.

Huxford gives July 7, 1828 as the appointment date. No original appointment register or postal location paper proving that date was found. The 1827 federal register has no Lowndes office, but that absence does not prove that a new office could not have opened before the 1829 report. The exact first appointment remains unresolved.[7,17]

The 1860 population census independently describes Smith as both hotelkeeper and postmaster at Troupville.[4] It does not establish when he began that later postal service.

Mount Zion deed and public roles¶

Huxford printed a Mount Zion deed transcription he said he copied from the original. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed about six acres, including the church, camps, and burying ground, to the trustees in 1831. The registration certificate says the deed was entered in Lowndes Deed Book A, pages 654-655, on February 26, 1833 by "WILLIAM SMITH, Clerk".[20]

The deed book later burned and no manuscript image was located. Huxford's original-based transcription is strong evidence that Smith recorded the deed. Smith was not a grantor, grantee, witness, trustee, or first tenter in that instrument.

Huxford also names Smith among Troupville's first commissioners under the act approved December 14, 1837.[17] The official act could not be inspected because the Digital Library of Georgia returned the same unavailable message twice. The commissioner claim remains strong secondary evidence pending the session-law page.

An October 1839 notice signed at Troupville provides direct residence evidence. Smith reported that halves of bank notes mailed to him had been lost and asked newspapers to send their accounts to him at Troupville.[21] The notice does not make him a banker or public officer.

In 1850 he advertised from Troupville that he would procure federal bounty-land warrants for eligible claimants.[22] This proves a claims-agent business, not Smith's own military service. No qualifying Lowndes militia return, commission, company roster, or Creek War report was found for him. Common-name military hits elsewhere in Georgia were rejected.

Tranquil Hall and movement to Valdosta¶

The 1850 census calls Smith a hotelkeeper, and the 1860 schedule calls him hotelkeeper and postmaster at Troupville.[3,4] Smith's obituary names the hotel as "Tranquil Hall" and says its table and hospitality were widely known.[9] Sharpe and later Lowndes histories agree on the basic business.[11,18]

The railroad bypassed Troupville and led residents to the new town of Valdosta. A January 1870 advertisement says the proprietors of Tranquil Hall, formerly of Troupville, had opened at Valdosta. It is signed by William and "Marget" Smith.[19] The 1870 and 1880 censuses confirm William's Valdosta hotelkeeping and later retirement.[5,6]

An 1870 newspaper advertisement also calls the house "Tranquil Hall" at Valdosta. The original obituary says the aging couple gave up the business about ten years before Smith's death and sold the building to D. M. Jackson.[9,19]

Slavery and wealth¶

The strong-probable 1840 household counted two enslaved people.[2] The 1850 Lowndes slave schedule lists William Smith as enslaving fifteen people. The name, county, and same-census hotelkeeper context make the assignment strong probable. The original image and index agree on the owner and total.[8]

The 1860 schedule is geographically specific: "William Smith" at Troupville enslaved thirty-six people. The original page and index agree. The population schedule valued his real estate at \$5,000 and personal estate at \$23,000.[4,8]

The schedules did not record the people's names. No identity can be carried responsibly across emancipation from age and sex alone. Sharpe wrote that the war was especially hard on Smith because his property consisted of enslaved people.[11] That is a contemporary acquaintance's retrospective statement. The schedules prove the holdings and their scale but do not prove that every dollar of the reported personal estate represented enslaved people.

Land, tax, and the Franklinville site¶

Huxford places Smith's Franklinville home on Land Lot 50 in the 11th District and says the post office moved there.[17] No original deed, grant, plat, tax row, or title chain tying this William Smith to Lot 50 was found online. The exact lot is strong local-history evidence, not original land proof.

Available original tax pages preserved in related Lowndes projects were checked, but no uniquely identified William Smith row could be assigned without district, land-lot, and neighbor context. The 1839 signed Troupville notice and later censuses prove the migration more securely than an unattributed tax-index hit.

Death, church, and burial¶

The original Valdosta Times obituary says Smith died Wednesday morning at his Valdosta residence. With the issue dated February 4, 1882, the date was February 1. Funeral services were held at the residence that afternoon, and burial occurred Thursday morning, February 2, in "our cemetery".[9]

Hamilton W. Sharpe's memorial says Smith had joined the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, many years earlier and became a regular attendant late in life.[11] No baptism, membership roll, or church minute was found online, so the statement remains a close contemporary's account rather than an original church record.

The obituary does not name the cemetery. Find a Grave and broader searches produced user-created leads but no inspected marker photograph, burial register, sexton record, cemetery deed, or contemporary notice naming the ground.[23] The exact cemetery and grave remain unresolved.

Polly Smith died at Valdosta on January 21, 1892, derived from the Thursday preceding the January 23 issue. She was reported to be in her ninety-fifth year.[10] An indexed probate entry for Mary A. Smith is consistent with the widow, but its manuscript contents were not recovered and cannot resolve the initial or support an heir or property claim.

Evidence summary¶

Claim Grade Reason
Franklinville settler, later Troupville/Valdosta hotelkeeper Verified Smith's letter, original obituary, censuses, and hotel ad
Born North Carolina about 1797-1800 Verified as reported range Four censuses and original obituary
1830 household Strong probable Age/place fit; common name and unstated relationships
1840 page 249 household Strong probable Correct adult ages and family structure; page 238 control excluded
Wife Mary/Polly of Hutchinson family Strong Census wife sequence and 1892 widow notice
"Marget Smith" was Mary/Polly Unresolved Printed hotel ad conflicts with census names
Sons William and Henry Verified Original 1882 obituary
Postmaster by 1829 through 1835 Verified Four federal registers
Exact July 7, 1828 postal appointment Unresolved Huxford only; original appointment not found
Superior Court clerk by 1828-era dateline Verified service Contemporary certification and 1831 control
Exact 1827/1830 election and commission sequence Unresolved conflict Sharpe, contemporary signature, and Huxford differ
Inferior Court and Court of Ordinary clerk Verified Signed contemporary extracts/notices
Mount Zion deed recorder Strong original-based transcription Huxford copied lost original
Troupville commissioner Strong secondary Huxford; official act temporarily inaccessible
Enslaved fifteen people in 1850 Strong probable Lowndes slave schedule and hotelkeeper context
Enslaved thirty-six people in 1860 Verified Troupville slave schedule
Military service Unresolved No qualifying record found
Death February 1, 1882 Verified Original Valdosta obituary
Exact cemetery or grave Unresolved Obituary says only "our cemetery"

Chronology¶

  • About 1797-1800: born in North Carolina.[3-6,9]
  • 1827-1828: settled at Franklinville; witnessed early Lowndes courts and later recalled them.[1,9,18]
  • By June 21, probably 1828: signing as Lowndes Superior Court clerk.[13]
  • September 30, 1829: federally listed as Franklinville postmaster.[7]
  • 1830: strong-probable Lowndes household of seven, with no enslaved people recorded.[2]
  • 1831-1832: verified Superior and Inferior Court clerk signatures.[14,15]
  • February 26, 1833: recorded the Mount Zion deed according to Huxford's original-based transcription.[20]
  • 1835: verified Court of Ordinary clerk and Franklinville postmaster.[7,16]
  • October 1839: signed a notice from Troupville.[21]
  • 1840: strong-probable household of ten, including two enslaved people.[2]
  • 1850: Lowndes hotelkeeper; strong-probable owner of fifteen enslaved people.[3,8]
  • 1860: Troupville hotelkeeper and postmaster; thirty-six enslaved people; \$5,000 real and \$23,000 personal estate.[4,8]
  • January 1870: Tranquil Hall advertised at Valdosta.[19]
  • 1870: Valdosta hotelkeeper.[5]
  • December 11, 1880: published his first-court recollection.[1]
  • 1880: retired hotelkeeper living with wife Mary; original-image middle initial appears "P", while the index reads "A".[6]
  • February 1-2, 1882: death and reported burial at Valdosta.[9]
  • January 21, 1892: widow Polly died at Valdosta.[10]

Search coverage and remaining targets¶

The main unresolved record targets are:

  1. Smith's original clerk election return, commission, and the Henry Blair handoff;
  2. the original Franklinville postmaster appointment and location paper;
  3. an original Lot 50 deed, plat, tax row, or title chain;
  4. William and Polly/Mary's marriage, Bible, probate, and named-heir records;
  5. proof of the "Marget Smith" identity;
  6. Tranquil Hall deeds and business records;
  7. church membership minutes;
  8. a cemetery register, marker image, sexton record, or burial deed.

This dossier describes the accessible online evidence checked through August 19, 2026. It does not imply that undigitized courthouse, church, cemetery, postal, or federal records do not exist.

docs.title: Birth, migration, and first-hand recollection
docs.text:
The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses consistently place Smith's birth in North Carolina and imply birth about 1797-1800.[3-6] His original obituary says he was born in North Carolina in 1797 and died in his eighty-fourth year.[9]

Smith's own letter in the Valdosta Times appeared on December 11, 1880. Newspapers.com's metadata assigns the image to December 18, but the photographed masthead clearly reads December 11; the printed issue controls. Signing "W. S.", Smith recalled the first Lowndes Superior Court at Sion Hall's house in January 1827, the next court at Francis Rountree's, and the severe cold. He closed by saying that after the 1828 term he rode eight miles to his "lonely domicile at old Franklinville, where we had settled but a short time before".[1]

The initials alone would be insufficient. The obituary identifies William Smith as the Franklinville settler who later wrote the first-court account, and Hamilton W. Sharpe's participant history names Smith as Franklinville's first settler.[9][18] That makes Smith's authorship and the basic settlement chain verified.

docs.title: Early households and the 1840 namesake problem
docs.text:
The 1830 Lowndes census lists a William Smith household with a man aged 30-39, a woman 20-29, three boys under ten, and three other adult men. It records no enslaved people.[2] The head's age and place fit the subject, but the common name and unstated relationships make this a strong probable, not verified, assignment.

Two Lowndes households were indexed under Wm Smith in 1840. The page 249 household is the stronger match. Its head and adult woman were both 40-49, matching the later William and Mary; it included three adolescent boys and other residents. Two enslaved people were counted: one boy under ten and one woman aged 24-35. The page 238 namesake had a man 30-39, woman 20-29, and boy under five, with one person in agriculture and no enslaved people.[2]

The later evidence says Smith had sons William and Henry, but it does not name every person in either early household. The page 249 household is therefore strong probable, while page 238 is retained as a same-name control.

docs.title: Wife and sons
docs.text:
The named census sequence is consistent:

  • In 1850 William, age 50 and a hotelkeeper, lived with Mary Smith, 50, Charles S. Rockwell, 28, Mary E. Rockwell, 18, and William Ashley, 26.[3]
  • In 1860 William, 60, was a hotelkeeper and postmaster at Troupville. Mary Smith, 59, Laura Smith, 9, and Mary Smith, 7, shared the household.[4]
  • In 1870 William, 73, kept a hotel at Valdosta. Mary N. Smith, 72, Laura C. Smith, 19, Mary N. Smith, 16, and five other residents shared the dwelling.[5]
  • In 1880 William, 80, was a retired hotelkeeper at Valdosta. The continuation page explicitly identifies his wife, age 80. Her written middle initial appears to be "P"; Ancestry indexes it as "A".[6]

The pre-1880 schedules do not state relationships. The Rockwells, Laura, and younger Mary cannot be labeled daughters or grandchildren merely because they shared the household.

The original 1882 obituary directly identifies two sons, William and Henry, both of whom had died after the Civil War leaving families. It says William Jr.'s family had all died, while Henry's widow, four children, and one or two grandchildren survived. No original birth, marriage, or probate record was found for either son.[9]

William's wife presents a real naming conflict. The censuses call her Mary and Mary N.; the 1880 image appears to read Mary P., while Ancestry indexes Mary A. A January 1892 Valdosta death notice calls her "Mrs. Polly Smith", identifies her as Uncle Billy Smith's widow, and says she was a sister of David Hutchinson of Adel.[10] The age, place, widowhood, and unique husband identification make Mary and Polly the same woman with strong confidence and establish her Hutchinson family connection.

An original January 1870 Tranquil Hall advertisement is signed "WM. SMITH / MARGET SMITH".[19] "Marget" may represent Margaret, a nickname, a printing error, or a different person involved in the hotel. No marriage or Bible record settles the issue. The safest wording is: Smith's wife was recorded as Mary during 1850-1880 and as Polly at death; the advertisement's Marget Smith remains an unresolved conflict. The modern form "Mary Hutchinson Smith" is plausible, but her full legal name has not been proved.

docs.title: Court service
docs.text:
The earliest contemporary clerk evidence conflicts with Huxford's later office table. A mortgage-foreclosure rule printed March 7, 1829 ends with Smith's certification of a May 5, 1828 Lowndes Superior Court minute, followed by "WILLIAM SMITH, Cl'k. Sup. Court, Lowndes county" and a "June 21" dateline. The year is not printed beside June 21, but the twelve-month publication sequence makes June 21, 1828 the strong-probable reading.[13]

A July 1831 equity extract again carries Smith's Lowndes Superior Court clerk signature.[14] In March 1832 he certified an Inferior Court estray extract as "c. i. c." In June 1833 he certified the Lowndes grand-jury presentments; his name appears as clerk, not as a juror.[15]

By 1835 Smith was signing probate notices as "c. c. o.", clerk of the Court of Ordinary. The same issue also shows him acting as administrator of John Sutton. Further signed Lowndes probate notices continue through the 1830s and 1840s.[16]

Huxford's officer table begins Smith's Superior Court clerk term on January 20, 1830 and assigns Henry Blair through 1830. Sharpe wrote shortly after Smith's death that Smith had been elected clerk in 1827.[11,17] The records prove Smith's service by the 1828-era dateline, but they do not show whether Huxford recorded a later commission or recommission. The exact Blair-to-Smith handoff, election, and commission sequence remains unresolved rather than neatly disproved.

Smith's obituary says he had more than once been Ordinary and had held the office about 1868-1870. That later elected service was not independently reconstructed. The antebellum signatures prove clerk work in ordinary business, not every later term as elected Ordinary.[9]

docs.title: Franklinville post office
docs.text:
The federal Official Register lists Smith at Franklinville on four reporting dates:

Register date Entry Compensation
September 30, 1829 "Franklinville, Ga. / Wm Smith" \$9.06
September 30, 1831 "Franklinville, Ga. / Wm. Smith" \$16.67
September 30, 1833 "Franklinville, Ga. / William Smith" \$26.96
September 30, 1835 "Franklinville / William Smith" \$28.08

These are direct federal records and verify Smith as postmaster by September 30, 1829 through the September 30, 1835 reporting date.[7] They do not prove that he served continuously between every register date.

Huxford gives July 7, 1828 as the appointment date. No original appointment register or postal location paper proving that date was found. The 1827 federal register has no Lowndes office, but that absence does not prove that a new office could not have opened before the 1829 report. The exact first appointment remains unresolved.[7,17]

The 1860 population census independently describes Smith as both hotelkeeper and postmaster at Troupville.[4] It does not establish when he began that later postal service.

docs.title: Mount Zion deed and public roles
docs.text:
Huxford printed a Mount Zion deed transcription he said he copied from the original. Sion and Enoch Hall conveyed about six acres, including the church, camps, and burying ground, to the trustees in 1831. The registration certificate says the deed was entered in Lowndes Deed Book A, pages 654-655, on February 26, 1833 by "WILLIAM SMITH, Clerk".[20]

The deed book later burned and no manuscript image was located. Huxford's original-based transcription is strong evidence that Smith recorded the deed. Smith was not a grantor, grantee, witness, trustee, or first tenter in that instrument.

Huxford also names Smith among Troupville's first commissioners under the act approved December 14, 1837.[17] The official act could not be inspected because the Digital Library of Georgia returned the same unavailable message twice. The commissioner claim remains strong secondary evidence pending the session-law page.

An October 1839 notice signed at Troupville provides direct residence evidence. Smith reported that halves of bank notes mailed to him had been lost and asked newspapers to send their accounts to him at Troupville.[21] The notice does not make him a banker or public officer.

In 1850 he advertised from Troupville that he would procure federal bounty-land warrants for eligible claimants.[22] This proves a claims-agent business, not Smith's own military service. No qualifying Lowndes militia return, commission, company roster, or Creek War report was found for him. Common-name military hits elsewhere in Georgia were rejected.

docs.title: Tranquil Hall and movement to Valdosta
docs.text:
The 1850 census calls Smith a hotelkeeper, and the 1860 schedule calls him hotelkeeper and postmaster at Troupville.[3,4] Smith's obituary names the hotel as "Tranquil Hall" and says its table and hospitality were widely known.[9] Sharpe and later Lowndes histories agree on the basic business.[11,18]

The railroad bypassed Troupville and led residents to the new town of Valdosta. A January 1870 advertisement says the proprietors of Tranquil Hall, formerly of Troupville, had opened at Valdosta. It is signed by William and "Marget" Smith.[19] The 1870 and 1880 censuses confirm William's Valdosta hotelkeeping and later retirement.[5,6]

An 1870 newspaper advertisement also calls the house "Tranquil Hall" at Valdosta. The original obituary says the aging couple gave up the business about ten years before Smith's death and sold the building to D. M. Jackson.[9,19]

docs.title: Slavery and wealth
docs.text:
The strong-probable 1840 household counted two enslaved people.[2] The 1850 Lowndes slave schedule lists William Smith as enslaving fifteen people. The name, county, and same-census hotelkeeper context make the assignment strong probable. The original image and index agree on the owner and total.[8]

The 1860 schedule is geographically specific: "William Smith" at Troupville enslaved thirty-six people. The original page and index agree. The population schedule valued his real estate at \$5,000 and personal estate at \$23,000.[4,8]

The schedules did not record the people's names. No identity can be carried responsibly across emancipation from age and sex alone. Sharpe wrote that the war was especially hard on Smith because his property consisted of enslaved people.[11] That is a contemporary acquaintance's retrospective statement. The schedules prove the holdings and their scale but do not prove that every dollar of the reported personal estate represented enslaved people.

docs.title: Land, tax, and the Franklinville site
docs.text:
Huxford places Smith's Franklinville home on Land Lot 50 in the 11th District and says the post office moved there.[17] No original deed, grant, plat, tax row, or title chain tying this William Smith to Lot 50 was found online. The exact lot is strong local-history evidence, not original land proof.

Available original tax pages preserved in related Lowndes projects were checked, but no uniquely identified William Smith row could be assigned without district, land-lot, and neighbor context. The 1839 signed Troupville notice and later censuses prove the migration more securely than an unattributed tax-index hit.

docs.title: Death, church, and burial
docs.text:
The original Valdosta Times obituary says Smith died Wednesday morning at his Valdosta residence. With the issue dated February 4, 1882, the date was February 1. Funeral services were held at the residence that afternoon, and burial occurred Thursday morning, February 2, in "our cemetery".[9]

Hamilton W. Sharpe's memorial says Smith had joined the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, many years earlier and became a regular attendant late in life.[11] No baptism, membership roll, or church minute was found online, so the statement remains a close contemporary's account rather than an original church record.

The obituary does not name the cemetery. Find a Grave and broader searches produced user-created leads but no inspected marker photograph, burial register, sexton record, cemetery deed, or contemporary notice naming the ground.[23] The exact cemetery and grave remain unresolved.

Polly Smith died at Valdosta on January 21, 1892, derived from the Thursday preceding the January 23 issue. She was reported to be in her ninety-fifth year.[10] An indexed probate entry for Mary A. Smith is consistent with the widow, but its manuscript contents were not recovered and cannot resolve the initial or support an heir or property claim.

docs.title: Chronology
docs.text:
• About 1797-1800: born in North Carolina.[3-6,9]
  • 1827-1828: settled at Franklinville; witnessed early Lowndes courts and later recalled them.[1,9,18]
  • By June 21, probably 1828: signing as Lowndes Superior Court clerk.[13]
  • September 30, 1829: federally listed as Franklinville postmaster.[7]
  • 1830: strong-probable Lowndes household of seven, with no enslaved people recorded.[2]
  • 1831-1832: verified Superior and Inferior Court clerk signatures.[14,15]
  • February 26, 1833: recorded the Mount Zion deed according to Huxford's original-based transcription.[20]
  • 1835: verified Court of Ordinary clerk and Franklinville postmaster.[7,16]
  • October 1839: signed a notice from Troupville.[21]
  • 1840: strong-probable household of ten, including two enslaved people.[2]
  • 1850: Lowndes hotelkeeper; strong-probable owner of fifteen enslaved people.[3,8]
  • 1860: Troupville hotelkeeper and postmaster; thirty-six enslaved people; \$5,000 real and \$23,000 personal estate.[4,8]
  • January 1870: Tranquil Hall advertised at Valdosta.[19]
  • 1870: Valdosta hotelkeeper.[5]
  • December 11, 1880: published his first-court recollection.[1]
  • 1880: retired hotelkeeper living with wife Mary; original-image middle initial appears "P", while the index reads "A".[6]
  • February 1-2, 1882: death and reported burial at Valdosta.[9]
  • January 21, 1892: widow Polly died at Valdosta.[10]

docs.title: Search coverage and remaining targets
docs.text:
The main unresolved record targets are:

  1. Smith's original clerk election return, commission, and the Henry Blair handoff;
  2. the original Franklinville postmaster appointment and location paper;
  3. an original Lot 50 deed, plat, tax row, or title chain;
  4. William and Polly/Mary's marriage, Bible, probate, and named-heir records;
  5. proof of the "Marget Smith" identity;
  6. Tranquil Hall deeds and business records;
  7. church membership minutes;
  8. a cemetery register, marker image, sexton record, or burial deed.

This dossier describes the accessible online evidence checked through August 19, 2026. It does not imply that undigitized courthouse, church, cemetery, postal, or federal records do not exist.

docs.title: Jacob Bryan
docs.text:
Jacob Bryan¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

Conclusion¶

Roster status: secondary-supported early Lowndes County officer; locality unresolved.

Barney relevance: broader county context only. No direct land, residence, institution, or descendant bridge to Barney is proved.

Evidence¶

Huxford states that the first Lowndes Inferior Court appointed John McCranie receiver of tax returns and Jacob Bryan tax collector in 1826. This is a clear secondary account of an early county office, but the original court minutes or appointment have not been inspected.

No Jacob Bryan household appears in Huxford's reconstructed list of families living in the portion of Lowndes that became Brooks County. No deed, tax return, probate record, or census household reviewed here places Jacob in that territory. His office was countywide and does not establish residence in the later Brooks portion.

No exact Jacob Bryan deed appears in the reviewed Lowndes index. John Bryan's District 12 transactions belong to a separate controlled identity and cannot establish Jacob's residence. See Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved.

Identity and Barney bridge test¶

Jacob remains separate from John Bryan, Timothy Bryan, Jose or Joseph Bryan/Bryant, and the later Barney Bryant surname occurrences. The 1900 Barney census includes Bryant Williams, where Bryant is a given name, and Joe Bryant as a boarder. Neither record identifies parentage or supplies a link to Jacob.

Sources and gaps¶

  1. Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), account of the first Lowndes County officers, p. 13.
  2. Early-settler master audit, identity-conflict row IC-009, which records the absence of a distinguishing future-Brooks chain.
  3. 1900 Barney household-link scope ledger, Bryant Williams and Joe Bryant entries; no lineage established.

The original Inferior Court appointment, Jacob's census household, land, tax, probate, spouse, and children remain unresolved.

docs.title: Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved
docs.text:
Regional figures — future-Brooks residence unproved¶

Back to the Early History Profiles index

William Hancock, David Platt, William Smith, and Jacob Bryan belong in early Lowndes County history. The surviving records do not yet place any of their homes inside the territory that became Brooks County in 1858. This page compares the four geography problems without merging their identities or replacing their individual profiles.

William Hancock¶

The original 1830 Lowndes County census names William Hancock. His identification as the county's early sheriff is strong probable, based on the name, county, and chronology, but the underlying commission and bonds remain uninspected. The reviewed deed index contains no exact William Hancock entry that locates his home in future Brooks County. The reported continuation into Columbia County, Florida, also lacks an identity-controlled chain.

Recommendation: retain Hancock as a verified regional settler. Do not describe him as a future-Brooks resident until a tax district, deed, sheriff bond, probate record, or Georgia-to-Florida family chain supplies the missing geography and identity evidence.

David Platt¶

The original 1830 Lowndes County census names David Platt, and his 1818 marriage to Mary Rowe is verified. A deed locator records David and Peter Platt conveying a grist mill and improvements in District 11 to James D. Shanks. District 11 does not establish residence in future Brooks County. Joshua Platt's District 12 land cannot be assigned to David merely because compiled genealogy identifies Joshua and Amy Newell Platt as his parents; that parentage remains secondary-supported.

Recommendation: retain Platt as a verified regional settler. The decisive records are his tax and deed chain, the readable 1840 household row, and an estate, Bible, church, or deed record naming his parents.

William Smith¶

Contemporary court notices and federal postal registers verify the Franklinville clerk and postmaster who later kept Tranquil Hall at Troupville and Valdosta. District 11 transactions fit that civic chain. The deed index also contains District 12 transactions under the common name William Smith, including Lot 435, but no inspected instrument connects those parcels to the clerk and postmaster. Two William Smith household heads in 1840 reinforce the namesake problem.

Recommendation: retain Smith as a verified regional official. Do not assign the District 12 deeds, a future-Brooks residence, or a direct Barney role to him without an instrument that supplies an office, associate, spouse, signature, or other distinguishing fact.

Jacob Bryan¶

Folks Huxford identifies Jacob Bryan as Lowndes County's 1826 tax collector. That specific retrospective account is secondary-supported because the appointment, bond, and returns have not been inspected. Countywide officeholding does not locate Bryan's home. No exact Jacob Bryan deed, census household, spouse, child group, probate record, or generation-by-generation Barney connection has been proved. John Bryan's District 12 deed chain belongs to a separate controlled identity and cannot be reassigned to Jacob.

Recommendation: retain Bryan as a secondary-supported early Lowndes officer whose locality is unresolved. The first inferior-court minutes, tax-collector bond and returns, and identity-controlled census, deed, and probate records are the next targets.

Comparison and publication rule¶

Person What is established Future-Brooks problem Current classification
William Hancock Original 1830 Lowndes household; sheriff identity strong probable No person-specific home or parcel locator Verified regional settler
David Platt Original 1830 household; Mary Rowe marriage; District 11 mill interest District 11 is not a future-Brooks locator Verified regional settler
William Smith Civic and postal identity chain District 12 deeds cannot be separated safely from namesakes Verified regional official
Jacob Bryan Specific retrospective 1826 office account No inspected appointment, household, or land record Secondary-supported early Lowndes officer; locality unresolved

These men should not be promoted to the broader future-Brooks group on countywide evidence alone. A later original may change an individual classification, but one man's proved parcel cannot supply another man's geography.

Source notes¶

  • 1830 U.S. census, Lowndes County, Georgia, William Hancock and David Platt household entries; original schedules inspected in the underlying research packets.
  • Lowndes County deed index, David and Peter Platt to James D. Shanks, District 11 grist mill and improvements, Deed Book A, p. 625; locator only, original instrument uninspected.
  • Federal postal registers and contemporary Lowndes court notices for William Smith; District 11 and District 12 deed locators remain identity-controlled separately.
  • Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), Jacob Bryan tax-collector account; original appointment and bond uninspected.

The individual profiles provide the fuller source coverage and unresolved-record lists.

The original 1830 Lowndes County census names David Platt, and his 1818 marriage to Mary Rowe is verified. A deed locator records David and Peter Platt conveying a grist mill and improvements in District 11 to James D. Shanks. District 11 does not establish residence in future Brooks County. Joshua Platt's District 12 land cannot be assigned to David merely because compiled genealogy identifies Joshua and Amy Newell Platt as his parents; that parentage remains secondary-supported.

Recommendation: retain Platt as a verified regional settler. The decisive records are his tax and deed chain, the readable 1840 household row, and an estate, Bible, church, or deed record naming his parents.

docs.title: William Smith
docs.text:
Contemporary court notices and federal postal registers verify the Franklinville clerk and postmaster who later kept Tranquil Hall at Troupville and Valdosta. District 11 transactions fit that civic chain. The deed index also contains District 12 transactions under the common name William Smith, including Lot 435, but no inspected instrument connects those parcels to the clerk and postmaster. Two William Smith household heads in 1840 reinforce the namesake problem.

Recommendation: retain Smith as a verified regional official. Do not assign the District 12 deeds, a future-Brooks residence, or a direct Barney role to him without an instrument that supplies an office, associate, spouse, signature, or other distinguishing fact.

docs.title: Jacob Bryan
docs.text:
Folks Huxford identifies Jacob Bryan as Lowndes County's 1826 tax collector. That specific retrospective account is secondary-supported because the appointment, bond, and returns have not been inspected. Countywide officeholding does not locate Bryan's home. No exact Jacob Bryan deed, census household, spouse, child group, probate record, or generation-by-generation Barney connection has been proved. John Bryan's District 12 deed chain belongs to a separate controlled identity and cannot be reassigned to Jacob.

Recommendation: retain Bryan as a secondary-supported early Lowndes officer whose locality is unresolved. The first inferior-court minutes, tax-collector bond and returns, and identity-controlled census, deed, and probate records are the next targets.

docs.text:

These men should not be promoted to the broader future-Brooks group on countywide evidence alone. A later original may change an individual classification, but one man's proved parcel cannot supply another man's geography.

docs.text:

  • Lowndes County deed index, David and Peter Platt to James D. Shanks, District 11 grist mill and improvements, Deed Book A, p. 625; locator only, original instrument uninspected.
  • Federal postal registers and contemporary Lowndes court notices for William Smith; District 11 and District 12 deed locators remain identity-controlled separately.
  • Folks Huxford, History of Brooks County, Georgia (1948), Jacob Bryan tax-collector account; original appointment and bond uninspected.

The individual profiles provide the fuller source coverage and unresolved-record lists.

docs.title: Sarah Adams: probable Adams estate successor
docs.text:
Sarah Adams: probable Adams estate successor¶

Sarah Adams belongs in the early-settler record because she appears independently in the land-and-tax history that followed the death of the elder Dennis Adams. Her exact relationship to Dennis remains unproved.

The land and tax record¶

A preserved land-history compilation associates Sarah Adams with District 12, Lots 402 and 403 in the 1830, 1834, 1835, 1838, 1840, and 1844 tax lists. The sequence begins immediately after an 1829 deed locator placed Lot 402 with the heirs of Dennis Adams and continues until the Adams estate-family land was transferred in the early 1850s.

That pattern is consistent with a widow or estate successor retaining and returning family property. It gives Sarah an independent role in the early future-Brooks land record rather than identifying her only through a husband.

Relationship to Dennis Adams¶

Sarah is the possible-to-strong-probable wife or widow of the elder Dennis Adams. No inspected deed, probate packet, marriage record, or tax row calls her Dennis's wife or widow. The repeated association with the same two lots supports family continuity, but it does not by itself state kinship or legal capacity.

A 1911 obituary for Cason Adams says the family moved after the husband's death, probably about 1830. Because the preserved text is retrospective and its opening context is incomplete, it supports the general chronology without naming Sarah as the widow.

Connection to future Brooks County¶

Lots 402 and 403 were in District 12, within the territory that became Brooks County. Sarah's repeated tax association therefore places her in the property history of future Brooks County, even though her residence, acreage, and role on each original tax row remain to be verified.

Evidence status¶

  • Secondary-supported: Sarah's repeated 1830–1844 tax association with District 12, Lots 402 and 403.
  • Possible to strong probable: wife or widow of the elder Dennis Adams and successor within his estate-family network.
  • Unresolved: residence, maiden name, parentage, children, legal capacity on the tax rows, and whether she held title or returned the property for an estate.

See the Dennis Adams profile and Adams surname audit for the wider identity and estate problem.

Sources¶

  1. Lowndes County Deed Book A, p. 248, conveyance to the heirs of Dennis Adams, executed September 12, 1829, and recorded December 4, 1829; preserved transcription and locator, original instrument uninspected.
  2. Preserved land-history compilation, District 12, Lots 402 and 403, identifying Sarah Adams in the 1830, 1834, 1835, 1838, 1840, and 1844 tax lists; original digest rows uninspected.
  3. Valdosta Daily Times, September 9, 1911, p. 5, Cason Adams obituary, Newspapers.com image 890588100.
  4. Brooks County deed index BCDI-018467 and Lowndes Deed Book C, p. 427, Lasa Adams conveyance associated with Lot 402, November 5, 1852; original instrument uninspected.

docs.title: Nancy King: widow and dower claimant
docs.text:
Nancy King: widow and dower claimant¶

Nancy King is named in a reproducible 1857 court locator as Willis King's widow. The locator ties her to a dower proceeding involving land in Districts 12 and 15, including territory that became Brooks County. Because the original minute-book pages remain uninspected, both the relationship and land claim are strong probable, not verified.

The 1857 dower application¶

A locator for Lowndes County Superior Court Minutes Book A, pages 49–51, records Nancy King's dower application dated October 19, 1857. The locator identifies her as the widow of Willis King and covers land in Districts 12 and 15.

This is more than a spouse's name in a later genealogy. If the locator accurately represents the original proceeding, the dower application reflects Nancy's own legal claim to an interest in the marital real property after Willis's death. The relationship and proceeding remain locator-anchored and strong probable until the original pages are inspected.

Connection to future Brooks County¶

Willis King's indexed land chain includes District 12, Lots 435 and 268, both in present-day Brooks County. Nancy's dower application spans Districts 12 and 15. The exact tracts included in her claim and their final disposition require the original court record, but the locator gives her an evidence-based connection to the future county's land history.

Evidence status¶

  • Strong probable from a reproducible court locator: Nancy was Willis King's widow and filed a dower application on October 19, 1857.
  • Locator-anchored: the reported legal claim involved land in Districts 12 and 15.
  • Unresolved: maiden name, parents, children, residence, the exact property schedule, and the outcome of the dower proceeding.

See the Willis King profile for the indexed land chain and the limits of the traditional 1823 relocation account.

Sources¶

  1. Lowndes County Superior Court Minutes Book A, pp. 49–51, Nancy King's dower application, October 19, 1857; reproducible locator, original pages uninspected.
  2. Lowndes County Deed Book B, p. 25, Solomon Walker to Willis King, District 12, Lot 435, May 15, 1837.
  3. Lowndes County Deed Book A, p. 91, Willis King to George Folsom, west half of District 12, Lot 268.
  4. Folks Huxford, The History of Brooks County, Georgia, 1858–1948, Willis King profile, pp. 497–498.

docs.title: Jane Bryan Hunter
docs.text:
Jane Bryan Hunter¶

Jane Bryan Hunter connects two early future-Brooks families. Federal census records document her as Abraham Hunter Jr.'s wife, while her 1912 obituary names John Bryan as her father and identifies Okapilco as her birthplace and her father's home.

Marriage and household¶

The 1850 census places Abram Hunter, age forty-four, and Jane, age nineteen, together in Lowndes County. The 1860 Brooks County census records Abraham and Jane as a continuing married couple. In 1880, Jane appears as Abraham's wife, with John M. and Virgil C. identified as sons in the household.

Those records verify Jane as Abraham Hunter Jr.'s wife. Theophilus W. Hunter's 1919 death certificate independently names his parents as Abraham Hunter and Jane Bryant.

Bryan or Bryant parentage¶

Jane's 1912 obituary identifies John Bryan as her father and says that she was born at Okapilco, described as her father's home. The obituary, household chronology, and later death certificate make Jane a strong-probable daughter of John Bryan.

The relationship is not graded verified because no inspected birth record, family Bible, probate file, or deed states it. The Bryan/Bryant spelling variation is historically common but must not be used to merge John with the unresolved Jose, Joe, or Joseph candidates.

Connection to future Brooks County¶

Jane's reported Okapilco birth, her documented marriage household, and her later Brooks County life give her a direct personal connection to the settlement region. She also carries the documented Hunter line forward through children including Theophilus W. Hunter, who became a Quitman physician and later supported the South Georgia Railroad.

Evidence status¶

  • Verified: wife of Abraham Hunter Jr.; mother of Theophilus W. Hunter.
  • Strong probable: daughter of John Bryan and native of his Okapilco household.
  • Unresolved: exact birth date and tract, mother, complete child group, and a parent-naming original for the John Bryan relationship.

See the Abraham Hunter profile, John Bryan profile, Hunter surname audit, and Bryan/Bryant identity audit.

Sources¶

  1. 1850 U.S. census, Division 53, Lowndes County, Georgia, dwelling 52, Abram and Jane Hunter household, p. 364A, Ancestry record 18778975.
  2. 1860 U.S. census, Brooks County, Georgia, Abraham and Jane Hunter household, p. 682, Ancestry record 10753357.
  3. 1880 U.S. census, Brooks County, Georgia, Abraham and Jane Hunter household, identifying Jane as wife and John M. and Virgil C. as sons.
  4. “Mrs. Jane Hunter, Brooks County,” Valdosta Times, April 10, 1912, p. 8, Newspapers.com image 889854125.
  5. Georgia death certificate for Theophilus Williams Hunter, December 13, 1919, Ancestry collection 2562, record 104019.
