docs.title: Early History Profiles
docs.text:
Early History Profiles¶

These 98 profiles separate people with a demonstrated Barney-area connection from settlers whose evidence belongs to the wider future-Brooks story.

Roster status describes the historical evidence. Barney relevance describes the connection to Barney: direct influence, a family or settlement bridge, broader county context, or none yet proved. A family bridge does not by itself prove residence at the later townsite.

Coffee Road figures¶

These officials directed or authorized the 1822–1823 state road project. They are included as infrastructure context, not as Barney settlers.

  • Governor John Clark — Status: context profile. Authorized the road and appointed its supervisors.
  • General John Coffee — Status: context profile. Surveyed the route and directed the road work carried out in 1823.
  • Thomas S. Swain — Status: context profile. Co-superintendent, surveyor, ferry operator, and public official.

Barney and immediate-area settlers¶

These people have documented influence on the later Barney area through roads, land, local institutions, residence, or a supported family and settlement bridge.

  • George Alderman — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: direct area connection. Documented regionally by 1830 and connected to the north-of-Barney Alderman land cluster.
  • William E. Dean — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: strong-probable family bridge. Robert Dean appeared in William's 1860 household and later headed Barney household #95; no parent-naming record proves the relationship.
  • Cornelius English — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: secondary-supported descendant bridge. Original records place him locally by 1830; compiled genealogy connects him through Matthew and John English to Andrew James English of Barney.
  • Ebenezer Folsom — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: family bridge. Documented through an 1840–1860 household chain and strong-probable father of Israel Lee Folsom.
  • Priscilla Jane Folsom — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: family bridge. Documented from 1850 through 1900 and as a Brooks landholder; Rogers parentage remains unresolved.
  • Lawrence Folsom — Status: verified · Barney relevance: family and institutional bridge. Irwin landowner by 1823, county-site commissioner, Mount Zion trustee, and Folsom patriarch.
  • William Folsom — Status: verified · Barney relevance: family and institutional bridge. Early resident, farmer, Methodist, estate holder, and probable courthouse commissioner.
  • Joel Gornto — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: immediate-area district connection. His 1836 militia service and 1860 estate are supported by original records.
  • James Groover — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: collateral family bridge. Reported first cousin of Sarah Reiser Groover, mother of Barney resident M. Franklin Jones.
  • John Groover Sr. — Status: traditional/secondary-supported · Barney relevance: collateral family bridge. His reported brother Charles begins the line through Sarah Reiser Groover to the Barney Jones family.
  • Enoch Hall — Status: verified · Barney relevance: land, mill, and family bridge. Farmer, mill-associated landholder, judge, legislator, and militia commander.
  • Sion Hall — Status: verified · Barney relevance: direct settlement influence. Coffee Road resident whose home became Lowndes County’s temporary court and election place.
  • James E. Hendry — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: secondary-supported family bridge. Compiled family history makes him Norman Campbell Hendry’s paternal uncle; Norman’s railroad connection is strong probable, but the James-to-Neal sibling link lacks an inspected parent-naming original.
  • Rebecca Yates Hiers — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: direct residence and family bridge. Brooks landholder and 1900 Barney resident; strong-probable daughter of William Yates.
  • James C. Hodges — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: strong-probable descendant bridge. Robertson or Robinson L. Hodges appeared in James's 1850 and 1860 households and later headed Barney household #8.
  • Nathan Hodges — Status: qualified supplemental · Barney relevance: secondary-supported collateral bridge. Compiled genealogy makes Nathan the brother of Joseph Hodges, ancestor of the principal Barney Hodges branch; no original parent-naming record verifies the upper generation.
  • James J. Joyce — Status: verified · Barney relevance: immediate-area institutional influence. Mount Zion trustee, minister, court official, landholder, and enslaver.
  • John Lawson — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: probable immediate-area land connection. His Barney-district land remains secondary-supported.
  • Angus Morrison — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: direct place connection. A 1937 newspaper identifies the old Angus Morrison home at Barney; the complete family descent remains secondary-supported.
  • James Rountree — Status: verified · Barney relevance: settlement-corridor influence. Early settler and Pulaski-to-Lowndes migrant killed on the Tallahassee road in 1834.
  • Drewry “Drew” Vickers — Status: verified · Barney relevance: settlement and family bridge. Farmer, landholder, enslaver, and member of the four-family settlement tradition.
  • Ely Webb — Status: traditional/secondary-supported · Barney relevance: family bridge. Probable father of Barney resident Malinda Webb Chambers; his own local residence remains unproved.
  • William Yates — Status: supplemental · Barney relevance: land and family bridge. Northern Brooks landowner and mill namesake linked on strong-probable evidence to Rebecca Yates Hiers.

Broader future-Brooks settlers¶

These people are independently documented in territory that became Brooks County, or have a strong evidence-based placement there, but no direct influence on Barney itself has been proved.

  • William Alderman — Status: supplemental. Documented in Lowndes by 1833; the reported 1828 arrival remains unproved.
  • Matthew Allbritton — Status: supplemental. Verified in Lowndes in 1830 and strongly associated with future-Brooks Baptist congregations.
  • Fleming Bates — Status: supplemental. The original 1830 census and a District 12 deed locator establish his local presence; no direct Barney influence is proved.
  • Alfred Belote — Status: verified. Early Lowndes settler, District 12 landholder, and member of the four-family settlement account.
  • Henry Blair — Status: verified. First county clerk, sheriff, legislator, militia colonel, farmer, and minister.
  • William Blair — Status: verified. County-site commissioner, judge, state senator, and Mount Zion trustee.
  • John Bryan — Status: verified supplemental. Original records document him from 1830 through 1850; Jose or Joe Bryant remains a separate unresolved identity.
  • Alexander Campbell — Status: supplemental. Indexed in Lowndes from 1830 through 1850.
  • Thomas Carlton — Status: supplemental. Household evidence supports regional presence, but his family and exact tract remain unresolved.
  • Henry Dean — Status: supplemental. Census transcriptions and District 12 deed locators place him in future-Brooks territory; no direct Barney influence is proved.
  • John Dean — Status: supplemental. Household and Tallokas office evidence support local residence; the Jane Allbritton marriage remains secondary-supported.
  • Edward Clinton Dukes — Status: supplemental. Original 1840 and 1850 schedules anchor his household; no descendant bridge to the later Barney Dukes families is proved.
  • Zachariah Fletcher — Status: supplemental. Verified in the future-Brooks 660th District by 1836; no descendant bridge to Barney is proved.
  • Israel Folsom — Status: supplemental. Pioneer household head kept separate from Israel Lee Folsom; their uncle-nephew link is secondary-supported.
  • John Folsom — Status: supplemental. Verified as an 1840 Lowndes household head; the Kelley John identity remains secondary-supported.
  • Pennywell Folsom — Status: supplemental. 1830 household head killed at Brushy Creek in 1836.
  • Thomas Folsom — Status: supplemental. 1830 household head and militiaman whose home served early Brooks public business.
  • Nathan Gornto — Status: verified. Tallokas settler, Nankin justice, and co-administrator of Joel Gornto’s estate.
  • John Hall — Status: supplemental. Verified in the 660th District in 1836; unresolved Hall identities prevent a family bridge.
  • William G. Hall — Status: verified. Landholder, Mount Zion trustee, and 660th District captain.
  • John Hendry — Status: verified. Liberty-to-Lowndes migrant, farmer, and early Mount Zion tenter.
  • William Hendry — Status: verified. Mount Zion trustee and grand juror with District 12 land near Mule Creek.
  • William Holloway Jr. — Status: supplemental. Bethel service and a District 12 deed locator support the profile; overlapping Sr./Jr. records remain qualified.
  • William G. Hunter — Status: supplemental. Tallokas captain, Bethlehem pastor, landholder, and courthouse committee member.
  • Jared Johnson — Status: supplemental. Documented by an 1840 household and District 12 land locators.
  • William Jones — Status: supplemental. Original records place him locally by 1828–1830, but the documented Barney line descends through Thomas Jones and no relationship to that family is proved.

docs.title: Site Updates
docs.text:
Site Updates

This page records substantial additions and corrections to the website. Minor wording, formatting, and maintenance changes are not listed.

October 6, 2026

1910 Census and Household Index

Added the complete 1910 census, a 308-household index, and individual household pages; final review remains pending.

Early-settler spouse profiles

Sarah Adams, Nancy King, and Jane Bryan Hunter now have separate profiles and appear beside their husbands in the Early History roster.

Remaining early-settlers campaign

John Kinsey and Willis King are now classified as locator-anchored future-Brooks landholders.

October 5, 2026

Hunter surname audit

The Hunter audit documents Abraham Hunter’s strong-probable Screven-to-Lowndes chain, the 1845 land transfer from Abraham Sr. to Abraham Jr., and the evidence-graded descendant line while keeping unrelated Barney families separate.

Bryan and Bryant surname audit

The Bryan and Bryant audit keeps Jose, Joe, John, Joseph, and the Irwin County sheriff separate and compares the conflicting accounts without merging them.

Swain surname audit

The Swain audit separates Thomas S., Canneth or Caneth, Morgan G., and the later Barney branch; no inspected record yet joins those branches.

Adams surname audit

The Adams family page now separates the Dennis represented by heirs in 1829 from later namesakes, grades his death by the transaction date as strong probable, grades Sarah and Lasa as probable estate-family links, and rejects the traditional 1836 arrival for the elder man.

Folsom surname audit

The Folsom family page now separates Elijah Folsom's compiled lineage from the documented Lawrence, William, Priscilla Jane, and Israel Lee branches.

Bryan, Hodges, and Jones profiles and surname audits

Added evidence-graded profiles for John Bryan, Nathan Hodges, and James C. Hodges while preserving the unresolved Bryan, Gornto, and Hodges family links.

Unresolved-evidence upgrades

William Hancock is now verified in the original 1830 Lowndes County census, while his identification as the county's first sheriff remains strong probable.

Joyce–Blair–Gornto family reconstruction

Updated the Blair, Joyce, and Gornto profiles with a probable family reconstruction while distinguishing it from the original records that do not name the full sibling group.

Three more early-settler profiles

Added profiles for Zachariah Fletcher, Angus Morrison, and Cyprian Brinson, with unresolved geography and family connections clearly marked.

Complete Dean surname audit

The Dean and Deen audit separates William E. Dean’s strong-probable family link from unresolved namesakes and removes unsupported family claims.

Dukes, Brinson, Adams, Bryan, and Kinsey profiles

Added profiles for Edward Clinton Dukes, Mills or Miles M. Brinson, Dennis Adams, and Jacob Bryan, and reviewed the Joseph Kinsley–John Kinsey identity question.

Full Alderman surname audit

The Alderman family page and the Barney household profiles for Mitchell Enoch, Jonathan Howell, George Washington, and James Carlton Alderman now reflect a 60-reference surname audit.

October 4, 2026

Dean, Hendry, Carlton, and Holloway profiles

Added profiles for Henry Dean, John Dean, James E. Hendry, Thomas Carlton, and William Holloway Jr.

Cornelius English descendant bridge

A new Cornelius English profile follows the best-supported line through Matthew Joseph English and John Cornelius English to Andrew James English, the later Barney railroad agent.

Jones, Bates, McMullen, and Burnett profiles

New profiles cover William Jones, Fleming Bates, William McMullen, James McMullen Jr., and James Burnett.

O’Steen, Robeson, Simmons, Selph, and Roberts profiles

Added profiles for John O’Steen, James T. Robeson, Ivy Simmons, Ezekiel Selph, and Elias Roberts.

Early History profiles reorganized by Barney relevance

The 67 Early History profiles are now divided into three evidence-based groups: 20 people with direct Barney-area influence or a documented family or settlement bridge, 36 broader future-Brooks settlers, and 11 traditional or unresolved candidates.

Newton, Rowell, and Wilson profiles

New profiles cover James Newton, James Rowell, Jeremiah Wilson Sr., Henry Rowell, and William Newton.

Strickland, Thigpen, McLeod, Campbell, and Lawson profiles

New profiles cover Simpson Strickland, Melus or Milus Thigpen, James McLeod, Alexander Campbell, and John Lawson.

Hall family identity and parentage update

The John Hall profile now separates John Hall Sr. from John Hall Jr.

Johnson, Hancock, Hunter, Lawson, and Yates–Hiers profiles

Added profiles for Jared Johnson, William Hancock, William G. Hunter, Ashley Lawson, William Yates, and Rebecca Yates Hiers.

October 3, 2026

Joshua and David Platt family evidence

A compiled genealogy identifies David Platt as a son of Rev. Joshua Platt and Amy Newell; original parent-naming proof remains unlocated.

Priscilla Folsom and Rogers evidence update

A new Priscilla Jane Folsom profile follows her from the 1850 Lowndes household through her 1900 widowed household in Quitman.

Rogers, Hall, Platt, and Strickland profiles

New profiles cover Uriah Rogers, John Hall, David Platt, Simeon Strickland, and Archibald Strickland.

Folsom family and Thomas F. Rogers profiles

Added profiles for John, Elijah, Pennywell, Israel, Thomas, and Ebenezer Folsom, together with Thomas F. Rogers.

Seventeen early-settler profiles reviewed

Reviewed seventeen early-settler profiles, separating original records from later tradition and marking unproved dates, relationships, land claims, and Barney connections.

October 2, 2026

Amos Emanuel and the proposed Little River ferry

A new Amos Emanuel profile brings together the 1827 ferry bill, Senate vote, census trail, Lowndes County tax entry, 1838 militia record, and later Ware County household.

William and Elizabeth Folsom original deeds

The William Folsom dossier now incorporates four administrator's deeds proving at least 2,080 acres in his estate.

October 1, 2026

Wider early-settler verification

The Early Settlers section now reports the results of an independent review of eighty additional roster names.

Expanded early-settler descendant crosswalk

The Families & Connections section now documents 22 residents of the 1900 Barney census through 29 graded paths to eight early settlers.

September 30, 2026

Folsom settler-descendant link

Jeremiah Walton Folsom's dossier now traces his reported line to early settler Lawrence Folsom and links to the Lawrence and William Folsom dossiers.

FamilySearch review of eleven contemporary-report identities

A FamilySearch review verified Rev. J. W. Folsom as Jeremiah Walton Folsom and strengthened two other identities; eight remain possible.

Contemporary-report dossiers and military review

The 1900 census page now links individual dossiers for all 15 people whose identities are verified or strong probable.

Original-record research on unresolved contemporary-report names

Original-record searches strengthen two identities.

Joyce and Culbreth second-round research

New records strengthen Janie Joyce as a daughter of John Wesley P. Joyce and verify Minnie Adelia Culbreth’s parentage.

Hall cluster second-round research

A second review separated the Hall references into at least two families.

Contemporary reports reconciliation

The 44 people named in contemporary reports but previously left unmatched were reviewed individually.

September 27, 2026

Hope and Jack Croft dossiers

The Hope Croft dossier identifies him as probably Abba or Abner Croft and possibly the later George A. Croft; the proposed fire connection remains unproved.

Initial website release

The first public edition was published at barneyga.com .

  • New research: expanded accounts of early settlement, Mount Zion, county formation, early roads, Folsom Bridge, and the communities along Little River.
  • New research: separate histories of the South Georgia Railway, the Tallokas-to-Barney tram, the Valdosta, Moultrie and Western, and the proposed Georgia, Alabama and Western Railroad.
  • New research: reorganized coverage of Barney before incorporation, the 1903 charter, early municipal government, commerce, postal service, community life, and public order.
  • Correction: the earlier 1910 census totals were withdrawn after a systematic extraction error was identified. Household information is used only where it has been checked, and a page-by-page reconstruction is underway.
  • New images: historical maps, photographs, restored images, and clearly labeled AI-generated reconstructions were added throughout the site.

docs.title: Pre-Incorporation Era, 1897-1903
docs.text: Barney developed around the South Georgia Railroad for nearly seven years before it became an incorporated town. A deed executed on November 20, 1896, already described property as being “in the town of Barney.” Within the next five weeks, Sallie A. Rozier acquired all of Land Lot 320, a court authorized Joel Mable's numbered plan in Land Lot 278, and Ancel Lawrence conveyed the railroad an undivided half interest in the proposed station parcel. That station deed leaves the land-lot number blank; its later marginal “LL321” notation is questionable, and the deed's boundary calls do not yet establish the parcel's land lot. The pages in this section follow the change from the Foster-area settlement to a railroad community with stores, schools, churches, mills, farms, public services, and local government.

docs.title: Explore the era
docs.text:
• Origins: Foster to Barney — the railroad, postal relocation, first residences, and the origin of the town's name.
  • Transportation and communication — passenger trains, mail routes, roads, and early telephone service.
  • Lumber, turpentine, and timber trams — the industries that supported the new station.
  • Farming, livestock, and markets — agriculture in the district and the railroad's effect on local trade.
  • Stores, trades, and the developing town — merchants, workers, fires, and Barney's business center.
  • People and community life — population, families, travel, and social ties.
  • Schools and churches — education and organized worship before municipal government.
  • Disease, fire, violence, and law — public health, disasters, crime, and local justice.
  • The road to incorporation — the 1903 campaign and act that created the town government.

Together, these records show that Barney already had the land plan, transportation links, businesses, schools, churches, and public life of a town before its incorporation on August 6, 1903.

docs.title: Origins: Foster to Barney
docs.text:
The earliest located public record using the place name Barney is a deed executed on November 20, 1896. Celia Davis conveyed Emma J. Anderson two acres in Land Lot 279, east of the South Georgia Railway, described as being “in the town of Barney.” The deed was recorded on April 22, 1897. A newspaper first called Barney a station on the South Georgia Railroad on June 3, 1897.[5][9]

The town's direct predecessor was Foster, a small postal, timber, and naval-stores settlement near Folsom Bridge. Federal records place Thomas A. Rozier as Foster's postmaster by April 4, 1890. Newspapers also document business activity involving Rozier and his partners during the early 1890s. Huxford later dated a Rozier, Connolly & Company turpentine still at Foster to 1892; the federal appointment and business notices are contemporary records.[2]

McNiel and Rozier assembled two separate landholdings in October 1890. On October 9, J. H. Croft conveyed McNiel & Rosier about 325 acres on the north side of Land Lot 227, the tract associated with Foster. Nine days later, Henry G. Turner conveyed James T. McNiel and Thomas A. Rozier the whole of Land Lots 320 and 325, 980 acres in all. The purchases were part of the same short period of expansion, but they were separate deeds from different sellers. Rozier, Conoly & Company did not make either original purchase; the Conoly brothers entered the Foster business in November 1891.[14]

A Post Office Department report dated February 9, with certification apparently dated February 11, proposed changing the office's name from Foster to Barney and moving it to the railroad. It located the proposed office in land lot 320 of the 12th district and put Foster in land lot 227, about three miles southeast. The application estimated roughly 100 people in the proposed village and 400 to 500 in the entire area the office would serve. Those are contemporary estimates, not census totals.[4]

docs.title: Four land lots become a town
docs.text:
Barney did not begin with one owner filing one subdivision. Four separate title histories met at the railroad and the crossing later known as Main Street and First Avenue:[9][10][11][12][13]

  • Land Lot 279: On October 3, 1896, C. M. Hitch and Robert Stroud granted the South Georgia Railway a 100-foot right-of-way across the southwest quarter. The November 20 Davis–Anderson deed shows that the Barney name was already in local legal use seven weeks later.
  • Land Lot 320: Henry G. Turner conveyed the whole of Land Lots 320 and 325—980 acres—to James T. McNiel and Thomas A. Rozier on October 18, 1890, nine days after McNiel & Rosier acquired the separate Foster tract in LL227. Rozier, Conoly & Company later conveyed LL320 and LL325 to Savannah Naval Stores Company on October 7, 1894. On December 1, 1896, the company sold the entire 490-acre LL320 to Sallie A. Rozier. Her later deeds created church, school, residential, and commercial parcels along named streets. The timing is consistent with planned development, although no located record states why she bought the lot.
  • Land Lot 321: Ancel Lawrence acquired a 245-acre tract described in K/721 as the west half. Later deeds record a series of small residence, business, church, and industrial parcels in LL321, but they do not establish that those town parcels came from the west half. A 1914 deed also shows Lawrence conveying 200 acres described as part of the east half, and the intervening title has not been found. His December 26, 1896, station deed cannot be assigned to LL321 from its operative description: the land-lot number is blank, and “LL321” appears only as a later marginal or index notation.
  • Land Lot 278: A December 19, 1896, order by Judge Hansell authorized a commissioner sale under a numbered town plan prepared by Joel Mable. The surviving deed identifies business and residence lots, a 50-foot First Street, a 20-foot alley, and residence lots measuring 140 by 200 feet. N/534 bounds the proposed half-acre station parcel north by Hodges land, east by Berryhill land, and south by church property. Those calls are consistent with the Hodges estate's LL278 holdings but do not establish the station parcel's land lot. The exact parcel remains unresolved because N/534 leaves the land-lot number blank, conveys only an undivided half interest, and does not identify the owner of the other half. The separate Joel Mable plat sheet has not been located.

This sequence shows a railroad town taking shape before the postal move was completed and nearly seven years before incorporation. Sallie Rozier controlled the southwest sector. Ancel Lawrence held the west half of LL321 under K/721 and later sold parcels identified as lying in LL321, but the present title chain does not place the platted town lots in that west-half tract; his later ownership also included part of the east half. He also conveyed an interest in the proposed station parcel. Several owners conveyed railroad and street-edge parcels in LL279, while the Hodges estate and commissioner C. W. Ryall used Joel Mable's numbered plan in LL278. The surviving deeds do not establish which land lot contained the station parcel, and the records do not identify one founder.[9][10][11][12][13]

AI-restored photograph of the open well that stood at the intersection of Main Street and First Avenue, where Land Lots 278, 279, 320, and 321 meet.

Barney's street center lies at the common corner of four land lots: 321 to the northwest, 278 to the northeast, 320 to the southwest, and 279 to the southeast. That four-lot corner falls in the center of the intersection of Main Street and First Avenue. Local history places an open deep well at the same point, in the middle of the crossing, where travelers watered their horses. The 1908 Brooks County map confirms the lot geometry but does not label the well.[8]

Detail from R. D. Flippen's 1908 Map of Brooks County, Georgia , showing Barney at the common corner of Land Lots 278, 279, 320, and 321. The map also labels the bank, depot, post office, hotel, gin, school, and still, but it does not label the open well. Source: Georgia Archives County Maps, cmf:285 .

Huxford dated an excursion between Heartpine and Quitman to February 2, 1897, while railroad reference works place regular service in March. The difference may reflect a ceremonial trip followed by regular operation, but the surviving evidence does not settle that point. Trains were using the line early in 1897.[3]

The earliest located newspaper reference to Barney appeared on June 3, 1897, when a report of J. J. Oglesby's broken leg called it a station on the South Georgia Railroad. Federal records name Thomas A. Rozier as Barney postmaster on July 26. A later questionnaire, dated October 28 and signed by Rozier on November 2, placed the office about 175 yards west of the track and described daily mail on the Quitman-to-Heartpine route. Together, these records document the move of the Foster post office to the railroad and its renaming as Barney. The deeds now prove that the name and a court-authorized town plan were already in use before the postal relocation, but they do not reveal who selected the name or when the first passenger train stopped.[2][4][5][9][13]

October 1897 Post Office Department application stating that the Barney post office stood 175 yards west of the South Georgia Railroad. Diagram attached to the October 1897 application, showing Barney in relation to the railroad and nearby post offices.

Two later traditions describe the first buildings at the new station. Huxford says the Rozier family moved from Foster and built Barney's first residence near present-day Third Avenue and Church Street. Stephen W. Edmondson recorded Pat Blease's account that mules moved a metal commissary building from Foster, with logs repeatedly carried from the rear to the front as rollers. The family's move and Rozier's postal role are documented, but no located deed, tax record, or contemporary newspaper proves the first-residence claim or the details of the commissary move. The two stories concern separate buildings.[1][2][6]

Mrs. D. H. Purvis and Folks Huxford said the station was named through the Oglesbys' relationship with the Barney & Smith Car Company of Dayton, Ohio. In the traditional story, local leaders were discussing what to call the new station while a Barney & Smith railroad car stood nearby. One of the men pointed to the company's name on the car and asked, "Why not Barney?" An October 1897 report confirms that the Oglesby mills were filling a large order for railroad-car sills involving Barney & Smith, but that order came after the Barney name was already in use. A 1901 notice mentioning "Messrs. Barney and Stevens of Dayton" also does not identify who selected the name. No located railroad minute, postal record, plat, letter, or contemporary article verifies the naming conversation. The Barney & Smith explanation is a plausible later tradition, not a documented naming event.[1][6][7]

AI reconstruction of the traditional “Why not Barney?” naming story.

docs.title: Station parcel land-lot correction
docs.text:
Correction

The Origins page no longer assigns Ancel Lawrence's December 26, 1896, station parcel to Land Lot 321. Deed N/534 leaves the land-lot number blank in its operative description; “LL321” appears only as a later marginal or index notation. The deed bounds the parcel north by Hodges land, east by Berryhill land, and south by church property, but those calls do not yet establish its land lot. The deed conveys only an undivided half interest, and the other half remains unresolved.

docs.title: LL321 parent-tract clarification
docs.text: The Origins page no longer says that Ancel Lawrence subdivided the west half of LL321 into town lots. Deed K/721 proves his 1893 purchase of a 245-acre tract described as the west half, but it does not connect the later platted parcels to that tract. A 1914 deed also places 200 acres of Lawrence's land in the east half. The title by which he acquired that additional interest remains unresolved.

docs.title: Foster and LL320 purchase chronology
docs.text: The Origins page now distinguishes the two October 1890 acquisitions. J. H. Croft conveyed McNiel & Rosier the Foster tract in LL227 on October 9. Henry G. Turner conveyed James T. McNiel and Thomas A. Rozier all of LL320 and LL325 on October 18. Rozier, Conoly & Company did not make either original purchase; the Conoly brothers entered the Foster business in November 1891.
